raw_record.support_text: A second case of reversible cholestatic liver injury was reported in a 49-year-old woman. Mild AST and ALT elevations developed 22 days after starting pioglitazone and, after 6 weeks of continued therapy, she developed jaundice, pale-colored stools, dark urine, pruritus, and pedal edema. At the time pioglitazone was stopped, AST was 94, ALT 84, alkaline phosphatase three times normal, and total bilirubin 21.5 mg/dL. CT and MRCP were normal and hepatitis virus serology was negative. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with bile duct injury, regenerative changes, and focal apoptosis without fibrosis. Serum bilirubin peaked at 34 mg%, then all liver chemistries normalized over 8 weeks; at 12 months follow-up the patient was asymptomatic with normal liver enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Second of two reported reversible pioglitazone-induced jaundice cases. Latency: mild AST/ALT elevations at 22 days after start; jaundice noted after 6 weeks of continued therapy. Labs at stop: AST 94, ALT 84, alkaline phosphatase 3x, total bilirubin 21.5 mg/dL; bilirubin peaked at 34 mg%. CT/MRCP normal; hepatitis virus serology negative. Liver biopsy: cholestasis with bile duct injury, regenerative changes, focal apoptosis, no fibrosis. All liver chemistries normalized over 8 weeks; asymptomatic with normal enzymes at 12 months.

raw_record.support_text: Cyclosporine causes necrosis of hepatocytes in zone 3 of the acinus, cholestasis, elevation of serum hepatocellular enzymes, and jaundice. Toxicity is clearly dose dependent, since early clinical use with large doses caused abnormal liver test results, while smaller doses were less toxic; trough cyclosporine blood levels greater than 400 ng/ml are associated with more hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocyte necrosis, cholestasis, jaundice, and elevated serum hepatocellular enzymes. Toxicity is dose dependent; trough blood levels >400 ng/ml associated with more hepatotoxicity. Incidence varies with clinical situation: 1/26 nontransplant patients developed hyperbilirubinemia; in a large renal transplant series half of patients developed hepatotoxicity; after marrow transplantation bilirubin elevation was attributed to cyclosporine in 10/21 and 3/22 cases; in one study 5/8 autopsied marrow-transplant patients had patchy zone-3 hepatic necrosis. Renal transplant patients on cyclosporine also had more gallstones and pancreatitis than azathioprine-prednisone controls, though persistent alkaline phosphatase elevations there are probably of bony origin.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol at the therapeutic dose (up to 4 g/day for adults and 50–75 mg/kg/day in children) has a safety profile, but an overdose can induce life-threatening adverse reactions like acute hepatic failure. In overdose (≥150 mg/kg or >10 g in an adult), liver glucuronidation capacity is saturated, more of the reactive intermediate N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) binds covalently to hepatocyte proteins and causes hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose threshold stated as ≥150 mg/kg or >10 g in an adult; single massive dose with delayed presentation (serum paracetamol level within therapeutic range at admission). Reactive metabolite NAPQI detoxified by glutathione conjugation at normal doses; CYP450-formed. Paper notes paracetamol is one of the most commonly reported products causing drug-induced liver injury. Case report of a patient; ALT and AST monitored since admission.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose in children causes hepatotoxicity. A British study of 417 children aged 5 years or younger who had taken an overdose of paracetamol found only three had significantly raised plasma concentrations of liver enzymes. A subsequent American study of 322 paediatric patients found that among 140 adolescents who deliberately ingested paracetamol, 26 developed liver toxicity, while only one of 172 young children with accidental ingestion developed elevated liver enzymes only, and one of ten patients with dosing errors developed liver toxicity. The reduced hepatotoxicity in young children is attributed to their greater capacity for sulphation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in children (ages 5 years or younger and adolescent subgroups); age-dependent susceptibility linked to greater sulphation capacity.
raw_record.extra_details: 417- and 322-patient paediatric overdose cohorts; 26/140 deliberate-ingestion adolescents developed liver toxicity; only 1/172 young children with accidental ingestion had elevated liver enzymes only; 1/10 dosing-error patients developed liver toxicity. Metabolism via glucuronidation and sulphation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports paracetamol overdose as a cause of acute liver injury (ALI) in humans: circulating miR-122 was about 100-fold higher in patients with established ALI than in healthy controls and overdose patients without ALI, and the marker was used to report liver injury in paediatric paracetamol-overdose patients. In a UK cohort of 129 patients (Edinburgh and Newcastle-upon-Tyne), miR-122 measured a median of 8 h post-overdose in those requiring NAC therapy was significantly higher in patients who developed subsequent ALI and correlated with peak ALT and INR.

raw_record.extra_details: Discussed as a paradigm of acute liver injury for biomarker (circulating miR-122) evaluation; miR-122 AUC 0.93 (95% CI 0.86-1.0, sensitivity at 90% specificity, P<0.0001) for separating ALI from non-ALI at an early time when ALT was still normal; correlated with peak hospital-stay ALT and INR.

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based study of 14,662 Victorian hospital admissions for paracetamol overdose between July 1, 2000 and June 30, 2007, complications were uncommon, with acute liver failure reported in 137 cases (0.9%) and acute renal failure in 163 (1.1%). Overall 30-day mortality was 1.1% (n=154), dropping to 0.2% (n=26) when death was attributed to paracetamol or liver failure on the death certificate; nine of these 26 deaths (34%) were in patients with accidental overdose and none in children under 15. The discussion refers to 'life-threatening paracetamol-induced acute liver failure.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (the whole recorded relationship concerns paracetamol overdose, whether intentional or accidental).
raw_record.extra_details: 14,662 hospital admissions for paracetamol overdose over 7 years (mean 2095/year), 71% in women, most aged 15-50. Of overdoses, 9157 (62.5%) intentional, 2149 (15%, 307/year) accidental, remainder unknown. Acute liver failure n=137 (0.9%) and acute renal failure n=163 (1.1%); 0.8% of pediatric (<15 y) overdoses had a complication vs 3.5% in adults. 30-day mortality 1.1% (n=154), but 0.2% (n=26) when death attributed to paracetamol/liver failure. 26% of patients referred to the Victorian Liver Transplant Unit had accidental overdose (P=0.01). Overdose admissions decreased from 46/100,000 (2001) to 39/100,000 (2006), with no reduction in liver transplant unit referrals or mortality.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of children and adolescents with acetaminophen overdose (a healthy population with no preexisting liver disease or other comorbidities), the authors observed significant elevations of plasma cytokines that reflect acetaminophen-related liver injury. Patients were stratified by the highest recorded AST and ALT values, and higher levels of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 were found in subjects with the most severe liver injury (ALT >1000 IU/L), with MCP-1 showing the strongest relationship to toxicity. The paper frames acetaminophen overdose as causing hepatotoxicity, referring to 'acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity'.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; pediatric population (children and adolescents); otherwise healthy cohort with no preexisting liver disease or comorbidities.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatoxicity severity stratified by highest AST and ALT; most severe liver injury defined as ALT >1000 IU/L. Elevated IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 associated with severity; MCP-1 showed the strongest relationship to toxicity, including correlation with prothrombin time (PT) and with time to initiation of NAC treatment. Reference is made to prior finding of association between IL-8 and severity of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, and to a study of adults with acetaminophen overdose (n=58; median age 36 years) reporting higher IL-8 in nonsurvivors than survivors. Supporting experimental findings (glutathione depletion, acetaminophen protein adducts, histologic hepatocellular injury in mice, CCR2 knockout increased toxicity) and hepatoprotective/regenerative cytokine mechanisms are noted.

raw_record.support_text: A 5-month-old child with intussusception received a 10-fold accidental overdose of 90 mg/kg intravenous paracetamol over an 8 h period (case 1). She was not initially treated with an antidote and developed hepatic impairment. The authors conclude that this case demonstrates intravenous paracetamol is a potentially dangerous drug, note that therapeutic errors such as 10-fold overdosing are relatively common in children, and recommend discussing significant overdose with the National Poisons Information Service, which suggests intervention with an antidote above 60 mg/kg.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (5-month-old infant, 6.9 kg) with intussusception; accidental 10-fold overdose; intravenous paracetamol formulation; no initial antidote treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 received 90 mg/kg IV paracetamol over 8 h and developed hepatic impairment without antidote treatment. A second infant (case 2, 6 months old) received a single 75 mg/kg IV dose, was treated with N-acetylcysteine, and remained well without hepatic impairment. Paper notes the oral overdose concentration-time nomogram should be used with caution after intravenous overdose; NPIS recommends antidote intervention above 60 mg/kg. The assertions on overdose frequency, nomogram caution, and NPIS guidance are considered context rather than independent DILI claims.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is a known consequence of iron overdose and that iron poisoning leads to periportal hepatic injury by free radical generation and lipid peroxidation. Two pediatric patients with intentional (suicidal) ferrous sulfate overdose rapidly developed fulminant hepatic failure severe enough to require liver transplantation despite deferoxamine treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (adolescents) with intentional suicidal ingestion of ferrous sulfate; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure context.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 17-year-old female ingested 10 pills ferrous sulfate (23 mg/kg elemental iron), serum iron 1000 µg/dL at 2h and 670 µg/dL at 4h; INR rose to 6.6 by 20h and >13; AST 2000 U/L, ALT 2424 U/L, total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL; developed Grade 1-2 then Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy and lactic acidosis; treated with deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour for 24h, intravenous N-acetylcysteine, and CVVH; emergent living-donor left lobe liver transplant 4 days post-ingestion; explant histology showed diffuse parenchymal collapse, severe cholestasis and massive hepatic necrosis compatible with toxin-induced liver injury; recovered, well at 1 year. Toxicology negative for acetaminophen, acetylsalicylic acid, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, opiates, ethanol. Posited mechanism: free radical generation and lipid peroxidation.

Two of the 157 pediatric subjects required liver transplantation, 155 recovered spontaneously, and there were no deaths; most overdoses were acute and NAC was administered to 90% of subjects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children and adolescents); overdose exposure. Population included 122 female and 35 male subjects, mostly >12 years old; 94.3% acute overdoses and 9 chronic overdoses.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP protein adducts used as a biomarker of occult APAP toxicity; in adults, adducts persisted up to 12 days after overdose with elimination half-life far exceeding the parent compound (APAP t1/2 in APAP-related ALF: 6.4 h without encephalopathy, 18.4 h with encephalopathy). Mean reported dose in acute overdose patients 633 (±1647) mg/kg; in chronic overdose patients 139 (±30) mg/kg/day. NAC given to 141 (90%) subjects; gastric decontamination used (activated charcoal 65, syrup of ipecac 1, gastric lavage 18). Two subjects required liver transplantation; no deaths; 155 (98.7%) recovered spontaneously. Adduct peak values did not vary by gender, race, ethnicity, age, or reported APAP dose.

raw_record.support_text: In a 10-year study of 322 pediatric patients presenting for acetaminophen overdose, hepatocellular injury developed in 27 patients (8.4%) and hepatic failure in 4 of these; 4 had severe hepatocellular injury and 1 died of multisystem organ failure, none required liver transplantation though 2 were accepted but recovered. Development of hepatocellular injury was associated with presentation more than 24 hours after ingestion (OR 335.0; 95% CI 40.8-275.0), age 10-17 years, intentional overdose, dose greater than 150 mg/kg, and white race.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (median age 4 years; overdose context including intentional and unintentional ingestions and dosing errors with therapeutic intent).
raw_record.extra_details: 322 patients over 10 years (268 from Kansas City, 54 from Seattle); ingested doses ranged 4-8333 mg/kg (median ~151 mg/kg); 27/322 (8.4%) developed hepatocellular injury, 4 developed hepatic failure, 4 had severe hepatocellular injury, and 1 died of multisystem organ failure; 2 were accepted for transplant but recovered before receiving an organ. Association factors: presentation >24 h after ingestion (OR 335.0; 95% CI 40.8-275.0), age 10-17 y (OR 36.9), intentional overdose (OR 37.2; 95% CI 5.0-278.2), dose >150 mg/kg (OR 17.9; 95% CI 2.3-139.2), white race (OR 2.8). 82 patients (25.5%) received N-acetylcysteine. One dosing-error case (11-year-old, repeated self-medication, ~120 mg/kg) developed hepatocellular injury with peak AST 454 U/L and recovered with N-acetylcysteine; none of the 10 dosing-error patients developed severe hepatocellular injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper is a retrospective case study of 25 children (aged 11-16 years) with severe acetaminophen poisoning, exploring the dose-response relationship between ingested acetaminophen and hepatotoxicity, early biochemical/clinical predictors, the impact of early N-acetylcysteine treatment on hepatotoxicity, and the incidence of nephrotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients aged 11-16 years with severe acetaminophen poisoning (overdose setting).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective case study (n=25 children). Hepatotoxicity was assessed by maximum INR and maximum ALT. Early predictors of hepatotoxicity included initial bilirubin (p=0.0003 vs max INR), initial phosphate (p=0.003 vs max INR), initial INR (p=0.0003 vs max ALT), initial creatinine (p=0.002 vs max ALT), prehospital vomiting episodes, and time of N-acetylcysteine initiation. Nephrotoxicity incidence was 12%. No significant relationship between the amount of ingested acetaminophen and degree of hepatotoxicity. The paper states that acetaminophen overdoses may cause hepatotoxicity and fulminant liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 41 pediatric patients included in the sensitivity and specificity analysis, 16 (39%) had hepatotoxicity after acute acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion: 9 'severe' (APAP dose range 190-819 mg/kg, 1 requiring transplantation, 8 fully recovered) and 7 'mild' (APAP dose range 146-500 mg/kg, all completely recovered). All patients had received NAC within the first 24 hours after ingestion, and 11 patients ingested >250 mg/kg of APAP by history without biochemical signs of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; acute deliberate/accidental overdose ingestion; all received N-acetylcysteine within the first 24 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: 16/41 patients (39%) developed hepatotoxicity; 9 severe (APAP dose 190-819 mg/kg; 1 required liver transplantation, 8 recovered) and 7 mild (APAP dose 146-500 mg/kg, all recovered). 11/41 (44%) ingested >250 mg/kg without biochemical hepatotoxicity. In patients with hepatocellular injury, postingestion APAP concentrations were not predictive of 'probable' toxicity per the Rumack-Matthews nomogram in 14% (mild) and 11% (severe) of cases. NAC administration within the first 9 hours in 11 patients. Mechanism (p10-11): APAP is bioactivated to NAPQI by hepatic cytochromes P450; NAPQI covalently binds protein thiols, disrupting enzymes/regulatory pathways and initiating an inflammatory cascade via interleukin-8, producing hepatocellular injury at the site and time of NAPQI formation.

raw_record.support_text: In a compiled case series of children with repeated accidental overdosage of acetaminophen (dosages estimated at 60–420 mg/kg/day for up to 6 weeks), hepatotoxicity was severe: only 20 of 43 (46.5%) survived, four additional patients survived only because of orthotopic liver transplantation, and 21 of 47 cases had histologic evidence of zone 3 (centrilobular) necrosis on biopsy or autopsy. This indicates that acetaminophen causes dose-related intrinsic hepatotoxicity in the supratherapeutic-exposure setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; repeated accidental supratherapeutic overdosage (estimated 60–420 mg/kg/day for 1 day to 6 weeks) rather than a single acute overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Compilation of 47 well-documented pediatric cases (20 previously unreported) plus 8 nonoverlapping cases from Rivera-Penera et al., totaling 55 cases. Peak serum AST (n=45) ranged 1,180–30,000 IU/L (median 10,000); peak ALT (n=34) ranged 440 to >22,000 IU/L (median 8,200); these were significantly higher than in non-acetaminophen fulminant hepatic failure. Of 30 cases with timing, 22 had serum levels above the Rumack-Matthews nomogram line associated with hepatotoxicity. 21/47 had zone 3 centrilobular necrosis histology. 9 patients received N-acetylcysteine (44% survived). This is described as the largest collection of liver injury from long-term acetaminophen administration in children; the number likely underrepresents true hepatotoxicity cases.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 25 pediatric patients with acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC), hepatotoxicity severity was assessed. There were highly significant relationships between maximum ALT and maximum INR (p < 0.0001), maximum AST (p < 0.0001), maximum bilirubin (p < 0.0001) and maximum pH (p < 0.0001), and a significant relationship between maximum ALT and minimum phosphate (p = 0.038). The mean time from acetaminophen intake to NAC initiation was 12.4 h (range 1.5–25.5 h), and multiple prehospital vomiting episodes were proposed as an early predictor of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity in this pediatric cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (25 children); overdose exposure treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC).
raw_record.extra_details: Mean time from acetaminophen intake to NAC initiation 12.4 h (range 1.5–25.5 h). Hepatotoxicity severity indicated by maximum ALT, INR, AST, bilirubin, pH, and minimum phosphate relationships. Prehospital vomiting (≥3 episodes in 60%, 15/25) proposed as an early predictor; significant relationship of vomiting episodes with maximum INR (p=0.013), maximum AST (p≤0.0001), maximum ALT (p=0.0005), and other biochemical parameters. Maximum ALT significantly related to maximum INR (p<0.0001), maximum AST (p<0.0001), maximum bilirubin (p<0.0001), maximum pH (p<0.0001), and minimum phosphate (p=0.038). Acetaminophen overdose hepatotoxicity treated with NAC.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of 109 children with acetaminophen supratherapeutic-dose severe hepatotoxicity (86% aged two years old and less) reported an overall case-fatality of 53%. Only 15% did not receive NAC during hospitalization; not receiving NAC was associated with increased hazard (HR 5.24, 95% CI 2.23-12.42), while completing the three-day NAC regimen was associated with survival (HR 0.015, 95% CI 0.005-0.047). No adverse effects were observed among the children.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (86% aged two years and less; children weighing less than 10 kg) with supratherapeutic-dose (overdose) acetaminophen exposure in a low-resource setting (BJTH, Monrovia).
raw_record.extra_details: 109 children with acetaminophen supratherapeutic-dose severe hepatotoxicity; overall case-fatality 53%. NAC (N-acetylcysteine, a DILI treatment/protectant) reduced mortality: completing the three-day regimen associated with survival (HR 0.015, 95% CI 0.005-0.047); not receiving NAC gave HR 5.24 (95% CI 2.23-12.42); NAC within 24 hours of hospitalization reduced death risk (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48-0.90). No adverse effects observed.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical characteristics of 51 children (6 males) with paracetamol induced significant hepatotoxicity are described. The median age was 14.7 years, with a bimodal distribution; 6/51 children were less than 7 years. In adolescent patients overdose was usually an impulsive act with female predominance (43/45). The median dose for single paracetamol ingestion was 345 mg/kg (range 91-645). Two patients who took supratherapeutic doses (97 and 127 mg/kg) showed significant hepatotoxicity without encephalopathy and survived. 27% with significant hepatotoxicity received N-acetylcysteine treatment despite paracetamol level being less than the nomogram treatment line.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged 0.8-16.1 years); overdose/supratherapeutic exposure, including single and accidental/intentional multiple cumulative overdoses.
raw_record.extra_details: 51 children; median single ingestion dose 345 mg/kg (range 91-645); two patients with supratherapeutic doses (97 and 127 mg/kg) developed significant hepatotoxicity without encephalopathy and survived; median time from ingestion to presentation 24 h in group I vs 44 h in group II; severe hepatocellular injury in 41% (10/40 group I, 11/11 group II); group I recovered with conservative management while group II had rapidly progressing encephalopathy ≥grade III; 6/11 underwent OLT with only 33% (2/6) survival, and 5/11 died awaiting OLT; survival 100% for encephalopathy ≤II vs 18% for ≥III; main cause of death was cerebral oedema (8/11, 73%), with 1/11 dying of fungal sepsis; histopathology of explanted/postmortem livers in 9/11 confirmed drug toxicity; peak ALT/AST up to 10000/7500 IU/l.

raw_record.support_text: Four children aged 1 to 3.5 years with colchicine poisoning are presented. Ingested doses were 0.37 to 1.72 mg/kg. Most findings of colchicine poisoning, including gastrointestinal symptoms, hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, hypocalcaemia and hair loss, were diagnosed in these patients. Two children given 0.37 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg colchicine, admitted 13 and 19 hours after poisoning, respectively, died. The paper explicitly lists hepatotoxicity as one of the findings attributed to colchicine poisoning in these cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged 1-3.5 years); overdose exposure with ingested doses of 0.37-1.72 mg/kg colchicine.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was diagnosed among the manifest multiorgan findings of colchicine poisoning. In Case 1, AST was 405 U/L and ALT 36 U/L. Two of four children (receiving 0.37 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg) died; mortality was also related to the duration between drug ingestion and hospital admission (admissions at 13 and 19 hours after poisoning). Colchicine is a highly active alkaloid used for gouty arthritis, pseudogout, familial Mediterranean fever and Behçet's disease.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective poison center chart review (11 centers) using the AAPCC 1986-1987 database, children aged 1-6 years who acutely ingested acetaminophen and were referred to hospital had risk of hepatic injury assigned on the basis of the Rumack-Matthew acetaminophen toxicity nomogram. The study sought referral strategies to identify children at risk of acetaminophen-induced hepatic injury after acute overdose while reducing the number of hospital referrals.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged 1-6 years), acute accidental ingestion of acetaminophen as a poisoning/overdose event.
raw_record.extra_details: Risk of hepatic injury assigned via the Rumack-Matthew acetaminophen toxicity nomogram. Of 2091 referred patients, 866 had timed serum acetaminophen concentrations; 3 were in the 'probable risk' nomogram area and 6 in the 'possible risk' area. A referral strategy referring only children ingesting >=200 mg/kg of an adult preparation could eliminate 82% of referrals without missing probable-risk patients, but no strategy identified all possible-risk patients. Average charge for an emergency department evaluation in 1992 was $272.00.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 71 children satisfying pediatric acute liver failure (PALF) criteria in South India, paracetamol overdose (19.7%) was identified as one of the major identifiable causes of PALF, alongside infection (29.5%). The study reports the etiological profile of PALF in this pediatric population.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged >28 days to ≤15 years); paracetamol overdose exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose accounted for 19.7% of the 71 PALF cases (approximately 14 cases). Study from South India over a 7-year period; survival at discharge was 61%. Infection (29.5%) and paracetamol overdose (19.7%) were the major identifiable causes of PALF; hepatitis A was the most common infection identified.

raw_record.support_text: In a pediatric study of 88 children, 64 presented with acetaminophen (APAP) overdose (Group C). Patients were evaluated for potential hepatotoxicity risk using the Rumack nomogram based on plasma APAP level versus time since ingestion, plus elevated ALT at presentation and antihistamine co-ingestion. Of the 64 overdose patients, 40 were judged at risk for liver injury by nomogram, bringing the overall proportion of Group C judged at risk for developing liver injury to 73%; there were no deaths or liver transplants. Eleven of 64 (17.2%) overdose subjects had ALT values above 1000 IU/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged ~1.5-18 years); overdose setting; all overdose patients received N-acetylcysteine (NAC), with timing of NAC stratified (<10 h, 10-24 h, ≥24 h); two patients had antihistamine co-ingestion; one subject had unknown time of ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 of 64 overdose patients at risk by Rumack nomogram; 73% of Group C overall judged at risk for liver injury; 11 of 64 (17.2%) had ALT >1000 IU/L; no deaths or liver transplants in the cohort; peak ALT for Group C median 29 IU/L (range 8-9909), higher than healthy controls (p=0.001) but not higher than Group A after early NAC treatment; serum APAP protein adducts (nmol/mL) differed significantly across all groups and were higher in overdose group, consistent with exposure/metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: This clinical metabolomics study compared six control subjects with 13 children/adolescents hospitalized for acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, and the results were consistent with previous findings in a rat model of APAP-induced hepatotoxicity. The time from overdose to hospital presentation and to N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment varied, and the authors noted the small cohort and need for further studies, while concluding the metabolomics findings were consistent with APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children ages 2-18); overdose exposure; NAC treatment administered; small cohort (6 controls, 13 overdose patients).
raw_record.extra_details: Metabolites from arginine and proline metabolism, TCA cycle, taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, glycine/serine/threonine metabolism, and glutathione metabolism pathways were significantly altered in the APAP overdose group; hydroxybutyrylcarnitine showed significant negative correlation with ALT; acylcarnitines proposed as biomarkers of reduced beta-oxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction; results consistent with prior rat model of APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In children and adolescents following acetaminophen overdose, significant hepatotoxicity (transaminases > 1000 IU/L) developed in 6 patients and mild hepatotoxicity in 6 patients. Acetaminophen-protein adducts were detected in serum only in the patient with the most severe hepatic injury (ALT or AST > 6000 IU/L), who received late NAC treatment after a late presentation, and the test is regarded as highly specific for acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children and adolescents); overdose setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum acetaminophen-protein adducts detected in only 1 of the overdose patients (the one with ALT/AST > 6000 IU/L, who received late NAC due to late presentation). Adducts considered of hepatic origin based on a murine model, but human liver sampling would be required to confirm. Plasma transaminase elevation up to >1000 IU/L in 6 patients. Acetaminophen-protein adduct measurement proposed as a confirmative biomarker for acetaminophen poisoning in children.

raw_record.support_text: This study provides the first published serum and urine miRNA profiles for APAP (acetaminophen) poisoning in children, serving as proof of concept that altered extracellular miRNA can represent hepatocellular injury. Overdose subjects presented in multiple stages of APAP poisoning (before injury, during peak toxicity, and during resolution), and all overdosed subjects received N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC), the standard-of-care treatment for APAP overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children with APAP poisoning); overdose exposure context with NAC (N-acetyl-cysteine) standard-of-care treatment administered to all overdosed subjects.
raw_record.extra_details: Study assessed serum and urine miRNA profiles as biomarkers of APAP-induced hepatocellular injury; serum miR-122 elevation in pediatric poisoning paralleled adult APAP poisoning. Groups included a therapeutic (APAP-treated) group and overdose groups at multiple time points after ingestion. Time-to-peak for biomarkers ranged 92-110 h (n=6). ALT and APAP protein adducts served as reference hepatotoxicity biomarkers. NAC serves as a GSH precursor and reduces oxidative stress.

The etiology table (Table 1) lists paracetamol overdose as the cause in 14 of the 19 drug-attributed FHF cases.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose accounted for 14 of 19 drug-attributed FHF cases in a UK cohort of 97 children with fulminant hepatic failure: 10 adolescents with deliberate self-overdose (median age 15 years) and 4 children, including 2 infants, deliberately poisoned by a caregiver. Injury phenotype was fulminant hepatic failure/acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Acute APAP (acetaminophen) toxicity is described as the most common identifiable cause of acute liver failure in children aged ≥3 years (21%), with an even higher frequency (40%) in adults. The mechanism involves formation of APAP-protein adducts: when usual APAP metabolism and excretion pathways are exhausted, the reactive APAP metabolite binds to intracellular proteins resulting in cell death; these serum adducts may serve as a biomarker of APAP toxicity. Instances of prolonged or inappropriate dosing (therapeutic misadventures) are noted as not easily captured by the study.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children ≥3 years of age); therapeutic-misadventure dosing (prolonged or inappropriate dosing) acknowledged but not captured by this study.
raw_record.extra_details: Most common identifiable cause of ALF in children ≥3 y/o (21%) and even more frequent in adults (40%). Mechanism: reactive APAP metabolite forms protein adducts when metabolism/excretion is exhausted, causing cell death; serum APAP-protein adducts may serve as a biomarker of toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: This study demonstrates significant increases in long-chain acylcarnitines (palmitoyl-, oleoyl- and myristoyl-carnitine) in children exposed to acetaminophen (APAP) in therapeutic doses or overdose, extending the preclinical model of APAP-induced hepatotoxicity to the clinical setting. In subjects with significant hepatotoxicity (ALT ≥1000 IU), median peak levels of the three long-chain acylcarnitines were 1.2–2.5-fold above those of the control group, indicating disruption of the fatty-acid β-oxidation pathway and mitochondrial dysfunction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children); all overdose subjects received N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment, with outcomes influenced by time to NAC (early ≤24 h vs late >24 h).
raw_record.extra_details: Significant hepatotoxicity defined as ALT ≥1000 IU in the overdose (group C) cohort. Long-chain acylcarnitines (oleoyl-, palmitoyl-, myristoyl-carnitine) elevated with APAP exposure; acetyl-carnitine decreased; increases indicate disruption of fatty-acid β-oxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction, validated with UPLC-TQ MS. Therapeutic-dose exposure also showed acylcarnitine elevations. No acute liver failure, transplantation, or death reported as outcomes.

raw_record.support_text: The study examined children who simultaneously ingested alcohol and acetaminophen; comparing patients with toxic versus nontoxic plasma acetaminophen levels, SGOT peaks were used as the indicator of hepatotoxic manifestation, and simultaneously ingested alcohol was associated with significantly lower SGOT peaks (P<.05), suggesting alcohol may be hepatoprotective. The study population required consumption of more than 150 mg/kg of acetaminophen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children); overdose exposure with inclusion requiring ingestion of more than 150 mg/kg acetaminophen; some patients simultaneously ingested alcohol, antihistamines, anticholinergics, codeine, or propoxyphene with acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was indicated by subsequent SGOT (AST) peaks in patients with toxic plasma acetaminophen levels; toxic plasma levels developed in only 13.2% of referred patients. No significant difference (P>.10) was found between amount ingested and toxic plasma levels. Plasma acetaminophen levels are interpretable only at least 4 hours after ingestion. Treatment with acetylcysteine (N-acetylcysteine) was recommended for plasma levels above the nomogram line, most effective if begun within 16 hours of ingestion. Death rate was zero in this series. Simultaneous alcohol ingestion was associated with lower SGOT peaks (P<.05); co-ingestants (antihistamines, anticholinergics, codeine, propoxyphene) were associated with toxic SGOT manifestation (P<.01) and with lethargy (P<.001).

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is a drug commonly ingested by children in potentially toxic amounts, and it has been recognized that children are less likely than adolescents or adults to suffer hepatotoxicity from overdose. The paper discusses predicting which children are at risk of hepatotoxicity from acetaminophen overdose and reports that only 0.59% of pediatric acetaminophen exposures in this study produced a potentially toxic serum concentration (patients whose concentrations fell in the probable or possible risk areas of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children, typically age 1-6 years); overdose/supratherapeutic ingestion setting.
raw_record.extra_details: In this retrospective series of 223 patients without GI decontamination, no patient ingesting less than 200 mg/kg (n=104) developed a potentially toxic serum concentration (0/104, upper 95% CL 2.9%); 6 patients (cases 1-6) had potentially hepatotoxic concentrations (probable or possible risk areas of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram), 3 ingesting unknown amounts and 3 greater than 200 mg/kg. No correlation was found between reported dose (mg/kg) and 4-hour acetaminophen concentration in the nondecontaminated group (n=69, R²=0.004, excluding one outlier of 2500 mg/kg with 600 µg/mL). Children are recognized as less likely than adolescents or adults to suffer hepatotoxicity from overdose; adult toxicity standards applied to children yield a low rate of documented toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The study compared a 52-hour regimen of IV-NAC with standard therapy with O-NAC for reducing the incidence of hepatotoxicity after acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose in a pediatric cohort (mean age 15.6 ± 3.2 years). In this cohort, no patients treated within 10 hours and only 9.8% treated between 10 and 24 hours after ingestion experienced hepatotoxicity, whereas other series reported 6.1%/26.4% (oral NAC) and 10%/27.1% (IV-NAC) depending on treatment timing. The hepatic injury is attributed to acetaminophen overdose, with the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (elaborated by CYP1A2 and CYP2E1) discussed as mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (mean age 15.6 years); overdose setting; one patient with hepatic encephalopathy reportedly abused ethanol (unresolved co-exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity incidence in acetaminophen overdose: 0% when NAC begun within 10 hours and 9.8% when begun 10-24 hours after ingestion in this cohort; compared to Smilkstein et al. reports of 6.1%/26.4% (oral NAC) and 10%/27.1% (IV-NAC). One patient developed hepatic encephalopathy: ALT/AST >3000 IU/L by 32 h, peak ALT/AST 10,600/9840 IU/L at 58 h, peak ammonia 138 µg/dl at 106 h, improved by day 6 and discharged without sequelae; O-NAC attempt at 11 h with multiple episodes of emesis. Coagulopathy was clinically apparent in two patients (epistaxis, menorrhagia), neither requiring fresh frozen plasma. Mechanism discussion: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (initially reported as N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine) produced via CYP2E1/CYP1A2; ethanol induced CYP2E1 and reduced glutathione may increase susceptibility; pediatric sulfation more prominent and possibly greater glutathione regeneration.

raw_record.support_text: In this series of 6 pediatric patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF), 2 cases were reported as induced by paracetamol (PCM) overdose (Patient A, a 14-year-old male with encephalopathy grade IV, and Patient D, a 9-year-old female with grade III). Both received MARS bridging treatment; Patient A underwent liver transplantation and survived, while Patient D recovered without transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that life-threatening complications of paracetamol poisoning follow liver injury, with liver injury typically peaking 3–5 days after ingestion and presenting with jaundice, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy; metabolic acidosis, seizures, and coma are also reported. The paper also compiles case reports of paracetamol overdose in neonates and infants, including a 7-month-old who received 1565 mg (233 mg/kg) due to inadvertent duplication of prescriptions, developed fulminant hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy/Reye's syndrome (ALT 22,235 IU/L, AST 8924 IU/L, PT 75 s) and died, and a 3-month-old with an IV dosing error (1500 mg, 300 mg/kg/day instead of 30 mg/kg) who had transient hepatotoxicity (peak ALT 1946 IU/L, AST 1633 IU/L) with recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population, specifically neonates and infants; all cases are supratherapeutic (overdose) dosing from dosing errors or inadvertent prescription duplication.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose doses ranged from 60 to 445 mg/kg via oral, IV, and IM routes in neonatal and infant cases tabulated by the authors. Fulminant hepatic failure/encephalopathy/Reye's syndrome case (Ebenezer): 233 mg/kg paracetamol over 36–48 h, ALT 22,235 IU/L, AST 8924 IU/L, PT 75 s, INR 4.7, paracetamol concentration 91.1 mcg/mL; death 24 h later despite intubation and antidote. Transient hepatotoxicity case (Aslan): 3-month-old, 300 mg/kg/day IV dosing error, peak ALT 1946 IU/L and AST 1633 IU/L, normalized after NAC. Most neonatal/infant overdose cases recovered fully with N-acetylcysteine (NAC); some showed only transient enzyme elevations. Liver injury typically peaks 3–5 days after ingestion; moderate-severe overdose may initially show nonspecific vomiting, appetite loss, lethargy, weakness. Renal dysfunction co-occurs with hepatotoxicity (about 25% of adults with significant hepatotoxicity, >50% with hepatic failure).; aliases: acetaminophen

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports on a pediatric population with acetaminophen overdose (suicide attempts) and the resulting hepatotoxicity. It states that the importance of early initiation of NAC treatment in acetaminophen overdose has been proved in several adult studies and that the present study confirmed these findings in a pediatric population, with a highly significant relationship between hepatologically relevant biochemical parameters and the latency time before NAC initiation. The conclusion further frames the outcome as moderate/severe hepatotoxicity in these acetaminophen-overdosed patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; exposure was deliberate acetaminophen overdose during a suicide attempt (overdose context).
raw_record.extra_details: Outcome described as moderate/severe hepatotoxicity with elevated transaminases (ALT/aspartate aminotransferase) and INR, and reduced coagulation parameters. Retrospective design. Number of prehospital vomiting episodes was a more sensitive risk factor for moderate/severe hepatotoxicity than the amount of acetaminophen ingested (only a sparse relationship between acetaminophen intake and biochemical parameters was found). Treatment with intravenous antidotal NAC (99% of study population received NAC); latency to NAC initiation significantly related to higher transaminases and lower coagulation. Illness prior to the suicide attempt was associated with more affected transaminases and INR.

raw_record.support_text: In response to a question about acetaminophen toxicity in a pediatric acute liver failure series, the authors note that of the nine children who survived, four were not teenage suicide attempts but younger children probably overdosed by their parents from either lack of information or lack of understanding of how to use the drug. Earlier discussion adds that in the Philadelphia experience, 32% of the 26 cases were acetaminophen ingestions.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; exposure was overdose—four survivors were younger children overdosed by parents who misunderstood drug dosing, while other acetaminophen cases were not teenage suicide attempts.
raw_record.extra_details: In a Philadelphia pediatric acute liver failure experience (26 cases), 32% were acetaminophen ingestions; nine children survived overall, and acetaminophen toxicity was associated with survival, likely due to early recognition and treatment with N-acetylcysteine and other support. Presenting features in this series included elevated transaminases with prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time; only 9 of 26 patients were clinically jaundiced at presentation.

raw_record.support_text: Rectal administration of acetaminophen was significantly associated with supratherapeutic dosing (mean 20.9 mg/kg, range 16.6-41.7 mg/kg). Previously reported cases of hepatotoxicity secondary to multiple supratherapeutic acetaminophen dosing per rectum included 5 children (ages 7 months to 8 years), with an overdose range of 17 to 70 mg/kg/dose or 102 to 420 mg/kg/d. Death occurred in a 2-year-old child who received 650-mg suppositories every 4 hours for a total of 17 doses. The paper also states that with greater than recommended doses the CYP450 pathway produces NAPQI, and excessive NAPQI leads to hepatic cellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; multiple supratherapeutic doses predominantly via the rectal route; at risk in children receiving >15 mg/kg/dose for more than 5 doses within 24 hours, children younger than 2 years who are ill and acutely malnourished, and children with chronic liver disorders or taking medications that stimulate CYP450 hepatic enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose range 17 to 70 mg/kg/dose or 102 to 420 mg/kg/d; mean rectal supratherapeutic dose 20.9 mg/kg (16.6-41.7); death in a 2-year-old given 650-mg suppositories every 4 h, 17 total doses; dosing errors attributed to parents (2), physicians (2), and pharmacists (1). Mechanism: therapeutic doses metabolized by sulfation and glucuronidation, but supratherapeutic doses saturate these pathways and activate CYP450, producing N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which is detoxified by glutathione conjugation; excessive NAPQI leads to hepatic cellular necrosis. Risk enhanced by CYP450 inducers (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, rifampin, ethanol, isoniazid) and by illness/malnutrition in young children.

raw_record.support_text: Untargeted metabolomic profiling was applied to high dose acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity by comparing the urinary metabolic pattern of 13 APAP-overdosed patients versus 6 controls in a pediatric population. Several identified metabolites belonged to pathways known to be involved in acetaminophen intoxication or were increased in a rat model. A further pediatric study used targeted metabolomic profiling to demonstrate a structure-dependent phospholipid alteration in the serum of acetaminophen-overdosed children. Acetaminophen is thereby treated as causing human liver toxicity in the overdose setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; overdose setting (13 APAP-overdosed patients compared with 6 controls).
raw_record.extra_details: Metabolomic biomarker context: untargeted urinary profiling of overdosed patients identified metabolites in pathways known to be involved in acetaminophen intoxication or increased in a rat model; targeted profiling of overdosed children showed structure-dependent serum phospholipid alterations.

raw_record.extra_details: Penna & Buchanan case series: 7 deaths and 11 hepatotoxicity cases in children; mortality associated with doses >300 mg/day/kg for 1-6 days; survival usually seen with hepatotoxic doses >150 mg/day/kg for 2-8 days; paracetamol may accumulate in paediatric patients after repeated therapeutic doses combined with adult volunteer evidence of glutathione depletion (0.5 g and 3 g doses separated by 4-10 days); current guidelines recommend not exceeding 90 mg/day/kg.

raw_record.support_text: The study shows that at an early stage of admission it is possible to predict subsequently elevated levels of transaminases, INR, and other hepatologically relevant biochemical parameters. Especially prehospital and in-hospital vomiting, latency time before initiation of NAC treatment, and illness prior to a suicide attempt by means of acetaminophen were identified as important early clinical risk factors of underlying evolving moderate/severe hepatotoxicity in a pediatric population.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; poisoning after suicide attempt (overdose exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Early clinical risk factors of evolving moderate/severe hepatotoxicity: prehospital and in-hospital vomiting episodes (highly significant relationship between number of prehospital vomiting episodes and elevated hepatologically relevant biochemical parameters), latency time before initiation of NAC treatment (longer delay associated with higher maximum GGT, maximum INR, initial/maximum AST, initial/maximum ALT), and illness up to 48 hours prior to the suicide attempt (significant relationships with initial/maximum INR, maximum AST, maximum ALT). No relationship between ingested acetaminophen amount (mean 10.01-11.29 g) and biochemical parameters in this pediatric population, unlike some adult studies; adults with severe liver failure may have different cytochrome P450 expression yielding higher hepatotoxic NAPQI at lower doses, and glucuronosyltransferase gene polymorphisms have been linked to acetaminophen-induced liver injury risk. None of the patients were candidates for liver transplantation; only 3 required referral to a tertiary pediatric department specialized in children's liver diseases. Study population: patients admitted to a general secondary-level pediatric department.

raw_record.support_text: The paper opens by stating that paracetamol (acetaminophen), although considered a safe over-the-counter analgesic and antipyretic, can cause liver injury with overdose, and notes that therapeutic misadventure is a unique problem where the acute-poisoning nomogram does not apply. raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; therapeutic misadventure type (unintentional multiple/supratherapeutic dosing); two of the six cases also co-administered mefenamic acid.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 6 children (April-December 2008) hospitalized after paracetamol overdose, doses ~90-367 mg/kg/day for 1-5 days. Introduction states poisoning may cause either isolated elevation of transaminases or acute liver failure (ALF). Three of 6 cases had abnormal LFT and PT, three had normal values; none documented to progress to ALF. N-acetylcysteine (oral or IV loading followed by 17 doses of 70 mg/kg every 4 h) was given empirically before biochemical evidence of liver injury; paracetamol levels 32-142 μg/mL (reference 10-20 μg/mL). Infants/young children noted to be less susceptible to acute paracetamol toxicity due to age-associated differences in drug metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity after unintentional ingestion is dose-dependent in young children. The author critiques a prospective observational case series (1,039 patients) that observed children at home after ingestions below 200 mg/kg with no decontamination. Because 93.4% ingested less than 150 mg/kg and only 68 patients (6.5%) ingested 150-200 mg/kg, the author argues low-dose ingestions are very unlikely to produce hepatotoxicity, whereas the risk in the 150-200 mg/kg subgroup is uncertain (upper 95% confidence limit for an adverse outcome 4.4%, 3/68, vs 0.3%, 3/971, in the low-dose group). The minimum acute hepatotoxic dose of acetaminophen in young children is described as not well defined.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric young children; unintentional acute ingestion (overdose setting); risk considered specifically in the 150-200 mg/kg dose range with no decontamination and home observation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute overdose doses: <150 mg/kg associated with very low likelihood of hepatotoxicity; 150-200 mg/kg subgroup (n=68) had no reported adverse outcomes but upper 95% CI for an adverse outcome was 4.4% vs 0.3% (3/971) in the low-dose group. Letter discusses proprioac-induced emesis <1 hour after ingestion as a mitigation option and questions whether adult (500-mg) formulations were miscounted. Primary data from Mohler et al. prospective observational case series (n=1,039).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is a common cause of pediatric ingestions and, in severe cases, may result in acute liver failure (ALF). It further reports that APAP overdose is a major cause of ALF in adults (~50% of cases) and accounts for ~13% of ALF cases in children, establishing a human DILI relationship for acetaminophen at overdose. Supporting these claims, the study found that of 157 adolescents and children presenting with APAP overdose at eight pediatric hospitals, two required liver transplantation while the others recovered spontaneously, and peak APAP protein adducts correlated with peak hepatic transaminase values.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric/adolescent population (157 patients at eight pediatric hospitals); overdose exposure setting.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose causes acute liver failure in adults (~50% of ALF cases) and in children (~13% of cases); morbidity in children is generally lower than in adults. In the study cohort, 2/157 patients required liver transplantation and the remainder recovered spontaneously. Peak APAP protein adduct concentrations correlated with peak hepatic transaminases, time-to-treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC), and Rumack-Matthews nomogram risk determination; model-derived adduct value at 48 h correlated with adduct Cmax, adduct Tmax, Rumack-Matthews risk, peak AST and peak ALT. Mechanism involves cytochrome P450 (CYP2E1, CYP1A2, CYP3A4) oxidation to the reactive metabolite NAPQI; covalent binding of NAPQI to cysteinyl sulfhydryl groups on cellular proteins (3-(cystein-S-yl)APAP protein adduct) under glutathione depletion underlies toxicity. APAP accounts for ~50% of adult ALF and ~13% of pediatric ALF.

raw_record.support_text: This study of 157 children and adolescents with APAP (acetaminophen) overdose who received timely NAC treatment found that APAP protein adducts correlate with measures of toxicity, and that the elimination characteristics of APAP adducts were similar to those reported for adults with acute liver failure (ALF) following APAP overdose. The paper confirms APAP protein adducts as a clinically relevant and specific biomarker of APAP toxicity, and discusses adults with ALF following APAP overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric/adolescent population (children and adolescents presenting with APAP ingestion); subjects received timely NAC treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (APAP, paracetamol) overdose leads to acute liver failure (ALF). Study measured APAP protein adducts as a toxicity biomarker; adduct elimination half-life exceeds that of the parent compound. Overdose context in pediatrics often involves inadvertent overdose, adult formulations, and OTC cough/cold remedies; opioid/APAP combination products are a target of adolescent drug abuse. NAC (N-acetylcysteine) was administered as treatment. Enrollment from 157 adolescents and children across eight sites of the Network of Pediatric Pharmacology Research Units.

raw_record.support_text: Actinomycin D (administered with vincristine) is reported as a cause of hepatopathy in children receiving chemotherapy for Wilms' tumour. In NWTS 4, 5 of 37 children receiving a single 60 µg/kg dose per 3-week course developed hepatic toxicity, while none of 63 children on the divided-dose regimen did; dose reduction to 45 µg/kg followed. In SIOP 9, 64 children suffered at least one episode of hepatotoxicity, with 41 of 511 (8%) classed as 'H-VOD', supporting a steep dose/toxicity relationship between 1.5 and 1.8 mg/m².
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children with Wilms' tumour; administered together with vincristine (and in some cohorts with abdominal radiation, which increases risk); infants and younger/lower-weight children appear more vulnerable, and right-sided tumours are associated with higher risk; dose and scheduling varied across study protocols.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic veno-occlusive disease ('H-VOD') was the reported syndrome. Dose/schedule data: NWTS 4 single dose 60 µg/kg per 3 weeks (approx 1.8 mg/m²) versus same total fractionated over 5 days; dose later reduced to 45 µg/kg. UKW1/UKW2 used pulsed 1.5 mg/m² 3-weekly, with 6/355 (1.7%) developing hepatopathy. SIOP 9 used 0.45 mg/m²/day x 3 days (later 15 µg/kg/day x 3) in weeks 1-2, repeated in weeks 4-5 for the 8-week arm; infants received 66% of doses; 64 children had at least one episode, 41/511 (8%) H-VOD. SIOP series: abdominal irradiation produced hepatopathy in 11/68 (16%) versus 30/443 (6.7%), multivariable P=0.001. Right-sided Wilms' tumour associated with more hepatopathy (5.6% vs 1.2%, P=0.0002); of 33 H-VOD cases from four series, 27 were right-sided. A newborn with fatal hepatopathy after 75 µg/day x 5 days (approx 100 µg/kg if ~3 kg) and one fatal hepatopathy in 5/9 infants on UKW3 new dosing were reported. A convincing case in a 3.8-year-old with rhabdomyosarcoma after 2.25 mg/m² in divided doses is also cited.

raw_record.support_text: Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) is described as a well-known serious complication, and the paper states that chemotherapeutic agents such as Act-D, as well as radiation, can damage small hepatic venules and sinusoids, recapitulating SOS in non-HSCT patients. The reported incidence of SOS ranges from 1.2% to 8% in children treated for Wilms' tumor, and this study describes a single-center experience where children with WT developed SOS during neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy that included Act-D.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children) treated for Wilms' tumor/clear cell sarcoma of the kidney under the SIOP-WT2001 protocol; SOS developed during neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy; one patient expired before surgery.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 104 children (4.8%) developed SOS while on Act-D therapy; median age 3.3 years (range 6 months-5 years); median interval from start of therapy to SOS diagnosis was 6 weeks (range 4-13); median 2 doses of Act-D received before SOS (range 2-6); Act-D given as single dose slow IV bolus of 45 mcg/kg, reduced to two-thirds in children <12 kg and half in children <6 months. SOS diagnosed clinically by modified McDonald criteria (jaundice with total bilirubin >2 mg/dL, tender hepatomegaly and/or right upper quadrant pain, 5% weight gain with/without ascites). All 5 had tender hepatomegaly and fluid accumulation; clinical jaundice, fever and recurrent vomiting in 4; CNS drowsiness/altered sensorium in 3; respiratory distress with bilateral infiltrates in 3; hypotensive shock requiring inotropes in 3; acute renal failure requiring dialysis in 1. All had significant thrombocytopenia and prolonged PT and aPTT; 4 each had conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, hypoalbuminemia, and transaminases >5x ULN. Viral hepatitis serology negative in all; no reversed/attenuated portal venous flow on Doppler. None of the patients received radiation. Papal (abstract) notes re-challenge of ACT-D can be performed in gradually escalating doses under close monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The authors discuss the frequency of severe hepatotoxicity in Wilms' tumor patients treated with actinomycin D, noting that single-dose actinomycin D caused severe hepatotoxicity in the UK Children's Cancer Study Group and American National Wilms Tumor Study (NWTS-4), which led to the dose being reduced from 60 µg/kg to 45 µg/kg.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric Wilms' tumor (nephroblastoma) patients receiving actinomycin D chemotherapy as part of cooperative-group treatment schedules.
raw_record.extra_details: On the 60 µg/kg single-dose schedule, raised liver function tests occurred in 4 of 33 patients (12%) with no case of severe hepatotoxicity; on the standard schedule (15 µg/kg daily ×5 days), 1 of 32 patients had severe hepatotoxicity and 2 others had raised liver function tests without ascites. Frequency of severe hepatotoxicity was 0/33 versus 1/32. A reduced single dose of 45 µg/kg was reported as well tolerated. Severe hepatotoxicity was previously reported in NWTS-4. The Brazilian study administered doses every six weeks rather than every three weeks as in NWTS-4, which the authors suggest may explain the lower frequency of severe hepatotoxicity with the 60 µg/kg regimen. Ascites was noted in the severe hepatotoxicity case.

raw_record.support_text: The letter presents a case of an HIV-infected man who developed acute hepatitis due to valproic acid (VPA) given concurrently with cytochrome P450 active drugs (ritonavir, nevirapine). The authors note that hepatotoxicity due to valproic acid is a known event and that VPA's use in psychiatry has enlarged the at-risk population; pediatric epilepsy risk factors include neurological disease, male gender, and concomitant use of hepatic P450-inducing drugs.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 51-year-old HIV-infected man with multidrug-resistant HIV and bipolar disorder; concurrent antiretroviral therapy (ritonavir 400 mg BID, saquinavir 400 mg BID, stavudine 40 mg, nevirapine 200 mg) with unresolved possible enhancement by P450 inhibitor ritonavir or inducer nevirapine; low serum carnitine.
raw_record.extra_details: VPA used for mood stabilization; VPA serum level remained therapeutic throughout. On Day 5 ascites and pleural effusions developed; all drugs discontinued on Day 5. Infectious workup (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV serology; urine, blood, CSF cultures) negative; LP negative. Liver-associated enzymes trended downward on Day 7 after levocarnitine (1 gm tid) started on Day 6; patient discharged on Day 11. LAEs later remained normal after antiretrovirals resumed with efavirenz replacing nevirapine. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (added for suspected UTI) was discontinued and its role as a competing cause was not implicated; rash deemed secondary to the sulfa drug.

raw_record.support_text: The paper clinically characterizes fatal cases of hepatic dysfunction associated with valproic acid (VPA), dividing them into a chronic progressive form (4-6 week course of lethargy, vomiting, nausea, anorexia, jaundice and edema, mostly in older patients, with unimpressive histology except cholestasis in a few cases) and an acute fulminating form usually occurring in children under 12 years of age, with abrupt onset of coma, markedly abnormal coagulation, elevated SGOT and ammonia, microvesicular fatty changes in hepatocytes with mitochondrial dissolution on biopsy, and all reported patients in this category dying.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute fulminating form is restricted to children under 12; chronic progressive form occurs mostly in older patients; severe cases may involve predisposing factors such as inborn partial deficiencies of mitochondrial enzymes, added stress of an acute viral illness, or concomitant use of other drugs metabolized by mitochondrial enzyme systems.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic form: 4-6 week course of slowly increasing lethargy, vomiting, nausea, anorexia, jaundice and edema; recovery if VPA stopped early; histology unimpressive except cholestasis in a few cases. Acute fulminating form: sudden onset of coma with signs of increased intracranial pressure, jaundice absent, marked coagulation abnormalities and elevated SGOT and ammonia at symptom onset, renal failure in some patients, liver biopsies showing microvesicular fatty changes and mitochondrial dissolution; all reported patients in this category died. Mechanism: VPA (2-n-propylpentanoic acid), a short-chain fatty acid; Haas et al (1981) showed VPA inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in isolated rat liver mitochondria; hypothesized mitochondrial decompensation spectrum from transient SGOT/ammonia elevations to chronic progressive hepatic dysfunction to acute generalized mitochondrial failure, hepatic failure, cerebral edema, coma and death.

raw_record.support_text: Conditioning regimens containing busulfan are described as well known to induce hepatotoxicity in human HPCT recipients, ranging from elevated liver enzyme levels to hepatitis and hepatic veno-occlusive disease (HVOD). In paediatric patients most autologous and allogeneic recipients had regimen-related grade 1–2 elevations of AST/ALT, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, or bilirubin with none of grade 4. In adult patients 15% of serious adverse events involved hepatotoxicity, and HVOD occurred in 8.2% of 61 adult allogeneic recipients (fatal in two patients) and in 2.5% of 42 autologous recipients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Administered as intravenous conditioning therapy prior to haematopoietic progenitor cell transplantation, co-administered with single-dose melphalan 140 mg/m2 or cyclophosphamide 50 mg/kg/day for 4 days; patients had underlying disease requiring transplant.
raw_record.extra_details: In paediatric patients (n=55, aged 0.3–17.2 y) most regimen-related elevations of AST/ALT, GGT or bilirubin were grade 1–2, none grade 4. In adults, 15% of serious adverse events involved hepatotoxicity; HVOD in 8.2% of 61 adult allogeneic HPCT recipients (fatal in two) and 2.5% of 42 adult autologous recipients; serious bilirubin elevations in three patients and AST elevations in one patient, two of these among those with HVOD. In a separate report, HVOD occurred in 4 of 31 autologous and 3 of 36 allogeneic paediatric recipients receiving bodyweight-based IV busulfan, all mild-to-moderate and resolving with symptomatic treatment within 18 days.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that cholic acid (CA) was chosen over chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) because of better tolerance and less hepatotoxicity, noting CA had been used without side effects since 1994 at Cincinnati Children's Hospital for inborn errors of bile acid metabolism and studied at doses up to 20 mg/kg per day in adults. In their study, no major adverse events were attributed to CA, although a few patients complained of diarrhea. They conclude that CA is not hepatotoxic and is overall well tolerated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Assessment based on a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in patients with lipodystrophies; CA was administered at 15 mg/kg per day (maximum 1500 mg/day).
raw_record.extra_details: No major adverse events were attributed to CA, apart from a few complaints of diarrhea. CA had previously been used without side effects since 1994 for inborn errors of bile acid metabolism and studied at doses up to 20 mg/kg per day in adults for gallstones, mild hypertriglyceridemia, bile acid kinetics, and cholesterol absorption. The study did not confirm the previously reported serum TG-lowering effect of CA. The paper also notes CDCA is a more potent FXR agonist than CA but was avoided due to better tolerance and less hepatotoxicity of CA.

raw_record.support_text: Laboratory studies are reported for 13 children and adolescents who had isoniazid hepatotoxicity during treatment for latent tuberculosis infection. Two additional patients were excluded (1 with Becker muscular dystrophy, 1 with uncertain number of ingested isoniazid doses). At onset, mean ALT was 401 U/L and mean AST 361 U/L, with peak ALT 559 U/L and peak AST 457 U/L; all patients had ALT >3x ULN at onset, with 5 (38%) having ALT >=10x ULN. Mean bilirubin at first or peak was 2 mg/dL. Viral hepatitis testing was negative in 11 (85%). Time for ALT/AST to decrease was 69 days on average.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children and adolescents (0-18 years) treated for latent tuberculosis infection.
raw_record.extra_details: N=13 patients. ALT at onset 401 +/- 448 U/L (range 100-2690, highest outlier), peak 559 +/- 523 (101-2925); ALT >ULN at onset: 0 <3-fold, 5 (38%) 3- to <5-fold, 3 (23%) 5- to <10-fold, 5 (38%) >=10-fold. AST at onset 361 +/- 580 (26-3589), peak 457 +/- 663 (26-4139); AST >ULN at onset: 5 (38%) <3-fold, 1 (8%) 3- to <5-fold, 3 (23%) 5- to <10-fold, 4 (31%) >=10-fold. Bilirubin first or peak 2 +/- 4 mg/dL (0.2-14.5). Viral hepatitis negative in 11/13 (85%); HBsAg negative only in 1 (8%); not tested in 1 (8%). Time for ALT/AST to decrease 69 +/- 63 days (21-232). One patient with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis had ALT decrease to 33 U/L and AST to 38 U/L after isoniazid discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Lennard et al. (1993) studied seven children previously treated with 6-MP in first remission who were subsequently given 6-TG for 3-10 months. TGNs accumulated rapidly in RBCs after oral 6-TG, reaching 3-7.5 times higher than from prior 6-MP. Most patients developed cytopenias with no hepatotoxicity during the second remission treatment period with 6-TG, and the authors suggested 6-TG for patients failing 6-MP due to high TPMT levels.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated during second remission, previously treated with 6-MP during first remission.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven children treated for 3-10 months; RBC TGN concentrations reached 3-7.5 times higher than with prior 6-MP after oral dosing; most developed cytopenias with no hepatotoxicity. Paper explicitly reports absence of hepatotoxicity, not inferred from silence.

raw_record.support_text: Valproate can induce liver failure in mitochondrial disorders. A 15-year-old girl developed liver failure after valproate exposure and was confirmed as carrying a POLG1 (polymerase γ) gene mutation, consistent with mitochondrial DNA depletion and Alpers' syndrome; her brother had died 15 years earlier after valproate-associated liver failure. The authors also saw 24 children with mitochondrial cytopathies and liver involvement, 18 of whom had a history of 'difficult-to-treat' atypical seizures.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children with mitochondrial cytopathies (Alpers' syndrome, POLG1 mutation) and 'difficult-to-treat' atypical/unclassified seizures; valproate should be avoided in children with early-onset developmental problems or a family history of severe hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: The authors discuss a newborn who developed a transient cholestatic hepatitis possibly induced by carbamazepine taken by his epileptic mother (400 mg/day) during gestation and breastfeeding. Applying the Naranjo algorithm, the causal relationship between the cholestatic hepatitis and transplacental carbamazepine exposure was judged probable. The hepatic adverse effects of carbamazepine are known, and because the drug crosses the placental barrier and is excreted in breast milk, infants of epileptic mothers may develop hepatic dysfunction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Exposure was via transplacental passage and breastfeeding; the affected individual is a newborn of an epileptic mother treated with carbamazepine 400 mg/day, not a directly treated adult patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report in French (RÉSUMÉ). Between the third and seventh week of life the infant developed marked increases in gamma-glutamyltransferase, conjugated bilirubin, and bile acids. Diagnostic work-up excluded biliary atresia and metabolic or infectious etiologies. The authors recommend updating the carbamazepine monograph to warn clinicians of this possibility. Transient course reported.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that although salicylates have little direct toxic effect on the liver in large therapeutic doses, there are increasing reports of children and adults with rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatic fever who developed hepatotoxicity while on high-dose aspirin therapy. In Case 2, a four-year-old girl with rheumatic fever treated with aspirin (100 mg/kg/day) developed nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain on day 12 with salicylate 26.8 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 1325 iu/l; after a two-day discontinuation and re-institution at a reduced dose (80 mg/kg/day), AST fell to 109 iu/l and liver function returned to normal. The paper concludes the hepatotoxicity is dose-related and reversible and not a hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose aspirin therapy; risk appears restricted to patients with connective tissue disorders (rheumatic fever, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus).
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2: 4-year-old girl, aspirin 100 mg/kg/day; symptoms of nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain on day 12 of therapy; serum salicylate 26.8 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 1325 iu/l (79.34 nkat); Hepatitis B antigen and mononucleosis spot tests negative; aspirin discontinued two days, then reinstituted at 80 mg/kg/day; after 10 days salicylate was 18 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 109 iu/l (6.53 nkat); liver function tests normal at three-month follow-up. Mechanism concluded dose-related (hepatotoxicity appears when salicylate concentrations exceed ~25 mg/dl) and reversible on dose reduction, not a hypersensitivity reaction; saturated formation of salicyluric acid and salicyl phenolic glucuronide at therapeutic doses increases minor metabolites, possibly hepatotoxic in uniquely sensitive connective-tissue-disorder patients. Typical features across reports: anorexia, malaise, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain; SGOT/SGPT elevation; hyperbilirubinaemia unusual; alkaline phosphatase normal or slightly increased; biopsy shows preserved lobular architecture, widened sinusoidal spaces, focal hepatocyte necrosis, degeneration and ballooning with anisocytosis and mitotic figures.

raw_record.support_text: Bucaretschi et al. (2014) reported a case of APAP-induced acute liver failure in a term neonate: after oral APAP (10 mg/kg/dose every 4 hours) for three consecutive days (total ~180 mg/kg), a 26-day-old boy was admitted with slight liver enlargement, increased serum aminotransferase activity, intestinal bleeding, shock signs, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, and hyperbilirubinemia, highlighting the risk of severe hepatotoxicity in neonates after multiple doses of APAP for more than two to three days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Neonatal patient (term, 26-day-old boy); therapeutic repeated oral dosing (10 mg/kg/dose every 4 h for 3 days, total ~180 mg/kg); detected rise in serum aminotransferase with multiple systemic features.
raw_record.extra_details: Presenting features: slight liver enlargement, intestinal bleeding, shock, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia; paper notes neonates/infants differ from older children and adults in APAP pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, making age important in APAP toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that MTX commonly causes liver function impairment. It reports that although a few studies found no correlation between MTHFR C677T mutations and liver function impairment, a large number of studies indicate a strong association, including a meta-analysis of 14 studies (1714 children) showing the C677T mutant gene was significantly associated with hepatotoxicity, and several reports confirming a significantly higher risk of hepatic impairment in patients with mutant genotypes. In the present study, the authors found significant differences in the incidence of hepatic impairment among MTHFR C677T genotypes, with a significantly higher risk in CT+TT mutant carriers than in CC wild-type carriers, a conclusion also supported by stratified analysis in the low-risk group.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia patients treated with high-dose MTX (HD-MTX); hepatic-impairment risk was significantly higher in MTHFR C677T CT+TT mutant carriers than in CC wild-type carriers in the study population and in the low-risk subgroup.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX use is limited by drug-related toxicities including bone marrow suppression, abnormal liver and kidney function, skin mucosal damage, and gastrointestinal reactions. Liver function impairment was assessed as a grade II or higher toxic reaction. Supporting literature: Zhu et al. meta-analysis of 14 studies (1714 children) found C677T mutant significantly associated with hepatotoxicity; El-Khodary et al. reported higher serum glutaminase levels in CT/TT carriers; the C677T mutation was suggested to cause a rapid increase in cysteine levels after MTX chemotherapy as a potential mechanism of liver function impairment.

raw_record.support_text: 6-Thioguanine (6-TG) is known to be associated with veno-occlusive disease (VOD) due to endothelial toxicity, and 6-TG-induced chronic hepatotoxicity involving chronic hepatic sinusoidal endothelial damage, portal venular obstruction, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) with parenchymal atrophy and nodular transformation is discussed. The paper reports a paediatric case series of children treated for ALL with maintenance 6-TG who developed 6-TG-induced portal hypertension with splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia and abnormal hepatic echo texture, noting a male predominance (7 of 10 in the series; 24 of 30 reported cases), a minimum incidence of 13.3% in this paediatric series, and variceal bleeding during follow-up.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paediatric patients treated for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) with maintenance 6-TG; male predominance noted (7 of 10 in series, 24 of 30 reported cases); follows ALL treatment.

raw_record.support_text: In 92 paediatric patients with IBD receiving mercaptopurine (mean dosage 1.25 mg/kg/day), patients with wild-type TPMT and mercaptopurine-induced hepatotoxicity showed significantly (p < 0.05) higher concentrations of 6-MMP (>5700 pmol/8 × 10⁸ red cells) than patients without hepatotoxic events. The paper suggests high TPMT activity and subsequent accumulation of 6-MMP could play an important role in the pathogenesis of mercaptopurine-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paediatric patients with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, indeterminate colitis); wild-type TPMT genotype; therapeutic dosing (mean 1.25 mg/kg/day).
raw_record.extra_details: Mercaptopurine-induced hepatotoxicity in patients with wild-type TPMT was associated with 6-MMP >5700 pmol/8 × 10⁸ red cells vs non-hepatotoxic patients (p<0.05); high TPMT activity and subsequent 6-MMP accumulation proposed as playing a role in the pathogenesis of hepatotoxicity. 6-MMP is a metabolite discussed mechanistically, not independently attributed as the causal entity.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective paediatric study, voriconazole-attributable hepatotoxicity occurred in 12.7% of children, comparable to previously reported rates of 14.3%–17.5%. None of the patients who developed voriconazole-attributable hepatotoxicity had voriconazole concentrations >5 mg/L, so an association with trough concentration could not be determined, consistent with other studies reporting no relationship with trough concentrations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paediatric population (children receiving therapeutic voriconazole); retrospective study setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity attributed to voriconazole occurred in 12.7% of children; comparable to previously reported rates of 14.3%–17.5%. No patient with voriconazole-attributable hepatotoxicity had voriconazole trough concentration >5 mg/L, and no concentration-association could be determined; other studies also reported no relationship with trough concentrations.
