raw_record.support_text: The authors state it is exceedingly difficult to assess the importance of azaserine in the production of hepatic injury, since many patients were in poor general condition, had received multiple blood transfusions, and often had liver involvement by neoplastic cells. Despite jaundice in some patients, there was no histological evidence of drug toxicity in the liver parenchyma, and in children treated with azaserine there was no evidence of hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with advanced Hodgkin's disease, poor general condition, prior multiple blood transfusions, and liver involvement by neoplastic cells; pre-existing hepatic damage possible.
raw_record.extra_details: No histological evidence of drug toxicity in liver parenchyma even among patients who became jaundiced, so jaundice was not attributed to azaserine; attributable to disease progression, transfusions (possible homologous serum jaundice), and hepatic neoplastic involvement. Fifteen children treated with azaserine showed no evidence of hepatic injury. The authors report that azaserine cannot be stated with certainty to produce serious systemic intoxication and recommend caution and prompt stopping in debilitated or pre-existing hepatic dysfunction patients.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate has proven useful in treating severe psoriasis but is not without problems; its hepatotoxicity was first described in 1955 in children treated for leukemia and later in psoriasis patients. The paper describes liver biopsies performed between 1974 and 1978 on psoriatics to assess their value in managing the psoriatic and monitoring liver damage due to methotrexate.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with heavy alcohol intake were excluded from methotrexate treatment; chronic use for severe psoriasis with pre-treatment and on-treatment liver biopsy monitoring.
raw_record.extra_details: 31 liver biopsies performed on 22 severe psoriasis patients (12 men, 10 women; ages 22-75, mean 53). Of 21 attempted pre-methotrexate biopsies, 4 were abnormal and 1 failed; 5 of 10 post-methotrexate biopsies were abnormal. Histological abnormalities were mild and cirrhosis was not seen. Three patients developed serious morbidity after biopsy (post-biopsy complication, not drug-related). Liver function tests were not found to be a reliable indicator of hepatic damage.

raw_record.support_text: Indicine N-oxide was used to treat leukemia. In a dose-seeking study, 22 patients with refractory acute leukemia received indicine N-oxide daily for five consecutive days; five patients had severe hepatic toxicity, probably due to veno-occlusive disease induced by indicine N-oxide. In a separate Phase II study of 31 children with leukemia, hepatotoxicity was mild (grade 1 or 2) in 63% and moderate (grade 3) in 9% of patients, and three patients (9%) experienced severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The abstract reports the first pediatric case of successful orthotopic liver transplantation for disulfiram-induced fulminant hepatic failure in a 16-year-old girl who developed an idiosyncratic reaction associated with short-term, low-dose disulfiram use, as evidenced by her liver biopsy and explanted liver. The paper notes that disulfiram has been reported in rare cases to cause fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (16-year-old female) patient with underlying alcohol use disorder; idiosyncratic reaction after short-term, low-dose disulfiram (500 mg twice weekly for 5 weeks); discontinued alcohol 1 week before disulfiram.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug discontinued 6 days prior to admission after nausea, vomiting, and malaise. Liver biopsy showed 80-90% hepatic necrosis, mild portal infiltrate with moderate-to-severe eosinophilia, and few plasma cells; damage predominantly hepatocellular with minimal ductal involvement. Strong temporal relation: symptoms of hepatocellular failure developed within 6 weeks of initiating disulfiram. No acetaminophen use and negative viral/autoimmune serologies except ANA 1:160. Progression to grade III hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy (INR 3.8), factor V decreased to 20%; underwent successful OLT on hospital day 5; normal liver function 84 weeks post-transplant.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatopathy-thrombocytopenia syndrome (HTS) is observed in patients with Wilms tumor undergoing actinomycin D (dactinomycin) treatment, describing it as a rare and often unrecognized syndrome. Actinomycin D-induced HTS is characterized as a rare syndrome, and the case study presents a 3.5-year-old pediatric Wilms tumor patient with actinomycin D-related HTS and multiple *MDR1* (ABCB1) gene mutations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (3.5-year-old girl) patient receiving actinomycin D as chemotherapy for Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma).
raw_record.extra_details: Actinomycin D (dactinomycin) is an antitumor agent used in the treatment of Wilms tumor for the past 40 years. The hepatopathy-thrombocytopenia syndrome (HTS) is described as rare and often unrecognized. This case study reports that the girl carried the following MDR1 (ABCB1) gene mutations: (−)1G>A, 1236C>T, 2677G>T, 3435C>T, and 61A>G; the authors hypothesize the mechanism underlying HTS may differ with individual MDR1 genotype, though MDR1 genotype is a susceptibility/mechanistic factor rather than an independently causal hepatotoxic agent.

raw_record.support_text: In the report of doxapram effects in 2 infants with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, the authors state that the other major complication associated with the maintenance doxapram infusion was hepatotoxicity. Liver size increased progressively during the infusion; at the time of abdominal surgery the liver was 6 cm below the right costal margin, yellow, and firm, and biopsy revealed severe fatty metamorphosis without necrosis or inflammation. Increased serum transaminase concentrations (SGOT 160 IU/L and SGPT 120 IU/L vs normal ranges 8-31 and 6-39 IU/L) provided additional evidence of hepatotoxicity, while serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase remained normal. Liver size and transaminase concentrations returned to normal within 10 days after stopping doxapram.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (infants) with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome; occurred during prolonged continuous maintenance doxapram infusion at 2 mg per kg body weight per hour, necessitating stopping the infusion after 5.2 days
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of 2 infants treated with doxapram. Hepatotoxicity occurred in Patient 2 during a 5.2-day maintenance infusion (loading dose 0.5 mg/kg/min for 14 min, then up to 7 mg/kg/h, stepped down to 2 mg/kg/h). Liver enlarged, yellow, firm; liver biopsy showed severe fatty metamorphosis without necrosis or inflammation; SGOT 160 IU/L and SGPT 120 IU/L vs normal 8-31 and 6-39 IU/L; bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase normal. Liver size and transaminases returned to normal within 10 days after discontinuation. Concurrent massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage required surgery the following day for a perforated duodenal ulcer, and hypoglycemia (25 mg/100 ml) occurred one day before the hemorrhage, confounding the clinical picture.

raw_record.support_text: In a CCSG randomized study of childhood leukemia patients free of disease for 2.5–3 years, those continued on chemotherapy developed serious chronic toxicity. Among 7 children continued, a child on daily methotrexate for 255 days developed hepatosplenomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, bony osteoporosis, and severe scoliosis; a percutaneous liver biopsy demonstrated cirrhotic changes, and liver function tests returned to normal after methotrexate was discontinued. Two other patients had clinical evidence of liver disease with altered liver function and hepatosplenomegaly after 461 and 1211 days of methotrexate maintenance, both improving after discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric childhood leukemia patients on chronic maintenance therapy; one patient also received methotrexate plus four other drugs cyclically as an unresolved co-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic methotrexate toxicity. CCSG randomized study (1966): 7 children continued treatment, 3 developed serious chronic toxicity. Daily methotrexate for 255 days led to hepatosplenomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, osteoporosis and scoliosis, with cirrhotic changes on biopsy; liver function normalized after discontinuation. Two further children on methotrexate maintenance for 461 and 1211 days had liver disease with altered liver function and hepatosplenomegaly, improving on discontinuation. Minnesota series: hepatic fibrosis in 12 children, usually asymptomatic despite abnormal BSP excretion and transiently elevated OCT/SGOT immediately after methotrexate. CCSG 903 maintenance methotrexate (30 mg/m² twice weekly p.o.): predominant clinical toxicity hepatic; of 216 patients on study >4 months, 80 had elevated liver enzymes (median time to definite elevation 167 days); liver biopsy showed significant cirrhosis in 5 and fibrosis in 9 (moderate fibrosis mean 389 days, cirrhosis mean 530 days on MTX); 9 of 11 with fibrosis/cirrhosis had prior acute methotrexate toxicity. Pathologic findings in MTX-induced liver disease (12 patients): portal fibrosis 10/12, enlarged/double-nucleated hepatic cells 9/12, portal inflammation 7/12, periportal fat 4/12, cholestasis 1/12, hepatic necrosis 1/12.

raw_record.support_text: Of 470 epileptic patients with measured VPA serum metabolites, 170 asymptomatic subjects served as a reference. Among 11 patients with early symptoms and signs of possible fatal VPA-associated hepatotoxicity, reversible or irreversible fulminant liver failure occurred in 5 children, and 4 children had a fatal outcome (3 with massive lactic acidosis). The paper states that VPA hepatotoxicity is considered dose-independent and idiosyncratic, and that the most toxic compound could be VPA itself, possibly unmasking an inborn or acquired metabolic defect in fatty-acid processing.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric epileptic patients; suspected underlying inborn or acquired defect in fatty-acid metabolism that VPA may unmask.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 470 epileptic patients; 11 patients with symptoms/signs of possible fatal VPA-associated hepatotoxicity, 5 with fulminant liver failure, 4 fatal (3 with massive lactic acidosis). Benign presentations included unusually severe side effect at initiation, high VPA dosage, reversible coagulation impairment with bleeding and slight transaminase increase (1 child), and reversible liver dysfunction with febrile illness (7 patients). Affected patients showed impaired VPA beta-oxidation and increased metabolites of omega- and omega1-hydroxylation and dehydrogenation; 2-PGA (omega-oxidation end product) was found in some children in prior reports. Pathogenesis described as dose-independent and idiosyncratic.

raw_record.extra_details: Primary outcome VCZ-induced hepatotoxicity defined as any-grade liver dysfunction attributed to VCZ within the first week of use, per CTCAE v4 (total bilirubin >1.5x ULN, or AST or ALT >3x ULN). raw_record.support_text: The paper records HD-MTX-related toxicities following methotrexate treatment in pediatric non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) patients, including hematological suppression, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, oral mucositis, vomiting, and diarrhea, with adverse events graded by CTCAE 3.0. A total of 355 courses of high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) therapy were analyzed across 93 pediatric patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric NHL patients treated with high-dose methotrexate as part of chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 93 pediatric patients (median age 8.8 years; LBL, BL, ALCL, DLBCL); 355 courses of HD-MTX analyzed; adverse events graded by CTCAE 3.0 and dichotomized into grade 0/I/II versus III/IV; plasma MTX level >0.2 umol/L at 48 h seen in 63 (17.7%) courses. Hepatotoxicity recorded as one of the HD-MTX-related toxicities; no specific pattern, severity, dose, or latency for the hepatic injury is provided.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a thirteen-year-old boy admitted in February 1969 with disabling rheumatoid arthritis who died from toxic hepatic necrosis attributed to phenylbutazone; phenylbutazone described as a potentially toxic drug but hepatotoxic hepatic injury is uncommon.

raw_record.support_text: After mandatory school-enrollment tuberculin skin testing, a 4-year-old girl who was at low risk for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection had severe isoniazid hepatotoxicity that was managed with a liver transplant. The case report states that severe isoniazid hepatotoxicity is very uncommon in children, and emphasizes that the patient was not taking any medications other than isoniazid that may have contributed to her hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (4-year-8-month-old girl); treated for latent tuberculosis infection after mandatory school-entry tuberculin skin testing despite low risk of TB infection.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose isoniazid 150 mg/day (9 mg/kg/day) for LTBI treatment. Hepatotoxicity appeared after 11 weeks of treatment with one week of episodic vomiting, irregular appetite, pale stools, progressive abdominal pain, and 4 days of eye yellowing; exam showed scleral icterus, abdominal tenderness, and tender enlarged liver palpable 3 cm below right costal margin. No other contributing medications were taken. Managed with a liver transplant.

raw_record.support_text: In this pediatric case series, INH (isoniazid) was listed among the toxic agents that caused acute liver failure (ALF) in a 4-year-old boy (Case 3) following ingestion as medical treatment; the prodromal period from ingestion to symptom appearance was 2 months. At admission he had grade II hepatic encephalopathy, AST 40–34 IU/mL, ALT 217–23 IU/mL, total bilirubin 22–25 mg/dL and INR 3.9 to >4.5, and the explanted liver showed massive necrosis. He required living-related liver transplantation (from his mother) 8 days after admission and was alive at 9 months follow-up.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (4-year-old male child); therapeutic medical-treatment setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Two-month latency from INH initiation to symptoms; progressed to ALF with grade II encephalopathy; laboratory values AST 40–34, ALT 217–23 IU/mL, total bilirubin 22–25 mg/dL, INR 3.9 to >4.5; explant histology showed massive necrosis; underwent living-related liver transplant from his mother 8 days after admission; survived (alive at 9-month follow-up). Paper recommends serial liver enzyme measurements after initiating INH.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure that resulted in the need for a liver transplant. A 9-year-old boy diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and treated with pemoline developed signs and symptoms consistent with liver failure; pemoline therapy was discontinued but hepatic function continued to deteriorate, and the patient ultimately required a liver transplant. Pemoline was associated with the development of hepatotoxicity, mostly in pediatric patients, and this is reported as the second case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure resulting in liver transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (9-year-old boy)
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Hepatic function continued to deteriorate after pemoline discontinuation. Reported as the second known case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure resulting in liver transplant; most reported cases occurred in pediatric patients. Mechanism of the adverse effect is unknown; hypotheses proposed include hypersensitivity reactions, dose-related phenomena, and autoimmune reactions. Authors advise against pemoline as first-line ADHD treatment and recommend liver function testing before and during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion identifies lamotrigine as the offending agent in a pediatric case of vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS), a rare ductopenia characterized by progressive loss of interlobular bile ducts that can result from drugs or toxins. The report notes that drug-induced hepatitis has been reported with lamotrigine and states this is the first report of bile duct injury associated with lamotrigine requiring liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient; single case report; no improvement with prednisolone and azathioprine so liver transplantation was contemplated and the child was waiting for it.
raw_record.extra_details: 6-year-old girl on lamotrigine developed progressive cholestasis and jaundice. Repeat liver biopsy showed marked ductular proliferation with paucity of interlobular bile ducts (absent in 7 of 8 portal tracts on CK7/CK19 immunostains) and bridging fibrosis; diagnosis of VBDS. Biochemical markers at month of worsening included AST 110 IU/L, ALT 59 IU/L, bilirubin 7.8 mg/dL; later worsening coagulogram. Treated with prednisolone 2 mg/kg and azathioprine 1.5 mg/kg/day without improvement; liver transplantation awaited.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports hepatic failure caused by isoniazid in children: among 20 children with isoniazid-induced hepatic failure, 10 had liver transplant, 6 died before transplant, and only 4 recovered without transplant; a second report of 2 children with severe isoniazid adverse events (2004–2008) included 1 liver transplant. The retrospective descriptive study (patients <18 years initiating isoniazid for LTBI) evaluated prevalence of hepatotoxicity caused by isoniazid, defining isoniazid hepatotoxicity as ALT >3x ULN with hepatitis symptoms/jaundice, or ALT >5x ULN without symptoms.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (<18 years) treated for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI); 9-month isoniazid therapy at 10–15 mg/kg/day (max 300 mg/day).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort reviewed 1582 patients aged <18 years initiating isoniazid for LTBI (2005–2011, California county). ATS-based definition: (1) ALT >3x ULN (female >93 U/L; male >120 U/L) with hepatitis symptoms or jaundice (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, unexplained fatigue), or (2) ALT >5x ULN (female >155 U/L; male >200 U/L) without symptoms. Literature cited: national sample of 2473 patients <20 years, hepatitis in 1/1000; Seattle study (11,141 patients) no hepatotoxicity in 1468 patients <14 years; San Diego County study no cases in 1277 patients <14 years, 6/1939 (0.3%) in patients aged 15–34 years. Known lower hepatotoxicity frequency in children; however severe outcomes (liver transplant, death) documented.

raw_record.support_text: In a pilot study of 58 children with newly diagnosed standard-risk ALL treated with multi-agent chemotherapy including CIVI-TG (480 mg/m²) and substitution of oral thioguanine (TG, 60 mg/m²/day) for oral mercaptopurine during maintenance, six patients (five males) experienced reversible veno-occlusive disease (VOD) while receiving oral TG. The study was amended to discontinue TG, switching all patients to oral MP, and the authors concluded that the development of VOD negatively impacts the risk:benefit ratio of substituting TG for MP.

raw_record.extra_details: Six of 58 patients (five males) developed reversible veno-occlusive disease (VOD) while receiving oral TG during maintenance; the study was amended to discontinue TG and change all patients to oral MP, concluding VOD negatively impacts the risk:benefit ratio. raw_record.support_text: Seven pediatric cases of halothane hepatitis are reported, all having received more than one documented halothane exposure (range 2-6, median 3) including the one immediately preceding jaundice, with no serological evidence of infective hepatitis or other known hepatotoxic drugs. The interval between the final halothane exposure and onset of jaundice was two to four days (median 3), and halothane antibodies were detected in six of seven children. One child (case 7) died of fulminant halothane hepatitis, while the six survivors had uneventful recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (ages 11 months to 15 years); all had repeated halothane exposures (2-6, median 3) with the penultimate-to-ultimate exposure interval 13 days to five months; two patients had halothane twice within three weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Unexplained postoperative fever after previous halothane anaesthesia in two patients and a maculopapular rash in one; none had drug allergy history or was obese; halothane antibodies detected in six of seven children (exception case 7); latency from final exposure to jaundice 2-4 days (median 3); maximum serum aminotransferases 960-5080 IU/l (ULN 40), maximum bilirubin 93-861 µmol/l (ULN 15); six survivors had no hepatic encephalopathy and recovered; case report of a 3½-year-old boy with grade III hepatic encephalopathy, prolonged prothrombin time, admitted 14 days after last halothane anaesthetic; in adults mortality of grade III/IV fulminant halothane hepatitis approaches 100%; child put on emergency list for transplant.

raw_record.support_text: In children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia receiving maintenance therapy that included daily oral 6-mercaptopurine (6MP), a group of patients developed gastrointestinal symptoms and 6MP-induced hepatotoxicity with elevated aminotransferases and jaundice. Other potential causes (viral hepatitis, sepsis, leukemic infiltration of the liver, and other hepatotoxic drugs such as methotrexate) were ruled out as far as possible: when 6MP was held, the symptoms and signs of hepatitis resolved despite continuation of methotrexate, and rechallenge with 6MP resulted in similar adverse effects. The paper states that 6MP has been reported to be toxic to the liver as well as to the bone marrow and intestine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (ages 3-17 years) with ALL on maintenance chemotherapy; received combination therapy including methotrexate, vincristine, and prednisone; small case series of 4 symptomatic children compared with asymptomatic children.
raw_record.extra_details: Symptomatic patients had AST 174-385 IU/L, ALT 204-558 IU/L, bilirubin up to 243 µmol/L (elevated direct bilirubin up to 213 µmol/L); doses 52-100 mg/m². Lower 6MP peak concentrations and AUC, longer time to peak in symptomatic patients suggested impaired absorption and/or hepatic accumulation. TPMT activity 10-27 units/ml pRBC consistent with homozygous wild-type genotype, ruling out low-TPMT-related hematologic toxicity as the mechanism. Possible proposed mechanisms include selective hepatic toxicity of methylated nucleotide (meMPN) metabolites or a hypersensitivity reaction developing after weeks to months of sensitization; rechallenge reproduced the adverse effects.

raw_record.support_text: In all seven children described, the most likely cause of the liver damage was halothane; other causes of postoperative hepatitis, including viral and bacterial infection, hypoxia, hypotension, and other drug toxicities, were absent. All cases had a history of previous halothane anaesthesia, and halothane-related antibodies were detected in six of the seven children. One of the seven children (case 6) died; at necropsy the liver showed confluent necrosis with extensive cell loss and reticulin collapse.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children aged 11 months to 15 years); all seven cases had a history of previous halothane anaesthesia (multiple exposures), and three had possible halothane sensitisation features (postoperative fever or rash). None had the risk factor of obesity; only one had a history of eczema.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven paediatric cases of halothane hepatitis (case series) referenced from the National Halothane Study and retrospective data. Adults: mortality 56% among 86 adults with severe hepatitis after halothane anaesthesia, similar in seropositive (~75% with halothane-related antibodies) and seronegative patients. Retrospective incidence in children was 2/165 400 halothane anaesthetics in one study and 1/200 311 in another. Laboratory findings included markedly elevated bilirubin (up to 861 µmol/l) and aspartate transaminase (>1500–5080 IU/l). Halothane antibody present in 6/7 children; in seronegative cases antibody may be bound to antigen/immune complexes. One child (case 6) died; another boy placed on the liver-grafting list started on methylprednisolone died on postoperative day 18 with a shrunken 480 g liver showing confluent necrosis and reticulin collapse. Adult National Halothane Study: unexplained severe massive liver cell necrosis incidence 1 per 35 000 anaesthetics, rising to 1 in 3500 after multiple exposures. Possible cross-sensitisation with enflurane is discussed but the halothane antibody did not react with the enflurane-related antigen.

raw_record.support_text: The life-threatening adverse events of aplastic anemia and hepatotoxicity have been associated with felbamate use in adults and children, and these events have not been identified as being dose related.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children aged 3-12 years, with six of 18 hepatic-failure cases); an independent evaluation found only seven of 18 reported cases could be solely related to felbamate therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: There have been 18 cases of hepatic failure in felbamate recipients (six in children aged 3-12 years). Signs and symptoms developed as early as 3 weeks after treatment initiation. Some cases resulted in liver transplant or death. Independent evaluation found only seven cases could be solely related to felbamate therapy; risk of hepatic failure estimated at 1:18,500-25,000 exposures; risk factors could not be established. Hepatotoxicity was not identified as dose related.

raw_record.support_text: A synopsis of 16 German patients, all children, describes liver failure while receiving VPA (valproate). Clinical signs of impending liver failure appeared >8 weeks before death in 6 of 16 patients, and pathological symptoms were seen in all patients 2-4 weeks before death. Reversible cases of VPA hepatotoxicity were noted, and the fatal outcome of liver failure might be avoided if nonspecific early symptoms are recognized as potentially dangerous side effects of VPA. Liver dystrophy leading to hepatic failure and coma hepaticum was the cause of death in all autopsy cases, and a hepatogenic cause of death was strongly suggested in the remaining patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children treated for epilepsy with VPA), representing 16 German cases
raw_record.extra_details: 16 patients with fatal VPA-associated liver failure; all died of hepatic failure/coma hepaticum (autopsy) or strongly suspected hepatogenic death. Liver histology was uniform: hepatocellular damage with cellular ballooning and microvesicular steatosis in all patients, acidophilic single-cell or cell-group necrosis mostly in central lobular areas, pseudoglandular hepatocyte arrangement with bile thrombi, destruction of liver architecture (cirrhosis criterion) in 9 of 10 examined patients, and striking bile duct proliferation; one case showed only microvesicular steatosis and cholesteatosis without bile duct proliferation. Associated findings included pneumonia (4), sepsis (3), shock (4), cerebral edema, and hemorrhagic necrotizing pancreatitis (patients 2, 7, 10). VPA treatment durations 6-22 weeks; maximum VPA doses 24-55 mg/kg; discontinuation of VPA within ≤1 week after first symptoms did not change the rapid fatal outcome in patients 1, 2, 6, 7.

raw_record.support_text: The study compared L-carnitine-treated and untreated children who developed valproate-induced hepatotoxicity (92 total patients, 42 treated with L-carnitine and 50 untreated). After onset of toxicity, valproate was stopped after a median of 7 days in the L-carnitine group and 8 days in the untreated group. The children often had poor nutrition and chronic illness, and 69% were below the 25th percentile for weight.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients treated for epilepsy (two with bipolar disorder); polytherapy with other anticonvulsants (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, clorazepate, clonazepam) or lithium was common; many had pre-existing chronic illness/poor nutrition.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 92 children with valproate-induced hepatotoxicity collected from US, German, and other centers; valproate median dose 39 mg/kg/d (treated) and 43 mg/kg/d (untreated), duration median 81 vs 72 days. Hepatic survival was 47% (20/42) in L-carnitine-treated vs 10% (5/50) in untreated patients (p < 0.001), indicating substantial mortality from valproate-induced hepatic failure; three patients who received prophylactic L-carnitine (stopped 60-100 days before the event) had this hepatic event delayed. L-carnitine is framed as a treatment/preventive measure, not the causal agent.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that high-dose and long-term use of 6-thioguanine (6-TG) in children with ALL leads to chronic hepatotoxicity and portal hypertension, with hepatic sinusoidal obstruction/veno-occlusive disease as the key liver-injury picture. This was originally described in the MRCALL97 randomized controlled trial by Vora et al. (2006), in which 11% of children in the 6-TG group developed nonfatal HVOD. Clinical manifestations are described as mild hepatomegaly, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminase, thrombocytopenia, and portal hypertension, and 6-TG-related HSOS during Baixiaoan treatment was associated with glutathione depletion and oxidative stress in hepatocytes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia during maintenance therapy; high-dose and long-term use; co-treatment context (e.g., Baixiaoan regimen, vincristine/methotrexate interactions).
raw_record.extra_details: 11% of children in the 6-TG arm of the MRCALL97 RCT (Vora et al., 2006) developed nonfatal hepatic veno-occlusive disease (HVOD). Main clinical manifestations: mild hepatomegaly, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminase, thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension; >90% showed transient mild hepatomegaly, mild-to-moderate hyperbilirubinemia with elevated transaminase, and moderate-to-severe thrombocytopenia. One child with HVOD-like features died of adenovirus infection (autopsy-confirmed), needing differentiation from HSOS. Most reversible HVOD patients in the American CCG-1952 trial had only HSOS manifestations. 6-TG-related HSOS during Baixiaoan treatment associated with glutathione depletion and oxidative stress in hepatocytes; interactions with vincristine and methotrexate-induced homocysteine increases proposed to reduce anticoagulant protein levels. Imaging (Doppler ultrasound, multislice spiral CT with MPR and liver CTA) aids HSOS diagnosis.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), no significant association between the SLC19A1 polymorphisms rs2838958, rs1051266 and the rs56292801 polymorphism of miR-5189 and MTX-induced side effects (hepatotoxicity, mucositis and other adverse events) was found. Logistic regression showed a significant association between the CT genotype of the rs1131596 SLC19A1 polymorphism and a higher risk of developing severe hepatotoxicity, and the combination of the TT genotype of rs1131596 with the AA genotype of rs56292801 conferred a statistically significant risk of severe hepatotoxicity. A statistically significant correlation between patient age and liver toxicity was also reported, with most hepatotoxicity cases in children aged 5-10 years.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) treated with MTX-based therapy at a single center
raw_record.extra_details: Paper investigates pharmacogenetic predictors of MTX-induced hepatotoxicity. No significant association of rs2838958, rs1051266 (SLC19A1) or rs56292801 (miR-5189) with MTX-induced hepatotoxicity when considered individually; CT genotype of rs1131596 and the combination of TT(rs1131596)+AA(rs56292801) significantly linked to severe hepatotoxicity risk. Hepatotoxicity statistically correlated with age, most cases in children aged 5-10. Study limitation: relatively small, genetically homogeneous population from one geographic area.

raw_record.support_text: In children with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis treated with aspirin, hepatotoxic effects manifested by modest SGOT elevations (< 400 IU) were frequently seen within one month after the start of therapy; most patients showed no clinical evidence of hepatitis, though some complained of nonspecific abdominal pain. In most of these patients (15 of 18), SGOT values returned to normal within the initial three months of therapy. For 93 patients, simultaneous serum salicylate levels and SGOT determinations showed a positive correlation between salicylate level and SGOT elevation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis; aspirin was given at doses up to and exceeding 100 mg/kg/day to achieve therapeutic serum salicylate levels (>20 mg/dL).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxic effects manifested by modest SGOT elevations (<400 IU) frequently seen within one month of therapy; 15 of 18 affected patients returned to normal SGOT within the first three months. Positive correlation between serum salicylate level and SGOT elevation (340 simultaneous determinations in 93 patients). Five patients developed symptomatic hepatitis requiring aspirin discontinuation; a total of 11 children had toxic reactions (including hepatitis) requiring withdrawal of aspirin therapy. Substantial decreases in SGOT within the first three months of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Indicine N-oxide was used to treat 46 children with malignant solid tumors at a dose of 2000 mg/m²/day for five consecutive days. Hepatotoxicity was experienced by 13 patients: 11 developed asymptomatic elevations of transaminases, 1 developed hyperbilirubinemia, and 1 developed ascites. The authors note that higher doses are associated with an unacceptably high incidence of severe, irreversible hepatotoxicity and recommend against further study of this agent in pediatric solid tumors.

raw_record.support_text: In this pediatric phase 1 study of clofarabine (Cl-F-ara-A, infused intravenously over 1 hour daily for 5 days, dose levels 11.25-70 mg/m²/day), the dose-limiting toxicity was reversible hepatotoxicity and skin rash at 70 mg/m²/day for 5 days; the maximum tolerated dose was 52 mg/m²/day for 5 days. The paper additionally notes that a prior adult phase 1 trial defined the MTD at 40 mg/m² daily for 5 days with hepatotoxicity as the dose-limiting toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients younger than 21 years with relapsed or refractory leukemia, heavily pretreated, enrolled in a phase 1 dose-escalation study.
raw_record.extra_details: Clofarabine was given IV over 1 hour daily for 5 days at six dose levels from 11.25 to 70 mg/m²/day with 30% dose escalation (modified 3+3 design). Dose-limiting toxicity was reversible hepatotoxicity and skin rash at 70 mg/m²/day; MTD was 52 mg/m²/day for 5 days. At MTD, clofarabine triphosphate in leukemia blasts ranged 6-19 µM with complete sustained inhibition of DNA synthesis. Adult phase 1 trial defined MTD at 40 mg/m² daily for 5 days with hepatotoxicity as the DLT. Activity: 5 CR and 3 PR of 25 patients (32%).

raw_record.support_text: Rare pediatric reports of vancomycin-induced DRESS syndrome describe a life-threatening condition with acute liver failure, aggravated encephalopathy, and azotemia, necessitating liver transplantation in one case and causing frank and refractory shock in another case. The patient in the present study developed vancomycin-induced DRESS fulfilling all RegiSCAR and Japanese Consensus Group criteria, with a benign outcome after prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; DRESS syndrome as the presenting systemic hypersensitivity drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS is a drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome whose systemic manifestations include acute liver failure; reagents: pediatric case series reported one case requiring liver transplantation and another with refractory shock. In the present case ALT rose from 72 to 353 U/L and AST from 32 to 341 U/L, with resolution after vancomycin discontinuation (ALT 88, AST 56); total bilirubin and ALP remained near baseline. Patch test to vancomycin was positive. Diagnosis fulfilled European Registry of Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions (RegiSCAR) Study Group and Japanese Consensus Group inclusion criteria. A prior study at Massachusetts General Hospital found vancomycin involved in 5 of 6 inpatient DRESS cases over 18 months.

raw_record.support_text: Six children were treated exclusively with VPA (valproic acid); one had received polytherapy previously but was on VPA monotherapy during the last months of life. Fatal hepatotoxicity occurred both at low (32 µg/ml, patient 2) and high (191 µg/ml, patient 16) VPA plasma concentrations. The majority of children died within the first 6 months of VPA therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (16 children aged 1 year, 1 month to 17 years, 10 months; median 5 years) treated for epilepsy; several had underlying neurologic diseases (e.g., history of encephalitis, ceroid lipofuscinosis); patient 4 received clonazepam in addition 3 days before first signs of apathy.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 fatal cases (11 boys, 5 girls): 5 had partial and 11 generalized epilepsy; 6 children treated exclusively with VPA; most died within the first 6 months of therapy, patient 16 in the twelfth month. Fatal hepatotoxicity occurred at both low (32 µg/ml) and high (191 µg/ml) VPA plasma concentrations. Symptoms included vomiting, nausea, abdominal pain, apathy; edema in 12/16. Liver enzymes elevated in 15/16, coagulation impaired in all (thromboplastin tests pathologic in all, fibrinogen test in 14/16, AT III in 7/7), serum bilirubin elevated in 16/16, blood ammonia elevated in 12/16, hypoglycemia in 3/16.; clinical_phenotype_note: Fatal hepatic failure reported (hepatic failure with impending liver failure symptoms); recorded as other_specific_phenotype because the hierarchy lacks an acute-liver-failure phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: The liver unit at King's College Hospital had experience of a fatal case of halothane hepatitis in a 3½ year old boy. The coroner's inquest recorded the cause of death as massive hepatic necrosis (halothane hepatitis) following three minor operations under general anaesthetic at another hospital in a 130-day period, with halothane used each time. The letter further cites Dr Roger Williams referring to five cases and Dr A P Mowatt describing four cases of halothane hepatitis in children.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (3½ year old boy, and further cases in children); repeated inhalational anaesthetic exposures (three minor operations under general anaesthesia within 130 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal outcome in a child; cause of death recorded as massive hepatic necrosis (halothane hepatitis). Anaesthetists were aware of halothane hepatitis in adults but not in infants, highlighting reporting problems. Coroner reported the case to the Committee on Safety of Medicines, the Faculty of Anaesthetists, and the National Anaesthetic Adverse Reaction Advisory Service. Additional cases in children: five (Roger Williams) and four (A P Mowatt).

raw_record.support_text: The stated aim of this work was to assess the therapeutic value of Black seed oil in protection against methotrexate induced hepatotoxicity in Egyptian children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Forty newly diagnosed ALL patients received MTX as part of their chemotherapy treatment protocol with delayed leucovorin rescue, and methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity is the attributed drug-related liver injury being protected against rather than being questioned.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (ages 4-13 years) with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia; methotrexate given as part of standard chemotherapy protocol with delayed leucovorin rescue after each MTX dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 40 consecutive newly diagnosed ALL children (28 males, 12 females; mean age 9.17±3.81 years, range 4-13) randomly assigned to MTX + Black seed oil (Baraka soft gelatin capsule 450 mg, 80 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for one week after each MTX dose, n=20) versus MTX + placebo for one week (n=20), with 20 healthy age/sex-matched controls. Leucovorin rescue (Ca leucovorin) dosed at 10 mg/m2 every 6 hours beginning 48 hours after MTX infusion, adjusted per methotrexate levels. MTX-induced hepatotoxicity is the target condition Black seed oil is tested to protect against (protective agent, not itself extracted as a DILI cause).

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as a well-known potential adverse effect of INH therapy, most likely due to reactive metabolites including acetylhydrazine and free-radical generation. Serum transaminase elevations were seen in 6.8–13.6% of children receiving INH monotherapy and in 6.4–22.9% of adults, with most patients asymptomatic and liver tests normalizing on discontinuation. Clinically overt hepatitis occurred in 0.1–3% of adults and 0.1–7.1% of children, and a surveillance study of 13,838 patients on INH for latent TB found clinically significant hepatitis in 0.1% of children versus 1.3% of adults.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged 0–17 years) receiving INH for tuberculosis/latent tuberculosis infection; findings specific to the pediatric transplant-referral setting.
raw_record.extra_details: INH (isoniazid) monotherapy or therapy for latent TB/active TB. Transaminase elevation incidence 6.8–13.6% (children) and 6.4–22.9% (adults); clinically overt hepatitis 0.1–7.1% (children) and 0.1–3% (adults); clinically significant hepatitis in 0.1% of children vs 1.3% of adults in a 13,838-patient surveillance study. Mechanism attributed to reactive metabolites (acetylhydrazine) via free-radical generation (mechanism only, acetylhydrazine not independently identified as the injuring entity). raw_record.support_text: Halothane hepatitis occurred in seven children aged between 11 months and 15 years, all of whom had received multiple halothane anaesthetics (range 2-6, median 3); one 3.5-year-old boy died with fulminant hepatic failure. In all cases other causes of liver diseases were excluded, and in all but one the diagnosis was confirmed serologically by antibodies to halothane-altered liver cell membrane antigens. The findings suggest halothane hepatitis occurs in children and should be considered when choosing anaesthetic agents for children requiring multiple anaesthetics.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged 11 months to 15 years); required repeated/repeated halothane exposure across multiple anaesthetics.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven affected children; multiple halothane anaesthetics (range 2-6, median 3); one 3.5-year-old boy died with fulminant hepatic failure; diagnosis confirmed serologically in six cases by antibodies to halothane-altered liver cell membrane antigens; other causes of liver disease excluded. Paper notes that in adults severe liver damage is an established but rare event after repeated halothane exposure, and this report extends it to children.

raw_record.support_text: Thirteen of 1582 patients (0.8%) who started isoniazid therapy for latent tuberculosis infection developed isoniazid hepatotoxicity; among 1235 patients who completed the 9-month isoniazid course the frequency of hepatotoxicity was 1.1% (13 of 1235). No significant difference in hepatotoxicity frequency was found between sex, age, or racial groups. All 13 patients were children or adolescents treated at therapeutic isoniazid dosages, and improvement of ALT occurred in all 13 at a mean 69 days after isoniazid discontinuation, with no deaths.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children and adolescents, age range 2-17 years); treatment for latent tuberculosis infection.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 of 1582 patients (0.8%) overall; 1.1% (13/1235) among those who completed the 9-month course. Mean time to hepatotoxicity onset 109 days (range 28-257); in 3 patients detection >6 months after start. Dosages 150-300 mg/d (mean 9 ± 4 mg/kg/d). Most had ALT elevation ≥5 times ULN; onset ALT mean 401 ± 448 U/L (range 100-2690), peak mean 559 ± 523 U/L (range 101-2925). Symptoms most commonly abdominal pain, anorexia, vomiting, nausea; jaundice in 3, hepatomegaly in 1, splenomegaly in 1. ALT improvement at mean 69 days after discontinuation; no deaths. No known viral hepatitis or HIV. Two additional patients excluded (1 with Becker muscular dystrophy, 1 with uncertain isoniazid dose count). Most patients (62%) were female and Hispanic. Half completed therapy with rifampin.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe human hepatocyte injury produced by valproic acid in children treated with the drug. Liver-biopsy tissue from two additional valproic-acid-treated children with abnormal liver-function tests (not in hepatic failure), along with one of the two children in the prior case report (whose late-biopsy and autopsy tissues showed hepatocyte injury), showed ultrastructural abnormalities of parenchymal cells, including alterations of mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, peroxisomes, and pericanalicular cytoplasm. The authors state that neither the mitochondrial injury nor the overall hepatocyte injury produced by valproic acid is similar to that in Reye's syndrome or to that produced by hypoglycin or 4-pentenoic acid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children being treated with valproic acid as an antiepileptic).
raw_record.extra_details: Evidence from ultrastructural examination of liver-biopsy and autopsy tissue in valproic-acid-treated children, including two with abnormal liver function but not hepatic failure and two from the earlier case report with late-biopsy and autopsy tissue. Findings: alterations in hepatocyte mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, peroxisomes, and pericanalicular cytoplasm. The authors explicitly conclude valproic acid causes hepatocyte injury, and that this injury is not similar to Reye's syndrome or to injury from hypoglycin or 4-pentenoic acid.

raw_record.support_text: A Canadian Association of University Teachers report described attempts by University of Toronto officials to discredit pediatric hematologist Nancy Olivieri, who published that the then under-development iron chelator deferiprone was associated with severe hepatotoxicity among children enrolled in a phase III clinical trial. Her findings were subsequently confirmed by regulatory agencies including the FDA worldwide.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children enrolled in a phase III manufacturer-funded clinical trial for the then undeveloped iron chelator deferiprone).
raw_record.extra_details: Report published by pediatric hematologist Nancy Olivieri; findings were countered by an industry-supported assessment written by two pharmaceutical employees and one university faculty member, but were later confirmed by regulatory agencies including the FDA worldwide. The manufacturer filed lawsuits, later settled in mediation after 18 years, and the clinician experienced career and legal consequences. A 2019 retrospective study of 41 deferiprone-treated patients identified ineffectiveness and significant toxicity and deaths.

raw_record.support_text: The study confirms that a significant proportion of children with ALL treated with 6-TG (6-thioguanine) as maintenance chemotherapy may develop chronic hepatotoxicity with portal hypertension, which can lead to variceal haemorrhage; the complication may present without antecedent veno-occlusive disease, and no children randomized to 6-MP maintenance were referred.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia) receiving 6-TG as maintenance chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic hepatotoxicity complicated by portal hypertension and oesophageal variceal haemorrhage; 10 children followed since hepatology assessment (5-46 months, median 30 months); one child had variceal bleeding 2 years after chronic hepatotoxicity was recognized and entered an endoscopic variceal banding programme; persistent splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia; 3 children had abnormal liver function tests at referral; variceal bleeding developed in 3 of the reported cases. On biopsy, 8 of 9 showed some sinusoidal dilatation, 1 had established nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) and 4 had features compatible with early NRH; the injury is proposed to represent a spectrum of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension including NRH and hepatoportal sclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: Valproic acid (VPA) is used to treat epilepsy; its hepatotoxicity is a major concern. In epileptic children, targeted metabolomics of serum acylcarnitines showed that VPA-induced abnormal liver function resulted in accumulation of serum long-chain acylcarnitines and reduced expression of beta-oxidation genes (CPT1, CPT2, LCAD), indicating disruption of fatty acid beta-oxidation. The introduction states VPA hepatotoxicity is the most common and life-threatening adverse drug reaction, has been associated with secondary carnitine deficiency, and intravenous carnitine has been used to treat severe symptomatic hepatotoxicity caused by VPA.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (epileptic children) receiving long-term therapeutic VPA; abnormal liver function context.
raw_record.extra_details: Proposed mechanism: disruption of fatty acid beta-oxidation with accumulated serum long-chain acylcarnitines and reduced CPT1, CPT2, LCAD expression; association with secondary carnitine deficiency; hepatic steatosis and reduced beta-FAO demonstrated in VPA-exposed mice; fenofibrate (PPARalpha agonist) showed a protective effect by reversing fatty acid metabolism. Introduction notes VPA hepatotoxicity is described as the most common and life-threatening adverse reaction limiting its use.

The paper explicitly states that no drug-related adverse events were shown to have a causal association with azithromycin therapy, and the discussion reiterates that standard azithromycin treatment was well-tolerated with no liver injury detected.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population treated for community-acquired respiratory infection; findings limited to the study cohort of 44 children.
raw_record.extra_details: Mild transient ALT elevation occurred in two patients (4.5%), normalized within 10 days of follow-up; hepatitis antibody tests negative and no history of hepatitis; no statistically significant difference in azithromycin trough concentration between children with and without liver injury (P>0.05). The authors concluded no drug-related adverse events had a causal association with azithromycin therapy and that standard treatment was well-tolerated with no liver injury detected.

raw_record.support_text: In a pharmacogenetic cohort of children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) treated with methotrexate (MTX), gastrointestinal- and liver-associated adverse events (AE) were the two main reasons for MTX discontinuation. Liver-associated AE ('hepatotoxicity') was attributed to MTX and was analyzed against genetic markers: 11 SNPs were significantly associated with hepatotoxicity. Carriers of MTRR rs1801394 had about a 2.5-fold higher hazard rate to develop hepatotoxicity and to discontinue MTX because of AE, and wild-type MTHFD1 rs2236225 had a 1.64-fold higher hazard rate for hepatotoxicity compared with mutated patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA); folic acid supplementation reduced hepatic AEs.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX was withdrawn due to adverse events in 10/119 patients (8.4%) in the cohort. Gastrointestinal- and liver-associated AEs were the 2 main reasons for MTX discontinuation. 11 SNPs were significantly associated with MTX hepatotoxicity; MTRR rs1801394 carried ~2.5x higher hazard for hepatotoxicity and for AE-related MTX discontinuation; wild-type MTHFD1 rs2236225 gave 1.64x higher hazard for hepatotoxicity. Results were consistent with prior JIA and rheumatoid arthritis studies.

raw_record.support_text: High-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) is used to treat malignant tumors in children and young adults, but systemic exposure to MTX often results in liver injury (drug-induced liver injury, DILI), which limits sustained administration. In a cohort of 374 patients receiving initial HD-MTX, moderate/severe DILI was the outcome modeled, with female gender, ABCB1 rs1128503 genotype, SLCO1B1 haplotypes, and MTX dosage identified as independent factors.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric/young-adult patients with malignant tumors (ALL, CNS tumors, NHL, osteosarcoma); high-dose MTX (above 20 mg/kg or 500 mg/m2) administration, which the authors explicitly note is a therapeutic dose.
raw_record.extra_details: HD-MTX is described as presenting a potentially lethal risk including DILI. Study of 374 patients with initial HD-MTX; moderate/severe DILI outcome. G allele of ABCB1 rs1128503, *1b/*1b and *1b/*15 haplotypes of SLCO1B1, female gender, and MTX dosage were independent factors for moderate/severe DILI. Predictive model ROC AUC = 0.805 including 24h MTX concentration. Patients with GA/AA genotype of ABCB1 rs1128503 had higher 24h MTX concentration than GG; SLCO1B1 *1b/*1b group had lower dose-adjusted concentration than *1a/*1a; IV plus triple intrathecal route gave higher C/D than IV alone. Mechanism/relevant genes: ABCB1 and SLCO1B1 (folic acid cycle transporters/enzymes).

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of seven premature infants undergoing nasogastric paracetamol for PDA closure, none of the patients presented high paracetamol blood levels or significant liver function disturbances, except for mild temporary elevation of GGT in 3 infants (Table 1). The authors note that the potential paracetamol hepatotoxicity concentration is unknown, and in their series no significant liver injury was observed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Preterm infants with hemodynamically significant PDA; off-label nasogastric paracetamol administration for PDA closure at doses recommended for pain control, with paracetamol blood levels and liver function monitored.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 7 premature infants; none presented high paracetamol blood levels or significant liver function disturbances; mild temporary GGT elevation in 3 infants only (recommended GGT range 12-132 units/l). Recommended plasma paracetamol concentration for analgesia/antipyresis 10-20 mg/ml; two infants had transient elevations of 24.3 and 27.1 mg/ml before dose 9, returning to the recommended range after treatment with normal liver function tests. The paper notes the potential paracetamol hepatotoxicity is attributed to production of N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine by hepatic cytochrome P-450, and that the paracetamol concentration causing such hepatotoxicity is unknown.

raw_record.support_text: These cases fit the reported spectrum of pemoline hepatitis. Hepatocellular injury is prominent. Pemoline hepatotoxicity is more common in children than in adults, and occurs late in the course of treatment; drug-induced hepatitis usually resolves after withdrawal. In our patients, treatment with pemoline lasted an average of 16 months before hepatotoxicity was evident. Liver biopsy specimens from children with jaundice or more severe symptoms showed hepatocellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported case series skewed to children (more common in children than adults) and males; one reported case with preexisting cholestatic liver disease; the most severe case involved concurrent use of methylphenidate, an unresolved co-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Treatment averaged 16 months before hepatotoxicity; injury occurs late in the course of treatment; biochemical recovery was slow and aminotransferases could take months to normalize; biopsy in jaundiced or more severely symptomatic children showed hepatocellular necrosis; the most severe patient had fulminant hepatic failure and required liver transplantation. Mechanism speculation includes metabolic idiosyncrasy and decreased pemoline metabolism with chronic use (half-life increases with chronic use and age); hypersensitivity considered less likely due to lack of fever/rash, though eosinophilia may occur and rechallenge caused rapid aminotransferase rises in only some patients. Chemical: phenylisohydantoin, an oxazolidinone derivative.

raw_record.support_text: Valproate-induced hepatotoxicity is described as rare, but often fatal, and is attributed to direct disruption of mitochondrial processes. It is heralded by nonspecific symptoms such as lethargy, nausea/vomiting, or worsening seizures, and occurs more frequently in at-risk populations such as mentally retarded individuals, young children, and those taking multiple drugs. One proposed mechanism is drug-induced carnitine deficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported more frequently in at-risk populations including mentally retarded individuals, young children, and patients taking multiple drugs; most children appeared malnourished (69% <25th percentile for weight, 38% <5th percentile).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective inception cohort from the International Registry for Adverse Reactions to Valproate; 92 patients with severe, symptomatic, valproate-induced hepatotoxicity (90 with epilepsy, 2 with bipolar disorder); outcome was hepatic survival (deceased and liver transplant combined as terminal hepatic failure). Valproate stopped after a median of 7 days in L-carnitine-treated and 8 days in untreated patients. 48% of 42 L-carnitine-treated patients survived vs 10% of 50 treated with supportive care only (p < 0.001).

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) therapy for tuberculosis carries a known risk for hepatotoxicity and leads to hepatic failure in a small subset of patients; the study aimed to estimate pediatric referrals for INH-related liver failure and describe outcomes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Restricted to pediatric patients on prophylactic INH for latent/asymptomatic tuberculosis infection (ages 1.3–17 years; mean age 9.8 years).
raw_record.extra_details: A 10-year survey of 84 U.S. pediatric liver-transplant centers plus UNOS statistics found 20 cases of INH-related liver failure: 4 (20%) recovered spontaneously, 10 (50%) underwent orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT), and 6 (30%) died awaiting OLT. Mean INH therapy duration was 3.3 months (range 0.5–9). Five patients with hepatitis symptoms were initially told not to stop treatment. INH-associated liver failure accounted for 0.2% (8/4679) of all pediatric OLTs and 14% (8/56) of transplants for drug hepatotoxicity. Estimated incidence of liver failure up to 3.2/100,000 among children on prophylactic INH. Case count, incidence, outcomes, therapy duration, and monitoring-context details are recorded here.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen serum concentrations were studied in 21 infants and children with fever after therapeutic single and repeated doses (66-81 mg/kg/day as elixir). Maximum serum concentrations ranged from 9.96 to 19.6 µg/ml after a single 12-14 mg/kg dose and 13.9 to 40.1 µg/ml after a single 22-27 mg/kg dose; ten patients were restudied at steady-state. The authors report there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity in these patients, concluding only that acetaminophen may accumulate after repeated therapeutic doses in children with fever.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Subjects were hospitalized febrile children (n=21, ages 0.5-6.4 years, weight 8.84-22.6 kg) with presumed/proven bacterial or viral infection receiving therapeutic oral acetaminophen elixir 66-81 mg/kg/day (12-14 mg/kg/4h or 22-27 mg/kg/8h) for 1-3 days; patients with abnormal liver or renal function, vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, or malnutrition were excluded; some patients received concomitant drugs (ampicillin, phenobarbital, diphenhydramine, theophylline, phenytoin, penicillin, cefaclor, moxalactam, gentamicin, nafcillin).
raw_record.extra_details: No evidence of hepatotoxicity or abnormal liver function at these therapeutic doses despite dose-normalized AUC increasing from 0.181 to 0.202 (ml/min/kg)^-1 from first dose to steady-state (p<0.05); five of ten steady-state patients showed 13-44% increase in AUC, one a 10% decrease, and four <6% change; conclusion was possible acetaminophen accumulation after repeated therapeutic doses in febrile children, not hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The rs2302387 (ABCB4 L59L) and rs4148115 (ABCB11) polymorphisms are associated with mithramycin-induced acute transaminitis in two independent studies in adult patients with thoracic malignancies and in pediatric patients with Ewing sarcoma; mithramycin toxicity is predicted to be most severe in patients harboring variant genotypes conferring low expression of ABCB4 and ABCB11. The paper concludes that mithramycin induces cholestasis in individuals harboring genetic profiles susceptible to bile acid accumulation (ABCB4 and/or ABCB11 gene variants), and a dose-escalation clinical trial (NCT01624090) is assessing mithramycin therapy in patients with wild-type alleles.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Susceptibility appears restricted to individuals harboring ABCB4 and/or ABCB11 variant genotypes conferring low bile transporter expression (bile acid accumulation); study populations were adult patients with thoracic malignancies and pediatric patients with Ewing sarcoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed human injuries include mithramycin-induced acute transaminitis, hepatotoxicity/LFT elevations, and cholestasis. Two independent clinical studies (adult thoracic malignancies; pediatric Ewing sarcoma) reported the association of rs2302387 and rs4148115 with transaminitis. Mechanism: inhibition of FXR gene expression and ligand-induced FXR activation, deregulation of bile transport, and intracellular bile acid accumulation; not a direct ABCB11 inhibitor and unlike CDCA/CsA did not decrease bile synthesis; CYP8B1 and RALBP SNPs were additionally associated with mithramycin-induced hepatotoxicity in the ongoing dose-escalation trial NCT01624090.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, noting that shortly after its introduction cases of severe and occasionally fatal hepatotoxicity in treated patients were reported, with fatal damage frequency roughly 1:10,000 in children and 1:40,000 in adults and higher with antiepileptic polytherapy; microvesicular steatosis is the principal histological finding and is attributed to decreased mitochondrial β-oxidation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic-dose exposure; case involved co-medication with clonazepam (6 mg/day) and aspirin (100 mg/day), a period of failed carbamazepine, and an antiepileptic polytherapy setting; patient had underlying multi-infarct syndrome and manic depressive disorder.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old woman with fatal valproate-induced hepatotoxicity; valproate 2400 mg/day with serum concentrations in therapeutic range. Frequency of fatal valproate-induced liver damage averages roughly 1:10,000 in children and 1:40,000 in adults and is higher with antiepileptic polytherapy. Microvesicular steatosis named as the principal histological finding in valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, attributed to decreased mitochondrial β-oxidation. Case showed bilirubin 145 µM, ALAT 35 U/l, ASAT 95 U/l, prothrombin ratio 39%, ammonia 75 µM, thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagulation and hepatorenal syndrome, ending in multiorgan failure and death five days after admission. Plasma and liver free/total carnitine decreased with increased short-chain acylcarnitine ratios; liver total CoA decreased by 84% with reduced CoASH, acetyl-CoA and long-chain acyl-CoA and increased succinyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that cholic acid (CA) is now recognized as the bile acid of choice for 3β-HSD and Δ⁴-3-oxo-R deficiencies because it is not hepatotoxic and is effective therapy, and concludes that prolonged oral CA therapy is safe. This is supported by prospective follow-up of 15 children with primary bile acid synthesis defects (initial mean dose 13 mg/kg, 6 mg/kg at last evaluation, median treatment follow-up 12.4 years) in which serum liver biochemistries and sonography normalized and post-treatment liver biopsies showed marked improvement, with CA tolerated well.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treatment in children (median age at start 3.9 years, range 0.3-13.1) with primary bile acid synthesis defects (3β-hydroxy-Δ⁵-C₂₇-steroid oxidoreductase [3β-HSD] or Δ⁴-3-oxosteroid 5β-reductase [Δ⁴-3-oxo-R] deficiency).
raw_record.extra_details: 15 patients (13 with 3β-HSD, 2 twin sisters with Δ⁴-3-oxo-R deficiency) from 10 families, followed prospectively from 1993 to 2007 at Bicêtre Hospital. Liver biopsies after at least 5 years of CA therapy in 14 patients showed marked improvement, especially in 3β-HSD deficiency. Atypical urinary metabolites reduced 500-fold (3β-HSD) and 30-fold (Δ⁴-3-oxo-R). Two women had normal pregnancies during treatment. Study aimed to assess long-term effectiveness and safety of oral cholic acid; the paper explicitly asserts CA is not hepatotoxic (vs. chenodeoxycholic acid also used for bile acid replacement).

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity after acute overdose is well documented in the literature, with more severe signs including hepatic damage. In the reported case a 28-year-old man intentionally ingested up to 250 g of acetaminophen (500-mg tablets) plus an unknown quantity of ibuprofen and developed acute renal and fulminant liver failure; his admission acetaminophen level was 316 µg/ml and liver tests were markedly elevated (AST 3993 U/L, ALT 5731 U/L, INR 5.3), and he underwent liver transplantation on hospital day 3.

raw_record.extra_details: Intentional overdose of up to 250 g of acetaminophen (500-mg tablets); admission acetaminophen level 316 µg/ml (critical value > 40 µg/ml); treated with IV acetylcysteine; acute renal and fulminant liver failure; AST 3993 U/L, ALT 5731 U/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl, INR 5.3, pH 6.9, lactic acid 13.7 mEq/L; liver transplantation on day 3 with necrotic bowel found at surgery; rhabdomyolysis was a rare co-occurrence and the Naranjo scale indicated a probable acetaminophen-overdose-associated reaction for rhabdomyolysis; the literature does not clearly associate acetaminophen with rhabdomyolysis because of other possible causes.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion concludes that a toxic hepatitis occurred twice in this patient after ingestion of psoralen (methoxsalen) during PUVA therapy. The rapid onset of symptoms 4-5 hours after methoxsalen ingestion on treatment days and rapid defervescence and resolution of liver enzymes with symptomatic therapy strongly suggest a toxic drug reaction rather than a viral origin or extrahepatic biliary pathology; a viral origin was considered unlikely due to negative HAA testing and repetition of the reaction after readministration of methoxsalen, and other medications were excluded because they were continued without recurrence.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient with psoriasis undergoing PUVA photochemotherapy; after a scheduled PUVA treatment she ingested 50 mg oral methoxsalen and received UVA (4 joules) 2 hours later. Four hours after ingestion temperature rose to 39.5 C, LDH to 905, SGOT to 870, and alkaline phosphatase to 111; she defervesced within 24 h and enzymes returned to normal over 5 days. HAA was negative; intravenous cholangiogram unsuccessful because liver function was too poor to excrete dye; no liver biopsy. The reaction recurred after repeat methoxsalen readministration (rechallenge), supporting causality. The same patient later used topical methoxsalen with no similar reaction. Note: the discussion heading refers to 'methotrexate-induced toxic hepatitis,' but the attributed administered causal agent throughout is methoxsalen (psoralen).

raw_record.support_text: Serum miRNA profiles were compared between a lethal case of acetaminophen overdose, previously measured non-lethal cases of acetaminophen overdose, and healthy controls. Acetaminophen-induced liver injury was corroborated by ALT/AST and TBIL levels; the lethal poisoning case showed the highest ALT and AST at the early time point, and one non-lethal overdose case without elevated ALT was indistinguishable from healthy participants. The degree of PCA shift was proportional to the degree of liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single lethal acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning followed longitudinally from hospitalization to death, compared with previously studied non-lethal acetaminophen overdose cases and healthy participants. Acetaminophen is described as the most commonly used analgesic/antipyretic with frequent supra-therapeutic poisonings. Liver injury was assessed via ALT, AST, TBIL, INR and MELD scores; the lethal case developed acetaminophen-induced lethal acute liver failure (ALF), with severe coagulopathy (INR reaching ~5 within 40 h of admission) and loss of liver function accompanied by rising TBIL and decreasing ALT; one non-lethal case without elevated ALT was indistinguishable from healthy participants. GSE analysis of PC1 implicated pathways related to autophagy, cell-cycle and Notch signaling consistent with molecular mechanisms of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity; PC2-related pathways involved fibrosis, coagulation and thrombosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old female being treated for porphyria cutanea tarda was mistakenly given a single 1250 mg dose of chloroquine instead of the intended 125 mg. In contrast to typical chloroquine toxicity (mainly cardiac arrhythmias), she died 13 days after ingestion in a coma caused by irreversible, acute decompensation of the liver. Forensic autopsy and histological and toxicological investigations confirmed the findings, and the authors explain the severe hepatotoxic effect of chloroquine in this case from its pharmacological mechanism of action in p.c.t. The authors warn against exceeding the recommended p.c.t. dose of 125-250 mg twice weekly and consider clinically manifest p.c.t. a contraindication to chloroquine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental overdose of 1250 mg instead of intended 125 mg; patient had porphyria cutanea tarda (chronic porphyria hepatica), which the authors consider a contraindication to chloroquine use.
raw_record.extra_details: Single oral dose of 1250 mg chloroquine (Resochin) instead of 125 mg; death occurred 13 days post-ingestion in a coma due to irreversible acute liver decompensation; confirmed by forensic autopsy and histological and toxicological investigations; the severe hepatotoxic effect is explained by chloroquine's pharmacological mechanism in p.c.t.; authors recommend p.c.t. dosing of 125-250 mg twice weekly and warn against exceeding it. Typical chloroquine overdose toxicity (cardiac arrhythmia) was not the course in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: Seven of 122 patients presented at least 18 hours after acute acetaminophen ingestions with no acetaminophen detectable in serum. Four manifested minor liver injury (AST >80 but <1,000 IU/L) and two, including one with high-dose alcohol use, experienced severe liver injury (AST >1,000 IU/L). All were hospitalized, six received NAC, all recovered, and none underwent liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute intentional acetaminophen ingestion with delayed presentation (>=18 hours) and undetectable serum acetaminophen, or multiple intentional overdoses within a single day; one severe case was associated with chronic high-dose alcohol use; outcomes limited to a population-based sample of all hospitalized cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Median age 17-28 years, predominantly female. Minor liver injury defined as AST >80 but <1,000 IU/L; severe liver injury as AST >1,000 IU/L. Six of seven delayed-presentation patients treated with NAC (first dose 18-33 h post-ingestion); one presented at 96 h with serum AST 762 IU/L. Three of four multiple-overdose patients treated as inpatients with NAC (presentation acetaminophen 240, 123, 38 µg/mL); all recovered without transplantation; one chronic high-dose alcohol consumer had highest AST 150 IU/L. Population-based incidence of acute acetaminophen ingestion 21.4/100,000/yr (95% CI 17.7-25.2); hospitalization for acute toxicity 4.8/100,000/yr (95% CI 3.0-6.5); hospitalization for acute and chronic poisoning 5.5/100,000/yr (95% CI 4.1-7.0). Cases not amenable to Rumack-Matthew nomogram comprised 44% of those hospitalized.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state there is little doubt that paracetamol was the primary cause of the hepatic necrosis in this case, although a single dose of chlorpromazine given on the third day may have been responsible for precipitating hepatic coma. At least 5 cases of hepatic necrosis following paracetamol overdosage in man have been reported, 3 of them fatal; the dose here was 35 g (0.5 g/kg). In the comment they classify the lesion as a dose-related toxic lesion rather than a drug-induced idiosyncratic reaction. The patient died, and autopsy biopsy showed acute hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic necrosis following deliberate paracetamol overdosage (35 g, 0.5 g/kg).
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as a case report of a patient who took a paracetamol overdose and died on September 7. Liver weighed 1100 g and post-mortem biopsy showed acute hepatic necrosis with collapse of the reticulin pattern, complete centrilobular necrosis, fatty infiltration, hydropic change, cloudy swelling, and prominent cholestasis, with no cell regeneration. Authors note at least 5 reported cases of hepatic necrosis after paracetamol overdosage in man, 3 fatal; the lowest fatal dose recorded was 'at least 15 g' versus the rat lethal dose of 3.71 ± 0.80 g/kg. A single dose of chlorpromazine on the third day may have precipitated hepatic coma. Patient also had extreme hypokalemia (1.4 mEq/L), severe hyperglycemia, cardiac arrest, oliguric renal failure and acute tubular necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old physically healthy extreme-sportswoman with a history of an eating disorder ingested 20,000 mg of niacinamide (Niacinamid) on a single day, based on Internet research, to improve training performance and treat constipation. She developed clinically apparent abdominal pain and within 3 days acute liver failure (INR > 8.9, factor V < 5%, transaminases 12,000–14,000 U/L; negative hepatitis markers and liver immunology). She met King's College criteria, was listed for liver transplantation, and received a donor liver; the explant histology showed subtotal hepatocyte necrosis. The conclusion section attributes the acute toxic liver failure and transplantation need to the vitamin B3 (niacinamide) overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional supratherapeutic overdose of 20,000 mg niacinamide taken in a single day; patient had a history of an eating disorder and took the dose to improve athletic performance and treat constipation.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency: acute liver failure developed within 3 days of ingestion. Coagulopathy with INR > 8.9 and factor V < 5%; transaminases 12,000–14,000 U/L. Hepatitis markers and liver immunology negative. Met King's College criteria and was placed on the liver transplant list; underwent transplantation with graft from a 63-year-old donor, extubated 2 h postoperatively, discharged after 19 days. Explant histology showed subtotal hepatocyte necrosis. The conclusion notes that acute toxic liver failure with transplantation need from vitamin B3 overdose was already described for the sustained-release (retard) galenic form and is now shown for the pure form; good interdisciplinary management averted the lethal outcome.

raw_record.support_text: A 29-year-old male soldier presented with abdominal pain, vomiting, and sudden-onset jaundice. Initially diagnosed as ischemic liver damage, raised liver function tests and elevated prothrombin time led to detection of acetaminophen in blood and urine by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, and ultrasound evidence of hepatic necrosis gave the final diagnosis of acetaminophen poisoning causing drug-induced liver injury. The paper states acetaminophen hepatotoxicity can occur when the drug is misused or after an overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; single 29-year-old male patient case
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic effects over 150 mg/kg single dose result in liver failure; ~10% of APAP is oxidized by CYP2E1 to the reactive toxic metabolite NAPQI, which depletes glutathione, causes oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, and depletes ATP stores; toxic metabolite NAPQI identified as the mechanism, not an independently causal entity. Patient's peak lab values included total bilirubin 938 µmol/L (day 4), ALT 7046 U/L (day 1), AST 5035 U/L (day 2), PT 20 sec (day 4), serum ferritin 63433 ng/ml; blood acetaminophen 9874 ng/ml (day 1) declining to undetectable by day 4; HBsAg, anti-HCV, CMV-PCR, and liver kidney microsomal antibodies negative. Four sequential stages of paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity described; Rumack-Matthew nomogram used for management; aminotransferases may rise above 10,000 IU/L.
