raw_record.support_text: In a multivariate analysis of 645 cases of single-dose acetaminophen poisoning, the acetaminophen dose was a risk factor for hepatotoxicity, especially in nonalcoholic patients. Doses resulting in death ranged from 15 to 125 g, and 28 cases of severe hepatotoxicity (alanine transaminase level greater than 1,000 U/L) resulted from ingestion of a single dose of less than 12 g. Time to N-acetylcysteine was the most important risk factor for death, hepatic encephalopathy, and liver transplant, with mortality rising from 0.42% (time to NAC <12 h) to 19% (time to NAC >48 h).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-dose acetaminophen poisoning (overdose); prognostic factors analyzed in 645 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose of acetaminophen was a risk factor for hepatotoxicity, most importantly in nonalcoholic patients. Doses associated with death ranged from 15 to 125 g; 28 cases of severe hepatotoxicity (ALT >1,000 U/L) followed a single dose <12 g, 21 of them in regular alcohol abusers. Time to N-acetylcysteine was the dominant risk factor: mortality was 0.42% (95% CI 0.05-2.7) when time to NAC <12 h, rising to 6.1%, 13%, and 19% at >12, >24, and >48 h, with corresponding rates of hepatic encephalopathy of 1.3%, 12%, 25%, and 38%. Chronic alcohol abuse was an independent risk factor for HE (OR 4.21; 95% CI 2.42-7.32) and mortality (OR 3.52; 95% CI 1.78-6.97); acute alcohol ingestion was protective for HE (OR 0.40) and mortality (OR 0.12), mainly in chronic abusers. Age was a risk factor for HE and death/orthotopic liver transplantation. No sex-specific differences or effect of other drugs were found.

raw_record.support_text: In case 2, a 16-year-old adolescent admitted to having taken methandrostenolone 10 mg three times daily for five days before symptom onset. Laboratory tests showed bilirubin 441 µmol/l, ALT 156 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 203 IU/l, and INR 1.1. Extended liver screening and abdominal ultrasound identified no other cause of the jaundice, so the diagnosis of methandrostenolone-induced cholestasis was made clinically. The bilirubin peaked at 635 µmol/l on day 7, and liver biopsy confirmed cholestatic liver disease with a weak inflammatory component. The patient was treated with cholestyramine, chlorphenamine, ursodeoxycholic acid, rifampicin, and naltrexone, with full liver recovery over four months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 16-year-old adolescent; first anabolic-steroid use; bodybuilding-related abuse (supratherapeutic dosing of 10 mg three times daily for 5 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of methandrostenolone (methandienone)-induced cholestasis in a drug-naïve adolescent. Laboratory values at admission: bilirubin 441 µmol/l (peak 635 µmol/l on day 7), ALT 156 IU/l, ALP 203 IU/l, INR 1.1. Presenting symptoms: severe pruritus, nausea, abdominal discomfort, jaundice for ~3 weeks. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic liver disease with mild lymphocytic and macrophage infiltrate (cholestatic hepatitis). Treated with cholestyramine, chlorphenamine, ursodeoxycholic acid, rifampicin, and naltrexone; prolonged 15-day hospitalization due to therapy-refractory pruritus; anxiety and low mood during hospitalization; complete liver function recovery over four months; no other cause of jaundice identified.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of fulminant hepatitis which was due to repeated sniffing of methoxyflurane as a euphoriant. They reference that hepatitis following methoxyflurane anesthesia has been reported and that methoxyflurane was incriminated as the causative agent, with a hypersensitivity reaction implicated in its pathogenesis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Abuse-related exposure via repeated sniffing of methoxyflurane as a euphoriant; past history of heavy alcohol use but no alcohol consumed in the three years prior to admission.
raw_record.extra_details: 42-year-old black man, a veterinarian's assistant, admitted to Houston VA Hospital on March 7, 1975. Two weeks before admission he developed nausea, vomiting, and vague intermittent midabdominal pain with temperature of 101-102 F (38.3-38.9 C) and chills. He admitted sniffing methoxyflurane for the two months before admission, confirmed by his family and employer. Methoxyflurane (Penthrane) is a fluorinated agent sharing the basic chemical structure of halothane; a hypersensitivity reaction has been implicated in the pathogenesis of halothane- or methoxyflurane-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 27 DILI patients analyzed, the authors could only select a unique case of acute hepatic failure attributable to abusive consumption of acetaminophen (APAP) over time, in a 40-year-old male with several suicide attempts and no relevant comorbidities. At emergency admission he had low blood pressure (70/40), drowsiness, peripheral cyanosis, conjunctival icterus, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and altered aspartate aminotransferase (AST > 4,600 U/L), creatinine (4.6 mg/dL), and leukocytosis; serum APAP measured at admission (>4 h post ingestion) was 220 µg/mL, indicating possible liver toxicity by the Rumack-Matthew monogram, and he was treated with N-acetylcysteine. Post-mortem liver analysis (2 days after emergency admission) showed extensive necrosis, congestion, infiltration, hemorrhage and ischemia, all compatible with a hepatotoxic etiology.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Abusive consumption of acetaminophen over time in a 40-year-old male with a history of several suicide attempts; overdose setting; no pre-existing relevant comorbidities reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Single acute liver failure case among a retrospectively selected cohort of 27 DILI patients. At admission: blood pressure 70/40, drowsiness, peripheral cyanosis, conjunctival icterus, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, AST > 4,600 U/L, creatinine 4.6 mg/dL, leukocytosis; serum APAP 220 µg/mL measured >4 h post ingestion, indicating possible liver toxicity per the Rumack-Matthew monogram. Treated with N-acetylcysteine. Patient died; post-mortem liver analysis (2 days after admission) showed extensive necrosis, congestion, infiltration, hemorrhage and ischemia.

raw_record.support_text: A 26-year-old man who habitually sniffed halothane to obtain a 'high' presented with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and anorexia, with deeply icteric skin, a tender enlarged liver, and markedly elevated SGOT (up to 1250 mU/ml), bilirubin (up to 34.5 mg/100 ml), AP, and LDH. A liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis, and he recovered over an uneventful hospital course. The paper reports this as an unusual manner of exposure to halothane in which the patient positively identified halothane by smell, attributing his acute hepatitis to weekly halothane inhalation abuse.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Abusive exposure by deliberate inhalation/sniffing to obtain a 'high' (unusual route, not standard anesthetic administration); single case report; possible confounding by prior thioridazine treatment (25 mg TID for 2 weeks, 6 weeks before admission).
raw_record.extra_details: 26-year-old male prison inmate; sniffed a volatile liquid weekly for 8 weeks before admission, continuing until 3 weeks before admission when he briefly lost consciousness after prolonged inhalation; positively identified halothane by smell and obtained it from an operating-room-contact friend. Symptoms (nausea, vomiting, jaundice, anorexia, light-colored stools, tea-colored urine) of ~1 month. Liver tender, 3 cm below right costal margin, span 13 cm. Peak SGOT 1250 mU/ml, bilirubin 34.5 mg/100 ml, AP up to 140 mU/ml, prothrombin time up to 19/11 sec. Heterophil, hepatitis-associated antigen, alpha-fetoglobulin, cultures and chest X ray negative; eosinophils 3%. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis; uneventful recovery and discharge.

raw_record.support_text: Outcomes of paracetamol overdose are reported from numerous countries. Paracetamol has been the main cause of DILI in the United States and England, and contributes roughly 10% of acute liver failure cases in European countries such as Portugal and Germany per the European Liver Transplant Registry. A study from Australia reported over 440 deaths from paracetamol in combination with codeine from accidental overdose, with roughly 25% also involving other sedating medications.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental and intentional overdose settings; some cases involved co-ingestion of codeine or other sedating medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Outcome data across countries, including Australia (440+ deaths from paracetamol with codeine, 25% with other sedating drugs such as antihistamines; 8.8% death in ALF cases, 39 deaths total), UK (2163 cases, 65% of total ALF; 36% deaths, 778 total; 147 transplants), US (120 cases, 39% of ALF; 27% mortality, 6% transplant, 44/120 suicide attempts), Portugal (5 cases/3yr, 11% of ALF; 1 transplant), Germany (10 cases, 9.2% of ALF; 3 transplants, 1 death). Mechanism thought to be glutathione depletion with buildup of harmful metabolites; mortality ~30% without liver transplantation; 5-year survival >70% after transplant.

raw_record.support_text: A 47-year-old man died from fatal massive peripheral zonal hepatic necrosis after accidentally ingesting a solution of methyl ethyl ketone peroxide (MEKP) in dimethyl phthalate (about 10% active oxygen). His course included temporary cardiac arrest, abdominal burns, severe metabolic acidosis, rapid hepatic failure, rhabdomyolysis and respiratory insufficiency, ending in death 4 days later from hepatic coma with blood coagulation disorders. Microscopy showed massive periportal hepatic necrosis with atypical pseudoductular proliferation; the suggested mechanism involves lipid peroxidation by free oxygen radicals derived from MEKP.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental ingestion while excessively inebriated, with co-exposure to alcohol during a fishing trip.
raw_record.extra_details: Ingested 50-100 ml of polymer-curing peroxide solution (MEKP in dimethyl phthalate) stored in a rum bottle; solution contains about 10% active oxygen. Course: cardiac arrest with successful resuscitation, metabolic acidosis (pH 6.86, base excess 28 mmol l-1), anuria, hepatic coma, fatal outcome 4 days later with blood coagulation disorders. Histology: massive periportal hepatic necrosis with atypical pseudoductular proliferation, probably bile-duct origin with atypia and mitoses. Suggested mechanism: lipid peroxidation by free oxygen radicals derived from MEKP. Report notes eight prior human cases of accidental or suicidal MEKP ingestion, with no prior reports of severe liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old man with a history of alcoholic liver disease and renal insufficiency mistakenly ingested Colchicum autumnale (autumn crocus) instead of wild garlic. After a 12-hour latency he developed nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, then somnolence, respiratory failure and cardiac deterioration. Laboratory tests revealed rhabdomyolysis, coagulopathy, and deterioration of renal and hepatic function. Toxicological analysis disclosed colchicine in urine (6 μg/l) and serum (9 μg/l) on day 2. The patient died on day 3 of asystolic cardiac arrest.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental off-label ingestion of Colchicum autumnale plant mistaken for wild garlic (supratherapeutic colchicine exposure); pre-existing alcoholic liver disease and renal insufficiency; 76-year-old patient; pneumonia as complicating infection.
raw_record.extra_details: Colchicine is an antimitotic alkaloid that blocks mitosis by preventing DNA synthesis and tubulin polymerization. Poisoning follows a latent period of 4-12 h with a second intoxication stage (24-72 h) that includes hepatic injury together with heart failure, arrhythmias, renal failure, respiratory distress, coagulopathy, bone marrow depression and neuromuscular involvement. Toxicology confirmed colchicine 6 μg/l in urine and 9 μg/l in serum on day 2. The patient died on day 3 of asystolic cardiac arrest (cardiovascular collapse), not from liver failure; phase 3 features leukocytosis and alopecia.

raw_record.support_text: A 71-year-old woman ingested a plant she thought was wild garlic (Allium ursinum) but which was actually Colchicum autumnale (autumn crocus). Toxicology analysis confirmed colchicine in gastric lavage, blood (5 µg/l) and urine (30 µg/l). She developed arrhythmias, liver failure, pancreatitis, ileus, and bone marrow suppression with pancytopenia, plus alopecia in the third week; treatment was supportive and five months later she had no clinical or laboratory signs of poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental oral overdose/poisoning from ingestion of Colchicum autumnale (autumn crocus) mistaken for wild garlic; 71-year-old woman; plant-source colchicine exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Colchicine binds tubulin and blocks mitosis (antimitotic), primarily affecting tissues with rapid cell turnover, producing gastroenterocolitis, bone marrow hypoplasia with pancytopenia, and alopecia; toxicity in tissues without rapid cell turnover caused arrhythmias, acute liver failure and pancreatitis. Blood colchicine 5 µg/l and urine 30 µg/l by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Managed with gastric lavage, oral activated charcoal and saline infusion; supportive care only. Patient recovered without clinical or laboratory signs five months later.

raw_record.support_text: The study used high-throughput sequencing to evaluate global profiles of circulating miRNAs in the serum of human subjects with an accidental overdose of acetaminophen (APAP). Thirty-six miRNAs were identified, including three novel miRNA-like snRNAs significantly enriched in the serum of APAP-overdosed patients that returned to baseline levels after treatment with NAC. Most serum miRNA profiles correlated with standard and emerging leakage biomarkers of liver injury (ALT, AST, MDH, GLDH) monitoring hepatocyte damage, and the paper frames DILI as a frequent cause of acute liver failure, confirming accidental APAP overdose as causing drug-induced liver injury in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental overdose (APAP poisoning); subjects treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC).
raw_record.extra_details: Serum from 24 APAP-overdosed patients studied. DILI framed in the paper as a primary cause of drug failures and up to half of acute liver failure cases. miRNA profiles correlated with ALT, AST, MDH, and GLDH (hepatocyte damage markers) and 8 miRNAs correlated with TBIL; novel miRNA-like snRNAs returned to baseline after NAC treatment.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old woman being treated for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia received a high-dose course of methotrexate (MTX) infused intravenously in less than 2 h instead of 24 h because the patient accidentally increased the infusion rate, constituting a high-dose MTX intoxication. In the aftermath, her alanine aminotransferase rose to 114 UI/L (~5x upper limit of normal) at h48 and her total bilirubin rose to 104 µmol/L by J4, alongside nausea/vomiting, oliguria, rising creatinine (up to 398 µmol/L), and pancytopenia; hemofiltration was started at J5. The paper frames this as an accidental high-dose MTX intoxication rather than explicitly labeling the hepatic abnormalities as hepatotoxicity or DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental overdose resulting from shortening of a 24 h intravenous infusion to less than 2 h (increase of infusion rate by the patient); single case in a 53-year-old woman with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia; co-administered tienam, amikacine, purinéthol, and folinic acid rescue.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of high-dose methotrexate intoxication. ALT 114 UI/L (~5x ULN) at h48, ~1.5x at J3, 24 UI at J4; total bilirubin 41 µmol/L at J3 and 104 µmol/L at J4 (ULN <17 µmol/L); methotrexate levels 99, 89, and 93 µmol/L at h48/J3/J4; creatinine rose from 65 to 398 µmol/L; oliguria; pancytopenia (platelets 42 G/L, hemoglobin 73 g/L, leukocytes 0.8 G/L); hemofiltration initiated at J5; folinic acid rescue increased to 50 then 200 mg/m²/6h. The paper describes the event as MTX intoxication with renal, marrow, mucocutaneous and digestive toxicity; it does not explicitly discuss the liver enzyme/bilirubin elevations as hepatotoxicity or DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A previously well 3-year-old (15.4 kg) girl accidentally ingested up to 150 mL of 24 mg/mL liquid paracetamol (3.6 g, 240 mg/kg), about 1 h before presenting. Four-hour paracetamol concentration was 105 mg/L (below nomogram threshold), but ALT rose from 52 U/L (4 h) to 219 U/L (17 h), peaking at 1393 U/L 5 days post-ingestion; INR peaked at 1.5. Intravenous acetylcysteine was started at 25 h, continued for 64 h, and she recovered uneventfully. CYP metabolites accounted for 11% of total metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that although the liver is well established as the primary site of toxicity after acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, strong clinical evidence also indicates APAP overdose can be nephrotoxic. In the context of overdose, the text notes that acute liver failure after APAP overdose can progress to multi-organ failure if the patient does not spontaneously recover or receive a liver transplant, and reports that data from 375 definitive APAP overdose patients indicate kidney dysfunction after APAP overdose strongly correlates with severe liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Discussed as dose-related direct toxicity initiated by CYP2E1-catalyzed generation of the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which forms protein adducts. Acute liver failure after APAP overdose can progress to multi-organ failure if the patient does not recover or receive a liver transplant. Data from 375 definitive APAP overdose patients show kidney dysfunction strongly correlates with severe liver injury; creatinine (kidney function) is included in the MELD score used for liver transplant decisions.

raw_record.support_text: In this acute liver failure (ALF) registry cohort (1998-2013, n = 2070), 955 patients were classified as having APAP (acetaminophen) toxicity, and approximately 90% of APAP-overdose patients received intravenous or oral N-acetylcysteine. The cohort represents APAP overdose as a cause of acute liver failure, with outcomes at 21 days including liver transplantation and transplant-free survival.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose; ALF registry/cohort population.
raw_record.extra_details: 955 patients with APAP toxicity in an ALF registry cohort (1998-2013; n=2070). Approximately 90% of APAP-overdose patients received N-acetylcysteine (88.7% early 1998-2005 vs 91.7% later 2006-2013; P=0.117). Outcomes at 21 d included liver transplantation (461/2070 received transplant), overall survival 1478/2070 (71.4%), and transplant-free survival 1054/2070 (50.9%). N-acetylcysteine is an antidote, not the causal agent.

The remaining 27 patients (meeting inclusion criteria) were divided into short-, intermediate-, and long-course NAC treatment groups, and hepatotoxicity, defined as a serum aminotransferase (AST or ALT) concentration >1000 IU/L, was the primary outcome measure.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity outcome was defined as serum AST or ALT >1000 IU/L. Study comprised 27 patients grouped by NAC therapy duration: short-course (<=36 h, n=17), intermediate-course (37-72 h, n=4), and long-course (>=73 h, n=6). Comparisons were made with historical controls receiving fixed-duration oral NAC for 72 h or intravenous NAC for 20 h. 2 NAC-noncompliant patients recovered; 41 patients with APAP below risk threshold developed no hepatotoxicity. No statistical analysis was performed due to small sample size.

The report describes two patients who each allegedly ingested greater than 13 gm of acetaminophen (APAP), in whom serial plasma concentrations and half-life were obtained by colorimetric and HPLC methods.

raw_record.extra_details: Plasma APAP half-life of elimination is presented as a prognostic indicator of potential hepatic toxicity; a half-life greater than 4 hr is often associated with liver injury. Serial plasma concentrations were measured by a colorimetric (nitrous acid chromophore; Glynn and Kendal) method and HPLC; the colorimetric method overestimates drug concentration below about 50-100 µg/ml, producing falsely prolonged half-lives. The purpose of the report is assay-method comparison rather than establishing the hepatotoxicity itself.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is a common complication following acetaminophen overdose and can lead to acute liver failure (ALF), noting that acetaminophen is one of the most common causes of ALF in the USA and UK. It reports that without treatment acetaminophen overdose leads to 0.4% mortality and that at least half of people with a blood acetaminophen level above the UK standard treatment line manifest with severe liver damage, with cerebral edema a major cause of death.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity described as a common consequence of acetaminophen overdose that may lead to acute liver failure. 64 acetaminophen-overdose patients (age 15-85, all male) studied. Prothrombin time is noted to show the severity of hepatic necrosis; PT rose from 13.9±0.36 s (admission, range 11-21) to 15.7±1.1 s (48 h). Severe liver damage documented in at least half of patients with blood acetaminophen above the UK treatment line; hepatotoxicity accounts for 42% of US acute liver failure cases at tertiary-care centers and one-third of deaths; without treatment mortality is 0.4%; cerebral edema is a major cause of death.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose causing fatal acute liver failure in two reported cases. Case 236: serum acetaminophen 24 µg/mL; AST and ALT both >3,000 U/L on admission, peaking near 6,000 U/L on the third hospital day; INR, bilirubin, and ammonia rose steadily despite lactulose and vitamin K; treated with activated charcoal, N-acetylcysteine, and ventilation; care withdrawn and patient died on the sixth hospital day. Case 237: ~250 tablets ingested ~48 h before presentation; serum acetaminophen 266 µg/mL, AST 577 U/L, ALT 594 U/L, bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, INR 4.7, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, platelets 87,000/µL; IV N-acetylcysteine initiated but discontinued when hypotension developed; transaminases peaked >4,500 U/L on the third hospital day; coagulopathy treated with phytonadione and fresh frozen plasma; patient died on the eighth day of hospitalization. The other cases in this window (brodifacoum rodentside, Conium maculatum/poison hemlock) caused coagulopathy or neurotoxicity but no attributed human liver injury and were not extracted.

raw_record.support_text: In 2540 patients treated with oral N-acetylcysteine after acetaminophen overdose, hepatotoxicity developed in 6.1% of patients at probable risk when antidote therapy was started within 10 hours of ingestion and in 26.4% when begun 10 to 24 hours after ingestion; among high-risk patients treated 16 to 24 hours after overdose, hepatotoxicity developed in 41%. Four records noted 11 deaths among the 2540 patients, with elevated aminotransferase values before N-acetylcysteine treatment in the nine fatal cases where measured.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose (suspected poisoning context, ingestions reported among 11,195 suspected overdose cases); all patients received oral N-acetylcysteine antidote treatment with a 140 mg/kg loading dose followed by 70 mg/kg every four hours for 17 additional doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity rates of 6.1%, 26.4%, and 41% depending on the interval (≤10 h, 10-24 h, and 16-24 h) between overdose and N-acetylcysteine start; 11 deaths (0.43%) among 2540 patients; aminotransferase values were elevated before N-acetylcysteine in nine fatal cases; no deaths clearly caused by acetaminophen among patients treated within 16 hours. N-acetylcysteine was protective when given within 8 hours regardless of initial plasma acetaminophen concentration.

raw_record.extra_details: Prospective Danish study (Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen). Hepatotoxicity defined as maximum ALT >1000 U/L without acute liver failure; hepatic encephalopathy/acute liver failure treated in a specialized liver intensive care unit. Study aimed to determine whether a half-life cutoff of 4 hours still predicts hepatotoxicity in N-acetylcysteine-treated patients. Earlier Prescott et al study (30 patients, pre-N-acetylcysteine era) found half-life >4 hours predicted significant hepatotoxicity, though hepatotoxicity was not clearly defined there.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with severe acetaminophen-associated acute liver failure (AALF) who fulfilled King's College criteria for liver transplantation yet recovered native liver function after bridging support with single-pass albumin dialysis (SPAD). The AALF was attributed to acetaminophen, consistent with an overdose setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose setting (AALF); patient fulfilled King's College criteria for liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Hyperacute liver failure with encephalopathy prior to seven days of jaundice, extensive hepatocellular necrosis, early clinical signs of cerebral edema, and multi-organ (including renal) involvement; patient met transplant criteria yet showed rapid hemodynamic improvements after SPAD initiation and recovered native liver function; bilirubin peaked at 538 mmol/L on day 35 then fell below 100 mmol/L; INR 1.9 and synthetic liver function improved by ICU discharge, normalizing later (INR 1.1, albumin 35 g/L). Paragraph 29 also cites a controlled trial by Schmidt et al of 13 patients with ALF due to acetaminophen or hepatitis B treated with MARS or mechanical cooling, showing early hemodynamic benefits but no survival advantage.

raw_record.support_text: The paper opens by stating established knowledge that a nomogram has been used for decades to predict acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, noting that this nomogram has not been validated in common scenarios such as chronic overdose or when the time from ingestion is unknown. In a prospective cohort of 117 acetaminophen-poisoned patients receiving N-acetylcysteine, plasma procalcitonin on admission was associated with liver injury and its rise preceded alanine aminotransferase elevation, highlighting the need for better biomarkers to identify patients at higher or lower risk of acetaminophen-related acute liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose/poisoning patients; patients received N-acetylcysteine treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury labeled LI, with acute liver injury (ALI) as outcome; 117 prospective patients in a toxicological ICU cohort (2012-2017). Plasma procalcitonin (PCT) on admission predicted liver injury with excellent accuracy and negative predictive value, and its rise preceded alanine aminotransferase rise by a median of 33 h. Other candidate biomarkers mentioned: acetaminophen protein adducts, miR-122, HMGB1, keratin 18, GLDH. Predictive nomogram covers time-from-ingestion and dose scenarios.

raw_record.support_text: This trial enrolled 60 patients (mean age 25.2 ± 7.3 years) hospitalized for acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning, who were treated with N-acetylcysteine alone or combined with cimetidine. Liver toxicity manifested as elevated serum aminotransferases, and the study states that 'the toxicity of the liver was treated successfully in all patients'; serum acetaminophen reached zero at 48 hours. At 12 hours, mean AST was significantly higher in the NAC-only group (110.0 ± 30.1 IU/L) than in the NAC plus cimetidine group (94.93 ± 26.38 IU/L; p = 0.044), with no significant differences in ALT between groups.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen poisoning (overdose) requiring hospital treatment; all patients treated with N-acetylcysteine, either alone or combined with cimetidine before or during admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Comparator trial of NAC alone vs NAC plus cimetidine in 60 patients (32 female, 28 male). Liver toxicity treated successfully in all patients; no deaths and no side effects reported. Mean AST at 12 h was 110.0 ± 30.1 IU/L (NAC) vs 94.93 ± 26.38 IU/L (NAC + cimetidine), p = 0.044. ALT showed no significant intergroup differences. Symptoms included loss of appetite (67%, 40/60), abdominal pain (9 patients), abdominal discomfort (12 patients), and pruritus (3 patients). Hospitalization averaged 1.2 ± 2.1 vs 1.4 ± 2.3 days (p = 0.523).

raw_record.support_text: In 107 acetaminophen-poisoned patients, all who developed hepatotoxicity (elevated transaminases) recovered and none developed hepatic encephalopathy; the study compared standard N-acetylcysteine therapy with N-acetylcysteine plus cimetidine, and found no statistically significant difference in mean peak transaminase levels, AST category distributions, or bilirubin between the cimetidine and control groups. One patient in the cimetidine group died from esophageal carcinoma 2 weeks after recovering, not from liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen poisoning (overdose) treated with N-acetylcysteine, with or without cimetidine co-administration.
raw_record.extra_details: All 107 poisoned patients who developed hepatotoxicity recovered; none developed hepatic encephalopathy. Peak AST up to 11,925 IU/L and AST >1000 IU/L occurred in 22% (NAC only) and 20% (NAC + cimetidine) of 105 analyzed patients; mean peak AST 1,259 ± 330 vs 1,301 ± 451 IU/L (p=0.94), mean peak ALT 1,724 ± 452 vs 1,212 ± 435 IU/L (p=0.42), mean total bilirubin 1.38 ± 0.19 vs 1.33 ± 0.25 mg/dL (p=0.86). Adding 300 mg IV cimetidine every 6 h throughout NAC treatment did not alter hepatotoxicity. One death was due to esophageal carcinoma, occurring 2 weeks after recovering from the acetaminophen ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of 677 acetaminophen poisoning cases, 511 were without opioid co-ingestion (mean acetaminophen concentration 74 µg/L, 72% intentional self-harm, 2% multiple acetaminophen products). Severe liver injury occurred in this group, with cases meeting King's College Criteria (3.1%), peak AST >1000 U/L (8.4%), two cases requiring liver transplant, and mortality of 0.5%. The paper frames these as acetaminophen poisoning cases with hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen poisoning/overdose setting without opioid co-ingestion; some patients used multiple acetaminophen products; 62-72% intentional self-harm.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort over 18 months at >40 urban hospitals affiliated with one PCC; primary outcome mortality; secondary outcomes transaminases >1000 U/L and positive King's College Criteria. Two of the four total liver transplants occurred in this non-opioid group; mortality 0.5%; KCC 3.1%; peak AST >1000 U/L 8.4%.

raw_record.support_text: At Prince of Wales Hospital, ~240 patients with acetaminophen poisoning required hospitalization during 1994–1996 in Hong Kong, and patients with fulminant hepatic failure were expected to be managed at a liver transplant center. The annual incidence of acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure was calculated at less than 0.03/100,000 in Hong Kong.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective study of acetaminophen poisoning, the authors report that an increase in episodes of vomiting at first presentation appears to be an important risk marker of subsequent nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity. Patients with a higher frequency of vomiting episodes after acetaminophen poisoning tended to have a worse general condition, and more vomiting episodes were associated with prolonged prothrombin time, elevated serum creatinine, reduced serum potassium, and elevated serum bilirubin.

raw_record.support_text: In this Acute Liver Failure Study Group cohort of 1564 ALF patients not listed for liver transplantation, acetaminophen (APAP) was a predominant etiology of acute liver failure, accounting for 635 of 1006 patients alive at day 21 (63.1%) and 208 of 558 deceased patients (37.3%); overdose intent was recorded (suicide attempt vs. unintentional) among these APAP patients. DILI was listed as a separate etiology category (71/1006 alive, 59/558 deceased).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen-related ALF in patients not listed for liver transplantation; overdose exposure (suicide attempt or unintentional) is the recorded setting.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP was the most common etiology in this ALF cohort. In multivariable analysis APAP etiology was independently associated with reduced 21-day mortality (aOR 0.58 [95% CI 0.38–0.87], p=0.009; univariate OR 0.35 [95% CI 0.28–0.43]). Cases of ALF with APAP: 635 alive vs 208 deceased at day 21 among nonlisted patients. Nonlisted patients had higher APAP etiology rates than listed patients (53.9% vs 29.1%, p<0.001); 'not sick enough' nonlisted survivors had higher APAP rates than nonsurvivors (64.7% vs 35.3%, p=0.014).

raw_record.support_text: In patients diagnosed with acute hydrogen cyanamide (Dormex) intoxication at Tanta Poison Control Center, laboratory investigations associated with unfavorable outcomes included significant elevation of liver enzymes (SGOT, SGPT), serum bilirubin, and serum creatinine, and prolonged prothrombin time. The association between elevated liver transaminases, prolonged PT, and liver impairment was described, and the changes in pathological hepatic involvement were applied to Dormex-induced hepatotoxicity. Contributing hepatotoxicity mechanisms cited were cellular lysis with release of transaminases, impaired hepatic synthesis of coagulation factors, and prolonged PT.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute accidental/intentional poisoning (Dormex intoxication) cases presenting to a poison control center, with multiorgan/systemic involvement; hepatic impairment was part of overall poisoning severity and outcome assessment in 35 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver enzyme elevation (SGOT up to 1575 U/L, SGPT up to 2480 U/L in the unfavorable-outcome subgroup), elevated total/direct/indirect bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time/INR were significantly associated with unfavorable outcomes; prolonged PT and impaired coagulation-factor synthesis linked to liver impairment. The obstruction of bile flow and acute drug-induced cholestasis were also suggested mechanisms (Zimmerman 1999). Dormex is a commercial form of hydrogen cyanamide used as a plant growth regulator.

raw_record.support_text: The study addresses patients with an acute acetaminophen overdose who are at greatest risk of having severe hepatotoxicity, recommending observation for at least 48 hours postingestion and NAC therapy to identify and treat patients at risk of severe acetaminophen-related liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute acetaminophen overdose (supratherapeutic ingestion)
raw_record.extra_details: 9 patients in the current report developed severe hepatotoxicity; most showed early evidence, but in some cases AST/ALT elevations appeared only after 24 hours (in the current report one of 9 had no elevation and 2 had minor elevations, AST/ALT <100 IU/L). Study supports shortened NAC courses (until 48 hours postingestion) in select patients depending on PT, AST, and ALT changes. raw_record.support_text: The risk of hepatotoxicity in nonalcoholic and abstinent alcoholic patients after an acute acetaminophen overdose was modeled at the 150 µg/ml at 4 h (37.5 µg/ml at 12 h) line, corresponding to the possible hepatotoxicity line on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, representing a 1.6% risk of hepatotoxicity at or below this line for non-alcoholic patients and a 10.7% risk for abstinent alcoholics. A lower 104 µg/ml at 4 h line equates to a 1.6% risk in abstinent alcoholics.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute acetaminophen overdose in patients with a history of chronic alcoholism (abstinent alcoholics), with a proposed lower treatment decision line for this population; the reported case was not treated with NAC.
raw_record.extra_details: Modeled risk: 150 µg/ml at 4 h (37.5 µg/ml at 12 h) line gives 1.6% hepatotoxicity risk for nonalcoholics and 10.7% for abstinent alcoholics; an equivalent 1.6% risk in abstinent alcoholics occurs at 104 µg/ml at 4 h (26 µg/ml at 12 h), and a proposed line of 100 µg/ml at 4 h (25 µg/ml at 12 h) equates to a 1.1% risk in abstinent alcoholics. Cheung et al. (1994) reported a 21-year-old female with chronic alcohol ingestion who overdosed on acetaminophen, with a serum acetaminophen level of 151 µg/ml at 3 h and 124 µg/ml at 4 h postingestion, was not treated with NAC, and subsequently developed fulminant hepatic failure. The FDA in 1998 mandated a public warning of acetaminophen risk with chronic alcohol use.

raw_record.support_text: In acute APAP (acetaminophen) poisonings, the CYP metabolite ratio APAP-Cys/APAP-Sul detects patients at risk of developing subsequent acute liver injury (defined as an increased serum ALT activity of 50% or more), with an AUC-ROC of 0.91 (0.83-0.98). The authors confirm this association for hepatotoxicity with a similarly high AUC-ROC, and note that a combination of traditional liver biomarkers, APAP body load, and APAP metabolites performs even better for predicting acute liver injury. The study reports that the number of patients with hepatotoxicity and fulminant hepatic failure was low, and further studies are needed to determine if metabolites aid in predicting outcomes such as liver transplant or death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute APAP (acetaminophen) overdose (poisoning) setting, the studied exposure context.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver injury defined as an increase in serum ALT activity of 50% or more. The CYP-pathway metabolite ratio APAP-Cys/APAP-Sul (reflecting glutathione depletion, CYP metabolism, and sulfation balance) predicted subsequent acute liver injury with AUC-ROC 0.91 (0.83-0.98); a combination of traditional liver biomarkers, APAP body load (APAP ratio), and APAP metabolites predicted acute liver injury even better. Some patients received early acetylcysteine before the 4-hour APAP concentration, and acetylcysteine treatment may increase sulfation and/or CYP metabolites, though results remained similar when those patients were excluded. Fulminant hepatic failure and hepatotoxicity cases were few; further studies are needed to validate whether metabolites aid prediction of liver transplant or death. Fomepizole is noted as a newly proposed adjuvant to acetylcysteine.; confidence: 0.0

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) is commonly taken in overdose and can cause acute liver injury via its toxic metabolite NAPQI formed by the cytochrome P450 pathway. In this Australian prospective observational (ATOM) study of 200 patients following acute APAP ingestion, 26 developed hepatotoxicity (peak ALT > 1,000 U/L) defined as the primary outcome; those who developed hepatotoxicity had higher CYP-metabolite concentrations on presentation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute APAP overdose (deliberate self-poisoning or accidental overdose); the paper notes APAP is safe at recommended doses in healthy individuals.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury occurs via the toxic metabolite NAPQI formed by CYP P450 2E1 and 3A4; in overdose glutathione becomes depleted and NAPQI binds to cellular sulfhydryl proteins, causing oxidative stress, mitochondrial injury, hepatocyte necrosis, and acute liver failure. APAP toxicity is described as a leading cause of acute liver failure in North America, Europe and Australia. Study details: median ingested dose 20 g; 191/200 patients received acetylcysteine at median 5.8 h post-ingestion; 26 patients developed hepatotoxicity. Hepatotoxicity patients had higher total CYP metabolite concentrations (36.8 vs 10.8 μmol/L), higher CYP-metabolite proportion (5.4% vs 1.7%, P<0.001), lower APAP-Sul concentration (49.1 vs 78.7 μmol/L) and lower APAP-Sul percentage (6.3% vs 13.1%). APAP-Cys and APAP-Mer (NAPQI conjugates) were measured as metabolites; NAPQI protein adducts quantified as APAP-Cys. Metabolites proposed for early identification of high-risk patients for possible adjunct therapy (e.g., fomepizole).

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of acute acetaminophen (APAP) overdose patients above the Rumack-Matthew nomogram treatment threshold, the incidence of hepatotoxicity and coagulopathy were uncommon when at least 5 h (200 mg/kg) but less than 21 h (300 mg/kg) of intravenous N-acetylcysteine was administered. Hepatotoxicity was defined as AST or ALT >1,000 IU/L, and hepatic injury as AST or ALT >100 IU/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute APAP overdose above the Rumack-Matthew nomogram treatment threshold (~150 µg/mL at 4 h); patients received a shortened i.v. NAC course (at least 5 h/200 mg/kg but less than 21 h/300 mg/kg).
raw_record.extra_details: Descriptive analysis of a large, multi-center dataset of acute APAP overdose patients who discontinued i.v. NAC before completing the full 21-h course. Hepatotoxicity defined as AST or ALT >1,000 IU/L; hepatic injury defined as AST or ALT >100 IU/L; low incidence of severe hepatotoxicity and coagulopathy. Anaphylactoid reactions were a likely common reason for NAC discontinuation. Patients with low pretreatment exposure psi (ψ) <5 mmol/L-h or an APAP x aminotransferase product <10,000 µmol/L-IU/L had low risk of hepatic insult. Findings not intended to identify a threshold for withholding treatment or recommending shorter NAC regimens.

Paper proposes a new composite predictor (serum APAP x aminotransferase product) for hepatotoxicity risk, applicable even when the Rumack-Matthew nomogram cannot be used. Data derive from the CAOS study cohort.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 77 patients with acute acetaminophen (APAP) overdose treated with IV N-acetylcysteine, hepatotoxicity occurred in 4 of 77 patients (5.19%; 95% CI = 0.24% to 10.14%), translating to 9.76% of the 41 patients with initial plasma APAP on or above the 200 mg/L nomogram line. Poor outcomes occurred in 2 of these 4 patients: hepatic transplantation in 1 patient and death in the other.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute APAP overdose setting; often ingested as combination products (APAP/diphenhydramine, APAP/hydrocodone, APAP/doxylamine), with some coingestants (ethanol, escitalopram, zolpidem); patients received IV NAC.
raw_record.extra_details: Median maximum plasma APAP was 195 mg/L (range 88-697 mg/L). 41 patients had max concentrations on or above the 200 mg/L nomogram line; 36 between the two lines. Time to IV NAC initiation 1-8 h (median 6 h). Standard 21-hour IV NAC sufficed in 70/77 (90.9%); 7 required prolonged IV NAC (>21 h) due to elevated plasma APAP, AST, ALT, or both at 21 h, with factors associated being older age, higher max APAP, and APAP-combination product ingestion. Two patients (Patients 1 and 2) had poor outcomes: one hepatic transplantation (T), one death (D); max ALT up to 15450 IU/L, max INR 14, hepatic encephalopathy present in both.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of acute acetaminophen (APAP) ingestions, the authors state that there are data showing some patients whose APAP concentrations plot below the Rumack-Matthew nomogram do go on to develop hepatotoxicity. The paper evaluates whether an early APAP concentration below 100 µg/mL drawn 1-4 hours after ingestion has adequate negative predictive value to exclude subsequent toxic concentrations and the need for treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute APAP overdose/ingestion setting; need for N-acetylcysteine therapy when concentrations plot above the nomogram.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of early APAP concentrations (<100 µg/mL drawn 1-4 h after ingestion) for predicting later toxic concentrations; NPV overall 98.8% (95% CI 93.5-99.8), with ≤ 100% NPV for the 2-4 h subgroup. Two patients with initial concentrations <100 µg/mL (54 µg/mL at 90 min; 38 µg/mL at 84 min) later rose above the nomogram line (240 µg/mL at 300 min; 193 µg/mL at 227 min); both received IV N-acetylcysteine and had no transaminase elevation or hepatic dysfunction. Recalculation of Douglas et al. data gave a 1-4 h NPV of 94.6% (95% CI 91.3-96.7).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in acute acetaminophen (APAP) poisoning, it is necessary to predict the onset of liver injury (肝障害) and to administer N-acetylcysteine (NAC) early. It further notes that prior evaluation of their own facility's cases showed the need for patients to receive NAC to prevent liver injury from worsening, framing APAP overdose as causing liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute APAP poisoning overdose setting; NAC administration is the evaluated intervention and its own (non-hepatic) side effects are explicitly not the focus.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 25 acute APAP-poisoning patients (3 excluded for unknown time since ingestion or estimated dose) compared serum APAP quantification by Acetaminophen Detection Kit® versus HPLC for the decision to administer NAC. In 23/25 patients both methods agreed (both above or both below the NAC administration line); in 2 patients the values straddled the line, giving different NAC decisions. The NAC administration decision was concordant in 23/25 cases, with the 2 discrepant values near the NAC line, considered practically likely to lead to NAC administration in emergency over-triage. The paper notes possible prior cases where patients needing NAC might not have received it, risking severe liver injury. Acetylcysteine (NAC) itself is described as causing mainly nausea/gastrointestinal side effects, not liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The study characterizes the time course of serum aminotransferase (AT) rise in patients after acute acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, describing hepatotoxicity as AT exceeding 1,000 IU/L, severe coagulation disturbances (INR), and an early leak from severely injured zone 3 hepatocytes. Nearly all patients developed elevated AT within 12–24 h after acute APAP ingestion, and two-thirds of cases destined to reach 1,000 IU/L did so within 48 h.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute drug overdose; patients treated with antidotal acetylcysteine; population recruited from regional tertiary care and referral hospitals.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as serum AT > 1,000 IU/L; initially abnormal AT doubled roughly every 8 h in patients who met the threshold within 48 h and developed severe coagulation disturbances; AT peak height not predictive of encephalopathy or death; early rise attributed to leak from severely injured zone 3 hepatocytes plus a later healing/turnover spike; all study patients were above the Rumack–Matthew nomogram treatment line and received antidote (20-h Prescott protocol); severe coagulopathy unlikely when serum AT is relatively low after 12 h of acetylcysteine therapy; INR, international normalized ratio; AT/aminotransferase is AST/ALT.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports acute iron toxicity with hepatotoxicity. It states that hepatotoxicity caused by acute iron poisoning is associated with a high mortality rate, and describes a case of severe hepatic injury in an adult who overdosed on iron tablets with suicidal intent. Peak serum iron level (340 µg/dL) was lower than the reported hepatotoxic threshold (>1,700 µg/dL), yet rapid and significant elevations in aminotransferases (>4,000 U/L), total bilirubin (5 mg/dL), and prothrombin time (50 s) occurred within 48 hours; tests for acetaminophen, hepatatrophic viruses, and other causes of acute liver injury were negative, and the patient had a full recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute iron overdose with suicidal intent: one-time ingestion of ~100 ferrous sulfate tablets (120 mg elemental iron/kg body weight) in an otherwise previously healthy 18-year-old woman; no other ingestion or co-medications except occasional ibuprofen.
raw_record.extra_details: Ingested as ferrous sulfate tablets. Peak serum iron 340 µg/dL, lower than the reported threshold associated with hepatotoxicity (>1,700 µg/dL); aminotransferases >4,000 U/L, total bilirubin 5 mg/dL, prothrombin time 50 s within 48 hours. Tests for acetaminophen, hepatatrophic viruses, and other causes of acute liver injury were negative. Treated promptly with deferoxamine followed by empiric N-acetylcysteine once liver injury was apparent. Paper notes iron is a known hepatotoxin and that acute iron-poisoning hepatotoxicity is associated with high mortality, and warns that unlike acetaminophen levels, iron levels do not offer reliable risk stratification for liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen-induced liver injury (LI) is the studied condition in this prospective registry of patients admitted after acetaminophen overdose. LI was defined as a peak increase in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) >100 IU/L, and acute liver failure (ALF) was defined as severe LI with encephalopathy and INR >1.5 at any time, prompting consideration for referral to a liver transplantation unit.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute or chronic overdose exposure in admitted patients; all patients received intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC); co-ingestions such as ethanol, codeine, tramadol, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, psychotropic, and cardiotoxic drugs were recorded and could delay gastrointestinal absorption.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen-induced liver injury defined as peak ALT increase >100 IU/L (corresponding to the French indication for continuing NAC therapy). ALF defined as severe LI with encephalopathy and INR >1.5. NAC dosing per French recommendations based on Rumack-Matthew nomogram (baseline acetaminophen >150 mg/L at 4 h), ALT>50 IU/L, or nonvalid nomogram. Study examines admission procalcitonin (PCT) as a diagnostic biomarker for LI using ROC analysis and multivariate Cox regression (HR with 95% CI). Plasma acetaminophen therapeutic range 5-25 mg/L.

The ongoing NACSTOP trial evaluates whether NAC can be ceased after 12 hours in low-risk patients, with hepatic injury as the primary outcome and hepatotoxicity (ALT > 1000 IU/L) as a secondary outcome.

raw_record.extra_details: NACSTOP trial: multicentre, open-label cluster-controlled pilot trial at six Australian emergency departments, recruitment from February 2016. Patients received a two-bag IV NAC regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 h then 100 mg/kg over 16 h). Primary outcome was 'hepatic injury' 20 h after NAC initiation, defined as ALT doubling with peak ALT > 100 IU/L; secondary outcomes were hepatotoxicity (ALT > 1000 IU/L) and peak INR. NAC cessation criteria at 12 h: ALT < 40 IU/L and paracetamol < 20 mg/L. No clinical outcomes are reported, as the trial is ongoing.

raw_record.support_text: Chloroform, a halogenated hydrocarbon, causes CNS depression, cardiac arrhythmias, and hepatotoxicity. A 19-year-old man who ingested approximately 75 mL of chloroform in a suicide attempt developed liver function abnormalities with peak AST of 224 IU/L, ALT of 583 IU/L, and total bilirubin reaching 16.3 mg/dL, and was successfully treated with intravenously administered N-acetylcysteine and supportive care without permanent sequelae. Serum chloroform on admission was 91 μg/mL. Hepatocellular toxicity is thought to result from free radical-induced oxidative damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute oral (ingestion) overdose in a suicide attempt by a 19-year-old man; treated with intravenously administered N-acetylcysteine; supportive care; recovery without permanent sequelae.
raw_record.extra_details: Ingested ~75 mL chloroform; admission serum chloroform 91 μg/mL (average fatal serum level in inhalational poisoning reported as 64 μg/mL). Liver test peaks: AST 224 IU/L, ALT 583 IU/L, total bilirubin 16.3 mg/dL, PT 21.3 s (INR 2.25); values normalized by hospital day 8. Mechanism described as free radical-induced oxidative damage; hepatocellular toxicity. Chloroform synonym trichloromethane.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of chloroform (halogenated hydrocarbon) intoxication diagnosed by an abdominal radiograph showing radiopaque material in the bowel, with associated hepatotoxicity. This is reported as the first documented case of chloroform ingestion with both diagnostic radiopacity and hepatotoxicity. Hepatotoxicity occurred on post-ingestion day 3, and liver enzyme elevation reached peak levels on post-ingestion day 5; the patient was treated with haemoperfusion, activated charcoal, laxatives, and N-acetylcysteine, improved from hepatic dysfunction, and was discharged on post-ingestion day 11.

Chloroform is a radiopaque halogenated hydrocarbon visible on abdominal radiograph; oral chloroform poisoning is rare.

raw_record.support_text: The cohort comprised patients who presented after acetaminophen overdose with hepatic encephalopathy (coma grades 1–4), grouped by whether 48 h had elapsed between overdose and admission, and by reported acetaminophen dose (cutoffs of 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 g). Outcomes were spontaneous survival (survival without liver transplantation) or death (a group that also included transplanted patients). Acetaminophen dose did not significantly predict spontaneous survival by multivariate analysis (P = 0.146; OR, 1.000), and no survival difference was found between patients ingesting more versus less than 10–50 g. Low-coma-grade patients (grades 1–2, n = 78) had a higher spontaneous survival rate than high-coma-grade patients (grades 3–4, n = 35): 83% vs 40% (P < 0.0001).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose ingestion (reported doses spanning thresholds of 10–50 g acetaminophen) in patients who developed hepatic encephalopathy after overdose; outcome analysis stratified by coma grade (grades 1–2 low vs 3–4 high) and whether 48 h elapsed between overdose and admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 115 patients with acetaminophen overdose and hepatic encephalopathy; spontaneous survival 83% in low-coma-grade (n=78) vs 40% in high-coma-grade (n=35) patients. Multivariate analysis: acetaminophen dose, admission ALT, sex, age, ethnicity, and dose/body-weight ratio did not significantly predict spontaneous survival. Death group included liver-transplanted patients. Chi-square analyses found no survival difference by dose cutoffs of 10, 20, 30, 40, or 50 g. Groups were predominantly female and white; no significant difference in age, acetaminophen dose, BMI, or opiate co-ingestion between coma groups. Encephalopathy/coma is a marker of severe (acute liver failure) liver injury.

raw_record.extra_details: The paper evaluates whether early post-ingestion acetaminophen concentrations predict a subsequent concentration above the nomogram treatment line (150 µg/mL at 4 hours), which defines potentially toxic exposure warranting antidote. A 2-4 h concentration ≥100 µg/mL (662 µmol/L) had sensitivity 0.96 (95% CI 0.94-0.97) and negative likelihood ratio 0.070 (95% CI 0.048-0.10); sensitivity was reduced by opioid and antimuscarinic coingestion. Peak aminotransferase ≥1000 IU/L occurred in 19/2454 (0.8%); death or transplant in 2/2454 (0.08%). Cohort median age 23 [IQR 17,34], 70.5% female. One described case: a 14-year-old with a 2-4 h level of 17.4 µg/mL, treated with a 48-h intravenous acetylcysteine protocol, with entirely normal aminotransferases for three days. Seifert et al. are cited as finding zero cases of hepatotoxicity in their poison-center cohort.

raw_record.support_text: The text describes human hepatotoxicity from acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, establishing that the risk of hepatotoxicity increases with both larger ingested dose and higher serum paracetamol concentration, with risk lines starting at 300 mg/L and 200 mg/L at 4 h post-ingestion carrying hepatotoxicity risks of 93% and 24%, respectively. Delayed initiation of antidotal treatment (acetylcysteine) leads to higher risk of developing hepatotoxicity. A single fatal case of liver failure is also attributed to paracetamol overdose in a patient who did not initially meet treatment-line indications.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose setting; nomogram use restricted to patients with a known time of ingestion; cases described include those where acetylcysteine was not administered; reported ingested dose may be inaccurate (retrospective data).
raw_record.extra_details: Nomogram used to determine acetylcysteine need after acute overdose (Rumack-Matthew, lines at 150/200/300/100 mg/L at 4 h post-ingestion). Hepatotoxicity risk 93% (300 mg/L) and 24% (200 mg/L); ~1% risk below the 150 mg/L threshold. Up to 10% of patients develop hepatotoxicity despite early acetylcysteine. Case series report hepatic injury with reported ingested dose of 3.5–10 g without acetylcysteine administration. Single fatal liver-failure case prompted UK lowering of treatment line to 100 mg/L at 4 h. Not validated in staggered ingestions, delayed presentations, unknown ingestion time, repeated supra-therapeutic ingestion, or modified-release paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is described as the most common pharmaceutical product involved in acute overdoses worldwide, able to result in life-threatening hepatotoxicity through conversion of acetaminophen to the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzo-quinoneimine, with the resulting hepatitis preventable by N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment. High acetaminophen concentrations at presentation and a delay in NAC therapy of more than 8 hours post-ingestion are associated with hepatotoxicity risk as high as 45%, and a larger psi parameter is associated with increased incidence of hepatotoxicity after acute acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose setting; study population limited to patients with acute acetaminophen ingestion of 150 mg/kg or more and NAC started when timed acetaminophen concentration was above the 150 line of the Rumack-Matthew Nomogram, aged 12 years or older, at Siriraj Hospital (Thailand).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurs through conversion of acetaminophen to the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzo-quinoneimine (NAPQI) via CYP2E1. Risk determinants include timed serum acetaminophen concentrations and delayed NAC onset (>8 h giving up to 45% hepatotoxicity risk); the psi parameter predicts hepatotoxicity risk. Retrospective cohort study (Siriraj Acute Acetaminophen Hepatotoxicity Project) evaluating whether being overweight/obese increases hepatotoxicity and acute liver injury (ALI) risk. NAPQI itself was only described as a mechanism, not independently attributed as the injuring agent.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents details of 17 patients with liver damage following acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, each having ingested between 6 and 50 g of paracetamol (with some cases also taking other drugs such as aspirin, ferrous sulphate, and barbiturates). Peak serum bilirubin levels ranged up to 5.3 mg/100 ml and peak serum alanine transaminase levels reached values above 800 to 4,000 units/ml, indicating paracetamol-induced liver injury in overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose/supratherapeutic ingestion of 6-50 g of paracetamol; some cases involved co-ingestion of other drugs (aspirin, ferrous sulphate, butobarbitone, carisoprodol and sodium amylobarbitone).
raw_record.extra_details: 17 patients with liver damage; peak serum bilirubin 0.4-5.3 mg/100 ml, peak serum alanine transaminase 46 to >4,000 units/ml. Jaundice described as the most obvious complication, and massive liver necrosis is noted; mortality in the present series 2.4%. In 56 published acute paracetamol poisoning cases (including the present series), jaundice occurred in 13, hypoglycaemia in 6, metabolic acidosis in 5, and there were 8 deaths. Authors advise knowledge of the drugs which produce massive liver necrosis for early diagnosis.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is a common analgesic and antipyretic and the most commonly overdosed therapeutic agent in Hong Kong, accounting for 8.4% of all poisoning cases. After the first human case report of paracetamol-induced liver injury in 1966, paracetamol overdose remains an important cause of acute liver failure with mortalities worldwide. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment is used to prevent paracetamol-induced liver injury, with treatment guided by plotting timed serum paracetamol concentration at 4-24 h post-ingestion on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram and initiating NAC when the concentration is on or above the treatment line.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinico-pathological study of 60 patients Clark et al. (1973) concluded that a dose of 13 g of paracetamol is sufficient to cause appreciable liver damage and that 25 g may be fatal. Twenty-seven of our patients admitted to taking 25 g or more and 21 of these (including 5 fatal cases) sustained severe liver damage, while several patients who took a considerably larger overdose had only moderately severe (grade II) liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute paracetamol overdose (doses of 13 g or more, 25 g or more in serious cases); single-episode exposure; general adult population.
raw_record.extra_details: Clark et al. (1973): 13 g sufficient for appreciable liver damage, 25 g may be fatal. In the present series, 27 patients took 25 g or more; 21 of these sustained severe liver damage including 5 fatal cases; some patients taking a larger overdose had only moderately severe (grade II) damage. Severe paracetamol poisoning shows centrilobular necrosis with acidophilic degeneration (hepatocytolytic vs acidophilic forms); lesion considered nonspecific and common to liver injury by various agents. Follow-up of the authors' own patients (20 rebiopsied at 3 months): all made complete clinical recovery with normal liver function except serum total bile acids; only 1 showed persistent centrilobular condensation of reticulin with scarring (mild residual fibrosis), and Clark et al. reported similar mild residual fibrosis in 2 of 11 patients rebiopsied 3 months after overdose. A single acute overdose was not shown to initiate severe lasting or progressive liver damage. Animal threshold data (hamster 200 mg/kg) cited but not the basis of the human claim.; reaction_type_override: None

raw_record.support_text: Among 21 patients admitted for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose over 13 months, the group with hepatotoxicity (n=3) had a significantly longer estimated plasma half-life (t1/2 = 8.5 h; range 3.6-8.7 h) than the group without hepatotoxicity (n=18; t1/2 = 2.4 h; range 1.6-4.3 h; p < 0.005). There was agreement between a positive (toxic) Rumack nomogram ratio and t1/2 > 4 h, and a negative ratio with t1/2 < 4 h.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute paracetamol overdose (self-poisoning), including cases where time of ingestion or multiple-timepoint (fractionated) ingestion was unknown or indeterminate.
raw_record.extra_details: 21 patients admitted to Son Dureta Hospital (Palma de Mallorca) and Clínic Hospital (Barcelona) over 13 months. Estimated t1/2 was computed as the quotient between 2 plasma paracetamol concentrations separated by 2 or more hours. The paper concludes Rumack's nomogram should be complemented with t1/2 estimation, especially when time of ingestion is unknown or there was multiple-timepoint ingestion. Severe hepatotoxicity or even multiorgan failure versus asymptomatic outcome or moderate transient transaminase elevations is discussed; plasma concentration relates to probability of liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses fatal paracetamol toxicity from paracetamol overdose in the UK. It notes only one death recorded over 20 years among patients in the 100–149 nomogram range of acute paracetamol concentrations, with high-risk patients treated with acetylcysteine. The impact of lowering the acetylcysteine treatment threshold on fatal paracetamol toxicity in other countries cannot be predicted from UK data.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute paracetamol overdose context; UK-specific treatment threshold and presentation patterns, including UK pack-size legislation limiting severe overdoses.
raw_record.extra_details: Two-year UK hospital study (three hospitals) of acute paracetamol overdose presentations; 23% had plasma concentrations above the 150-line and lowering the acetylcysteine treatment threshold from 150 to 100 line would increase treated proportion from 23% to 39% (70% relative increase); one death recorded in UK over 20 years in the 100–149 nomogram range, a group described as very low risk of hepatotoxicity and higher risk of adverse reactions to acetylcysteine. International response to the UK position has been negative, with Ireland the only adopters.

raw_record.support_text: For paracetamol overdose in Hong Kong, the failure rate of the 150-treatment line is 0.45%. Lowering the treatment threshold to the 100-treatment line may lower the failure rate to 0.22%, incurring an annual cost of HK$189,131 (US$24,248), 37 more patients per year needing treatment, and an additional 1.83 anaphylactoid reactions per year. The number needed-to-treat to potentially reduce one significant liver injury is 112.

raw_record.support_text: The study of 100 patients with acute paracetamol poisoning evaluated plasma paracetamol levels and risk-assessment tools for identifying patients at risk of hepatotoxicity, in a resource-limited setting in Sri Lanka. The conclusion endorses colorimetry for assessing the risk of hepatotoxicity in acute paracetamol poisoning patients, treating paracetamol overdose hepatotoxicity as a known clinical consequence.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute paracetamol poisoning (overdose) in a resource-limited setting in Sri Lanka.
raw_record.extra_details: Plasma paracetamol levels were measured by HPLC (reference) and colorimetry in 100 patients; colorimetry had a post-test likelihood of toxicity of 68% and no-toxicity of 91%, with sensitivity 81% and specificity 86%. The 150 mg/kg dose threshold had sensitivity 89% and specificity 5%, and would have indicated antidotal therapy in about 95% of patients with no hepatotoxicity risk; the AUC for the history of ingested dose was 0.578, indicating no discriminatory power. Colorimetry (30 min, US$2) was faster and cheaper than HPLC (180 min, US$20).

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe 132 patients with acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, all with admission plasma paracetamol concentrations above the prognostic line (200 mg/l at 4 hours to 70 mg/l at 12 hours) who, based on previous figures by Prescott et al, were considered destined for severe hepatotoxicity. Of 96 given oral methionine within 10 hours of ingestion, none died from hepatic failure, but 7 suffered severe liver damage (aspartate transaminase > 1000 IU/l). When methionine was delayed beyond 10 hours, severe hepatic damage ensued in 17 of 36 patients, and the table shows 2 deaths from hepatic failure in that delayed group.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute paracetamol poisoning (overdose) with severe exposure, defined by plasma concentrations above the prognostic line (200 mg/l at 4 h to 70 mg/l at 12 h); patients were treated with antidotes (oral methionine, N-acetylcysteine, cysteamine) which modified outcome.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver damage defined as AST > 1000 IU/l. Among 96 given oral methionine within 10 h: 7 (7%) severe liver damage, 1 (1%) acute renal failure, 0 deaths. Among 36 treated after 10 h: 17 (47%) severe liver damage, 2 (5%) acute renal failure, 2 (5.5%) deaths from hepatic failure. Comparison groups: oral N-acetylcysteine (49 within 10 h: 8 [17%]; 51 after 10 h: 23 [45%], 0 deaths), intravenous cysteamine (23 within 10 h: 0; 13 after 10 h: 8 [62%], 1 [8%] death), intravenous N-acetylcysteine (62 within 10 h: 1 [2%]; 38 after 10 h: 20 [53%], 1 [5%] death), supportive therapy only (57: 38 [58%], 6 [17%] renal failure, 3 [6%] deaths). Hepatic failure deaths and acute renal failure attributed to paracetamol poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: In the study's acute paracetamol poisoning group (n=180), transaminase elevation >3x ULN secondary to paracetamol was found in 7 cases (3.9%); causality assessment via the RUCAM algorithm classified 6 as probable and 1 as possible, and the Capellá–Laporte system classified 4 probable and 3 possible. Paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (ALF) occurred in 4 patients (2.2%) and 2 deaths (1.1%) were recorded. Maximum ALT reached 5260 UI/L and maximum AST 3785 UI/L in the acute group, evidencing paracetamol-attributed human liver injury after acute overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute poisoning/overdose setting (median ingested dose 7.25 g, range 1–80 g); some cases had co-ingestion of other drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Transaminases >3x ULN in 7/180 (3.9%) acute cases; paracetamol-induced ALF in 4 (2.2%); 2 deaths (1.1%). Causality: RUCAM probable 6, possible 1; Capellá–Laporte probable 4, possible 3 (among 10 transaminase-elevation cases across groups). Maximum ALT 5260 UI/L, AST 3785 UI/L, GGT 4445 UI/L; maximum total bilirubin 12.6 mg/dL (acute). Reason for paracetamol level request mostly suicide attempt (169 cases, 93.9%).

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 100 episodes of paracetamol (paracetamol) poisoning treated with intravenous NAC, the proportion developing severe hepatic necrosis (plasma transaminases >1000 IU/L) ranged from 0 to 82% depending on treatment interval, versus 89% in historical controls, who developed liver necrosis. Fifteen patients with paracetamol levels above 200 mg/L at 4 hr to 60 mg/L at 12 hr were treated with intravenous NAC (total 300 mg/kg over 20.25 hr).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute poisoning/overdose; timing of antidote (NAC, cysteamine or methionine) therapy influenced outcome, with risk of necrosis rising when antidote was given later.
raw_record.extra_details: In the Prescott series, 15 patients above the 200 mg/L at 4 hr / 60 mg/L at 12 hr line were treated with IV NAC (150 mg/kg over 15 min, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hr and 100 mg/kg over 16 hr). In 100 episodes, severe hepatic necrosis (transaminases >1000 IU/L) after NAC at intervals up to 8 hr, 8-10 hr, 10-12 hr, 12-15 hr, 15-24 hr was 0, 7, 43, 56 and 82%, respectively, vs 89% in historical controls; only 11 patients treated after 15 hr. Severe liver damage occurred in 1/62 treated with NAC, 0/27 with cysteamine and 3/15 with methionine; liver-function abnormalities were less common after NAC (26%) than cysteamine (59%) or methionine (60%). Renal dysfunction developed in 13% after NAC given after 10 hr. In the US National Multicenter Study (11,195 suspected poisonings, 2540 treated with oral NAC, n=2023 above the 200 mg/L/4 hr to 50 mg/L/12 hr line), hepatic toxicity developed in 6% treated within 10 hr vs 34% treated 10-24 hr; severe liver necrosis occurred in 41% of 283 high-risk patients treated 16-24 hr.

raw_record.support_text: A 28-year-old man was admitted to the intensive care unit for acute acetaminophen poisoning after ingesting 25 g of acetaminophen in a suicidal attempt 24 hours earlier. His plasma acetaminophen concentration on admission was 55.7 µg/ml (371 µmol/l), which plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram indicated a high risk for hepatotoxicity. Laboratory studies showed elevated liver enzymes (ASAT 4790 IU/l, ALAT 3275 IU/l, LDH 6230 IU/l), prothrombin time 30 s, factor V 19%, and total bilirubin 68.2 µmol/l, with hepatomegaly on ultrasound.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute self-poisoning overdose by a 28-year-old man; pre-existing bronchial asthma treated with salbutamol inhalation.
raw_record.extra_details: Suicidal ingestion of 25 g acetaminophen; plasma concentration 55.7 µg/ml (371 µmol/l) at admission (24 h post-ingestion) plotted as high risk on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram (levels <10 µg/ml expected at 24 h). Right-sided abdominal pain/tenderness, painful liver palpable 6 cm below costal margin, hepatomegaly. Biologic/chemistry: LDH 6230, ASAT 4790, ALAT 3275 IU/l peaking at 48 h (LDH 24150, ASAT 13840, ALAT 7540 IU/l); prothrombin time 30 s rising to 35 s and factor V fell to 7% at 48 h, all then normalizing; treated with IV N-acetylcysteine; patient left ICU on day 6. Discussion states ingestion of as little as 150 mg/kg of acetaminophen can cause liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective secondary analysis of 59 hospitalized acute acetaminophen (APAP) overdose patients treated with <21 h of i.v. N-acetylcysteine, hepatotoxicity (aspartate aminotransferase or alanine aminotransferase >1,000 IU/L) occurred in one patient (1.7%; 95% CI 0.04–9.1), and eight additional patients developed hepatic injury (AST or ALT >100 IU/L); no fatalities occurred. The paper attributes this hepatic injury to the APAP overdose despite shortened NAC treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute single acetaminophen overdose; patients received a shortened (<21 h) course of i.v. N-acetylcysteine, which was initiated a median of 11.3 h post ingestion and given for a median of 11.0 h.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 59 patients hospitalized for APAP poisoning. Hepatotoxicity defined as AST or ALT >1,000 IU/L (1.7% of patients) and hepatic injury as AST or ALT >100 IU/L (8 additional patients). No fatalities; hepatotoxicity and coagulopathy incidence was low despite delays to NAC treatment. Low-risk predictors reported: APAP x AT product <10,000 µmol/L/IU-L, or pretreatment psi (ψ) parameter <5 mmol/L-h.

raw_record.support_text: Approximately 50,000 patients present to US emergency departments each year due to acetaminophen (APAP) exposure. Patients with acute ingestions are risk-stratified by plotting APAP concentrations on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, and those with toxic concentrations require treatment, reflecting the established hepatotoxic risk of APAP in overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute single APAP ingestion in ED-presenting patients
raw_record.extra_details: Rumack-Matthew nomogram is validated only for concentrations drawn 4 hours or later after acute ingestion; nomogram starts at 4 hours to include delayed absorption, although therapeutic-dose PK suggests peak within 1 hour. Douglas et al. retrospective analysis of APAP concentrations drawn within 4 hours reported negative predictive values of 76% within 1 hour, 88% at 1-2 h, 98% at 2-3 h, and 99% at 3-4 h (recalculated NPVs 80%, 90%, 94% respectively); APAP <100 microg/mL between 1 and 4 h had NPV 94.6%. The study aims to prospectively validate whether APAP <100 microg/mL obtained 1-4 h after acute ingestion predicts a nontoxic 4-hour concentration.

raw_record.support_text: This study of patients presenting after acute single paracetamol overdose found a positive correlation between reported paracetamol dose ingested and subsequent plasma paracetamol concentration, but reported dose was a poor predictor of which patients would require antidotal (NAC) treatment. The authors note that using reported dose to decide treatment could lead to both overtreatment and under-treatment, the latter carrying a risk of hepatotoxicity, and they conclude there is no safe threshold reported dose below which NAC could be withheld without measuring a plasma paracetamol concentration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute single paracetamol ingestion (overdose).
raw_record.extra_details: Over-the-counter paracetamol availability in the UK (8 g and 16 g packs, each 11 % of ingestions) and Australia (10 g) was analysed against 100 mg/L (UK) and 150 mg/L (Australia) plasma paracetamol treatment lines for NAC use. Of 446 patients with reported ingestion <8 g, 87 % had plasma paracetamol below the 100 mg/L line and 90 % below the 150 mg/L line; among 61 patients ingesting >32 g, 90 % were above the 100 mg/L line and 85 % above the 150 mg/L line. Reported ingestion >18 g predicted being above the 100 mg/L line in 80 % of cases and >26 g predicted being above the 150 mg/L line in 80 % of cases. Back-extrapolation of plasma concentrations to C4 gave a moderate correlation coefficient of 0.58 with ingested dose. PPV/NPV for commonly ingested amounts were insufficient to guide antidote use.

raw_record.support_text: Case 2: a 51-year-old man ingested 23,600 mg of acetaminophen (279.6 mg/kg) in a single acute overdose and was admitted ~8 h later; N-acetylcysteine was administered. By the second day GOT and GPT rose to 2508 and 1473 IU/L, respectively, with a blood acetaminophen level of 116.9 μg/mL. GOT and GPT decreased over subsequent days and returned to normal by follow-up, indicating acetaminophen-overdose-induced liver cell damage from which the patient recovered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute single-dose overdose of 23,600 mg (279.6 mg/kg); N-acetylcysteine administered ~8 h after intake
raw_record.extra_details: GOT rose to 2508 IU/L and GPT to 1473 IU/L by day 2 of admission; blood acetaminophen 116.9 μg/mL; PCT elevated to 45.66 ng/mL at ~56 h after intake; ultrasound showed mild fatty liver with hepatomegaly without bile duct dilatation; no fever or infection signs; liver enzymes returned to normal (GOT 32, GPT 31 IU/L) at follow-up. Discussion notes high PCT in acute liver failure due to acetaminophen intoxication without infection and 'acetaminophen-induced liver cell damage' with sterile inflammation via IL-1 beta and tumor necrosis factor alpha as proposed mechanisms (Tschiedel et al., PCT-acetaminophen r = -0.45, P = .15; PCT-GPT r = 0.66, P = .02).

One patient received a liver transplant and one patient died (of respiratory failure secondary to aspiration 30 hours post-ingestion). Most patients received acetylcysteine treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: Of the 200 included patients, 140 (70%) were female, median age 25 years, median weight 65 kg; 152 immediate-release, 48 modified-release/combo ingestions. 26 (13%) developed hepatotoxicity; 15 had INR > 2.0 (5 with INR > 5.0); 4 developed severe acute kidney injury (AKIN stage 3). One liver transplant and one death (respiratory failure secondary to aspiration 30 h post-ingestion). 42 patients developed peak ALT > 100 U/L. 191 (96%) received acetylcysteine. Cohorts compared immediate-release vs modified-release ingestions.

raw_record.support_text: A 24-year-old woman presented a few hours after ingesting a large (>7000 mg) amount of sustained-release sodium valproate together with 10 mg of alprazolam in a suicidal attempt; liver function tests initially normal rose six hours later (AST 3.3x and ALT 4.5x normal), with blood valproate of 1380 µmol/l, and evolved to severe VPA-induced liver failure (peak ALT 174x normal, PT 28%, factor V 24%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute suicidal overdose (>7000 mg sustained-release sodium valproate) co-ingested with 10 mg alprazolam; no preexisting liver or metabolic disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute biopsy-proven reversible VPA-associated hepatic failure. Liver biopsy showed diffuse massive panlobular clarification with focal hepatocellular necrosis and predominant microvesicular steatosis (oil red O); electron microscopy showed swollen mitochondria with disorganized cristae and fluffy matrix. Peak ALT 174x normal, PT 28%, factor V 24%, blood lactate 3.8 mmol/l, blood valproate 1380 µmol/l (therapeutic range 350-700). Patient recovered without liver transplantation; valproic acid was not reintroduced.
