raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old boy ingested an unknown quantity of potassium dichromate in a suicide attempt and developed vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and acute renal and liver failure in January 1996. Supportive treatment and dimercaprol did not prevent deterioration of renal and liver function within two days. On day 6 orthotopic cadaveric liver transplantation was performed; histopathological examination of the explanted liver showed diffuse hepatocellular necrosis. The patient recovered after transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adolescent (16-year-old boy); intentional suicide ingestion of an unknown quantity, i.e., overdose exposure; poison obtained from a school chemical laboratory.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure progressed over six days leading to orthotopic cadaveric liver transplantation. Histopathology of the explanted liver showed diffuse hepatocellular necrosis. Serum chromium levels decreased over time, suggesting chromium accumulation in the liver. Plasmapheresis and hemodialysis did not remove substantial chromium from circulation as documented by filtrate measurements. Dimercaprol (250 mg IV twice daily) was administered as chelation treatment. Patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 14 with normal laboratory findings; normal liver and kidney function at two-year follow-up. Authors recommend delaying liver transplantation to allow the native liver to extract chromium.

raw_record.support_text: A 17-year-old male was admitted with acute liver failure after he admitted ingesting an unspecified amount of over-the-counter niacin to obscure the results of an upcoming drug test. Autoimmune, infectious, and alpha-1 antitrypsin testing were negative, and his ALF was attributed to this use of niacin, with no further workup undertaken. His liver transaminases and coagulation studies returned to normal within two weeks. The paper describes the case as ALF secondary to niacin-induced toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Given negative acetaminophen, salicylate, and alcohol testing and negative viral hepatitis, pancreatitis, or other explanations for the transaminase elevation, coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis and lactic acidosis, the authors conclude the adolescent patient's symptoms, including his resulting hepatitis, were likely due to severe niacin toxicity following a large intentional niacin ingestion (overdose). The patient also developed severe myalgias and his symptoms and laboratory studies resolved with supportive care.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adolescent patient; severe intentional niacin overdose (reported as the third adolescent niacin overdose case); suspected dose-dependent toxidrome; the patient ingested significantly more niacin than two prior reported adolescent cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Case presented with elevated liver enzymes (transaminases), coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis, and lactic acidosis; formed a hepatic and myalgia syndrome. Negative acetaminophen, salicylate, and alcohol screens and negative viral hepatitis/pancreatitis supported niacin attribution. Resolution of symptoms and laboratory findings after a few days of supportive care. Prior reported high-dose niacin exposure in 4 patients (attempting to alter urine drug tests) included 2 with more severe presentation (adolescents, 14 and 17 years old) who developed elevated liver enzymes, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia and abnormal coagulation studies that resolved; no muscular pain. No death from acute overdose has been reported.

raw_record.support_text: A letter to the editor reports that Nyquil, an over-the-counter cold remedy containing ephedrine, doxylamine, promethazine, dextromethorphan, and 700 mg of acetaminophen per ounce in a 25% alcohol elixir, was consumed in a 12-oz (360 ml) amount over 12 hours by an alcoholic 45-year-old man, causing massive hepatic necrosis. The high alcohol level led this alcoholic patient to consume the elixir, and the resulting hepatic injury was attributed to the acetaminophen, for which he was treated as for a possible acetaminophen overdose with N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Alcoholic 45-year-old man with a history of chronic heavy beer consumption; exposure was via a supratherapeutic 12-oz (360 ml) ingestion of Vicks Nyquil (25% alcohol elixir containing 700 mg acetaminophen per ounce, ~8.4 g total acetaminophen) consumed over 12 hours; urine showed high concentrations of Nyquil ingredients.
raw_record.extra_details: Admission labs indicated severe liver injury: total bilirubin 9.6 mg/dL (indirect 5.4), prothrombin time 27.1 seconds, aspartate aminotransferase 10,100 IU/dL, albumin 3.8 g/100 ml; alkaline phosphatase and amylase normal. Treated with N-acetylcysteine (Mucomyst) for possible acetaminophen overdose and vitamin K; prothrombin time and aspartate aminotransferase normalized within 8 days; patient discharged with total bilirubin 17 mg/dL and still icteric two weeks later; no coagulopathy-related death or transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a 37-year-old alcoholic presenting with metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, hypoprothrombinemia, and a markedly elevated SGOT level; despite absence of volunteered information, acetaminophen hepatotoxicity was considered the probable cause and this diagnosis was eventually supported. The patient died of widespread hepatic necrosis, as did most previously reported late-presentation acetaminophen overdose patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Alcoholic patient; associated alcohol ingestion; late presentation of overdose (diagnosis considered ~48 hr after admission); antagonist n-acetylcysteine no longer effective at this stage.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical presentation included metabolic acidosis with increased anion gap, hypoglycemia, severe coagulopathy with early hypoprothrombinemia at a time of minor hyperbilirubinemia, abdominal pain with elevated serum amylase, and markedly elevated SGOT (peak 13,500 IU/liter). Histology showed extensive centrilobular-midzonal confluent injury with hepatocellular loss, foamy Kupffer cells, hepatocellular ballooning and fat vacuolization, spared periportal hepatocytes, and increased centrilobular collagen. The patient presented ~24 hr after ingestion and died. The authors also tabulate nine other reported late-presentation acetaminophen overdose patients, six of whom died; the constellation (lactic acidosis, hypoglycemia, early severe hypoprothrombinemia, very high SGOT) is proposed as highly suggestive of well-established acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. Proposed mechanism involves a rapid alteration in hepatocyte redox state hindering lactate metabolism and impairing gluconeogenesis, with early involvement of rough endoplasmic reticulum; supporting findings are in experimental animals.

raw_record.support_text: This prospective phase I/II study enrolled sequential patients admitted with acute liver failure (ALF) due to acetaminophen overdose to the Liver Intensive Therapy Unit at King's College Hospital (inclusion criteria: age 16-60, INR >= 4, less than 20 h from admission). raw_record.support_text: William M. Lee reports that more than half of all acute liver failure (ALF) instances in the ALFSG registry from 25 U.S. sites are due to DILI, and that 3/4 of the DILI cases are accounted for by acetaminophen. Acetaminophen-induced ALF cases have increased, with acetaminophen accounting for 51% of all ALF cases over the last two years, and more than half of these involved 'unintentional' cases in which narcotic/acetaminophen combinations were over-represented.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: ALF patients in the ALFSG registry; many cases were unintentional, with narcotic/acetaminophen combinations over-represented
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen accounted for >50% of ALF cases and 3/4 of DILI cases; 51% of all ALF cases over the last 2 years. Acetaminophen adducts were a highly specific and sensitive assay for hepatotoxicity, remaining positive up to nine days after ingestion, and were detected in serum of 20% of previously 'indeterminate' ALF cases.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients presenting after staggered paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, three suffered adverse hepatic consequences and one died. Case 3, a 20-year-old woman with depression who took 48 paracetamol plus aspirin tablets over 24 hours before admission, developed severe hepatic injury with paracetamol level 129 mg/l, ALT rising from 171 U/l, INR peaking at 14.5 on day 5, grade III encephalopathy and acute renal failure, and died of adult respiratory distress syndrome with multi-organ failure on day 10 despite full NAC support. Two other staggered-overdose patients had marked transaminase elevation (ALT up to 9300 U/l) with raised INR and recovered on NAC.

raw_record.extra_details: Aliases: acetaminophen. From 160 suspected paracetamol overdose cases; three staggered-overdose patients had adverse hepatic consequences with one death. Laboratory findings included serum ALT up to 9300 U/l, INR up to 14.5, hypoglycaemia, severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.18), and bilirubin 30 umol/l. 18 cases (11.3%) presented >24 h after ingestion; six cases involved staggered overdose. All treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Death occurred on day 10 from ARDS and multi-organ failure after transfer to King's College Hospital liver unit.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective series of 170 paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdoses taken by 152 patients (103 females, 49 males, age range 9 months to 83 years) was analyzed. Fifty-seven additional patients who ingested small amounts of paracetamol (<125 mg/kg over 24 h) were excluded as not significant overdoses. Patients fell into two groups: 131 whose primary management was at the Austin and Repatriation Medical Centre, and 21 referred to the Victorian liver transplant unit from other hospitals because they had developed severe paracetamol hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All patients had taken paracetamol as an overdose (therapeutic threshold considered >125 mg/kg over 24 h); thirteen overdoses were accidental or inadvertent, including eleven in young children who accessed paracetamol liquid/tablets and two patients (aged 6 and 15 years) given excessive therapeutic amounts.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol was taken alone in 28% of cases; co-ingested with alcohol in 32%, benzodiazepines in 20%, codeine in 15%, and aspirin in 8%. Mean amount taken in group A was 20.7±14.0 g (range 2.5–107 g); mean delay to hospital was 8.8±12.5 h. NAC therapy and peak ALT were assessed. Annual presentations trended upward over the last 3 years from a baseline of 7–13 cases/year (1988–1992).

raw_record.support_text: Plasma samples were collected from acetaminophen (APAP) overdose patients. ALT and ASS were measured in healthy volunteers (n=6), APAP overdose patients with normal liver test results (n=9), and APAP overdose patients with abnormal liver test results indicating liver injury (n=13). In the abnormal-liver-test group peak ALT was 4,382 ± 668 U/L, peak prothrombin time was 60.4 ± 12.7 seconds, and survival was 85%, establishing that APAP overdose caused clinically severe liver injury and associated mortality in these human patients.

raw_record.support_text: Blood analysis of patients with APAP overdose on admission to emergency departments revealed a heterogeneous pattern of increased bile acid (BA) concentrations and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity, with some patients showing elevated BA and almost normal ALT, others both increased ALT and BAs, a third group with increased ALT and normal/close-to-normal BAs, and some with both normal BAs and ALT. A time-resolved analysis was performed on a 19-year-old woman who ingested 86.5 g of APAP (blood concentrations 3.7 mM and 2.2 mM at 1.7 h and 4 h post-ingestion); from 28.5 h post-ingestion the sum of BAs and ALT was elevated, with the BA increase preceding and declining while ALT remained high, indicating APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: APAP overdose without documented time of intoxication in most patients; one 19-year-old woman ingested 86.5 g APAP (blood levels 3.7 mM and 2.2 mM at 1.7 h and 4 h post-ingestion); time-resolved analysis limited to this single patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Heterogeneous admission pattern in APAP-overdose patients; no significant correlation between BA and ALT levels observed. In the indexed patient, sum of BAs rose before ALT (increase at ~28.5 h post-ingestion) and declined while ALT stayed elevated; various patient groups likely correspond to early (high BA, normal ALT), intermediate (high BA, high ALT), and late (high ALT, moderately increased/normal BA) stages of overdose. Supporting mouse data (hepatotoxic APAP dose) showed transient BA increase at ~2 h preceding ALT rise and pericentral (Cyp2e1-positive zone) cell death by programmed necrosis (no cleaved caspase-3 increase), plus bile canalicular dilatation/blebbing and loss of mitochondrial membrane potential in pericentral hepatocytes.

raw_record.support_text: Carbon tetrachloride is described as a directly cytotoxic drug, with evidence of liver involvement usually occurring within 48 hours of exposure. Abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly and/or jaundice are usually the earliest signs, and liver function tests show changes suggesting hepatocellular damage that may closely mimic viral hepatitis; in the reported case the serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase level was elevated within 12 hours and rose to extremely high levels before falling. The hepatic injury is characterized histologically by centrilobular ballooning, fatty metamorphosis, necrosis, and leucocytic infiltration, referred to as carbon tetrachloride hepatitis, and if death from liver disease occurs it is within the first ten days after ingestion, usually from liver-cell failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Carbon tetrachloride poisoning by ingestion (supratherapeutic/overdose exposure) rather than ordinary therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Evidence of liver involvement usually within 48 hours; earliest signs were abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly and/or jaundice. SGOT (glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase) elevated within 12 hours, rising to extremely high levels then falling rapidly, and such levels are rarely seen except in viral hepatitis and active chronic hepatitis. Hyperbilirubinaemia occurred within 12 hours and returned to normal in seven days; prothrombin depressed at first estimation and rapidly normalized; alkaline phosphatase usually within normal limits; bromsulphalein retention 13% at 45 minutes on day 7 (sensitive index of hepatic function). Histology showed typical carbon tetrachloride hepatitis: centrilobular (occasionally whole-lobule) ballooning, fatty metamorphosis, eventual necrosis with leucocytic infiltration, mild portal inflammation, lipofuscin staining of Kupffer cells; a second biopsy at 45 days showed minimal residual fatty metamorphosis, focal necrosis and prominent lipofuscin. If death from liver disease occurs it is within the first ten days after ingestion, usually from liver-cell failure with or without ascites and hepatic coma; survivors rarely have residual damage, though post-necrotic scarring reported in two cases. High transaminase levels also noted by Fry 1959, Dawborn 1961, New 1962; pathology descriptions per Moon 1950, Klatskin 1963.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen has been identified as the leading cause of acute liver injury in the United States from 1998 to 2003, with unintentional overdose accounting for 48% of acute liver injury cases, and combination APAP products remain a leading cause of fatalities. In the present case series of 40 patients with APAP-attributed hepatotoxicity, 2 patients died, 1 underwent liver transplantation, and 30 survived to discharge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases were unintentional (non-recidivating) APAP overdoses taken for excessive pain; most patients consumed multiple APAP-containing products, frequently a prescription 500 mg APAP product combined with OTC APAP or with hydrocodone, oxycodone, or butalbital/caffeine, so co-exposure to coprescribed opioids/caffeine occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 cases; 29 (73%) female; ages 19–90 years; APAP use duration 24 h to 4 weeks; cumulative APAP doses 10.5–49 g in 14 cases with clear histories; AST ≥1000 IU/L in 38 (95%) patients (mean 5,861 ± 5,424 IU/L, range 772–24,406 IU/L); ALT ≥1000 IU/L in 37 (93%) patients (mean 3,383 ± 2,953 IU/L, range 486–14,883 IU/L); all patients received acetylcysteine (60% oral, 33% IV, 5% both); outcomes: 30 survived, 2 died, 1 liver transplant, 6 lost to follow-up. Discussion cites APAP as leading cause of acute liver injury in the US 1998–2003 and Larson et al. finding combination APAP products account for 63% of unintentional APAP poisonings.

raw_record.support_text: Case 216: a 39-year-old woman who chronically took acetaminophen (and acetaminophen with codeine) for headaches over 2 months presented dehydrated with an upper GI bleed. After N-acetylcysteine was started, repeat labs showed AST 6,800 U/L and ALT 6,700 U/L with a rising PT and bleeding at several sites; she required intubation, vasopressors, and glucose and died on the fourth day of admission. The case attributes the severe hepatic injury to the chronic acetaminophen exposure.

raw_record.extra_details: Presenting labs: acetaminophen 51 µg/mL, salicylate 2.5 mg/dL, INR >10, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, AST 144 U/L; repeat acetaminophen was 24 µg/mL 20 h later at which time N-acetylcysteine was started; subsequent labs AST 6,800 U/L, ALT 6,700 U/L; rising PT with bleeding, respiratory distress requiring intubation, vasopressors and glucose support; died on day 4 of admission.

raw_record.support_text: In the study's chronic paracetamol poisoning group (n=20), transaminase elevation >3x ULN secondary to paracetamol was found in 8 cases (40%); causality via RUCAM classified 7 as probable and 1 as possible, and Capellá–Laporte classified 6 probable and 2 possible. Paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (ALF) occurred in 3 patients (15%) and 2 deaths (10%) were recorded. Maximum ALT reached 4800 UI/L, AST 12798 UI/L, and total bilirubin 19.9 mg/dL in the chronic group, evidencing paracetamol-attributed human liver injury after chronic (unintentional) overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic (unintentional) poisoning/overdose setting; chronically higher median age (54.6 years); daily dose median 4 g/day (range 2–32).
raw_record.extra_details: Transaminases >3x ULN in 8/20 (40%) chronic cases; paracetamol-induced ALF in 3 (15%); 2 deaths (10%). raw_record.support_text: The report describes cases of severe liver damage and toxic hepatitis in patients who chronically ingested moderately excessive amounts of acetaminophen. The first patient's severe liver damage from chronic ingestion of moderately excessive acetaminophen was attributed to concurrent chronic alcohol abuse (which presumably induced his cytochrome P-450 enzyme system, increasing susceptibility), and a second patient developed toxic hepatitis after ingesting excessive acetaminophen doses on two occasions, with negative nitrogen balance/cachexia and low serum albumin possibly lowering hepatic glutathione stores.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic abuse of moderately excessive acetaminophen doses in metabolically susceptible patients; concurrent chronic alcohol abuse (case 1) or cachexia with low serum albumin and suspected reduced hepatic glutathione stores (case 2).
raw_record.extra_details: Cases of serious liver damage from chronic abuse of acetaminophen in susceptible patients. Reported post-cessation serum acetaminophen levels of 37 and 15 µg/ml more than 24 h after stopping ingestion, described as in the toxic range (normal therapeutic 4-h level <9 µg/ml). In supporting animal work, alcohol and glutathione-depleting agents (diethylmaleate) potentiate acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis in mice, and protein restriction depletes glutathione in rats; diethylstilbestrol and ethacrynic acid also deplete glutathione in animals.

raw_record.support_text: Among 27 DILI patients analyzed, a unique case of acute hepatic failure was caused by abusive consumption of paracetamol (APAP) over time, without other relevant comorbidities. The 40-year-old male patient presented with hypotension, drowsiness, peripheral cyanosis, icterus, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and altered laboratory values (AST > 4,600 U/L, creatinine 4.6 mg/dL). Serum APAP at admission (220 μg/mL) indicated possible liver toxicity, N-acetylcysteine was given, and post-mortem liver analysis 2 days after admission showed extensive necrosis, congestion, infiltration, hemorrhage and ischaemia, all signs compatible with a hepatotoxic etiology.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic abusive (supratherapeutic) consumption over time; single male patient (40 years) with several prior suicide attempts; no other relevant comorbidities.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient presented with hypotension (blood pressure 70/40), drowsiness, peripheral cyanosis, conjunctival icterus, right upper quadrant abdominal pain; laboratory values AST > 4,600 U/L, creatinine 4.6 mg/dL, leukocytosis; serum APAP concentration 220 μg/mL at admission (>4 h post ingestion), indicating possible liver toxicity by the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Treated with N-acetylcysteine. Post-mortem liver examination showed extensive necrosis, congestion, infiltration, hemorrhage and ischaemia.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 2, a 38-year-old black male chronic alcohol abuser, ingested 4400 mg/d of acetaminophen over 48 hours (as Regular-Strength Tylenol and Tylenol #3 with codeine) for chronic back pain, while drinking about 100 g of alcohol per day. He developed severe hepatic necrosis; the acetaminophen level 24 hours after the presumed last dose was 15.6 µg/mL, in the toxic range. The paper attributes the liver injury to acetaminophen and concludes that chronic alcoholics must be cautioned about its potential serious adverse effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcohol abuser (~100 g alcohol/day); concurrent codeine co-exposure via Tylenol #3; supratherapeutic intake of 4400 mg/d of acetaminophen over 48 h.
raw_record.extra_details: On admission AST 13,496 IU/L, ALT 4,744 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 60 IU/L, total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dL, platelets 9000/mm3, positive DIC screen (PT 30 s, PTT 60 s), creatinine 3.2 mg/dL; acetaminophen level 15.6 µg/mL (toxic range) 24 h after last dose; treated with oral N-acetylcysteine, FFP, packed erythrocytes, platelets; laparoscopy showed Mallory-Weiss tear; patient improved and was discharged 3 weeks later with normal clotting studies/aminotransferases and bilirubin 20 mg/dL.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse and excessive daily use of paracetamol of approximately 20 tablets (500 mg each) for the past 2 months presented with jaundice, fever, hepatomegaly, and acute ischemia of the left leg. Hematology showed prothrombin time 29.0 s, INR 2.90; biochemistry showed severe hepatic enzyme elevation (AST 4840 U/L, ALT 2713 U/L, LDH 4114 U/L, GGT 682 U/L, total bilirubin 7.81 mg/dL). The patient had significant coagulopathy with acquired deficiencies of antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S; after successful thrombectomy and intensive treatment he recovered fully and was discharged on acenocoumarol.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcohol consumption co-exposure; excessive daily use of approximately 20 tablets (500 mg each, about 10 g/day) for the past 2 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Alcohol-paracetamol syndrome presenting with hepatic failure and acute limb arterial thrombosis. Jaundice, fever up to 38.8°C, hepatomegaly; transaminases AST 4840 U/L, ALT 2713 U/L, LDH 4114 U/L, GGT 682 U/L, total bilirubin 7.81 mg/dL (4.42 mg/dL direct); co-existing significant coagulopathy (PT 29.0 s, INR 2.90) with acquired deficiencies of antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S. Patient discharged 20 days after admission with complete recovery, on acenocoumarol. Diagnosis ascribed to alcohol-paracetamol syndrome rather than graded by a causality instrument.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old male chronic alcoholic ingesting about 10 g of acetaminophen over two days developed severe hepatotoxicity. On autopsy the liver showed massive hepatic necrosis with only a rim of remaining hepatocytes around the portal areas; these findings were thought to be typical for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. The patient progressed to hepatic encephalopathy and died on the fourth hospital day.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholics with a history of heavy alcohol abuse; three patients (case 1 survived, case 2 died, case 3 survived).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported acetaminophen amounts: 10 g/48 hr (case 1), 10 g/24 hr (case 2), 50 g/72 hr (case 3). Case 1 showed severe centrilobular necrosis with preservation of periportal hepatocytes typical of severe acetaminophen liver toxicity; case 2 showed massive hepatic necrosis with residual periportal hepatocytes showing degeneration and microvesicular fat. Peak SGOT values 6,960, 9,940, and 7,720 IU; peak bilirubin 17, 8, and 7 mg/dL. Case 2 developed acute tubular necrosis, oliguria, delirium tremens, progressive hepatic encephalopathy, respiratory arrest, and died on day 4; autopsy additionally showed diffuse petechial myocardial hemorrhages and acute tubular necrosis, both previously associated with acetaminophen toxicity, although other factors (e.g., pancreatitis, shock) may have contributed.

raw_record.support_text: The case is described as APAP-induced acute liver injury with significant elevation in transaminases, in a patient who ingested large/unknown amounts of extra-strength acetaminophen (APAP) over days to weeks for chronic pain, with chronic alcoholism. Laboratory findings included an APAP level of 126.3 ug/ml, AST 2,175 U/l, ALT 896 U/l, total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dl, INR 1.6, and lactate 3.9 mmol/L; hepatic encephalopathy was present and King's College criteria were calculated daily. Treatment included N-acetylcysteine and fomepizole, and liver and kidney function returned to baseline four weeks after admission.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholism and long-term use of staggering unknown doses of extra-strength acetaminophen for chronic pain; exact ingested amount and time of last ingestion (6-18 h prior) uncertain; co-administration of an N-acetylcysteine rescue regimen; the overdose context is implied by amounts but explicit dose is unavailable.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 58-year-old female. Admission labs: APAP 126.3 ug/ml, ethanol <0.01 gm/dl%, AST 2,175 U/l, ALT 896 U/l, total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dl, INR 1.6, lactate 3.9 mmol/L, CK 151 U/L. Hepatic encephalopathy improved ~one day after admission; acute kidney injury occurred with differential diagnoses including APAP-induced hepatotoxicity, hepatorenal syndrome, and acute tubular necrosis; kidney function improved ~80 h post-admission without hemodialysis. N-acetylcysteine i.v. given (21-hour protocol, then dose increased to 12.5 mg/kg/h then 6.25 mg/kg/h until serum APAP undetectable at ~40 h); one-time fomepizole 15 mg/kg i.v. load then 10 mg/kg every 12 h x4, first dose ~30 h after admission (~36-48 h after last ingestion). King's College criteria did not indicate transplant evaluation. Liver and kidney function returned to baseline four weeks post-admission. Mechanism stated: CYP2E1 forms NAPQI, which depletes glutathione causing hepatocyte necrosis and hepatic failure in overdose.; confidence: 0.9; needs_more_context: False

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old man with chronic daily ketamine abuse presented with weeks of vomiting, constant abdominal pain, alkaline phosphatase of 123 IU/L (AST/ALT and bilirubin normal), and CT/ultrasound showing intrahepatic dilation of the common bile duct (16 mm) with an enlarged gallbladder; he was ultimately diagnosed with ketamine-induced cholangiopathy (KIC) and concomitant ketamine-induced uropathy (KIU). The discussion states ketamine is a rare but recognized cause of cholangiopathy in heavy ketamine abusers, and case reports from Asia show cholestatic liver injury that improves after cessation of ketamine abuse.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic daily/heavy ketamine abuse (recreational drug-abuse setting); concurrent ketamine-induced uropathy.
raw_record.extra_details: 35-year-old man; weeks of vomiting and constant abdominal pain; alkaline phosphatase 123 IU/L with normal AST/ALT and bilirubin; intrahepatic CBD dilation from 8 mm to 16 mm over 8 months; enlarged gallbladder without cholecystitis/stones/sludge; MRCP/HIDA showed no choledocholithiasis, obstruction, stricture, or cholecystitis; mechanism of injury unclear; Asian case reports show cholestatic injury improving after cessation of abuse.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients (33 and 55 years old) who were chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) carriers were treated with buprenorphine for addiction and hospitalized with clinical hepatitis and jaundice after intravenous administration. Aminotransferase rose to 100 and 21 times normal. Co-factors included alcohol consumption in the first patient and high-dose aspirin in the second. After discontinuing IV buprenorphine, hepatitis did not recur with oral buprenorphine. Using the Naranjo adverse-event criteria, and also the CIOMS and Maria-Victorino (M&V) scales, the relationship between buprenorphine and acute hepatitis was categorized as probable in both cases. Acute hepatitis was followed by HCV RNA disappearance.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic HCV carriers; misuse of buprenorphine by intravenous route; co-factors included alcohol consumption (patient 1) and high-dose aspirin (patient 2); competing co-exposures unresolved.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases (ages 33 and 55). Aminotransferase increased to 100 and 21 times normal; severe hepatitis with jaundice. Causality scored probable by Naranjo, CIOMS, and Maria-Victorino (M&V) scales. Hepatitis was followed by HCV RNA clearance. Suggested mechanism is a mitochondrial defect aggravated by co-factors (HCV, alcohol, drugs). Patients tolerated buprenorphine well at recommended sublingual doses; risk of acute hepatitis applies to IV intravenous misuse. Drug intended for treatment of opioid addiction.

raw_record.support_text: In the discussion the authors state that acetaminophen, like aspirin and phenacetin, has the potential for chronic abuse, and that all three patients took rather large amounts of acetaminophen during long periods and eventually developed biochemical and histologic evidence of a toxic hepatitis that resolved when acetaminophen use was discontinued.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic heavy-dose therapeutic use (5.2 to 6.5 g/day for weeks, termed chronic abuse); patients had underlying fever/pain (one with neoplasm); no alcohol use reported in Patient 3.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients (Patients 1-3) described. Patient 1 showed very severe pericentral necrosis on liver biopsy; Patient 2 had improved liver tests after initial withdrawal, but rechallenge with 5.2-6.5 g/day for 7 days raised SGOT to 121 IU and total bilirubin to 2.4 mg/dl with biopsy showing moderately severe pericentral necrosis and increased lipofuscin pigment (serum acetaminophen 37 µg/ml 24 h after stopping; SGOT fell to 27 IU in 2 days); Patient 3 had SGOT 400 IU, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dl, mild pericentral necrosis with lipofuscin, improving after withdrawal and normalizing within 4 weeks. Mechanism attributed to saturation of sulfate/glucuronide conjugation and cytochrome P450-dependent reactive electrophilic metabolite with glutathione depletion and covalent binding to hepatocyte membranes; alcohol/barbiturates may induce this pathway (Wright & Prescott retrospective overdose data cited).

The patient ingested approximately 5.0 to 6.5 g of acetaminophen daily for 6 to 8 weeks via multiple medications, with no alcohol abuse, P450-inducing medications, or massive dosing. raw_record.extra_details: 54-year-old woman; presented with altered mental status, lethargy, hepatic encephalopathy (asterixis, elevated ammonia up to 131 UM/L), INR 10.4, and severe coagulopathy. Peak AST 7816 U/L, ALT 3066 U/L on day 2, elevated total bilirubin up to 6.5 mg/dL, elevated alkaline phosphatase up to 183 U/L, and elevated creatinine (5.4 mg/dL on admission). Concurrent medications included carisoprodol, citalopram, fexofenadine, celecoxib, estradiol, and gabapentin. Patient denied alcohol use (confirmed by family), smoking, and fasting. Underlying medical history included hypercholesterolemia, depression, rheumatoid arthritis, gastric bypass, and cervical spine fusion.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old hemodialysis patient on colchicine for pericarditis (escalated from 0.5 mg to 1 mg once daily) developed diarrhea, confusion, and hypotension, followed by multiple-organ failure with leucopenia, acute liver failure, and rhabdomyolysis; he died 36 hours after ICU admission. The final diagnosis was colchicine poisoning, confirmed by characteristic mitotic arrests found at post-mortem examination of the esophagus, small bowel, and bone marrow.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic kidney disease/dialysis patient with kidney transplant and chronic allograft nephropathy; colchicine dose escalated from 0.5 mg to 1 mg o.d.; on cyclosporin, prednisolone, and rosuvastatin (possible drug-drug interactions).
raw_record.extra_details: Laboratory worsening: AST rose to 5330 IU/l, ALT to 1361 IU/l, LDH to 7260 IU/l, INR to 3.52 24 h after ICU admission. Colchicine poisoning staging described: initial GI symptoms (day 1), multiple-organ failure with bone-marrow suppression and myopathy (days 2–7), possible recovery. Mechanism: binds tubulin, disrupts microtubules. Diagnosis based on toxidrome; no correlation between plasma level and severity. Post-mortem mitotic arrests in esophagus, small bowel, bone marrow. Patient died 36 h after ICU admission from refractory shock.

raw_record.support_text: In a single case, a 38-year-old male with a six-year history of chronic methamphetamine addiction died from complications of prolonged substance abuse. Histopathological examination of his liver tissue, stained with hematoxylin and eosin, showed cholestasis with degeneration of hepatocytes and inflammatory cellular infiltrates; representative images showed hepatocyte cholestasis with bile salt accumulation, minimal portal mononuclear/lymphocyte inflammation, and no significant fibrosis. The discussion characterizes this as METH-induced hepatocellular damage and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic methamphetamine (METH) substance abuse/addiction in a single male patient who died; findings based on one autopsy case only.
raw_record.extra_details: 38-year-old male with a 6-year history of chronic methamphetamine addiction who died; liver histology showed cholestasis (bile salt accumulation inside hepatocytes), hepatocyte degeneration, minimal portal inflammation with mononuclear lymphocytes, and no significant fibrosis. Study also reported elevated liver enzymes including GGT (with diagnostic accuracy assessed via AUC and a meaningful cut-off value, interpreted with caution as GGT can rise with alcohol, medications, hepatitis or bile duct obstruction) and elevated blood urea as a sensitive marker of METH-related metabolic disturbance reflecting disrupted protein metabolism and impaired liver processing (METH-induced hepatotoxicity).

raw_record.support_text: In humans, cocaine hepatotoxicity was first reported in 1967, when chronic abusers of both heroin and cocaine had high serum transaminase levels, some with jaundice. One human case report describes fulminant hepatic failure and rhabdomyolysis from regular cocaine use, with histologic features of coagulative-type perivenular and midzonal necrosis and periportal microvesicular fatty changes. Another report of four patients described similar zone-III morphological changes as those seen in mice given cocaine.

raw_record.extra_details: First human report of cocaine hepatotoxicity was in 1967 (Marks and Chapple), describing high serum transaminases and some cases of jaundice in chronic heroin/cocaine abusers. One case report of fulminant hepatic failure with rhabdomyolysis from regular cocaine use, histology showing coagulative-type perivenular and midzonal necrosis and periportal microvesicular fatty changes. A second report of four patients showed similar zone-III morphological changes as in mice. Cocaine use is also associated with sudden deaths, cardiovascular disorders, and birth defects.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes an infant who received a chronic supratherapeutic overdose of acetaminophen (162 mg/kg/day of acetaminophen for several days, due to a maternal dosing error) and developed hepatotoxicity with markedly elevated transaminases (ALT 455 U/L, AST 1907 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 603 U/L), elevated total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, ammonia 135 µmol/L, and prolonged PT 53.5 s / INR 2.5. The child was treated with N-acetylcysteine for 18 doses, the liver enzymes returned to near normal by the fifth hospital day, and she made a complete recovery over 3 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic supratherapeutic dosing (162 mg/kg/day for several days) rather than acute single ingestion, in an infant; overdose resulted from a maternal medication-dose confusion between acetaminophen and amoxicillin. raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism attributed to formation of N-acetyl-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) via cytochrome P-450 mixed function oxidase pathway. Other labs included total protein 4.6 g/dL, albumin 3.1 g/dL, WBC 29,700/mm3 with 67% neutrophils, platelet 676,000/mm3, glucose 30 mg/dL, hypoglycemia with seizure corrected by IV glucose, BUN 8 mg/dL, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. Treated with N-acetylcysteine loading dose plus 18 total doses (oral regimen 140 mg/kg then 70 mg/kg q4h for 17 doses); transferred to regional transplant center; complete recovery over 3 weeks. Paper notes acute single-ingestion toxic dose of >140 mg/kg in adults or >150 mg/kg in a child.

raw_record.support_text: In this human case series of chronic hypervitaminosis A, cirrhotic patients had consumed significantly more vitamin A than patients without cirrhosis (mean daily intake 135 ± 31.4 × 10³ IU/day vs. 65.7 ± 9.2 × 10³ IU/day; mean total cumulative intake 366 ± 94 × 10⁶ IU vs. 91 ± 40 × 10⁶ IU). A minimal continuous daily consumption of 25,000 IU/day over 6 years produced similar histological liver lesions to 100,000 IU/day over 2½ years, and discontinuous consumption of 300,000 IU/day over 10 years also resulted in cirrhosis, attributing chronic high-dose vitamin A intake as the cause of the cirrhosis.

Duration of intake 9.3 ± 2.6 vs 3.8 ± 1.05 years (n.s.). Clinical features included hepatomegaly (18), splenomegaly (14), ascites (9), icterus (8); plasma retinol below normal in 4, above normal in 9 of 24 cases; moderate transaminase elevation and slight anicteric cholestasis; mild-severe hepatocellular-function alteration with ¹⁴C-aminopyrine breath test 2.21%±0.21% (normal ≥2.8%); elevated IgG 125%, IgA 146%, IgM 218%; esophageal varices in 21 patients (16 grade 3) and bleeding varices in 10.

raw_record.support_text: Serum samples from 28 transplant-free survivors and 30 nonsurvivors of acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver failure were obtained from the Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) biorepository. ALF was diagnosed by ALFSG investigators (INR >= 1.5, hepatic encephalopathy, illness < 26 weeks, absence of chronic liver disease), and APAP toxicity was determined as the etiology based on patient-reported history of APAP overdose, a detectable APAP level documenting ingestion, and aminotransferase levels >= 1000 IU/l. Ten healthy volunteers with reported recent therapeutic APAP exposure served as controls for the effects of APAP itself.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cohort restricted to APAP overdose-induced ALF patients enrolled in the ALFSG biorepository; the 10 control volunteers had only recent therapeutic APAP exposure and no liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: ALF definition: INR >= 1.5, hepatic encephalopathy, duration of illness < 26 weeks, absence of chronic liver disease. APAP etiology determined from patient-reported APAP overdose history, detectable APAP level documenting ingestion, and aminotransferase >= 1000 IU/l. Study cohorts: 28 transplant-free survivors and 30 nonsurvivors of APAP-induced ALF; 10 healthy volunteers with recent therapeutic APAP exposure. Clinical phenotype: acute liver failure (acute hepatic failure) in the overdose cohort. Paper is a methods/biomarker-discovery proteomics study (dataset PXD029576); APAP is the established causal agent in the studied population.

raw_record.support_text: In this large, single centre cohort study of severe paracetamol-induced acute liver injury, patients with staggered paracetamol overdoses had reduced survival compared with single intentional overdoses, despite ingestion of significantly lower total amounts of paracetamol. Delay to hospital presentation at >24 h following overdose was independently associated with increased mortality or requirement for orthotopic liver transplantation following single time point overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cohort restricted to severe paracetamol overdoses requiring tertiary-level care at a single liver transplant unit (Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit), representing severe cases (overall mortality 32.7%), with selection bias that may limit generalizability to emergency-department overdose presentations.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospectively defined cohort of 344 paracetamol ALF patients, analysed overall and separately for single time point (n=211) and staggered (n=90) overdoses. King's College poor prognostic criteria (KCC) sensitivity was 89.9% (95% CI 85.8-92.7) for single time point vs 77.6% for staggered overdoses; overall mortality rate 32.7%. Staggered overdoses showed reduced survival despite lower total paracetamol dose ingested. Delayed presentation (>24 h) following single time point overdose was an independent risk factor for death or OLT. Concomitant P450 enzyme inducers or recent fasting were noted to increase hepatotoxicity risk after repeated ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, including a case series by Bray et al describing seven cases of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity in patients (ages 16-29) on phenytoin therapy, of whom six who did not receive NAC died from fulminant hepatic failure and the seventh, who received NAC, survived. Additional reported cases (Minton et al, McClements et al) describe acetaminophen overdose in suicide attempts leading to liver failure, hepatic encephalopathy, and in one case death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent chronic phenytoin therapy; cases were adolescents and young adults (ages 14-29); overdose by suicide attempt.
raw_record.extra_details: Bray et al: seven cases of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity on phenytoin therapy; six without NAC died of fulminant hepatic failure, one with NAC survived. Minton et al: 20-year-old male on chronic phenytoin ingested an unknown quantity (serum acetaminophen 94 µg/ml, below toxic threshold on nomogram), developed liver failure, renal failure and hepatic encephalopathy and died. McClements et al: 14-year-old boy on phenytoin ingested 45 g acetaminophen, AST 1630 U/L, treated with cimetidine without NAC, developed hepatic encephalopathy and recovered. Index case lab values: ALT >6600 U/L, AST >8800 U/L, total bilirubin 12 mg/dl, INR 30, pH 7.2. Phenytoin was discussed as a possible enzyme inducer but Rumack concluded it did not enhance acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase I trial, paracetamol was administered at escalating doses up to 20 g/m² in combination with BCNU and NAC. Grade IV AST elevations occurred in two patients and constituted dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) in the 20 g/m² cohort. One of these patients also developed grade III prothrombin time prolongation and grade IV decreased level of consciousness. The paper attributes the persistently elevated paracetamol levels at 24 h (71 µg/ml) to impaired drug clearance secondary to liver injury caused by paracetamol.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate high-dose investigational (supratherapeutic) use in a phase I trial at doses up to 20 g/m², combined with carmustine (BCNU) and N-acetylcysteine (NAC); one affected patient received numerous concomitant Parkinson's disease medications that may have altered paracetamol metabolism.
raw_record.extra_details: DLT in the 20 g/m² cohort comprised grade IV AST elevation in two patients, one of whom also had grade III prothrombin time prolongation and grade IV decreased consciousness, then aspirated and developed pneumonia requiring intubation (the latter scored as grade IV pulmonary toxicity). Affected patient had peak serum paracetamol 392 µg/ml at 4 h and 71 µg/ml at 24 h post-ingestion with persistently elevated serum levels; another patient also had elevated levels (>20 µg/ml) at 24 h. raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old man developed jaundice of the skin and sclerae by the sixth hospital day after intentionally inhaling an unknown quantity of laboratory-grade chloroform from a soaked towel while intoxicated with beer. A percutaneous liver biopsy on the 11th day, 10 days after chloroform exposure, showed resolving centrilobular necrosis with fatty droplets in mid-zonal surviving cells, dropout of hepatocytes, and dilated sinusoids lined by Kupffer cells. The jaundice rapidly resolved and the patient was discharged in good condition.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate inhalational abuse of laboratory-grade chloroform (unusual route, non-therapeutic self-exposure); concurrent alcohol ingestion (serum ethanol 112 mg/dl); no suicidal intent; healthy young male without prior exposure to chloroform or recent acetaminophen use.
raw_record.extra_details: Unknown quantity inhaled from a chloroform-soaked towel after drinking beer; jaundice developed by hospital day 6, resolved rapidly; liver biopsy on day 11 showed resolving centrilobular necrosis, hepatocyte dropout, fatty droplets in surviving cells, dilated sinusoids lined by Kupffer cells, and inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils, eosinophils, and few plasma cells; elevated admission total serum bilirubin with initially normal hepatocellular enzymes attributed partly to mild intravascular hemolysis (low haptoglobin 2 mg/dl, elevated free hemoglobin 29.9 mg/dl); negative hepatitis B surface antigen; patient discharged on day 12 and remained well at one-month follow-up; other features included metabolic acidosis, hypotension, bradycardia, ventricular tachycardia, aspiration pneumonia.

raw_record.support_text: In Case 190, a 17-year-old girl who was reported to have taken a whole bottle of acetaminophen 4 days earlier presented with altered mental status and markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 5441 IU/L, ALT 9559 IU/L), bilirubin 4.9 mg/dL, PT 25 s, INR 4.33, and ammonia 183 µmol/L; she developed progressive neurologic deterioration and worsening hepatic dysfunction and was pronounced brain dead within 24 hours. In Case 196 a pregnant woman with a serum acetaminophen concentration of 465 µg/mL died of multisystem organ failure 48 hours after a presumed overdose of up to 100 acetaminophen tablets, and her stillborn infant's death was attributed to massive maternal acetaminophen overdose. In Case 214 a 41-year-old man who ingested an unknown amount of acetaminophen 48 hours earlier had an acetaminophen concentration of 180 µg/mL, total bilirubin 10.6 mg/dL, AST 8272 U/L, ALT 7400 U/L, and PT 46.4 s, and died of hepatic failure on the eighth hospital day despite N-acetylcysteine and bioartificial liver support.

Case 196: pregnant woman, serum acetaminophen 465 µg/mL (post-delivery 398 µg/mL), up to 100 tablets for back/labor pain; DIC, multisystem organ failure, death; stillborn infant death attributed to massive maternal overdose. Case 214: 41-year-old man, acetaminophen 180 µg/mL, total bilirubin 10.6 mg/dL, AST 8272 U/L, ALT 7400 U/L, PT 46.4 s, PTT 40.5 s; treated with oral N-acetylcysteine and 5 days of bioartificial liver support; died of hepatic failure on hospital day 8. raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective case series of patients requiring tertiary referral after paracetamol overdose, most patients (96.6%) had evidence of acute liver dysfunction defined by a PT≥25 s. The paper frames paracetamol poisoning as a cause of hepatic injury (toxic metabolites generate liver injury monitored by rising hepatic transaminases and prothrombin time) and reports KCHC poor-prognosis criteria (17.6–36.5% across ingestion-to-presentation intervals) and mortality in this overdose cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate paracetamol overdose (acute single and staggered ingestion); highly selected population with severe poisoning referred to a tertiary liver unit; acute liver dysfunction defined by PT≥25 s (96.6% of the cohort).
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury monitored by hepatic transaminase rises (referral ALT 1960±264 IU/l presenting ≤24 h up to 7887±875 IU/l presenting >48 h) and prothrombin time; toxicity attributed to toxic paracetamol metabolites generated by local metabolism; KCHC poor prognosis 17.6% (≤24 h), 36.5% (>24–48 h), 26.2% (>48 h); mortality 15.3%, 28.3%, 23.8% by ingestion-to-presentation interval; stated single paracetamol doses ~27–39 g in acute ingestions without a dose-response relation to renal risk. No biochemical pattern classification was stated.

raw_record.support_text: In the discussion of this liver unit series, the authors state that paracetamol poisoning is associated with serious hepatotoxicity when patients who have taken a significant overdose are not treated early, and that early treatment with N-acetylcysteine (within 12 hours) is almost completely successful in averting significant liver damage. This constitutes an explicit human attribution of hepatotoxicity to paracetamol overdose, set against the presented series of 92 consecutive patients admitted with paracetamol poisoning, 10 of whom underwent liver transplantation and 6 of listed-but-not-transplanted patients who died.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate paracetamol overdose (poisoning) with significant overdose; several patients also had established renal failure requiring dialysis; a number presented late or were not treated early with N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: 92 consecutive patients admitted to the liver unit with paracetamol poisoning. 17 were considered transplant candidates; 10 underwent transplantation (median 79 h from poisoning, range 64-98); 7 were listed but not transplanted, 6 of whom died (median 98 h from poisoning). Early N-acetylcysteine treatment (<12 h) was almost completely successful in averting significant liver damage; only 7 of 92 presented within 12 h of poisoning, and the 3 treated at presentation survived. Hepatotoxicity averted with early treatment, but delayed treatment is associated with increasing severity.

raw_record.extra_details: Fourteen autopsy cases of paraquat poisoning. Laboratory: five of twelve patients had elevated serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (cholestasis); all but one patient showed laboratory evidence of liver cell damage, most marked in patients surviving more than 8 days. Histopathology: liver weight 450-1,940 g, preserved lobular architecture, centrolobular (coagulation) necrosis, fatty metamorphosis, acidophilic and hydropic degeneration, feathery degeneration, bile plugs and bile-filled Kupffer cells, bile duct injury, and portal inflammatory infiltration. Seven of eight patients dying within 4 days of ingestion had hepatocytic injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of deliberate self-injection of T-61®, a veterinary euthanasia agent containing embutramide, mebezoniom and tetracaine dissolved in the organic solvent dimethylformamide (DMF), and states that delayed hepatotoxicity observed in nonfatal cases can be attributed to the solvent DMF or its metabolites. In the present case, the injection of about 0.12 to 0.16 mL/kg resulted in moderate hepatic impairment that peaked on day 14; the contribution of other factors such as sepsis, renal failure, parenteral feeding and drugs could not be excluded but was considered unlikely.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate self-injection (overdose) of the veterinary euthanasia agent T-61® in a non-therapeutic setting; competing factors (sepsis, renal failure, parenteral feeding, concurrent drugs) could not be excluded but were judged unlikely.
raw_record.extra_details: DMF-delayed hepatotoxicity is described as DMF-induced hepatotoxicity, also documented in the literature with liver function abnormalities and fulminant hepatic failure within 3-22 d following T-61® at DMF doses of 0.18-0.6 mL/kg. Present case dose 0.12-0.16 mL/kg produced moderate hepatic impairment peaking on day 14. Liver biopsy (electron microscopy) showed lipid-containing lysosomes and abundant vesicular endoplasmic reticulum. DMF is metabolized to N-hydroxymethyl-N-methylformamide (NMF), NMF and N-acetyl-S-(N-methyl-carbamoyl) cysteine identified in urine; significant NMF was found in hemodialysis and CAVH fluids. Authors question N-acetylcysteine since toxicity does not appear related to lysosomal destruction, lipoperoxidation or glutathione depletion. Acute renal failure also developed and recovered within three weeks.

raw_record.support_text: This case series describes 177 patients hospitalized for acetaminophen deliberate self-poisoning (overdose), all managed with stomach wash, activated charcoal, and intravenous N-acetylcysteine after estimating serum acetaminophen concentrations, which reflects management of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity risk. The study reports that overall two patients were admitted to the intensive care unit, but no patient died or needed a liver transplant as a result of the acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate self-poisoning (overdose) context; in this cohort no patient died or required liver transplantation as a result of the overdose.

raw_record.support_text: In India many rodenticides contain hepatotoxic drugs leading to acute liver failure, of which yellow phosphorus (in 3% yellow phosphorus rodenticide paste) is most lethal. A consecutive series of 101 patients admitted with alleged yellow phosphorus rodenticide paste poisoning was analyzed; 42 (41%) developed acute liver injury, 21 (21%) developed acute liver failure, and the overall mortality was 19%. Conclusion states that a lethal dosage and late presentation led to development of acute liver failure and mortality.

raw_record.extra_details: 101 consecutive patients over 6 months; 62% female, 38% male; age 15-65 yr (peak 20-30 yr); ingestion mode: 34% raw, 30% with water, 20% with alcohol, 17% with food; first symptom <6h in 41%, 6-12h in 42%, >12h in 17%; care sought within 3h in 46%, 3-10h in 41%, after 10h in 13%. Liver injury spectrum: acute liver injury 42 (41%), acute liver failure 21 (21%), acute kidney injury 19%, multiple organ failure 19%, 3 acute pancreatitis, 2 myocarditis, 1 atrial fibrillation. INR <2 in 69, 2-3 in 11, >3 in 21; MELD <10 in 9, 11-20 in 30, 21-30 in 35, >30 in 27; all MELD >40 died. Overall mortality 19% (22% females, 13% males); 82 recovered (mean stay 8.88 days). raw_record.support_text: In the present series of epileptic patients who took paracetamol overdose, one patient who received NAC 8 h after overdose developed fulminant hepatic failure and died, and two others given NAC 8 and 12 h after ingestion developed fulminant hepatic failure and survived. The effectiveness of NAC as an antidote against paracetamol overdose is described as well established, and the authors note the NAC treatment threshold recommendations for overdose. They report features of evolving hepatic necrosis (rising prothrombin time or development of encephalopathy).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Epileptic patients taking anticonvulsant drugs; some received NAC; acknowledged potentiation by concurrent sodium valproate and barbiturate co-therapy via increased reactive-metabolite formation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol hepatotoxicity in the overdose setting; one death and two cases of fulminant hepatic failure with survival among NAC-treated epileptics. NAC is well established as an antidote when given within 10 h of overdose. Authors propose NAC for all anticonvulsant-treated overdose patients if plasma paracetamol is detectable or with rising prothrombin time/encephalopathy. Mechanism discussion includes potentiation by enzyme induction, macrophage activation, and competition with glucuronidation.

raw_record.support_text: In a US ALFSG prospective study of 275 consecutive patients with acetaminophen (ACM)-related acute liver failure (ALF), the annual incidence of ALF due to ACM rose from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2004. Nearly 50% of cases were nonintentional 'therapeutic misadventures', with 48% of ALF-ACM cases nonintentional; most were taking excessive doses, about 50% of the nonintentional group consuming 4-10 g/day and 7% of the entire cohort ingesting less than 4 g/day. The majority (81%) of nonintentional overdose patients had an acute or chronic painful medical condition and 63% were taking a narcotic-ACM analgesic chronically.

raw_record.extra_details: US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) prospective data, 275 consecutive ACM-related ALF patients. Annual ALF incidence due to ACM rose from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2004. 48% were nonintentional overdose cases; ~50% of these consumed 4-10 g/day and 7% of the entire cohort ingested <4 g/day. 81% of nonintentional patients had acute or chronic painful conditions, 63% used narcotic-ACM analgesics chronically. Nonintentional patients had lower serum ACM (median 106 vs 554 µmol/L, P<0.001), lower ALT (3319 vs 5326 U/L, P<0.001), and more advanced encephalopathy (53% vs 39% grade 3-4). Outcomes: 9% vs 7% required liver transplantation, 28% vs 29% fatal. 87% of intentional and 95% of nonintentional patients received N-acetylcysteine. Reference to 60,000 intentional ACM overdose cases/year in the US with 500 fatalities.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective series of 207 patients presenting to the emergency department with acetaminophen overdose, 52 (25%) received hepatology consults due to the severity of their liver injuries, and 36 were transferred to the liver transplant unit. Of 36 LTU patients, 12 were ill enough to be considered for transplant; five were approved, three underwent successful liver transplantation, and two died before they could be transplanted. Across the cohort, liver injury took the form of acute liver injury hepatitis, fulminant liver failure was present in 16 LTU patients (44.4%), and there were two deaths, establishing acetaminophen overdose as a cause of severe human hepatotoxicity including acute liver failure, transplantation, and death.

raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 207 acetaminophen overdose patients; NAC was administered to 135 with known ingestion timing (41 first dose within 8 hrs, 31 within 8-24 hrs, 6 within 24-72 hrs, 2 after 72 hrs). LTU vs non-LTU comparisons showed higher tablet amounts (90.7±94.0 vs 39.1±36.2), peak ALT (8235±6344 vs 667±2008), peak AST, acute liver injury hepatitis (94.4% vs 10.3%), fulminant liver failure (44.4% vs 0%), coagulopathy, acute renal failure, and encephalopathy. Three patients received liver transplantation (ALT peaks 8100, 13900, 8720); two patients died (one after 75 g acetaminophen; the other after 150 tablets). One fatal case also ingested alcohol and opiates.

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective population-based cohort, 2010–2017, Iceland (only and largest university hospital). 542 cases identified via serum paracetamol concentrations (≥66 µmol/L). raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients with severe paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity managed in intensive care, survival was 63% following a deliberate overdose and 58% after therapeutic misadventure. Acute liver failure complications were frequent: grade III–IV encephalopathy occurred in 58% and 55% of the therapeutic misadventure and deliberate overdose groups respectively, 54% (278/515) of deliberate overdose cases and 56% (21/38) of the therapeutic misadventure group required renal dialysis, and 37 patients fulfilled transplant criteria and received a transplant. Survival, need for inotropic support, transplant criteria fulfilment, and encephalopathy were independent of both the amount of paracetamol taken and the level of alcohol consumption.

raw_record.support_text: The paper examines phospho-JNK expression in human liver tissue from cases of paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (ALF). Compared with a normal control human liver, cytoplasmic and dense nuclear phospho-JNK staining in hepatocytes (around central veins) was markedly increased in paracetamol-induced ALF human livers (n = 8 cases in each group), establishing acetaminophen (paracetamol) as a cause of acute liver failure in humans, consistent with a paracetamol poisoning context.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Human tissue assessment derived from paracetamol-induced ALF cases (n=8), in a paracetamol-poisoning context; the majority of the supporting experiments are in a murine model.
raw_record.extra_details: Synonyms: acetaminophen. Mechanism focus is hepatic JNK (c-Jun N-terminal kinase) activation that precedes onset of hepatocyte death; peak JNK activity 2 h after paracetamol, peak serum ALT 5 h after injection in mice (350 mg/kg IP). JNK inhibitors SP600125 (ATP-competitive) and D-JNKI1 (peptide inhibitor), given 1 h before paracetamol, potently inhibited phospho-JNK, markedly reduced mortality over 72 h, reduced histological liver injury and hepatic necrosis scores, and reduced hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis in mice. Delayed JNK inhibitor administration was more effective than NAC in limiting liver injury. Human ALF tissue showed increased hepatocyte cytoplasmic and nuclear phospho-JNK.

raw_record.support_text: Of 110 subjects with indeterminate acute liver failure (ALF), 20 (18%) had serum APAP-CYS adduct levels ≥1.0 nmol/mL (median 9.2 nmol/mL), suggesting that the ALF was secondary to an acetaminophen overdose; these 20 (Group 2) were similar to 188 clinically defined acetaminophen-overdose control patients (Group 3), with median ALT values >4,000 IU/L and lower bilirubin concentrations than adduct-negative indeterminates.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Indeterminate ALF patients identified as acetaminophen overdose on the basis of serum APAP-CYS adducts ≥1.0 nmol/mL; in 12 of 20 cases retrospective evidence made APAP a possible or likely ('ill-defined overdose') diagnosis, and 8 were clinically unrecognized acetaminophen overdoses.
raw_record.extra_details: From 1,115 registry cases, 158 (14%) were indeterminate ALF; 110 had day 1-2 sera and 20 (18%) were APAP-CYS positive (median 9.2 nmol/mL; cutoff ≥1.0 nmol/mL, quantitation limit 0.03 µM). Of 199 clinically defined APAP overdose sera, 188 (94.5%) were above the toxicity threshold (median 11.1 nmol/mL). Adduct-positive groups had median ALT 4,025 (Group 2) and 5,156 IU/L (Group 3) with bilirubin <10 mg/dL in 90% and 93%. In a previous study a cutoff ≥1.1 nmol/mL at ALT>1000 IU/L gave 96.8% sensitivity and 95% specificity. Assay: gel filtration, protease digestion, APAP-CYS adducts by HPLC-EC.

raw_record.support_text: In 1968 Hashimoto et al. described a 48-year-old schizophrenic woman who drank 500 ml of carbon tetrachloride. She became acutely ill, developed progressive toxicity with oliguria and coma, and died 2 days later. Autopsy examination of the liver revealed massive centrilobular and midzonal necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion of 500 ml carbon tetrachloride (supratherapeutic / self-poisoning).
raw_record.extra_details: Case reported by Hashimoto et al. 1968 in a 48-year-old schizophrenic woman; acute onset, oliguria, coma, death 2 days later. Autopsy showed massive centrilobular and midzonal hepatic necrosis. Carbon tetrachloride caused a large increase in neutral lipid fraction of total liver lipids, with conjugated diene configurations indicating extensive peroxidative degeneration of hepatic-cell structural lipids similar to that demonstrated in rats. Thioacetamide hepatotoxicity and postmortem autolysis studies in rats suggested the lipid peroxidation was not due to necrobiologic changes or autolysis.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old man with a history of chronic analgesics, alcohol, and illicit drug abuse developed acute liver failure in relationship with the ingestion of largely supra-therapeutic doses of acetaminophen over the days preceding admission. The patient received the classical N-acetylcysteine treatment regimen for acetaminophen overdose, but his neurological condition worsened to grade IV encephalopathy with persistent coagulopathy (factor V <10%). He fulfilled criteria for liver transplantation, but this was rejected after psychiatric evaluation; his serum unconjugated bilirubin increased progressively until death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion of largely supra-therapeutic doses over the days preceding admission; history of chronic analgesics, alcohol, and illicit drug abuse; liver transplantation rejected after psychiatric evaluation.
raw_record.extra_details: Received standard N-acetylcysteine overdose regimen; progressed to grade IV encephalopathy; persistent coagulopathy with factor V <10%; progressive increase in serum unconjugated bilirubin until death without evidence of hemolysis, with Gilbert's syndrome excluded; attributed mechanism is damage to endoplasmic reticulum in relation to centrilobular necrosis caused by toxic metabolism of acetaminophen; the paper notes that a persistent unconjugated bilirubin rise may reflect defective bilirubin conjugation and that the ratio of unconjugated/conjugated bilirubin has insufficient data to serve as a prognostic factor.

raw_record.support_text: A 65 year old man had acute hepatitis, thought to be caused by exposure to 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D), a selective weedkiller. The patient ingested 2,4-D as a result of habitual licking of his golf ball. Clinical and histological data together with a challenge test confirmed the diagnosis of 'golf ball liver'.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion via habitual licking of golf ball (oral herbicide exposure, not therapeutic use); 65-year-old retired consultant engineer; no other drugs, alcohol, travel, or infection.
raw_record.extra_details: Two-month history of lethargy, two-week history of dark urine and upper abdominal discomfort, jaundice. Liver function at admission: bilirubin 142 µmol/l, AST 205 U/l, ALT 380 U/l, γ-GT 210 U/l, ALP 412 U/l. Liver biopsy showed preserved architecture with pronounced canalicular and intracellular cholestasis plus acute hepatitis features (lobular and portal inflammation, periportal oedema, mixed infiltrate with mononuclear cells and eosinophils). Viral, bacterial, and parasitic serology negative. Dechallenge: after ceasing golf ball licking, liver function tests returned to normal within two months. Labelled 'golf ball liver'.

raw_record.support_text: The patient described in this case report had a severe episode of acute liver failure following monochlorobenzene ingestion. Although factor V decreased to 14% of normal (a value seen in fatal fulminant hepatitis B), encephalopathy did not develop and the patient ultimately recovered. Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) was administered, but no beneficial effect could be demonstrated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion/poisoning case; chronic alcohol consumption may have contributed to severity of the liver lesions.
raw_record.extra_details: Erythema was noted and was likely related to monochlorobenzene ingestion, not phototoxic (face uninvolved). Factor V fell to 14% of normal; no encephalopathy developed and the patient recovered. Treated with prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) with no demonstrable benefit. Proposed mechanism: metabolism likely similar to bromobenzene, via cytochrome P450 to a reactive epoxide causing reactive-metabolite formation and glutathione depletion; alcohol-induced CYP2E1 induction may have exaggerated hepatotoxicity. Monochlorobenzene blood concentrations exceeded benzene concentrations in exhaled breath.

raw_record.support_text: Chloroform intoxication produces hepatic injury seen after two to five days, which is the result of liver cell necrosis; prothrombin time and transaminase values are markedly elevated while bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase tend to be minimally abnormal. Alcohol or barbiturates that induce hepatic microsomal enzymes increase chloroform-induced liver cell damage, whereas enzyme inhibitors such as disulfiram prevent hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion/poisoning context; in this report chloroform was voluntarily inhaled or ingested at 'chloroform parties', either accidentally or as a suicidal gesture.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 19-year-old boy who ingested chloroform; liver function tests showed SGOT rising to 8,080 IU, SGPT to 10,250 IU, and LDH to 9,280 IU by days 3-4, with total bilirubin up to 2.7 mg/100 ml and prolonged prothrombin time (patient 19.3 sec vs control 11.9 sec); values normalized by day 90. Hepatic injury is attributed to liver cell necrosis from toxic metabolites formed by hepatic enzymes rather than direct injury; alcohol/barbiturate enzyme induction worsens the injury and disulfiram prevents hepatotoxicity. Also associated with renal damage appearing within 24-48 hours.

raw_record.support_text: Three adolescents with a history of drug abuse developed acute hepatic injury after inhaling Carbona cleaning fluid, a commercial preparation containing trichloroethylene. Hepatic biopsies in two patients showed acute centrilobular necrosis, and both also showed mild centrilobular fibrosis, probably from previous injury from trichloroethylene exposure. The authors attribute the hepatic injury to inhalation of the trichloroethylene-containing solvent.

raw_record.extra_details: Three cases reported; two patients had acute hepatic and renal damage (renal tubular necrosis) and one had centrilobular hepatic necrosis; hepatic biopsies showed acute centrilobular necrosis and mild centrilobular fibrosis; icterus present; electrocardiographic and electroencephalographic abnormalities also noted.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion explicitly attributes liver injury to acute arsenic poisoning: 'Hepatic injury due to acute arsenic poisoning is uncommon,' noting that large doses may induce massive hepatic necrosis or Milian's syndrome (a hypersensitivity reaction with fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, arthralgia, eosinophilia and hepatitis), that arsphenamine-related damage shows intrahepatic cholestasis, and that hepatic veno-occlusive disease has been related to acute arsenic poisoning. In both reported cases, liver biopsy after acute arsenic poisoning showed hepatocytic alterations with increased mitotic activity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional (homicidal) acute arsenic poisoning rather than therapeutic use; both patients poisoned by their household companion. Case 2 also had acute pancreatitis, tubular necrosis, rhabdomyolysis and polyneuropathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (37-year-old man, day 1 1978): acute poisoning suspected via urinary arsenic 10 mg/24 h; liver biopsy on day 11 showed preserved architecture, portal infiltration, hepatocytic ballooning, granular cytoplasm, acidophilic bodies, enlarged nuclei, cholestasis and increased mitotic activity; PC10 positive in 18% (0.3% control), Ki 67 in 15% (0.1% control); AST peaked ~278-234 IU/l, ALT ~368 IU/l, prothrombin fell to 30%; treated with dopamine, haemodialysis and BAL; recovered and discharged day 26. Case 2 (26-year-old man, day 1 1990): abdominal pain/vomiting, liver biopsy on day 8 suggested acute arsenic intoxication confirmed day 9 by urinary arsenic 867 µg/ml (normal <25 µg/ml); biopsy showed granular hepatocytic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, multiple mitotic figures, acidophilic bodies, periportal cholestasis; PC10 8.4%, Ki 67 6%; treated with BAL and 2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid; died on day 25 from cerebral oedema due to meningeal bleeding. Discussion also notes large-dose arsenic may cause massive hepatic necrosis, Milian's syndrome (hypersensitivity hepatitis), and hepatic veno-occlusive disease.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old female ingested 54 tablets of ferrous sulfate (358 mg/kg elemental iron) during an intentional overdose following a conflict. She presented with blood-tinged emesis, abdominal tenderness, serum iron >1000 µg/dL, and elevated liver enzymes. Her liver function worsened with massive transaminase elevations (AST 10378 U/L, ALT 9045 U/L), profound coagulopathy (INR >13), and stage 2 hepatic encephalopathy; she underwent emergent deceased donor liver transplantation on day 4, with explanted liver histology showing massive acute panlobular hepatic necrosis, centrilobular congestion/hemorrhage, and cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional overdose in an adolescent (16-year-old female) with depression; co-ingested omeprazole, diphenhydramine, and ibuprofen; treated with deferoxamine and IV N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 358 mg/kg elemental iron; serum iron >1000 µg/dL initially falling to 404 µg/dL; initial AST 67/ALT 79 U/L and INR 1.1 rising to AST 10378/ALT 9045 U/L, INR >13, ammonia 137 µg/dL with stage 2 hepatic encephalopathy by day 3; transplant on day 4; explant showed massive acute panlobular hepatic necrosis with centrilobular congestion/hemorrhage and cholestasis; recovered with normal graft function at one year. Discussion notes hepatotoxicity is dose-related, with single-center study of 73 iron-intoxicated patients of whom 13 developed hepatotoxicity (AST/ALT >5x ULN), 9 severe, 5 died; serum iron >1000 µg/dL associated with clinically important hepatotoxicity while <700 µg/dL within 12 h unlikely hepatotoxic; coagulopathy can occur without hepatotoxicity via thrombin inhibition; fifth-stage GI strictures/fistulas not seen in these patients.

raw_record.support_text: Two hundred intentional paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose cases were identified (median dose ingested 50 g, IQR 45–60 g, median time to presentation 3.5 h). Twenty-eight (14%) patients developed hepatotoxicity, with a further 9 (5%) having a peak ALT between 150 and <1000 U/L. Those who developed hepatotoxicity had a significantly longer time to treatment (13.9 h) than those who did not (6 h, p<0.001). One patient required a liver transplant despite acetylcysteine being commenced 2.5 h post-ingestion; there was one death unrelated to paracetamol ingestion. The 200 patients were identified across four sites with comparable data.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional paracetamol self-poisoning (median dose 50 g, 0.7 g/kg); co-ingestion of ethanol (27%) and gut-slowing medications (33%) in a portion of patients; treated with acetylcysteine in 193 (97%) of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 28/200 (14%) developed hepatotoxicity and 9/200 (5%) had peak ALT 150–1000 U/L. Median time to treatment 13.9 h in hepatotoxic patients vs 6 h in non-hepatotoxic (p<0.001). Six patients who developed hepatotoxicity had treatment within 8 h (paracetamol ratios 2.7, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.5, 5.8); one patient required liver transplant despite acetylcysteine started 2.5 h post-ingestion; one death unrelated to paracetamol. Median paracetamol ratio 1.9; 79 (40%) had initial concentration more than double the 150 mg/L 4-h nomogram line. Activated charcoal within 4 h associated with 45% decrease in paracetamol ratio (adjusted RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.43–0.69).

raw_record.support_text: This study concerns paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning. Among 16 severely poisoned patients with 4 h paracetamol concentrations above 300 µg/ml who received only supportive therapy, all suffered severe liver damage, 3 died in hepatic failure, and 4 developed acute renal failure. The severity of poisoning was reflected by the average urinary recovery of 18·6 g of paracetamol despite incomplete collections. These findings attribute severe liver injury to paracetamol overdose in humans.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional poisonings/overdose (average urinary recovery of 18·6 g paracetamol); among the 16 supportive-therapy-only patients with 4 h paracetamol concentrations above 300 µg/ml, all developed severe liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 of 16 supportive-therapy patients died in hepatic failure and 4 developed acute renal failure. Cysteamine given within 10 h of ingestion protected against severe liver damage; cysteamine, methionine (3 failures in patients treated within 10 h), and penicillamine are discussed as protectants/treatments, not as causal agents.

raw_record.support_text: In an observational study (n=48, mean age 29) of rat killer compound (yellow phosphorus) poison consumption, all patients developed acute liver failure; 29 (60%) underwent therapeutic plasma exchange based on the presence of acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity. Despite plasma exchange, mortality was 18%. Factors associated with poor outcome included no gastric lavage within 2 hours, hemodynamic instability, hepatic encephalopathy, high toxin dose, higher admission lactate (>4), delayed presentation (>72 hours), and worsening liver/renal function despite plasma exchange. Case formulation of the toxin appeared less toxic than paste.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional rat killer (yellow phosphorus) poison consumption; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Rat killer compound (yellow phosphorus) is a protoplasmic poison causing multiorgan failure; dose >1 mg/kg is stated as nearly always fatal. Mean age 29; 50% (n=24) presented within 24 hours of consumption; 19% (n=9) had bone marrow toxicity at presentation (most commonly neutropenia with increased absolute monocyte count). 29 (60%) patients underwent therapeutic plasma exchange for acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity; 3 developed hypotension during the procedure; number of sessions was based on LFT and coagulopathy. 18% mortality despite plasma exchange. Indication for exchange: acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity; new-onset diabetes insipidus seen in 4 patients. Cake formulation appeared less toxic than paste.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of 72 paraquat-poisoned patients, of the 52 survivors all had renal damage, 47 had toxic hepatitis, 7 pulmonary oedema and pneumonitis, 4 pneumomediastinum, and 1 pneumothorax. Five deaths were attributed to multiple organ failure, mainly hepatic and renal.
