raw_record.extra_details: 72 poisoned patients; 47 of 52 survivors had toxic hepatitis (C0019193). Raised ALT (mean 305 IU/l, range 26-1290), raised alkaline phosphatase (mean 157 IU/l, range 62-448), hyperbilirubinaemia (mean 43 mg/l, range 13-262). 5 deaths from multiple organ failure mainly hepatic and renal; 12 deaths from pulmonary complications. Overall mortality since the dexamethasone/cyclophosphamide regimen fell to 28%; historical 68% mortality prior to the regimen. Therapy included steroids (dexamethasone), cyclophosphamide, Fuller's earth, charcoal, lavage.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that even when paraquat (PQ) is ingested in a small amount it is extremely toxic and that immediately after ingestion the compound accumulates in different organs, with a spectrum of complications—including gastrointestinal injuries, respiratory failure, renal failure, hepatotoxicity, and lung fibrosis—evolving over time; the suggested mechanism of toxicity is production of reactive oxygen species causing cell damage. raw_record.support_text: The abstract reports three cases of massive acetaminophen (APAP) overdose with an unusual double-hump APAP concentration pattern. A 38-year-old woman ingested 2 g hydrocodone/65 g acetaminophen, a 25-year-old man ingested 2 g diphenhydramine/26 g APAP, and a 16-year-old boy ingested 5 g diphenhydramine and 100 g APAP; each developed liver injury, with peak AST values of 1603, 1153, and 8686 IU/L and peak INR of 1.6, 2.1, and 5.9, respectively. The paper states that patients with double-hump APAP concentrations may be at risk for liver injury, with AST elevations and peaks occurring later than typical for acute APAP overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: The study states that acetaminophen (APAP) overdose results in hepatic injury, attributed to increased production of the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), and that N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is highly effective at preventing hepatotoxicity if given within 8 h of acute overdose. In a retrospective cohort of 1425 APAP overdose cases, 104 met the definition of massive APAP overdose (single acute overdose with an APAP concentration exceeding 300 mcg/mL at 4 h post-ingestion); 25 (24%) of these developed hepatotoxicity, and receiving NAC after 8 h carried 5.5-fold higher crude odds of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive APAP overdose, defined as single acute overdose with APAP concentration exceeding 300 mcg/mL at 4 h post-ingestion, reported to a regional poison center.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective single-center cohort (2010-2019) of 1425 APAP overdoses; 104 met massive overdose criteria; 25 (24%) developed hepatotoxicity while 79 (76%) had no acute liver injury or hepatotoxicity. Of cases receiving NAC within 8 h, 9% (n=4) developed hepatotoxicity and 91% (n=40) were protected. Crude odds of hepatotoxicity were 5.5-fold higher with NAC after 8 h. Mechanism cited as increased production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI. NAC administered at standard IV dose of 300 mg/kg over 21 h.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen toxicity is caused by a highly reactive minor metabolite which is formed by, and damages, the liver, kidneys and certain other vital organs, and that biochemical and symptomatic evidence of acetaminophen toxicity is usually delayed for several days and can be reduced or prevented by early N-acetylcysteine. This is described in the context of a case report of a 28-year-old woman who ingested an estimated 58 g acetaminophen (plus 9 g propoxyphene) 20 h before hospitalization, with a serum acetaminophen concentration of 485 µg/mL at 22 h and complete recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive intentional overdose (estimated 58 g acetaminophen) taken as ~90 Darvocet-N 100 tablets (each containing propoxyphene napsylate 100 mg and acetaminophen 650 mg), with co-ingestion of 9 g propoxyphene; 20 h delay before hospitalization; prior barbiturate exposure (enzyme inducers); patient on methadone maintenance (80 mg/day).
raw_record.extra_details: Serum acetaminophen concentration 485 µg/mL at 22 h, declining with unusually long half-life of 14 h; hemodialysis for 4 h (started at 36 h) reduced concentration from 250 to 32 µg/mL; N-acetylcysteine prevented inorganic sulfate depletion and may have increased acetaminophen sulfate formation; patient recovered completely. Hepatotoxicity attributed to a highly reactive minor metabolite; predictable dose-related overdose mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: A 36-year-old female presented ~72 hours after intentional ingestion of about 200 pills of 500 mg acetaminophen in an overdose. Labs showed severe acidosis (pH 6.9), AST 23,356 IU/L rising to a peak of 28,254 IU/L, and INR 2.8; the patient met King's College Criteria for acidemia and was deemed unfit for liver transplantation. She was treated with N-acetylcysteine and Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System (MARS, liver dialysis) for 3 days and survived to discharge, recovering from the massive acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure without sequelae.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive intentional overdose of ~200 x 500 mg acetaminophen (~100 g) taken approximately 72 hours before presentation; late presentation; patient met King's College Criteria (acidemia) and was deemed unfit for liver transplantation; treated with N-acetylcysteine and MARS liver dialysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure with severe hepatocellular injury (AST peak 28,254 IU/L, initial 23,356 IU/L), INR 2.8, severe metabolic acidosis (pH 6.9 rising to 7.0), initial APAP 28 mcg/mL declining to 14 mcg/mL. MARS (liver dialysis) used for 3 days as extracorporeal therapy; EXTRIP recommendations referenced for ECT when acetaminophen concentrations exceed 800 mg/L or with altered mentation/lactic acidosis at >500 mg/L. Patient survived to discharge without sequelae.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that even if the patient survived the acute CNS depressant effects of propoxyphene, long-term survival appeared questionable because of the likelihood of severe liver damage by acetaminophen. Plasma-acetaminophen concentrations above 400 µg/mL at 4 h after ingestion are associated with very severe intoxication; the patient's concentration was 485 µg/mL at 22 h and probably over 1000 µg/mL at 4 h. Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is increased by prior exposure to barbiturates and other enzyme-inducing drugs that enhance formation of its hepatotoxic reactive metabolite.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive overdose combined with propoxyphene; patient on methadone maintenance and abused barbiturates prior to ingestion; N-acetylcysteine antidote treatment delayed ~24 h (considered ineffective after 10 h).
raw_record.extra_details: Ingestion of 58.5 g (1.22 g/kg) acetaminophen, among the largest known ingestions; back-extrapolated plasma concentration 1470 mg/L equivalent to 1.40 g/kg. Acetaminophen biologic half-life is 2-3 h at therapeutic doses but averages ~8 h in intoxicated patients, and long half-lives are usually associated with severe liver damage and a high fatality rate. Hepatotoxic reactive metabolite formed by mixed-function oxidase; toxicity increased by barbiturate-induced enzyme induction. Propoxyphene was attributed to coma, respiratory depression, and hypothermia rather than liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the classic clinical course of iron poisoning, divided into five phases. The fourth phase, occurring 12-48 h post ingestion, is characterized by hepatotoxicity. The described case matched this classic description of iron poisoning, with liver injury shown by rising total bilirubin (to 253.1 µmol/L/14.8 mg/dL) and alanine aminotransferase (SGPT) rising to 2843 U/L by 48 h post ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive overdose ingestion of an iron-containing product; the patient survived with recovery and treatment was given.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of iron poisoning in which hepatotoxicity marked the fourth phase (12-48 h post ingestion). Peak serum iron was 2992 µmol/L (16,706 µg/dL) at 5 h. Total bilirubin rose to 253.1 µmol/L (14.8 mg/dL) and SGPT/ALT to 2843 U/L by 48 h; LDH 2014 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 248 U/L. Treated with high-dose intermittent-infusion DFO (deferoxamine) mesylate chelation; the patient left hospital ~4 months after ingestion in good condition with good oral intake and was neurologically normal. Gastric outlet obstruction (phase-five complication) also developed and subsequently improved.

raw_record.support_text: An 18-year-old male presented 1 hour after consuming 125 grams of acetaminophen (APAP) with a peak APAP level of 738.6 µg/mL. He was treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine, fomepizole, intermittent hemodialysis, and CVVH at a high replacement rate. His AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase remained low (AST 50 U/L, ALT 55 U/L, both <100 U/L during hospitalization), and no liver failure developed; the early NAC and fomepizole were credited with protecting him from APAP-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive overdose of 125 g APAP (single-agent ingestion); no prior liver disease noted.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP level rose from 630.6 to 730 µg/mL despite 4 hours of intermittent hemodialysis, attributed to continued GI absorption and high tissue distribution. Treated with intravenous NAC (initially 150 mg/kg then 12.5 mg/kg/h, with oral NAC 70 mg/kg q4h) and fomepizole (15 mg/kg then 10 mg/kg q6h) during high-rate CVVH (replacement 90 mL/kg/h). Discussion notes APAP toxicity can be fatal if acute liver failure develops; prior massive tylenol ingestion cases delayed beyond the NAC effective window had AST/ALT in the thousands; this patient's AST and ALT remained <100 U/L throughout and liver enzymes returned to normal.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old man ingested 90 g of paracetamol and was admitted 36 hours later. He developed hepatic failure (serum bilirubin 5.2 mg/100 ml, SGOT >2,000 units) as well as hypotension from massive upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, an ECG conduction defect, and renal failure. Post-mortem revealed massive hepatic necrosis with preservation of the normal reticulum structure (centrilobular necrosis), and the patient became comatose and died three days after admission.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive paracetamol overdose (90 g ingested); patient had simultaneous massive upper GI haemorrhage with hypotension, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, anuria/renal failure, and extensive atheromatous coronary artery disease found at post mortem.
raw_record.extra_details: Admitted 36 hours after ingestion with serum paracetamol 152 µg/ml, fully conscious. Findings: systolic BP 60 mm Hg; pH 7.20, PaCO2 16, base excess -21 mEq/L; prothrombin time 33 s (control 13), partial thromboplastin time 74 s (control 37), thrombin time 9 s (control 7), platelet count 60,000/cmm; gross intraventricular conduction defect; anuria. Hepatic failure with bilirubin 5.2 mg/100 ml; SGOT >2,000 units the next day. Histology: massive centrilobular necrosis with preservation of normal reticulum structure. Treated with hepatic coma regime, sodium bicarbonate, mannitol, lasix, 10% dextrose, fresh frozen plasma, blood, dimercaprol 5 mg/kg, and intragastric noradrenalin irrigation for haematemesis; died 3 days after admission.

raw_record.support_text: This study of 'massive' paracetamol overdose highlights prolonged absorption and persistently high concentrations in these patients, with some showing delayed paracetamol peak concentrations out to 60 h suggesting pharmacobezoar formation. Acetylcysteine within hours of the overdose did not prevent severe liver injury in several patients. The paper confirms that very high early paracetamol concentrations are an independent risk factor for hepatotoxicity even when acetylcysteine is given, with hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 U/L in this high-dose cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive paracetamol overdose (ingestion of at least 40 g, high-dose cohort) rather than ordinary therapeutic exposure; some patients had delayed/double peaks out to 60 h suggesting pharmacobezoar formation.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 U/L despite IV acetylcysteine given within 8 h of ingestion; high early paracetamol ratio (above the 300 mg/L at 4 h nomogram line) was an independent risk factor for hepatotoxicity even when adjusted for time to acetylcysteine and ratio. In patients presenting within 16 h of ingesting ≥40 g receiving 'standard' treatment (no activated charcoal, standard acetylcysteine dose), hepatotoxicity rate was 11% (n=10/87), vs 5% (n=4/87) with activated charcoal or increased acetylcysteine. Toxic intermediate NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) discussed as the metabolite acetylcysteine detoxifies; NAPQI not independently blamed as separate causal entity. Activated charcoal within 4 h associated with reduced paracetamol concentrations and reduced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The study systematically assessed outcomes of massive paracetamol overdose. Key findings were that, despite receiving standard therapy with acetylcysteine, patients with massive overdoses were more likely to develop significant liver injury (hepatotoxicity), kidney injury, and coagulopathy, with the APAP p1:APAP t ratio predicting organ toxicity. This relationship persisted even when acetylcysteine was administered within 8 hours of reported ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive paracetamol overdose setting; patients received standard acetylcysteine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred despite acetylcysteine started within 8 hours of reported ingestion; risk was higher in the highest plasma paracetamol concentration subgroups; delayed absorption (double plasma peaks), extended half-life with progressive hepatotoxicity, and NAPQI generation after acetylcysteine infusion may explain injury in early presenting poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: A 78-year-old man reportedly ingested approximately 96 immediate-release acetaminophen 500-mg tablets (48 g) over one hour in an apparent suicide attempt. Following intravenous NAC for 21 hours, therapy was discontinued despite a residual acetaminophen concentration of 116 µg/mL, and the patient experienced hepatotoxicity, coagulopathy, and renal injury. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed prolonged acetaminophen absorption with a second peak concentration of 228 µg/mL at about 48 hours postingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive single overdose (~48 g as ~96 tablets of 500 mg immediate-release acetaminophen) in a 78-year-old patient following a suicide attempt; erratic gastrointestinal absorption with double serum concentration peaks occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: Peak acetaminophen concentration 281 µg/mL at 6.25 h postingestion (264 µg/mL at 2.25 h, residual 116 µg/mL at end of 21-h IV NAC course, second peak 228 µg/mL ~48 h postingestion). Hepatotoxicity and coagulopathy developed despite 21 h of intravenous NAC; renal injury also occurred. Case suggests standard 21-h NAC course may be inadequate in massive ingestion due to erratic absorption.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of massive acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion (125 g) associated with GSH depletion, prolonged APAP half-life, increased NAPQI production, and hepatotoxicity, treated with an increased IV NAC regimen (400 mg/kg over 29 hours vs the standard 300 mg/kg over 21 hours). It states that the standard NAC dose may not provide adequate protection against hepatotoxicity in massive APAP ingestion, and discusses predictors of poor prognosis after APAP toxicity (decreased pH, increased lactate, increased PT/INR, increased serum creatinine).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive single-ingestion overdose (125 g ingested by a 70 kg patient; massive ingestion defined as a single APAP intake >40 g), requiring an increased NAC dose and duration.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: GSH depletion and increased NAPQI production with prolonged APAP half-life; NAC regimen raised to 400 mg/kg IV over 29 h vs standard 300 mg/kg IV over 21 h because optimal regimen for massive ingestions is uncertain. Chiew et al 2017 retrospective analysis: 79 patients with serum APAP above the 300-line at 4 h treated with NAC within 16 h; clinical_hypothesis the increased NAC dose reduced hepatotoxicity. Predictors of poor prognosis after APAP toxicity: decreased pH, increased lactate, increased PT/INR, increased serum creatinine. Concomitant diphenhydramine may slow GI absorption and prolong APAP half-life.

raw_record.support_text: The case report documents hepatotoxicity occurring after a massive suicidal acetaminophen (APAP) overdose. A 78-year-old man reportedly ingested approximately 96 tablets of APAP IR (each 500 mg) over one hour. IV N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was started 5 hours after ingestion, but was discontinued after 21 hours despite a residual APAP concentration of 116 µg/mL. The patient subsequently experienced hepatotoxicity, coagulopathy, and renal injury, with pharmacokinetic analysis revealing prolonged, erratic APAP absorption and a second peak APAP concentration of 228 µg/mL approximately 48 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive suicidal overdose in a 78-year-old man; approximately 96 tablets of APAP IR (500 mg each, ~48 g) ingested over one hour; IV NAC started 5 hours after ingestion and prematurely discontinued after 21 hours despite a residual APAP concentration of 116 µg/mL.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP serum concentrations were 264 µg/mL at 2.25 h post-ingestion and 281 µg/mL at 6.25 h; a second peak of 228 µg/mL appeared approximately 48 h post-ingestion. Erratic and prolonged APAP absorption led to toxic serum concentrations persisting beyond the standard 21-hour IV NAC course. The patient also developed coagulopathy and renal injury; re-ingestion was deemed unlikely due to direct hospital monitoring. No specific biochemical pattern (e.g., hepatocellular vs. cholestatic) was reported.

In another case a mother developed severe liver damage after an overdose of aspirin and paracetamol (maternal plasma paracetamol 160 mg/l at 16 h after ingestion). These passages attribute acute maternal liver damage to paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Maternal overdose during pregnancy; one described case involved co-ingestion of aspirin.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose hepatotoxicity can be fatal: muscle necrosis was found histologically in all of 26 patients with fatal hepatic failure, including six who had taken a paracetamol overdose. Muscle damage was proposed on the basis of increased plasma creatine phosphokinase, though many patients were alcoholics or had taken other drugs. Includes cases of transient mild maternal liver damage and severe liver damage with recovery.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in a moderate-overdose group of patients taking roughly 4 to 10 g of acetaminophen within 24 hours. Sixty percent of the patients in this group who developed severe hepatotoxicity were chronic acetaminophen users, several of whom had taken such amounts for weeks or months without problems; the paper proposes that another factor, such as illness leading to prolonged fasting, precipitated hepatotoxicity, with ample acetaminophen present in the liver to cause hepatocyte necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Moderate-overdose exposure (4-10 g within 24 hours); prolonged fasting (e.g., from illness) proposed as a precipitating factor; chronic alcoholism was much less common in this group and not required; chronic alcohol use or recent alcohol intake alone did not account for most cases.
raw_record.extra_details: This study (see Table, patients 3 and 7) suggests fasting may be an important predisposing factor for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in the moderate-overdose range. Alcohol may potentiate the effect of fasting by inducing microsomal enzymes; genetic factors such as diminished glucuronidation capacity may increase susceptibility. Benson previously showed patients with chronic liver disease including alcoholic cirrhosis had no ill effects with 4 g/day up to 14 days, and cases of hepatotoxicity at recommended doses (4 g/24 h) in chronic alcoholics are almost absent. Acetaminophen plasma toxic level given as >300 µmol/L (>5.0 mg/dL).

raw_record.extra_details: Two of 29 NAC-treated patients achieved peak ALT >1000 IU/L (threshold for paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity): 58/M with 75,840 mg (945 mg/kg) and peak ALT 1232 IU/L at 89 h; 17/M with 19,950 mg (249 mg/kg) and peak ALT 7516 IU/L at 67 h. raw_record.support_text: This cohort study reports on modified-release paracetamol overdose treated with acetylcysteine and evaluates the paracetamol × aminotransferase multiplication product as a predictor of hepatotoxicity. Regardless of ingestion type (acute vs. staggered), a product ≥10,000 mg/L × IU/L was associated with a high likelihood of developing hepatotoxicity despite acetylcysteine treatment, while a product <1500 mg/L × IU/L was highly sensitive in excluding the development of hepatotoxicity. The paper frames paracetamol overdose as the cause of the hepatotoxicity and ALI observed in the exposed patients, discussing risk of progression to fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Modified-release paracetamol formulation; poisoning context treated with acetylcysteine; includes both single and staggered (staggered) overdose presentations.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of patients with modified-release paracetamol overdose treated with acetylcysteine; 5 patients developed hepatotoxicity (4/5 with calculable serial multiplication products) and 68 did not. Outcome definitions: hepatotoxicity by traditional biochemical criteria; ALI defined as at least a doubling of ALT and >50 IU/L. Paracetamol × ALT multiplication product cut-offs: ≥10,000 mg/L × IU/L (LR 27, 95% CI 4-207 for ALI; LR 28, 95% CI 7-107 for hepatotoxicity with single ingestion), 1500-10,000 (LR 0.9), <1500 (LR 0.3 for ALI; highly sensitive to exclude hepatotoxicity). Product within 8 h of ingestion mildly elevated and fell quickly in patients without ALI/hepatotoxicity; delayed repeat testing improves specificity. Acetylcysteine started within 8 h of overdose prevented hepatotoxicity despite high product. Severity outcome discussed: 'patients are unlikely to develop fulminant hepatic failure unless meeting the traditional biochemical criteria of hepatotoxicity first', with product proposed as an inclusion criterion for trials of intensified acetylcysteine to prevent fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG), examining acute liver failure across 22 academic centres over 6 years, found paracetamol (acetaminophen) accounted for 42% of all ALF cases in the US, increasing from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2003, and stabilizing at 52% and 46% in 2004 and 2005. ALF mortality was cited at roughly 30%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most US paracetamol-associated ALF was from unintentional (48%) or intentional (44%) overdose; only ~10% of paracetamol ALF cases occurred at dosages <4 g/day. Among unintentional-overdose ALF patients, the median paracetamol dose was 7.5 g/day (range 1.0-78 g/day), use was rarely for more than 7 days, and 63% used an opioid-paracetamol product.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol is also known as acetaminophen. ALFSG data: 42% of all US ALF cases attributed to paracetamol; proportion rose from 28% (1998) to 51% (2003), then 52% (2004) and 46% (2005). ALF is rare (~1.4 cases per million per year in Spain) with a mortality rate of ~30%. Among unintentional-overdose ALF patients, 81% reported pain and 62% used a single product. The 2009 FDA Advisory Committee recommended dose limits (3.25 g/day), single-tablet limits (325 mg), and removal of opioid-paracetamol products; in January 2011 the FDA required limiting paracetamol to 325 mg/tablet in opioid-paracetamol products and label revisions on the risk of severe liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old male was admitted to the Regional Poison Center after inadvertently ingesting a toxic resin-curing dimethyl aniline-based formulation (dimethyloaniline/dimethylaniline) at work. During hospitalization he developed massive intravascular hemolysis requiring blood products and showed signs of liver dysfunction with cholestatic liver damage and jaundice; the case is presented as evidence that severe organ damage can result from even a small amount of this toxicant. The patient stayed in the Toxicology Clinic for 3 weeks.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of an occupational intoxication; patient also had massive intravascular hemolysis requiring blood products; stayed 3 weeks in the Toxicology Clinic; jaundice attributed to cholestatic liver damage. raw_record.support_text: Of the 132 patients identified as having acetaminophen overdose, 22 developed acute liver failure (ALF). Among these patients, hepatic encephalopathy (OR 75.46; 95% CI 8.73–3335) and hepatic necrosis (OR 9.15; 95% CI 2.96–28.46) were the most discriminative liver-related diagnostic codes for identifying ALF. When restricted to patients identified as having acetaminophen hepatotoxicity, the ALF algorithm had sensitivity of 89% (17/19 cases), specificity 63%, PPV 53%, and NPV 93%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurs in the setting of acetaminophen overdose, including patients with multiple time-point (e.g., unintentional) ingestions within a population-based hospitalization administrative database.
raw_record.extra_details: Study validated ICD-9-CM (965.4) and ICD-10 (T39.1) principal codes for identifying acetaminophen overdose (sensitivity 90%, specificity 83%, c-statistic 0.87). Of 132 overdose cases, 59 had hepatotoxicity (n=59 in Table 5) and 22 developed ALF. Hepatotoxicity: hepatic necrosis (570, K71.1) OR 17.16 (4.65–92.85), toxic hepatitis (573.3, K71.2, K71.6, K71.9) OR 7.85 (3.01–21.98). ALF: hepatic encephalopathy (572.2, K72.0, K72.9) OR 75.46 (8.73–3335), hepatic necrosis OR 9.15 (2.96–28.46); diagnostic algorithm requiring hepatic encephalopathy or necrosis code predicted ALF with OR 58.8 (12.5–276.0). Codes for jaundice and hepatorenal syndrome were not recorded in any patient.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective case series reported that, although the frequency of paracetamol poisoning is lower in older subjects, when paracetamol intoxication does occur it is more frequently associated with fulminant hepatic failure and death, and age is considered an independent risk factor of morbidity and mortality in these cases. The paper also notes there is a lack of good quality clinical evidence that older people have a clinically significant difference in paracetamol metabolism or are at increased risk of toxicity at either therapeutic or supra-therapeutic doses.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Older/elderly people; overdose (intoxication) setting; age is an independent risk factor for morbidity and mortality in these cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure and death are more frequent in older people when intoxication occurs. Metabolism/age data are inconsistent: some PK studies suggest increased toxicity risk with age (prolonged t1/2, reduced clearance, increased oxidation from reduced glucuronidation/sulfation, reduced liver volume), whereas others find no age effect (t1/2, AUC, oral clearance unrelated to age; Cmax not translating to ALT changes). Two population-based studies found paracetamol poisoning rates decrease with age from a peak in adolescence/early adulthood. The paper states there is a lack of good quality clinical evidence that older people have a clinically significant difference in paracetamol metabolism or increased toxicity risk at therapeutic or supra-therapeutic doses.

raw_record.support_text: This report presents two human cases of monensin poisoning by oral ingestion. Patient 1, with a history of chronic bronchitis and hypertension, presented with severe rhabdomyolysis, hepatotoxicity, and hypoxemia; his condition deteriorated and he suffered irreversible cardiopulmonary arrest. Patient 2 was diabetic on oral hypoglycemic drugs and had obvious rhabdomyolysis, recovered after fluid replacement, urine alkalinization, and CRRT, and was discharged 1 month later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Oral ingestion (self-poisoning) of monensin 5 days prior to admission; Patient 1 carried comorbidities of chronic bronchitis and hypertension and died from irreversible cardiopulmonary arrest; Patient 2 was diabetic and taking oral hypoglycemic drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Monensin is a sodium-selective carboxyl ionophore polyether antibiotic produced by Streptomyces cinnamonensis used to prevent coccidiosis in poultry/livestock; overdose leads to lethal poisoning in animals. The paper frames the cases as monensin-induced rhabdomyolysis and hepatotoxicity. Two patients (a couple), latency ~5 days. Patient 1 died; Patient 2 recovered after fluid replacement, urine alkalinization and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Mechanism attributed to dysfunction of cell membranes and mitochondria due to disorder of cellular ion transporters.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 16-year-old boy in whom vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and acute renal and liver failure developed in January 1996 after he ingested an unknown quantity of potassium dichromate in a suicide attempt (obtained from his school's chemical laboratory). Supportive treatment including continuous hemofiltration and intravenous dimercaprol (250 mg twice daily) was started, yet renal and liver function deteriorated within two days. An accompanying general statement notes that oral ingestion of potassium dichromate is followed by renal and hepatic failure, with a lowest reported lethal dose of 0.1 g.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old patient died 24 hours after ingesting an abortifacient/laxative preparation containing 1,2-dichloroethane, from therapy-resistant cardiovascular failure. Along with the typical gastroenterocolitis and acute yellow liver dystrophy (acute liver failure), a severe hemorrhagic diathesis was observed. The complex coagulation disorder with thrombocytopenia and decreased activity of factors I, II, V, VII and XIII was interpreted as consumptive coagulopathy with secondary hyperfibrinolysis. Treatment recommendations, including immediate gastric lavage with paraffin oil and intensive liver protection, were given for acute liver failure from oral 1,2-dichloroethane poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Oral poisoning after ingestion of a preparation (an 'Ereibemittel') containing 1,2-dichloroethane; overdose setting.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old patient died 24 h after ingestion from therapy-resistant cardiovascular failure. Along with acute yellow liver dystrophy (acute liver failure) there was gastroenterocolitis and a severe hemorrhagic diathesis; the coagulation disorder (thrombocytopenia, reduced activity of factors I, II, V, VII, XIII) was interpreted as consumptive coagulopathy with secondary hyperfibrinolysis. The paper states the tolerated single human dose should not exceed 1 ml of dichloroethane, with a daily maximum of 3 ml, and that no specific antidote exists. Mechanisms discussed include possible cardiogenic-shock-driven or cor pulmonale-related intravascular coagulation, with small thrombi in the pulmonary circulation noted histologically.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old pregnant woman (35 weeks) presented 3 days after intentional ingestion of 30 grams of acetaminophen, with elevated ALT (785 IU/L) and AST (630 IU/L), a detectable acetaminophen level of 14 mg/dL, and INR of 1.7, consistent with delayed acetaminophen toxicity. She was treated with n-acetylcysteine, but developed worsening coagulopathy, fulminant hepatic failure with peak AST 6693 IU/L and peak ALT 5566 IU/L, acute renal injury, congestive heart failure, and acute lung injury requiring ventilation. She recovered and was discharged on day 14; the fetus delivered stillborn 72 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (30 g intentional ingestion) in a 35-week pregnant patient; developed coagulopathy requiring reversal with vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma; treated with n-acetylcysteine; fetal death (stillbirth) occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: Delayed acetaminophen toxicity; fulminant hepatic failure attributed to acetaminophen-induced liver injury; presenting ALT 785 IU/L and AST 630 IU/L, INR 1.7 rising to 3.0; peak AST 6693 IU/L and peak ALT 5566 IU/L; acetaminophen level 14 mg/dL; acute renal injury, congestive heart failure, acute lung injury; n-acetylcysteine continued until hepatic improvement; discharged day 14 after complete recovery. NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) toxic byproduct forms in fetal liver at a lower rate than adults due to immature P450 system; acetaminophen crosses the placenta with fetal levels approximating maternal levels.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen was the most common ALF etiology in this multi-center ALFSG registry study (64% of TH-treated vs 47% of control patients). raw_record.support_text: In the authors' single-center series of acute liver failure (ALF), 104 patients underwent liver transplantation, with similar 30-day posttransplant survival in the acetaminophen cohort (69%) and the non-acetaminophen cohort (78%). Mortality on the transplant waiting list was double in the acetaminophen cohort (31.8%) versus the non-acetaminophen cohort (15.7%), and patients with acetaminophen-induced ALF listed for emergency transplantation had an increased incidence of organ failure with cerebral edema, inotropic support, and renal dialysis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (acetaminophen poisoning) exposure; some patients had concurrent active or resistant alcohol dependence or alcohol/drug use, noted as a factor excluding them from transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose/poisoning causes acute liver failure (acetaminophen-induced ALF), including cases requiring emergency listing for liver transplantation. King's College poor prognostic criteria were used for transplant decisions; lactate was introduced into listing criteria. 327 in-hospital deaths were attributed to acetaminophen overdose in Scotland over 1995-2003 (27-53 deaths/year); ~600 adult (ages 20-69) admissions per quarter followed acetaminophen overdose. In the current cohort (2002-2005), 4 of 81 acetaminophen ALF patients received liver transplant vs 13 of 99 in 1993-1996; transplant waiting-list mortality for the acetaminophen cohort was 31.8%. In 80% of 2002-2005 cases there were contraindications to transplantation, frequently active/resistant alcohol dependence.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 11,195 cases of acetaminophen exposure from the 1988 prospective US multicenter trial, where an ALT/AST greater than 1000 IU/L was used as the toxic threshold on the study nomogram. Some patients treated with acetylcysteine still developed elevated ALT/AST (e.g., 2.84% of those below the 150 mg/L line treated between 10 and 16 h), and the paper notes that despite treatment protocol refinements 'unexpected deaths still occur although such events appear very rare.' This frames acetaminophen (overdose) exposure as a human cause of hepatotoxicity, with acetylcysteine used as its treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is a safe antipyretic-analgesic if a maximum dosage of 4 g/day is not exceeded; ingestion of higher doses can lead to acetaminophen poisoning with hepatotoxicity (10–15 g/day) and may be fatal (20–25 g/day). raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (approximately 15 g, one-half bottle extra-strength acetaminophen) ingested in a suicide attempt; concurrent heavy alcohol intake (~4 L vodka) with a history of chronic alcohol abuse.
raw_record.extra_details: 41/43-year-old African-American man presented with chest pain; initial labs showed hepatocellular injury (AST 14000 U/L, ALT 6400 U/L), then AST 11 000 U/L, ALT 6510 U/L, total bilirubin 395 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 207 µmol/L; treated with N-acetylcysteine and nitroglycerin; referred for concern of progression to fulminant hepatic failure; author states hepatotoxicity occurs at 10–15 g/day and fatal poisoning at 20–25 g/day.

raw_record.support_text: The paper tabulates clinical findings on the effect of chronic alcohol exposure on paracetamol-related hepatotoxicity following paracetamol overdose, either deliberate (suicidal/parasuicidal) or accidental for therapeutic purposes. Series include a national cohort of 662 consecutive patients with at-risk paracetamol levels (Rumack), 247 London patients (Read), 79 patients (Bray), 553 patients with paracetamol-related hepatotoxicity (Makin & Williams), 38 Swedish patients (Denison), and a report of higher serum transaminases in those with chronic alcohol intake (Smilkstein & Rumack).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (either deliberate with suicidal or parasuicidal intent or accidental for therapeutic purposes); assessment of whether chronic alcohol abuse modifies severity.
raw_record.extra_details: Mortality higher (67% vs 34%) in high alcohol intake group in the Bray series (79 patients) though rates of cerebral oedema, dialysis, or ventilation were not significantly more prevalent; Makin & Williams (553 patients) found no association between chronic alcohol consumption and severity as reflected by inotropic support, renal dialysis, grades III/IV encephalopathy, or transplant criteria. Smilkstein & Rumack reported higher serum liver transaminases after overdose in those with chronic alcohol intake.

raw_record.support_text: The paper emphasizes the importance of excluding drug (paracetamol) overdosage in jaundiced patients, noting that patients who survive paracetamol induced hepatic necrosis do not develop chronic liver disease, unlike non-A, non-B hepatitis patients. It also stresses that a positive history of paracetamol overdose and its temporal relation to symptom onset avoids unnecessary viral serological tests, and that patients with concealed paracetamol overdose may present late.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (including concealed overdose) setting; patients presenting with jaundice; overdose may occur more than 10 hours prior to presentation when antidotes are too late.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis carries a good prognosis once the patient survives the acute episode; survivors do not develop chronic liver disease. The magnitude of the alanine aminotransferase (ALT) rise can help differentiate from viral hepatitis; in the authors' case 2, ALT activity was 13,450 U/l, far exceeding the maximum 5300 U/l (mean 2122 U/l, SD 1565 U/l) recorded in 69 jaundiced patients with proved viral hepatitis in 1981. Paracetamol induced hepatitis was mentioned alongside hepatic/liver necrosis with identical causal attribution.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is frequently taken as an overdose in suicidal attempts, and hepatic damage of all grades of severity, from minor to fulminant hepatic failure, may result, with bleeding often being a major problem and not infrequently the direct cause of death. Low clotting factor levels were attributed in part to impaired hepatic synthesis and increased consumption from intravascular coagulation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (including suicidal overdose) in adults.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic damage of all grades from minor to fulminant hepatic failure. In 66 patients, early coagulation changes included low clotting factors II, V and VII within 24 hours; prothrombin time ratio exceeded 2.2 within 30 hours of overdose in all patients who eventually died (9 deaths in the series), and the ratio was less than this in those developing only moderate hepatic damage. Severe hepatic damage was defined as plasma bilirubin >69 umol/l and was the group from which all 9 deaths occurred. A controlled trial of fresh frozen plasma (300 ml every 6 hr) in 20 patients with prothrombin time ratio >2.2 reduced the maximum prothrombin time ratio abnormality but did not reduce morbidity or mortality. Coagulation disturbance was of short duration, with prothrombin time ratio returning to normal within one week of overdose.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old woman was admitted 24 h after ingestion of 25 g paracetamol in a suicide attempt. Her plasma paracetamol concentration on admission was 5.2 mg/l and transaminases were moderately elevated; the next day she was transferred to a transplant unit because of a significant further rise in her liver enzymes, although hepatic function improved subsequently. Peak plasma ALT reached 5032 U/l and prothrombin time fell to 32%, reflecting paracetamol-overdose-related liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (ingestion of 25 g paracetamol in a suicide attempt) treated with N-acetyl cysteine; single-patient case context.
raw_record.extra_details: Plasma paracetamol on admission 5.2 mg/l; peak plasma ALT 5032 U/l, AST 4174 U/l, bilirubin up to 4.2 mg/dl; prothrombin time fell to 32%; patient transferred to a transplant unit because of rising liver enzymes but hepatic function subsequently improved. Paper notes paracetamol overdose is thought to damage liver cells through similar mechanisms to those affecting the renal tubule, involving reactive arylating metabolites trapped by glutathione that become toxic after glutathione depletion. The paper's primary focus is renal toxicity (acute tubular necrosis) and hypophosphataemia.

raw_record.support_text: In a 1988 NEJM-based analysis of 11,195 acetaminophen (APAP) poison exposures at our center, hepatotoxicity was minimal regardless of initial APAP plasma concentration when NAC treatment was started within 8 hours of ingestion, with increased frequency of hepatotoxicity when the treatment delay reached 8–16 hours and some retained benefit even beyond 16–24 hours. Paragraph 22 adds that of the 11,195 exposures, 517 had APAP levels below the nomogram line or otherwise did not meet protocol criteria, and an outcome nomogram showed the percentage of toxic cases related to initial plasma level and time of ingestion among patients treated with a full NAC course.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (ingestion) setting from a national multicenter study of 11,195 exposures; outcomes reflect patients treated with NAC (full course in the outcome nomogram); 517 cases with sub-nomogram levels or non-protocol entries were analyzed separately.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity frequency rose with treatment delay (minimal when NAC started within 8 h; increased at 8–16 h; diminished but still present after 16 h). Outcome nomogram (previously unpublished) plots percent toxic cases against initial plasma APAP level and historical time of ingestion. Some patients with initial plasma level below the nomogram line showed toxicity, attributed to inaccuracy of patient histories and time dependence. APAP levels of 300 µg/mL (4 h) referenced in risk analysis nomogram; cases with SGOT ≥ 1000 IU were plotted. Toxicity follows a threshold effect related to plasma level; height above threshold did not further refine severity. Hepatic damage occurs at ~70% glutathione depletion; ~4% of an APAP dose converts to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), with calculated ~15.9 g APAP absorbed in a 70 kg human to reach threshold toxicity (~0.635 g NAPQI). NAC (N-acetylcysteine) administration discussed as the antidote, not as a cause.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 23 patients presenting more than 15 h after a paracetamol overdose, 20 (87%) developed hepatotoxicity and four died of hepatic failure. The text frames paracetamol poisoning as a cause of hepatotoxicity and of paracetamol-related acute liver failure, describing established hepatotoxicity in overdose. A table of 24 reported paracetamol-poisoning cases lists peak AST/ALT, INR/PT, and outcomes including death from hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol poisoning) context only; many cases involved co-ingested drugs (temazepam, salicylate, codeine, sulphasalazine, aspirin, pine oil, dextropropoxyphene, cinnarizine); some patients received NAC, bicarbonate, haemodialysis/haemofiltration or charcoal treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causing early lactic acidosis/early metabolic acidosis of uncertain cause and later hepatotoxicity with established hepatotoxicity and paracetamol-related acute liver failure. Reported ingestions up to ~200 g with peak paracetamol concentrations up to 1614 mg/L. In the series of 23 late-presenting (>15 h) overdose patients, median plasma lactate 3.6 mmol/L, 11 (48%) acidotic, 20/23 (87%) hepatotoxicity, 4 died of hepatic failure. In a cohort of 103 with severe paracetamol-related ALF (King's College Hospital 1998-1999), 10 transplanted/excluded, 57 survived, 36 died; early arterial lactate significantly higher in non-survivors (median 8.5 vs 1.4 mmol/L, P<0.0001); pH and lactate were the only independent mortality predictors (cut-offs 3.5 mmol/L admission, 3.0 mmol/L post-resuscitation). King's College criteria for liver transplantation in paracetamol-related ALF: arterial pH <7.3 ≥24h after overdose or creatinine >300 umol/L with grade 3-4 encephalopathy and PT >100 s; modified criteria added lactate-based criteria. Lactate proposed as prognostic marker for transplant decisions.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports acute hepatotoxicity after paracetamol overdose in nine patients. GST and F protein concentrations in plasma were more sensitive than ALT activity for detecting this hepatotoxicity: all nine patients had abnormal GST concentrations and eight had abnormal F protein concentrations at some time after the paracetamol overdose, whereas ALT became abnormal in only six. Five of the patients developed moderate or severe liver damage with maximal ALT activities 9.4 to 390 times the upper reference limit, and abnormal hepatocellular damage markers were measurable as early as 4 h after overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol poisoning) exposure; series of nine patients who took a paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Five of nine patients developed moderate or severe liver damage with maximal ALT activities ranging from 9.4 to 390 times the upper reference limit; GST maxima ranged from about 300 to 3000 times the upper reference limit. Hepatocellular damage was measurable as early as 4 h after overdose. GST, ALT, and F protein concentrations continued to increase after treatment with N-acetylcysteine was begun. Admission GST >10 µg/L distinguished the five patients who developed severe or moderate liver damage from the four who did not. The paper's focus is on comparing GST and F protein (more sensitive) with ALT for detecting acute hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The letter critiques a study of paracetamol poisoning that investigated risk factors for severe outcomes (hepatic encephalopathy, renal dysfunction and hepatotoxicity). It reports mortality from paracetamol poisoning of 9.3% (46 of 492) among patients transferred from other hospitals, with no deaths among 179 patients presenting directly, and 0.1% mortality (2 in 1939 patients) in the authors' own poisoning unit. The underlying study identified liver cell damage as a marker of severe paracetamol poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol poisoning) setting; the letter also notes the studied population mixed tertiary and primary referral cases of differing severity, which it argues limits generalization.
raw_record.extra_details: The study examined risk factors for severe paracetamol poisoning including hepatic encephalopathy, renal dysfunction and hepatotoxicity (liver cell damage). Mortality was 9.3% (46/492) in transferred, severely poisoned patients, 0% (0/179) in directly presenting patients, and 0.1% (2/1939) in the authors' own unit. The letter disputes the study's claim that co-ingested benzodiazepine overdose (OR 1.91 for hepatic encephalopathy; OR 1.79 for renal dysfunction; OR 1.75 for liver cell damage) was an independent risk factor, arguing the analysis had methodological flaws and results were of borderline significance.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 80 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) referred to the Victorian Liver Transplant Unit in Australia, paracetamol poisoning was the etiology in 29 cases (the second largest etiologic group after non-A non-B hepatitis). Among these paracetamol-poisoning cases, survival without transplantation was 20/27 (74%) and with transplantation was 1/2 (50%). The discussion describes these as cases of paracetamol-induced FHF.

raw_record.extra_details: 29 of 80 FHF patients due to paracetamol poisoning; survival without transplant 74%, with transplant 50%. FHF here denotes fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: In this trial, paracetamol-intoxication was the cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in 54% of patients in the high volume plasmapheresis (HVP) group and 64% in the standard medical treatment (SMT) group. The authors also compared paracetamol-induced ALF with ALF due to other aetiological causes and noted that patients with paracetamol-induced ALF have a better prognosis than most other etiological causes of ALF.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol intoxication accounted for 54% of ALF cases in the HVP group and 64% in the SMT group of 182 ALF patients; paracetamol-induced ALF patients had a better prognosis than most other etiological causes (viral and autoimmune hepatitis among others).

raw_record.support_text: 524 patients underwent psychiatric assessment for potential OLT after presenting to the SLTU with paracetamol overdose (POD)-induced acute liver failure (AHF) between 2006 and 2024. 102 (19.5%) died within their index admission without undergoing OLT; among these, 46 were identified for whom absolute psychiatric contraindications (APCIs) precluded transplant despite otherwise being medically suitable, representing 8.8% of all assessed and 45% of deaths.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (POD) setting in patients with AHF referred to the Scottish Liver Transplant Unit for emergency orthotopic liver transplantation assessment; the cohort consists of patients receiving psychiatric assessment for transplant suitability.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-centre retrospective cohort analysis at SLTU (Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh), 2006-2024, identified via ICD codes for AHF prompting psychiatric assessment (n=524). Of 46 in-episode deaths with APCIs to OLT despite medical suitability: 27 (59%) female, average age 44.6 years (range 19-72); most common primary psychiatric diagnosis was Alcohol Dependence Syndrome in 31 patients (67%). APCIs (absolute psychiatric contraindications) alone precluded transplant and led to death; 8.8% of all patients assessed for urgent OLT and 45% of all in-episode deaths. Study context: paracetamol overdose is the established cause of AHF in these patients.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports on fifteen patients with admission plasma-paracetamol concentrations above a line joining 200 µg/ml at 4 h to 60 µg/ml at 12 h, i.e. paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning by overdosage, in whom severe liver damage (defined as serum AST or ALT >1000 I.U./l) was the criterion monitored. Twelve treated within 10 h had normal or only slightly disturbed liver-function tests except patient 12; patients 13-15 treated after 10 h all sustained severe liver damage without hepatic encephalopathy, and patient 14 also developed acute renal failure. Thus paracetamol overdose is the agent causing the liver injury that N-acetylcysteine was used to treat/prevent.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (poisoning) exposure with admission plasma-paracetamol 4 h concentrations roughly 210-633 µg/ml; some patients had co-ingestion of other drugs (Distalgesic/dextropropoxyphene-paracetamol in patients 1,4,9,13; Para-Hypon containing caffeine, codeine phosphate and phenolphthalein in patient 7); patient 12 had taken unknown drugs and a warfarin rodenticide the prior week; five patients were at particular risk of severe hepatic necrosis due to alcoholism or prior microsomal-enzyme-inducing drugs; N-acetylcysteine (and comparators cysteamine, methionine) were given therapeutically to prevent/treat the liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver damage defined as serum AST or ALT >1000 I.U./l. Patient 12 had maximum AST 2520, ALT 3260 I.U./l; patient 13 had AST 10400, ALT 5020 I.U./l with max bilirubin 3.2 mg/dl; patient 14 had ALT 13600, max bilirubin 5.3 mg/dl and prothrombin-time ratio 2.4 plus acute renal failure; patient 15 had ALT 10300, bilirubin 3.5 mg/dl. Patients 13-15 (treated after 10 h) sustained severe liver damage without hepatic encephalopathy. Patient 1 died of a cerebrovascular accident 9 days after admission (not liver-related). Treated with N-acetylcysteine ('Airbron') 300 mg/kg IV over 20 h; mouse data cited showing N-acetylcysteine protects against paracetamol hepatotoxicity. The paper frames paracetamol hepatotoxicity and severe hepatic necrosis in the setting of paracetamol poisoning; the anti-dote agents (N-acetylcysteine, cysteamine, methionine) are protectants, not attributed DILI causes.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdosage causes acute centrilobular hepatic necrosis, with plasma aspartate and alanine aminotransferases sometimes exceeding 10,000 IU/l (normal 10-40), plasma bilirubin rising to 60-100 µmol/l, and prothrombin time ratio to 2.0-3.0 in severely poisoned patients. Regeneration is rapid and liver function tests usually return to normal in 7-14 d, but repeated episodes of severe paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis may progress to cirrhosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (poisoning) setting, not therapeutic use; individual susceptibility reported with ~25% of poisoned patients developing liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: AST/ALT sometimes exceed 10,000 IU/l (normal 10-40); bilirubin 60-100 µmol/l; prothrombin time ratio 2.0-3.0; liver function tests return to normal in 7-14 d with no permanent sequelae; histology shows acute centrilobular hepatic necrosis (e.g., a 54-yr-old woman who died 6 d after paracetamol overdosage); repeated severe episodes may progress to cirrhosis. Overall mortality from hepatic failure without treatment is 1-3%; ~25% of patients develop liver damage. N-acetylcysteine treatment line joins 200 µg/ml at 4 h and 30 µg/ml at 15 h; protective antidotes cysteamine, methionine, and N-acetylcysteine are effective only if given within 8 h.

raw_record.support_text: In paracetamol overdose patients at severe risk, the relation between plasma alanine aminotransferase and 3-(cystein-S-yl)paracetamol protein adducts at admission supports a dominant mechanistic role of this protein binding, described as the first direct evidence of a similar mechanism of paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis in man and in laboratory animals.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (poisoning) setting; most patients in the series were treated immediately with intravenous N-acetylcysteine 300 mg/kg.
raw_record.extra_details: Based on 30 patients presenting with paracetamol poisoning at Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen; 11 were at high risk, 3 at moderate risk, and 16 at low risk of hepatotoxicity on the Prescott classification. Hepatic necrosis attributed to oxidation of paracetamol to the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine, which after overdose overwhelms glutathione detoxification and forms 3-(cystein-S-yl)paracetamol protein adducts; serum alanine aminotransferase rise accompanied adduct appearance. An immunoassay for 3-(cystein-S-yl)paracetamol adducts was used; the metabolite is framed as a marker rather than an independent causal entity.

raw_record.support_text: In patients with acetaminophen overdose, hepatic encephalopathy developed in 21 patients (acute liver failure group, 13 died and 2 underwent liver transplantation, all with ALT >1000 U/L). 43 patients without encephalopathy had ALT above 1000 U/L (median 9000 U/L; the hepatotoxicity group) and 48 had peak ALT below 1000 U/L but no encephalopathy (the nonhepatotoxicity group). The study relates acetaminophen exposure to hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure across these overdose patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (poisoning) setting; patients received antidote treatment; analysis restricted to acetaminophen-overdose patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 112 acetaminophen-overdose patients grouped by outcome: 21 acute liver failure (3 grade II, 6 grade III, 12 grade IV encephalopathy; 13 died, 2 transplanted), 43 hepatotoxicity (ALT >1000 U/L; median 9000, range 1020-21,500), 48 nonhepatotoxicity (max ALT <1000; median 25, range 8-850). Median half-life 5.4 h overall, 3.0 h nonhepatotoxicity, 6.4 h hepatotoxicity, 18.4 h acute liver failure group; half-life >5.5 h gave PPV 91% and NPV 74% for hepatotoxicity; half-life correlated with delay from intake to antidote (r=0.61) and with age (r=0.20) but not ingested dose.

raw_record.support_text: Self-poisoning with paracetamol is increasingly common. Although paracetamol is a remarkably safe drug at therapeutic doses, hepatic necrosis is a life-threatening complication of overdosage. The study investigated plasma concentrations and half-life of paracetamol in relation to liver damage in thirty patients admitted to the Regional Poisoning Treatment Centre, Edinburgh, after paracetamol overdosage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (self-poisoning) exposure after paracetamol overdosage; hepatic necrosis is presented as a complication of overdosage, not therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 30 patients overdosed with paracetamol at the Regional Poisoning Treatment Centre, Edinburgh. Hepatic necrosis occurred in 17 patients, one of whom developed fatal hepatic coma. Metabolism of paracetamol was impaired in patients with hepatic injury, with statistically significant correlations between biochemical indices of liver damage and paracetamol half-lives. Plasma-paracetamol half-life was the most reliable early prognostic guide, with liver damage expected if half-life exceeds 4 hours.

raw_record.support_text: This is a case series of 737 patients with paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose. Median paracetamol overdose was 25 g (interquartile range, 18–50 g; range, 1.5–300 g) and median time to N-acetylcysteine was 17 h. Orthotopic liver transplantation was performed in seven patients with severe fulminant hepatic failure, resulting in six recoveries and one death due to post-operative complications, demonstrating paracetamol overdose as the cause of severe human hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (self-poisoning) exposure; deliberate in 624 cases, accidental in 113 (15%); alcohol co-ingested by 21% and 25% were regular alcohol abusers; concomitant drug overdosing in 30%; 73% of patients transferred from other hospitals.
raw_record.extra_details: 737 patients, median age 33 years (range 12–88), 487 women/250 men. Median paracetamol overdose 25 g (IQR 18–50 g; range 1.5–300 g); median time to N-acetylcysteine 17 h (IQR 6–36 h). Seven patients received orthotopic liver transplantation for severe fulminant hepatic failure with six total recoveries and one death due to post-operative complications. Hepatic dysfunction defined as INR >= 3; hepatocellular injury defined as ALT > 1000 U/L. Synonyms: acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: In serial liver biopsies taken after paracetamol overdose, confluent centrilobular necrosis was the striking change seen in biopsies taken up to 6 days after the overdose; later, collapse of the reticulin framework and fatty microvacuoles in surviving liver cells occurred, with probable bile ductule reduplication in extensively necrotic areas. These findings attribute extensive hepatic necrosis directly to paracetamol overdose in patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (self-poisoning) in a series of 76 patients with liver biopsies; assessment includes 14 patients with measured plasma half-life.
raw_record.extra_details: Confluent centrilobular necrosis was the dominant finding on biopsies up to 6 days after overdose; later the lesion showed reticulin collapse, pigmented macrophages, and fatty microvacuoles in surviving hepatocytes. Grade 4 encephalopathy was associated with deaths, and hepatocyte volume fraction (HVF) below 40% was associated with greater maximal prothrombin-time prolongation in the first 10 days; residual scarring occurred in the three cases with initial HVF below 40%. Cholestasis was usually evident in surviving parenchyma in more seriously affected cases and corresponded in time with deep cholestatic jaundice lasting 4-8 weeks before gradual recovery, with liver function tests eventually returning to normal.

raw_record.extra_details: Severe paracetamol hepatotoxicity reported in 15 patients who also overdosed an NSAID, only one of whom developed hepatic encephalopathy. Concomitant benzodiazepine or ASA overdose was associated with a more severe outcome, whereas opioid or NSAID co-overdose was associated with improved outcome. Increased hepatic prostaglandin synthesis has been suggested as a mediator of paracetamol hepatotoxicity; cyclooxygenase inhibition by ASA/NSAID may be protective.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes that after serious paracetamol overdose, patients suffer hepatic damage, including grade III-IV hepatic encephalopathy, and that charcoal haemoperfusion and/or high-flux dialysis were used to treat this. Among 73 patients with serious paracetamol overdose seen from 1983 to 1993 who had not received N-acetylcysteine within the first 15 h, 51 received haemoperfusion and/or dialysis; peak prothrombin time, bilirubin, and creatinine were lower in patients admitted within 42 h, and mortality was 2/18 (11%) vs 15/33 (45%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (self-poisoning) setting; patients had not received N-acetylcysteine within the first 15 h after overdose; inclusion required paracetamol levels above/near the 'Helliwell line' (high risk of severe liver damage) or peak AST/ALT > 5000 U/l, indicating significant hepatic damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 73 patients with serious paracetamol overdose reported; 51 received charcoal haemoperfusion and/or daily long-hours high-flux dialysis for grade III-IV hepatic encephalopathy or risk thereof. Peak AST/ALT > 5000 U/l (normal AST 5-45, ALT 5-43 U/l). Mortality lower among patients admitted within 42 h versus after 42 h (2/18, 11% vs 15/33, 45%; p<0.05), with lower peak prothrombin time, bilirubin, and creatinine. Cascade/liver injury included hepatic encephalopathy grades III-IV and fatal hepatic failure; death due to self-poisoning with paracetamol first described in 1966. Patients also received cimetidine, vitamin K, neomycin, and lactulose.

raw_record.support_text: Following the UK pack-size legislation for paracetamol, there was an estimated reduction of 17 deaths per quarter in England and Wales involving paracetamol alone (with or without alcohol) that received suicide or undetermined verdicts, a 43% reduction or about 765 fewer deaths over 11¼ years. There was also a 61% reduction in registrations for liver transplantation for paracetamol induced hepatotoxicity, though no significant reduction in actual transplantations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (self-poisoning/accidental) context; paracetamol alone with or without alcohol.
raw_record.extra_details: National data for England and Wales (suicide/undetermined verdicts); 17 fewer deaths/quarter (95% CI −25 to −9), 43% reduction, ~765 fewer deaths over 11¼ years after September 1998 pack-size legislation restricting packs to a maximum of 32 tablets in pharmacies and 16 for non-pharmacy sales. 61% reduction in registrations for liver transplantation for paracetamol induced hepatotoxicity (−11 (−20 to −1)/quarter), with no significant reduction in actual transplantations (−3 (−12 to 6)). Paper references paracetamol as a common cause of hepatotoxicity and liver unit admissions.

raw_record.support_text: A 29-year male soldier presented after acetaminophen overdose with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. By day 2 of referral he developed acute fulminant hepatitis attributed to paracetamol poisoning; acetaminophen blood level was 6358 ng/ml. He then progressed to multisystem organ failure with ascites and neurological symptoms and was deemed a poor liver transplant candidate, with confirmed admission acetaminophen blood level of 9874 ng/ml. N-acetylcysteine was given to inactivate the toxic metabolite NAPQI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (supratherapeutic exposure); single adult male patient case report; initially misdiagnosed as ischemic liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen blood levels: 9874 ng/ml (admission), 6358 ng/ml (day 2 of referral), declining then undetectable; serum ALT up to 7046 U/l, AST 5035 U/l, total bilirubin rising to 938 µmol/l, prolonged prothrombin time (20 sec), LDH 9928, ferritin 63433 ng/ml, elevated CK/CK-MB; toxic metabolite NAPQI inactivated/converted by N-acetylcysteine treatment; patient showed acute fulminant hepatitis and progressed to multisystem organ failure with ascites and neurological symptoms; deemed poor candidate for liver transplant due to poor prognosis and multiple organ system failure. Indication context: overdose poisoning rather than therapeutic use.

raw_record.support_text: In patients who had taken paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdoses, the dose of paracetamol absorbed was related to liver damage: as little as 6.2 g caused a severe hepatic lesion in one patient (SGOT 2760 i.u./l) while 15.3 g in another did not produce liver damage, one patient who absorbed 18.3 g died in hepato-renal failure, and another survived a dose of 34.9 g. A separate section describes a 32-year-old woman with fatal hepatic necrosis following paracetamol overdosage, and the paper reports patients dying with hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (supratherapeutic) exposure setting; individual susceptibility varied widely (hepatic lesion at 6.2 g, no damage at 15.3 g).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported doses absorbed ranged from 6.2 to 34.9 g in the analysed patients. One patient developed a severe hepatic lesion (SGOT 2760 i.u./l) after 6.2 g; a 32-year-old woman died of fatal hepatic necrosis following paracetamol overdosage; some patients died in hepatic failure and one in hepato-renal failure; some developed acute renal failure. Patients with liver damage showed reduced overall elimination and metabolite formation rate constants compared with those without.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that at therapeutic doses paracetamol is metabolized to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, detoxified by hepatic glutathione, but at much higher (overdose) doses NAPQI production overwhelms cellular glutathione and induces hepatic cellular damage; onset of hepatic disturbances typically occurs within 12–36 hours after ingestion, with peak liver dysfunction delayed until around day 3. The reported three cases provide further evidence that paracetamol overdose is associated with these hepatic effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (supratherapeutic) exposure; case 1 co-ingested 3 g ibuprofen alongside 8 g paracetamol (co-exposure); adolescent patient (16-year-old girl); treated with N-acetylcysteine infusion.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic mechanism attributed to accumulation of the NAPQI metabolite overwhelming cellular glutathione. Case series of three paracetamol-overdose patients presenting prothrombin-time prolongation without overt hepatic failure; the paper emphasizes that prothrombin-time prolongation in this setting should not alone be interpreted as severity/accuracy of liver failure. Case 1: ingested 8 g paracetamol, initially mild ALT elevation (173 UI/L, later 207 UI/L), prothrombin index fell 85% to 38% while factor V was low-normal (60%); on day 3 abrupt transaminase rise peaking at 7873 UI/L, prothrombin index 21%, factor V 33%, bilirubin and renal function normal, no jaundice or encephalopathy; transferred to a transplant unit and improved with normalization of transaminases, prothrombin index and factor V.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 746 patients transferred with signs of severe paracetamol intoxication, logistic regression analysis identified age ≥40 years as an independent risk factor for fulminant hepatic failure (odds ratio 2.33, 95% CI 1.50-3.64) and for death or orthotopic liver transplantation (odds ratio 4.18, 95% CI 2.17-8.05). The paper repeatedly refers to 'paracetamol induced hepatotoxicity' and 'paracetamol induced FHF', attributing fulminant hepatic failure and death to paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (supratherapeutic) setting; increased risk in patients aged ≥40 years, with regular alcohol abuse, late presentation (delay to N-acetylcysteine), and co-overdoses (benzodiazepine, acetylsalicylic acid, opioid).
raw_record.extra_details: 746 patients transferred with signs of severe paracetamol intoxication (roughly the 5% most severe cases in Denmark, representing ~1% FHF and ~0.5% fatality rate in the referral base). Logistic regression risk factors for fulminant hepatic failure: time to N-acetylcysteine OR 1.36 per 12 h, regular alcohol abuse OR 2.92, age ≥40 years OR 2.33, acute alcohol ingestion OR 0.39 (protective), benzodiazepine co-overdose OR 1.75. Risk factors for mortality: regular alcohol abuse OR 3.72, age ≥40 years OR 4.18, time to NAC OR 1.25 per 12 h, acute alcohol ingestion OR 0.13 (protective), acetylsalicylic acid co-overdose OR 3.78, female sex OR 1.95. FHF is described as paracetamol induced.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (N-acetyl-p-aminophenol, Paracetamol), a widely used over-the-counter analgesic, is described as a leading cause of drug-induced acute liver failure in western countries, with an intake of more than 10-15 g at one time being harmful. The toxic course is staged, with AST/ALT, bilirubin and prothrombin time rising within 2-3 days and potentially lethal hepatocellular necrosis occurring at 72-96 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose by intentional self-poisoning: an 18-year-old man ingested 75 tablets of 325 mg acetaminophen followed by 30 more tablets over 24 hours (total 34,125 mg within 24 hours) in an attempted suicide, admitted 48 hours after the second dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient had severe liver failure with impaired liver function; admitted to Loghman Hakim Hospital Poison Center 72 hours after attempted suicide with lethargy, icterus, right upper quadrant tenderness and refractive vomiting; acetaminophen was not detectable in blood; AST peaked at 3650 U/L (day 3), ALT peaked at 2700 U/L (day 4), total bilirubin up to 11.7 mg/dL, PT up to 52 sec and INR 6; treated with extended high-dose intravenous N-acetylcysteine beyond 72 hours and survived. The paper also states acetaminophen is a main cause of drug-induced liver failure and that hepatocellular necrosis occurs 72-96 hours after ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old man with chronic analgesic abuse, alcohol use disorder, and chronic cocaine/cannabis use was admitted to the ICU with fulminant liver failure. He was treated daily with clonazepam, pregabalin, oxycodone, and acetaminophen, and during the last months his daily acetaminophen consumption frequently reached 6 g or more; he admitted greater acetaminophen ingestion (6 g/day) over the last 3 days. Liver tests showed AST >7000 IU/L, ALT 5600 IU/L, INR >7, and hyperbilirubinemia. The patient received N-acetylcysteine treatment for acetaminophen overdose, progressed to grade IV encephalopathy and hepatic failure, and died on hospital day 8; liver transplantation was judged inappropriate.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context (frequently 6 g/day during last months, greater 6 g/day ingestion over the last 3 days); coexisting chronic analgesic abuse, alcohol use disorder, and chronic cocaine/cannabis use; no evidence of chronic liver disease before admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure with icterus, flapping tremor, grade IV encephalopathy, factor V <10%, serum acetaminophen 24 µg/mL at ICU admission (≥24 h after last exposure), serum glucose 27 mg/dL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, total bilirubin 7.94 mg/dL (conjugated 5.8 mg/dL); no hemolysis; G6PD 7 IU/g Hb; UGT1A1 *1/*1 genotype excluding Gilbert syndrome; received N-acetylcysteine; died on hospital day 8 from complications of fulminant liver failure. Discussion describes centrilobular (zone III) necrosis with possible spread to zones I-II at toxic doses, and the mechanism of rising unconjugated bilirubin.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a patient who survived but had profound hepatic necrosis after consuming roughly 7 g of acetaminophen, an amount not usually associated with such severe necrosis. The paper notes that a recent binge of heavy drinking may negate the suggested hepatoprotective effect of ethanol, and that although the antihistamines doxylamine and promethazine in the elixir may contribute to Nyquil's appeal, the presence of acetaminophen may contribute to a more harmful effect. The case involved over-the-counter polypharmacy with an alcohol-containing elixir.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context (~7 g acetaminophen ingested in an alcohol-containing Nyquil elixir) during a recent heavy-drinking binge; co-exposure to ethanol, doxylamine, and promethazine; the paper suggests recent heavy alcohol intake may negate any ethanol hepatoprotective effect; over-the-counter polypharmacy.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient survived the profound hepatic necrosis; case report illustrates the deadly potential of over-the-counter polypharmacy; dose of roughly 7 g is not an amount usually associated with such profound hepatic necrosis; doxylamine and promethazine are Antihistamine sedatives in the elixir but are not themselves attributed as causes of the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The study enrolled 67 adult patients transferred to the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit with acute liver injury (ALI) secondary to APAP (acetaminophen) ingestion from single overdose, staggered overdose, or therapeutic excess. ALI was defined as serum ALT activity above 3× upper limit of normal with sudden deterioration in liver function and coagulopathy in the absence of chronic liver disease, with a clear history of excess APAP ingestion. All patients received intravenous N-acetylcysteine treatment; outcomes recorded included survival, death, or liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context comprising single overdose, staggered overdose, or therapeutic excess of acetaminophen; patients with ALI were managed in a liver transplantation unit and all received intravenous N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: ALI defined as serum ALT activity above 3× upper limit of normal with sudden deterioration in liver function and coagulopathy, in the absence of chronic liver disease. Outcomes recorded included survived, died, or underwent liver transplantation; an additional group of 7 acetaminophen-overdose patients without liver injury (normal ALT <50 U/L) served as a comparison. Plasma KIM-1 was investigated as a predictor of patient outcome.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 177 patients with paracetamol overdose (median ingested dose 10 g, IQR 8–15 g), paracetamol overdose caused hepatotoxicity: 14 (7.9%) patients developed coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5), of whom 11 had evidence of hepatocellular injury, and 12 (6.8%) had bleeding events. Nausea and/or vomiting (83.1%) was the most frequent overdose symptom.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context with supratherapeutic doses; mixed ingestions were common (54.8%), mainly caffeine (20.3%) and alcohol (19.2%) as co-ingestants; both intentional (76.8%) and unintentional (22.6%) overdoses included.
raw_record.extra_details: Median dose 10 g (IQR 8–15 g); 79.7% ingested ≥ 7.5 g; coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5) in 14 (7.9%) patients, 2 of whom had no elevated transaminases and 1 only mild transient transaminitis, with 11 showing hepatocellular injury; bleeding in 12 (6.8%) patients; jaundice in 4 (2.3%); N-acetylcysteine (NAC) instituted in 76.3% of patients (135), with anaphylactoid reactions in 24.4% of NAC-treated patients; patients with higher predicted nomogram risk ingested higher mean doses.

raw_record.support_text: In the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group prospective cohort of 1126 patients with ALF, 499 of 1016 patients (49.1%) younger than 60 years had acetaminophen-induced ALF, a rate significantly higher than the 22.7% seen in patients aged ≥60 years. Acetaminophen toxicity causing ALF was confirmed using a history of ingestion exceeding package labeling (>4 g/24 hours) within 7 days of presentation, detectable plasma acetaminophen, and characteristic ALT levels ≥3500 IU/L.

raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of acetaminophen-induced ALF used: (1) ingestion history >4 g/24 h within 7 days, (2) plasma acetaminophen detection, and (3) ALT ≥3500 IU/L. raw_record.support_text: The background states that acetaminophen overdose can lead to fulminant hepatic failure, and the study performs a retrospective analysis of 983 acetaminophen overdose cases (2010–2019) requiring treatment with N-acetylcysteine, evaluating sensitivity and specificity of the King's College criteria and ANZ referral criteria for predicting death or liver transplant.

raw_record.extra_details: 983 acetaminophen overdose cases from 2010 to March 2019 at Austin Hospital (Australia); primary outcome was death or transplant; compared King's College criteria (KCC) and Australia and New Zealand (ANZ) referral criteria using sensitivity, specificity and ROC curves. Fulminant hepatic failure (acute liver failure) is the injury phenotype attributed to overdose.

raw_record.support_text: The study objective was to assess whether intravenous acetylcysteine improves outcome in patients with fulminant hepatic failure after paracetamol overdose. This attributes the fulminant hepatic failure (acute liver failure) to paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Prospective randomised controlled study of intravenous acetylcysteine. 50 consecutive patients (21 male), aged 16-60, with fulminant hepatic failure after paracetamol overdose; setting: Institute of Liver Studies, King's College Hospital, London.
