raw_record.support_text: In paracetamol poisoning there are no specific early features and clinical and biochemical evidence of liver injury is delayed, with maximum abnormalities of liver function tests usually occurring 3-5 days after ingestion. Most severely poisoned patients develop nausea and vomiting within a few hours, followed by upper abdominal pain and hepatic tenderness; mild jaundice may appear after 2-3 days and a minority progress to fulminant hepatic failure after 3-6 days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context; severe poisoning is assessed by plasma paracetamol concentration to identify those needing sulphydryl-compound treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver-function test abnormalities peak 3-5 days after ingestion; nausea/vomiting within hours, then upper abdominal pain and hepatic tenderness; mild jaundice after 2-3 days; minority progress to fulminant hepatic failure after 3-6 days. Reviews cited: Prescott 1975-1980.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes five patients who took paracetamol overdoses of 17.5–45 g and developed imminent acute hepatic failure; they were treated with N-acetylcysteine and MARS albumin dialysis, four recovered without liver transplantation and one died. Paracetamol overdose is described as causing acute liver failure, with prognosis depending on the ingested amount and the time between ingestion and treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (17.5–45 g ingested). One patient also co-ingested 1800 mg codeine and was on chronic metoprolol and enalapril for hypertension.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol-overdose hepatic failure. Treatment comprised activated charcoal to reduce absorption, NAC to replenish hepatic glutathione, and supportive care; prognosis depended on the ingested amount and time to treatment. MARS albumin dialysis was used to support native-liver recovery and avoid liver transplantation. Of five overdosed patients, four recovered without transplantation and one died. Patient 1: 45 g overdose, high serum paracetamol levels (1731 µmol/l at 24 h, 922 µmol/l at 30 h, 540 µmol/l at 39 h after ingestion), grade I encephalopathy, anuria/oliguria needing haemofiltration, fulfilled high-urgent liver-transplant criteria, pH 7.22, Factor V 7%, thromboplastin time (TT) 18%.

raw_record.support_text: A patient was admitted about 60 hours after ingesting 100 Tylenol tablets (33 gm of acetaminophen) and twenty 0.15 mg L-thyroxine tablets, presenting with nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain. Laboratory values showed severe hepatic injury: total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl, SGOT greater than 5,000 IU, alkaline phosphatase 327 IU, and prothrombin time 48 sec, with a blood acetaminophen of 7.1 mg/dl.

Case 1 also ingested twenty 0.15 mg L-thyroxine tablets; Case 2 additionally ingested an unknown cough syrup and injected intravenously five to ten dissolved tablets, with a remote history of IV amphetamines two or three months prior.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: latency of symptoms about 16 hours before admission, 60 hours after ingestion; progressed to stage IV hepatic encephalopathy with ten days of encephalopathy requiring intubation on the sixth hospital day; peak serum bilirubin 33 mg/dl on day 11; acidosis (arterial pH 6.94, lactate 129 mg/dl). Liver biopsy one month after overdose showed extensive collapse with bridging lesions, regenerating nodules, and cholestasis; follow-up biopsy at eight months showed residual portal-tract fibrosis without active disease or cirrhosis. Case 2: admitted four days after ingestion with scleral icterus, bilirubin 3.9 mg/dl, SGOT greater than 2,750 IU, prothrombin time 35 sec; acetaminophen not detectable in blood; serum creatinine remained normal.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old male presented with abdominal pain after taking 50 x 500 mg acetaminophen tablets (25,000 mg total) over the preceding two days. Labs showed acetaminophen 337 mg/L, AST 137 IU/L, ALT 194 IU/L, pH 7.24, and lactate 4.1 mmol/L. He was treated with IV N-acetylcysteine and a single 15 mg/kg fomepizole dose, with a peak AST 198 IU/L, peak ALT 301 IU/L, and peak INR 3.1. The paper frames this as severe acetaminophen toxicity, with multiple markers of poor expected outcome (cross product over 10,000 mg/L x IU/L, chronic ethanol use, delayed NAC, long APAP half-life) yet peak transaminases stayed below 1000 IU/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (50 x 500 mg tablets over two days = 25 g); history of chronic ethanol/alcohol abuse; delay to NAC administration of over eight hours; complaint of abdominal pain, not self-harm.
raw_record.extra_details: Initial APAP level 337 mg/L; initial AST 137 IU/L, ALT 194 IU/L; peak AST 198 IU/L, peak ALT 301 IU/L, peak INR 3.1; hepatic dysfunction with INR peaked at 3.1. Cross product (higher transaminase x APAP) over 10,000 mg/L x IU/L (positive likelihood ratio 250 for hepatotoxicity defined as peak transaminase >1000 IU/L). Serum APAP half-life 10.2 hours (above the 4-hour threshold for hepatotoxicity). Hepatotoxicity attributed to the hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI generated via CYP 2E1 upregulation (mechanistic/preclinical data, not independently causal). Treated with IV NAC and a single 15 mg/kg fomepizole dose; patient recovered and was medically cleared, INR normalized within 3 days. No blood products, no liver transplant needed, no death.

raw_record.support_text: In this randomized trial of antidotes for paracetamol poisoning, patients who ingested paracetamol overdose (mean ingested amounts 25.5-29.3 g across groups) developed liver injury evidenced by elevated AST (geometric mean peak 1046 U/l in the supportive-therapy group), elevated bilirubin, and histological hepatic necrosis grades, with grade III (severe) necrosis occurring significantly less often with cysteamine or methionine treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (accidental/deliberate paracetamol poisoning) treated with supportive therapy or an antidote (cysteamine or methionine).
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized trial of cysteamine vs methionine vs supportive therapy for paracetamol poisoning. Mean ingested paracetamol 25.5 g (S), 29.3 g (C), 28.4 g (M); mean delay to treatment ~7 h. One death (previously reported) occurred in the supportive-therapy group: a 24-year-old patient transferred 10 h after ingesting 15 g paracetamol and treated by charcoal haemoperfusion. Geometric mean peak AST 1046 U/l (S), 96 U/l (C), 139 U/l (M); significant AST reduction with cysteamine (p<0.002) and methionine (p<0.01); bilirubin significantly lower with cysteamine (p<0.05). Histology showed hepatic necrosis grades; grade III severe necrosis significantly reduced with cysteamine (p<0.01) and methionine (p<0.05). Peak plasma creatinine lower in treatment groups. Cysteamine and methionine were antidotes (treatments), not themselves causative. No randomized control group receiving placebo; supportive therapy served as comparator.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old young woman was admitted with acute liver failure secondary to acetaminophen overdose (AOD). On arrival she had cold peripheries, arterial pH 7.42, INR of 9.48, and serum creatinine of 38 µmol/L; she subsequently developed grade IV encephalopathy requiring intubation, INR greater than 15, vasopressor dependence, and persistent hyperlactataemia (blood lactate 3 mmol/L despite high-volume hemodiafiltration), and was super-urgently listed for liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (acetaminophen overdose, AOD) in a 16-year-old adolescent; case required super-urgent listing for liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. On arrival: arterial pH 7.42, INR 9.48, serum creatinine 38 µmol/L without renal replacement therapy. Progressed to grade IV encephalopathy with intubation, INR > 15, vasopressor dependence, persistent hyperlactataemia (blood lactate 3 mmol/L despite high-volume hemodiafiltration). Undergoing auxiliary partial orthotopic liver transplantation (APOLT). Core evidence is the acute liver failure outcome secondary to acetaminophen overdose; individual lab values, encephalopathy grade, and transplant listing detail.

raw_record.support_text: Of 452 delayed paracetamol ingestions treated with acetylcysteine, 10 (2%) patients had or developed hepatotoxicity (defined as peak ALT >1000 IU/L), 5 with established hepatotoxicity at presentation (initial ALT range 2366–10116 IU/L, INR range 1.4–2.6). In the staggered overdoses (n=426), 13 cases of hepatotoxicity occurred (peak INR 1.5–4.4; ALT up to 10956 IU/L), and one supratherapeutic ingestion had an initial multiplication product >10 000 mg/L × IU/L with ALT 3042 IU/L. The paper attributes these episodes of hepatotoxicity to paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (acute single acute, staggered, delayed, and supratherapeutic ingestions); patients treated with the antidote acetylcysteine, so risk reflects treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as peak ALT >1000 IU/L. Cohort: 452 delayed ingestions (10 hepatotoxicity cases, 5 with established hepatotoxicity, initial ALT 2366–10116 IU/L, INR 1.4–2.6); 426 staggered overdoses (13 hepatotoxicity cases, peak INR 1.5–4.4, ALT up to 10956 IU/L); 202 supratherapeutic ingestions (1 case with initial multiplication product >10 000 mg/L × IU/L, ALT 3042 IU/L, peak INR 1.7). Novel risk instrument is the paracetamol–aminotransferase multiplication product (APAP × ALT); product >10 000 mg/L × IU/L strongly associated with hepatotoxicity, product <1500 mg/L × IU/L highly unlikely. All patients with undetectable paracetamol concentrations survived.

raw_record.support_text: In a descriptive study of 662 patients enrolled by the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group, 275 (41.5%) had acetaminophen (APAP) overdoses meeting ALF criteria of coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy. Both unintentional (staggered) and intentional suicidal overdoses produced nearly equally high aminotransferases, and the paper attributes acute liver failure to APAP overdose, with toxicity enhanced by glutathione depletion from alcohol or starvation. The text also notes paracetamol was understood in the UK as responsible for a rising number of deaths as a suicide agent, and a 1975 Lancet editorial urged replacing paracetamol because it 'cannot cause liver damage.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (both intentional self-harm and unintentional/staggered overdoses); not therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: US ALF Study Group cohort of 662 patients, 275 (41.5%) APAP overdose meeting ALF criteria (coagulopathy INR ≥1.5 and encephalopathy); 7% reported less than 4 g, suggesting possible enhanced sensitivity, possibly via alcohol or starvation depleting glutathione; APAP half-life about 2-3 h; both phenotypes with nearly equally high aminotransferases and similar antidepressant/other substance use; ~2/3 of unintentional patients habituated/adicted to high-dose hydrocodone/APAP products; Dangers recognized in UK case reports from 1970; paracetamol used as a suicide agent with rising UK deaths; 1975 Lancet editorial ('cannot cause liver damage'); UK 1998 legislation limiting package size (16 convenience stores, 32 pharmacies) and requiring blister packing.

The answer key confirms this death resulted from an overdose of drugs (possible accident or suicide), i.e., not a natural cause.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of 184 patients with acute APAP (acetaminophen) overdose (167 intentional, 17 unintentional), hepatotoxicity was documented in cases presenting with elevated serum AST and ALT, with peak AST 15,616 IU/L and peak ALT 7,726 IU/L. raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 184 APAP overdose patients, median age 22 years, 79.9% female; median ingested dose 10.5 g (range 4.5-50 g). Severe hepatotoxicity was predefined as AST or ALT ≥10xULN with INR >2.11; ALF was predefined as hepatotoxicity with INR >1.5 and any hepatic encephalopathy. Peak AST 15,616 IU/L and peak ALT 7,726 IU/L in documented hepatotoxicity cases, peaking 10-18 h (1-105 h) after acute overdose. 11 patients (6%) developed AKI (max creatinine 5.37 mg/dL). Treatment included N-acetylcysteine; 59 patients had serum APAP above the Rumack-Matthew treatment line. APAP (acetaminophen) is also referred to as paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: Forty-four patients underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for acute liver failure caused by paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose during a 14-year period, representing 35% of transplants for acute liver failure in the unit. Nine patients (20.5%) presented following a staggered overdose, only four (9.1%) had an accidental overdose, and the median number of paracetamol tablets ingested was 50 (25 g), range 10-125.

raw_record.extra_details: 44 orthotopic liver transplants for paracetamol overdose-induced acute liver failure, 35% of all ALF transplants in the unit over 14 years; median 50 tablets (25 g) ingested, range 10-125; 9 patients (20.5%) staggered overdose, 4 (9.1%) accidental overdose. On admission to the Scottish Liver Transplant Unit, 29 (65.9%) were jaundiced, 21 (47.8%) encephalopathic, 11 (25%) acidotic (pH < 7.30). Median admission values: ALT 9490 U/l (range 694-18269), bilirubin 85 µm, prothrombin time 70.3 s, creatinine 198 µm; 37/44 (84%) required renal support. All 44 met King's College criteria for transplantation; 18 deaths occurred (13 during index admission, 5 later), all transplant-related except one case.

raw_record.support_text: This case series describes seven psoriasis patients with acute methotrexate toxicity resulting from overdosing of methotrexate. The acute cumulative dose of methotrexate ranged from 35 mg to 150 mg taken over 3–7 days and was responsible for acute toxicity, which included deranged liver function (hepatotoxicity). All cases presented with ulceration, bleeding and pain in skin lesions; five had oral mucosal ulceration and two had genital mucosal involvement. Five cases recovered and two expired after receiving injectable folinic acid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure in psoriasis patients: acute cumulative methotrexate dose 35–150 mg taken over 3–7 days. Case 1 co-ingested paracetamol and diclofenac with methotrexate for joint pain; cases 5 and 6 were alcoholic, and both expired.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases (6 male, 1 female; ages 35–57 years). Deranged liver function tests included SGOT up to 510 U/L and SGPT up to 420 U/L (normal 0–37 and 0–40 U/L). Two cases died due to grossly deranged liver function tests, renal function tests and pancytopenia leading to septicaemia; the other five recovered. Serum methotrexate levels (available in cases 2,3,4,5,7) ranged 0.21–97 μmol/L. Acute methotrexate toxicity is attributed to inhibition of DNA synthesis in rapidly proliferating cells, with higher doses causing deranged liver function, lowered blood counts and skin/mucosal necrosis. All patients treated with intravenous folinic acid (leucovorin) 20 mg 6-hourly then 10 mg 6-hourly until counts normalized. No patients had pre-existing renal or hepatic disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol overdose is the main cause of acute liver failure in both the United Kingdom (60.9%) and the United States (46%), and is becoming a common cause of ALF in other European countries. Intentional overdose-related ALF predominates in the UK, whereas in the US paracetamol hepatotoxicity is usually secondary to accidental overdose (multiple doses for pain relief without suicidal intent). A comparison of 122 subjects with intentional and 131 with unintentional overdose showed that unintentional overdose patients were older (median 38 vs 32 years, P=0.002), more frequently used multiple paracetamol-containing preparations (38% vs 5%), were less likely to report depression (24% vs 45%), had lower serum paracetamol (16 vs 84 µg/dL), and were more likely to have severe (grade 3 and 4) hepatic encephalopathy on admission.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure only (both intentional suicidal overdose and accidental repeated-dose overdose analyzed)
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose accounted for 46% of ALF in a US survey (1998-2008, 1147 patients; paracetamol also implicated in 11% drug-related ALF and as a contributing factor in an acute hepatitis A series), 60.9% of fulminant hepatic failure in the UK, 20% of the French series (1986-2006, 500 patients), and 8% of transplanted fulminant hepatic failure in the European Liver Transplantation Registry (1972-2007). Comparison of 122 intentional vs 131 unintentional overdose subjects detailed: age, multiple preparation use, depression history, serum paracetamol, and encephalopathy grades.

raw_record.support_text: At the international level, acetaminophen (paracétamol) overdose has become one of the leading causes of acute liver failure, ahead of viral infections. The European SALT study, covering 600 cases of drug-induced acute liver failure requiring transplantation, identified acetaminophen overdose in 1 in 6 cases, 10% of which were unintentional. Unintentional overdoses present a higher mortality than massive intoxications, due partly to a slow, progressive onset of hepatotoxicity and later medical care.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure only (intentional and unintentional, including self-medication); not a therapeutic-dose claim.
raw_record.extra_details: The SALT study registered 600 cases of drug-induced acute liver failure requiring transplantation, of which acetaminophen overdose accounted for 1 in 6 (10% unintentional). Unintentional overdoses were reported to have higher mortality than massive intoxications, linked to slow, progressive onset of hepatotoxicity and delayed care. Paper is in French (paracétamol); French regulatory context limits self-medication unit dose to 1 g and packaging to 8 g per box.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states in summary that paracetamol overdose remains a common cause of liver injury in humans, and that prompt treatment with NAC helps keep severe liver injury to a minimum. The authors' clinical experience with paracetamol overdose patients is also described, including eight patients with deep hepatic coma who fulfilled King's College criteria, one of whom died following a liver transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure setting (deliberate or excessive paracetamol intake).
raw_record.extra_details: Authors' clinical experience with paracetamol overdose; eight patients with deep hepatic coma fulfilled King's College criteria for poor outcome prediction, one of whom died following liver transplantation. Authors questioned sole reliance on the first King's College criterion (arterial pH <7.3 failing to correct with volume replacement) and would proceed to transplantation only with persistent/worsening coagulopathy and grade IV coma. NAC treatment emphasized to minimize severe liver injury. Comparison made to United Kingdom outcomes.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective observational study of suspected overdose patients admitted to an emergency unit (2010), an acute liver failure (AST 102 N, ALT 143 N) was observed in a patient with an acetaminophen overdose (plasmatic level 49.7 mg/l), and a 55-year-old patient died from an unintentional acetaminophen overdose (plasmatic level 33.2 mg/l) in a context associated with acute pancreatitis. The median plasmatic acetaminophen concentration among the 21 overdosers was 39.5 mg/l.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure setting; one case was an unintentional overdose in a 55-year-old patient where death was associated with concurrent acute pancreatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure with AST 102x upper limit of normal and ALT 143x upper limit of normal at a plasmatic acetaminophen level of 49.7 mg/l. A separate unintentional acetaminophen overdose (plasmatic level 33.2 mg/l) was associated with death in a 55-year-old patient with acute pancreatitis. Median plasmatic acetaminophen concentration was 39.5 mg/l (range 15-200.5); 21 of 62 symptomatic toxic-concentration patients were acetaminophen cases.

raw_record.support_text: Thirty-five patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) progressing to grade IV encephalopathy were studied; the etiology was attributed to paracetamol overdose in 23 patients, hepatitis A virus in three, hepatitis B virus in one, non-A, non-B hepatitis in five, and halothane-associated hepatitis in three. This lists paracetamol overdose and halothane as the causative agents of the DILI (fulminant hepatic failure) in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure setting; part of a cohort of patients who progressed to grade IV hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose was the attributed etiology in 23 of 35 FHF patients; the condition involved massive cell necrosis. Patients received intensive care with hemodialysis or charcoal hemoperfusion with prostacycline as platelet-protective agent. No zinc or trace elements were given during the study.

raw_record.support_text: In this population-based surveillance study of acute liver failure (ALF) in the Metropolitan Atlanta area, APAP-related ALF was the most common etiology among patients admitted to community hospitals as well as among those transferred to liver transplantation centers. The paper states that APAP-related hepatotoxicity is a preventable condition and asks the medical community and pharmaceutical industry to investigate ways to decrease the potential hepatotoxic risk to patients related to APAP.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure setting; population restricted to the Metropolitan Atlanta surveillance area (GaHD3); the paper notes data collection on medication/alcohol intake was limited by altered mental status in ALF patients, and the calculated incidence is considered a low estimate.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP-related ALF was the most common etiology both among adults admitted to community hospitals and among those transferred to liver transplantation centers. The study highlights note that unintentional acetaminophen overdose accounts for 25% of ALF cases in children. Overall ALF incidence was at least 5.5 cases/million, extrapolating to approximately 1,600 cases/year nationwide; ALF of unknown etiology and APAP overdose are important causes of ALF in children.

This is the only human DILI-related claim in the paper, the surrounding evidence being from acetaminophen-treated mice.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure setting; single historical case report of acetaminophen overdose with concurrent impaired glucose tolerance.
raw_record.extra_details: Case reported by Thomson and Prescott (1966): patient with acetaminophen overdose developed liver damage and impaired glucose tolerance; the patient recovered and glucose tolerance reverted to normal over a period of weeks. The rest of the paper concerns acetaminophen-treated mice (β-cell toxicity, serum ALT/insulin) and is not human DILI evidence.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that acetaminophen overdose, including both intentional and accidental ('therapeutic misadventure') overdose, led to hospitalizations and acute liver failure (ALF) in a Canadian population-based study. It cites US ALF Study Group findings that 50% of ALF cases due to acetaminophen were accidental, and estimates approximately 500 ALF cases and 150 deaths attributable to unintentional acetaminophen overdoses annually in the US, noting that accidental ingestions have been linked with a greater risk of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure, both intentional/suicidal and accidental (therapeutic misadventure); no required co-exposure stated, though alcohol-related diagnoses occurred in 33% of the cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjusted annual hospitalization rate for acetaminophen overdose 15.5 per 100,000 population (1995-2004) in a Canadian health region, with a 41% decline over the period; accidental ingestions comprised 13% of the study population; US ALF Study Group reported 50% of ALF cases due to acetaminophen were accidental, with ~500 ALF cases and 150 deaths attributable to unintentional overdoses annually in the US; accidental ingestions linked with greater risk of hepatotoxicity; sociodemographic risk factors for overdose included Aboriginal status (RR 4.04) and social assistance (RR 5.16).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen overdose (AO) is the most common cause of acute liver failure, and in the background that acetaminophen is the most commonly implicated drug in cases of acute liver failure, predominantly due to its widespread availability. A cohort of 1,543 patients hospitalized for acetaminophen overdose in the Calgary Health Region (1995-2004) was examined using administrative data.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure, including both intentional and accidental ingestions; cohort based on hospitalizations in a Canadian health region.
raw_record.extra_details: 1,543 patients hospitalized for acetaminophen overdose in the Calgary Health Region (population ~1.1 million) between 1995 and 2004 identified via administrative data. Age/sex-adjusted hospitalization rate fell 41% from 19.6 to 12.1 per 100,000 (1995 to 2004). Intentional overdoses fell (RR 0.49); accidental overdoses rose above baseline by 2004 (RR 1.24). Risk factors included female sex (RR 2.19), Aboriginal status (RR 4.04), and social assistance (RR 5.15). Background notes toxic quantity ~150 mg/kg, <5% develop acute liver toxicity, and roughly one-third of those developing encephalopathy die and 8% require transplantation. US ALF Study Group data identified acetaminophen as etiology in ~50% of acute liver failure cases.

raw_record.support_text: In a single-centre cohort from the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit, among 938 cases of severe acute liver injury admitted over 16 years (1992-2008), 663 (70.7%) were due to paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity; 161 (24.3%) had taken a staggered paracetamol overdose. Staggered overdose patients had higher mortality than single time-point overdose (37.3% vs 27.8%; p=0.025), with worse clinical outcomes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure, including staggered (repeated supratherapeutic) ingestions; staggered pattern associated with older age and chronic alcohol abuse, with worse outcomes (more encephalopathy, renal replacement therapy, mechanical ventilation, multi-organ failure).
raw_record.extra_details: 663/938 severe acute liver injury cases due to paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity; 161 staggered overdoses (24.3%). Staggered patients had lower total ingested doses and lower admission serum ALT but higher mortality (37.3% vs 27.8%, p=0.025) and more frequent encephalopathy/renal replacement/ventilation. Pain relief (58.2%) was the most common rationale for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion.

The most common etiology of ALF was paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, affecting 23 patients (57%). Within 90 days from admission, 12 patients were transplanted (30%) and 12 died (30%), including one after liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper confirms cases of acetaminophen toxicity leading to acute liver failure (ALF) using standard criteria: a history of ingestion of doses exceeding package labeling (>4 gm/24 hours) within 7 days of presentation (usually greatly exceeding this value), combined with detection of acetaminophen in plasma of a patient meeting other ALF qualifications and characteristic alanine aminotransferase levels ≥3,500 IU/L. Most patients met at least 2 of these 3 criteria. In this prospective US ALF Study cohort, 80 of 206 ALF patients were classified in the acetaminophen etiology group.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure: ingestion exceeding the package-labeling dose of >4 gm/24 hours within 7 days of presentation, in most cases greatly exceeding that value.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis confirmed via standard criteria requiring at least 2 of 3: history of supratherapeutic ingestion, acetaminophen detected in plasma, and alanine aminotransferase ≥3,500 IU/L. Acetaminophen group comprised 80 of 206 ALF patients, with 61 (76%) overall 3-week survival (59 spontaneous survivors, 19 died without transplant, 2 transplanted).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is the serious adverse effect most commonly reported in acetaminophen overdoses, with the mechanism attributed to glutathione depletion and covalent binding between the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) and sulfhydryl-containing hepatic enzymes. This claim appears in the discussion of a case report in which a patient ingested 75 g of acetaminophen (150 500-mg Extra Strength Tylenol tablets) along with salicylate and Pine Sol, and whose laboratory results subsequently normalized.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure: ingestion of 75 g acetaminophen (150 500-mg Extra Strength Tylenol tablets); the paper dissociates metabolic acidosis/comatose presentation from progression to hepatic damage in acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism stated as glutathione depletion and covalent binding of the toxic metabolite NAPQI to sulfhydryl-containing hepatic enzymes. Case report context: patient also ingested 1.95 g acetylsalicylic acid (Midol) and two sips of Pine Sol; all laboratory results normalized after three days. Metabolic acidosis and coma were still noted to occur early in severe acetaminophen overdoses without inevitable progression to hepatic damage.

raw_record.support_text: A large multi-country study of acute liver failure leading to registration for liver transplantation (ALFT) reported by Gulmez et al. identified 600 ALFT cases in 52 of 57 eligible transplant centers across European countries between 2005 and 2007. Of the 600 cases, 114 were from overdose, and 111 (97.3 %) of these were from acetaminophen (AAP); most overdoses were intentional (63 %). The highest proportion was in Ireland (52 %), followed by the UK (28 %), France (18 %), the Netherlands (8 %), and Italy (1 %), with none in Greece.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; 63% of acetaminophen overdoses were intentional.
raw_record.extra_details: Multi-country ALFT study of 600 acute liver failure cases registered for liver transplantation in France, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, and the UK, 2005-2007; 111 of 114 overdose-related ALFT cases were due to acetaminophen (97.3%). Geographic distribution: Ireland 52%, UK 28%, France 18%, Netherlands 8%, Italy 1%; none in Greece.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a retrospective review of APAP (acetaminophen) overdose cases from 1996-1999 at the University of Colorado in which APAP accounted for 7.5% of all poisoning admissions. Among 93 cases, peak ALT greater than 1,000 was more frequent in accidental overdose cases (39% vs 12% in suicidal), as was death (15% vs 0%). Chronic alcohol abuse was twice as common in the accidental overdose group (39% vs 18%). This supports APAP overdose as a cause of human drug-induced liver injury culminating in acute liver failure and death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; accidental (unintentional pain-relief) overdoses with delayed medical attention showed higher peak ALT and mortality than suicidal overdoses; chronic alcohol abuse was more common among accidental overdose cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 93 overdose cases reviewed (80 suicidal, 13 accidental); APAP 7.5% of all poisoning admissions at University of Colorado 1996-1999; women outnumbered men 2:1; peak ALT >1000 in 39% of accidental vs 12% of suicidal; death in 15% of accidental vs 0% of suicidal; chronic alcohol abuse in 39% of accidental vs 18% of suicidal. Higher arterial blood lactate (>3.5 mmol/L) was an early predictor of nonsurvival.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes 247 patients treated at King's College Hospital in 1982 and 1983 after a paracetamol overdose. Survival in local patients was 100%, whereas in patients referred because of severe liver damage it was 49% and 63% (1982 and 1983). Delay in presentation (median 30 h in referred, 8 h in local patients) precluded antidote administration to most referred patients, and patients dying from liver failure included those with serum paracetamol concentrations in the 'non-toxic' range. One patient with a chronic alcohol history (>200 g/day) who received N-acetylcysteine at 12 h died from liver failure, yet in the complete series prior or concomitant alcohol consumption had no significant effect on outcome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; concurrent alcohol use did not significantly worsen prognosis in the series.
raw_record.extra_details: 247 patients, 147 referred from other centres due to severe liver damage and 100 local; deaths from liver failure including fulminant hepatic failure. Delay to presentation median 30 h (referred) vs 8 h (local); lack of antidote in 11 treatable cases led to death in all 11. Mechanism described: paracetamol is metabolized to an electrophilic metabolite that initiates hepatocyte damage and liver necrosis (Mitchell et al., 1973). Antidote N-acetylcysteine and methionine are considered effective only within <15 h after overdose.

raw_record.support_text: The paper frames paracetamol as a hepatotoxic substance whose intoxication causes liver damage, stating that taurine is lost from the liver early after hepatotoxic substance intoxication and that plasma taurine concentration may predict the severity of liver damage following paracetamol overdose. Plasma taurine was measured in 217 paracetamol-positive poisoned patients, 100 paracetamol-negative poisoned patients, and 90 healthy controls, and the paracetamol-poisoned group showed significantly elevated taurine (mean 26.4 mg/l) versus controls (P<0.0001) and the non-paracetamol group (P<0.01).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; liver damage assessed following paracetamol self-poisoning.
raw_record.extra_details: The central aim is evaluating plasma taurine as a biomarker for liver damage following paracetamol overdose, with liver enzymes (ALT/AST) and prothrombin time cited as comparator biomarkers; no specific dose, latency, histology, or severity outcomes are reported. Taurine itself is an endogenous biomarker, not an injuring agent.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, the patient had a large acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose; continued elevation of serum bilirubin, SGOT, and prothrombin time beyond five days was associated with fulminant hepatic failure in the patient, and higher maximum SGOT was associated with a higher frequency of liver damage in acetaminophen overdosage. Histology showed severe centrilobular necrosis with cholestasis and bile plugs, while non-necrotic areas showed prominent hepatocellular rough endoplasmic reticulum.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; occurred after suicidal ingestion of large amounts of adult-strength Tylenol, with concurrent phenobarbital overdose and prior administration of a phenacetin-containing compound; liver had pre-existing features and therapy was developed for overdose management.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe centrilobular necrosis with sparing of midzonal portal area, cholestasis with bile plugs, basophilia and cytoplasmic vacuolization in remaining hepatocytes, abundance of hepatocellular rough endoplasmic reticulum by electron microscopy. Fulminant hepatic failure developed with continued elevation of serum bilirubin, SGOT, and PT beyond five days; a bilirubin above 4 mg/dl and PT ratio of 2.2 or greater by days 3-5 portends poor prognosis (12 of 19 such patients died in one series). Reported mortality for hospitalized acetaminophen overdose is 3%-27%. Liver function test abnormalities generally appear 2-3 days after onset.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen, one of the most widely consumed OTC analgesics, is one of the most common medications toxicologists encounter in overdose, and toxicity can result in severe liver damage culminating in acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure. This retrospective cohort study of patients aged ≥14 with a discharge diagnosis of acetaminophen-induced hepatic failure (confirmed by a documented toxic serum acetaminophen concentration or a history consistent with ingestion) compared hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and lactic acidosis with the King's College criteria for predicting a composite endpoint of death or transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; patients aged 14 years or older; retrospective hospital cohort with manual adjudication of eligibility.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury manifests as acute/fulminant hepatic failure. Standard therapy is N-acetylcysteine (NAC); orthotopic liver transplant is considered when medical management fails. The study compares hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and lactic acidosis with the King's College criteria (pH <7.3 regardless of encephalopathy; or PT >100 s, creatinine >3.4 mg/dL, and grade III/IV encephalopathy) for predicting a composite endpoint of death or transplant. Reported severity is acute liver failure among enrolled patients; death/transplant was the predicted endpoint.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the histological appearances of the liver damage occurring after a paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose in liver biopsies from 104 patients, of whom 38 developed fulminant hepatic failure. The injury featured confluent centrilobular necrosis of varying extent followed by rapid disappearance of necrotic cells with reticulin collapse and a usually mild inflammatory reaction. Histological recovery was remarkable even in the most severe cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; patients with a hepatocyte volume fraction below 40% in a biopsy within 10 days of overdose all died, whereas some survivors beyond 10 days could recover below this level.
raw_record.extra_details: 104 patients with paracetamol overdose were biopsied; 38 developed fulminant hepatic failure. Histology showed confluent centrilobular necrosis with a usually mild inflammatory reaction. Of 17 survivors whose initial biopsy showed interlobular bridging/confluent necrosis (grade II), only one had appreciable residual fibrosis on follow-up biopsy after ~1 year. A morphometric hepatocyte volume fraction (HVF, normal 85 ± 5%) under 40% was found only in patients who died. Survival for two patients correlated with prothrombin time prolongation and peak plasma bilirubin in the first 10 days.

raw_record.support_text: N-acetylcysteine has an established role to prevent hepatic necrosis associated with APAP (acetaminophen) overdose. The paper's study cohort comprised patients with APAP overdose, and earlier discussion references a retrospective cohort of patients admitted with APAP-induced hepatotoxicity who developed severe hepatotoxicity with metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, renal failure, hypoglycemia, encephalopathy, and thrombocytopenia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; patients with high m-MELD (≥2.9) had worse outcomes including AKI, dialysis, longer ICU/hospital stay, and higher 28-day mortality.
raw_record.extra_details: Aliases: APAP. Mentions APAP-induced hepatotoxicity and acute hepatic failure as a consequence of overdose. Hypothesized mechanism shared between hepatic and renal toxicity involves local production of a quinone imine; the direct APAP metabolite p-aminophenol is suggested as the likely nephrotoxin after oxidation to a quinone imine intermediate. NAC is reported to have an established role in preventing APAP-overdose hepatic necrosis but has not been shown beneficial for nephropathy. Study included 138 APAP-overdose patients (low m-MELD n=68, high m-MELD n=70); outcomes reported include liver transplant (0% vs 1%), hypoglycemia (9% vs 13%), 28-day mortality (3% vs 20%).

raw_record.support_text: The paper compiles multiple studies documenting hepatotoxicity (AST/ALT > 1000 IU/L) after paracetamol overdose, including patients with paracetamol levels below 1000 µmol/L at 4 h and between 1000 and 1300 µmol/L at 4 h, with reported fatal cases (e.g., four deaths in one series and one death in another) following paracetamol overdose. Chronic alcohol abuse and glutathione depletion are described as increasing the risk and severity of paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity, with mechanisms involving increased microsomal metabolism and hepatic GSH depletion leading to hepatocellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; risk and/or severity increased by chronic alcohol abuse, glutathione depletion (recent severe fasting, anorexia nervosa, bulimia, AIDS, malignancy), microsomal-inducing co-medications (barbiturates, carbamazepine, rifampicin, isoniazid, omeprazole, oral contraceptives), and underlying hepatic impairment.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as AST/ALT > 1000 IU/L. Compiles studies showing hepatotoxicity even at paracetamol levels below the 1300 µmol/L (200 mg/L) at 4 h treatment line (e.g., 2/10 and 1/16 untreated patients below 1000 µmol/L; 0.4% of 297 and 1.4% of 214 NAC-treated patients; Grade II biopsy changes at levels < 660 µmol/L, Grade III in 1/12). Deaths reported with paracetamol levels below the treatment line in association with chronic ethanol use. Mechanisms: increased microsomal metabolism in alcoholics, lower hepatic GSH, hepatocellular necrosis when GSH depleted below critical threshold. A retrospective case series of 49 patients suggested recent severe fasting may be a more important predisposing factor than chronic alcohol abuse.

raw_record.support_text: In studies of APAP-induced cell injury in human HepaRG cells, the authors found no significant caspase activation and a pan-caspase inhibitor did not prevent injury, with loss of viability correlating with PI uptake and LDH release (indicators of necrotic cell death). They note that the absence of apoptosis in human HepaRG cells is consistent with a case report on APAP (acetaminophen) overdose in which no markers of apoptosis were detectable in human plasma, supporting necrotic (oncotic) cell death as the mode of APAP-induced liver injury in humans.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; the human reference is a single case report on acetaminophen overdose in which plasma lacked markers of apoptosis; primary study evidence is from HepaRG/HepG2 cell-culture mechanistic work.
raw_record.extra_details: Paper focuses on cell-culture mechanism (HepaRG human hepatocyte-like cells): APAP-induced cell death proceeds by oncotic necrosis rather than apoptosis, without significant caspase activation, and was not prevented by a pan-caspase inhibitor. Mode in human is inferred from a cited overdose case report lacking plasma apoptosis markers; supporting mechanistic findings (GSH depletion, protein adducts, mitochondrial oxidative stress/peroxynitrite, MPT loss) are cell-based.

raw_record.support_text: A 29-year-old woman ingested 18 gm of acetaminophen, with resultant hepatic necrosis and acute renal failure. The paper notes that since 1966, eighty-six cases of hepatic necrosis secondary to acetaminophen overdose have been described, and concludes that acetaminophen overdosage should be considered one of the causes of acute hepatorenal failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose in a suicide attempt (60 tablets, 18 gm); patient was an habitual oral user of barbiturates and amphetamines.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver biopsy on hospital day 8 showed centrilobular necrosis with regenerating hepatocytes and disorganization of cords, minimal bile stasis, and a moderate chronic inflammatory infiltrate, consistent with acute toxic hepatitis. Combined liver necrosis and renal failure followed acetaminophen overdosage. Patient recovered without further therapy (initially treated with bed rest and sulfisoxazole, which was discontinued; given IV dextrose and vitamin K). Hepatitis-associated antigen, smooth muscle antibody, and anti-mitochondrial antibody tests were negative. Since 1966 eighty-six cases of hepatic necrosis secondary to acetaminophen overdose have been described; this was reported as the first such combined case published in the United States.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states it has been shown clearly that the risk of hepatotoxicity with paracetamol overdose is related to the plasma paracetamol concentration at any given time, with a treatment line above which antidotal treatment is recommended to prevent liver damage (Prescott, 1978). In the reported case, the patient was not given antidotal therapy after a paracetamol overdose and developed severe liver damage, defined as an AST of 1000 i.u./l (Prescott, 1983). Enzyme-induced patients (e.g., those on barbiturates) were cited as developing significantly more severe hepatic necrosis despite similar plasma paracetamol concentrations at ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose not treated with antidote; patient co-exposed to the enzyme-inducing drug carbamazepine (200 mg daily).
raw_record.extra_details: Risk of overdose hepatotoxicity related to plasma paracetamol concentration at time of ingestion (Prescott treatment line). Reported patient had AST 1000 i.u./l defining severe liver damage. Carbamazepine recomenced at 200 mg daily for 14 days reduced paracetamol AUC by 30%, indicating enzyme induction; t1/2 14% shorter. Discussion notes enzyme induction may increase hepatic necrosis risk in overdose (Wright & Prescott, 1973) although Prescott argued otherwise; paracetamol t1/2 is prolonged in patients who develop hepatotoxicity. Competing explanations considered: earlier ingestion (denied), unusual paracetamol sensitivity, or inaccurate single concentration measurement.

raw_record.support_text: Ingestion of paracetamol in quantities greater than 10 g (about 20 tablets) usually causes severe centrilobular necrosis of the liver, which may result in fatal hepatic failure several days after ingestion of the drug. Paracetamol is among the commonest drugs involved in self-poisoning episodes in the UK with over 5000 overdose cases a year, of which 50 to 100 die. The effects are attributed to depletion of hepatic glutathione, allowing the toxic P-450-derived metabolite to bind cellular proteins and cause cell degeneration and necrosis. The study uses NMR analysis of urine and plasma from subjects who took paracetamol at therapeutic doses or in self-poisoning episodes (fatal and nonfatal), with overdose subjects showing elevated amino acid levels indicative of drug-induced hepatic damage and severe liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose of 10-50 g taken with suicidal intent; some cases involved co-ingestion of alcohol, dextropropoxyphene, and aspirin. Subjects who recovered were treated with N-acetyl-L-cysteine or L-methionine.
raw_record.extra_details: Also known as acetaminophen, N-acetyl-4-aminophenol. Ingestion >10 g usually causes severe centrilobular necrosis of the liver with fatal hepatic failure several days later. Mechanistically, ~4% is metabolized by cytochrome P-450 to a toxic metabolite that is detoxified by glutathione conjugation once hepatic glutathione is depleted ~70%; the toxic metabolite then covalently binds cellular proteins causing necrosis. Subjects with fulminant hepatic failure developed grade III/IV encephalopathy and oliguric renal failure, usually fatal. Overdose urines showed unusually high glucuronide:sulfate conjugate ratios, elevated cysteinyl and N-acetyl cysteinyl conjugates, and high amino acid excretion (Phe, Tyr, His, Gln, Pro, Ala, Val, Lys, Met, Ser, Thr) in plasma indicating severe liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Ten patients presenting with hepatic toxicity from acetaminophen overdose (12-50 g acetaminophen, including Tylenol, Darvocet, and Extra Strength Tylenol products, some with co-ingestion of ethanol, hydrocodone, diazepam, cocaine, or amphetamines) were treated with the Liver Dialysis System plus oral N-acetylcysteine (Mucomyst). raw_record.extra_details: 10-patient case series. Mean peak ALT 9,120 and AST 10,115; mean pre-treatment PT 17 s (INR 2.3) with 2 patients showing marked further increase; some patients had coma (NA-graded confusion/coma), hyperammonemia, elevated bilirubin (up to 7.1), elevated lactate, and one developed DIC and ARDS. No patient progressed to hepatic failure, kidney failure, or coma from the overdose; all recovered and were discharged on days 5-7 (5.5 +/- 1.0 days). Patients were treated with the Liver Dialysis System (DT System, extracorporeal sorbent-based device) 1-3 times. Acetaminophen levels ranged from 4.8 to 310 ug/mL at various times post-ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old woman ingested 15 grams of acetaminophen 36 hours prior to admission, with a plasma acetaminophen level of 179 mg/dL, for which she was treated with N-acetylcysteine. She developed severe acetaminophen toxicity with acute liver failure: plasma AST 7,090, ALT 6,710, and LDH 3,110 IU/L; total and direct bilirubin 12.9 and 6.3 mg/dL; and ensuing hepatic encephalopathy with cerebral edema, increased ICP (17-25 mm Hg), and placement on the liver transplant list. She recovered slowly and woke up approximately 180 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose of 15 g acetaminophen in a 22-year-old female patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose-induced acute liver failure (ALF). Latency/onset: encephalopathy developed ~72 hours after ingestion; patient comatose with decerebrate posturing at about 102 hours. Peak labs: AST 7,090, ALT 6,710, LDH 3,110 IU/L; total bilirubin 12.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.3 mg/dL; serum phosphate 1.8 mg/dL; blood pH 7.50, pCO2 34 torr. Treated with N-acetylcysteine, lactulose, intubation and ventilation; ICP 17-25 mm Hg via epidural monitor; placed as Stage IVA on liver transplant list (coma score 6) but recovered spontaneously, moving all extremities by 180 hours after ingestion. Sequenced plasma ammonia and glutamine in relation to neurological status described in the paper.

Her paracetamol was 1056 umol/l, indicating severe poisoning. She received one oral dose of methionine (2.5 g). Although she had no clinical signs of liver damage after delivery, 50 hours after paracetamol ingestion her aspartate transaminase rose to a maximum of 4300 IU/l, bilirubin to 30 umol/l, and prothrombin time to 22 seconds (control 13), with liver function returning to normal by 126 hours and no sequelae.

raw_record.extra_details: The infant of 29 weeks' gestation was exposed transplacentally and treated with exchange transfusions due to the risk of severe hepatic necrosis from paracetamol's reactive arylating intermediate. The paper notes sulphation is the major metabolic pathway and mixed function oxidase activity sufficient at this gestational age to produce hepatotoxic metabolic products, and that liver necrosis is likely unless the reactive intermediate is conjugated with glutathione.

raw_record.support_text: A 24-year-old female self-poisoned with >30 g of paracetamol (acetaminophen), taken as both co-proxamol (dextropropoxyphene and paracetamol) and paracetamol, presenting >18 h after ingestion. Her paracetamol level was 943 µmol/l, which at that time of ingestion implied a very high risk of hepatocellular damage as well as fulminant liver failure despite n-acetylcysteine treatment; however her liver function tests remained entirely normal and she recovered rapidly, possibly due to profound therapeutic hypothermia (rectal temperature 19°C).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose of >30 g with delayed (>18 h) presentation; paracetamol ingested partly via co-proxamol (dextropropoxyphene and paracetamol); patient had profound hypothermia which may have protected the liver, as liver tests remained normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol level 943 µmol/l; the paper states paracetamol poisoning causes ~200 deaths/year in the UK and is the most frequent cause of fulminant hepatic failure in the UK, and that high paracetamol levels imply very high risk of hepatocellular damage and fulminant liver failure. Treated with n-acetylcysteine; made rapid and complete recovery with normal liver function tests, attributed to therapeutically induced hypothermia.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of an adolescent who developed acute hepatic failure despite early and complete acetylcysteine treatment started 5 hours after ingestion. Persistently elevated serum acetaminophen (653 µg/mL at 4 h; 470 µg/mL at 45 h); rising transaminases; mild hepatic encephalopathy; INR peaked at 4.8 on hospital day 4; placed on the liver-transplant list but removed as transaminases fell and encephalopathy resolved on hospital day 6. Received a second acetylcysteine bolus; treated with fresh-frozen plasma, vitamin K, and factor VII for coffee-ground emesis; also received cefotaxime for Haemophilus influenzae bacteremia.

raw_record.support_text: The correspondence discusses a case of overdose with an extended-release acetaminophen product. Because of the delay between the overdose and arrival, the pattern of acetaminophen elimination in the case could not be timed to peak level or assessed with the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, but the observed elimination pattern is 'similar to that seen with acute acetaminophen overdose when hepatotoxicity has developed.' The text frames acetaminophen overdose as leading to hepatotoxicity and gives management and nomogram guidance for extended-release acetaminophen overdoses.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose of an extended-release acetaminophen formulation; severe overdose context in which the delay between ingestion and arrival precluded timing of peak level or application of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of extended-release acetaminophen overdose; elimination pattern consistent with acute acetaminophen overdose hepatitis. Management discussion: measure plasma acetaminophen at least 4 h post-ingestion and again 4-6 h later; if either exceeds the Rumack-Matthew nomogram line, complete acetylcysteine antidotal therapy; if the specific product is unknown, manage as an extended-release overdose. Refers to Poisindex Information System for management.

raw_record.support_text: In the present case report, acute liver failure (ALF) was induced by an overdose of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) taken in a suicide attempt; the resulting serum salicylate concentration was 1,180 µg/mL. The authors note that ASA-induced hepatic injury is a well-known dose-related phenomenon tied to the intrinsic hepatotoxicity of salicylate, whereas ASA-induced ALF is rare. The patient developed ALF with hepatic coma and received emergency living donor liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose of ASA in a suicide attempt by an adult without an antecedent viral infection; patient presented with ALF with hepatic coma.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum salicylate concentration 1,180 µg/mL (toxic range considered 350–700 µg/mL; severe poisoning ≥700 µg/mL). Histopathology showed swelling and microvesicular steatosis consistent with Reye's syndrome, but presence of cholestasis and periportal neutrophil infiltration contraindicated Reye's; loss of hepatocytes and cholestasis were also noted. Patient received emergency LDLT; ALF score at transplantation was 4.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' reply regarding a patient who overdosed on extended-release acetaminophen (Tylenol Extended Relief), they state that recent data show little or no prolongation of elimination after overdose in patients without hepatotoxicity, and they agree that slowed drug elimination in their patient was due to hepatic dysfunction rather than unusually prolonged drug absorption. This frames acetaminophen overdose as capable of causing hepatotoxicity and attributes the patient's hepatic dysfunction to the overdosed drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose of the extended-release (Tylenol Extended Relief) formulation; the affected patient was a 13-year-old girl who ingested an extended-release acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Extended-release (Tylenol Extended Relief) formulation; overdose management involved measuring serum acetaminophen levels every 2 hours from 4 to 16 hours after ingestion and treating with acetylcysteine if a value exceeded two thirds of the potentially toxic level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, with treatment discontinued if the value never reached the potentially toxic range and liver-function tests were normal 36 hours after ingestion. Prolonged drug absorption was noted after actual and simulated overdoses (50 tablets gave only 64 percent dissolution at 8 hours). Peak acetaminophen levels after supratherapeutic nontoxic doses of the extended-release form were about two thirds of those after equivalent immediate-release doses, with nearly identical AUCs. The case patient was described by Graudins et al.

raw_record.support_text: The letter, responding to a case report by Graudins et al. of an overdose of extended-release acetaminophen (Tylenol Extended Relief, McNeil), states that the subsequent pattern of acetaminophen elimination in this case is similar to that seen with acute acetaminophen overdose when hepatotoxicity has developed. It then provides management guidance for extended-release acetaminophen overdose, including measuring plasma acetaminophen levels at least four hours after ingestion and again four to six hours later, using the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, and possibly completing acetylcysteine antidotal therapy if values fall in the potentially toxic range.

raw_record.extra_details: Extended-release bilayered caplet formulation containing 650 mg acetaminophen total (325 mg immediate-release plus 325 mg slow-release matrix). In vitro dissolution: 2 caplets (1.3 g) release 88% within 3 hours and 95% within 5 hours; 20 caplets (13 g) release 84% and 93%, respectively. Case details insufficient to establish time-to-peak level or to assess Rumack-Matthew nomogram utility; elimination pattern similar to acute acetaminophen overdose with developed hepatotoxicity. Management includes serial plasma acetaminophen measurement and acetylcysteine therapy per Rumack-Matthew nomogram; Poisindex Information System referenced.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 17 year old boy sought medical attention 72 hours after an overdose of 20-30 tablets of paracetamol (acetaminophen). Prothrombin time was prolonged to 120 seconds, he developed clinical cerebral oedema and progressed to deep grade 4 hepatic coma (fulminant hepatic failure), complicated by oliguric renal failure. The paper frames this as acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure, describing permanent neurological sequelae in a patient who otherwise recovered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (20-30 tablets of paracetamol); patient also had oliguric renal failure requiring fluid ultrafiltration.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose of 20-30 paracetamol tablets taken 72 hours before seeking care; prothrombin time prolonged to 120 s (control 13); progressed to grade 4 hepatic encephalopathy/coma with cerebral oedema and respiratory arrest; treated with charcoal haemoperfusion, mannitol, and hyperventilation; recovered but with permanent neurological deficits (left third nerve palsy, facial weakness, spastic hemiparesis). A prior 1977 report by the same group described permanent cortical and optic atrophy after acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure in a young woman.

raw_record.support_text: Multiple case reports in this paper attribute acute hepatotoxicity to acetaminophen overdose. A 15-year-old female died 40 h after an acetaminophen overdose, having taken 36 tablets of Lobak (each tablet containing 450 mg paracetamol and 100 mg chlormezanone); autopsy revealed centrilobular liver necrosis and fatty degeneration of the hepatocytes. In additional cases, a 40-year-old woman ingesting 30 g acetaminophen became jaundiced and comatose 5 days later and died; a 41-year-old patient taking acetaminophen 12.5 g (plus phentermine and barbiturate) developed hepatic encephalopathy with biopsy-confirmed centrilobular necrosis that resolved after 6 months; and a 26-year-old woman after an acetaminophen overdose (60–80 tablets) developed hepatic encephalopathy on hospital day 4, then jaundice and coma, and died on hospital day 8.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (36 tablets of Lobak with chlormezanone in one case; 30 g ingestion; 12.5 g plus phentermine and a small quantity of barbiturate; 60–80 tablets). Reported cases include a 15-year-old female, a 40-year-old woman, a 41-year-old patient, and a 26-year-old woman.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: death 40 h after overdose; autopsy showed centrilobular liver necrosis, hepatocyte fatty degeneration, renal tubule fatty degeneration, hyperemic zones, myocardial necrosis and fatty degeneration. Case 3 resolved spontaneously with centrilobular necrosis seen on liver biopsy resolving after 6 months. Case 4: AST 2320, alkaline phosphatase (KA units) 8, hepatic encephalopathy on hospital day 4, jaundice and coma on day 5, death on day 8; autopsy showed sub-endocardial hemorrhage, diffuse myocardial fibrosis, and focal left ventricular necrosis. Non-hepatic manifestations (sinus tachycardia, hypotension, ECG ST changes) reported in several cases.

raw_record.support_text: This study analyzed 746 patients transferred with signs of severe paracetamol intoxication for age-specific risk of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) and death or liver transplantation. Among these, 170 developed FHF and 83 either died or required orthotopic liver transplantation; the paper identifies 'time to N-acetylcysteine' and regular alcohol abuse as risk factors of paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity, and age ≥40 years was associated with a significantly increased risk of FHF (risk ratio 3.15; 95% CI 2.33–4.24) and death or OLT (risk ratio 5.78; 95% CI 3.37–9.91).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (accidental and suicidal paracetamol overdose); findings apply to patients transferred with signs of severe paracetamol intoxication; age ≥40 years was associated with higher risk of FHF, death, or OLT; co-overdoses (acetylsalicylic acid, benzodiazepines, opioids) and regular alcohol abuse present; outcome analysis dependent on time to N-acetylcysteine administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) as the attributed outcome. Of 746 transferred patients, 170 developed FHF and 83 died or required OLT. In transferred patients, FHF was more common with older age (median 48 y with FHF vs 33 y without, p<0.00001). Liver transplantation counts: 2 (0.5%) in <40 y vs 9 (2.7%) in ≥40 y; deaths: 13 (3.1%) vs 59 (18%). Age ≥40 y risk ratios: FHF 3.15 (95% CI 2.33–4.24), death or OLT 5.78 (95% CI 3.37–9.91), mortality in FHF 1.84 (95% CI 1.17–2.88). Ten of 11 transplanted patients survived to discharge. Older patients had delayed presentation and time to N-acetylcysteine, higher regular alcohol abuse, and benzodiazepine co-overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Among 208 registered adult patients with measurable paracetamol serum concentrations (2005-2010), 180 had acute and 20 chronic paracetamol poisoning. Only 7 of 98 (7.14%) patients with acute poisoning at toxic doses showed hepatotoxicity, whereas 8 of 10 (80%) with chronic poisoning at toxic doses presented hepatotoxicity and 3 (30%) met ALF criteria. Transaminase elevation >3 ULN due to paracetamol overdose occurred in 3.9% of acute and 40% of chronic cases, and ALF was recorded in 2.2% versus 15% respectively, with an odds ratio for liver failure in the chronic group of 28.80 (95% CI 1.974-892.96, p=0.007), identifying paracetamol overdose as a cause of human hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (acute and chronic paracetamol poisoning); 57.2% of patients also ingested other drugs (most frequently ATC group N neurological); 10.6% were chronic alcohol consumers.
raw_record.extra_details: 208 patients over 18 years with measurable paracetamol concentrations; median age 33 years (18-92), 68.3% female; median acute ingested dose 7.25 g once vs 4 g/day chronic; annual overdose incidence rose from 2.0 to 3.4 cases per 10,000 patients (2005-2010); 5 patients died and none underwent liver transplantation; acute poisoning hepatotoxicity 7/98 (7.14%), chronic 8/10 (80%) with 3 ALF criteria cases; ALF 2.2% acute vs 15% chronic; transaminases >3 ULN 3.9% vs 40%; OR liver failure chronic vs acute 28.80 (95% CI 1.974-892.96, p=0.007); NAC, gastric lavage, and activated charcoal used mainly in acute poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective human study of 18 patients presenting to the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh following paracetamol (APAP) overdose, 9 developed drug-induced liver injury (DILI) with serum ALT over 100 U/L (ALT = 4571 ± 3089 U/L), while 9 patients did not develop DILI (ALT = 16 ± 6.63 U/L). raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses the interpretation of aminotransferase abnormalities following APAP (acetaminophen) overdose, and states that very little published information exists regarding the AST:ALT (De Ritis) ratio in 'the most common cause of fulminant hepatic failure, APAP poisoning.' This explicitly attributes fulminant hepatic failure to acetaminophen poisoning in the overdose setting. Additional context from paragraph 40 notes that hepatotoxicity (crossing the 1000 IU/L AST/ALT threshold) followed APAP exposure in this cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (APAP poisoning); findings reflect aminotransferase kinetics in patients presenting after acetaminophen overdose rather than ordinary therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Descriptive analysis of aminotransferase (AST/ALT) rise and fall kinetics following APAP overdose. 55 subjects who received N-acetylcysteine (N-AC) were analyzed; death and a surviving liver-transplant patient are shown. A stopping criterion of aminotransferase decrease to 50% of peak was reached in 43 subjects using AST and 38 using ALT; the AST:ALT ratio half-decay time after N-AC was approximately 24.7 hours. No patient with a normal ALT at presentation developed hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is being increasingly used as a suicidal agent. About 10 g produces hepatic necrosis but the dose actually ingested is difficult to assess because of the early onset of vomiting and the difficulty in obtaining a reliable history. Shortly after ingestion the patient becomes nauseated and vomits; after about 48 hours recovery seems in progress when the condition deteriorates and jaundice appears on the third or fourth day. Serum transaminase levels and prothrombin times are extremely high, and acute liver failure supervenes. The overall mortality for 201 patients admitted to a district general hospital was 3.5%. Hepatic histology shows centrilobular necrosis, some fatty change and very little inflammation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (increasingly used as a suicidal agent); about 10 g produces hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism involves the electrophilic metabolite of paracetamol conjugating with hepatic glutathione; when glutathione is exhausted the metabolite arylates essential nucleophilic macromolecules, producing hepatic necrosis. Clinical course: nausea and vomiting shortly after ingestion, jaundice on approximately the third or fourth day, extremely high serum transaminase and prothrombin times, acute liver failure, prominent myocardial and renal damage and hypoglycaemia. Mortality was 3.5% among 201 patients admitted to a district general hospital. Histology shows centrilobular necrosis, some fatty change and little inflammation; reticulin collapse may be confluent and massive but cirrhosis is not a sequel. Prognostic factors include prothrombin ratio of 20%, hepatic coma, and paracetamol blood levels (normal plasma half-life 2 h; toxicity likely if >4 h, severe damage probable if >12 h; plasma level >300 µg/ml at 4 h gives 100% incidence of hepatic toxicity, <120 µg/ml no danger; >50 µg/ml at 12 h likely toxicity, <50 µg/ml no danger). Cysteamine treatment discussed.

raw_record.support_text: Clinical demonstration of alcohol-exacerbated paracetamol hepatotoxicity was made in 2 studies totaling over 850 patients with paracetamol overdose hepatitis (dose about 25 g). Hepatitis was more severe in heavy drinkers: lower prothrombin time nadir (13% vs 28%) and higher percentage of death or emergency transplantation (26% vs 5.3%), with no difference in ingested paracetamol doses. On multivariate analysis, chronic alcohol intake was an independent prognostic factor for poor outcome with an odds ratio of 3.5 (95% CI 1.78-6.97); the second study showed similar results for hepatic encephalopathy and greater hepatitis severity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (ingested dose about 25 g); chronic alcohol consumption is an independent prognostic factor worsening the course (OR 3.5).
raw_record.extra_details: Two studies totaling >850 overdose patients; hepatitis more severe in heavy drinkers with lower prothrombin nadir (13% vs 28%) and higher death/emergency transplantation rate (26% vs 5.3%) despite identical doses (25 g); multivariate OR 3.5 (95% CI 1.78-6.97); second study showed similar findings for hepatic encephalopathy and severity; these studies did not address impact of therapeutic doses in chronic alcoholics.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) remains the leading cause of acute hepatic failure in the USA. The Acute Liver Failure Study Group's prospective evaluation of 275 consecutive patients (1998-2003) at 22 tertiary care centers found these cases represented 42% of all acute liver failure patients (criteria: acute coagulopathy and encephalopathy, aminotransferases >1000 IU/l, intake of >4 g/day within 7 days, no other cause). Median dose ingested was 24 g (range 1.2-180 g); 44% were intentional (suicidal) overdose (often with a narcotic), 42% unintentional overdose, and 8% of unknown intent. Mortality was 27%, with 8% undergoing liver transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (intake of >4 g/day within 7 days); 44% intentional/suicidal overdose (often combined with a narcotic-containing drug), 42% unintentional overdose (usually for pain control), 8% unknown intent.
raw_record.extra_details: Also referred to as paracetamol; leading cause of acute hepatic failure in the USA. ALFSG prospective study of 275 consecutive patients over 6 years (1998-2003) across 22 tertiary care centers (~30% of transplant facilities). Cases were 42% of all ALF cases (declined from 51% peak in 2003, from 28% in 1998). Median dose 24 g (range 1.2-180 g). Mortality 27%; 8% underwent liver transplant; survival and transplant rates similar between intentional and unintentional overdose.

raw_record.support_text: In this population-based study of paracetamol overdoses in the NUH catchment area of Iceland, the occurrence of acute liver failure (ALF) was very low and more often associated with accidental overdose; N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was used in all patients with clinically significant liver injury and serious outcome was very rare. Among the 7 ALF patients (Table), one patient (case 1) had mortality listed as the liver injury outcome within 2 years of follow-up, and one (case 5) experienced a 2nd ALF.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (intentional and accidental self-poisoning); ALF more often associated with accidental overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Annual incidence of paracetamol overdose declined from 30 to 16 per 100,000 inhabitants over 6 years (down 47%), with a step-change in 2005 coinciding with removal of paracetamol/codeine combinations as OTC drugs; paracetamol accounted for 18.4% of all drug-related overdoses in the catchment area. 326 patient visits and 182 hospitalized index visits; 7 patients developed ALF (median ALT 7402 IU/l, median peak ALT range 2778-8844 IU/l; peak PT up to 61.4 s; up to 6 days in ICU). ALF patients were older (51 vs 30 years) and more often had accidental overdose (67% vs 7%) and alcohol abuse (100% vs 31%). NAC used in all patients with clinically significant liver injury. One ALF death (case 1) and one recurrent ALF (case 5) within 2-year follow-up. Young females (16-25 years, 75% female) dominated intentional overdoses; no gender difference in accidental overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: Among 182 paracetamol overdose patients, severe hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 IU/l was 10-fold more common in accidental overdose (31%) than intentional overdose (3%, p<0.001). Risk of severe hepatotoxicity increased with age (OR 1.89 per 10 years, 95% CI 1.30–2.73, p=0.001). Paracetamol overdose was thus an attributed cause of dose-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (intentional or accidental); all 7 ALF patients had a history of alcohol abuse; one malnourished patient developed ALF after ~4 g paracetamol; only death occurred in a 48-year-old female with a contraindication for liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity (ALT >1000 IU/l) in 31% of accidental vs 3% of intentional overdoses (p<0.001); abnormal aspartate/alanine aminotransferases (>50 IU/l) in 31% of males vs 17% of females; 78% of the 182 patients had normal liver tests. Acute liver failure occurred in 7/182 (3.8%) index visits (3 females 2.3%, 4 males 7.8%); 4/16 (25%) accidental vs 2/161 (1.2%) intentional overdoses (p=0.001). Median peak serum paracetamol 83 µmol/l in ALF vs 326 µmol/l in non-ALF (p<0.05); median creatinine 339 vs 68 µmol/l (p<0.001). ALF risk OR per 10 years 1.75 (95% CI 1.14–2.69). All ALF patients received N-acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: The authors discuss paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose in north east England, where 43% of all overdoses are due to paracetamol. They estimate about 58,000 paracetamol overdoses annually in England and Wales, with about 5,500 patients above the current treatment line and 3,500 above a proposed lower line. They mention the deaths of three patients treated above the lower line, note uncertainty about risk of paracetamol toxicity, and state that more information on the occurrence of death and liver failure in this group is needed, noting as many as 200 patients may die each year of paracetamol poisoning. The accompanying text frames paracetamol overdose toxicity as causing death and liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (paracetamol self-poisoning); discussion concerns uncertain timing of blood sampling, susceptibility factors such as alcoholism, enzyme-inducing drugs, poor nutrition and cachexia influencing treatment decisions.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective data on patients presenting with paracetamol poisoning in north east England (43% of all overdoses); estimated ~58,000 annual paracetamol overdoses in England and Wales; ~5,500 above current treatment line and ~3,500 above proposed lower line; three patient deaths in the debated group; up to ~200 deaths per year attributed to paracetamol poisoning; discusses treatment nomogram lines (200 mg/l at 4h, 25 mg/l at 16h current vs 150 mg/l at 4h, 30 mg/l at 12h proposed).

raw_record.support_text: This observational cohort comprised 6455 patients with acetaminophen (APAP) overdose who were treated with the 21-h intravenous N-acetylcysteine protocol for acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. Of these overdose patients, 136 died (including 34 who did not exhibit clinical signs of hepatotoxicity) and 16 underwent liver transplantation, reflecting severe human liver injury attributed to acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (peak APAP concentrations median 126 µg/mL; reported ingested dose median 15 g); pre-existing heavy/acute ethanol co-ingestion present in part of the cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Study patients received the 21-h IV NAC protocol; 136 deaths occurred of which 34 lacked clinical signs of hepatotoxicity, and 16 underwent liver transplantation. The paper's primary focus was NAC anaphylactoid reactions (528/6455, 8.2%), not acetaminophen DILI characterization.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic necrosis is the major manifestation of acetaminophen overdose. In these patients it became clinically evident one to five days after ingestion, with maximal SGOT elevation two to six days after ingestion. Severity varied from mild SGOT elevation to prolonged prothrombin time (four patients) and massive hepatic necrosis with encephalopathy (two patients). Liver biopsies and postmortem examination demonstrated centrilobular necrosis, characteristic of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (self-ingestion of 10-34 g acetaminophen, sometimes in combination with propoxyphene); 10-patient case series.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of 602 patients transferred to a specialized unit with severe paracetamol poisoning plus 212 unselected local patients, fulminant hepatic failure occurred in 148 patients, of whom 118 (80%) had an elevated serum amylase (>100 U/L). Hyperamylasaemia was associated with excess mortality (odds ratio 5.0, 2.6–9.7 for amylase >150 U/L), indicating paracetamol poisoning presenting with fulminant hepatic failure in the overdose setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (severe paracetamol poisoning transferred to a specialized unit)
raw_record.extra_details: 148 of the patients developed fulminant hepatic failure; hyperamylasaemia (serum amylase >100 U/L) was present in 118/148 (80%) of those, 218/602 (36%) of transferred patients, and 28/212 (13%) of unselected patients. Serum amylase >150 U/L predicted non-survival (sensitivity 76%, specificity 85%, PPV 33%, NPV 97%) and was associated with excess mortality (OR 5.0, 2.6–9.7). 33 cases of paracetamol-associated acute pancreatitis were also diagnosed, but this record concerns the liver-injury (fulminant hepatic failure) endpoint.

raw_record.support_text: The POP Trial's primary objective was to assess adverse events and serious adverse events associated with calmangafodipir co-treatment with the SNAP NAC treatment regime in patients with paracetamol overdose, with a secondary objective of measuring clinical and exploratory biomarkers of acute liver injury. Patients admitted within 24 h of a single acute or staggered paracetamol overdose and deemed to require treatment with NAC were eligible, and NAC continuation depended on ALT activity more than doubling, ALT ≥ 2× ULN (100 U/L), INR > 1.3, or paracetamol > 20 mg/L, indicating hepatotoxicity in the overdose setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (single acute or staggered paracetamol overdose within 24 h of admission, in patients deemed to require NAC treatment); mixed overdoses including other medications were permitted.
raw_record.extra_details: EudraCT 2017-000246-21 / ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03177395; all patients received NAC infusion (100 mg/kg IV over 2 h, then 200 mg/kg over 10 h, continued if ALT doubled, ALT ≥ 100 U/L, INR > 1.3, or paracetamol > 20 mg/L). Paracetamol-induced liver injury is the disease under study; 24 patients planned (NAC alone n=6; NAC + calmangafodipir 2, 5, or 10 μmol/kg n=6 each). ALT = alanine aminotransferase; ULN = 100 U/L.
