raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case series of 11 patients poisoned with carbon tetrachloride via accidental ingestion or inhalation (e.g., drinking a mouthful of carbon tetrachloride instead of gin or beer, drinking a vermifuge of carbon tetrachloride plus paraffin, or inhaling vapors while varnishing). Multiple patients were jaundiced, and autopsies showed severe liver injury such as diffuse or pronounced centrilobular necrosis and pronounced fatty degeneration; several patients died (e.g., Patients II, VI, X, XI).

raw_record.extra_details: 11 patients poisoned with carbon tetrachloride; two died without medical treatment and nine were hospitalized. Presenting features included jaundice (icterus), oliguria/anuria, uraemia, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhoea. Autopsy findings in fatal cases included diffuse or pronounced centrilobular necrosis of the liver, fatty degeneration/pronounced fatty infiltration, and enlarged liver (e.g., 2280 g, 3100 g). Latency was short (ingestion/inhalation hours to a few days before admission). Route varied (ingestion, inhalation); patient IX was a medicolegal case presumed to have drunk carbon tetrachloride.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acetaminophen overdose in a 22-yr-old woman who ingested 15 g of acetaminophen and 36 hours later showed biomarker changes (ammonia, glutamine, aspartate aminotransferase) and Glascow Coma Score changes consistent with acute liver failure (ALF) and encephalopathy with increased intracranial pressure. raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure: single ingestion of 15 g acetaminophen in a 22-yr-old woman, with biomarker and encephalopathy onset noted 36 hrs after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (1 patient) presented as a biochemical demonstration of the osmotic gliopathy theory for the final common pathway to encephalopathy in acute liver failure. Reported biochemical interrelationships between serum ammonia, glutamine, and aspartate aminotransferase and the Glascow Coma Score (surrogate for depth of encephalopathy) with increased intracranial pressure; deep encephalopathy persisted 96-144 hrs after ingestion and neurologic improvement began at ~180 hrs when plasma glutamine normalized. Paragraph 4 reiterates acetaminophen poisoning as one of the listed causes of hyperammonemia and acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman presented with altered mental status, icteric sclera, jaundice, and markedly elevated transaminases (AST 1240 U/L, ALT 1450 U/L, AP 238 U/L) with INR 3.07, diagnosed as acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure. She was treated with a complete 20-hour IV N-acetylcysteine regimen and recovered without serious sequelae.

raw_record.support_text: Ten patients with hepatic toxicity after acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose were characterized at the time of Liver Dialysis treatment. Ingested amounts ranged from 12 g to 50 g (e.g., 100 Extra Strength Tylenol/50 g, 50 Extra Strength Tylenol with ethanol/50 g, >30 Darvocet tablets/>15 g), with markedly elevated AST and ALT (up to AST 9,640; ALT 7,550), prolonged PT, and in several cases altered consciousness including coma; all patients recovered and were discharged. One patient developed fulminant hepatic failure after acetaminophen overdose, with residual plasma acetaminophen concentration near 100 µg/mL at 84 hours.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure; ingestions ranged 12-50 g, some with concurrent ethanol, beer, cocaine, amphetamines, hydrocodone, or diazepam; standard oral therapeutic exposure not addressed.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 patients (A1-A14; 17-64 y, mostly female) treated with liver dialysis; oral and one NG N-acetylcysteine (Mucomyst) therapy; acetaminophen levels at presentation, marked AST/ALT elevations, PT up to 40.8, and hyperbilirubinemia in some; coma and intubation in one; fulminant hepatic failure case treated 84 h post-ingestion; all recovered and were discharged; dialysis cleared an average ~1,150 mg acetaminophen per treatment (clearance 140 mL/min, treatment 240 min) with ~73% average decrease in plasma acetaminophen per treatment; paper frames injury as 'acetaminophen hepatitis' and 'hepatic toxicity' following overdose.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes acetaminophen hepatotoxicity causing fulminant hepatic failure in an overdose setting. Among 28 patients with fulminant hepatic failure described by Record et al., three had taken an acetaminophen overdose and had a severe anion gap metabolic acidosis with lactic acidosis confirmed in two. A case of a 37-year-old woman who chronically ingested 10 g acetaminophen per day with anion gap acidosis and hypoglycemia is also cited, establishing acetaminophen overdose as a cause of severe human liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure; the cited cases involved an acetaminophen overdose or chronic ingestion of 10 g per day (a case of chronic high-dose ingestion in a 37-year-old woman).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity was associated with type B lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia. Record et al. (20) found a markedly reduced lactate elimination rate in patients with liver damage from acetaminophen overdose; another study (21) found mild transient fasting hypoglycemia in four patients with mild-to-moderate liver damage from acetaminophen overdose. The authors note the degree of lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia exceeds that seen with other apparently equally severe liver disease, and suggest impaired gluconeogenesis, though they consider it unlikely that acetaminophen or its metabolites are directly responsible for these metabolic abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: In case 10, a 21-year-old woman ingested approximately 25 g of a cantharides mixture in an attempted self-abortion, became comatose 23 h later and died 24 h after ingestion; forensic pathology showed mild toxic hepatopathy (spotty necrosis of liver cells with low neutrophilic infiltration), and gas chromatography detected cantharidin in the gastric content and in the medicine residue, with the cause of death being toxic nephropathy and circulatory failure caused by cantharidin. In case 11, an 18-year-old woman who ingested cantharides in an attempted abortion was found at autopsy to have slight toxic hepatic disease (slightly fatty degeneration of hepatic cells with focal neutrophilic infiltration); GC analysis confirmed cantharidin in her gastric content, and the cause of death was toxic nephropathy from cantharidin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic ingestion of a cantharides mixture in attempted self-abortion; case 10 ingested ~25 g and was pregnant (~3-month fetus); case 11 ingested cantharides during suspected pregnancy.
raw_record.extra_details: Cantharidin confirmed by gas chromatography in gastric content (and in the medicine residue in case 10). Liver injury was mild (mild toxic hepatopathy with spotty hepatic necrosis and low neutrophilic infiltration in case 10; slight toxic hepatic disease with fatty degeneration and focal neutrophilic infiltration in case 11). Cause of death in both cases was toxic nephropathy/circulatory failure, not liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that among thirty-one patients with severe paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdosage seen before cysteamine was available, twenty-two of thirty-one (71%) had disastrous liver damage (serum A.S.T. > 1000 units/l) and three died in hepatic failure. Seven other patients who could not be given cysteamine for 11.5-26.5 h after overdosage all developed severe hepatic necrosis (mean max A.S.T. > 4470 units/l). This establishes paracetamol overdose as a cause of human hepatic necrosis and liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic ingestion; some patients were additionally at risk due to alcoholism or prior consumption of hepatic microsomal enzyme-inducing drugs; comparison group and treated-group outcomes are described in the setting of paracetamol poisoning.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 31 patients without cysteamine, 22 (71%) had disastrous liver damage (A.S.T. > 1000 units/l) and 3 died in hepatic failure; 7 patients with delayed (11.5-26.5 h) cysteamine developed severe hepatic necrosis (mean max A.S.T. > 4470 units/l). Histologically/outcome-relevant hepatic failure deaths recorded. Acute hepatic damage also indicated by elevations in A.S.T. (mean max 3419 units/l) and A.L.T. (mean max 2760 units/l) in the untreated comparison group.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old white female who ingested 15 grams of acetaminophen 36 hours prior to admission developed acute liver failure shortly thereafter, becoming confused, irritable and agitated at approximately 72 hours after ingestion. The case report frames this as a hyperammonemic patient who overdosed on acetaminophen, with acute liver failure as the underlying hepatic event and hyperammonemia contributing to encephalopathy via the osmotic gliopathy theory.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose: 15 grams acetaminophen ingested 36 hours prior to admission by a 22-year-old white female.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient developed confusion, irritability and agitation about 72 hours after ingestion, then cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure; treated with intubation, ventilation and lactulose; improved by 180 hours and woke up shortly thereafter. Paper focuses on hyperammonemia as a contributor to the encephalopathy of acute liver failure and presents evidence for the osmotic (glutamine-induced) gliopathy theory.

raw_record.support_text: The letter states that acute paracetamol poisoning is a well-known cause of centrilobular hepatic necrosis and renal tubular damage, and reports a further necropsy case, a 15-year-old girl who died 40 hours after taking 36 tablets of Lobak (each containing 450 mg paracetamol and 100 mg chlormezanone). At necropsy, histology showed obvious centrilobular hepatic necrosis with fatty change in viable and necrotic liver cells, hyperaemic central and mid zones, and early bile ductular proliferation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose: 36 tablets of Lobak (each 450 mg paracetamol plus 100 mg chlormezanone) taken by a 15-year-old adolescent girl; death occurred 40 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Necropsy case; liver showed obvious centrilobular hepatic necrosis, fatty change in viable and necrotic cells, hyperaemic central/mid zones, patchy polymorphonuclear leucocytic infiltration in portal tracts with early bile ductular proliferation. Maximum hepatotoxic effect of paracetamol is reported to occur between two and four days from ingestion; recommended therapeutic dose about 1 g and minimum toxic dose may be as low as 6 g. Renal tubular damage also described.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old female presented after allegedly ingesting 10 mL of 20% paraquat (PQ) following a familial dispute, experiencing projectile vomiting, dizziness, and generalized body aches. On the second day after ingestion she became icteric and developed shortness of breath and a 'paraquat tongue'; liver function tests showed drastic elevations in bilirubin, AST, and ALT (Day 2: total bilirubin 18.4 mg/dL, AST 724 U/L, ALT 339 U/L), and the authors state the patient had 'now developed acute kidney injury and hepatitis.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose: deliberate ingestion of 10 mL of 20% paraquat following a familial dispute.
raw_record.extra_details: 45-year-old female; developed jaundice (scleral icterus), tongue ulcers ('paraquat tongue'), ARDS, and acute kidney injury. LFT values from ingestion: Day 0 total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, AST 55 U/L, ALT 61 U/L; Day 2 total bilirubin 18.4 mg/dL (direct 15.4), AST 724 U/L, ALT 339 U/L; Day 3 total bilirubin 25.8 mg/dL (direct 22.0), AST 531 U/L, ALT 396 U/L. Managed with gastric lavage, activated charcoal, IV methylprednisolone (125 mg then 40 mg thrice daily), antibiotics, antiemetics, and IV fluids in ICU; supplemental oxygen avoided.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old female consumed multiple ferrous sulfate (iron) tablets with suicidal intention. She developed fulminant hepatic failure with marked elevation of liver enzymes (ALT 1982 IU/L), high bilirubin, and INR 5.7, and died of multiorgan failure within 48 h of admission despite chelation with desferrioxamine. The cause of death was attributed to multiorgan failure due to iron poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of paracetamol overdose treated with cysteamine, paracetamol overdose produced mild liver damage. In Case 1, on the third admission the G.O.T. and G.P.T. activities rose to 160 and 288 IU/L respectively, the maximum prothrombin-time ratio was 1.6/1, and plasma bilirubin peaked at 1.8 mg/100 ml 18 hours after admission before falling to normal. Case 2 (20 g paracetamol) showed very mild transient liver damage (G.P.T. and G.O.T. to 192 and 180 IU/L, max bilirubin 1.0 mg/100 ml, max prothrombin ratio 1.4/1), while Cases 3-5 showed no clinical or biochemical evidence of hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose (20-37.5 g) in patients treated with cysteamine as antidote; only some cases showed liver damage while others had none.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose amounts ranged from 20 g (Cases 2, 3) to 37.5 g (Case 5) plus 25-50 Distalgesic tablets (325 mg paracetamol each) in Case 4. Initial plasma paracetamol 396, 194, 141, and 220 mcg/mL in cases 2-5. Liver injury was mild and transient (elevated transaminases, mild bilirubin rise, slight prothrombin-time prolongation) and did not progress to hepatic necrosis in these reports. Cysteamine is the antidote being studied and is not itself implicated as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose (POD) is described as a major cause of acute liver failure (ALF) requiring liver transplantation in the United Kingdom. Of 127 liver transplants performed for ALF in the Scottish Liver Transplant Unit over 1992–2006, 44 were for POD; post-transplant mortality during the index admission was 30% (13 patients) with five further deaths during follow-up, and actuarial 5-year patient survival was 54.5%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose (POD) leading to ALF requiring liver transplantation; in 18/44 (63.7%) patients POD was associated with alcohol/other drugs, 9 (20.5%) had a staggered overdose, and 4 (9.1%) accidentally overdosed.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper states paracetamol is one of the most widely used analgesics with a lack of adverse effects at therapeutic doses, but overdosage can lead to acute liver failure requiring liver transplantation. 44 liver transplants for POD over 14 years (out of 608 POD patients managed; 436 did not meet King's College criteria; 172 assessed; 68 suitable; 44 transplanted). Post-transplant index-admission mortality 30% (13 patients) plus 5 late deaths; 5-year patient survival 54.5%, graft survival 49.5%; 23% re-transplanted (primary nonfunction 1, hepatic artery thrombosis 3, chronic rejection 2). Median age 30 (18–51); median follow-up 7 years; 19 (43.2%) had prior overdose/psychiatric illness.

raw_record.support_text: The letter discusses paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning and states that severe liver damage occurred in 58% of patients with plasma paracetamol concentrations above the treatment line who received supportive therapy, and in 89% of high-risk patients (plasma paracetamol above a line joining semilogarithmic plots of 300 µg/ml at four hours and 45 µg/ml at 15 hours after ingestion) receiving supportive therapy alone. It reports severe hepatotoxicity following paracetamol overdose and notes that only one of 33 high-risk patients treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine within 10 hours developed severe liver damage, and none treated within eight hours.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose (poisoning) exposure setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver damage occurred in 58% of patients above the treatment line on supportive therapy and in 89% of high-risk patients (plasma paracetamol above a line joining 300 µg/ml at 4 h and 45 µg/ml at 15 h after ingestion) with supportive therapy alone. Of 33 high-risk patients treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine within 10 hours, only one developed severe liver damage; none treated within 8 hours developed it, with a mean maximum alanine aminotransferase of 27 IU/l. An accompanying patient developed acute renal failure despite oral methionine given within 10 hours. N-acetylcysteine and oral methionine are discussed as treatments for the poisoning, not as causes.

raw_record.support_text: This study included 57 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF); the aetiologies were paracetamol overdose in 47 patients and non-A non-B hepatitis in 10. Ten patients (five paracetamol overdose) underwent orthotopic liver transplant. The paracetamol overdose cohort is presented as the responsible cause of FHF in these 47 patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose (supratherapeutic exposure) in FHF patients; no co-exposure or restriction reported besides the overdose context.
raw_record.extra_details: 47 of 57 FHF patients had paracetamol overdose as aetiology; median AST 2673 U/l (range 100-10200), median prothrombin time 7.3 INR, median bilirubin 93 µmol/l; 5 of these patients underwent orthotopic liver transplant; 18 of 47 died. A further 8 FHF liver-tissue patients also had paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of paracetamol overdose patients managed in Hong Kong, the authors report that lowering the NAC treatment line from 150 to 100 would require treating an additional 112 patients to potentially prevent one case of paracetamol-induced liver injury, giving a number-needed-to-treat of 112. The paper frames paracetamol overdose as a cause of liver injury that NAC treatment can prevent.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose (supratherapeutic exposure) setting; patients in a Hong Kong paracetamol overdose cohort for whom NAC treatment was considered based on serum paracetamol treatment lines.
raw_record.extra_details: The study concerned clinical management of paracetamol overdose. Using the 100-treatment line instead of the 150-treatment line would increase the number of patients indicated for NAC from 187 (20.9%) to 299 (33.5%), adding 112 NAC courses. NNT to potentially prevent one case of paracetamol-induced liver injury is 112. In one case (case 1), NAC was initiated based on presentation and clinical judgement; 23 of 112 patients between the 100- and 150-treatment lines were prescribed NAC, so 89 additional NAC treatments would actually be needed. Anaphylactoid reactions occurred in 4.9% of NAC-treated patients. The study may underestimate liver injury incidence because patients discharged below the treatment line might have developed chemical hepatitis without readmission.

raw_record.support_text: Data from Prescott (1978) on 83 untreated patients who ingested paracetamol overdose are presented, stratified by estimated dose based on blood paracetamol concentration at presentation using a paracetamol risk nomogram. The data show dose-dependent hepatic toxicity, with liver injury (ALT >1000 IU L–1) developing in 93% of patients above the >300 mg L–1 line (25/27), versus 0% below the 100 mg L–1 line, and deaths occurring only in the highest-dose group (3/27, 12%).

raw_record.support_text: In a study of patients admitted after paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and treated with mercaptamine, serum alanine aminotransferase (SGPT) concentrations over 1000 IU/l denoted severe liver damage and from 30 to 1000 IU/l mild to moderate liver damage. One patient with a serum bilirubin of 142 µmol/l and a prothrombin time ratio of 3.9 was considered to have severe liver damage despite a maximum SGPT of only 783 IU/l. Severe liver damage occurred in eight and mild to moderate in four late mercaptamine-treated patients, and severe in three and mild to moderate in 11 early mercaptamine-treated patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose context; liver damage graded by serum alanine aminotransferase (SGPT) criteria; patients were treated with mercaptamine as an antidote after the overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Severity was graded by SGPT: >1000 IU/l severe liver damage; 30-1000 IU/l mild to moderate. One patient was classified as severe based on bilirubin 142 µmol/l and prothrombin time ratio 3.9 despite a maximum SGPT of 783 IU/l. Case counts: 8 severe and 4 mild-moderate (late mercaptamine); 3 severe and 11 mild-moderate (early mercaptamine). One death occurred (late mercaptamine group) in a patient admitted moribund who died 22 hours later with multiple-system failure but only moderate liver damage. Paracetamol (active agent) is the studied cause of the overdose-related liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Liver-cell necrosis after paracetamol overdose is mediated by a chemically active intermediate metabolite of the drug, which combines irreversibly with hepatic macromolecules. After therapeutic doses of paracetamol (0.5 to 1 g orally up to five times daily) the metabolite is conjugated with hepatic glutathione to form nontoxic mercapturates; only when the dose is large enough to deplete hepatic glutathione reserves does the excess metabolite remain free to exert harmful effects leading to cell death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose exposure
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients died in acute hepatic failure, all showing subtotal lobular necrosis with only small islets of altered hepatocytes surviving periportally. In survivors, grade III (severe) centrilobular necrotic zones were reconstituted by 3 months with only minor residual changes, including one patient with mild centrilobular fibrosis and reticulin scarring. Injury mechanism: a chemically active metabolite depletes hepatic glutathione, releasing the reactive metabolite to cause cell death; experimental animal data showed a dose threshold for paracetamol-induced centrilobular necrosis. No close dose-damage relationship could be established from stated/estimated overdose size, but plasma paracetamol levels above 400 g/l at 2 h to 30 g/l at 18 h were frequently associated with severe (grade III) damage, while lower admission levels were usually associated with mild (grade I) damage.

raw_record.support_text: This retrospective study analyzed patients who experienced hepatotoxicity following paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose presenting after two different scenarios, single or multiple ingestion, with a common feature of a delay of 12 h or more for the initiation of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) therapy. It is noted that most patients with an acute paracetamol overdose will not develop hepatotoxicity provided NAC is administered within 8 h of overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose setting, either single or multiple ingestion; all patients had a delay of 12 h or more before NAC therapy initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of patients with paracetamol overdose experiencing hepatotoxicity. Poor outcome was noted in 29% of patients with single ingestion versus 54% with multiple ingestions; subgroups differed for peak ALT, bilirubin, factor V, ammonia, minimal arterial pH, maximal lactate, AST/ALT ratio, half-lives of AST and ALT, and APAP x AT. Patients with poor outcome were significantly older (p=0.005). Among accidental overdose following multiple ingestion, lactate was higher in those with bad outcome (5.2 mmol/L vs 2.1 mmol/L, p=0.001). Multivariate analysis showed significant association of maximal lactate and creatinine with bad outcome; ROC AUC confirmed predictive value. NAC = N-acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: Prescott and colleagues' 1971 observations of 30 patients admitted to the Royal Infirmary in Edinburgh with paracetamol overdose reported clinical and biochemical evidence of severe hepatic poisoning in 17 patients, one of whom died. Plasma paracetamol concentrations above 1980 µmol/L (300 µg/mL) at 4 h were always associated with severe hepatic toxicity, and hepatic necrosis developed in 16 of 18 patients with a 12 h level greater than 330 µmol/L (50 µg/mL).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose setting; hepatic poisoning severity was related to the plasma paracetamol level at 4–12 h after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Prescott 1971 study of 30 overdose patients with no antidote (supportive treatment only): severe hepatic poisoning in 17, one death. Plasma concentration >1980 µmol/L (300 µg/mL) at 4 h always associated with severe hepatic toxicity; 12 h level >330 µmol/L associated with hepatic necrosis in 16/18 patients, with no liver damage in 11/12 patients below this; no biochemical evidence of liver damage when 4 h level <793 µmol/L (120 µg/mL); a paracetamol half-life >4 h was the most reliable indicator of hepatic damage. Centrilobular necrosis linked to glutathione depletion. In a survey response, one department reported a specific case of raised transaminases after a 4 h paracetamol level of 770 µmol/L.

raw_record.support_text: One case of paracetamol poisoning was managed at the authors' hospital and the patient died. The timing and circumstances of the poisoning were considered clear-cut: the time of paracetamol purchase from a local shop and the time immediately after when help was sought concurred with the given history. The paracetamol concentrations at four hours were 22% below the national standard treatment line, and the authors argue the nomogram should allow a safety margin of 22%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol poisoning (overdose) in acute self-harm context; authors note alternative explanations such as particular individual susceptibility to paracetamol or a possible sequential overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning fatality; 4-hour paracetamol concentration was 22% below the national standard treatment line (nomogram), prompting advocacy for a 22% safety margin. The authors' hospital changed its treatment protocol to a lower treatment line since 1994, treating about 60 extra patients per year with acetylcysteine who would not have been treated under national guidelines; one third were considered normal risk and two thirds high risk of hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In 746 transferred patients with severe paracetamol poisoning plus 273 unselected local patients, paracetamol poisoning most frequently occurred in those aged 15-24 years, whereas FHF and death occurred most frequently in patients aged 40 years or above. Logistic regression showed 'age ≥40 years' was associated with excess risk of fulminant hepatic failure (OR 2.33, 95%CI 1.50-3.64) and of death or liver transplantation (OR 4.18, 95%CI 2.17-8.05), and older age was also associated with regular alcohol abuse and late presentation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol poisoning (overdose) setting; age ≥40 years associated with excess risk of FHF and of death or liver transplantation, and with regular alcohol abuse and late presentation.
raw_record.extra_details: Study population: 746 patients transferred to a specialised unit with severe paracetamol poisoning and 273 unselected patients admitted locally over a 10-year period; partly retrospective chart-based study with multivariate analysis. Transferred patients were older than local patients (median 37 vs 29 years, p=0.0006). Paracetamol poisoning most frequent in ages 15-24 years; FHF and death most frequent at age ≥40 years.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of patients with paraquat poisoning, five of the six patients who survived more than 8 days after ingestion of paraquat showed intrahepatic cholestasis without bile duct injury, characterized by bile plugs in bile canaliculi and bile-filled Kupffer cells mainly in the centrolobular zone. Separate patients (Cases 5, 7, 8) showed necrotizing bile duct injury affecting bile ductules, interlobular, septal, and extrahepatic bile ducts, with intraductal and periductal neutrophil infiltration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paraquat poisoning by ingestion (overdose context); findings based on autopsy/liver tissue examination of the affected patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases (5, 7, 8) showed necrotizing injury of the bile ductules, small/medium interlobular, septal, and (in Case 8) extrahepatic bile ducts, with epithelial swelling, necrosis, inspissated bile, and neutrophil infiltration. Five of six patients who survived more than 8 days showed intrahepatic cholestasis without bile duct injury. In Case 8 electron microscopy showed bile canaliculi with dilatation, wall thickening, and microvilli degeneration, though the authors noted this finding was not reliable due to postmortem autolysis.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen overdose is reported as the most common cause of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) in the United States, accounting for 39% of cases. The Acute Liver Failure Study Group noted that 48% of acetaminophen overdoses are unintentional (therapeutic misadventures) and 44% are suicidal. The paper frames a timely transfer to a liver transplantation center as crucial for management.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose is the most common cause of FHF in the US (39% of cases); Acute Liver Failure Study Group data: 48% of overdoses unintentional, 44% suicidal. Illustrative case: 28-year-old woman ingested a full bottle of sixty 325 mg acetaminophen tablets (~19.5 g) plus several methamphetamines and alcohol, presenting with lethargy and confusion 12 hours later, with discussion of liver transplantation candidacy for fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes patients with paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) who had been taking anticonvulsant drugs. A table lists 18 such patients, most with overdose paracetamol doses (e.g., 7.5, 15, 25, 50, 75 g), whose outcomes were predominantly death. The fatal cases included one patient given N-acetylcysteine 8 h after ingestion; mortality among the 15 not given NAC was 93.3% (14/15), significantly higher than the historical series.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients concurrently taking anticonvulsant drugs (phenytoin, phenobarbitone, primidone, valproate, carbamazepine, troxidone, methylphenobarbitone); overdose exposure (7.5-75 g).
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) attributed to paracetamol overdose. 18 patients; overall mortality 83.3% (15/18), mean 6 d from admission to death; mortality among the 15 not given NAC 93.3% (14/15) vs the 1986-88 series (33/57, 57.9%) and 1973-85 group (192/297, 64.6%); mortality 33.3% in three cases given NAC before referral. Two patients from a general context had accidental overdoses (e.g., 7.5 g/24 h). One fatal case had received NAC 8 h after ingestion. NAC (N-acetylcysteine) used as treatment and not itself a liver-injury cause.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents three cases of fulminant hepatic failure attributable to the acetaminophen contained in Vicodin (an acetaminophen/hydrocodone combination). All three patients had chronic pain requiring opioids and received large amounts of Vicodin for pain relief; two of the three also took plain acetaminophen in addition, and the second patient was at further risk because she was also taking antiseizure medications. The authors recommend caution in prescribing Vicodin to patients at increased risk for acetaminophen toxicity, including those with chronic alcohol consumption or concurrent use of anticonvulsants, isoniazid, or additional acetaminophen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had chronic pain requiring opioids and received large amounts of Vicodin; two of three also took plain acetaminophen simultaneously; the second patient was on antiseizure medications (increased risk). Cautions cited for chronic alcohol consumption or concurrent anticonvulsant, isoniazid, or extra acetaminophen use.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure attributable to the acetaminophen in Vicodin (acetaminophen plus hydrocodone); N-acetylcysteine is the treatment of choice for acute acetaminophen overdose (oral, 140 mg/kg first dose then 70 mg/kg every 4 h for 17 doses, appropriate within 24 h); patients with fulminant hepatic failure unresponsive to antidote/supportive therapy may require emergency liver transplantation; acetaminophen overdose may also cause acute renal failure and acute cardiac toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective case series of patients admitted with unintentional paracetamol overdose secondary to dental pain, excessive paracetamol consumption caused blood toxicity in a significant proportion of patients (96%) as well as one case (2%) of acute hepatic failure which required active medical intervention. The authors also note dentists have a role in recognizing unintentional paracetamol overdose cases to prevent hepatotoxicity and death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients presenting with unintentional paracetamol overdose secondary to acute dental pain; overdose exposure (removal/change of the 150 mg/kg threshold lowered to 75 mg/kg under MHRA guidelines September 2012).
raw_record.extra_details: 48 (41%) of unintentional paracetamol overdose cases were secondary to a cause associated with dental pain (average ~2 cases/month). 96% of the dental-related cases had blood toxicity; one case (2%) developed acute hepatic failure requiring active medical intervention. 81% of patients were not registered with a general dental practitioner. The authors developed an algorithm/training package for dentists to improve early recognition of paracetamol overdose and prevent hepatotoxicity and death.

Among 36 evaluable heavier patients, hepatotoxicity (defined as alanine transaminase >1000 U/L) occurred in 12/36 (33.3%) and death in 4/36 (11.1%), consistent with APAP overdose causing hepatic injury.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as alanine transaminase >1000 U/L; occurred in 12/36 (33.3%) patients; death in 4/36 (11.1%). Median weight 110 kg (range 101-160). raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl presented 19 hours after ingesting two handfuls of Tylenol Extended Relief, an extended-release acetaminophen formulation containing 650 mg per caplet. She developed vomiting, abdominal pain, elevated alanine aminotransferase (peaking at 7459 U/L) and international normalized ratio (peaking at 4.2) consistent with acetaminophen-induced liver injury following overdose; she was treated with acetylcysteine and sent home on day 4 with resolving liver-function values. Serial acetaminophen levels showed a linear decline with an elimination half-life of 11.08 hours.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (13-year-old) patient; overdose by ingestion of two handfuls of the extended-release formulation Tylenol Extended Relief (650 mg per caplet).
raw_record.extra_details: Ingestion occurred 19 hours before presentation; vomiting and abdominal pain began six hours after ingestion. Serum acetaminophen 89 µg/mL, ALT 180 U/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, INR 1.5 at presentation; ALT peaked at 7459 U/L and INR at 4.2 at 59 hours. Treated with acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg oral load then 6 x 70 mg/kg and 11 x 100 mg/kg). Patient remained clinically well and was discharged on day 4 with resolving liver function. Apparent elimination half-life 11.08 hours, linear decline (Fig. 1).; extra_details_note: Severity not explicitly labeled as acute liver failure; patient remained clinically well.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl presented 19 hours after ingesting two handfuls of Tylenol Extended Relief (extended-release acetaminophen, 650 mg per caplet) with vomiting, abdominal pain, and epigastric and right-upper-quadrant tenderness. Serum acetaminophen was 89 µg/mL with ALT 180 IU/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, and INR 1.5; ALT (7459 IU/L) and INR (4.2) peaked 59 hours after ingestion. She was treated with acetylcysteine, remained clinically well, and was sent home on day 4 with resolving liver-function values. The author notes that unless acetaminophen levels after such an overdose are in the potentially toxic range, the nomogram is of doubtful value, and even elevated nontoxic levels do not exclude subsequent hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (13-year-old) patient; overdose of the extended-release formulation Tylenol Extended Relief; delayed presentation 19 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Vomiting and abdominal pain began 6 hours after ingestion; serum acetaminophen 89 µg/mL on arrival; ALT peaked at 7459 IU/L and INR at 4.2 at 59 hours post-ingestion; bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL initially; apparent elimination half-life 11.08 hours with linear decline in drug concentrations; treated with oral acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg loading, then 6 doses of 70 mg/kg and 11 doses of 100 mg/kg); patient remained clinically well and was discharged on day 4 with resolving liver-function values. Authors discuss uncertainty over whether slowed elimination reflected prolonged absorption or hepatic dysfunction and question the value of the immediate-release acetaminophen nomogram for sustained-release overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: A case report described an 18-month-old male infant who presented with acute liver failure (ALF) after parental accidental overdosage of acetaminophen. He was treated with N-acetylcysteine and, when no improvement occurred within 24 h, continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) was added as rescue therapy; the infant recovered uneventfully after 10 days.

raw_record.extra_details: NAC given at 150 mg/kg over 1 h, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h and 100 mg/kg over 16 h; no improvement in first 24 h; CVVH used as rescue and infant recovered after 10 days.

raw_record.support_text: A 6-year-old, 18.2-kg boy with cervical adenitis received acetaminophen elixir and acetaminophen-with-codeine elixir over 30 hours, totaling 3.6 g (198 mg/kg) of acetaminophen, which was a subacute overdose (recommended maximum 1.9 g). At presentation he had diaphoresis and emesis, and laboratory testing showed elevated AST (251 IU/L), ALT (175 IU/L), LDH (1507 IU/L) and GGT (84 IU/L) with a prothrombin time of 14.4 seconds; the acetaminophen level drawn 5 hours after the last dose was <10 µg/ml. He was treated with N-acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg loading, then 70 mg/kg every 4 hours for 17 doses) and, per the paper's abstract, manifested stage II hepatic toxicity that resolved and all laboratory values returned to normal within 24 hours.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (6-year-old) subacute/multiple-dose (30-hour) overdose of 198 mg/kg (3.6 g total, recommended maximum 1.9 g), given with codeine elixir and treated with N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: Case resolved fully; stage II hepatic toxicity reported in abstract; initial labs AST 251 IU/L, ALT 175 IU/L, LDH 1507 IU/L, GGT 84 IU/L, bilirubin 0.7 mg/dl, PT 14.4 s (normal 11.4-13.4 s); post-dose acetaminophen level <10 µg/ml. Mechanism: in overdose, glucuronidation/sulfation saturate, excess NAPQI forms, depletes glutathione, then binds covalently to hepatocyte proteins causing liver damage. Abstract states acetaminophen in toxic doses can cause liver dysfunction ranging from mild transaminase elevations to fulminant liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case report of a 12-year-old (64-kg) girl with a total estimated ingestion of 1742 mg/kg acetaminophen (paracetamol) and 19 mg/kg diphenhydramine. Despite early treatment with n-acetylcysteine (NAC), she developed hepatic failure with plasma ALT activity peaking at approximately 8000 IU/L around 90 hours after ingestion. This human case attributes hepatic failure/DILI to a massive paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric case (12-year-old, 64-kg girl) of massive overdose (total estimated ingestion 1742 mg/kg acetaminophen) with co-ingestion of 19 mg/kg diphenhydramine; treated with n-acetylcysteine (NAC).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic failure developed despite early NAC treatment, with plasma ALT peaking at approximately 8000 IU/L around 90 hours after ingestion; 22 ALT concentration values from 0 to 250 hours were extracted for model fitting. The paper presents the case to demonstrate/validate a mathematical model of ALT biomarker release after paracetamol overdose, and assumed a linear relationship between parent drug concentration and the toxic metabolite NAPQI and that diphenhydramine had no effect on the ALT release profile.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-year-old, 40-kg girl with SMA type II developed postoperative APAP-induced liver injury and acute liver failure after receiving acetaminophen (APAP) rectally at 69 mg/kg/d for 4 days, together with hydromorphine, diclofenac and propofol; APAP and propofol were discontinued once liver injury was detected, N-acetylcysteine was started on day 4, and the acute liver failure with encephalopathy resolved. In a second patient (17-year-old, 55-kg, congenital muscular dystrophy with carnitine deficiency), acetaminophen was given rectally (average 40 mg/kg/d, max 90 mg/kg/d) and acute liver failure developed on day 11 despite immediate discontinuation and N-acetylcysteine; she died of refractory shock on day 14. Serum APAP protein adducts (APAP-CYS) were quantified in both patients to confirm acetaminophen exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric critically ill patients (12-year-old with SMA type II and 17-year-old with congenital muscular dystrophy and carnitine deficiency); APAP given rectally; coexisting post-operative/procedural medications (patient 1: hydromorphine, diclofenac, propofol; patient 2: amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, cefuroxime, clarithromycin, fentanyl, rocuronium) as potential concurrent factors.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1: 12-year-old, 40 kg, APAP rectally 69 mg/kg/d for 4 days after spinal fusion; transaminases >2x normal at 3 days post-op; ALF with encephalopathy requiring ventilatory support; N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg IV bolus then 50 mg/kg/dose every 4h x17 doses started day 4; resolved, extubated day 6. Patient 2: 17-year-old, 55 kg, APAP rectally average 40 mg/kg/d (max 90 mg/kg/d); icterus, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting day 11; ALF; developed multiple organ failure with severe hypotension and died day 14 of refractory shock. APAP protein adducts (APAP-CYS) measured in serum to confirm acetaminophen involvement; AST and APAP levels relative to dosing shown in figures.

raw_record.support_text: An infant presented with hepatomegaly and markedly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 455 U/L, AST 1907 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 603 U/L), total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, ammonia 135 µmol/L, PT 53.5 s, and INR 2.5. The child had received an inadvertent acetaminophen overdose: the mother gave 200 mg/dose every 4 hours (~162 mg/kg/day for several days) because a language barrier led her to misuse the acetaminophen and amoxicillin doses. Plasma acetaminophen was 78.5 µg/mL approximately 96 hours after the first dose. The patient was treated with N-acetylcysteine (loading dose plus 18 doses), transferred to a regional transplant center, and made a complete recovery over 3 weeks. The paper states acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is well described in acute overdosage and results from formation of N-acetyl-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) via the cytochrome P-450 pathway.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric infant; chronic supratherapeutic dosing (~162 mg/kg/day for several days) due to a caregiver medication-dose error (acetaminophen switched with amoxicillin) related to a language barrier; plasma level was from chronic supratherapeutic dosing, not a single acute ingestion, so the Rumack-Matthew nomogram did not apply.
raw_record.extra_details: Plasma acetaminophen 78.5 µg/mL measured ~96 h after the last/first dose; 2 mL of 80 mg/0.8 mL (200 mg/dose) every 4 h. Initial labs: hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, WBC 29,700/mm3, PT 53.5 s, PTT 75 s, INR 2.5, ammonia 135 µmol/L, total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL (conjugated 1.9), ALT 455 U/L, AST 1907 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 603 U/L. Transferred to regional transplant center; treated with NAC (oral loading 140 mg/kg plus 18 doses) and recovered completely over ~3 weeks with near-normal liver enzymes by hospital day 5. Mechanism attributed to NAPQI formation via cytochrome P-450. The paper notes acute adult ingestions >140 mg/kg (≥7.5 g) or >150 mg/kg in a child are potentially toxic, and prognostic factors for severe liver damage/transplant include PT >37 s, pH <7.3, creatinine >3 mg/dL, and grade 3-4 encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl arrived at the hospital 19 hours after ingesting two handfuls of Tylenol Extended Relief (McNeil Pharmaceuticals), a new extended-release formulation of acetaminophen containing 650 mg per caplet. After the overdose she developed epigastric and right upper quadrant tenderness, and laboratory testing showed an elevated serum acetaminophen level (89 µg/mL), alanine aminotransferase 180 IU/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, and an INR of 1.5. The alanine aminotransferase (7459 U/L) and INR (4.2) peaked 59 hours after ingestion, and the patient was sent home on day 4 with resolving liver-function values after acetylcysteine therapy. The paper discusses the risk of hepatotoxicity from this acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (13-year-old girl); overdose of an extended-release formulation (Tylenol Extended Relief, 650 mg per caplet) with delayed presentation (19 h after ingestion) and underestimated peak levels; concern that high acetaminophen levels represented a massive overdose warranting higher-than-usual acetylcysteine dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: Migrated toxicokinetics: apparent elimination half-life 11.08 h with linear decline in serum acetaminophen concentrations; hypothesis that sustained-release overdose causes plateau rather than peak levels, so nomogram based on immediate-release acetaminophen may underestimate antidote need. Peak ALT 7459 U/L and INR 4.2 at 59 h post-ingestion; epigastric/RUQ tenderness; patient remained clinically well, discharged at day 4 with resolving liver-function values. Treated with initial oral acetylcysteine 140 mg/kg followed by 6 doses of 70 mg/kg and 11 doses of 100 mg/kg. Initial labs: acetaminophen 89 µg/mL, ALT 180 IU/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, INR 1.5.

raw_record.support_text: Case 184: a 3-year-old boy given both over-the-counter and prescription formulations containing acetaminophen over the previous 4-5 days presented with lethargy, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and liver failure (ALT 2,453 U/L; PT 32.6 s; bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL; acetaminophen 11 µg/mL). raw_record.support_text: A 3.5-year-old child who received repeated acetaminophen overdose (320 mg, two 160-mg tablets, every 2 hours for at least 48 hours) developed hepatotoxicity, as confirmed by toxic blood acetaminophen concentrations. The dose, about 25 mg/kg every 2 hours, exceeded the recommended therapeutic dose of 10 to 20 mg/kg every 4 hours. Liver enzymes returned to normal by hospital discharge (day 17), and the patient recovered after N-acetylcysteine treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (3.5-year-old child); repeated supratherapeutic dosing (320 mg every 2 hours for at least 48 hours); concurrent acute renal failure requiring peritoneal dialysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Blood acetaminophen 187.2 mg/L at ~22 h from last dose; subsequent 75.0, 41.9, and 6.5 mg/L at 14, 20, and 31.5 h. Peak AST 9,158 U/L and ALT 11,282 U/L (day 1), normalizing by day 17 discharge. Treated with oral N-acetylcysteine (18 doses over 72 h). Also developed pancytopenia with hypoplastic bone marrow (day 6) and acute renal failure; the paper notes no prior report of bone marrow toxicity after chronic acetaminophen overdose in children.

raw_record.support_text: Case 1 describes a 4-year-old girl treated at home for 4 days with unknown quantities of acetaminophen (APAP) given by three caregivers who were unaware of each other's dosing; toxicologic screening revealed a serum APAP level of 450 µmol/L (67.8 mg/L), and hepatic function tests showed markedly elevated AST (6,640 IU/L), ALT (2,926 IU/L), and LDH (5,930 IU/L) with low GGT and near-normal total bilirubin. This APAP intoxication was treated with N-acetylcysteine, and the patient's hepatic function worsened markedly before she improved; the injury was attributed to acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (4-year-old girl); overdose from unknown quantities of acetaminophen administered by three caregivers unaware of each other's dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum APAP 450 µmol/L (67.8 mg/L) on presentation; AST peaked at ~37,820 IU/L, ALT ~16,660 IU/L, LDH ~35,250 IU/L on transfer day; GGT low (24 IU/L then 41 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase 223 IU/L; prolonged prothrombin time (17.6-19.2 s) and elevated serum ammonia; viral hepatitis A/B/C ruled out and ceruloplasmin normal. Treated with oral N-acetylcysteine and vitamin K; transferred for preevaluation for liver transplant but showed marked improvement; complicated by transient renal dysfunction (peak BUN 55 mg/dL, creatinine 4.5 mg/dL), hypertension treated with prazosin, and residual mild renal tubular acidosis. Acetaminophen is also known as paracetamol (APAP).

raw_record.support_text: The report notes that the most common organ affected by acetaminophen intoxication is the liver when the drug is administered in supratherapeutic doses, and that repeated therapeutic doses can also be toxic. In the presented case, a 5-year-old female was treated by her mother with different acetaminophen formulations (250 mg suppositories and 500 mg tablets) every 3 hours for three consecutive days, an approximate dose of 90 mg/kg/24h over 72 hours, and developed fulminant hepatic failure. Acetaminophen poisoning was strongly suspected and confirmed by a blood acetaminophen level of 32.9 mg/l 10 hours after the last dose; viral serologies and blood culture were negative, and the child was treated with NAC.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (5-year-old female); repeated supratherapeutic/repeated dosing via suppositories and tablets every 3 hours for 3 days (about 90 mg/kg/24h over 72 hours) without other concomitant medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure with grade II-III encephalopathy, jaundice, hepatomegaly; ALT 5794 U/L, AST 6000 U/L, total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dl, INR 3.86; blood acetaminophen 32.9 mg/l 10 h after last dose; viral serologies (HIV, HEV, HAV, HCV, HBV, Coxsackie, influenza A/B, adeno) negative and blood culture negative; treated with 140 mg/kg NAC loading then 70 mg/kg every 4 h for 18 doses; coagulopathy with melena/hematemesis; suspected acute pancreatitis (hyperamylasaemia 255 U/L, hyperlipasaemia 514 U/L); child recovered with improving liver enzymes. Paper also states risk of toxic reactions is generally lower in children than adults.

raw_record.support_text: The patient presented with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure, and laboratory investigations corroborated this suspected diagnosis. The patient deteriorated with cerebral edema, was evaluated for liver transplantation and deemed ineligible, but ultimately recovered. The discussion notes acetaminophen is the most common drug taken in overdose and describes classic clinical acetaminophen poisoning progressing through stages to fulminant hepatic failure with cerebral edema as a common cause of death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a pediatric patient with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure and fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy, cerebral edema (CT showing diffuse edema, sulcal/basal cistern effacement and uncal herniation), and elevated liver transaminases. She was evaluated for liver transplantation but deemed ineligible due to poor neurologic prognosis; treated with N-acetylcysteine, mannitol, vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma; recovered with a residual right third and sixth cranial nerve palsy. Discussion frames acetaminophen as the most common drug taken in overdose in pediatric and adult populations, with classic poisoning in 4 stages (nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain, hepatic injury with elevated transaminases, fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy/coagulopathy), and cerebral edema leading to herniation as a common cause of death.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a psychiatric patient (Ms. A) who developed fulminant liver failure from acetaminophen, presented as the lowest acetaminophen dose resulting in fulminant liver failure reported to date. Her heightened sensitivity to acetaminophen's toxic effects was attributed to a combination of low body weight, malnutrition, and treatment with carbamazepine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric-free adult patient with low body weight, malnutrition, and concurrent carbamazepine treatment (CYP450 induction) that increased acetaminophen sensitivity; psychiatric illness context of overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the lowest acetaminophen dose to date causing fulminant liver failure. Mechanism: small fraction metabolized by CYP450 mixed oxidases to toxic metabolites detoxified by glutathione; hepatonecrosis occurs when glutathione stores are depleted and toxic metabolites accumulate (paragraph 38). Doses of acetaminophen as low as 7500 mg have been shown to cause transient hepatotoxicity. Carbamazepine and fasting induce CYP450; protein-poor diets lower glutathione and increase acetaminophen toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The study assessed APAP-induced hepatotoxicity among poison-center-reported poisonings using NAC therapy as a surrogate for hospitalization and hepatotoxicity. Comparing 2013 (pre-mandate) and 2015 (post-FDA mandate) cohorts (n=9130 and n=7758), it found no significant difference in APAP-induced hepatotoxicity; analysis excluding cases of unknown intent further confirmed the null finding.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Poison-center-reported ingestions in an overdose context; surrogate outcome NAC therapy used as an indication of hospitalization; intent (intentional vs unintentional) often inferred and sometimes unknown.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity prevalence data from NPDS poison-center database for 2013 and 2015: AST elevation 175 (1.92%) vs 183 (2.36%); AST >100 but <1000 111 (1.22%) vs 117 (1.51%); AST ≥1000 49 (0.54%) vs 42 (0.54%); other LFT disturbances 15 (0.16%) vs 21 (0.27%). NAC therapy used as surrogate for hepatotoxicity (prevents AST >1000 IU/L). Study compared periods around the FDA mandate limiting opioid-APAP combination products; exposures to opioid-APAP combinations declined from 48,051 calls (2009) to 38,142 (2013), a 20.6% reduction. No significant difference in APAP-induced hepatotoxicity before vs after the mandate.

raw_record.support_text: This population-based study (National University Hospital of Iceland, 2004-2009) reviewed 1913 drug-related poisoning episodes, of which 352 (18%) were paracetamol overdoses. Of 182 hospitalized index visits, ALF occurred in 3.8% (7/182, incidence 0.7/100,000/year); in the intentional group 1.2% (2/163) developed ALF versus 25% (4/16) of the accidental group (p=0.001). Only one patient died from ALF and none underwent liver transplantation. The paper states paracetamol is the most common cause of acute liver failure in the USA and many European countries and emphasizes its dose-dependent hepatotoxicity, with risk factors for hepatotoxicity described.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Population-based study of paracetamol overdoses; findings in intentional (mostly young females) and accidental (mostly older) overdoses; accidental overdose associated with higher aminotransferases and a higher ALF rate.
raw_record.extra_details: Annual incidence of paracetamol overdoses declined from 30.0 (2004) to 16.0/100,000/year (2009), p<0.05; female/male ratio 3.0, largest age group 16-25 years; 26% discharged after initial examination; 182 hospitalized index visits with 16 (9%) accidental overdoses; ALF incidence 0.7/100,000/year; hepatotoxicity described as dose-dependent and paracetamol cited as the most common cause of ALF in the USA and many European countries.

raw_record.support_text: In the described case, instead of the intended 125 mg chloroquine the 10-fold higher dose of 1250 mg was given, which almost inevitably had to lead to liver damage in the sense of a 'Flu' syndrome. The entire symptomatology of this 'Flu' syndrome, an expression of liver damage, occurred in the present case. No evidence for another cause of the neurological symptomatology was found, and the temporal course left no reasonable doubt of a causal relationship between the fatal liver damage and the chloroquine administration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Porphyria cutanea tarda patient; 10-fold dosing error (1250 mg instead of 125 mg).
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxic 'Flu' syndrome; temporal course supports causality; transaminase (GOT/GPT) elevation occurred; peak urinary porphyrin excretion ca. 163 mg on day 3 after chloroquine, largely preserving the P.c.t. excretion pattern (uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyporphyrin markedly increased; delta-aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen normal).

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old at 19-20 weeks gestation presented with elevated liver enzymes after self-treating a toothache with approximately 6 g of acetaminophen daily for 2 weeks. Following rapid hepatic decompensation with stage III hepatic encephalopathy, the differential diagnosis excluded viral, HELLP, and acute fatty liver of pregnancy causes, and FHF was deemed secondary to unintentional acetaminophen overdose on the basis of recent ingestion and elevated acetaminophen levels. The patient was listed status 1 and underwent liver transplantation; the previable fetus subsequently expired.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy (second trimester, ~20 weeks gestation); unintentional overdose (approximately 6 g/day for 2 weeks).
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure with stage III hepatic encephalopathy. Admission labs: AST 1064 U/L, ALT 1436 U/L, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL, pH 6.99, glucose 30 mg/dL, APAP 31.5 µg/mL; later AST>2250 U/L, ALT>3000 U/L, total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, INR 3.4, APAP 35 µg/mL. Treated with N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate. No prior liver disease, IV drug use, or alcohol use. Differential excluded hepatitis A/B/adenovirus, HELLP, acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Listed status 1; liver transplant performed; the previable fetus expired despite preservation attempts. Reported as the first case of acetaminophen overdose requiring liver transplantation during a second-trimester pregnancy.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old at 17-week gestation was diagnosed with acute liver failure secondary to acetaminophen overdose taken for dental pain management. raw_record.support_text: A case of fetal demise and maternal recovery after acetaminophen overdose is presented. Fetal liver and maternal serum concentrations indicated overdose to be the cause of fetal death, and maternal disseminated intravascular coagulation may have been related to maternal acetaminophen-induced liver disease alone or a combination of liver disease and the presence of a dead fetus. The paper is framed as a hepatotoxicity (acetaminophen/paracetamol) case report.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patient (27-28 week fetus); overdose ingestion; maternal DIC may reflect liver disease and/or retained dead fetus.
raw_record.extra_details: 24-year-old gravida 2 para 1 woman ingested a total of 29.5 g acetaminophen over less than 24 hours for severe dental pain, followed by impending liver decompensation; maternal recovery occurred. Fetal death attributed to overdose; treatment with oral N-acetylcysteine (9 g, then 4.5 g q8h) began 20 hours after last dose, vomited after each dose; serum acetaminophen 56 µg/mL. Authors state a causal relationship between maternal toxic ingestion and fetal death is very likely.

raw_record.support_text: In this single patient case report of iron ingestion, highly pathological serum aminotransferase levels were registered 12 hours after ingestion (aspartate 19 microcat/l, alanine 15 microcat/l), peaking after 36 hours (aspartate 130 microcat/l, alanine 100 microcat/l) with a subsequent slow decrease. Serum bilirubin rose progressively from 40 micromol/l at 12 hours, particularly after day 4, with about 90% conjugated. Most serologic tests for viral hepatitis (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HAV) were negative, while anti-HBc was positive.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patient undergoing cesarean section at time of iron ingestion; requires co-exposure/intensive care context not defaulting to general adult therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Iron overdose/poisoning case report. Latency: aminotransferase elevation at 12 h, peak at 36 h. Peak aspartate 130 microcat/l and alanine 100 microcat/l; bilirubin rose from 40 micromol/l at 12 h, ~90% conjugated. Viral hepatitis serologies (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HAV) negative; anti-HBc positive. Deferoxamine treatment instituted 26 h after ingestion (1 g IM, total 8 g over 40 h). Other systemic findings: transient creatinine rise day 2, thrombocytopenia, coagulation dysfunction, metabolic acidosis, fever.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of 36 pregnant patients exposed to paraquat (from the Ramathibodi Poison Center Toxic Exposure Surveillance System), all had oral exposure. Systemic effects mainly comprised acute kidney injury (AKI), found in 13 patients (36.1%), and the paper reports that AKI, hepatotoxicity, and maximum white blood cell count significantly differed between dead and surviving patients, indicating paraquat hepatotoxicity as a clinical feature in these human overdose cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patients (restricted population); oral ingestion of the herbicide (poisoning/overdose exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: 36 pregnant patients (mean age 22.7 years, mean gestational age 23.1 weeks), all with oral paraquat ingestion over a 5-year period. Hepatotoxicity, AKI, and maximum WBC count significantly differed between dead and surviving patients. Overall pregnant-patient mortality 25% and in-hospital offspring mortality 44.4%, all deaths in patients with systemic toxicity; median hospital stay 6 days; treatment included intravenous dexamethasone and cyclophosphamide. Paraquat = 1,1'-dimethyl-4,4'-bipyridylium dichloride; toxicity attributed to redox cycling generating reactive oxygen species.

raw_record.support_text: In this ICU cohort of 62 patients with acute liver failure, etiology was attributed to toxic hepatitis in 11 cases and 'associated with ecstasy consumption' in five cases; the diagnosis of ecstasy-induced acute liver failure was made in five cases, representing 8% of the total series and 31% of those due to a toxic agent. The five ecstasy cases (all young males, ages 17-20) showed peak ALT 2623-5282 U/l, high bilirubin, low prothrombin index, latency 7-15 days, positive rechallenge in one case, and resolution over 3-12 months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Recreational (abusive) ecstasy use in young males, not therapeutic use; competing etiologies systematically excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Ecstasy = MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine). Five patients (all male, ages 17-20); ecstasy consumption 1 tablet/week to 1-2/2 weeks, duration 4-48 weeks; latency 7-15 days; peak ALT 2623-5282 U/l, peak AST 1755-4800 U/l, serum bilirubin up to 38.9 mg/dl, prothrombin index 21-37% at admission; one case had positive rechallenge; resolution time 3-12 months. No hepatic encephalopathy in some patients but severe hypoglycemia and prolonged prothrombin time.

raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant/acute liver failure with encephalopathy grades III–IV; a single series of 10 Ecstasy-ingestion cases treated with OLT had 50% mortality, with causes of death being sepsis (75%) and MODS/acute rejection (25%); several anecdotal reports of severe reactions after single or massive ingestion; signs of severe hepatic damage with and without hyperthermia (core temperature >41°C, acidosis, renal failure, encephalopathy, INR >7; or malaise, GI symptoms, hyperbilirubinemia, rising AST/ALT, progressive coagulopathy and encephalopathy); encephalopathy grade III–IV associated with poor prognosis even after LT.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report an unusual manner of exposure to halothane in a 26-year-old man who sniffed a volatile liquid weekly to obtain a 'high' and presented with 1 month of nausea, vomiting, jaundice, anorexia, light-colored stools, and tea-colored urine. He positively identified halothane by smell from among volatile anesthetic liquids, and a liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis. The elevated SGOT, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase improved and he recovered after halothane exposure ceased, with the hepatitis attributed to repeated inhalational (sniffing) halothane exposure.

raw_record.extra_details: 26-year-old prison inmate who sniffed halothane weekly for 8 weeks, continuing until 3 weeks before admission when he briefly lost consciousness after prolonged inhalation; halothane obtained from a friend who worked in the operating room. Presentation with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, anorexia, light-colored stools, and tea-colored urine for about 1 month. Liver tender, 3 cm below right costal margin, span 13 cm; deep icterus without lymphadenopathy, palmar erythema, or spider angiomata; no splenomegaly. Liver tests included SGOT rising to 1250 mU/ml and bilirubin peaking at 41 mg/100 ml, alkaline phosphatase up to 140 mU/ml, LDH up to 395 mU/ml, prothrombin time 19/11 sec; hemoglobin 15 g/100 ml, leukocyte count 5500/mm3 (44 PMNs, 47 lymphocytes, 6 monocytes, 3 eosinophils). Heterophil, hepatitis-associated antigen, alpha-fetoglobulin, BUN, urinalysis, platelets, and chest X-ray within normal limits; urine and blood cultures negative. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis; he had an uneventful hospital course and was discharged, with dechallenge and recovery.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 12 patients presenting with MDMA (ecstasy) intoxication after recreational use at raves, acute liver injury (ALI) is defined as transaminases >1000 U/L with abnormal prothrombin time/International Normalized Ratio or partial thromboplastin time. Serum toxicology in several patients confirmed MDMA and MDA, and coroner investigations attributed deaths to sequelae of MDMA intoxication.

raw_record.support_text: The authors cared for three patients who developed hepatitis after repeated sniffing of halothane to produce a drug 'high.' Patient 1 had sniffed concentrated halothane for more than a year (about 1250 mL consumed in this manner) and died; postmortem liver showed acute yellow atrophy with extensive, predominantly centrolobular hepatic necrosis, portal inflammatory reaction, moderate bile stasis, and Kupffer cell hyperplasia. Elevated transaminases (SGPT 1370 IU/L, SGOT 2810 IU/L) and total bilirubin of 6.5 mg/dL were recorded.

raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 3 patients (Patient 1: 25-year-old Mexican female scrub technician). Patient 1 sniffed concentrated halothane for >1 year, ~1250 mL in the month before death, multiple times daily. Patient 1 died after coma and hypotension; postmortem: acute yellow atrophy, extensive predominantly centrolobular hepatic necrosis, portal inflammatory reaction, moderate bile stasis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, plus pulmonary hemorrhage/pneumonia and proximal tubular degeneration. Laboratory peaks: SGPT 1370 IU/L, SGOT 2810 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 124 IU/L, total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dL, prothrombin time 28.7 s. Patient 2: SGPT 455, SGOT 677; Patient 3: SGPT 144, SGOT 190.

raw_record.support_text: A case series in the Singapore Medical Journal described cholestasis and biliary dilatation in three recreational ketamine abusers (a 27-year-old man with a 4-year history of intranasal ketamine abuse who developed a dilated biliary system requiring ICU admission and bile duct stenting, a 27-year-old man with 2 years of abuse, and a 26-year-old man with 7 years of misuse). All three patients had concurrent urinary tract issues and abnormal liver function tests were found in all 3 cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Recreational ketamine abusers (inhalational/intranasal misuse), with concurrent urinary tract issues; not ordinary therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Biliary dilation from ketamine abuse first reported in 2007; a case of ketamine-induced cholangiopathy was reported in 2011. First case required ICU admission and a 10F plastic biliary stent, with 4 additional admissions on continued abuse; second case developed colicky epigastric pain 4-5 hours postingestion and was lost to follow-up; third case had gallbladder dyskinesia and coexisting bladder problems. Abnormal liver function tests were found in all 3 cases. Potential mechanism proposed as NMDA-receptor blockade in smooth muscle or through the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.

raw_record.support_text: The paper lists gastrointestinal complications of ketamine use to include epigastric pain, gallbladder malfunction (e.g., biliary dilation), and hepatic toxicity. A retrospective study of 28 subjects with upper GI symptoms among 37 inhalational ketamine abusers (exclusion criteria included concomitant substance abuse, Helicobacter pylori, NSAID use, and GI disorder history) found epigastric pain only in 23 (62.2%) subjects and gastritis confirmed by biopsy in 11 subjects; relief from GI symptoms correlated with abstinence from ketamine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Recreational ketamine abusers without other substance abuse, H. pylori, NSAID use, or GI disorder history.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic toxicity is listed as a GI complication of ketamine use. In the retrospective study of 37 inhalational ketamine abusers (mean duration of ketamine use 4 years before admission), 28 had upper GI symptoms; endoscopy done in half of subjects diagnosed gastritis in 12, gastroduodenitis in 1; biopsy confirmed gastritis in 11 and intestinal metaplasia in 1. Treatment includes cessation of ketamine use.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of MDMA-induced severe hepatitis with autoimmune features in a 22-year-old male who used three to five pills of MDMA daily for one month and was admitted with jaundice. Liver biopsy revealed acute hepatitis with mild interface hepatitis and a mixed portal inflammatory reaction with plasma cells. His liver enzymes normalized after one month of corticosteroid therapy, and the authors note that steroid therapy is not traditionally part of ecstasy-induced hepatitis management.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Recreational, non-therapeutic use of MDMA (3-5 pills daily for one month); case exhibited autoimmune-like features (plasma cell infiltration) and responded to corticosteroid therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 22-year-old male with jaundice. Labs: total/direct bilirubin 24/20 mg/dL, ALT 1825 IU/L, AST 1268 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 111 IU/L, GGT 99 IU/L, albumin 4 g/dL, INR 1.1 (normal coagulation). HAV IgM, HCV, HBcIgM, ANA, AMA, ASMA, LKM-1 negative; IgG normal; normal ceruloplasmin (36 mg/dL); normal hepatobiliary ultrasound. Biopsy showed acute hepatitis with mild interface hepatitis and mixed portal inflammation with plasma cells (<10%). Treated with prednisolone 40 mg oral/day for 1 month with complete normalization of liver enzymes and bilirubin. The paper notes ecstasy is associated with acute hepatitis and liver failure; management is usually conservative.

raw_record.support_text: A 17-year-old female patient who regularly used ecstasy (MDMA) over a six-month period developed nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and jaundice two days after her last use, progressed to acute liver failure within 10 days, and was listed for urgent orthotopic liver transplantation. The paper frames the hepatic damage as ecstasy-related ('Ecstasy'-bedingten Hepatotoxizität), noting dose-independent toxicity with a latency of days to weeks after the last use.

raw_record.support_text: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion of acetaminophen is presented as an important cause of acetaminophen-related poisoning, hepatic injury, and death; one study cited estimates that 30% of patients acquired hepatic injury after a repeated supratherapeutic ingestion pattern of misuse. In the poison-center case series (N=249), no patient with an initial aspartate aminotransferase level below 50 IU/L died or developed significant hepatotoxicity, whereas 6 (16%) with an initial aspartate aminotransferase greater than 1,000 IU/L died or required liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Repeated supratherapeutic (chronic, >8 hours) ingestion pattern rather than acute single overdose, representing deliberate misuse/excessive dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: A study estimated that 30% of patients acquired hepatic injury after repeated supratherapeutic ingestion. Of US poison-center acetaminophen deaths in 2002, 31 (16%) were designated as chronic (occurring over >8 hours). In the 18-month poison-center series (N=249), 6/38 (16%) patients with initial AST >1000 IU/L died or required liver transplantation; none with initial AST <50 IU/L died or developed significant hepatotoxicity. Treatment with acetylcysteine noted; the nomogram cannot be applied to repeated-ingestion cases. Variable data collection, recording, and treatment limited definition of precise exposure-therapy-outcome relationships.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients presenting with repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI) of paracetamol, hepatotoxicity was defined as alanine transaminase (ALT) >1000 IU/L and acute liver injury as ALT ≥50 IU/L. Among 91 paracetamol RSTI presentations, 9 (17%) in the non-abbreviated group developed hepatotoxicity (median peak ALT 3834 IU/L) and 36 had acute liver injury without hepatotoxicity, attributing these liver injuries to paracetamol ingested at supratherapeutic doses.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI) overdose context; patients presenting after supratherapeutic paracetamol doses, with some receiving an abbreviated or full acetylcysteine treatment regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 IU/L (9 of 91 patients, all in the non-abbreviated group; median peak ALT 3834 IU/L, IQR 1973-5171); acute liver injury defined as ALT ≥50 IU/L (36 patients). Median reported paracetamol dose 179-203 mg/kg over 24-48 hours of ingestion. No patients re-presented with developing liver injury or acute liver failure. Paracetamol hepatotoxicity managed with acetylcysteine infusion.

raw_record.support_text: Rodenticide-induced hepatotoxicity (yellow phosphorus as the toxic protoplasmic agent) is described as a major cause of acute liver failure in southern and western India. Yellow phosphorus is a protoplasmic toxin with no specific antidote; management is supportive and may require liver transplantation. The Tamil Nadu Chapter of the Indian Society of Gastroenterology reported a retrospective series of 685 patients consuming rodenticide, of whom 450 developed hepatotoxicity; 396 were managed conservatively, 54 required plasma exchange and 1 patient additionally required a liver transplant. 35% had an adverse outcome with 131 deaths and 28 discharged in a moribund state.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial states that hepatotoxicity due to yellow phosphorus poison (YPP) is being increasingly recognized as a cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in parts of the Indian subcontinent, largely from southern and western India, analogous to paracetamol overdose causing toxic liver necrosis and death in the West.

raw_record.extra_details: A statewide multicenter survey across 6 districts in Tamil Nadu (Jan-Jun 2019) on causes of toxic hepatitis found a rodenticide (yellow phosphorus) ingestion to paracetamol overdose ratio of 75:1; among 450 YPP-induced hepatotoxicity cases, 131 (31%) died and 28 (6%) were discharged moribund; extrapolation to all 35 districts estimated a six-month case burden of 1584 rodenticide-induced hepatotoxicity patients (95% CI 265-6119) with ~554 projected poor outcomes. Only 1 of 450 (0.2%) underwent urgent liver transplantation. Plasma von Willebrand factor (vWF) levels predicted survival with AUC 0.92 vs MELD score 0.66 in 24 patients with YPP-induced hepatotoxicity (20 ALI, 3 ALF, 1 uncomplicated acute hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: In nine patients with self-administered paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, plasma levels of glutathione S-transferase B1 subunits, F protein, and ALT were measured. GST exceeded the reference interval in all patients on admission, and F protein was increased in seven, whereas abnormal plasma ALT was seen in only one. Patients whose admission GST exceeded 10 µg/L subsequently developed moderate or severe liver damage despite N-acetylcysteine treatment, leading the authors to conclude that paracetamol poisoning causes acute liver dysfunction with predominantly centrilobular damage, which GST and F protein detect more sensitively than ALT.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-administered overdose (poisoning) exposure context; not therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine overdose patients studied; admission GST was abnormal in all 9, F protein in 7, but ALT in only 1 (a patient admitted 12 h after poisoning). Post-admission, abnormal GST/F protein/ALT were seen in 9, 8, and 5 patients respectively. GST >10 µg/L on admission predicted moderate or severe liver damage despite N-acetylcysteine treatment. Paper's focus is biomarker performance (GST and F protein vs ALT) for detecting minor degrees of acute liver dysfunction, particularly centrilobular damage, rather than on characterizing paracetamol hepatotoxicity.
