raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol (acetaminophen, N-acetyl p-aminophenol) is described as a commonly used analgesic that is hepatotoxic when taken in overdose. The authors report 220 patients admitted after a paracetamol overdose, of whom 200 showed evidence of liver damage and 29 died from fulminant hepatic failure, with the first case of acute hepatic necrosis related to the drug reported in 1966. The paper describes the histological appearances of the liver damage in 104 patients who had a liver biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-poisoning overdose of 10 to 100 g; 25 of the 104 patients had concurrently ingested alcohol or another drug (e.g., barbiturates, nitrazepam, diazepam, chlordiazepoxide), representing unresolved co-exposure in those cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 220 patients admitted to the Liver Unit, King's College Hospital up to 1 Jan. 1974 after paracetamol overdose; 200 showed evidence of liver damage and 29 died from fulminant hepatic failure. In the 104 biopsied patients (65 females, 39 males, aged 15-58 yr), liver function became abnormal in all, 38 developed fulminant hepatic failure with grade 3 or 4 encephalopathy and 27 died. Histological grades: grade 0 (swelling, minor vacuolation/inflammation, no necrosis), grade I (confluent necrosis of centrilobular hepatocytes), grade II (confluent necrosis continuous between adjacent lobules), grade III (massive necrosis leaving a rim of liver cells around portal tracts). Dose-related injury with characteristic delay in appearance of liver damage; plasma paracetamol levels and coagulation disturbance studied.

raw_record.support_text: This paper reports patients with severe paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, treated with supportive care, cysteamine and methionine, or acetylcysteine. Among 57 patients given supportive treatment, mean maximum serum ALT activity exceeded 2022 IU/l, mean maximum plasma bilirubin was 56 µmol/l, mean prothrombin-time ratio was 1.9, and 33 (58%) developed severe liver damage (AST or ALT >1000 IU/l). Acetylcysteine given within 10 hours reduced severe liver damage to 1/62 (2%), whereas given 10-24 hours after ingestion it did not prevent it (20/38, 53%). Deaths from hepatic failure occurred in the supportive-treatment group (3/57) and in late-treatment groups. The liver damage is attributed to paracetamol poisoning.

raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver damage defined as serum AST or ALT activity exceeding 1000 IU/l. In supportive-treatment patients mean maximum serum ALT >2022 IU/l, plasma bilirubin 56 µmol/l, prothrombin-time ratio 1.9; 33/57 (58%) developed severe liver damage; 6 (11%) had renal impairment (3 requiring haemodialysis); 3 (5%) died from hepatic failure. Acetylcysteine within 8 hours was almost completely protective (serum ALT normal in 89% of 19 high-risk patients treated <8 h); protection declined with treatment at 8-10 h (7% severe damage), 10-12 h (43%), 12-15 h (56%), and was ineffective after 15 h (82%). Comparison groups: acetylcysteine and cysteamine+methionine, which are treatments not causes. High-risk defined by plasma paracetamol concentration.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the development of the acetaminophen (paracetamol, APAP) nomogram using 30 previously published untreated cases from the Edinburgh Poisons Unit plus 34 additional unpublished untreated cases, plotting initial plasma APAP levels against time to discriminate patients who subsequently developed hepatotoxicity (defined as serum AST > 1000 IU) from those who did not. All 64 cases were untreated with antidotes (NAC, methionine, or cysteamine). The 1971 publication had stated that plasma levels greater than 300 µg/mL at 4 hours and 50 µg/mL at 12 hours were associated with toxicity, and the additional untreated cases led to lowering the 4-hour level to 200 µg/mL, so the nomogram line was drawn from 200 µg/mL at 4 hours to 50 µg/mL at 12 hours (a 4-hour half-life slope). The nomogram was intended to predict whether patients would develop hepatic toxicity after a single acute APAP overdose, based on an initial plasma level obtained 4 or more hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single acute oral overdose with a measured initial plasma level obtained 4 or more hours after ingestion; nomogram not intended for chronic ingestions.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as serum SGOT/AST greater than 1000 IU at any time during the hospital course. Based on 30 published plus 34 unpublished untreated cases (all untreated with N-acetylcysteine, methionine, or cysteamine). The 1971 publication correlated levels >300 µg/mL at 4 h and >50 µg/mL at 12 h with toxicity, and a half-life >4 h with likely toxicity and >12 h with likely hepatic coma; the revised nomogram threshold was 200 µg/mL at 4 h to 50 µg/mL at 12 h (4-hour half-life slope). Therapeutic oral absorption of APAP is 70-90% with peak plasma values at 20-90 min. Co-ingested propoxyphene was noted to delay gastric emptying, favoring sampling at 4 h or later.

Collateral history revealed she had taken an overdose of an unknown quantity of paracetamol-containing flu tablets three days prior, and a diagnosis of delayed paracetamol overdose (approximately 60 h) with suspected hepatic encephalopathy was made. raw_record.support_text: Several hours after admission, the patient became hemodynamically unstable with hypotension and hypoglycemia, disorientation, and an ammonia level of 122 µmol/L. The working diagnosis was fulminant acute liver failure with multiorgan dysfunction secondary to staggered supratherapeutic niacin ingestion; investigations for other causes of liver failure (hepatitis screen, ceruloplasmin, autoimmune screen) were negative. She was placed on the liver transplantation list and treated with NAC, inotropes, and later CVVHDF.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-case report of staggered supratherapeutic (overdose) niacin ingestion; the patient was placed on the liver transplantation list but recovered without transplant.
raw_record.extra_details: Working diagnosis of fulminant acute liver failure with multiorgan dysfunction secondary to niacin. Biopsy showed subacute necrosis with loss of 90% of sampled hepatocytes; CT showed patchy perfusion. Peak ALT 14,300 U/L (day 1), total bilirubin 134 µmol/L, INR >10, ammonia 122 µmol/L. Other causes excluded (negative hepatitis, ceruloplasmin, autoimmune screens); LFTs one month earlier unremarkable. Treated with NAC infusion, ICU support, inotropes, broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem, anidulafungin) and six days of CVVHDF; liver function resolved on outpatient follow-up. Authors note dialysis did not significantly clear niacin.

The study aimed to predict the occurrence of HE, which complicates paracetamol-induced liver injury following overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: 161 noncomatose overdose patients (50 men, 111 women) studied; in the 86-patient learning set, 15 developed hepatic encephalopathy (hepatic coma grade II or more) treated per established guidelines; median dose 25 g (range 9–150 g); delay to N-acetylcysteine and degree of liver dysfunction (ALAT max up to 24,000 IU/l, bilirubin max up to 498 µmol/l, prothrombin index nadir) differed between HE and non-HE groups; the study focused on predicting HE as a complication of paracetamol-induced hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (ALF) in an 18-year-old girl who presented 3 days after a paracetamol overdose (30 g) and was treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine. She met King's College criteria for poor prognosis and, because of uncontrolled intracranial hypertension, underwent hepatectomy, remained anhepatic for 14 h, and was successfully bridged to liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-patient case; overdose context (30 g paracetamol, 3 days prior) in an 18-year-old female who also subsequently required hepatectomy and transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose of 30 g presented 3 days later; treated with IV N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg/day. Laboratory findings on admission: pH 7.3, pCO2 3.9 kPa, bilirubin 119 umol/l, ALT 8756 IU/l, creatinine 190 umol/l, lactate 3.9 mmol/l, WBC 9.7 x 10^9/l. Met King's College criteria for poor prognosis (prothrombin time >100 s, Grade III hepatic encephalopathy, creatinine >300 umol/l). Developed severe uncontrolled intracranial hypertension (ICP >40 mmHg), underwent hepatectomy, was anhepatic for 14 h, and was successfully bridged to orthotopic liver transplantation. Authors noted the necrotic liver may release pro-inflammatory cytokines contributing to intracranial hypertension.

raw_record.support_text: The first report of hepatic injury resulting from acetaminophen appeared in the British Medical Journal in 1966: two Scottish residents who each ingested 50 or 150 acetaminophen tablets in suicide attempts both died of fulminant hepatic necrosis. Thereafter, severe hepatotoxicity occurring during the course of acetaminophen overdose was increasingly recognized, reaching epidemic proportions in the UK by the early 1970s, with the first US case reported in 1971.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Suicidal overdose ingestion of 50-150 tablets; first two reported cases both died of fulminant hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic injury from acetaminophen overdose first reported in 1966 (BMI 1966;3). Recognized increasingly in the UK through the early 1970s, with the first US case report in 1971. Contrasted with the otherwise marketed 'safety' of the compound.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol predictably produces acute liver injury when taken in suicidal overdose. After an initial two to three days of irritability, jaundice and other signs of acute liver failure appear; by the fourth day the liver is tender and histologically shows uniformly distributed centrilobular coagulative necrosis with vacuolation of adjacent surviving hepatocytes. Of 200 patients admitted to the Liver Unit at King's College Hospital with signs of liver damage after an overdose of between 10 and 100 g of paracetamol, 29 died in fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Suicidal overdose of 10-100 g of paracetamol.
raw_record.extra_details: Centrilobular coagulative necrosis with vacuolation of adjacent surviving hepatocytes in early stages; two to three day initial period of irritability followed by jaundice and signs of acute liver failure by the fourth day; 29 of 200 overdose cases died in fulminant hepatic failure (Portmann et al., 1975).

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective series of 25 paracetamol overdose cases with suicidal intent hospitalized at Clínica Las Condes (2000–2006), the mean ingested dose was 11.7 g (range 5–45 g, 188 mg/kg, range 63–550). Only 3 cases developed acute hepatitis, corresponding to probable toxicity levels per the Rumack and Matthew nomogram; these showed mean peak GOT 1,892 U/L, GPT 3,388 U/L, and prothrombin time 60%. All were treated with N-acetylcysteine with good outcomes. Women mostly co-ingested benzodiazepines, antidepressants, and antipsychotics, and men co-ingested alcohol.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (N-acetyl-p-aminophenol), an active metabolite of phenacetin, marketed as Tylenol, Liquiprin, Datril, Tempra, and Liquiprim. Acetaminophen poisoning is described as one of the most common causes of hepatic failure in England; until 1970 only 56 such cases were reported in the US. The paper notes there was no established effective therapy to prevent organ damage, and Mucomyst (acetylcysteine) might be of value in treatment. Case 1: 33-year-old female, 13 g acetaminophen, lethargic, not hypotensive.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old white female attempted suicide by injecting 0.5 mL of chloroform intravenously and drinking half a cup the next morning. Sequential measurement of biomarkers in serum for liver cell necrosis, liver function, and liver regeneration indicated the presence of initial liver damage followed by recovery, showing acute chloroform toxicity caused human liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Suicide attempt by 0.5 mL intravenous injection followed by 120 mL (half cup) oral ingestion of chloroform; patient was otherwise reportedly healthy with no competing liver disease. She remained asymptomatic during hospitalization and recovered fully after treatment with hyperbaric oxygen, cimetidine (10 g IV over 24 h for 3 days), and N-acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg load then 17 doses of 70 mg/kg q4h); liver functions returning to normal by day 6 and she was discharged on full recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Plasma chloroform levels declined rapidly by headspace GC; initial laboratory values on arrival showed AST 21 IU/L, ALT 40 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, PT 13.4 s, APTT 28.4 s; WBC 14,400 with 79% neutrophils. Acute exposure causes hepatic necrosis generally between day 2 and 5 peaking day 5-7; death may occur secondary to hepatic and renal failure. Cimetidine was given to inhibit cytochrome P450 and arrest metabolism of chloroform to the more toxic metabolite phosgene, and N-acetylcysteine to replenish glutathione stores.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is described as the predominant cause of acute liver failure in the United States. Biomarkers of mitochondrial damage and nuclear DNA fragmentation were measured in plasma from APAP-overdose patients, and the authors conclude that mitochondrial damage and nuclear DNA fragmentation are likely critical events in APAP hepatotoxicity in humans, resulting in necrotic cell death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Supertherapeutic exposure (overdose, both accidental and intentional) is required; the paper explicitly notes that APAP is safe at therapeutic doses.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose is stated to be the most common cause of acute liver failure in most Western countries and the predominant cause in the US (~56,000 ER visits, ~26,000 hospitalizations, and nearly 500 deaths per year; about half intentional). Patient cohort (n=40 overdose patients; 20 abnormal LT group with peak ALT >=1,000 U/l and peak PT >=18 s, 20 normal LT controls) plus 6 healthy volunteers. Mechanism: CYP-mediated formation of reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) after saturation of glucuronidation/sulfation, GSH depletion, mitochondrial protein binding, mitochondrial permeability transition and nuclear DNA fragmentation via AIF/EndoG, without caspase activation (necrotic, not apoptotic, cell death) leading to centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis. Plasma biomarkers GDH and mtDNA elevated in abnormal-LT patients; peak ALT up to 8,545 U/l, peak AST up to 26,000 U/l, peak PT up to 374s, peak bilirubin up to 25 mg/dl; 6/20 abnormal-LT patients had encephalopathy grade >=1 and 95% survived.

raw_record.support_text: Case 2: A 28-year-old man developed jaundice, abdominal pain, and oliguria after self-treating with acetaminophen 'extra strength' capsules, taking two to four every 4-6 hours, estimating 10-12 capsules (5-6 g) over a 24-hour period, and denying a single massive dose or suicidal intent. He drank beer daily and frequently abused glutethimide, methaqualone, and nonprescription cough syrups but denied parenteral drug abuse. At admission he was deeply icteric with hepatomegaly. His serum acetaminophen drawn 17 hours after admission was 237 µg/ml, and he experienced hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis), then cardiac and respiratory arrest after an emesis with aspiration, and died; autopsy was refused.

raw_record.extra_details: SGOT 19,750 IU and SGPT 12,550 IU with massive enzyme elevation; total bilirubin 23.9 mg/dl (15.4 conjugated); prothrombin time 27 s (control 11 s); serum creatinine 7.2 mg/dl; second acetaminophen level 137 µg/ml 24 hours later; hemolytic anemia diagnosed with low-normal G6PD; progressed to fulminant hepatic failure with confusion and asterixis, treated with peritoneal dialysis and lactulose, then cardiac and respiratory arrest.

raw_record.support_text: The infant had received acetaminophen every 4 h since circumcision on the second day of life; dosing was 80 mg (26 mg/kg) every 4 h for the first 24 h, then 40 mg (13 mg/kg) every 4 h for the next 2 days. Acetaminophen concentration measured 16 h after the last home dose was 109.8 µg/ml, well above the therapeutic range of 10 to 30 µg/ml, confirming an oral acetaminophen overdose in this term newborn.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Term newborn (neonatal) infant; oral acetaminophen overdose with supratherapeutic blood concentration; also presented with oliguric renal failure and a presumptive initial diagnosis of sepsis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 4-day-old term male neonate with oral acetaminophen toxicity. Presented with episodic emesis, decreased arousal, hypoglycemia (glucose 27 mg/dl), elevated AST 718 IU/l and ALT 978 IU/l, PT 51.9 s, INR 5.4, factor V 57%, fibrinogen 61 mg/dl, serum bilirubin 9 mg/dl (conjugated 1.4 mg/dl), ammonia 114 µmol/l, creatinine 3.2 mg/dl, and blood-tinged gastric aspirates. Developed hepatic encephalopathy, liver failure, coagulopathy, and oliguric renal failure. Successfully treated with a 20 h intravenous N-acetylcysteine infusion (NAC) without adverse effects. Paper notes acetaminophen toxicity is well documented and can lead to liver failure and death, with risk generally lower in children than adults, and supports NAC treatment for neonatal acetaminophen toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Initial laboratory investigations for the 3 patients with hepatocellular necrosis secondary to acetaminophen ingestion are shown. Across the three patients AST ranged from 7080 to 18012 U/L and ALT from 3540 to 12286 U/L, with acetaminophen concentrations measured at approximately 24, 96, and 48 h after ingestion for patients 1, 2, and 3, respectively (1218, <66, and 78 µmol/L). The paper attributes the hepatocellular necrosis to acetaminophen ingestion in all three patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Three patients with acetaminophen ingestion/overdose (concentrations measured ~24, 96, and 48 h after ingestion for patients 1, 2, and 3 at 1218, <66, and 78 µmol/L).
raw_record.extra_details: Patient lab values: patient 1 AST 8330 U/L, ALT 3540 U/L; patient 2 AST 7080 U/L, ALT 12286 U/L; patient 3 AST 18012 U/L, ALT 4119 U/L; LDH levels 8075, 4871, 10147 U/L; lactate 22.5, 1.2, 5.1 mmol/L. The report's focus is spurious ethanol elevation on the Siemens Advia 1650 assay caused by endogenous dehydrogenase interference in these hepatotoxicity samples; patient 3's acetaminophen-toxicity diagnosis and N-acetylcysteine therapy were delayed after a presumptive alcoholic gastritis diagnosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old male unintentionally ingested a mouthful of methyl ethyl ketone peroxide (MEKP), a fiberglass fixing agent, while working on his boat. Approximately 12 hours post-ingestion his liver function tests worsened, with ALT rising to a peak of 761 U/L and AST to 576 U/L, and INR slightly elevated at 1.3. The paper states MEKP is highly toxic, causing corrosive effects in the gastrointestinal tract, hepatic necrosis, renal impairment and cardiovascular collapse, and concludes that despite a small ingestion it caused hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unintentional (accidental) ingestion of a small amount (~mouthful) of liquid while working on a boat; treated with acetylcysteine infusion and supportive care.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset of worsening LFTs approximately 12 hours post-ingestion; ALT peaked 761 U/L, AST 576 U/L, INR peaked 1.3; ALT remained slightly elevated at 89 U/L on day 14 follow-up while AST was normal; patient clinically well at 14 days; MEKP confirmed in blood by headspace gas chromatography-mass spectrometry; presentation included profuse watery diarrhoea, diaphoresis, compensated metabolic acidosis with lactate 6.0 mmol/L, haemoconcentration (Hb 210 g/L); MEKP generally described as causing hepatic necrosis, renal impairment and cardiovascular collapse.

raw_record.support_text: Regarding acetaminophen safety for OA pain in older adults, the paper states that acetaminophen toxicity was the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States from 1998 to 2003, and that unintentional overdose is the leading cause of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, with the vast majority of these cases having taken acetaminophen to treat pain. These data led the FDA in January 2011 to recommend capping acetaminophen at 325 mg in prescribed combination products and to run public awareness campaigns focused on the risk of acetaminophen-related liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unintentional overdose in patients who took acetaminophen to treat pain (OA-related).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (up to 4 g daily) modestly effective for OA pain vs placebo (SMD -0.13; 95% CI -0.22 to -0.04); acute liver failure data from 1998-2003 US; FDA January 2011 recommendation to cap prescribed combination products at 325 mg and public awareness campaigns regarding acetaminophen-related liver injury; larger population-based cohort found increased risk of hospitalization for GI events when older adults combined NSAIDs with acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: The authors' analysis of 40 poison-center cases found all involved patients taking multiple acetaminophen (APAP)-containing products with a cumulative dose exceeding the FDA maximum daily dose of 4 g per 24 h. The paper concludes that therapeutic exposure to multiple APAP-containing products, alone or with OTC formulations, can lead to severe liver injury and death, calling these unintentional APAP poisonings. The FDA statement cited notes that severe liver injury including acute liver failure resulting in liver transplant and death has been reported with acetaminophen use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unintentional overdose/poisoning from taking multiple acetaminophen-containing products concurrently; cumulative daily dose exceeded the FDA maximum of 4 g per 24 h in all 40 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 cases from retrospective poison-center data. FDA recommends not exceeding 4 g/day total daily dose and advises against alcohol use while taking acetaminophen. Acute liver failure resulting in liver transplant and death reported. Authors note imprecise total dose/duration histories and inability to exclude other ingested substances or co-morbidities affecting liver function.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is a commonly ingested drug, and up to 25% of intentional drug-overdose patients volunteer that they ingested it. Because rapid serum acetaminophen testing is the only way to determine whether NAC antidote treatment is needed and because the ingestion history is often unreliable, many physicians routinely order rapid serum acetaminophen levels in all overdose patients regardless of history.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unsuspected/overdose exposure setting; applies to patients presenting with drug overdose at a busy urban emergency department.
raw_record.extra_details: In an ED cohort, approximately 1 in 70 drug-overdose patients had unsuspected acetaminophen ingestion and approximately 1 in 500 had unsuspected but potentially hepatotoxic serum acetaminophen levels identifiable only by routine screening. Authors suggest routinely screening all drug-overdose patients for acetaminophen. References document acute liver necrosis following paracetamol overdose and reversal of paracetamol toxicosis with N-acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old schizophrenic man developed hepatic toxicity after a daily dose of 9 g nicotinamide, presenting with nausea and vomiting and increased serum transaminase and bilirubin concentrations. A liver biopsy showed increased portal fibrosis and cholestasis. After discontinuation of nicotinamide the symptoms disappeared rapidly and all liver function tests returned to normal in 3 weeks; a nicotinamide rechallenge produced reappearance of symptoms and increased transaminase concentrations in less than 2 weeks. The paper concludes this report illustrates that very large doses of nicotinamide can be hepatotoxic in susceptible people.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Very large dose (9 g/day); heightened susceptibility in this individual; male patient with schizophrenia as the treated/clinical setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Positive dechallenge (symptoms disappeared and LFTs normalized within 3 weeks) and positive rechallenge (symptoms and elevated transaminases recurred within <2 weeks). Nausea and vomiting, increased serum transaminase and bilirubin, liver biopsy showing increased portal fibrosis and cholestasis. Single case report.

In Cases 1 and 3, liver biopsy demonstrated centrilobular necrosis, a finding characteristic of chlorinated hydrocarbon hepatotoxicity, and fibrous tissue in the centrilobular zones suggested that repeated exposure may produce permanent hepatic alterations.

raw_record.support_text: A 17-year-old girl with a psychiatric disorder was admitted after voluntary poisoning with 16 g of Paracetamol. A blood Paracetamol assay 5.5 hours after ingestion gave 195.4 mg/L, which on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram indicated a high risk of probable liver injury, prompting N-acetylcysteine treatment. A follow-up level returned to 2.5 mg/L at 48 h, antidote was stopped, and evolution was favorable.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Voluntary drug overdose (16 g) in a 17-year-old girl with a psychiatric disorder; disorder-specific/suicide context.
raw_record.extra_details: Blood Paracetamol 195.4 mg/L taken 5.5 h after ingestion, interpreted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram as high risk of probable liver injury; follow-up level 2.5 mg/L at 48 h; treated with N-acetylcysteine (loading 150 mg/kg then maintenance); evolution favorable. Paper also notes transaminase increase usually occurs ~24 h after a toxic dose and that transaminase measurement contributes to risk assessment.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 1's condition was diagnosed as fulminant hepatitis from VPA (valproic acid) intoxication. After withdrawal of VPA and glucagon-insulin therapy, consciousness returned to normal, and SGOT, SGPT, and blood ammonia levels returned to normal within 12 days. Two patients with acute encephalopathy due to VPA intoxication were described; the liver injury was attributed to VPA intoxication.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: VPA intoxication (overdose) in two patients with acute encephalopathy
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatitis diagnosed from VPA intoxication; SGOT, SGPT, and blood ammonia normalized within 12 days after VPA withdrawal plus glucagon-insulin therapy, and consciousness returned to normal within 10 days. In patient 2 a lymphocyte stimulation test was positive with a stimulation index of 49.2 vs standard 2.0. Liver histology differed from Reye's syndrome: mitochondria were not swollen and matrix granules did not disappear; enlarged mitochondrial matrix granules (111 ± 22 nm in patient 1, 80 ± 22 nm in patient 2 vs ~32-40 nm in five chronic-hepatitis controls) and calcium content detected by energy-dispersive X-ray microanalysis in patient 1 (not patient 2).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports three patients in whom hepatitis developed in relation to halothane anesthesia. The authors conclude that the evidence supports the diagnosis of a halothane-induced sensitization reaction with hepatitis, based on the characteristic temporal relation between halothane exposure and fever/jaundice, onset with chills and high fever, significant eosinophilia, antecedent atopy and drug-hypersensitivity reactions, occurrence of the hepatitis after a second halothane exposure in two of the three cases, and histologic features consistent with drug-induced hepatitis. Biopsies showed severe hepatitis with bridging necrosis, and all three patients recovered fully.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Antecedent atopy and drug-hypersensitivity reactions; hepatitis occurred after a second (re)exposure to halothane in two of the three cases; one patient (Patient 3) was diabetic with a fish allergy.
raw_record.extra_details: Serial SGOT (normal 15–35 IU/ml) and serum bilirubin (normal 0.1–1.4 mg/dl) values were recorded after halothane exposure for each patient (e.g., Patient 1 SGOT 1600 IU/ml at 2 days, bilirubin 2.66 mg/dl at 7 days; Patient 2 SGOT 2480 IU/ml at 6 days, bilirubin 13.50 mg/dl at 13 days). Histology showed severe hepatitis with bridging necrosis and, in one case, granulomata and giant cells; Patient 3 had eosinophilia rising to 11%. The authors noted absence of epidemiologic or serologic evidence of type B hepatitis and excluded postoperative cholestasis or centrilobular necrosis attributable to shock/multiple transfusions. All patients recovered fully.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled study of extended-release naltrexone (XR-NTX) in opioid-dependent patients with a very high prevalence of chronic HCV infection, there was no evidence of drug-induced liver injury during treatment relative to placebo (Lucey et al., 2008). Liver enzyme (ALT, AST, GGT) elevations >3x ULN occurred in both arms without significant differences between XR-NTX and placebo, no patient had total bilirubin >2x ULN combined with ALT >3x ULN, elevations resolved toward baseline with continued treatment, and no jaundice, variceal hemorrhage, ascites, or encephalopathy was associated with the elevations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Opioid-dependent patients with high prevalence of chronic HCV infection; XR-NTX given as extended-release intramuscular formulation.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial. ALT >3x ULN at any postbaseline visit in 21/107 (19.6%) XR-NTX vs 11/85 (12.9%) placebo (p=.876); AST in 15/107 (14.0%) vs 9/85 (10.6%) (p=.713); GGT in 25/107 (23.4%) vs 18/85 (21.2%) (p=.811). No bilirubin >2x ULN with ALT >3x ULN in either arm. Peak ALT 578 IU/ml in a placebo patient and 402 IU/ml in an XR-NTX patient. Elevations improved and returned toward baseline in all patients with follow-up; no jaundice, variceal hemorrhage, ascites, or encephalopathy. Elevations >3x ULN occurred primarily, but not exclusively, in patients with chronic HCV. AST comparison in HIV-positive vs HIV-negative XR-NTX patients yielded p=.018, not significant after Bonferroni correction (requires p<.003).

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, on weekly intramuscular methotrexate (increased from 7.5 mg to 15.0 mg), developed cirrhosis (Roenigk grade IV) on repeat liver biopsy when cumulative MTX reached 1,300 mg; MTX was then discontinued and she showed no deterioration in hepatic function over the following year. The paper frames this as MTX hepatotoxicity, and the patient had no other hepatotoxic medications (diabetes precluded prednisone, and azathioprine was refused).

raw_record.extra_details: 51-year-old woman with 16-year history of severe seropositive erosive nodular RA and 7-year history of poorly controlled IDDM; no alcohol abuse. Prior unsuccessful therapy with intramuscular gold and D-penicillamine; offered azathioprine but refused; no prednisone due to IDDM. MTX started at 7.5 mg intramuscularly weekly and increased to 15.0 mg; monthly liver enzymes and albumin remained normal although alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamic acid were persistently elevated. Cirrhosis (Roenigk IV) confirmed on second biopsy at cumulative MTX dose 1,300 mg; MTX discontinued with no deterioration in hepatic function over the past year.

Liver biopsy in 17 patients after a mean cumulative dose of 1,950 mg of methotrexate (range 915 to 3,125 mg) showed mild fibrosis in six and no cirrhosis. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the first case of hepatic injury induced by Venoplant®, an extract of Aesculus hippocastanum (horse chestnut) with antiinflammatory activity. A 37-year-old man who received a 65 mg i.m. injection of Venoplant® developed jaundice and pruritus about 60 days later, with moderate elevation of total bilirubin, ALP, and γ-GTP, mild eosinophilia, and a positive lymphocyte stimulation test. Liver biopsy showed marked cholestasis with zonal necrosis in the centrilobular areas, features consistent with drug-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-case report; product (extract of Aesculus hippocastanum) administered by intramuscular injection; patient had a pathological left brachial bone fracture and giant cell tumor of bone.
raw_record.extra_details: 65 mg single i.m. injection several hours before admission. Liver function tests normal at admission; mild abnormality from Jan 12, 1984; jaundice and pruritus from Feb 14, 1984 (about 60 days after injection). Labs: total bilirubin 2.9 mg/dl, direct 1.1 mg/dl, SGOT 19 IU/l, SGPT 31 IU/l, ALP 649 IU/l (normal <280), γ-GTP 155 IU/l (normal <20), 8% eosinophils. CT and ERC excluded extrahepatic biliary obstruction. Liver biopsy: marked cholestasis with centrilobular zonal necrosis, little/no portal tract change. Lymphocyte stimulation test positive (index 290%) on exposure to Venoplant. Authors describe this as the first documented case of Venoplant-induced hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a young man with a previously unrecognized POLG-1 mutation who developed valproic acid-associated acute liver failure and was treated successfully with liver transplantation. It also notes that patients with POLG-1 gene mutations have an increased risk of valproic acid-induced acute liver failure, that severe valproate hepatotoxicity most commonly arises in children within the first 3 months of treatment with an estimated incidence of 1 in 40,000 treated patients, and that many experts consider valproic acid-induced acute liver failure in patients with mitochondrial disorders a contraindication to liver transplant due to high mortality among transplanted children.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was a young man harboring a previously unrecognized POLG-1 gene mutation (mitochondrial disorder), which increases the risk of valproic acid-induced acute liver failure; report is a single case successfully managed with liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure explicitly reported; severe valproate hepatotoxicity most commonly arises in children within the first 3 months of treatment, with an estimated overall incidence of 1 in 40,000 treated patients; high mortality among transplanted children underlies expert consideration of valproic acid-induced acute liver failure in mitochondrial disorders as a contraindication to liver transplant; case treated successfully with liver transplantation. Aliases: valproate, VPA.

raw_record.support_text: Liver injury was observed in 2.00% of patients treated with troglitazone in this study, higher than the known incidence in Japan; prescription of the drug had been suspended in hospitals where troglitazone-induced liver injury was encountered early. Although complicating diseases such as chronic hepatitis C and fatty liver were considered possible causes, all patients had normal ALT before taking troglitazone, so troglitazone appeared to be responsible, and histology did not suggest viral hepatitis or other diseases.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury incidence 2.00% in this study, above the known incidence in Japan, with >5% frequency in two hospitals. All patients had normal ALT before starting troglitazone; chronic hepatitis C and fatty liver were assessed but not supported by histology. Concurrent medications were analyzed and none played a role in the liver injury. Reported death was nearly three times more frequent in Japan (0.0042%) than in North American/European Caucasian populations (0.0017%). CYP2C19 poor metabolizer frequency is higher in Japanese (18-23%) versus Caucasians (3-5%); CYP2C19 homozygote frequency was 50% in affected patients. Glibenclamide co-administration did not differ significantly between those with and without liver injury (P=0.33).

raw_record.support_text: Phase II clinical data in 878 patients with HCV G1 infection demonstrate that the unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia arising from faldaprevir administration is benign and not associated with hepatotoxicity. The frequency of hyperbilirubinemia was 47.8% and 83.8% in the 120- and 240-mg q.d. dose groups, respectively; discontinuation due to hyperbilirubinemia and/or jaundice was ≤1%. In phase III studies, hyperbilirubinemia was predominantly unconjugated, rapidly reversible, and determined not to result from liver injury based on prospectively defined criteria. Toxicology studies in rhesus monkeys showed a dose-dependent increase in unconjugated bilirubin not associated with microscopic evidence of hepatotoxicity, elevations in liver enzymes such as ALT, or hemolysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Faldaprevir (an HCV NS3/4A protease inhibitor) dose-dependently increased unconjugated bilirubin, but this hyperbilirubinemia was explicitly determined to be benign and not to result from liver injury or hepatotoxicity. In phase II data (878 HCV G1 patients, 120 or 240 mg q.d. plus Peg-IFN/RBV, 24 weeks), hyperbilirubinemia frequency was 47.8% (120 mg) and 83.8% (240 mg) with ≤1% discontinuation due to hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice; not associated with ALT elevations, microscopic hepatotoxicity, or hemolysis; rapidly reversible on cessation of therapy. Proposed mechanism is reversible inhibition of bilirubin uptake (OATP1B1/OATP1B3), glucuronidation (UGT1A1), and biliary efflux (MRP2), with UGT1A1 inhibition considered likely most important.

raw_record.support_text: In an open trial of stanozolol (10 mg daily, anabolic steroid with fibrinolytic-enhancing activity) for severe post-surgical low-back pain, many patients withdrew from a larger initial cohort because of toxic side-effects attributed to the treatment, including weight gain, hypertension, hepatotoxicity, acneiform rash, and hirsutism with voice changes in females. Only the 18 patients completing at least 12 months of therapy were included in the analysis; all had normal hepatic biochemical profiles prior to treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Open trial, stanozolol 10 mg daily for severe back and radicular pain after lumbar disc surgery. Hepatotoxicity was one of several toxic side-effects (along with weight gain, hypertension, acneiform rash, hirsutism, voice changes in females) causing withdrawal from the initially recruited larger cohort; only the 18 completers (at least 12 months therapy) were analyzed. No pre-existing hepatic disease; all had normal plasma hepatic profiles before treatment. Hepatotoxicity was not further characterized (no phenotype, severity, or case count reported).

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 8451 patients taking azathioprine (AZA) for prevention of renal transplant rejection and treatment of inflammatory conditions, 1503 (17.8%) stopped AZA due to intolerable adverse drug events that included hepatotoxicity, with hepatitis in 4.6% of patients. The paper groups these as AZA-induced adverse events (also including leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, GI discomfort, alopecia, and allergy), and notes that concomitant use of allopurinol increased the risk of adverse-event development.
raw_record.extra_details: AZA is described as having a high potential for adverse drug effects including hepatotoxicity (para 24). In the cohort of 8451 AZA users, 17.8% (1503 patients) discontinued treatment due to intolerable ADEs, with hepatitis accounting for 4.6% of patients. Indications included renal transplant rejection and inflammatory conditions (SLE, Sjogren's syndrome, RA, other connective tissue disorders, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, severe atopic dermatitis). Concomitant allopurinol increased ADE risk. Hepatotoxicity was not analyzed for biochemical pattern or restriction in this evaluation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the case of a 44-year-old woman with chronic paranoid schizophrenia given clozapine, 400 mg/day, as monotherapy. During the fifth week of treatment her previously unremarkable transaminase levels dramatically rose to 675 U/liter for ALT and 369 U/liter for AST, with only a slight increase in gamma-glutamyltransferase (67 U/liter) and unremarkable bilirubin and cholestatic parameters; she developed 28% eosinophilia, and serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were negative. This case is presented as toxic hepatitis caused by clozapine treatment in a letter titled 'Toxic Hepatitis by Clozapine Treatment'. A previously reported clozapine case of toxic hepatitis accompanied by jaundice and bone marrow damage showed enzymes increased to 133 (ALT) and 268 (AST) U/liter.
raw_record.extra_details: Clozapine given at 400 mg/day as monotherapy; toxic hepatitis developed during the fifth week of treatment. ALT 675 U/liter, AST 369 U/liter, gamma-glutamyltransferase 67 U/liter; bilirubin and other cholestatic parameters unremarkable; 28% eosinophilia; negative serology for hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus; testing for autoimmune-chronic-active-hepatitis autoantibodies reported. Named phenotype 'toxic hepatitis' with eosinophilia. A prior published clozapine case described toxic hepatitis with jaundice and bone marrow damage (ALT 133, AST 268 U/liter). Background: transient moderate asymptomatic transaminase increases in about 50% of clozapine-treated patients (mean ALT 55, max 172 U/liter; mean AST 34, max 96 U/liter) have been suggested to be an adaptive reaction, but this is not presented as DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A 10-year prospective study of 248 patients with severe psoriasis, most treated with 25 mg methotrexate weekly as a single oral dose, found that the risk of hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis seemed related to total dose and duration of treatment, being most prevalent in patients receiving greater than 2,000 mg of methotrexate over a 4- to 8-year period. The paper frames this as methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity and notes that liver biopsy is the only reliable method for assessing hepatotoxicity because liver enzymes may remain normal despite ongoing hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic low-dose treatment for severe psoriasis; fibrosis/cirrhosis risk related to total cumulative dose and duration, most prevalent with >2000 mg of methotrexate over 4-8 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective 10-year study of 248 psoriasis patients; 25 mg methotrexate weekly as a single oral dose. Approximately 50% incidence of abnormal liver biopsies in patients 40-60 years old prior to methotrexate therapy; development of fibrosis/cirrhosis was not more common in psoriatics with abnormal pretreatment biopsies. Liver biopsy stated to be the only reliable method for assessing hepatotoxicity, since liver enzymes may remain normal despite ongoing or preexisting hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: In the Brazilian Cooperative Group Wilms' Tumor Study, patients treated with a 60 µg/kg single dose of actinomycin D showed raised liver function tests in 4 of 33 patients (12%) with no case of severe hepatotoxicity; in the standard 15 µg/kg-for-5-days schedule, 1 of 32 patients had severe hepatotoxicity and two others had raised liver function tests without ascites. The frequency of severe hepatotoxicity was similar across the two treatment arms (0/33 versus 1/32), and the authors relate the lower frequency with the 60 µg/kg regimen to the longer six-week (versus three-week) interval between doses used in Brazil.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) patients on an oncology treatment protocol.
raw_record.extra_details: Two regimens compared: 60 µg/kg single dose every 6 weeks gave raised LFTs in 4/33 (12%) and no severe hepatotoxicity; standard 15 µg/kg/day for 5 days gave severe hepatotoxicity in 1/32 plus raised LFTs without ascites in 2. After the US NWTS-4 group noted severe hepatotoxicity at 60 µg/kg, its dose was reduced to 45 µg/kg. Pritchard reported the frequency of severe hepatotoxicity with single-dose actinomycin D in the UK Children's Cancer Study Group Wilms' Tumour Study.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a life-threatening case of phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome, a rare reaction primarily characterized by fever, skin eruptions, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and hepatotoxicity. The reaction developed in a 27-year-old black man treated with phenytoin for one month for exercise-induced sustained ventricular tachycardia; phenytoin was discontinued and he was treated with corticosteroids, with improvement five days after admission. The authors note the reaction usually develops within six weeks of starting phenytoin therapy and may be fatal in up to 40 percent of patients who develop hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 27-year-old man with surgically corrected tetralogy of Fallot treated for exercise-induced sustained ventricular tachycardia; taking no other medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenytoin 300 mg/d for one month; reaction developed approximately four weeks after starting therapy; last dose taken about 36 hours before admission; life-threatening presentation with elevated liver function tests, scleral icterus, hepatosplenomegaly; treated with discontinuation of phenytoin plus intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g/d for three days, then 90 mg/d for three days, converted to oral prednisone; paper states reaction may be fatal in up to 40% of patients who develop hepatotoxicity and usually develops within six weeks of starting phenytoin.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of recurrent severe acute hepatitis induced by omeprazole, noting that isolated reports of fulminant hepatic failure exist but that their described patient's injury recurred with rechallenge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 30-year-old man with advanced renal failure secondary to diabetic nephropathy; omeprazole was the only new medication after ranitidine was stopped; prior co-medications included ranitidine, calcium carbonate, furosemide, and nifedipine.
raw_record.extra_details: Omeprazole 20 mg once daily. Nine days after starting, acute liver injury developed (AST 1788 U/L, ALT 1294 U/L) with prothrombin time normal; liver tests normalized within 4 weeks of discontinuation. Six months later a rechallenge produced acute liver injury within 1 week (AST 954 U/L, ALT 762 U/L), again resolving on discontinuation. Viral (hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, HSV, CMV), immunologic, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, and alpha-1-antitrypsin evaluations were negative/normal. Authors state the time association plus positive rechallenge strongly suggests a cause-and-effect relation, and that the mechanism is probably idiosyncratic because an allergic or direct toxic reaction is unlikely.

raw_record.support_text: A drug lymphocyte stimulation test performed on a patient who presented with fever, skin rash, and brown urine after taking ibuprofen tested positive only for ibuprofen. A liver biopsy supported the diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury, and the patient's skin lesions were diagnosed as multiform exudative erythema, supporting a definitive diagnosis of allergic-type drug-induced liver disease caused by ibuprofen and complicated by systemic hypersensitivity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 36-year-old female taking over-the-counter ibuprofen 4 times daily for 20 days for intermittent headaches; she had stopped ibuprofen 5 days before presentation due to gastrointestinal side effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented with fever (39°C), skin rash (multiform exudative erythema), and brown urine; admission labs: AST 1,492 U/L, ALT 1,860 U/L, ALP 323 U/L, total bilirubin 15.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 10.4 mg/dL, INR 1.76, elevated IgE 11,900 IU/mL; negative for hepatitis B, C, antinuclear antibodies and HHV-6; drug lymphocyte stimulation test positive only for ibuprofen; liver biopsy 14 days after discontinuation supported DILI; treated with IV methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 3 days followed by tapered oral corticosteroid; rash resolved and liver tests normalized over 4 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: Use of the Naranjo probability scale indicates that sulfone syndrome associated with dapsone was probable in our patient. The patient had primarily a cholestatic type of liver injury with exfoliative dermatitis, fever, malaise, and methemoglobinemia. One month after discontinuation of dapsone, all symptoms resolved and laboratory values began to normalize, supporting the diagnosis of sulfone syndrome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 42-year-old HIV-infected man; no pre-existing liver disease reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Sulfone syndrome (dapsone hypersensitivity) developed 4 weeks after dapsone was started. Naranjo probability scale rated the association as probable. Features included predominantly cholestatic liver injury with exfoliative dermatitis, fever, malaise, and methemoglobinemia; liver biopsy was not performed. Symptoms resolved and laboratory values began to normalize ~1 month after dapsone discontinuation. Sulfone syndrome is described as not dose-related, resolving within 1-14 days (time course) after stopping dapsone; fatal reactions have been reported in the literature. Peak labs at 11 weeks on dapsone: ALP 2078 U/L, AST 533, ALT 127, total bilirubin 5.7 mg/dL (conj. 4.7), methemoglobin 5.0%. Prednisone used for symptomatic relief.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the occurrence of fulminant hepatic failure, pancreatitis, acute renal failure, and rhabdomyolysis in a healthy 52-year-old adult taking valproic acid (as divalproex sodium) for migraine prophylaxis. The patient presented with altered mental status and jaundice; liver function tests 3 months earlier were unremarkable and the divalproex dose was doubled at that time to 500 mg twice a day. He was also using dihydroergotamine nasal spray and, rarely, naproxen and acetaminophen with codeine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 52-year-old adult; migraine prophylaxis; co-exposure to dihydroergotamine nasal spray and occasional naproxen and acetaminophen-with-codeine; divalproex dose doubled to 500 mg twice a day 3 months before presentation; no history of liver or kidney disease or alcoholism.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of multiorgan failure attributed to valproic acid toxicity, comprising fulminant hepatic failure, pancreatitis, acute renal failure, and rhabdomyolysis; patient survived. Presented with 24 hours of altered mental status and jaundice; reported by the authors as an occurrence of this multisystem toxicity not previously described in an adult taking valproic acid.

raw_record.support_text: Case 2: a 55-year-old male physician on generic simvastatin 80 mg/day (which had replaced atorvastatin 12 weeks before) presented with jaundice; admission showed ALT 2,867 U/l, AST 2,812, ALP 167, bilirubin 63 µmol/l, INR 1.3 and no detectable paracetamol. Simvastatin was stopped and a transjugular biopsy showed acute hepatitis with mixed expanded portal tracts, mixed inflammatory infiltrate with prominent eosinophils, liver cell dropout, moderate macro- and microvesicular steatosis without Mallory bodies and moderate balloon degeneration. ALT normalized within three weeks; rechallenge with a statin was considered contraindicated. RUCAM score was 9 (probable) and the ALT-ULN/ALP-ULN ratio (25.75) classified the injury as hepatocellular.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old obese male with subacute spongiotic dermatitis developed jaundice after 16 days of azathioprine therapy (50 mg twice daily). Liver function tests revealed a cholestatic type of liver injury; work-up for viral and autoimmune liver disease was negative. Liver biopsy showed moderate canalicular and intrahepatocytic cholestasis with maintained lobular architecture. RUCAM score was 9, indicating highly probable/definite drug-induced liver injury. The patient improved clinically and biochemically after azathioprine cessation and ursodeoxycholic acid supplementation.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first drug for improving insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes, was reported to cause severe hepatotoxicity in patients in Japan and the U.S. The U.S. FDA and Japanese government issued liver-monitoring recommendations. The authors report a patient who developed liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and Graves' disease; concurrently treated with gliclazide, pravastatin, aspirin, and levothyroxin; troglitazone 400 mg/day added in combination with gliclazide.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of 19 months from troglitazone start to abrupt transaminase rise (AST 308 U/l, ALT 470 U/l); earlier marginal elevations (AST 39, ALT 55) at 9 months. Withdrawal led to rapid improvement (AST 36, ALT 43 four weeks after discontinuation). Liver biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis around the central vein with mild lobular infiltration and portal inflammatory infiltrate and fibrosis, compatible with protracted acute hepatitis. DLST and patch tests were negative for troglitazone and other drugs; no allergic clinical signs. The paper states the mechanism is idiosyncratic rather than allergic and the injury is hepatocellular in most cases; it also references a reported autopsy case of fulminant hepatitis with hypersensitivity to troglitazone.

raw_record.support_text: An autopsy case of fatal subacute hepatic failure after administration of troglitazone is described. The liver dysfunction developed about five months after a 63-year-old woman was initially treated with troglitazone, and she died despite hepatic auxiliary treatments such as plasmapheresis. Autopsy findings revealed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis, and steatosis with infiltration of lymphocytes and neutrophils and lack of regenerative activity. The authors state the hepatic failure was due unequivocally to troglitazone, and propose a mechanism of metabolite aberration with accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s), categorized as idiosyncratic.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 63-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism, who also received glibenclamide (2.5 mg/day) and thyroxine (0.05 mg/day) as co-medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose history: troglitazone started at 200 mg twice daily on May 21, 1997, increased to 600 mg/day on June 16, then reduced to 400 mg/day after 2 weeks because treatment failed to improve her condition. Liver dysfunction developed about 5 months after initial treatment; malaise without fever or eruption began during that summer; on October 14, 1997 jaundice and liver dysfunction were found and all drugs were withdrawn. The patient developed hepatic failure and died despite plasmapheresis and other auxiliary treatments. Autopsy showed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis, steatosis, infiltration of lymphocytes and neutrophils, and lack of regenerative activity. Proposed mechanism: metabolite aberration due to accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s), in an idiosyncratic category. FDA (US) and MHW (Japan) had issued warnings about troglitazone liver-function side effects, and reports of liver dysfunction after several months of continuous use were accumulating.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 65-year-old man who developed hepatic injury while taking the benzodiazepine bentazepam and state that a causal relation between the use of bentazepam and hepatic injury can confidently be established, because alternative explanations were ruled out and drug withdrawal was followed by rapid clinical improvement and normalization of laboratory findings; rechallenge was not attempted for ethical reasons. The mechanism is attributed to an idiosyncratic metabolic aberration rather than hypersensitivity, based on the injury type, absence of rash/fever/eosinophilia/granulomatous inflammation, and a long latency of about 4 months between drug intake and presentation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 65-year-old man with prior peptic ulcer, chronic constipation, transient ischaemic attacks, and right carotid occlusion; co-treated with oral lactulose; prior triflusal had been stopped because of GI bleeding.
raw_record.extra_details: Bentazepam given at 25 mg three times daily (manufacturer's recommended dose), later reduced to 25 mg/day without symptomatic improvement; total drug use ~13 months with symptoms appearing about 4 months after starting. Labs: AST 152 U/L, ALT 142 U/L, total bilirubin 18.6 µmol/L (direct 6.8), γ-GT 109 U/L; normal ALP, copper/ceruloplasmin, iron/transferrin/ferritin, thyroid hormones; viral hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV ruled out; autoantibodies negative. Liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis: dense lymphocytic/monocytic portal infiltrate disrupting the limiting plate, swollen hepatocytes, lymphoid follicles, marked portal-to-portal fibrosis with evident transition to cirrhosis, and parenchymal collapse. AST 66, ALT 53, γ-GT 85 by week 11 after stopping; findings normal by 4 months. Rechallenge not performed for ethical reasons.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 68-year-old female with jaundice, total bilirubin 21.3 mg/dl, AST/ALT 702/790 IU/L and Alk phos 269 IU/L; liver biopsy showed marked acute lobular inflammation, balloon degeneration, spotty and bridging necrosis over a background of chronic injury. Her only medication, lisinopril, had been restarted 3 months prior. Hepatic function rapidly declined to grade III encephalopathy and acute liver failure (MELD 33 on day 10), and she expired on admission day 13 following bowel perforation and septic shock.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 68-year-old female; lisinopril restarted 3 months prior without other medications or alcohol; no personal/family history of autoimmune or liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatotoxicity/ALF case; Naranjo criteria for drug-induced reaction probability applied, concluding lisinopril is the probable cause of her ALF. Only few prior reports of ACE inhibitor hepatotoxicity (enalapril, captopril) and only 3 prior reports of lisinopril-induced hepatotoxicity. Laboratory values (day 1): AST 702, ALT 790, Alk phos 269 IU/L, total bilirubin 21.3, direct bilirubin 12.4 mg/dl; INR 1.5. Negative tests: acetaminophen, ethanol, illicit drugs, viral hepatitis, EBV, CMV, HSV, VZV PCR, AMA/ASMA/ALKA, HFE mutation; ferritin 6554 ng/ml. Biopsy: hepatocellular injury without cholestasis, moderate reactive iron deposition in Kupffer cells and hepatocytes, negative copper stain. Outcome: grade III encephalopathy, ALF (MELD 33 day 10), ileus with bowel perforation, septic shock, death on day 13.

raw_record.extra_details: Metronidazole 250 mg b.i.d. per os added to vancomycin/netilmicin therapy for Bacteroides fragilis abscess; netilmicin stopped at the same time. Hepatotoxicity appeared 4 days after metronidazole initiation with drowsiness, vomiting, nausea, right-upper-quadrant pain and moderately enlarged liver; AST 1,450 IU/l (normal <27), ALT 650 IU/l (normal <20), no evidence of cholestasis. Pre-treatment values were unremarkable (AST 17, ALT 14). After metronidazole withdrawal enzymes decreased within 4 days and returned to normal in 15 days. Viral hepatitis A/B/delta and HIV serologies negative. Authors attribute toxicity partly to age and impaired renal function (hydroxy metabolite accumulation), since the parent drug half-life is not altered in renal impairment. Only 2 prior published cases of metronidazole-associated hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old Japanese woman with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy had received 215 g of amiodarone over six years and presented with hepatic encephalopathy; liver biopsy revealed drug-induced steatohepatitis and no urea-cycle genetic variants. raw_record.extra_details: Presentation with hepatic encephalopathy and hyperammonemia; abdominal non-contrast CT showed diffusely increased attenuation of the liver parenchyma (bright liver); liver biopsy confirmed drug-induced steatohepatitis; elevated ammonia, total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, AST, and ALT consistent with amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity. Mechanism described: amiodarone accumulates in hepatocytes, impairs beta-oxidation causing steatohepatitis-like damage with potential progression to cirrhosis, and impairs the urea cycle. raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old male developed acute-onset, long-lasting cholestasis after taking atorvastatin 20 mg/day for 40 days for mixed dyslipidaemia. He presented with asthenia, nausea, painless icterus, acholic stools and hyperchromic urine, with marked bilirubin elevation (total bilirubin 22 mg/dL; direct bilirubin 21 mg/dL) and alkaline phosphatase up to 4-fold normal. Liver histology showed cholestasis with cholangiolitis and interlobular bile duct damage. Liver tests normalized within 5 months after withdrawal (ALK phosphatase after 8 months). The Maria and Victorino clinical scale and Naranjo ADR Probability Scale rated atorvastatin as the probable cause of prolonged cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 72-year-old male with type 2 diabetes, mild hypertension, and chronic cerebral ischaemia; low daily alcohol intake reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Atorvastatin 20 mg/day for 40 days, onset of symptoms 40 days after commencement. Labs: AST 85 IU/mL (2.3x), ALT 81 IU/mL (2.2x), ALP 816 U/L (4.0x), GGT 455 U/L (7x), total bilirubin 22.44 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 21.15 mg/dL; INR 1.1. Histology showed cholangiolitis, lymphocytic infiltration of interlobular duct epithelium with cholangiocyte damage, ductular reaction, centrolobular bilirubinostasis with cholestatic rosettes and feathery degeneration. Non-liver causes (viral hepatitis A-E/G, CMV, EBV, autoimmune serology, biliary obstruction) excluded; no gallstones on ultrasound or MR-cholangiography. Transaminases/bilirubin normalized in 5 months (150 days), ALP after 8 months (237 days). Causality rated probable by Maria-Victorino clinical scale and Naranjo ADR Probability Scale.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state this is the first published report of cholestatic hepatitis related to repaglinide. They note the putative role of repaglinide in this case of acute cholestasis is strongly supported by its temporal eligibility, the careful exclusion of alternative causes, the histological features, and the rapid improvement after drug withdrawal, and that the presence of some eosinophils in the liver inflammatory infiltrate suggests an immune mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes
raw_record.extra_details: Repaglinide started at 1 mg/day 2 months before presentation and increased to 2 mg/day 1 month before presentation; patient presented with 2-week history of itching and jaundice and was hospitalized. No other drugs or herbal remedies, no toxic habits. Labs: aspartate aminotransferase 83 units/l (<37), alanine aminotransferase 183 units/l (<40), alkaline phosphatase 307 units/l (<136), gamma-glutamyltransferase 303 units/l (<85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl with direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dl, serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dl. Viral serology negative, autoantibodies negative, MR cholangiography negative. Liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with mild bile duct proliferation and moderate inflammatory infiltrate (mainly lymphocytes and some eosinophils) with hepatocyte ballooning. Repaglinide discontinued; laboratory findings normal within a month. Authors note presence of eosinophils suggests an immune mechanism may be operating. Clinical phenotype: acute cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 74-year-old man developed DRESS (drug hypersensitivity) syndrome after allopurinol was prescribed for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia. Diagnosis was based on clear exposure to allopurinol, a time frame with cutaneous rash 14 days after medication start, clinical signs including fever and acute hepatocellular injury with abnormal liver enzymes (ALAT 474 IU/L, ASAT 350 IU/L, earlier ASAT 212 U/L, ALAT 280 U/L), worsened renal function, adenopathy, rash and leucocytosis, and lack of exposure to another drug. Hepatic cytolysis with vesicular lithiasis and febrile hepatic failure (cholestatic jaundice, cytolysis, coagulation abnormalities, prothrombin time 34%) were diagnosed, and a favourable clinical evolution followed allopurinol withdrawal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 74-year-old male patient; prescribed for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia; allergic/hypersensitivity (DRESS) reaction
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS (drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms) syndrome; DRESS is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening idiosyncratic drug reaction with lethal visceral involvement in 6-10% of cases. Cutaneous rash appeared 14 days after starting allopurinol; hepatic cytolysis, febrile hepatic failure with cholestatic jaundice, coagulation abnormalities (prothrombin time 34%), elevated liver enzymes (ALAT 474 IU/L, ASAT 350 IU/L), high serum creatinine (171 µmol/L) and leucocytosis (18.1 × 10⁹/L). HBV, HCV, HIV, CMV, Epstein-Barr virus, syphilis and Toxoplasma serologies negative. Favourable clinical evolution after allopurinol withdrawal; allopurinol was initially suspected but not halted, after which the patient deteriorated.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of cholestatic hepatitis induced by the oral fungicidal drug terbinafine, characterized by a prolonged course and mild reduction in the number of interlobular bile ducts (ILBD). In the discussion they explicitly conclude terbinafine is the offending agent, noting its four-week latency to jaundice, normalization of bilirubin and aminotransferases within three months of cessation, and exclusion of other causes of liver disease, while concurrent medications (nicergoline, fenofibrate) taken for four years were considered unlikely to be responsible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 75-year-old female patient treated for cutaneous candidiasis; concurrent nicergoline (5 mg daily) and fenofibrate (100 mg daily) were deemed unlikely offending agents because both had been taken for four years before terbinafine.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral terbinafine 250 mg/day for three weeks; onset of asthenia, anorexia, weight loss a few days after discontinuation, jaundice within ~4 weeks of start, followed by pruritus. Laboratory values ~2 weeks after discontinuation: total bilirubin 89 µmol/L (conjugated 70), ALT 277 IU/L, AST 242 IU/L, γGT 321 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 375 IU/L; normal eosinophil count and prothrombin time. Cholestyramine relieved pruritus; bilirubin normalized 10 weeks after stopping terbinafine, but anicteric cholestasis persisted, with γGT still elevated 17 months later. Percutaneous liver biopsy 6 months after withdrawal showed reduction of interlobular bile ducts (visible in 16 of 23, 70%, portal tracts; ILBD/portal tract ratio 0.7 vs 0.9-1.8 in normal liver), occasional lymphocytes between biliary cells, minimal portal/periportal fibrosis, mild mononuclear infiltration, mild centrilobular canalicular cholestasis and minimal hepatocyte necrosis; negative copper stains. The authors note terbinafine-induced hepatitis is considered uncommon (five prior self-limited cases; liver tests showed cholestatic and cytolytic features resolving within 2-6 months, with cholangitis and centrilobular cholestasis in two biopsied cases), and asymptomatic transaminase elevations occur at an estimated incidence of 1/120,000.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old man with normal baseline liver function had been given amiodarone 400 mg orally once daily for 17.8 months for atrial fibrillation and heart failure and developed nausea, vomiting and muscle weakness. Liver biopsy showed microvesicular steatosis, foam cells in the hepatic sinusoids and Mallory bodies in the periportal hepatocytes with features of chronic hepatitis, and electron microscopy showed pleomorphic mitochondria with crystalloid inclusions; the authors state both findings strongly suggested amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity. Liver enzymes improved by day 3 after amiodarone withdrawal (AST 31, ALT 27 IU/L) and the patient fully recovered at 1 month.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose 400 mg orally once daily for 17.8 months. Admission labs: AST 123 IU/L, ALT 146 IU/L, albumin 2.5 g/dL, bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 99 IU/L, platelets 212,000/uL, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL; hepatitis B/C/A and VDRL negative; ANA positive with other autoantibodies negative. Liver biopsy: microvesicular steatosis, foam cells in sinusoids, Mallory bodies, chronic hepatitis features (grade 2 lobular, grade 1 porto-peripheral, stage 1 portal fibrosis); electron microscopy showed pleomorphic mitochondria with crystalloid inclusions and concentric membranous arrays. Dechallenge: liver enzymes improved by day 3 after withdrawal (AST 31, ALT 27 IU/L); full recovery at 1 month. Sural nerve biopsy showed demyelination; nerve conduction showed mixed sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old man with severe aplastic anemia was treated with cyclosporin A, steroid pulse therapy, and metenolone acetate. Marked transaminase elevation appeared after starting metenolone acetate, followed by hepatic failure and death. Autopsy findings were compatible with drug-induced liver injury, and metenolone acetate was considered the most likely causative agent. Metenolone acetate was given at 25 mg/day beginning July 18 for less than 1 month; on August 14 AST rose to 1609 IU/l, ALT to 2173 IU/l, gamma-GTP to 126 IU/l, and total bilirubin to 6.5 mg/dl. After discontinuation transaminases decreased immediately, but the patient fell into hepatic coma on August 15 and died on August 28. The authors caution that liver impairment from this drug, usually regarded as mild, reversible, and infrequent, warrants extreme caution in debilitated patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 75-year-old man with severe aplastic anemia (debilitated state); prior treatment with cyclosporin A and steroid pulse therapy; co-administered cimetidine and antibiotics; the authors caution on use in debilitated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: MA given 25 mg/day for <1 month (from July 18). Liver tests normal until MA; on Aug 7 AST 108 and ALT 163 IU/l (cimetidine discontinued), on Aug 14 AST 1609, ALT 2173, gamma-GTP 126 IU/l, total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dl; MA discontinued, transaminases fell immediately (AST 1355, ALT 1248) but hepatic coma Aug 15; died Aug 28. Autopsy liver 1550 g with marked degeneration/regeneration of hepatocytes, lymphocytic infiltration and pseudo-bile-duct formation in portal areas, compatible with drug-induced liver injury. Lymphocyte stimulation test for MA was negative; IgE normal; patient positive for hepatitis-B virus antibodies but negative for anti-HCV and anti-CMV. Liver impairment from metenolone acetate had been considered mild, reversible, and infrequent. Plasma exchange with glucose-insulin therapy (10 times) was ineffective.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old woman who had received an average daily dose of 200 mg of amiodarone since December 1979 for recurrent supraventricular tachycardia developed progressive liver enzyme elevations (alkaline phosphatase, then aspartate aminotransferase), hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, abdominal pain, anorexia, and wasting. While still on amiodarone she died of hepatic encephalopathy; autopsy showed cirrhosis with prominent fibrosis, bile duct proliferation, severely damaged hepatocytes, and widespread Mallory bodies. The authors interpret this as evidence that asymptomatic amiodarone-induced liver function disturbance, especially with prolonged treatment, can herald irreversible liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 76-year-old woman; prolonged (approximately 3-year) amiodarone treatment; recurrent supraventricular tachycardia indication
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 200 mg/day from December 1979; asymptomatic two- to three-fold increases in alkaline phosphatase (195 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (85 U/L, later 225 U/L) noted from 1982-1983; 2 weeks after referral patient died of hepatic encephalopathy while still on amiodarone. Autopsy: cirrhosis, scant fatty infiltration, prominent fibrosis, bile duct proliferation, severely damaged hepatocytes, widespread Mallory bodies. Authors note hepatotoxicity appears concentration-dependent and that amiodarone induces alcohol-like changes (lamellar osmiophilic lysosomal inclusions); Rotmensch and associates held the traditional view that hepatic enzyme elevation is transient and clinically insignificant.

raw_record.extra_details: Celecoxib 200 mg twice daily; latency 12 days. Naranjo probability scale suggested a probable association with hepatorenal syndrome. Hepatorenal syndrome with jaundice, pitting edema, elevated AST (576), ALT (396), GGT (140), ALP (696), bilirubin (2.4 mg/dL), INR (5), and creatinine; GFR 15 mL/min/1.73 m². Dechallenge led to rapid symptomatic and biochemical improvement; rechallenge not done for safety; no known interaction with co-medications. Discussion notes rare reported celecoxib-induced hepatitis/hepatorenal syndrome and states celecoxib-induced hepatotoxicity may show hepatocellular, cholestatic, or combined pattern; allergic or idiosyncratic mechanism considered probable.

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old man being treated for essential hypertension with losartan developed hepatocellular and renal damage. He had been prescribed losartan 50 mg/d but, due to a misunderstanding of directions, took 150 mg/d (50 mg three times a day). Six weeks later he presented with asthenia, anorexia, and weight loss; laboratory tests showed SCr 1.9 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, AST 115 U/L, ALT 410 U/L, and GGT 89 U/L with normal alkaline phosphatase. Losartan was discontinued (other medications continued) and within one month his clinical condition and laboratory results returned to normal; rechallenge was not attempted.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatocellular pattern with elevated AST 115 U/L, ALT 410 U/L, GGT 89 U/L, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL and normal alkaline phosphatase; transient ischemic attack context; renal damage also present (SCr rose from 0.9 to 1.9 mg/dL); viral (HAV, HBV, HCV, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune liver serology negative; symptoms asthenia, anorexia, 5-kg weight loss; recovered within 1 month after discontinuation and remained asymptomatic over 18 months; authors note two 1996 case reports of possible losartan (50 mg/d) hepatotoxicity and that elevation in ALT occurred at 1.9% incidence in controlled trials (not significantly different from placebo); authors conclude mechanism unlikely dose-related given 150 mg/d used in trials and, with absence of hypersensitivity, suggest a metabolic idiosyncrasy; losartan (angiotensin II antagonist) used for hypertension.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of curcumin-induced hepatocellular DILI in a 78-year old female admitted with jaundice after a one-month latency, with unremarkable evaluation for alternative etiologies. The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score of 6 for the supplement indicated a probable association. Peak AST and ALT were >20 times the upper limit of normal, a 48% decrease in AST/ALT occurred 7 days after discontinuation, and transaminitis resolved in 42 days; no re-challenge was performed. The authors conclude that curcumin supplements should be recognized as DILI triggers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 78-year-old female patient; the culprit was an over-the-counter curcumin supplement taken once daily; long-standing co-medications (aspirin, citalopram, losartan, metformin, oxybutynin) taken for at least a year were not implicated.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score of 6 indicated probable association (score >8 would indicate highly probable). Latency about one month. Jaundice with acholic stools for one week; no fever, abdominal pain, pruritus, or alcohol use. Peak AST and ALT >20x upper limit of normal. 48% decrease in AST/ALT at 7 days after supplement discontinuation; full resolution of transaminitis in 42 days. No re-challenge performed. Manifestation reported as Grade 3 DILI (severe hepatotoxicity) with complete recovery on discontinuation. Curcumin is a constituent of turmeric (Curcuma longa); supplement curcumin levels higher than the 3.14% curcuminoid content of turmeric powder.

raw_record.support_text: A 79-year-old male with radiation-induced sarcoma received trabectedin (1.5 mg/m² over 24 h, dose-reduced to 1.2 mg/m²). He developed progressive hepatic and renal failure during a 2-week hospitalization. Viral hepatitis and ischemic hepatitis were ruled out, ultrasounds showed no focal abnormality. Gastroenterology and nephrology consults concurred that his liver failure was most likely due to his trabectedin treatment. The patient died on Day 54 from irreversible hepatic and renal insufficiency, with causes of death ruled as fulminant hepatic failure and acute renal failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 79-year-old male; concurrent as-needed acetaminophen use; dose reduction from 1.5 to 1.2 mg/m² per product recommendations; concurrent acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis; liver biopsy not performed due to thrombocytopenia.
raw_record.extra_details: Trabectedin is an orphan chemotherapy for soft-tissue sarcoma used when patients are not candidates for ifosfamide or anthracyclines. Clinical trials report hematological and hepatic toxicities as dose-limiting; in trials trabectedin-induced hepatic failure is described as transient and reversible, with transaminase increases within 2-5 days, peaking days 5-9, resolving within 3-4 weeks. Laboratory findings included rising total bilirubin (2.4 on Day 39 to 12.0 mg/dL on Day 54), AST up to 1053 U/L, ALT up to 502 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 473 U/L. Death occurred Day 54.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of cholestatic hepatitis associated with flutamide (4'-nitro-3'-trifluoromethyl-isobutyranilide) therapy, an antiandrogen. They note that jaundice after 1 to 3 months of flutamide therapy during clinical trials and fatal liver failure in the setting of flutamide treatment had been reported but without details. The case is a 79-year-old man who received flutamide 750 mg/d orally after prostatectomy for adenocarcinoma and developed cholestatic hepatitis 5 weeks later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 79-year-old man; prostatic adenocarcinoma indication; recent prostatectomy; treated with flutamide 750 mg/d orally; jaundice onset 5 weeks after therapy start.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis. Laboratory: serum bilirubin 74 µmol/L (normal <20); AST 120 U/L; ALT 158 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 1070 U/L (normal <110); gamma-glutamyltransferase 405 U/L; ESR 75 mm/h; leukocytes 18.6 x 10^9/L with 16% eosinophils. Viral and extrahepatic causes excluded; non-A non-B hepatitis considered less likely. On drug discontinuation liver enzymes and bilirubin declined, peripheral eosinophilia disappeared, values returned to normal within 3 weeks; follow-up at 4 months, 1 year, and 18 months unremarkable. Authors describe flutamide as 'the most likely cause' and 'the cause of cholestatic hepatitis,' with uncertain mechanism, speculating on androgen-related cholestasis or an immunoallergic reaction (repeated eosinophilia 10-16%).
