raw_record.support_text: The diagnosis of drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis was established after reasonably excluding other possible etiologies. Among all the drugs the patient was receiving, metformin appears the most probably responsible agent, per the Nierenberg protocol: prior published cases of metformin-associated hepatotoxicity exist, latency from exposure onset to symptoms was a few weeks, the clinical picture improved to resolution after drug withdrawal, and other causes of hepatitis were excluded. No rechallenge was performed.

raw_record.extra_details: Metformin (dimetilbiguanida) 1700 mg/day. Presented with 2-3 weeks of dyspepsia/abdominal discomfort, then intense asthenia, anorexia, jaundice, coluria and generalized pruritus. Peak liver tests: total bilirubin 256 µmol/l, direct bilirubin 210 µmol/l, AST 1198 U/l, ALT 596 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 164 U/l, GGT 260 U/l. Injury resolved (analytical normal) within 3 months and remained normal at 9 months follow-up; no specific treatment given, insulin used to control diabetes. Viral, autoimmune, and tumor serologies, imaging (ultrasound, CT, cholangio-MRI) all negative. Liver biopsy not performed (patient refused). MEDLINE (1966-2004) search 'Metformin/adverse effects AND Hepatitis or Cholestasis' identified only 4 prior published cases; metformin hepatic toxicity described as extraordinarily rare. Comparison table of the 5 cases (Babich, Desilets, Nammour, Deutsch, present case) shows resolution in 4-12 weeks; one published case (Nammour) had rechallenge/concomitant pathology.

In the cohort, all DIAIH patients scored as probable on the RUCAM scale, and nitrofurantoin (together with statins) was implicated in three fourths of DIAIH cases. raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of fatal hepatitis associated with troglitazone. An 85-year-old man with type 2 diabetes developed severe hepatic dysfunction after troglitazone therapy (started 5 months prior, increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks); abdominal pain, malaise and jaundice developed and alanine aminotransferase reached 608 U/L. A diagnosis of troglitazone-induced hepatitis seemed likely, symptoms progressed to confusion, agitation, ascites and edema, and liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis; the patient died 8 weeks after presentation. The paper notes that in rare cases troglitazone use is associated with fatal hepatotoxicity and that news of six deaths and one liver transplantation led to withdrawal of the product from the British market.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 85-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes; co-medication with insulin, metoprolol, and levothyroxine during the episode.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone dosed at 400 mg/day for about 5 months; initial ALT 608 U/L then 287 U/L (normal 10-45), total bilirubin 15.6 mg/dL (normal 0.1-1.1), albumin 2.5 g/dL, normal prothrombin time, glycosylated hemoglobin 5.2%; serology negative for hepatitis A, B, C; normal hepatic ultrasonogram; liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis (lobular, cholestatic hepatitis with areas of confluent necrosis); death 8 weeks after presentation; paper cites six deaths and one liver transplantation associated with troglitazone prompting British market withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: An 85-year-old woman was prescribed a 7-day course of telithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia with no other drugs taken. She was admitted 15 days after initiation with weakness; the following day total bilirubin was 4.3 mg/dL, AST 5,525 IU/L, ALT 3,870 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 132 IU/L. She progressed to liver failure and died a few days later; blood cultures and serology for hepatitis viruses were negative. This case was assessed as DILIN severity grade 5 and assigned causality to telithromycin as Probable.

raw_record.support_text: In a jaundiced patient with thyrotoxicosis, hepatitis A was excluded by negative serology, and the probable cause of jaundice was carbimazole since it developed three weeks after it was recommenced. Eosinophils on liver histology suggested an allergic aetiology for the hepatobiliary damage. Carbimazole-induced hepatic damage is described as allergic in aetiology and typically predominantly cholestatic, as depicted in this patient.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: A contributory effect from hormonal contraceptive use could not be excluded; liver enzyme tests from 25 September 2003 before carbimazole initiation were already mildly deranged.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice developed three weeks after carbimazole was recommenced; eosinophils present on liver histology. Thionamide-induced hepatobiliary damage usually occurs within three months of therapy and may occur despite prior uneventful exposure. Jaundice resolved over three months; carbimazole was discontinued and cholestyramine, atenolol, and later radioactive iodine therapy were used.

raw_record.support_text: Tolcapone (Tasmar) was associated with severe hepatotoxicity leading to the EMEA recommendation to suspend its marketing authorization. Three cases of acute, unpredictable hepatitis with fatal outcome had been reported, including a fulminant hepatitis in a 74-year-old woman 9 weeks after starting tolcapone as add-on therapy for Parkinson's disease (liver biopsy showed severe centrolobular necrosis and a lobular inflammatory infiltrate mostly of plasma cells and eosinophils) and a US patient who died from hepatic necrosis. A third case of fulminant hepatitis related to tolcapone occurred in a patient already under close liver-enzyme monitoring. The underlying mechanism was considered possibly a severe idiosyncratic reaction, similar to that seen with isoniazid or diclofenac.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Add-on therapy for Parkinson's disease; mechanism described as unpredictable, with possible genetic/environmental susceptibility, but no required co-exposure or restricted population is specified.
raw_record.extra_details: Three fatal human cases of acute unpredictable hepatitis reported after tolcapone marketing (approximately 100,000 patients worldwide treated). Index case: 74-year-old woman, fulminant hepatitis 9 weeks after starting tolcapone, biopsy showing severe centrolobular necrosis with lobular inflammatory infiltrate of plasma cells and eosinophils; a US patient died from hepatic necrosis. EMEA mandated liver-function monitoring (ALT threshold of 3x upper normal for discontinuation) before mandating suspension of EU marketing authorization on 12 November 1998; FDA did not suspend but revised the label to adjunctive use only with monitoring (baseline then every 2 weeks for year 1), discontinuing if ALT/AST exceeds upper limit. In Phase II/III double-blind placebo-controlled trials, asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations (ALT more often than AST) occurred in 1.76% (16 of 906) patients, were reversible, and were considered not of significance. Possible immune-mediated/mixed mechanism and role of hepatic COMT inhibition/catabolism (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, CYP oxidation) considered unknown.

raw_record.support_text: A first-in-human phase I dose-escalation trial of ursolic acid liposomes (UAL) enrolled 63 subjects (4 patients with advanced solid tumors and 35 healthy adult volunteers for the toxicity study, plus 24 healthy volunteers for pharmacokinetics). Dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) was encountered at 74, 98, and 130 mg/m² and consisted of hepatotoxicity and diarrhea; the maximum tolerated dose was 98 mg/m².
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Administered as a liposomal formulation (UAL) by 4-h intravenous infusion; single-dose dose-escalation setting with DLT manifesting at 74, 98, and 130 mg/m²; study population included healthy adult volunteers and patients with advanced solid tumors.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I MTD/DLT trial (registration ChiCTR-ONC-12002385). Doses evaluated: 11, 22, 37, 56, 74, 98, and 130 mg/m². Hepatotoxicity was a dose-limiting toxicity; MTD 98 mg/m². Other adverse events included grade 1 nausea, grade 2 abdominal distention, grade 1 microscopic hematuria, grade 2 elevated serum sodium, grade 1 vascular stimulation, and grade 1 skin rash. Linear pharmacokinetics for Cmax, AUC0-24h, and AUC0-inf.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty-one of 92 patients underwent placement of hepatic arterial pumps at the time of liver resection and received hepatic arterial infusional (HAI) floxuridine at doses previously demonstrated as safe. Significant biliary sclerosis developed in six patients in the HAI group, requiring chronic indwelling stents in four patients, and one patient died of progressive liver failure associated with this toxicity. The authors conclude that biliary toxicity is an important potential side effect of hepatic arterial chemotherapy.

raw_record.extra_details: 6 of 21 HAI patients developed significant biliary sclerosis; 4 required chronic indwelling biliary stents; 1 patient died of progressive liver failure associated with this toxicity. Floxuridine was given via implanted hepatic arterial pump at doses previously demonstrated as safe. The authors note prior studies in unresectable disease were plagued by high rates of biliary toxicity.

Only one patient (6% of 18 evaluable) developed 5-fluorouracil-induced hepatitis. The other hepatic arterial infusion-related toxicities were hepatic arterial thrombosis or arteritis in three patients (17%), and six patients (33%) required cessation or dose reduction because of systemic 5-fluorouracil toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic toxicity was frequent in the pump studies of hepatic arterial FUDR infusion for liver metastases: bilirubin elevations above 3 mg/ml occurred in 20% of patients, transaminase elevations in 71%, and two patients developed strictures of the bile ducts resembling biliary sclerosis. In most of the pump studies one-fourth to one-third of patients had hyperbilirubinemia. A serum SGOT elevation pattern at the end of each FUDR infusion occurred in 23 of the original 45 patients, was present in all patients who later developed severe hepatic toxicity (bilirubin >= 3 mg/ml), and in 11 of 12 who developed ulcers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Administered via hepatic arterial infusion (regional route) for colorectal cancer liver metastases; patients had pre-existing liver metastases. Two patients developed bile duct strictures resembling biliary sclerosis.
raw_record.extra_details: 20% of patients had bilirubin elevations above 3 mg/ml; transaminase elevations in 71%; hyperbilirubinemia in one-fourth to one-third of patients across pump studies. Characteristic SGOT elevation at end of FUDR infusion with normalization before the next dose occurred in 23 of 45 patients, preceded severe hepatic toxicity (bilirubin >= 3 mg/ml). Hepatic toxicity findings are grouped with gastrointestinal ulceration complications of hepatic arterial FUDR therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic toxicity was commonly observed during hepatic artery FUDR (floxuridine) infusion: bilirubin rose above 3 mg/100 mL in 9 (22%) patients and returned toward baseline in five while on saline, suggesting a drug effect. SGOT rose in 29 (71%) of 41 patients, exceeding three times baseline in 19 (46%), with levels normalizing during saline infusion. Two patients developed bile duct strictures unrelated to tumor progression requiring biliary drainage, and histopathologic examination in three patients showed periportal inflammation and cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Administered via hepatic artery pump infusion (unusual route) as cancer therapy; dose reductions were required in 34 of 41 patients, with 15 reduced to <0.1 mg/kg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Floxuridine (FUDR; 5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine) hepatic artery infusion. Bilirubin >3 mg/100 mL in 9/41 (22%) patients; SGOT elevation in 29/41 (71%), >3x baseline in 19/41 (46%); alkaline phosphatase occasionally rose in 7/29 with SGOT elevation; LDH did not increase. Abnormalities returned to baseline on saline infusion (dechallenge supports drug effect). Bile duct strictures in 2 patients requiring biliary drainage. Histology in 3 patients: periportal inflammation and cholestasis. Ten patients (24%) complained of generalized weakness, improved with dose modification. 23 patients showed cyclic SGOT rise at end of infusion with normalization before next dose.

raw_record.extra_details: Case performed in March 1980; first published in French in 1982 and in English in 1985 as part of the first series of partial liver grafts. The patient died of graft rejection at postoperative day 22 from agranulocytosis after immunosuppression withdrawal; the acute liver failure itself was the attributed valproic-acid injury, not the cause of death. Mechanistic details (e.g., intrinsic vs idiosyncratic mode) and biochemical pattern not stated.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I study, 32 patients with solid malignant tumors received intoplicine (RP60475F) by 24 h continuous infusion every 21 days at doses of 12-640 mg/m² via a central venous catheter. Liver toxicity was dose limiting. One patient died in a hepatic coma after the first course at 640 mg/m², which was associated with intoplicine treatment, and one sudden death probably occurred due to intoplicine toxicity. Liver toxicity was also seen in studies employing other dosages and infusion durations. The recommended phase II dose for the 24 h infusion was 384 mg/m².
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult cancer patients with solid malignant tumors in a phase I dose-escalation trial; intoplicine given by 24 h continuous intravenous infusion every 21 days.

raw_record.support_text: A single 28-year-old woman developed severe liver injury and jaundice after treatment with zileuton 400 mg four times daily for approximately 6 weeks. At discontinuation she was jaundiced with AST 19×ULN, ALT 33×ULN, alkaline phosphatase 1.3×ULN and total bilirubin 6.6×ULN; all viral hepatitis serology was negative and no alternative aetiology was identified. Total bilirubin reached 12.8×ULN 8 days after stopping zileuton; within 35 days ALT and AST returned to normal and bilirubin fell to 2.6×ULN, and the patient fully recovered with normal bilirubin after 70 days. This case was the basis for a long-term liver surveillance study.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult female (28 years old); no pre-existing liver disease noted; no alternative aetiology identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency approximately 6 weeks; dose 400 mg four times daily; symptoms fatigue, nausea, itching, influenza-like symptoms; AST 19×ULN, ALT 33×ULN, ALP 1.3×ULN, total bilirubin 6.6×ULN at discontinuation, rising to 12.8×ULN 8 days after stopping; ALT/AST normalized within 35 days, bilirubin normal after 70 days; full recovery; viral hepatitis serology negative; no alternative aetiology identified; motivated a 12-month surveillance study of zileuton liver safety.

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old woman with Cushing's syndrome treated with mifepristone (escalated to 1,200 mg daily about a month prior) presented with abdominal pain, jaundice, and itching. Labs showed total bilirubin 20.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 18.6 mg/dL, ALT 27 U/L, AST 49 U/L, and ALP 258 U/L with normal PT/INR. Transjugular liver biopsy revealed diffuse canalicular and cytoplasmic bile stasis consistent with drug-induced cholestasis, and a diagnosis of mifepristone-associated DILI was made. Mifepristone was discontinued and her symptoms and liver tests gradually improved.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult female patient with Cushing's syndrome receiving chronic high-dose mifepristone (escalating from 300 mg to a final 1,200 mg daily); concurrent stable levothyroxine therapy; no rechallenge performed.
raw_record.extra_details: 35-year-old woman; biopsy showed diffuse canalicular (long arrow) and cytoplasmic (short arrow) bile stasis, consistent with drug-induced cholestasis (intrahepatic cholestasis). Peak values: total bilirubin 20.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 18.6 mg/dL, ALT 27 U/L, AST 49 U/L, ALP 258 U/L; PT/INR normal. RUCAM score calculated as 7, making mifepristone a 'probable' cause; authors note that without rechallenge full RUCAM categories could not be assessed and the score may be under-calculated, possibly making mifepristone 'highly probable'/'highly likely'. Viral hepatitis serologies and autoimmune/metabolic workup negative. Following discontinuation biochemistry improved (T. Bili 1.7 mg/dL by one month); ursodeoxycholic acid was started; symptoms resolved. Authors state this is one of the first reported cases of mifepristone-associated DILI, citing one prior case report.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old East Indian woman treated with flutamide, 250 mg orally twice daily, for hirsutism developed severe jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools about 6 weeks after starting the drug. Laboratory results included bilirubin 263 µmol/L (peaking at 480 µmol/L), INR 1.9, alkaline phosphatase 180 IU/L, and alanine aminotransferase 1481 IU/L. Other causes of liver disease were excluded, flutamide was discontinued, and her condition improved with return of liver enzyme levels to normal within 6 weeks. Liver biopsy near the height of illness showed changes typical of drug toxicity, including zonal hepatic necrosis with cholestasis and ballooning degeneration of surviving zone 1 hepatocytes. The authors report this as the first association of flutamide with serious hepatotoxicity in a woman using the drug for hirsutism, saying the features of the case are quite conclusive.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult female treated for hirsutism (off-label indication); continued oral contraceptive (Demulen-30) use as co-medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset about 6 weeks after starting flutamide with GI symptoms and pruritus; bilirubin peaked at 480 µmol/L; INR 1.9; ALT 1481 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 180 IU/L; dechallenge led to biochemical recovery within 6 weeks and resolution by early June 1993; pruritus responded to subcutaneous naloxone, not hydroxyzine; biopsy showed zonal hepatic necrosis with cholestasis and ballooning degeneration of surviving zone 1 hepatocytes; ultrasound of liver normal, biliary tree not dilated; prior treatments with spironolactone and cyproterone were ineffective for hirsutism but not attributed to the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Data from three European centers confirmed a high frequency of hepatotoxicity in patients treated with 6-thioguanine (6-TG) for IBD: 8/45 patients (18%) receiving 6-TG for 8-119 weeks showed nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH), and an equal number had equivocal findings possibly related to NRH. A further international multicentric dataset of 296 IBD patients on 6-TG found 7 discontinued due to laboratory signs of hepatotoxicity, pathological findings in 31/60 (52%) liver biopsies, and probable or definite NRH in 11/38 (29%) silver-reticulin-stained samples. Case reports described elevated liver enzymes, splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia after 44 weeks of 6-TG that resolved after discontinuation, while two other cases failed to resolve after dose reduction or cessation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult IBD patients on chronic 6-TG therapy; NRH is dose-related (high doses associated with more NRH, while a 20 mg/day regimen showed almost no NRH); signs of portal hypertension (splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia) reported.

raw_record.support_text: Case 1/307, a clear Hy's Law case, was a 42-year-old man with T2DM. At study visit 8 (day 57) he had a marked ALT elevation (>30x ULN), AST (>15x ULN), and rising TBIL, with an AE of 'hepatitis acute' and dark urine that was upgraded to an SAE; liver tests normalized by day 120. The LSEC consensus causality assessment was that a causal role for fasiglifam was highly likely (75-95% likelihood).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult male (42 y) with type 2 diabetes mellitus in a clinical trial.
raw_record.extra_details: At day 57 ALT rose to >30x ULN and AST >15x ULN with TBIL then exceeding 2x ULN (Hy's Law case). AE 'hepatitis acute' with dark urine, upgraded to SAE; study drug interrupted day 59; recovery by day 120. Tests for acute viral hepatitis (HAV, HBV, HCV, CMV, HEV, EBV) and autoimmune hepatitis (ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM) were negative; abdominal ultrasound showed only fatty liver; no concomitant or herbal medication. LSEC consensus likelihood 75-95%.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old patient with recurrent depressive disorder developed a fulminant increase in transaminases 6 weeks after first taking nefazodone, which did not normalize despite stopping the drug. The subsequent severe uncontrollable liver failure required orthotopic liver transplantation, and the patient died weeks later from transplant complications. The temporal relationship of the antidepressant intake, the histological finding consistent with drug-toxic liver damage, and the absence of other plausible diseases argue for nefazodone-mediated liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult male patient with recurrent depressive disorder; nefazodone given at 300 mg/day in two doses; no pre-existing liver disease identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of 6 weeks after initiation of nefazodone; transaminase elevation did not normalize after drug discontinuation; histology consistent with drug-toxic liver damage (fulminant transaminase increase); this is reported as the 7th case of likely nefazodone-mediated acute liver failure; patient underwent liver transplantation and died weeks later from complications of transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present the case of a patient with Stevens-Johnson syndrome and severe liver injury in which warfarin was confirmed as the culprit drug; they report this as the first case of warfarin-induced SJS/TEN in an adult. Using the RUCAM score they confirmed the diagnosis of warfarin-induced DILI, and the MELD score verified seriously impaired liver function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patient with concurrent SJS/TEN; reported as the first adult case of warfarin-induced SJS/TEN.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver injury with significantly elevated transaminase values. Diagnosis of warfarin-induced DILI confirmed with the RUCAM score; the MELD score was applied to evaluate the degree of liver injury and verified seriously impaired liver function. Warfarin causality for SJS/TEN was also confirmed by ALDEN score and IFN-γ ELISPOT assay, and its discontinuation was essential for patient recovery. The authors note that in a retrospective study of 748 patients with DILI, only 36 (4.8%) presented with both SJS/TEN and DILI, with a higher mortality rate of 22%, though this does not specifically attribute those cases to warfarin.

raw_record.support_text: A case of a 61-year-old female with sitaxsentan-induced acute severe liver failure is presented. Despite withdrawal of therapy, her liver tests failed to improve, and after six weeks of monitoring she was given high-dose corticosteroids with a good clinical and biochemical response. The paper notes endothelin receptor antagonists are postulated to cause hepatitis by inhibition of a bile salt transporter pump, but an immune-mediated or idiosyncratic mechanism should be considered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patient with pulmonary arterial hypertension and a background of atrial septal defect repair, atrial flutter, atrioventricular node ablation and pacemaker insertion, with no known liver disease; unclear contribution of concomitant medications (warfarin, diltiazem, furosemide, vitamin D, calcium).
raw_record.extra_details: Sitaxsentan given at 100 mg/day for 16 weeks; liver enzymes became abnormal after 8 weeks and sitaxsentan was discontinued 6 weeks later; dechallenge was negative (continued worsening of all liver parameters over the next 6 weeks and admission); treated with high-dose corticosteroids with good clinical and biochemical response. Baseline near-normal liver tests (ALT 24 U/L, AST 28 U/L, ALP 112 U/L, bilirubin 11.6 µmol/L). Postulated mechanism: inhibition of a bile salt transporter pump; immune-mediated or idiosyncratic mechanism considered. Sitaxsentan is a selective endothelin A receptor antagonist.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective observational cohort of 52 adult patients with pulmonary drug-susceptible TB on PZA-containing first-line regimens, 6 (11.5%) had to discontinue PZA due to hepatotoxicity (outcome defined as an increase in liver enzymes leading to discontinuation of PZA). By CTCAE grade, 2 (33.3%) had grade 2, 3 (50.0%) had grade 3, and 1 (16.6%) had a grade 4 hepatotoxic adverse event. Hepatotoxicity occurred at a median of 22 days (IQR 11-43 days) after starting TB treatment, and female patients had a significantly higher risk of PZA-associated hepatotoxicity (OR 10.4, 95% CI 1.2-135.8).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patients with pulmonary drug-susceptible TB treated with PZA-containing first-line regimens; in one of the six cases isoniazid was also not reintroduced after treatment interruption.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper states PZA is associated with the highest risk of hepatotoxicity among first-line TB drugs, with reported incidence ranging from 5-58%. Cohort results: 6/52 (11.5%) discontinued PZA due to hepatotoxicity; CTCAE (v5.0) grades 2 (n=2), 3 (n=3), and 4 (n=1); median latency 22 days (IQR 11-43); female sex risk OR 10.4 (95% CI 1.2-135.8). Mechanism proposed to involve PZA metabolic intermediates. Main study aim was to identify differentially expressed genes predictive of PZA-hepatotoxicity. General context notes hepatotoxicity can present as asymptomatic elevation of liver enzymes, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and GGT and can escalate to life-threatening acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: In discussing pexidartinib for TGCT, the paper notes that although the drug was generally well tolerated, a few cases of severe irreversible liver toxicity were seen. Based on these results, pexidartinib was granted FDA approval only in a restricted population of adult TGCT patients with severe symptomatic disease not expected to benefit from surgery, with frequent liver-function monitoring and prompt drug discontinuation on adverse events.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patients with symptomatic TGCT not amenable to surgical resection; FDA approval restricted to severe symptomatic disease with no expectation that surgery will stabilize or improve the condition; close liver-function monitoring and prompt discontinuation advised. Indication: tenosynovial giant cell tumor.
raw_record.extra_details: A few cases of severe, irreversible and potentially life-threatening hepatic toxicity were observed in the clinical trial program (phase I-II and phase III studies; phase III part one n=120, phase II extension n=23). FDA approval accompanied by a REMS program/patient registry and recommendation of frequent monitoring of liver function with prompt drug discontinuation on adverse events; approval under EMA evaluation. Other side effects: hypertension and hair-color changes (mostly low-grade). Agent is an oral selective CSF1R inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: A total of 151 galactose tolerance tests (GTT) and liver biopsies were performed in a consecutive study of 45 psoriatic patients with methotrexate-induced liver fibrosis; of these, 23 had cirrhosis. The authors conclude that an oral GTT is not sensitive enough to reveal methotrexate-induced liver fibrosis or cirrhosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult psoriatic patients on chronic methotrexate therapy, with serial liver biopsy monitoring; fibrosis/cirrhosis developed during MTX treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 45 psoriatic patients with biopsy-confirmed methotrexate-induced liver fibrosis, 23 (51%) had cirrhosis. Cirrhosis usually occurred after a cumulative total of about 2200 mg of MTX had been given. MTX described as a hepatotoxic drug also affecting bone marrow, requiring regular monitoring of leukocytes, thrombocytes, liver function and liver histology. GTT results: 18 abnormal GTT among the cohort (8 with cirrhosis, 15 with fibrosis, 3 normal).

raw_record.support_text: In this sample of 110 West Algerian RA patients treated with MTX monotherapy (mean dose 12.67 mg/week for at least 6 months) with folic acid supplementation, Methotrexate-related adverse drug reactions were defined to include liver events: hepatic cytolysis, metabolic hepatic steatosis, cirrhosis, hepatic fibrosis, and transaminase levels, i.e., drug-related liver injury attributed to MTX. In a related methods statement, the MTX dose was reduced to 10 mg/week in patients who developed severe MTX-related toxicity including liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 14,271 patients treated with methimazole (MMI) for Graves' disease, severe DILI occurred in 198 patients (1.4%), with incidence 0.26% in male and 1.69% in female patients (females significantly higher, p<0.0001). Median MMI dose at DILI diagnosis was 15 mg/day (range 5-30 mg), median time to DILI was 25 days, and 93.9% had hepatocellular, 2.5% cholestatic, and 3.5% mixed type injury; 7 patients required hospitalization. There was no correlation between MMI dose and severity of liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adults treated for Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism); marked female predominance with significantly higher incidence in females; no MMI dose-severity correlation observed.
raw_record.extra_details: 198/14,271 cases (1.4% overall); median age 49 years (range 10-82); median MMI daily dose 15 mg (range 5-30 mg); median peak T-bil 0.8 mg/dL (range 0.3-15.7), peak ALT 235 U/L (range 16-1424); median time to DILI 25 days (range 7-155) and to recovery 29 days; hepatocellular 93.9%, cholestatic 2.5%, mixed 3.5%; 7 hospitalized; alternatives chosen included RAI, PTU, surgery, potassium iodide; 23 continued MMI after recovery.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 4,287 patients treated with propylthiouracil (PTU), 272 (6.3%) developed PTU-induced DILI, with overall incidence 1.43% in male and 6.51% in female patients (females significantly higher, p=0.015). Median PTU dose at DILI diagnosis was 300 mg/day (range 50-500 mg), median time to DILI was 33.5 days (significantly longer than MMI-DILI, p<0.001), and 98.9% had hepatocellular type injury; 7 patients required hospitalization. There was no correlation between PTU dose and severity of liver injury. Prevalence of DILI was significantly higher with PTU than MMI (6.3% vs 1.4%, p<0.001).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adults treated for Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism); marked female predominance with significantly higher incidence in females; no PTU dose-severity correlation observed.
raw_record.extra_details: 272/4,287 cases (6.3% overall); median age 33 years (range 17-66); median PTU daily dose 300 mg (range 50-500 mg); median peak T-bil 0.8 mg/dL (range 0.4-18.6), peak ALT 240 U/L (range 32-1329); median time to DILI 33.5 days (range 8-314), longer than MMI (p<0.001); hepatocellular 98.9%, mixed 0.7%, cholestatic 0.4%; 7 hospitalized; alternatives included RAI, MMI switch, surgery, potassium iodide; 12 continued PTU.

raw_record.support_text: In the German Diabetes and Dialysis Study (4D Study), 1255 adult hemodialysis patients with type 2 diabetes and LDL cholesterol of 80–190 mg/dl were randomized to 20 mg of atorvastatin or placebo. After 3 years the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint was similar between groups, and the authors report that atorvastatin was very well tolerated, with no liver or muscular side effects and no premature withdrawal due to adverse events. This is an explicit statement that no liver injury was observed with atorvastatin in this trial population.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adults with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and type 2 diabetes; atorvastatin 20 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: 4D Study: 1255 patients, 3 years follow-up; composite primary endpoint similar between atorvastatin (31.9%) and placebo (30.5%) (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.77–1.10; p=0.37); 42% LDL reduction at 4 months; authors explicitly report no liver side effects.

raw_record.support_text: Percutaneous liver biopsy specimens from patients receiving methotrexate for inflammatory bowel disease (30 Crohn's disease, two ulcerative colitis) were graded by a liver pathologist blinded to methotrexate dose according to Roenigk's criteria for methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity. Histologic findings ranged from mild steatosis (grade I) to severe fibrosis (IIIB) and cirrhosis (IV). Clinical interpretation was that grade I/II allows continued methotrexate, grade IIIA allows continuation with repeat biopsy after about 6 months, and grade IIIB/IV requires stopping methotrexate.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adults with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease in 30, ulcerative colitis in 2); one patient reported significant alcohol intake during methotrexate therapy; some had obesity (5) or diabetes (1) reflecting long-term steroid effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Methotrexate given at 5-50 mg weekly, taken orally, parenterally, or in combination; 20 of 32 patients underwent liver biopsy during therapy (biopsies not done in 12: 8 discontinued, 2 refused, 2 had contraindications). Biopsies graded per Roenigk criteria (I normal/mild steatosis; II moderate-severe steatosis/portal expansion/inflammation/necrosis; IIIA mild fibrosis; IIIB moderate-severe fibrosis; IV cirrhosis). No clinical evidence of hepatotoxicity was present in patients who discontinued.

raw_record.support_text: After chronic treatment with the anti-hypertensive drug dihydralazine, a large number of patients with hepatitis were reported. This drug-induced hepatitis affected more female than male patients, and most patients were slow acetylators. Development of hepatitis was usually delayed by a lag period of several months, resolved after discontinuation, and was reinduced upon rechallenge. Patients had liver microsomal (LM) antibodies recognizing a single band identified as cytochrome P450 1A2.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Affected more female than male patients; most affected patients were of the slow acetylator phenotype.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-hypertensive drug used chronically. LM autoantibodies did not stain kidney sections and recognized a single band in human liver microsomes identified as cytochrome P450 1A2; despite high sequence identity, P450 1A1 was not recognized.

raw_record.support_text: The current study monitored 74 alcoholic patients who received 25 mg of naltrexone (NTX) daily in the first week and then 50 mg daily for the remaining 12 weeks. After 12 weeks, hepatic enzyme alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels showed no elevation except in one subject, and the results strongly supported that NTX did not induce abnormalities in liver function tests or elevate liver enzymes; a statistically significant decrease in ALT and AST was observed. The paper concludes NTX is not hepatotoxic at the recommended daily dose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Alcoholic patients; ordinary recommended therapeutic dose (25-50 mg/day); open-label prospective monitoring rather than a randomized controlled design.
raw_record.extra_details: 74 patients; 25 mg/day week 1 then 50 mg/day for 12 weeks; no ALT/AST elevation except in one subject; statistically significant decrease in ALT and AST during the study; authors state NTX is not hepatotoxic at recommended daily dose and may benefit patients with elevated liver enzymes.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents 11 patients who developed jaundice at intervals of 1-14 days after halothane anesthesia, each with prior halothane anesthetics; laboratory findings included elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (SGOT up to >1,250-2,700), prolonged prothrombin time, hepatic encephalopathy grades up to 4, and granular immunofluorescence, consistent with immune-mediated halothane hepatitis (halothane-induced liver injury). Sera showed antibody-dependent microcytotoxicity against halothane-exposed hepatocytes and, in some cases, liver-kidney microsomal antibody or smooth-muscle antibody.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All 11 cases had one or more prior halothane anesthetics (time since last anesthetic 1 week to 20 years); hepatic encephalopathy (grades 1-4) was reported in several cases.
raw_record.extra_details: SGOT values up to >1,250 and 2,700; prothrombin time up to >120 sec; encephalopathy grades up to 4 in cases 5, 6, 8, 9, 10. Granular immunofluorescence on halothane-exposed hepatocytes and per cent cytotoxicity values (23-79%) consistent with an antibody-dependent immune mechanism. Operations included appendectomy, fracture repairs, ureterocelectomy, mastectomy, etc. Postoperative pyrexia noted in most cases.

raw_record.support_text: The laxative (phenolisatin) hepatitis, which runs under the mask of various liver and biliary diseases, is only reliably unmasked by the rechallenge test with phenolisatin. Glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) proved a particularly sensitive parameter, and transaminases (GOT, GPT) generally supported the proof by clear activity increases; bilirubin elevation was not obligatory. The paper reports 14 female patients with phenolisatin-induced liver diseases, whose histologic findings ranged from periportal liver fibrosis to advanced postnecrotic liver cirrhosis and scarring liver, with chronic-active hepatitis among the diagnostic forms.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All 14 reported cases were female; onset followed chronic long-term oral laxative use of 2 to 20 years; re-exposure (rechallenge) confirmed the diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge with 2 x 10 mg triacetyl-diphenolisatin on two consecutive days produced rises in GLDH (particularly sensitive), GOT and GPT; bilirubin elevation was not obligatory. Histologic spectrum included chronic-aggressive hepatitis (with transition to cirrhosis), acute recurrent and protracted hepatitis, chronic-persistent hepatitis, periportal liver fibrosis, postnecrotic scarring liver/cirrhosis, and one case of chronic-aggressive hepatitis with cholestasis (Fall 10, allegedly on oxyphenisatin-free laxatives). In six of ten examined cases low-titer antibodies against nuclei and smooth muscle were found by immunofluorescence; five of 14 were treated with immunosuppressives and/or glucocorticoids before the final diagnosis. Symptoms resembled acute/chronic liver or gallbladder disease. Before publication all 14 patients were fully investigated in hospital with entirely normal laboratory findings and histologically inactive stage. Reported hospitalizations and estimated total costs (e.g., 150,000 DM in Fall 1); some cases were reported as infectious disease or recognized as occupational disease, and some underwent cholecystectomy.

raw_record.support_text: All 15 patients with terbinafine hepatotoxicity enrolled as high causality cases in the Drug Induced Liver Injury Network were more than 40 years old (median 57 years), 53% female, with a median latency to onset of 38 days (range 24-114 days). At DILI onset 80% were jaundiced, median ALT was 448 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 333 U/L; one subject required liver transplantation for acute liver failure and several showed ongoing injury at 6 and 24 months. The conclusions state that terbinafine hepatotoxicity most commonly presents with a mixed or cholestatic liver injury profile with frequent residual chronic cholestatic injury, and confirmed a strong genetic association of HLA-A*33:01 with terbinafine DILI among Caucasians.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All 15 patients were older than 40 years (median 57); genetic susceptibility restricted to HLA-A*33:01 carriers in European ancestry participants (also one African American HLA-A*33:01 carrier and two East Asians with HLA-A*33:03).
raw_record.extra_details: Antifungal agent associated with rare instances of hepatotoxicity. Enrolled high-causality cases from the Drug Induced Liver Injury Network; median latency 38 days (range 24-114 days); 80% jaundiced at onset; median ALT 448 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 333 U/L. One subject required liver transplantation for acute liver failure; 7/13 (54%) remaining subjects had ongoing liver injury at 6 months and 4 had persistently abnormal liver biochemistries at month 24. Presenting profile most commonly mixed or cholestatic with frequent residual chronic cholestatic injury. High-resolution HLA genotyping confirmed 10/11 (91%) European ancestry participants carried the HLA-A*33:01, B*14:02, C*08:02 haplotype (carrier frequency 1.6% in European controls); one African American carried HLA-A*33:01 and two East Asian patients carried HLA-A*33:03. Molecular docking studies indicated terbinafine may interact with HLA-A*33:01 and A*33:03.

raw_record.support_text: In a preliminary study, 3 patients with cholestatic hepatitis due to ticlopidine were genotyped for CYP2C19 and evaluated for T cell reactivity and cytokine levels after therapy withdrawal. All patients carried 'slow metabolizer' CYP2C19 genotypes (CYP2C19*2/CYP2C19*2 and CYP2C19*2/CYP2C19*3), and T cell reactivity to ticlopidine was present in all patients during follow-up, with a positive correlation between decreasing ticlopidine-specific responses, decreasing Th1 cytokine serum concentrations, and clinical markers of liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All 3 reported patients were CYP2C19 'slow metabolizers' (CYP2C19*2/CYP2C19*2 and CYP2C19*2/CYP2C19*3); the authors conclude this genetic polymorphism is directly responsible for susceptibility to ticlopidine-induced liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 patients with cholestatic hepatitis due to ticlopidine. Genotyping for CYP2C19*1/*2/*3 by PCR-RFLP; T cell reactivity assessed by proliferation assay on days 0, 90, 150 and 210 after therapy withdrawal; serum INF-γ, IL-2, IL-4, IL-10, TNF-α, sFas, sFasL measured by ELISA. T cell reactivity present throughout follow-up; positive correlation between decline in ticlopidine-specific responses, decline in Th1 cytokines, and clinical markers of liver damage. Authors attribute pathogenesis to Th1-type immune reactivity and note a direct association between metabolic (CYP2C19) and immunological mechanisms in drug-induced cholestatic liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: Cases 3-7 describe chronic alcohol consumers who took therapeutic-to-high therapeutic oral doses of acetaminophen (ranging from 4 g/day up to about 6.5 g/day for 2-5 days) and developed severe acute hepatotoxicity, with marked transaminase elevations, hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy. Cases 5 and 7 died (case 5 from progressive coagulopathy, ARDS, and seizures on hospital day 8; case 7 with acute renal failure, seizures, and ARDS). The paper attributes the liver injury to acetaminophen taken concurrently with alcohol in these alcoholics.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All affected patients were chronic heavy alcohol consumers (approximately 12-18 beers/day, 0.5-2 pints of alcohol/day) who took acetaminophen at therapeutic-to-high-therapeutic doses concurrently with alcohol; one case (case 7) was confounded by confirmed rhinocerebral mucormycosis and sepsis.
raw_record.extra_details: Individual cases: case 3 (47-year-old man, 5-6 g/day acetaminophen for 4 days; AST 4472 U/L, ALT 3984 U/L); case 4 (49-year-old man, 20 x 325 mg tablets/day = 6.5 g/day for 5 days, with recurrent pancreatitis; AST 21660 U/L); case 5 (37-year-old woman, 6 g/day for 2 days; died day 8 with worsening coagulopathy, variceal bleeding, ARDS); case 6 (37-year-old man, 4 g acetaminophen plus 0.75 L whiskey/day for 3 days, from acetaminophen/codeine elixir); case 7 (40-year-old man with type II diabetes, Darvocet-N 100 [propoxyphene napsylate + acetaminophen] plus Tylenol, later died; acetaminophen level <10 ug/mL on transfer; underlying mucormycosis). Clinical findings included tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, and prolonged PT; ultrasound showed no biliary disease. Alcohol is a co-exposure and likely susceptibility factor; the acetaminophen component is attributed as the injuring agent.

raw_record.support_text: Six women were diagnosed with halothane-induced hepatitis based on criteria of no pre-existing liver disease, hepatitis onset within two weeks of halothane exposure, and no alternative explanations. All had jaundice and high transaminase levels, all were female, and most were obese; the interval between anesthesia and hepatitis was two days in the one previously exposed patient and six to ten days in the others. Three patients died with autopsy findings consistent with post-halothane hepatitis, and no other causes such as prior hepatotoxin exposure, shock, or hepatitis B infection were found.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All affected patients were women, markedly obese or at upper limits of normal weight, and from closely related families of common ethnic origin; only the patient with prior halothane exposure had a short (two-day) latency.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane anesthesia exposure; all six cases satisfied the diagnostic criteria for hepatitis induced by halothane. Clinical features included jaundice, high transaminase levels, fever rising to 40°C (104°F) in five of six, peripheral eosinophil counts above 500/mm3 in three, and two-to-ten day interval from anesthesia to hepatitis. Three patients died; autopsy findings were consistent with post-halothane hepatitis, and alternative causes (prior hepatotoxin exposure, shock, hepatitis B virus) were excluded. Survivors remained healthy with no recurrence. Anti-HBs testing was performed on three surviving patients; a four-to-five-generation survey of 154 blood relatives revealed no additional cases of postoperative hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: Four patients with metastatic colon cancer receiving oxaliplatin, 5-fluorouracil and elvorin developed a progressive increase in gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and alkaline phosphatase despite tumour regression. Liver biopsies showed sinusoidal dilatation in all cases, with perisinusoidal fibrosis and centrilobular vein lesions in 3, peliosis in 1 (a patient receiving oxaliplatin by intraarterial hepatic route), and nodular regenerative hyperplasia in 1. The patient with peliosis developed ascites and died from hepatic failure despite drug withdrawal. The patient with nodular regenerative hyperplasia developed jaundice, ascites and severe infection after a right hepatectomy. In the three surviving patients liver function tests improved after oxaliplatin withdrawal, and in one deteriorated again after reintroduction of the drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All four patients received combination chemotherapy with oxaliplatin together with 5-fluorouracil and elvorin (leucovorin); one patient received oxaliplatin by intraarterial hepatic route. All patients had metastatic colon cancer.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as a case series of 4 cases described as 'oxaliplatin-imputable sinusoidal lesions'. Histology: sinusoidal dilatation (all), perisinusoidal fibrosis and centrilobular vein lesions (3), peliosis (1), nodular regenerative hyperplasia (1). Laboratory hallmark was elevated gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and alkaline phosphatase. One patient died from hepatic failure with ascites; one developed jaundice, ascites and severe infection following right hepatectomy. Dechallenge improved liver tests in all three survivors; rechallenge with oxaliplatin led to deterioration in one. Paper concludes the prevalence of oxaliplatin-induced liver sinusoidal lesions is probably underestimated and recommends GGT and ALP monitoring, especially in adjuvant therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluated predictors of time to lapatinib-induced hepatotoxicity in a retrospective cohort. Lapatinib was the treatment under study, and hepatotoxicity was defined as an outcome attributable to lapatinib. Concomitant use of H2 blockers significantly increased the hazard of time to lapatinib-induced hepatotoxicity (adjusted HR 1.855, 95% CI 1.190–2.892), and use of CYP3A4 inducers significantly increased the incidence of lapatinib-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All participants were female patients with metastatic breast cancer, so sex differences could not be assessed; retrospective single-center design.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort study of lapatinib-treated patients. H2 blocker use was an independent predictor of time to hepatotoxicity (unadjusted and adjusted HR 1.855, 95% CI 1.190–2.892 in Model I; HR 1.842, 95% CI 1.181–2.872 in Model II), while PPI use appeared protective (unadjusted HR 0.602, 95% CI 0.394–0.919; age, height, and BSA were not significant predictors). CYP3A4 inducers significantly increased the incidence of hepatotoxicity, attributed mechanistically to increased reactive-metabolite formation. CYP3A4 inhibitors were not a significant factor. Concomitant H2 blockers and CYP3A4 inducers were concluded to be important factors increasing hepatotoxicity incidence.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of patients who had all undergone previous anaesthesia, repeat exposure to halothane was associated with liver damage (halothane-associated hepatitis). The outcome and severity of liver damage showed no significant correlation with the number of previous anaesthetics or the interval between the final two anaesthetics; intervals ranged up to 12 yr in those who developed encephalopathy and up to 11 yr in those without, indicating no 'safe interval' beyond which repeat halothane exposure will not result in liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All patients had undergone previous (repeat) halothane anaesthesia; findings concern repeat exposure rather than single-agent first exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of presumed halothane-associated hepatitis cases in the U.K.; patients predominantly middle aged and female. Encephalopathy (hepatic) occurred in a subset, indicating severe liver injury, and the authors note a potentially fatal complication might have been avoided if prior adverse reactions had been known. About one-third of patients had a documented previous adverse reaction following halothane. No safe interval exists between repeat halothane exposures for producing liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: Losartan was reported as the cause of hepatic toxicity with liver fibrosis and necrosis in humans. Toxic reactions occurred from 6 weeks to 5 months after starting the drug (mostly at 50 mg/day), all in patients over 45 years of age. Plasma transaminases increased 6-60 times the upper limit of normal and total bilirubin ranged from 1.3 to 9.6 mg/dL, and all cases improved after drug withdrawal (Tabak et al., 2002).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All reported cases occurred in patients over 45 years of age.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency 6 weeks to 5 months after starting the drug; dose mostly 50 mg/day; transaminases increased 6-60 times ULN; total bilirubin 1.3-9.6 mg/dL; liver fibrosis and necrosis as the attributed injury; all cases improved after drug withdrawal; source Tabak et al. 2002. The paragraph also notes the U.S. FDA is considering labeling changes for losartan (and valsartan), though a class hepatotoxicity warning for all angiotensin II inhibitors is not warranted by current data.

raw_record.support_text: It seems highly probable that in the reported patient, lamotrigine was the cause of a mixed liver injury, based on a close temporal relationship between first intake and onset of symptoms, rapid improvement of liver enzymes after lamotrigine withdrawal, and exclusion of alcohol, viral hepatitis, autoimmunity, and extrahepatic bile duct obstruction. Valproic acid was considered an unlikely cause because the patient had taken it for years without side effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All three cases, including the index patient, occurred when lamotrigine was added to chronic valproic acid (valproate) administration; valproate blocks lamotrigine elimination and may raise lamotrigine levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: maculopapular rash, hyperthermia, headaches, diplopia, moderate creatinine kinase increase, laboratory signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Liver histology showed mild portal inflammation with scant eosinophils and hepatocyte clarification/microvesicular fatty infiltration; AST higher than ALT, suggestive of rhabdomyolysis; suggested immunoallergic rather than direct toxic mechanism. Two prior reported cases: a 22-year-old woman developed fulminant hepatic failure with acute hepatic necrosis three weeks after starting lamotrigine (liver function improved after withdrawal but she died of a massive pulmonary embolism two months later), and an 8-year-old boy developed acute cytolytic hepatitis three weeks after introduction with prompt enzyme decrease and uneventful recovery on withdrawal. Recommended maintenance dose 1-5 mg/kg/day with valproate, 5-15 mg/kg/day without; all three cases followed dose adaptation. Rechallenge should be avoided.

raw_record.support_text: Tacrine treatment in an eight week crossover trial for Alzheimer's disease was associated with raised liver enzyme activities: six patients dropped out because of high liver enzyme activities and two others had raised activities at the end of the study. The patient with the highest liver enzyme activities (a 76 year old woman) was admitted to an intensive care unit; liver biopsy showed extensive centrilobular necrosis without steatosis, consistent with acute cytolytic hepatitis. In all patients with hepatitis, liver enzyme values returned to normal three to four weeks after withdrawal of tacrine and remained normal six to 12 months later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Alzheimer's disease patients; all patients also received oral lecithin during the trial (combined tacrine and lecithin treatment).
raw_record.extra_details: Crossover study of tacrine (maximum 125 mg daily) in 60 Alzheimer's disease patients; 8 of 60 had raised liver enzyme activities (tolerance section). One 76-year-old woman with highest liver enzyme activities required ICU admission; biopsy showed extensive centrilobular necrosis without steatosis. Dechallenge: liver enzyme values returned to normal 3-4 weeks after tacrine withdrawal and remained normal 6-12 months later. In the follow-up study, additional patients were withdrawn from tacrine treatment because of hepatitis. No steatosis on biopsy; plasma tacrine concentrations ranged 49-1140 mmol/l.

raw_record.support_text: In univariate logistic regression and Fisher's exact tests in the Caucasian PAH cohort, CYP2C9*2 was the only polymorphism significantly associated with occurrence of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) in patients treated with bosentan (odds ratio 95% CI = 2.29–∞; P = 0.003), while a SNP in SLCO1B1 (rs11045819) showed only a trend for association with bosentan-induced liver injury. This documents DILI events attributed to therapeutic bosentan exposure in PAH patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Analysis was restricted to the 56 Caucasian patients from a 92-patient, predominantly female (71%) PAH cohort; more than half (57.1%) were coadministered an OATP1B1 inhibitor (most commonly sildenafil).
raw_record.extra_details: Larger study cohort of 92 ethnically diverse PAH patients (61% Caucasian). CYP2C9*2 (rs1799853) was also significantly associated with increases in ALT (beta=2.16, P=0.024) and AST (beta=1.92, P=0.016) in multivariate regression adjusted for BMI; SLCO1B1 rs11045819 showed only a trend for DILI. Bosentan is metabolized to Ro 48-5033 (hydroxylation) and Ro 47-8634 (O-demethylation), further hydroxylated to Ro 64-1056; in vitro CYP2C9 formed only Ro 48-5033. The study investigated reduced-function SNPs in CYP2C9, CYP3A4, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, BSEP, and MRP2 as potential biomarkers for stratifying PAH treatment. In vitro microsome and recombinant-enzyme findings are supporting preclinical data.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that Cases 1 and 2 demonstrate good evidence of liver damage due to rifampicin. In Patient 1 (a 30-year-old woman treated for tuberculous peritonitis with streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampicin and prednisolone), jaundice developed after 2 weeks of therapy with bilirubin 7.0 mg/100 ml and A.S.T. 240 I.U./litre; a second biopsy showed hepatitis with cholestasis closely resembling viral hepatitis, and liver-function tests returned to normal within a week after rifampicin was stopped. In Patient 2, a second biopsy showed widespread liver-cell swelling, acidophilic bodies, increased mitoses and mild fatty change with raised serum bilirubin and A.S.T.; rifampicin was resumed uneventfully later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Anti-tuberculosis combination therapy with co-administered streptomycin, isoniazid, prednisolone, ethambutol and pyridoxine.

raw_record.support_text: The drug-induced liver disease (DILD) diagnosis for patients was based on International Consensus Meeting criteria: alanine aminotransferase >2 times ULN, conjugated bilirubin >2 times ULN, or a combined increase of ASAT, alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin with one >2 times ULN; identification of phenprocoumon with a temporal relationship to elevated liver enzymes; and exclusion of other causes of liver or biliary-tract disease and excessive alcohol use.

raw_record.extra_details: 30 phenprocoumon-induced liver injury cases. Liver injury pattern classified per International Consensus Criteria as hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed. In the two biopsied patients, lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis was described; no evidence of autoimmune hepatitis (no relevant autoantibodies, normal IgG). Liver enzymes and clinical symptoms normalized after withdrawal (dechallenge). In reexposed patients injury latency was significantly shorter (mean 91 days, median 90, range 3-180 days) than in first-exposure patients (mean 500, median 150, range 1-3700 days; p<0.05).

raw_record.support_text: A prospective study revealed that a single heterozygous variant in POLG (p.Gln1236His) was strongly associated with VPA-induced hepatotoxicity (odds ratio 23.6, p=5.1×10^-7), attributed to non-apoptotic cell death not mediated through mtDNA defect or impairment of fatty acid oxidation. Additional iPSC-derived hepatocyte work with the POLG p.Ala467Thr variant showed that VPA led to increased apoptosis via a mitochondrial permeability-transition pore-opening pathway, with carnitine or N-acetylcysteine supplementation seeming to rescue VPA-induced toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Association observed in the context of POLG-related mitochondrial disease; strong association reported specifically for carriers of a heterozygous POLG p.Gln1236His variant.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective study reported an odds ratio of 23.6 (p=5.1x10^-7) for the POLG p.Gln1236His variant with VPA-induced hepatotoxicity; toxicity was described as non-apoptotic cell death not mediated through mtDNA defect or impairment of fatty acid oxidation. Supporting iPSC-derived hepatocyte data (POLG p.Ala467Thr) indicated VPA increased apoptosis via a mitochondrial permeability-transition pore-opening pathway; carnitine or N-acetylcysteine appeared to rescue VPA-induced toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients on valproic acid (Divalproex) therapy developed acute hepatic dysfunction; patient 1 presented with hepatic failure and concurrent rhabdomyolysis leading to acute renal failure, while abdominal CT on patient 2 suggested hepatosteatosis. Their ARDS was deemed secondary to community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), which is considered a predisposing factor for hepatic dysfunction by VPA, and VPA therapy was continued in both patients because the treating team did not realize it could contribute to the hepatic failure and rhabdomyolysis. Patient 1's serum VPA level of 38 µg/mL was subtherapeutic with home Divalproex ER 500 mg oral twice daily. The calculated Naranjo score for both patients was 5, indicating probable adverse drug events.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe admitting two patients with severe hepatotoxicity on sitaxentan sodium, an endothelin receptor antagonist approved for pulmonary arterial hypertension, to their Pulmonary Hypertension Unit. Both patients developed severe acute drug-induced liver injury attributed to sitaxentan that resolved following drug discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Both patients had severe pulmonary arterial hypertension treated with sitaxentan 100 mg once daily; patient 2 was also concurrently taking aspirin, doxazosin XL, valsartan/hydrochlorothiazide, and frusemide.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1 (47-yr male, PAH with congenital heart disease) developed nausea, vomiting, anorexia and icterus ~4 months after starting 100 mg q.d.; LFTs worsened after discontinuation; INR peaked at 1.6 on vitamin K; transjugular biopsy consistent with severe acute drug-induced liver injury showing ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes, bile stasis and eosinophilic infiltration; no other hepatotoxic medications; recovered on ursodeoxycholic acid. Patient 2 (70-yr female, idiopathic PAH) had AST and ALT peak at 1,198 and 1,040 IU, bilirubin peak 426 umol/L, INR 1.6 off anticoagulation ~3 months after starting; biopsy showed moderate portal and parenchymal lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered eosinophils, extensive active hepatocyte injury and confluent necrosis; recovered from acute liver injury then died of respiratory failure from lobar pneumonia. Both had positive parietal cell antibodies; viral/autoimmune serologies otherwise negative. Authors note initial 300 mg sitaxentan studies showed potential for liver injury following the death of one patient, whereas a follow-up 100 mg study caused no significant liver enzyme elevation; they attribute delayed injury and prolonged recovery to nonlinear-pharmacokinetics-related drug accumulation.

The authors note that, based on pharmacogenetic investigations of lapatinib-associated hepatotoxicity and previously reported work implicating HLA-mediated mechanisms in drug-induced liver injury, carriage of specific HLA alleles (HLA-DQA*02:01/DRB1*07:01) is considered a strong and possibly diagnostic indicator of DILI caused by specific drugs; a breast cancer patient carrying at least one copy of these alleles is more susceptible to lapatinib-associated liver injury.

All patients exhibited CTCAE grade 3 or 4 hepatitis, with DILI network severity mild in 18, moderate in 3, and severe in 1 patient, with no hepatitis-related deaths. raw_record.extra_details: 19 of 22 total cases of CDK4/6 inhibitor-induced liver injury involved ribociclib. All patients had CTCAE grade 3-4 hepatitis; DILI network severity mild (18), moderate (3), severe (1); no hepatitis-related deaths. Hepatitis improvement was significantly slower in corticosteroid-treated patients (106.62 +/- 54.75 vs 49.36 +/- 40.74 days, p=0.009). Liver biopsies showed acute centrilobular hepatitis with foci of necrosis and lymphocytic infiltrate.

raw_record.support_text: In a breast-cancer patient case, the temporal evidence was judged to favour anastrozole as the most probable cause of the observed liver injury. The authors note that over the past 6 years more than 30,000 breast-cancer patients treated with third-generation aromatase inhibitors showed a good liver safety profile and no similar cases were found in the WHO database, indicating an uncommon, post-marketing-surveillance-detected drug-related event.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Breast-cancer patient on anastrozole; co-administration of valsartan was considered but an interaction was deemed unlikely; genetic polymorphism of cytochromes (CYP3A4/CYP2C9) was hypothesized as a susceptibility factor.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic biopsy showed extensive hepatocellular necrosis in zone 3 of the liver acinus, with cholestasis and middle macrovesicular steatosis also evident, and absence of inflammatory changes; injury was judged compatible with metabolically mediated hepatocellular liver injury. Anastrozole is extensively metabolised by N-dealkylation, hydroxylation, and glucuronidation; it (but not its metabolites) inhibits P450 1A2, 2C8/9, and 3A4. A later separate case of anastrozole-related hepatitis (without documented histology) was reported after submission. No similar cases were found in the WHO database; more than 30,000 aromatase-inhibitor-treated patients showed a good liver safety profile.

raw_record.support_text: In this pharmacokinetic study of CB 3717 in cancer patients, the CB 3717 peak plasma levels were about three times greater than in the earlier study (Alison et al.) because similar doses were given over shorter infusions, yet the incidence of hepatic toxicity was similar in both studies, confirming a lack of correlation between maximal plasma concentrations of CB 3717 and the drug-related hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cancer patients receiving CB 3717 as an investigational thymidylate synthase inhibitor antimetabolite.
raw_record.extra_details: CB 3717 is a thymidylate synthase inhibitor (PDDF-class antimetabolite). An earlier study (Alison et al.) reported a weak correlation between CB 3717 peak plasma levels and GPT peak levels when the drug was given as a 1 h infusion; the authors failed to confirm this correlation. Peak plasma levels here were about three times greater than the prior study because similar doses were given over shorter (bolus) infusions, while the incidence of hepatic toxicity was similar in both studies. The paper notes hepatic toxicity is not correlated with maximal plasma concentration and suggests the mechanism of hepatic (and renal) toxicity differs from that underlying antitumoral activity, arguing that non-hepatotoxic analogs should be developable.

Histology showed diffuse inflammation without lymphoid follicles, distinguishing it from viral acute hepatitis. Imatinib is an anticancer agent for CML and GIST.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first association of flutamide with serious hepatotoxicity in a woman using the drug for the treatment of hirsutism, noting hepatotoxicity is an infrequent complication of treatment with the oral antiandrogen flutamide and citing prior reports in 19 patients with benign and malignant prostatic diseases. They conclude that the features of this case are quite conclusive and that the potential for a life-threatening adverse effect should dissuade physicians from using the drug for a benign condition such as hirsutism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case in a 20-year-old woman using flutamide for off-label treatment of hirsutism, while concurrently taking an oral contraceptive pill (Demulen-30) and after prior use of spironolactone and cyproterone.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg orally twice daily started in late January; presented in March with 3 days of severe pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools, deeply jaundiced. Labs: bilirubin 263 umol/L (normal 3-20), INR 1.9, alkaline phosphatase 180 IU/L (normal 40-130), ALT 1481 IU/L (normal 5-55); bilirubin peaked at 480 umol/L. Viral serology and history excluded other causes; ultrasound normal with no biliary dilation. Flutamide discontinued; liver enzymes returned to normal within 6 weeks and bilirubin by early June. Liver biopsy near the height of illness showed changes typical of drug toxicity: zonal hepatic necrosis with cholestasis and ballooning degeneration of surviving zone 1 hepatocytes. AUthor states this is the 'first association' and describes the features as 'quite conclusive'; prior reports by Wysowski described 19 patients treated for benign and malignant prostatic diseases.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute hepatitis probably caused by terfenadine, an H1-receptor antagonist used as an antiallergic agent. A 43-year-old woman taking terfenadine 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria developed asthenia and jaundice; her serum bilirubin was 160 µmol/L, ALT 920 U, and alkaline phosphatase 188 U, with HBsAg absent and normal liver/biliary ultrasonography. Jaundice resolved after the drug was stopped. After she continued terfenadine intermittently, jaundice recurred a second time (bilirubin 70 µmol/L, ALT 512 U, alkaline phosphatase 484 U), with hepatitis A, B, and infectious mononucleosis serologies negative; jaundice and liver tests again normalized in October 1984.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case in a woman treated for recurrent urticaria; jaundice recurred after rechallenge-like continued intermittent use and resolved on dechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 60 mg/d. Onset with asthenia and jaundice; bilirubin 160 µmol/L, ALT 920 U (normal 5-40 U), alkaline phosphatase 188 U (normal 50-100 U), 3% eosinophils, HBsAg absent, normal hepatic/biliary ultrasonography. Second episode after intermittent continuation: bilirubin 70 µmol/L, ALT 512 U, alkaline phosphatase 484 U; HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, IgM anti-HAV absent, mononucleosis negative. Recovery documented in October 1984.

raw_record.support_text: A patient developed chronic active hepatitis and ascites attributed to nitrofurantoin; the drug was stopped, prednisolone was started for the severity of the liver damage, and liver function tests returned to normal within 4 weeks with resolution of ascites and oedema. The report notes this was a male patient, whereas all 24 previously reported cases of nitrofurantoin-related chronic active hepatitis had been in women, with negative hepatitis B surface antigen, raised immunoglobulins, and antinuclear factor suggesting the lupoid form.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case is a male patient, unlike all previously reported cases which were in women; authors suggest females are not preferentially susceptible given the drug is more commonly used by women.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic active hepatitis related to nitrofurantoin first reported in 1975; 24 cases now reported, all with negative hepatitis B surface antigen and raised immunoglobulins and antinuclear factor ('lupoid' form). In this case ascites and oedema were present with severe liver damage; nitrofurantoin was stopped and prednisolone given, with recovery of liver function in 4 weeks and falling antinuclear factor and smooth-muscle antibody titers. Holmberg's 10-year Swedish adverse-reaction analysis found an 86% female preponderance of nitrofurantoin reactions.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of acute reversible liver injury with the use of trazodone in a 38-year-old woman, who had taken trazodone for about 18 months while on corticosteroids. The diagnosis of trazodone-induced liver injury was confirmed by an inadvertent rechallenge with trazodone (taken for 2 days while off all other medications), after which bilirubin and transaminases rose again, and the patient improved upon stopping. The authors describe this as a well documented instance of trazodone-induced liver injury.

raw_record.extra_details: 38-yr-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presented with itching, nausea, vomiting and jaundice requiring hospitalization. Peak labs: bilirubin 11.0 mg/dl (conjugated 7.1), AST 625 U/L, ALT 1092 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 206 U/L, albumin 3.5 g/dl. Biopsy showed zone 3 feathery degeneration and ballooning, modest lymphocytic inflammation, and cholestasis (no fat, fibrosis, or iron). On rechallenge (2 consecutive days of trazodone), bilirubin rose to 10.3 mg/dl, AST 824 U/L, ALT 1476 U/L; tests normalized ~14 days after last dose. Serologies for hepatitis A/B/C negative. One prior report of five cases of trazodone hepatotoxicity exists (one chronic; others acute cellular and cholestatic injury).

raw_record.extra_details: Presenting illness was valproate-associated hepatic encephalopathy with hyperammonaemia (serum ammonia rising from 43 to 215 umol/l, normal <33 umol/l) and low carnitine (free 7.6, total 15.4 umol/l) despite normal routine liver function tests; delirium and asterixis resolved within three days after valproate reduction (3 g to 2.75 g/day) and oral L-carnitine 330 mg four times daily. raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 44-year-old female developed anorexia, nausea, and jaundice after six months of isoniazid (INH) monotherapy for latent tuberculosis. Other causes of liver injury were ruled out, and liver biopsy showed submassive necrosis, hepatocellular dropout, and lobular inflammation with no fibrosis; she also had acute portal hypertension. She was diagnosed with drug-induced liver injury (DILI), treated with NAC, ursodiol, and vitamin K, and recovered without liver transplantation. The paper notes severe hepatitis occurs in up to 1% of INH patients and supports monitoring of liver tests during INH therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case of a 44-year-old female also taking pantoprazole for gastroesophageal reflux disease; latent TB prophylaxis monotherapy setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Six months of INH monotherapy for latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis before symptom onset (~2 weeks of anorexia, right-sided abdominal pain, jaundice). Labs on day 1: ALT 651 U/L, AST 1134 U/L, ALP 186 U/L, total bilirubin 14.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.7 mg/dL, INR 1.75, MELD-Na 24; subacute liver failure with concurrent acute portal hypertension; biopsy showed submassive necrosis, hepatocellular dropout, lobular inflammation, no fibrosis; treated with N-acetyl cysteine, ursodiol, and vitamin K; recovered without liver transplant. Paper also cites up to 20% asymptomatic aminotransferase increases and severe hepatitis in up to 1% of INH patients.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed characteristic features of the anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) with multisystem organ dysfunction, including liver and kidney dysfunction, after treatment with phenytoin. The diagnosis of AHS was essentially established by the characteristic clinical picture together with skin biopsy findings, eosinophilia, absence of a septic focus, negative culture and serology results, and response to corticosteroid therapy, excluding infection and connective tissue disease as causes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) with multisystem organ dysfunction, including liver and renal dysfunction; single adult patient.
raw_record.extra_details: AHS case report. Liver tests initially: AST 532 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 392 IU/L, total bilirubin 3.3 mg/dl (56 µmol/L), alkaline phosphatase 321 IU/L; by third hospital day AST rose to 2710 IU/L and total bilirubin to 5.0 mg/dl (85 µmol/L). Myoglobinuria, creatine kinase 4522 IU/L (100% MM); platelet count fell to 18 x 10^3/mm³. Serology negative for hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, CMV, EBV; negative blood/urine/skin lesion cultures. Skin biopsy showed mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with upper dermal edema consistent with a drug reaction. Liver and renal function improved after discontinuing antibiotics/inotropes and starting high-dose methylprednisolone (40 mg IV every 4 h); patient discharged 4 weeks after admission without reported liver transplantation or death.

raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old male presented with pruritus, rash, nausea, and diarrhea after taking ciprofloxacin (4 days prior) for a recent urinary tract infection, and was found to have acute renal failure and hepatic dysfunction. Labs showed total bilirubin 2.9, alkaline phosphatase 351, AST 832, ALT 959, with LFTs peaking on hospital day 3 (bilirubin 3.6, AP 493, AST 1059, ALT 1231) and INR 2.04. After gastrointestinal workup, viral (EBV, CMV, HIV, Hepatitis A-C) and autoimmune (SMA, ANA) etiologies were negative, and the patient was diagnosed with ciprofloxacin-induced liver injury (CILI). Given deteriorating hepatic failure he was treated with N-acetylcysteine and steroids with rapid improvement in hepatic and renal function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case patient had dilated cardiomyopathy, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, obesity, concurrent acute renal failure, and was taking multiple co-medications (spironolactone, allopurinol last dose 4 weeks earlier, lisinopril, furosemide, metolazone); DRESS due to allopurinol was considered in the differential but excluded because the patient met only 2 of 3 RegiSCAR and 2 of 5 DIHS criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Ciprofloxacin taken for urinary tract infection, exposure 4 days before presentation. R-ratio of 5.83 suggested hepatocellular injury. Symptoms included pruritus, rash, nausea, diarrhea; LFTs peaked on hospital day 3 (bilirubin 3.6, AP 493, AST 1059, ALT 1231), INR 2.04. Mechanism thought to be a hypersensitivity response to fluoroquinolones; steroid and N-acetylcysteine therapy led to rapid improvement (AP 97, AST 298, ALT 341, INR 1.2, Cr 1.5). Discussion states CILI carried a 15% mortality rate in one study, consistent with 10-80% mortality for DILI with acute liver failure. CT showed hepatic steatosis, normal triglycerides/ceruloplasmin/iron saturation.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 30 patients with clometacin hepatitis, all treated with clometacin for various rheumatic conditions, 29 were females aged 32-84 years. Daily dose was 150-750 mg (mean 396 mg) with regular intake in 66% of cases; onset of hepatitis followed drug intake by 10 to 2,190 days. The study retained 7 'definite' rechallenge-positive and 23 'probable' cases of clometacin-induced chronic active hepatitis (CIH) after excluding other causes and applying the imputability method of Dangoumau.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case series of 29 females and 1 male treated for rheumatic conditions; indication and predominant sex noted descriptively, not a strict susceptibility restriction.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 patients with clometacin hepatitis; 7 'definite' rechallenge-positive and 23 'probable' cases; 26 'possible'/'doubtful' cases eliminated. Daily dose 150-750 mg (mean 396 mg), one patient (case 25) up to 2,000 mg/day; onset 10-2,190 days (median 230); prodromal symptoms (asthenia 64%, fever >38°C 36%, nausea/vomiting/anorexia 64%). Biologically mainly cytolytic hepatitis with mild cholestasis; bilirubin 20-509 µmol/l; ASAT 2-57xN, ALAT 3-100xN; prothrombin time <30% in 4 cases, all fatal of hepatic failure (cases 15, 19, 25, 29). Autoantibodies detected (anti-smooth muscle, anti-nucleus, anti-actin) in most sera; blood eosinophilia in 13%. Other causes (hepatitis A/B, CMV, HSV, EBV, alcoholism, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson's disease) excluded.
