raw_record.support_text: Tables 6, 7, and 8 list the clinical features demonstrated by 10 patients with halothane hepatitis in both their initial and their second, or challenging (rechallenge) episodes. The paper cautions that these rechallenged patients constitute a highly selected and biased group and cannot be assumed to represent a random sample of halothane hepatitis. In challenged patients, jaundice was a feature of all but one initial episode but of only half of the second episodes, and features thought to indicate a hypersensitivity reaction (myalgia, arthralgia, skin rash, nasal congestion, cough, allergic history) were noted in only one-third or less of both groups.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases are 10 deliberately rechallenged patients (highly selected and biased sample), including 2 anesthesiologists with chronic occupational exposure to low halothane concentrations who took 3.5 months and 1 year to become sensitized.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge (second/exposure) episodes confirm halothane hepatitis. Initial-episode features: jaundice in 9 of 10, hepatic enlargement 3, hepatic tenderness 3, myalgia 2, skin rash 1, nasal congestion 1, cough 1, allergic history 3; second episodes: jaundice 5, hepatic enlargement 2, hepatic tenderness 3, myalgia 2, nasal congestion 1, cough 1, allergic history 3. Onset of illness ranged from several hours to 1 year after halothane exposure; single anesthetic exposures had onset of several hours to 10 days. Fever over 100 F in 6 patients, chills in 2, eosinophilia in 3, one case with leukocytosis (23,300/mm3), one with leukopenia (1,750/mm3); maximum bilirubin 33.5 mg/100 ml, alkaline phosphatase 57 Bodansky units, SGPT 1,590 units; elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and SGOT in nearly every measured instance. Dark urine appeared about 1 week after nonspecific illness onset in the 2 anesthesiologists.

raw_record.support_text: In 14 patients with isoniazid-associated hepatitis, clinical signs and symptoms of hepatitis had developed in 12 of them, and all had increased serum SGOT (AST) concentrations ranging from 140 to 1,640 IU. Patients were taking daily doses of 300 mg of isoniazid (INH) for chemoprophylaxis, denied other hepatotoxic drugs or hepatitis exposure, and had no hepatitis-associated antigen. Most discontinued INH within a few days of symptom onset.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases occurred during chemoprophylaxis with daily 300 mg oral isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid introduced in 1952 for tuberculosis treatment/chemoprophylaxis; hepatic damage generally reported, usually after excessive dosages. Immunologic hypersensitivity was suggested as pathogenesis based on occasional fever, rash, urticaria, and rarely eosinophilia. In the 14 study patients, in vitro lymphocyte transformation to INH showed A/C ratios <2 (no sensitization), failing to support an immunologic basis. All patients lacked hepatitis-associated antigen (cross immunoelectrophoresis, hemagglutination, complement fixation), no injection/narcotic/transfusion history.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report 3 cases of allopurinol-induced hypersensitivity syndromes admitted with fever, generalized exanthematous rash, eosinophilia and liver dysfunction shortly after starting allopurinol for non-symptomatic hyperuricemia. Case 2 (34-year-old female) presented with severe liver dysfunction and recovered only after 9 weeks of corticosteroid therapy; case 3 (66-year-old male) developed severe liver dysfunction and renal failure and ultimately died with liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases occurred in patients treated for non-symptomatic asymptomatic hyperuricemia; patients with liver dysfunction and renal impairment appear at greater risk for allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) is described as an infrequent but potentially lethal adverse reaction of allopurinol therapy, with features resembling EBV infection including fever, exanthematous rash, leukocytosis, eosinophilia, impaired renal function, hepatocellular injury, and severe reactions such as toxic epidermal necrolysis and acute vasculitis. Reactions are considered cell-mediated immunity directed toward allopurinol and, more importantly, to its oxypurinol metabolite, which has a markedly longer half-life. One fatal case also complicated by iatrogenic diabetes, oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis, and severe ethmoidal rhinomucormycosis, with death due to liver failure from amphotericin B therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Bupropion is approved for mood disorders and smoking cessation. It was reported that acute cholestatic hepatitis was induced by bupropion when a 49-year-old female took it to stop smoking; after 20 days she presented a dramatic increase in direct bilirubin (up to 28 mg/dl) and transaminases (up to 68-fold normal). In a case of a 55-year-old man with jaundice and severe hepatic injury about 6 months after starting bupropion for smoking termination, laboratory evaluations confirmed a mixed hepatocellular injury and cholestasis picture, and the patient eventually died. Other controversial studies on bupropion for smoking cessation reported no adverse hepatic events.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases were adults using bupropion for smoking cessation (therapeutic use).
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 49-year-old female, acute cholestatic hepatitis after 20 days, direct bilirubin up to 28 mg/dl, transaminases up to 68-fold normal. Case 2: 55-year-old man, jaundice and severe hepatic injury about 6 months after start, mixed hepatocellular injury and cholestasis, eventually died. Other 7- and 9-week smoking-cessation studies reported no adverse hepatic events.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a series of four cases of biopsy-proven cholestatic hepatitis following treatment with flucloxacillin, presenting 17 to 28 days after commencing the drug. Liver biopsies showed centrilobular canalicular cholestasis with portal and lobular inflammation and eosinophil infiltration, consistent with drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Flucloxacillin was attributed as the cause of the liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases were in elderly patients aged 62-81 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Four cases (1M, 3F) with severe delayed cholestatic hepatitis; jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale faeces appeared 17-28 days after commencing flucloxacillin and 7-14 days after cessation before presentation. Marked elevations of serum bilirubin, ALP, GGT and AST in all patients; extrahepatic biliary obstruction excluded by ERCP in three and ultrasound/CT in one; negative serology for hepatitis A/B, CMV, ANA, AMA. Biopsy showed centrilobular canalicular cholestasis, hepatocyte swelling, mild lobular inflammation, sinusoidal eosinophil infiltration, portal infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils; no portal oedema or bile duct proliferation. Symptoms resolved with bilirubin normalisation in 19-60 days in all patients; two patients had persistent ALP/GGT elevations 111 and 380 days after cessation. One patient had mild peripheral eosinophilia; none had rash or fever.

raw_record.support_text: In AFCAPS/TexCAPS, treatment with lovastatin 20 to 40 mg daily was explicitly not associated with hepatotoxicity. Small increases in mean liver transaminase levels were observed, but data from nearly 7,000 participants receiving placebo or lovastatin in EXCEL and AFCAPS/TexCAPS showed no significant differences in frequency of confirmed AST or ALT elevations >3×ULN. Among over 100,000 liver transaminase tests in AFCAPS/TexCAPS, only 18 lovastatin-treated participants had clinically important confirmed elevations >3×ULN, no cases of lovastatin-induced hepatitis were identified, and the risk of transaminase elevation was independent of treatment, indicating lovastatin does not increase the risk of clinically important transaminase elevations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: CHD primary-prevention cohort (AFCAPS/TexCAPS) with average cholesterol and no symptomatic CHD; long-term lovastatin 20-40 mg daily in a trial setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized controlled trial AFCAPS/TexCAPS. No significant differences vs placebo in confirmed AST/ALT elevations >3×ULN across nearly 7,000 participants (EXCEL + AFCAPS); only 18 lovastatin participants with clinically important elevations among >100,000 transaminase tests; no cases of lovastatin-induced hepatitis; half of elevations occurred in the first year, as did half the tests; risk of elevations independent of treatment; ~30% sporadic elevations >1×ULN in both arms. Small increases in mean transaminases observed with statins generally. Also no new drug-related adverse experiences and no clinically important increase in muscle side effects.

raw_record.support_text: A 6-year-old girl developed severe anicteric hepatitis with greatly elevated liver enzymes, prolonged prothrombin time, leukopenia, and eosinophilia during intravenous oxacillin therapy for staphylococcal osteomyelitis. Clinical symptoms resolved and laboratory data returned to normal after withdrawing oxacillin and substituting cefazolin. The authors conclude this hepatotoxicity appears to be specific to oxacillin and not to other β-lactams.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Child (6-year-old girl) treated for staphylococcal osteomyelitis of the left big toe; prolonged intravenous oxacillin therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Intravenous oxacillin 200 mg/kg/day divided every 4 hours; symptoms (fever 39-40°C, chills, abdominal pain, vomiting) developed on day 14 of therapy. ALT 2257 U/mL, AST 2247 U/mL, normal alkaline phosphatase (430 U/mL), total bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, albumin 3.7 g/dL, prolonged PT 17.8 s with INR 2.3; leukopenia (WBC 2,800/mm3) and eosinophilia (13%). Anicteric course. Anicteric hepatitis with variable transaminase elevation and normal or slightly elevated alkaline phosphatase; reversible with no apparent long-term injurious effects. Excluded acute viral hepatitis (HAV, HBV, HCV, EBV, CMV), toxicology (acetaminophen, salicylates), autoimmune markers, copper/ceruloplasmin/alpha-1-antitrypsin. Recovered after oxacillin discontinuation and substitution with cefazolin. Authors state hepatitis specific to oxacillin, not other β-lactams; predisposing factors and mechanism unknown.

raw_record.support_text: In osteosarcoma patients receiving high-dose methotrexate (MTX) chemotherapy, MTX-induced hepatic toxicity was graded: 61 patients had grade 1-2 and 48 had grade 3-4 hepatic toxicity. Patients with severe (grade 3-4) hepatic toxicity had a remarkably higher incidence of the MTHFR rs1801133 TT genotype than those with mild toxicity (33.3% vs 14.8%, p=0.04), and the T allele added 1.98-fold risk (95% CI 1.15-3.41, p=0.01) for severe hepatic toxicity. MTX concentration at 72 h was also significantly related to the severity of hepatic toxicity (0.20 ± 0.26 vs 0.13 ± 0.05 μmol/L, p=0.03).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children and adults (10-65 years) with osteosarcoma; high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy regimen given for therapeutic treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 109 patients treated; hepatic toxicity graded by CTCAE (grade 1-2, n=61; grade 3-4, n=48). Severe hepatic toxicity (grade 3-4) more frequent in MTHFR rs1801133 (C677T) TT genotype carriers (33.3% vs 14.8%, p=0.04); T allele OR 1.98 (95% CI 1.15-3.41, p=0.01). MTX plasma level at 72 h higher in severe hepatic toxicity group (0.20 ± 0.26 vs 0.13 ± 0.05 μmol/L, p=0.03). No association of rs1801133 with hematological or renal toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A cohort of 109 Chinese osteosarcoma patients who sequentially received high-dose methotrexate (MTX) therapy was studied. The extent of MTX-induced toxicity, including hematological toxicity, hepatic toxicity, renal toxicity and mucositis, was scored from grade 1 to 4, with severe toxicity defined as a grade score of ≥3. Patients with severe hepatic toxicity had a remarkably higher incidence of the TT genotype of the MTHFR rs1801133 (C677T) variant than those with mild toxicity (33.3% vs. 14.8%, p = 0.04).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chinese osteosarcoma patients treated with high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy
raw_record.extra_details: 109 patients; MTX-induced hepatic toxicity graded 1-4 with severe defined as grade ≥3; severe hepatic toxicity associated with MTHFR rs1801133 (C677T) TT genotype (33.3% vs. 14.8%, p=0.04); MTHFR genotyping proposed to predict MTX-induced toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The conclusion states that, given the pharmacological adverse effects of azathioprine therapy and the increasing descriptions of morphological liver changes in the form of nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH), patients on chronic azathioprine therapy should have regular laboratory monitoring of hepatic parameters so that a 'transaminitis', which may be an early marker of NRH, is detected early. In the case, the patient on 4 years of azathioprine for Crohn's disease developed NRH confirmed by liver biopsy with consequent portal hypertension and variceal bleeding; azathioprine was discontinued.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic (4-year) azathioprine maintenance therapy for Crohn's disease (disease duration 18 years) leading to nodular regenerative hyperplasia and portal hypertension.
raw_record.extra_details: 45-year-old patient presented with hematemesis and melena; EGD showed grade III esophageal varices and signs of fundus variceal bleeding; thrombocytopenia and mildly elevated serum bilirubin and GOT/ASAT; MRI showed a splenorenal venous convolution with a patent portal vein and splenomegaly, indicating an intrahepatic cause of portal hypertension; liver biopsy showed low-grade non-active hepatitis with mild fibrosis consistent with NRH; treated with sclerotherapy of fundus varices, azathioprine was discontinued and beta-blocker therapy started; patient remains asymptomatic. NRH is noted as an increasingly described liver morphology change under azathioprine, with transaminitis as a possible early marker.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reviewed 61 cases from the literature (MEDLINE 1966-1995) plus 2 new case reports, identifying 53 patients with acetaminophen-alcohol syndrome (hepatotoxicity from acetaminophen in chronic alcohol users). The quantity of acetaminophen taken per day ranged from 1.3 g to 20 g, with 46 of 53 patients using over-the-counter preparations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcohol use (acetaminophen-alcohol syndrome); cases took 1.3-20 g/day including some supratherapeutic amounts.
raw_record.extra_details: 53 patients total (51 literature cases + 2 new case reports), 21 women/32 men, age 23-66 years (mean 42). Peak AST ranged 841-30,000 U/L (mean 9,432 U/L). 26 patients had liver biopsy or autopsy; all but one showed centrilobular necrosis typical of acetaminophen toxicity. Interval from ingestion to presentation 1-45 days; diagnostic delay of 2-7 days in 19/53 (36%). 46/53 (87%) took over-the-counter acetaminophen preparations.

raw_record.support_text: The authors defend their prior report of acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis from modest therapeutic doses in chronic alcoholics, emphasizing that the article aimed to draw attention to the danger of recommending acetaminophen as the analgesic of choice in the chronic alcoholic. They disagree with dismissal of the enhanced susceptibility of alcoholics to acetaminophen liver injury raised in Hall and coworkers' letter.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholic patients with enhanced susceptibility to acetaminophen; modest (therapeutic) doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Six case patients described; the authors rebut criticism of lack of assessment of other hepatotoxic agents (exposure to other hepatocellular poisons sought but not identified) and of unreported hepatitis serology in two patients. Fever in three of six patients (mild in one, associated with alcohol withdrawal in another) was noted as at least as common in acetaminophen injury as in viral hepatitis B or non-A, non-B hepatitis. Authors emphasize potential danger of recommending acetaminophen as analgesic of choice in chronic alcoholics.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that hepatotoxicity may occur in chronic alcoholics ingesting acetaminophen for therapeutic reasons and not as a suicide attempt. The amount consumed by such alcoholic patients may be considerably less than that normally considered necessary to cause severe hepatic necrosis, indicating severe liver cell necrosis at therapeutic exposure when chronic alcohol use is present.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholics; therapeutic (non-suicidal) ingestion with substantially lower amounts than normally needed for severe hepatic necrosis; co-exposure to chronic ethanol use.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases reported previously where alcohol was suggested to augment acetaminophen hepatotoxicity; possible mechanisms include hepatic microsomal enzyme induction by ethanol, inadequate dietary protein/low hepatic glutathione, and depressed serum vitamin E and selenium in alcoholics; in the three patients in the study two cases of acute tubular necrosis and one of cardiac damage were also reported; SGOT levels ranged from 5,000 to 10,000 IU, more than tenfold higher than normally seen with alcoholic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Thirteen patients met the criteria for severe acetaminophen hepatotoxicity over a 5-year study period; six had therapeutic misadventures (not attempting suicide) and seven were attempting suicide. Five of six patients in the therapeutic misadventure group were chronic alcoholics, three were taking other drugs reported to cause hepatic microsomal enzyme induction, and all six had nausea, vomiting, or starvation. One patient died in each group, and the authors describe these features as part of the spectrum of acetaminophen toxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity documented by SGOT >500 with acute or chronic acetaminophen ingestion; 4/6 patients in this group developed acute tubular necrosis; one death; 5-year study (1977-1982) of 13 consecutive patients referred to Gastroenterology Services at University of Minnesota Teaching Hospitals.

raw_record.support_text: The summary states that use of acetaminophen by the alcoholic is potentially lethal and warns of the potential hepatocellular damage resulting from the combination of chronic alcoholism and modest increases above therapeutic doses of acetaminophen. Of the seven patients in the series, three died, although in two of the three instances other factors may have contributed to their deaths. The paper frames this as the 'alcohol-Tylenol syndrome' caused by acetaminophen ingestion combined with chronic alcoholism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholism; all patients ingested acetaminophen for pain relief; dosing described as modest increases above therapeutic doses; one nonalcoholic patient took the drug in a suicide attempt (overdose) during the same interval.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients with severe acute liver injury; markedly elevated serum transaminases and prothrombin times; AST exceeded 10,000 U/L in four patients and exceeded 4,000 U/L in all; this elevation argues against alcoholic hepatitis (usually <300 U/L). No serologic evidence of acute hepatitis A or B; hepatitis C could not be excluded but such transaminase activity is unusual for viral etiology. Mechanism: acetaminophen partly metabolized by cytochrome P-450 reductase to a toxic intermediate detoxified by glutathione conjugation; alcohol induces P-450 and depletes glutathione, enhancing toxicity; preexisting liver disease may increase risk. Histology from prior reports showed centrilobular necrosis, with some features of alcoholic hepatitis, 'toxic hepatitis,' or chronic hepatitis; established cirrhosis not necessary. Three of seven patients died; in two of three other factors may have contributed. Suggested management: supportive care and acetylcysteine/cimetidine as antidotes within 24 hours.

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old woman had been taking nitrofurantoin (100 mg daily) for 2 years for urinary tract infections and developed nausea, vomiting and jaundice; after nitrofurantoin was withdrawn she improved biochemically (bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, SGOT 60 IU, albumin 3.2 g/dL), and rechallenge with nitrofurantoin caused worsening that again resolved upon withdrawal. The paper as a whole (title and case series) attributes chronic active hepatitis to nitrofurantoin therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic daily therapy (months to years) for urinary tract infections, predominantly female patients; index patient also co-treated with prednisone and the case series includes patients on other medications (e.g., patient 5 also received a spironolactone/hydrochlorothiazide diuretic).
raw_record.extra_details: Case series comprises 20 patients (index case plus patients 1-20 from AFIP files and cited references). Index case (patient described in p23-24): clinical deterioration with progressive encephalopathy, ascites, coagulopathy and renal failure after nitrofurantoin was restarted; patient died; autopsy showed small shrunken liver (940 g) with massive hepatocellular necrosis, stromal collapse, inflammation, pseudoductule formation, endophlebitis of central veins, portal inflammation, nodular regeneration and marked canalicular cholestasis. Patient 5: total bilirubin 5.9 mg/dL, SGOT 520 IU, alkaline phosphatase 252 IU, 3% eosinophilia, elevated gamma globulin, positive smooth muscle antibody; liver biopsy performed; recovered after withdrawal (bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, SGOT 60 IU, albumin 3.2 g/dL). Chronic active hepatitis features include positive antinuclear/smooth muscle antibodies, hypergammaglobulinemia and response to withdrawal/rechallenge pattern.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a spectrum of toxic reactions to nitrofurantoin from an acute self-limiting hepatitis or cholestatic injury associated with short-term use to a chronic active hepatitis or granulomatous reaction associated with long-term use. Immunologic responsiveness and genetic factors appear to play a role in chronic active hepatitis associated with nitrofurantoin. The paper reports a series of 20 patients with nitrofurantoin-associated chronic liver disease, with elevated transaminases in 20/20, elevated bilirubin in 12/17, circulating autoantibodies, and two deaths; symptomatic or biochemical relapse occurred in five patients on rechallenge with nitrofurantoin.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 100 patients with rheumatoid arthritis chronically treated with methotrexate (MTX, mean cumulative dose 3595 mg, mean 7.07 years), a statistically significant correlation was found between liver stiffness (LS) assessed by FibroScan and MTX cumulative dose (r²=0.64, p<0.0001) and duration of treatment (r²=0.36, p<0.0001), with only a weak correlation to ALT. Liver biopsy in 5 of 11 patients with LS >7.0 kPa showed mild or moderate perisinusoidal fibrosis (Kleiner score 1A and 1B) in two. The authors state that MTX-induced liver injury is dose-dependent, interpreted as direct toxic damage related to increased oxidative stress, and that significant liver fibrosis has been reported in patients with RA and psoriasis chronically treated with MTX (incidence up to 23%, and 8.2% in a psoriasis cohort with cumulative doses exceeding 1500 mg).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic long-term therapeutic use (mean 7.07 years, ~10 mg/week) for rheumatoid arthritis; study patients had no diabetes mellitus or metabolic syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver stiffness (LS) assessed by transient elastography (FibroScan), whole-population mean LS 4.93±1.87 kPa; correlation with cumulative MTX dose r²=0.64 (p<0.0001), treatment duration r²=0.36 (p<0.0001), weak ALT correlation r²=0.050 (p=0.0250), weak BMI and γGT correlations; mean LS significantly higher in patients with cumulative dose >4000 mg (n=22) vs <4000 mg (n=76) (p<0.0001); liver biopsy in 5 patients (cumulative dose 3510–13,000 mg, LS 7.1–11.6 kPa) showed Kleiner score 1A and 1B perisinusoidal fibrosis in 2 and lobular inflammation (Kleiner 1) in 4; fibrosis incidence reported earlier as up to 23% in RA/psoriasis and 8.2% in a psoriasis cohort with cumulative doses >1500 mg; sequential biopsy studies found no severe fibrosis or cirrhosis after ~4 years/2000 mg. Injury interpreted as direct toxic damage related to increased oxidative stress, dose-dependent.

raw_record.support_text: The main concern of long-term treatment with methotrexate is the development of hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis. Raised transaminases were found in 18 of 306 patients treated in trials for 16 weeks or more (prevalence 6%; 95% CI 4-9%), with the rise noted between 3 weeks and 6 months, usually transient. Of 20 patients having a liver biopsy after a mean cumulative dose of 2633 mg over a mean of 132 weeks, only one had fibrosis; it was concluded that surveillance biopsy is unnecessary in inflammatory bowel disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic long-term treatment in inflammatory bowel disease; risk of liver damage depends partly on the nature of the disease being treated.
raw_record.extra_details: Raised transaminases in 18 of 306 trial patients (6%, 95% CI 4-9%), rise between 3 weeks and 6 months, usually transient; abnormal LFTs may be absent despite hepatotoxicity. Liver biopsy: 1 of 20 patients had fibrosis after mean cumulative 2633 mg methotrexate over mean 132 weeks; authors concluded surveillance biopsy is unnecessary in IBD.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies methotrexate (MTX) hepatic toxicity as the major problem in psoriatic patients treated chronically with MTX, citing chronic toxicity such as steatosis hepatitis and liver cirrhosis. In the study cohort of 104 patients, serum enzyme increase (mostly transaminase) was a frequent finding in both acute and chronic MTX toxicity, mostly grade 1 and 2 requiring dose adaptation, and one case of cirrhosis grade 2 was observed (<1%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic MTX therapy in patients with psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis; alcohol abuse identified as a major risk factor for liver cirrhosis; only 10% of patients underwent liver biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum enzyme (mostly transaminase) increases were frequent in both acute and chronic MTX toxicity, mostly grade 1-2 requiring dose adaptation. One case of cirrhosis grade 2 among 104 patients (<1%), lower than other psoriasis studies reporting up to 20% cirrhosis; reported frequency up to five times lower in rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. Haematopoietic and hepatic adverse effects appear more frequent/severe with concomitant drugs.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old woman with CML-CP developed histology-confirmed imatinib-induced liver toxicity after 6 months of treatment with standard-dose imatinib (400 mg/day). She presented with jaundice, nausea, and epigastric pain; lab tests showed acute liver dysfunction (ALT 1638 U/l, AST 1182 U/l, GGT 69 U/l, ALP 94 U/l, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dl, INR 1.33). Viral and autoimmune hepatitis and a vascular event were ruled out. Early corticosteroid therapy led to rapid and complete hepatic recovery, and treatment was resumed safely with dasatinib.

raw_record.support_text: In late 2018 the authors observed a case of acute imatinib hepatotoxicity in a 32-year-old woman with CML. Grade III hepatotoxicity (ALT 354 u/l, AST 183 u/l) developed after six months of imatinib treatment. The hepatotoxicity resolved within two weeks of imatinib withdrawal on 20 mg prednisolone tapered and withdrawn after 45 days; viral hepatitis by PCR was negative and no offender concomitant drug causing interaction was identified. Imatinib was restarted at a reduced dose of 300 mg/day with simultaneous prednisolone after the hepatitis resolved, and liver tests stayed within normal range during four months of the restart, after which imatinib was increased to 400 mg/day.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic myeloid leukemia patients; therapeutic use for CML; one grade III case and a previously reported case; a previously reported case had absent early molecular response (3-month BCR-ABL1IS 17.241%) and was switched to nilotinib rather than restarted.
raw_record.extra_details: 32-year-old woman: grade III hepatotoxicity (ALT 354 u/l, AST 183 u/l) after six months of imatinib; resolved within two weeks on prednisolone (20 mg, tapered and withdrawn after 45 days); restarted at 300 mg/day then increased to 400 mg/day after four months with normal liver tests. Prior reported case: grade III hepatotoxicity with absent early molecular response led to imatinib withdrawal and switch to the second-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor nilotinib. Imatinib-induced liver cirrhosis was not identified.

raw_record.support_text: This case series describes six patients with liver injury after exposure to alpha-methyldopa, ranging from 24 to 96 months before symptom onset. The disease developed chronically with gradually increasing epigastric pain, dyspepsia, nausea, and weakness; patient 4 was jaundiced. Withdrawal of the drug resulted in improvement of symptoms. Histology showed reactive hepatitis in five patients, one case of chronic aggressive hepatitis-like changes with massive necrosis, and cirrhosis in patient 4.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic exposure (onset after 24-96 months of use); chronic, gradual development of symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients. Symptoms: mild epigastric pain, dyspepsia, nausea, weakness for several months; patient 4 jaundiced. Withdrawal improved symptoms. Liver histology: reactive hepatitis in five patients; one patient had chronic aggressive hepatitis-like changes with massive necrosis; patient 4 developed cirrhosis, and cirrhosis appears in patient 4 (fibrosis content 16%). Five patients showed slight Kupffer cell proliferation at follow-up. Morphometry quantified fatty infiltration and fibrosis percentages in individual patients (e.g., severe fatty infiltration 30.5%, mild 2.5%).

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluated transient elastography (TE) for detecting methotrexate (MTX)-induced liver fibrosis among Chinese psoriasis patients receiving MTX. The paper repeatedly frames MTX as the cause of liver injury and fibrosis (e.g., detecting 'MTX-induced liver injury, defined as Roenigk grade ≥3a'), confirming the robust performance of TE in detecting significant liver fibrosis in this cohort, and noting that TE-based LS measurements were associated with BMI, diabetes mellitus, and obesity but not correlated with the total cumulative dose of MTX.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic MTX treatment for psoriasis in a Chinese (Hong Kong) patient population; patients with pre-existing metabolic risk factors (obesity, diabetes mellitus) showed higher fibrosis on TE; some patients met only TCD or only TE criteria for biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective observational diagnostic-performance study of 34 psoriasis patients receiving MTX. Significant liver fibrosis defined as Roenigk grade ≥3a on liver biopsy; TE LS cut-off 7.1 kPa gave 100% sensitivity and 68% specificity, PPV 26.7%, NPV 100%, AUROC 0.76 (95% CI=0.59-0.93). TE-based LS correlated with BMI (r=0.441, P=0.009), body weight, and waist circumference but not with total cumulative dose of MTX (r=0.202, P=0.25) or duration of use (r=0.004, P=0.98). Comparison with other cohorts (Rongngern: AUROC 0.78, PPV 50%/NPV 84% for Roenigk ≥3a; Khandpur: TE detected 4/19 Ishak ≥F1 fibrosis cases; Berends: 50% sensitivity/88% specificity).

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes most of the severe histological liver changes seen in psoriatic patients treated with methotrexate to the treatment. Nearly half of methotrexate-treated patients had hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis (46%), with mild to moderately severe fatty change in all but two of those, a combination uncommon in the U.K. except in alcoholic liver disease; no patient had a history of alcoholism and features of alcoholic hepatitis were consistently absent. These changes are said to be similar to those previously attributed to methotrexate in psoriasis and other conditions.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic treatment in patients with severe psoriasis.
raw_record.extra_details: In the methotrexate-treated group, 7 (19%) had cirrhosis and 10 (27%) had fibrosis; 46% had fibrosis or cirrhosis overall. Bromsulphthalein retention was inadequate as a diagnostic test: one patient who had discontinued methotrexate four months previously had normal bromsulphthalein retention (4%) but established cirrhosis on biopsy. Of 20 methotrexate-treated patients without cirrhosis or fibrosis, all but three showed more severe fatty change, nuclear vacuolation, and inflammation than the untreated group.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports two patients who developed chronic active hepatitis secondary to prolonged nitrofurantoin therapy, resembling cases reported in Scandinavian patients. The presence of severe necroinflammatory liver disease with hypergammaglobulinemia and high titers of antinuclear and smooth muscle antibodies initially suggested the lupoid form of chronic active hepatitis. Discontinuation of nitrofurantoin therapy resulted in immediate clinical improvement, and laboratory values became normal in 4 to 6 weeks without specific treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic/prolonged nitrofurantoin therapy; both patients recovered with resolution of laboratory values in 4-6 weeks after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients (Cases 1 and 2). Features of chronic active hepatitis with hypergammaglobulinemia, high titers of antinuclear and smooth muscle antibodies, and biopsy showing chronic aggressive hepatitis suggestive of the lupoid form. Case 1 biopsy: moderate hepatocellular unrest, spotty centrilobular necrosis, focal acidophilic degeneration, portal/periportal inflammation and piecemeal necrosis with prominent plasma cells, minimal fibrosis. Repeat biopsy showed progression possibly evolving into cirrhosis. Case 2 showed marked enhancement of lymphocyte transformation by nitrofurantoin (ratio 13.8) at first study, gone in follow-up (ratio 1.4); Case 1 showed no enhancement. Discontinuation led to clinical improvement.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes 23 cases of nitrofurantoin-induced liver injury from the Latin American DILI Network (LATINDILI) and the Spanish DILI Registry, with causality assessed using the RUCAM and RECAM scales. Hepatocellular damage was the most frequent biochemical pattern (83%), and 5 patients (22%) developed nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (NI-AILH), of whom two had persistent transaminase increases requiring immunosuppressive treatment. Neither death nor liver transplantation was documented in this series; the median time to resolution was 81 days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic/prolonged therapeutic use (prophylaxis of recurrent UTI at 50-100 mg/day); 96% of the cohort were women; median drug exposure 175 days (IQR 96-760), with 11 patients treated for more than six months.
raw_record.extra_details: 23 DILI cases from LATINDILI and the Spanish DILI Registry; causality assessed with RUCAM and RECAM; mean age 61 years; hepatocellular damage 83%; 52% asymptomatic; 65% positive autoantibody titres; median time to resolution 81 days (IQR 57-141), 83% recovered within 6 months; 5 patients (22%) developed nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (NI-AILH), 2 of whom required immunosuppressive treatment for persistent transaminase increase. General spectrum of nitrofurantoin DILI ranges from transient liver enzyme increases, icteric hepatitis, acute liver failure to death. Incidence reported as 1 in 1,369 patients (Iceland population study); nitrofurantoin accounts for 4.2-4.7% of DILI cases in prospective registries; paraphernalia: high ALT with increased gamma globulin and positive ANA/ASMA titres mimicking AIH.

raw_record.support_text: In a Japanese randomized, parallel, multicenter, controlled trial, NAT2 genotype-guided dosing stratification of isoniazid improved the tolerability of the standard 4-drug 6-month TB regimen. The incidence of isoniazid-associated DILI was 78% among slow acetylators in the standard treatment group versus none in the NAT2 genotype-guided treatment group. A Taiwan study also showed patients with NAT2 slow acetylator genotypes were more likely to develop TB DILI than rapid acetylators (26.4 vs 11.1%; OR 2.87; 95% CI 1.32–6.23).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Claims refer to the standard 4-drug 6-month TB regimen (required combination therapy) in pulmonary TB patients; risk was higher in NAT2 slow acetylators.
raw_record.extra_details: Japanese RCT: 172 patients with confirmed pulmonary TB (9.3% slow, 53.5% rapid acetylators); isoniazid-associated DILI was 78% in slow acetylators on standard dosing versus 0% in genotyping-guided arm. Taiwan study OR 2.87 (95% CI 1.32-6.23) for TB DILI in slow versus rapid acetylators. Also reported: HLA-B*52:01 associated with isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity among Europeans (OR 2.67, 95% CI 1.63-4.37); GSTM1/GSTT1 gene deletion linked to isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity risk and severity, with GSTT1 possibly increasing risk only among NAT2 slow acetylators; CYP2E1 allele associations with INH DILI risk in slow acetylators were inconsistent across reports.

raw_record.support_text: Sudoxicam, an NSAID from the early 1970s, had clinical trials discontinued due to multiple deaths related to hepatotoxicity, so it was never approved for marketing. Studies later implicated thiazole bioactivation as the source of reactive metabolites capable of initiating toxic responses arising from sudoxicam exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Clinical trial development setting; the drug was never approved for marketing.
raw_record.extra_details: Multiple deaths related to hepatotoxicity led to discontinuation of clinical trials in the early 1970s; thiazole bioactivation (C4-C5 epoxidation yielding a thioamide protoxin) implicated as source of reactive metabolites initiating the toxic response; structural analog of meloxicam differing only by a methyl group at the C5 position; bioactivation catalyzed by CYP2C8, 2C19, and 3A4, with CYP2C8 dominating.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine was brought to clinical trial before its pharmacokinetic profile was fully understood. Its half-life was underestimated at 30 hours instead of the predicted 2.5 hours, and volunteers received the drug for a much longer period than had been previously tested. The result was severe hepatotoxicity in seven subjects, attributed to uncoupling of hepatic mitochondrial oxidative metabolism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Clinical trial setting in healthy volunteers; fialuridine was given for a longer dosing period than previously tested because its true 30-hour half-life was unrecognized.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven subjects affected. Mechanism: uncoupling of hepatic mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. Half-life measured at 30 hours versus predicted 2.5 hours.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman on peritoneal dialysis for 20 years, diagnosed with EPS, was treated with tamoxifen (10 mg) and prednisolone (20 mg) for 8 months. CT showed the left hepatic lobe was hardly illuminated, leading to a diagnosis of liver infarction; one month later she was re-admitted with extensive deep vein thrombosis of the leg. The patient was concluded to have liver infarction and extensive venous thrombosis as a side effect of tamoxifen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-administered prednisolone (20 mg) for EPS; patient had end-stage renal disease on peritoneal dialysis for 20 years (switched to hemodialysis) and did not receive heparin during hemodialysis; tamoxifen used therapeutically for EPS management (non-standard indication).
raw_record.extra_details: Tamoxifen 10 mg/day with prednisolone 20 mg/day for 8 months. Left hepatic lobe barely illuminated on CT, diagnosed as liver infarction attributed to hepatic artery thrombosis. Patient later suffered extensive deep vein thrombosis of the leg; tamoxifen was stopped and prednisolone reduced to 10 mg. Patient subsequently died of gram-negative sepsis (death not attributed to the liver injury). Tamoxifen's thromboembolic effect is noted to relate to factor V Leiden mutation and other mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, when given with insulin, improves glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes, but in rare cases its use is associated with fatal hepatotoxicity. The case emphasized adherence to current prescribing and monitoring guidelines recommended by the manufacturer and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and whether adherence would prevent similar cases remained uncertain. The accompanying liver biopsy figure shows lobular, cholestatic hepatitis with areas of confluent necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-administered with insulin in a patient with type 2 diabetes treated for glycemic control
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of fatal hepatotoxicity in a letter. Liver biopsy showed lobular, cholestatic hepatitis with areas of confluent necrosis; inflammatory cells associated with areas of collapse (hepatic plates devoid of hepatocytes) on Masson trichrome stain. Paper notes the rare occurrence of fatal hepatotoxicity and discusses relevance of manufacturer/FDA prescribing and monitoring guidelines for prevention.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case of levetiracetam-induced drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome presenting with pneumonitis and hepatitis that resolved with levetiracetam withdrawal. The patient was classified as a definitive DRESS case by the RegiSCAR scoring system, and the adverse drug reaction was considered probable by the Naranjo probability scale.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-administration of dexamethasone during treatment; single case in a 31-year-old male with low-grade astrocytoma and tonic-clonic seizures.
raw_record.extra_details: Levetiracetam given at 1 g twice daily for seizures; onset of symptoms ~45 days after initiation. Presenting with pneumonitis and hepatitis as part of DRESS; impaired liver function (alanine aminotransferase 60 U/L [ref <56], aspartate aminotransferase 53 U/L [<30], LDH 516 U/L). Symptoms and hepatitis resolved after levetiracetam withdrawal; liver function returned to normal during a 2-month follow-up. Classified as definitive DRESS by RegiSCAR and probable by the Naranjo scale. Previously only one other levetiracetam-induced DRESS case had been reported.

raw_record.support_text: Lorlatinib is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4 and UGT1A4. When lorlatinib was combined with a strong CYP3A4 inducer such as rifampin, severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 10 of 12 patients. Therefore, lorlatinib use is contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inducers and should be avoided with moderate inducers such as efavirenz, nevirapine, and etravirine; if concomitant use is unavoidable, ALT, AST, and bilirubin should be monitored 48 hours after initiation and at least three times during the first week of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 33-year-old woman presented with jaundice and pruritus after a 5-day course of azithromycin followed by one day of erythromycin for a flu-like syndrome. Total bilirubin, serum transaminases, and alkaline phosphatase were highly elevated, other causes of cholestasis were ruled out by laboratory tests and imaging, and liver biopsy showed drug-induced cholestasis. She was diagnosed with azithromycin-induced cholestasis, treated with cholestyramine and six courses of plasmapheresis, with normal biochemical liver tests at her 4-year follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity due to valproate often necessitates discontinuation of the drug, and reports a patient with unstable epilepsy in whom valproate was an irreplaceable anticonvulsant. Hepatic encephalopathy in this patient was reversed and remained controlled by combining L-carnitine supplementation with an essentially unchanged valproate schedule, framing valproate as the cause of the hepatotoxicity-related encephalopathy. The patient, a 35-year-old previously healthy woman, developed delirium with asterixis and hyperammonemia (serum ammonia rising to 215 µmol/l) with low serum carnitine while on a valproate 3 g/day regimen together with phenobarbitone; the encephalopathy resolved after valproate reduction to 2.75 g/day and addition of L-carnitine 330 mg four times daily.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-exposure to phenobarbitone as part of a multidrug anticonvulsant regimen; patient had viral encephalitis with status epilepticus and prior withdrawal of carbamazepine for abnormal liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: 35-year-old woman; hepatic encephalopathy with delirium, asterixis, and hyperammonemia (serum ammonia rising from 43 to 215 µmol/l; normal <33 µmol/l) while serum liver function tests were normal and valproate concentration was therapeutic (83 mg/l); low serum free carnitine 7.6 µmol/l (normal 19.0-60.0) and total carnitine 15.4 µmol/l; valproate reduced from 3 g to 2.75 g/day with L-carnitine 330 mg four times daily; encephalopathy resolved over three days with normal serum ammonia (25 µmol/l) and therapeutic valproate (93 mg/l). Paper also notes valproate can cause reduced serum carnitine and hyperammonemia in children, especially with multidrug regimens and within a few months of starting, and that carnitine has been used/reported to reverse such hepatotoxicity in children.

raw_record.support_text: The first of two cases of reversible pioglitazone-induced jaundice was a 49-year-old diabetic man who presented with scleral icterus and acholic stools 6 months after starting pioglitazone. Serum bilirubin was 5.7 mg/dL with AST approximately threefold elevated, ALT approximately eightfold elevated, and alkaline phosphatase 2.5 times normal. Ultrasound was normal and other causes of liver injury were excluded. Liver biopsy showed a mixed hepatocellular cholestatic injury pattern with cholestasis, portal inflammation, and bile duct injury. After pioglitazone was discontinued the bilirubin and AST declined, with liver enzymes normal by 48 weeks. The patient was also taking glyburide, metformin, lisinopril, and omeprazole, but jaundice did not occur until pioglitazone was added.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-medications (glyburide, metformin, lisinopril, omeprazole); 49-year-old diabetic male; jaundice appeared only after pioglitazone was added to the regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: First of two reported reversible pioglitazone-induced jaundice cases. Latency ~6 months after starting drug. Lab values: bilirubin 5.7 mg/dL, AST ~3x, ALT ~8x, alkaline phosphatase 2.5x. Normal abdominal ultrasound; other causes excluded. Liver biopsy: mixed hepatocellular cholestatic injury with cholestasis, portal inflammation, bile duct injury. Recovery: bilirubin and AST declining at 2 weeks; liver enzymes normal by 48 weeks and still normal 3 months later.

raw_record.support_text: Among 647 metastatic breast cancer patients receiving docetaxel chemotherapy, 329 had abnormal liver function tests, of whom 67 were diagnosed with docetaxel-DILI (41 hepatocellular, 16 cholestatic, 10 mixed type), giving an overall docetaxel-DILI incidence of 10.35%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cohort restricted to metastatic breast cancer patients receiving docetaxel chemotherapy; patients with active HBV infection were excluded and chemotherapy was postponed until liver function normalized; all patients received prophylactic liver protectants.
raw_record.extra_details: Docetaxel-DILI was diagnosed by three independent experts using DILIN criteria; eligibility required ALT/AST >5x ULN, ALP >2x ULN, or ALT/AST 5x baseline or ALP 2x baseline on two consecutive draws, or bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL with any transaminase/ALP elevation. Overall incidence 10.35% (67/647); median time from initial exposure to DILI occurrence 14.01 days; most frequent clinical presentations were fever, jaundice, pruritus, and right upper abdominal pain, with jaundice and liver region pain more common in cholestatic type.

raw_record.support_text: The study's objective was to evaluate oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy (OBC)-induced hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity detected on contrast-enhanced CT and its influence on liver metastasis response, based on the assumption that such heterogeneity may indicate the presence of chemotherapy-induced sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Colorectal cancer patients with hepatic metastases receiving oxaliplatin-based combination chemotherapy as treatment; SOS presence was inferred from CT hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity rather than confirmed histologically.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 104 patients with hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer (male:female 66:38, age 20-80) treated with OBC and serial CT. Hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity scored on a 5-point scale (interobserver kappa=0.825). Conclusion: post-OBC hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity may indicate the presence of SOS, and more severe SOS predicts worse hepatic metastasis tumor response to oxaliplatin. Suggestion that oxaliplatin-based therapy induces sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (vascular liver injury).

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old woman with multiple myeloma developed severe hepatotoxicity attributed to thalidomide while being treated with dexamethasone and daily thalidomide 200 mg/day. By week 6 of therapy her AST and ALT rose to more than 50 times the upper limit of normal, and a liver biopsy showed acute injury with chronic changes of underlying steatosis and bridging fibrosis from previously undiagnosed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Her liver tests improved after thalidomide was discontinued (AST/ALT fell to 86 and 165 U/L seven days later). The authors conclude the case demonstrates severe hepatotoxicity as a rare but potentially serious adverse effect of thalidomide therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Combination therapy with dexamethasone 40 mg/day (4 days twice/month); pre-existing undiagnosed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis with steatosis and bridging fibrosis; elderly (76-year-old) female patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Thalidomide 200 mg/day, started ~5 weeks before admission alongside intermittent dexamethasone; no prior liver disease or baseline liver test abnormalities; AST/ALT rose to >50x ULN by week 6 with jaundice; AST and ALT at 4 weeks were 179 and 218 U/L; total bilirubin 0.33 mg/dl initially; liver biopsy showed acute injury with underlying steatosis and bridging fibrosis; dechallenge led to improvement (AST 86 U/L, ALT 165 U/L after 7 days); authors note hepatotoxicity is an extremely rare listed adverse effect and ask whether preexisting liver disease increases risk.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of 318 tuberculosis patients treated with a standard antituberculosis regimen, 49 (15.4%) were diagnosed with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper states that most cases with antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis have been attributed to isoniazid, and that isoniazid is the main drug to induce hepatotoxicity among antituberculosis regimens.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Combination therapy with rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol in standard antituberculosis regimen; genetic susceptibility factors central to the study (CYP2E1 c1/c1 genotype and slow acetylator [NAT2] status); Taiwanese population.
raw_record.extra_details: 49/318 (15.4%) patients diagnosed with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; CYP2E1 c1/c1 genotype raised hepatotoxicity risk (20.0% vs 9.0% for c1/c2 or c2/c2; OR 2.52, P=.009; adjusted OR 2.38, P=.017), and risk rose from 3.94 (c1/c1 with rapid acetylator) to 7.43 (c1/c1 with slow acetylator) relative to the c1/c2/c2 rapid reference. Isoniazid withdrawn when aminotransferases exceeded 3-5x ULN with gradual rechallenge after normalization. Mechanism: isoniazid metabolized by hepatic NAT and CYP2E1; metabolic intermediates (e.g., acetylhydrazine oxidized to hepatotoxic intermediaries) rather than isoniazid per se are incriminated.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a 58-year-old woman on atorvastatin who presented with altered liver tests and repeated epigastric abdominal pain over a year, with a mixed pattern of statin-induced liver injury. Laboratory values showed elevated ALT (peak 1026 U/L), AST (503 U/L), ALP (826 U/L) and total bilirubin (5.0 mg/dL). Liver biopsy revealed portal and lobular inflammation with cholangiolysis, and the patient's liver function tests normalized following cessation of atorvastatin therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Four cholecystectomized patients with gallstones and an interrupted enterohepatic circulation were intraduodenally infused with taurohyodeoxycholic acid at 0.8 to 1 g/h for 3 hours, and blood liver function tests were performed before and after the infusion. No alteration in liver function test results was observed after taurohyodeoxycholic acid infusion, and the authors concluded that, in the conditions of the study, taurohyodeoxycholic acid was not hepatotoxic.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Conclusion applies to 4 cholecystectomized patients with gallstones and an interrupted enterohepatic circulation who received intraduodenal infusion of taurohyodeoxycholic acid at 0.8-1 g/h for 3 hours on separate occasions.
raw_record.extra_details: Blood liver function tests were performed before and after the infusions because of the 3-hour 0.8-1 g/h intraduodenal infusion; no liver function test alteration was observed, so the authors explicitly stated taurohyodeoxycholic acid was not hepatotoxic in these study conditions. The related animal (rat biliary-fistula) finding of no liver-function-test alteration was preclinical and not used as the human evidence basis.

Cholestatic hepatitis without bile duct involvement (pericentrolobular bile thrombi on liver biopsy), favorable course in 5 months after treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of Stevens-Johnson syndrome with hepatic involvement in a 37-year-old woman. Ibuprofen taken Aug 22 - Sept 1, 2005. Cholestatic hepatitis: ASAT 77 UI/L (N<35), ALAT 181 UI/L (N<35), alkaline phosphatase 386 UI/L (N<105), gamma GT 560 UI/L (N<55), total bilirubin 220 µmol/L (conjugated 179) rising to 320 µmol/L; normal prothrombin; liver biopsy showed pericentrolobular bile thrombi without bile duct damage; no steatosis on ultrasound; viral and autoimmune serologies negative; treated with ursodeoxycholic acid with favorable outcome in 5 months; no signs of hepatocellular insufficiency or portal hypertension.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first biopsy-proven case of efavirenz-induced hepatitis. Hepatitis and hepatic laboratory abnormalities resolved after the entire antiretroviral regimen was stopped, and although dechallenge was not with efavirenz alone, the authors state that the causal role of efavirenz is obvious because zidovudine and lamivudine had been taken for 2 years without problems and efavirenz was the only new drug. They concluded that HCV infection played a limited role because HCV RNA remained negative throughout the course of hepatitis and no HCV-related abnormalities were found on liver biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concomitant HIV and HCV (serotype 1) infection; continued co-treatment with zidovudine and lamivudine; dechallenge involved stopping the entire antiretroviral regimen rather than efavirenz alone; initial supratherapeutic intake of 1200 mg/day for the first 3 days before settling at the prescribed 600 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: 45-year-old man with HIV infection; hepatitis and cutaneous rash developed within 4 weeks of switching indinavir to efavirenz (600 mg/day). Symptoms: nausea, right upper quadrant pain, rash, fever (38°C). Laboratory: ALT 718 IU/l (normal <38), AST 336 IU/l, GGT 1180 IU/l rising to 1611, ALP 684 IU/l rising to 928, eosinophilia (460 to 1110/mm3), bilirubin 18 µmol/l (no jaundice). Biopsy showed dense portal infiltrate of histiocytes, lymphocytes and eosinophilic polymorphonuclears with some apoptotic bodies; no interlobular bile duct damage and no microvesicular steatosis. Liver tests and eosinophilia returned to normal within 1 month after stopping antiretroviral treatment. Autoantibodies (antimitochondrial, anti-smooth muscle, anti-endoplasmic reticulum, anti-LKM, anti-nuclear) negative; HCV RNA negative throughout. No rechallenge attempted because of possible immuno-allergic mechanism. Efavirenz is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (1,4-dihydro-2H-3,1-benzoxazin-2-one), extensively metabolized by P450 cytochromes to 8-hydroxylated metabolites then conjugated as glucuronides.

raw_record.support_text: The report attributes fatal liver failure to valproic acid (VPA) therapy in a 21-year-old patient on VPA for seizures/status epilepticus; no other cause of the hepatic injury could be substantiated, and necropsy showed hepatic steatosis, necrosis, fibrosis, and destroyed hepatic architecture. The paper states that pancreatitis associated with hepatic failure under VPA has a poor prognosis mainly because of the VPA hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent antiepileptic co-medications (clonazepam, phenobarbital) present; phenytoin failed initially; patient was a 21-year-old mentally retarded male with seizures evolving into status epilepticus.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal liver insufficiency 18 weeks after starting VPA; initial dosing 25.5 mg/kg/day increased to 39.2 mg/kg/day; VPA serum level remained within therapeutic range (50-100 mg/L; 350-700 µmol/L). Elevated AST, ALT, GGT (max 600 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase (max 665 IU/L), bilirubin (up to 50 µmol/L), and persistent severe coagulopathy. Necropsy: hepatic steatosis, necrosis, fibrosis, destroyed architecture; coexistent pancreatitis, pancreatic pseudocyst, 5 L serous icteric peritoneal fluid, ascites. Literature review: until March 1991, 24 cases of isolated pancreatitis and 6 cases of pancreatitis with hepatic failure under VPA published; overall pancreatitis mortality approaching 21%; pancreatic side effects range from asymptomatic hyperamylasemia to fatal pancreatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report another case of liver failure in close temporal relation to intake of the antidepressant nefazodone. Extensive internal medicine workup found no alternative explanation, excluding pre-existing liver disease, other toxic substances, alcohol/drug use, viral causes (hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr, cytomegalovirus), autoimmune liver failure, Wilson disease, and hemochromatosis. The liver biopsy histology (inflammatory portal infiltrates, periportal group necroses, cellular cholestasis) confirmed the hypothesis of drug-induced, probably nefazodone-mediated liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent comedication included doxepin, moclobemide, Moradorm, and dihydroergotamine; no reports of liver dysfunction exist for Moradorm or the dihydroergotamine product. Nefazodone had already been discontinued 8 days before admission to the internal hospital.
raw_record.extra_details: Nefazodone given at 300 mg for depression. At admission liver parameters: GOT 836 U/l, GPT 1947 U/l, gamma-GT 88 U/l, Quick 53%, PTT 37.8 s, LDH 466 U/l, bilirubin total 13.9 mg/dl, ferritin 10080 ng/ml. Liver biopsy showed marked cellular and canalicular cholestasis with inflammatory portal infiltrates and periportal-accentuated group necroses with collapse fibrosis. Patient developed hepatic encephalopathy 43 days after first clinical symptoms; liver transplantation was performed 10 days later. Patient died about 4 weeks post-transplant from an uncontrolled Aspergillus infection. MRI showed shrinking liver with ascites without portal hypertension or cirrhosis; ascites cytology unremarkable.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 39-year-old male agricultural worker who developed a severe cholestatic hepatitis 8 weeks after a 3-day course of itraconazole 400 mg/day for genital candidiasis and shortly after exposure to a herbicide. Clinical and morphologic data ruled out common causes of acute liver injury, and on the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) diagnostic scale the final score was 7, leading the authors to conclude the liver injury was most likely caused by itraconazole, even after a short period of treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent cutaneous exposure to a herbicide containing atrazine and simazine, which the authors hypothesize may have aggravated the severity of itraconazole-induced liver lesions; short 3-day therapeutic course.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old agricultural worker admitted with asthenia and jaundice; itraconazole 400 mg/day for 3 days for genital Candidiasis. Peak values: total bilirubin rose to 578 µg/dl, ALT 2426 rising to 1976 U/L, AST 1549 U/L, GGT 95 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 225 U/L. Liver biopsy showed distortion of lobular architecture, disruption of hepatocyte plates, diffuse lobular leukocyte/eosinophil infiltration, multiple foci of liver cell necrosis, moderate intracellular cholestasis, and enlarged portal tracts with loose collagenous fibrosis forming incomplete porto-portal bridges. Serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, leptospira, CMV, EBV, HSV and autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, AMA) were negative. Treated with tapering prednisone 30 mg; liver function parameters normal 6 weeks later. CIOMS scale final score 7.

raw_record.support_text: Case 1: a 65-year-old man with maturity-onset diabetes and osteomyelitis developed marked jaundice after 6 weeks of flucloxacillin (Heracillin) 1500 mg/24 h orally. Biochemically there was cholestasis with markedly elevated serum bilirubin (peak 364 mmol/l, normal <22) and slightly elevated ALP (32 U) and ASAT (33 U). After flucloxacillin withdrawal bilirubin returned to normal over 8 weeks, and a biopsy showed moderate cholestasis; the diagnosis of drug-induced canalicular cholestasis was established. The abstract frames the two patients as developing reversible cholestatic jaundice during treatment with oxacillin derivatives.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent glibenclamide (Daonil) for diabetes continued unchanged during recovery; indication osteomyelitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Flucloxacillin 1500 mg/24 h perorally for 6 weeks for osteomyelitis of proximal phalanx of left big toe. Marked jaundice, hepatic tenderness. Serum bilirubin peaked at 364 mmol/l (normal <22) on day 7 and normalized over 8 weeks; ALP 32 U (normal <10), ASAT 33 U (normal <20). Biopsy two weeks after admission showed moderate cholestasis (canalicular cholestasis); ERCP and ultrasound normal; Coombs' direct test negative, no hepatitis-associated antigens, no eosinophilia or fever. Repeat biopsy at 3 months showed Kupffer cell proliferation, enhanced intracytoplasmic vacuolization with scattered hepatocyte necroses. Bilirubin normalized while glibenclamide was maintained, supporting flucloxacillin as the causal agent.

raw_record.support_text: An epileptic 48-year-old woman treated with phenobarbital (100 mg/d) had been taking acetaminophen (1 g/d) for headaches for 3 months and presented with generalized discomfort and weakness, a palpable liver, and elevated transaminases (AST 170, ALT 456, ALP 131, GGT 498 mIU/mL). Acute hepatitis A/B, cytomegalovirus, herpes, and EBV were excluded, and the dramatic fall of serum transaminases to normal within 2 weeks of acetaminophen withdrawal strongly supported drug-induced liver damage. The authors note only seven prior cases of hepatotoxicity from therapeutic acetaminophen doses and propose that concurrent phenobarbital induced mixed-function oxidase activity, increasing toxic metabolite production beyond glutathione binding capacity, concluding that persons taking phenobarbital with even low therapeutic doses of acetaminophen are at risk of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent phenobarbital treatment (100 mg/d) as enzyme inducer; suggested metabolic predisposition; low therapeutic acetaminophen doses (1 g/d).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen 1 g/d taken for headaches for 3 months. Lab values: AST 170 mIU/mL (normal <30), ALT 456 mIU/mL, alkaline phosphatase 131 mIU/mL, 5'-nucleotidase 17 mIU/mL, GGT 498 mIU/mL. Seronegative for IgM-HVA, HBsAg, IgM-HBc; persistent low IgM/IgG ruled out CMV, herpes, EBV; sporadic non-A, non-B hepatitis not fully excluded. Transaminases returned to normal within 2 weeks of acetaminophen withdrawal. Authors state only seven previously reported cases of hepatotoxicity from therapeutic acetaminophen doses. Proposed mechanism: phenobarbital-induced mixed-function oxidase, increased toxic metabolites exceeding glutathione binding capacity.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old man treated for sympathetic ophthalmia with prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) and azathioprine (1.4 mg/kg/day) developed jaundice and diffuse abdominal pain with elevated liver enzymes (ALT 282, AST 105, ALP 230, GGT 992 U/L and bilirubin 35 µmol/L). Percutaneous liver biopsy showed a portal inflammatory infiltrate with granulomatous aspects and destruction of bile ducts, consistent with destructive cholangitis. After azathioprine was changed to Endoxan, abdominal pain resolved within 2 days and liver function tests normalized within 8 weeks. The authors judged the diagnosis of azathioprine-related liver toxicity likely because liver tests were normal before therapy, other causes of cholangitis (no stones, no antibodies, no other drug-induced cholestasis) were excluded, symptoms appeared 4 weeks after starting azathioprine, and symptoms/biochemistry resolved after azathioprine withdrawal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) co-medication; indication sympathetic ophthalmia; azathioprine dose 1.4 mg/kg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice and diffuse abdominal pain with posterior irradiation; LFTs: ALT 282 (N=60 U/L), AST 105 (N=50), ALP 230 (N=110), GGT 992 (N=50), bilirubin 35 µmol/L, prothrombin time normal; liver biopsy showed portal tract granulomatous mononuclear infiltrate without eosinophils and bile duct destruction (destructive cholangitis); latency ~4 weeks after starting azathioprine; dechallenge: pain resolved in 2 days, LFTs normalized at 8 weeks after substitution with Endoxan (cyclophosphamide); azathioprine is hepatically metabolized to 6-mercaptopurine; author hypothesis of idiosyncratic reaction of the metabolite type.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the death of a 64-year-old man from acute hepatic failure attributable to beclobrate, a lipid-lowering agent. He had taken beclobrate 100 mg daily for 6½ months before becoming anorexic and jaundiced, with total bilirubin 304 µmol/l (normal <17) and very much raised transaminases; acute hepatitis was diagnosed and he died 7 days after admission. No infectious (viral or toxoplasmosis) or obstructive cause was found, and there was no history of self-medication or alcohol abuse; he also received chondroitin sulphate 500 mg thrice daily for osteoarthrosis.

Most probably both disorders were caused by propafenone (450 mg/day); withdrawal of the drug resulted in normalization of elevated enzyme and threshold levels.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 95 patients with active tuberculosis treated with isoniazid (INH) 10 mg/kg, rifampicin (RMP) 10 mg/kg, and ethambutol (EMB) 25 mg/kg, the authors investigated the influence of acetylator phenotype on isoniazid hepatotoxicity. They found a 12.6% incidence of isoniazid hepatitis (SGOT, SGPT >200 U/l) and a significantly higher risk of isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity in slow acetylators (p <0.01): 26/56 slow acetylators (≈46.4%) vs 4/30 rapid acetylators (≈13.3%) had transaminases >50 U/l, and all 12 patients with the most severe hepatotoxic side effects (SGOT/SGPT >200 U/l) were slow acetylators. Women developed severe hepatic injury more often than men (p <0.05). In isoniazid hepatitis cases therapy was stopped or reduced to RMP+EMB; transaminases normalized within 2-4 weeks and no new elevation occurred upon resuming full therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Confirmed active pulmonary tuberculosis; triple therapy with rifampicin and ethambutol as co-medication; slow acetylator phenotype carries higher risk; women affected more often than men.
raw_record.extra_details: Doses: isoniazid 10 mg/kg, rifampicin 10 mg/kg, ethambutol 25 mg/kg (INH 10 mg/kg mentioned). Isoniazid hepatitis defined as SGOT/SGPT >200 U/l, incidence 12.6% of treated. Transaminase elevations >50 U/l in 46.4% of slow vs 13.3% of rapid acetylators. Onset constant in the 2nd-4th week (19 +/- 7 days); transaminases normalized within 2-4 weeks; no new transaminase elevation on rechallenge with full triple therapy. Authors propose an interaction between rifampicin and isoniazid metabolism limited to the early phase of chemotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: Vanscheidt et al. treated 114 of 231 patients with lower-limb oedema secondary to chronic venous insufficiency with 90 mg coumarin and 540 mg troxerutin daily for 16 weeks in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, monitoring ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT at baseline and weeks 4-16. No hepatotoxicity was reported; relative risk of elevations greater than 1.25 times the physiological range of GGT, ALT and AST was 4.9% in the active group vs 2.1% in placebo, and values returned to normal during or after treatment. A separate safety publication concluded coumarin treatment is safe and well-tolerated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Coumarin was administered in combination with troxerutin (90 mg coumarin + 540 mg troxerutin daily); patients had lower-limb oedema secondary to chronic venous insufficiency
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Germany, 231 patients total (114 active); liver function monitored at baseline and after 4, 6, 8, 12, 16 weeks; no hepatotoxicity reported; minor reactions in 25 cases (21.9%) active vs 14 (12.0%) placebo; elevations >1.25x physiological range of GGT/ALT/AST 4.9% active vs 2.1% placebo, resolving during or after treatment; separate publication concluded coumarin is safe and well-tolerated.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, the diagnosis of amiodarone-induced hepatitis is based on drug history, temporal relationship, time course of liver dysfunction, exclusion of other causes, and rapid improvement after amiodarone withdrawal. Although no bioptic or autoptic features of liver damage were obtained, the cause-effect relationship between amiodarone infusion and hepatitis was rated 'probable' according to the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability score (total score +7). A peculiarity was the very short latency between infusion and transaminase elevation, and the authors advise monitoring liver function during the first hours of intravenous amiodarone loading in critically ill elderly patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Critically ill elderly patient with intravenous amiodarone loading; the authors call for heightened alertness and liver-function monitoring in this population.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability score total +7, classified as probable. Very short latency between intravenous amiodarone infusion and transaminase elevation (earlier reports showed intervals of a day or more with lower transaminase elevation). Rapid improvement after amiodarone withdrawal; no biopsy or autopsy confirmation of liver damage. Intravenous loading route.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine (AZA), a corticosteroid-sparing treatment for Crohn's disease, can be associated with varying forms of hepatotoxicity, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) of the liver can arise 1 to 5 years after starting azathioprine. The presented 53-year-old man with Crohn's disease developed NRH after azathioprine exposure, with portal hypertension and esophageal varices; multiple case reports have documented NRH as an adverse effect of AZA.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Crohn's disease patient; co-treatment with 5-ASA and subsequently MTX/infliximab; azathioprine dose 150 mg/day; no prior liver disease or alcohol abuse.
raw_record.extra_details: Biochemical markers (albumin, GGT, ALP, bilirubin, AST, ALT) were within normal limits at diagnosis; NRH presented with new anemia and thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension, and esophageal varices (controlled by beta-blocker); high-dose thiopurine NRH frequency reported up to 62% vs low-dose, with dose-dependent, irreversible portal hypertension; hepatic function preserved after elective surgery.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine-induced peliosis hepatis is reported as idiosyncratic in humans. The authors describe a Crohn's disease patient who developed peliosis hepatis during azathioprine therapy most likely due to concomitant alcohol binging; the patient improved after azathioprine was stopped, with peliosis hepatis diagnosed by liver biopsy showing sinusoidal ectasia in zones II and III. Alcohol binging was concluded to be an additional risk factor via hepatic glutathione depletion increasing azathioprine endothelial toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Crohn's disease patient; concomitant episodic alcohol binging identified as most likely precipitating co-factor; required combination immunosuppression with steroids (prednisolone) and prior mesalazine/metronidazole; male gender noted as a possible azathioprine-peliosis risk factor.
raw_record.extra_details: Azathioprine dosed at 2.5 mg/kg/day. Hepatic toxicity only appeared after three episodes of alcohol binging (800 g over 3 d followed by two episodes of 20 g/day); liver enzymes were normal in April 2006 under azathioprine alone. Presenting features: progressive fatigue, abdominal discomfort, pruritus, pancytopenia, portal hypertension. Lab values: GGT 121 U/L, ALP 220 U/L, total bilirubin 4.03 mg/dL, transaminases normal, hyaluronic acid 166 ng/mL, TPMT 44 nmol/g Hb x h. Liver biopsy: sinusoidal ectasia zone II/III without venous obliterations, minimal portal tract fibrosis, no cirrhosis, no bile duct alterations. Syndrome grouped among azathioprine liver reactions (hypersensitivity, idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction, endothelial cell injury). Improvement after azathioprine withdrawal; proposed mechanism (murine in vitro) is glutathione depletion in sinusoidal endothelial cells increasing azathioprine toxicity; alcohol binging depletes hepatic glutathione ~60%.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old Caucasian female with Cushing disease, without prior liver disease, was started on mifepristone and semaglutide. Ninety days after initiating mifepristone she developed deep jaundice, severe pruritus, fatigue, and nausea; liver tests showed a mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic pattern, serologies were negative, and liver biopsy showed severe cholestasis without bile duct injury plus focal endothelialitis within a central venule. Symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized four months after stopping mifepristone. The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score indicated probable causality for mifepristone.

raw_record.extra_details: Latency 90 days; symptoms of deep jaundice, severe pruritus, fatigue, nausea; mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic pattern on liver tests; biopsy showed severe cholestasis without bile duct injury and focal endothelialitis within a central venule; RUCAM indicated probable causality; symptoms subsided over one month and completely resolved with normal liver tests four months after stopping mifepristone.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized trial of hepatic arterial infusion (HAI) after resection of liver metastases, a significantly higher rate of biliary sclerosis was noted in the HAI group than in the non-HAI group. Six of 17 patients receiving HAI therapy (35%) developed persistently elevated serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels indicative of biliary sclerosis; five underwent cholangiography documenting a pattern of stricturing consistent with this diagnosis, and four were managed with chronic indwelling stents. In the five patients with available treatment plans, the dose of FUDR given did not exceed 0.2 mg/kg/d. Three of the six patients received concomitant systemic chemotherapy (two with 5-FU/LV and one with CPT-11).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Delivery by hepatic arterial infusion (local/unusual route) in patients with resected hepatic metastases; three of the six affected patients also received concomitant systemic chemotherapy as part of adjuvant therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Biliary sclerosis (bile-duct stricturing injury) developed in 6/17 (35%) of HAI-treated patients, significantly more than controls; 5 confirmed by cholangiography, 4 managed with chronic indwelling stents, and 1 (patient 4) required intrahepatic Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy for a dominant hilar stricture. FUDR dose did not exceed 0.2 mg/kg/d in the five patients with available plans. One patient (paragraph 33) died of cirrhosis and subsequent liver failure associated with HAI therapy. Two patients in the HAI group died postoperatively (of sepsis and liver failure respectively), and one pump was removed for suspected infection.

raw_record.support_text: During a developmental study of the fluorinated thymidine analog fialuridine for HBV infection, 7 of 15 treated patients developed severe hepatotoxicity and lactic acidosis, with 3 patients showing milder changes. Treatment with intravenous thymidine or uridine was of no benefit. Subsequently, 5 participants died, and 2 patients survived after liver transplantation. Pancreatitis, neuropathy, and myopathy often accompanied the syndrome, and liver histologic findings showed macrovesicular and microvesicular steatosis and abnormal mitochondria.
