raw_record.support_text: In three of the diabetic patients who had recovered from jaundice after Neoteben (INH) was stopped and liver-function tests normalized, cautious rechallenge with small doses of Neoteben for a few days rapidly reproduced intolerance symptoms (fullness, belching, loss of appetite, inner restlessness) together with deterioration of carbohydrate tolerance with pronounced glycosuria. In one case the Takata-Ara fell from 80 to 60 mg%, and the Ehrlich urobilinogen test became positive in the others. The medication was promptly withdrawn and symptoms disappeared. The authors conclude that this behavior indicates liver damage, possibly a hypersensitivity reaction, rather than homologous serum hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Diabetic patients with tuberculosis; authors state the diabetic liver reacts more readily with damage than that of non-diabetic tuberculous patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Five jaundice cases among 15 Neoteben-treated diabetic patients (case series); rechallenge in 3 reproduced symptoms. Weicksel is cited as observing jaundice in 3 additional diabetics. The decrease of the glucose equivalent under Neoteben in 4 of these patients was attributed to hepatogenic insulin resistance from toxic liver damage. Animal experiments were conflicting (Freerksen: marked glycogen depletion of liver cells in rabbits fed high INH doses; Emmerich & Petzold: no regeneration inhibition or liver fatty change in rat liver regeneration test). Alias: INH.

raw_record.support_text: The author concluded that rechallenge of rifampicin, rifampicin/isoniazide, then ethambutol produced no recurrence of symptoms, establishing imputability of pyrazinamide for the DRESS syndrome in this patient; the diarrhea and hyperuricemia, classic pyrazinamide adverse effects, reinforced imputability. Within this DRESS syndrome the patient developed severe hepatic failure (cytolysis, low prothrombin, HHV6 reactivation) and died of severe hepatic failure two weeks after discharge. The conclusion states that DRESS syndrome induced by pyrazinamide with HHV6 reactivation is a rare clinical entity.

raw_record.extra_details: 35-year-old male with first episode of pulmonary tuberculosis; RHEZ fixed combination 150/75/400/275 mg, 3 tablets/day (dose adjusted to 41 kg). Symptoms (rash, jaundice, facial edema, fever 40°C, diarrhea) appeared ~20 days after treatment start. Liver tests rose after treatment resumed: AST 94->406->2011 UI/L, ALT 69->501->1437 UI/L (ALAT >10x ULN), conjugated bilirubin 3.28 mg/dl, total bilirubin 5.46 mg/dl, prothrombin 33%, albumin 14.2 g/L, alkaline phosphatase 488 UI/L; eosinophilia 4790/µL. RegiSCAR and DiHS diagnostic criteria met. Antitubercular treatment stopped; systemic corticosteroids 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks led to hepatic normalization, but patient died at home 2 weeks after discharge from severe hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of 6 HIV/TB coinfected patients with rifampicin-associated DRESS, rechallenge reactions to rifampicin produced hepatitis with eosinophilia in cases 1-3, 5, and 6 (4 of 6 cases), with initial DRESS presentations showing ALT >5x ULN in most cases. Isoniazid rechallenge produced hepatitis in cases 1, 2, and 4; moxifloxacin produced hepatitis in case 2; and in case 6 hepatitis was attributed to moxifloxacin and/or terizidone and/or ethionamide with unresolved co-attribution.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: DRESS syndrome hypersensitivity reaction; HIV/TB coinfected patients; rechallenge setting with clinical/laboratory monitoring for 96 h.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge reactions to rifampicin: rash 6/6, itch and eosinophilia 5/6, hepatitis 4/6, edema 3/6, fever/hypotension/diarrhea once; CTCAE severity mild-moderate-severe across cases; 19/88 (22%) reacted to rifampicin in the parent RCT; all 6 successfully switched to therapeutic-dose rifabutin. Initial DRESS presentations included ALT >5x ULN in 5/6 cases. Discussion references prior reports of rifampicin-associated hepatotoxicity with successful switch to rifabutin.

raw_record.support_text: In this prospective cohort of tuberculosis patients treated with isoniazid (INH)-containing regimens, the frequency of drug-induced hepatitis (DIH) was 11.76%, and a slow-acetylation (NAT2) profile was associated with DIH, with significantly lower AcINH AUC0-6h in patients with DIH suggesting impaired INH acetylation. The paper frames INH as the cause of drug-induced liver injury, noting that three INH metabolites (acetylhydrazine/AcHz, hydrazine/Hz, and a metabolite from bioactivation of INH itself) have been proposed to be responsible for INH-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: During multi-drug anti-tuberculosis therapy (regimen including rifampicin); DIH associated with NAT2 slow-acetylation phenotype.
raw_record.extra_details: DIH is drug-induced hepatitis, the study outcome attributed to INH-containing treatment; DIH frequency 11.76% in the cohort; AcINH AUC0-6h significantly lower in patients with DIH and AcINH plasma level proposed as a DIH biomarker; metabolites proposed to cause INH-induced liver injury: acetylhydrazine (AcHz), hydrazine (Hz), and an INH bioactivation metabolite (Metushi et al., 2011) - described only as proposed mechanism, not independently confirmed injuring entities; GSTM1-null genotype (59% of cohort) showed no effect on DIH; CYP2E1*6 (rs6413432) associated with INH pharmacokinetic changes but no direct demonstration of contribution to DIH.

raw_record.support_text: In the direct hepatotoxicity section, NNRTIs such as nevirapine (NVP) and efavirenz (EFV) are reported to cause pathological features resembling direct hepatotoxicity (centrilobular and panlobular necrosis), with EFV-associated submassive necrosis linked to significant morbidity and mortality. A case identified by Elsharkawy and colleagues reported the first adult EFV-induced acute liver failure that required liver transplantation within 5 months after initiating therapy; this 43-year-old woman was a slow drug metabolizer, contributing to the severe presentation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: EFV used within combination antiretroviral regimens; index case was a slow drug metabolizer whose genotype contributed to severe presentation.
raw_record.extra_details: Direct hepatotoxicity producing acute hepatic necrosis with centrilobular/panlobular necrosis and submassive necrosis with an immune-allergic pattern (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils); acute liver failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy; liver transplantation required within 5 months in a 43-year-old woman; EFV-associated submassive necrosis on liver biopsy associated with significant morbidity and mortality. EFV was also the most common cause of skin rashes (incidence 10-17%) and CYP2B6 slow-metabolizer genotype was associated with increased risk of EFV adverse reaction.

raw_record.support_text: After receiving metformin 500 mg/d for 3 weeks, a 73-year-old Japanese woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presented with fatigue, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal pain and laboratory findings of severe hepatotoxicity (elevated AST, ALT, ALP, and total bilirubin). Immediate hospitalization and discontinuation of metformin led to improvement in liver function and resolution of symptoms within 3 weeks. The probability of an adverse drug reaction assessed with the Naranjo ADR probability scale was 4 (probable). The authors concluded metformin appeared to have caused mixed-type (hepatocellular and cholestatic) hepatic damage, and although rare, severe hepatotoxicity might be associated with metformin use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (73-year-old) Japanese woman with low body weight (33.5 kg) and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus.
raw_record.extra_details: Metformin 500 mg/day for 3 weeks before presentation. Symptoms included fatigue, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal pain. Laboratory findings: elevated aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin. Naranjo ADR probability scale score 4 (probable). Liver function improved and symptoms resolved within 3 weeks after metformin discontinuation and hospitalization. Authors note hepatotoxicity is rare but may be associated with metformin. Metformin hydrochloride is widely used for type 2 diabetes mellitus; only 2 prior cases of possible metformin-induced acute hepatitis reported worldwide.

raw_record.support_text: A case report described a 77-year-old female who developed acute hepatic failure after receiving quetiapine 12.5 mg twice daily for 9 days to manage agitation and insomnia. She reported no other medication use. After an extensive workup, she had significantly elevated aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and γ-glutamyl transferase levels and prolonged prothrombin time/international normalized ratio; liver function tests 3 weeks prior were normal. The hepatic failure was attributed to quetiapine, which was discontinued with subsequent improvement in liver function, although the patient died shortly afterward from multiorgan system failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old man with stage IIIB lung adenocarcinoma developed drug-related acute hepatitis complicated by renal deterioration (aspartate aminotransferase 1400 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 1299 U/L, creatinine 4.4 mg/dL) 12 days after starting erlotinib 100 mg/day. Viral causes and liver metastases were excluded, and Roussel-Uclaf causality assessment classified the erlotinib-related hepatitis as probable. Fatal lactic acidosis caused death 2 hours after admission. The authors report this as the second case of fatal erlotinib-induced liver toxicity in a lung cancer patient, noting the previous case died after about 11 days from fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (77-year-old) patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus on concomitant metformin; advanced lung adenocarcinoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg/day; onset of hepatitis 12 days after erlotinib initiation; AST 1400 U/L, ALT 1299 U/L, creatinine 4.4 mg/dL, urea nitrogen 55 mg/dL; RUCAM causality score classified as probable; viral hepatitis and liver metastases excluded; fatal lactic acidosis within 2 hours of admission; discussion attributes lactic acidosis to erlotinib-related hepatitis with initial liver failure plus metformin-induced lactate production and metformin accumulation from acute renal deterioration; authors note this is the second fatal erlotinib liver toxicity case in a lung cancer patient (prior case died ~11 days from fulminant hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of fatal hepatitis associated with troglitazone in an 85-year-old man with type 2 diabetes. Troglitazone therapy had been started 5 months before presentation and increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks; abdominal pain, malaise, and jaundice developed. A diagnosis of troglitazone-induced hepatitis was made, liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis, and the patient died 8 weeks after presentation. The paper notes that troglitazone use is in rare cases associated with fatal hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (85-year-old) male patient with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin; troglitazone added for glycemic control.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks of therapy; fatal case. Symptoms included abdominal pain, malaise, and jaundice; ALT 608 U/L initially then 287 U/L at presentation, total bilirubin 15.6 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, normal prothrombin time, glycosylated hemoglobin 5.2%; serology negative for hepatitis A, B, and C; normal hepatic ultrasonogram. Liver biopsy showed lobular cholestatic hepatitis with areas of confluent necrosis (submassive hepatic necrosis); patient died 8 weeks after presentation despite aggressive therapy. Concomitant medications included metoprolol (50 mg) and levothyroxine (0.05 mg daily). Author note that postmarketing reports of troglitazone-related death and transplantation led to withdrawal from the British market.

Liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis, and despite aggressive medical therapy the patient deteriorated and died 8 weeks after presentation. The authors describe this as a case of fatal hepatitis associated with troglitazone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (85-year-old) man with type 2 diabetes, on insulin for 10 years, receiving concurrent metoprolol (50 mg) and levothyroxine (0.05 mg daily).
raw_record.extra_details: Presented with abdominal pain, malaise, jaundice; ALT 608 U/L initially then 287 U/L (normal 10-45), total bilirubin 15.6 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, normal prothrombin time, glycosylated hemoglobin 5.2%; serology negative for hepatitis A, B, and C; normal hepatic ultrasonogram; later confusion, agitation, ascites, edema; liver biopsy showed lobular cholestatic hepatitis with confluent necrosis/submassive hepatic necrosis (Masson trichrome, x63); troglitazone started 5 months before presentation and discontinued upon referral; patient died 8 weeks after presentation. Authors also note that, according to clinical trial experience, troglitazone-related hepatotoxicity is usually asymptomatic, mild, and reversible, and that news of six deaths and one liver transplantation associated with troglitazone led to withdrawal of the product from the British market.

The introduction documents the spectrum of reported CPA hepatotoxic reactions including immunoallergic cytotoxic reactions, cholestasis, autoimmune hepatitis, acute hepatitis, and fulminant hepatic failure, and notes that only 1 of 14 reported patients with CPA-induced hepatic failure has survived. In this case, hepatic failure developed months after starting daily 200 mg CPA; laboratory findings included AST/ALT 529/223 IU/L, total/direct bilirubin 10.6/5.2 mg/dL, ammonia 294, INR 2.4; the patient died 20 days after admission of multi-organ failure. Viral hepatitis and autoimmune hepatitis markers were negative.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) preventive treatment is associated with hepatotoxicity. The 1977 Public Health Service (PHS) Cooperative Surveillance Study showed increasing age was associated with increasing risk of INH toxicity up to age 64, with a fall in risk thereafter, and a rate of eight probable hepatotoxicity cases per 1000 individuals over 65 was used as a high limit for serious toxicity. The International Union Against Tuberculosis (IUAT) study of 28,000 people under age 65 found 5.2 cases of hepatitis per 1000 in those receiving INH for 12 months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (over 65) preventive-treatment setting; monthly serum AST (SGOT) monitoring model assumed; decision-analysis context
raw_record.extra_details: PHS 1977 Cooperative Surveillance Study: risk rose with age to 64 then fell; 8 probable hepatotoxicity cases per 1000 individuals over 65 used as high limit; PHS did not monitor liver enzymes routinely, only on symptom. IUAT study (~28,000, age <65): 5.2 hepatitis cases per 1000 with 12-month INH. Death from toxicity: 8 deaths among 174 hepatitis cases (case fatality 4.6%, 0.58 deaths per 1000 taking medication); none in people over 65, 7 of 8 in Baltimore; most had other conditions such as severe alcoholism or other hepatotoxic medications.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports an unusual case of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI) due to pirfenidone presenting as acute liver failure (ALF). A 77-year-old man with Parkinson's disease and IPF had been taking pirfenidone 200 mg three times daily for 1 month; he presented with jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, and ALF. Other etiologies were ruled out, and a RUCAM score of 7 suggested possible DILI-ALF; the postmortem liver biopsy revealed centrizonal confluent hepatic necrosis and bridging necrosis consistent with DILI, with a final RUCAM score of 10 (highly probable). The patient died on day 4 of illness.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly 77-year-old man with IPF and Parkinson's disease; concomitant levodopa/carbidopa considered incompatible on timing with reaction onset; no pre-existing liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose pirfenidone 200 mg three times daily for 1 month without liver function monitoring. RUCAM score 7 initially (possible DILI-ALF) and final RUCAM score 10 (highly probable). Labs: total/conjugated bilirubin 12.8/7.5 mg/dL, AST 1260 U/L, ALT 526 U/L, ALP 434 U/L, INR 2.1. Postmortem biopsy: centrizonal confluent hepatic necrosis, bridging necrosis, Kupffer cells/macrophages with lipofuscin, portal lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils. ALF with grade III hepatic encephalopathy, MELD 31, King's College criteria; liver transplant declined; patient died on day 4.

raw_record.support_text: An 83-year-old male admitted for possible community-acquired pneumonia received azithromycin and ceftriaxone. After 2 doses of azithromycin, AST and ALT exceeded 3 times the upper limit of normal and continued rising with subsequent doses; total bilirubin stayed within normal limits and abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly. Liver enzymes, INR, and aPTT continued to climb until hospital day 5, when azithromycin was discontinued, after which all values decreased over days 6-8. The authors conclude a potentially serious liver injury occurred with azithromycin initiation and began resolving quickly after discontinuation, describing it as the third reported case of direct hepatocellular injury (cholestatic injury being well described with azithromycin).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly 83-year-old male; indication of possible community-acquired pneumonia; concurrently received ceftriaxone; rosuvastatin and fenofibrate were held on admission and not resumed; rivaroxaban held for renal function.
raw_record.extra_details: After 2 doses: AST and ALT >3x ULN, rising with subsequent doses; total bilirubin remained normal; hepatomegaly on ultrasound; INR, aPTT, and LDH climbed until hospital day 5 then decreased over days 6-8 after azithromycin discontinuation (dechallenge improvement). Hepatitis serologies negative. Paper states it is the third reported case of direct hepatocellular injury with azithromycin, whereas cholestatic injury is well described.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of 22 males (70 ± 8 years, range 54–83) with prostate cancer treated with cyproterone acetate (CPA) 150 ± 50 mg/day (range 50–200) who developed CPA-induced liver injury was collected from 1993 to 2013. Latency was 163 ± 97 days. Most patients were symptomatic showing hepatocellular injury (91%) and jaundice. Severity was mild in 1, moderate in 7, severe in 11 and fatal in 3 (14%); five developed ascites, four encephalopathy, and one had liver injury resembling autoimmune hepatitis. RUCAM was 'highly probable' in 19 (86%), 'probable' in 1, and 'possible' in 2. The authors conclude CPA-induced liver injury is severe, can be fatal, and may occasionally resemble autoimmune DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly male prostate-cancer patients (70 ± 8 years; range 54–83); therapeutic daily dose 50–200 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 cases. Latency 163 ± 97 days. Liver tests at onset: ALT 18 ± 13 x ULN, ALP 0.7 ± 0.7 x ULN, total serum bilirubin 14 ± 10 mg/dl. INR >1.5 in 14 (66%). Severity: mild 4%, moderate 32%, severe 50%, fatal 14%. Ascites in 5, encephalopathy in 4; 4 developed ALF features; 11 (50%) hospitalized. One case resembled autoimmune hepatitis; 3 required steroids (two with high ANA titres). Liver biopsy in 7 patients: two hepatocellular collapse, one submassive necrosis, two cholestatic hepatitis, one cirrhosis with iron overload, one autoimmune hepatitis. RUCAM highly probable 86%, probable 4%, possible 9%.

raw_record.support_text: Cholestatic jaundice developed in a 64-year-old woman who had received phenytoin sodium for more than 40 years. Discontinuation of phenytoin resolved the hepatic abnormalities, which recurred on rechallenge, strongly suggesting a causal relation. Re-discontinuation gave complete resolution; a liver biopsy taken during therapy showed cholestasis compatible with biliary obstruction, although no obstruction was ever demonstrated. The biochemical and histologic findings were interpreted as an unusual response to phenytoin therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old male patient with advanced prostate adenocarcinoma, treated with cyproterone acetate (CPA) 200 mg/day for advanced prostate cancer, developed severe drug-induced hepatotoxicity after about four months, presenting with marked fatigue, jaundice and dark urine. Laboratory values included total bilirubin 22.3 mg/dL, AST 1,487 IU/mL, ALT 2,044 IU/mL, AP 223 IU/mL, GGT 335 IU/mL, and prothrombin index 43% at a later point. Drug-induced hepatitis caused by CPA was suspected, other causes of liver injury were excluded, and the patient was diagnosed with toxic acute hepatitis according to the CIOMS scale with a score of 9. Liver biopsy showed extensive periportal necrosis, intense interface hepatitis, and evolution to active cirrhosis, improving after CPA withdrawal and corticosteroid treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (66 years) with advanced prostate adenocarcinoma; treated with prolonged high-dose CPA (200 mg/day); prior treatment with bicalutamide and goserelin; comorbid corticosteroid-induced hyperglycemia/diabetes during management.
raw_record.extra_details: CPA, an oral anti-androgen, 200 mg/day; symptom onset after approximately 4 months of treatment. CIOMS/RUCAM causality score 9; rechallenge not performed for ethical reasons. Laboratory peaks: total bilirubin up to 29.1 mg/dL, AST 1359-1487 IU/mL, ALT 1655-2044 IU/mL, AP 223-242 IU/mL, GGT 195-335 IU/mL, PI 43%. Histology: extensive periportal necrosis, intense interface hepatitis with lymphocyte predominance, inflammatory septa, progressing to active cirrhosis; moderate steatosis on ultrasound; transient elastography fell from 72 to 19 kPa over two years. Managed with prednisone, budesonide, and ursodeoxycholic acid; patient recovered. The paper notes direct hepatotoxicity mediated by an idiosyncratic mechanism was hypothesized by some authors, and that adverse hepatic reactions may be more common in elderly patients with malignant disease on prolonged high doses.

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presented with itching and jaundice after 2 months on repaglinide (started at 1 mg/day, increased to 2 mg/day). Laboratory testing showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (83 U/l), alanine aminotransferase (183 U/l), alkaline phosphatase (307 U/l), γ-glutamyl-transferase (303 U/l), and total bilirubin (12.2 mg/dl with direct 9.4 mg/dl); serology ruled out viral causes, autoantibody screening was negative, and imaging including MR cholangiography was normal. A liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with mild bile duct proliferation and a moderate inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes and some eosinophils) with hepatocyte ballooning. Repaglinide was discontinued and laboratory findings normalized within a month.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (72-year-old man); renal impairment with estimated creatinine clearance of 46.59 ml/min (Cockcroft-Gault). Dose was escalated from 1 mg/day to 2 mg/day within the therapeutic range.
raw_record.extra_details: First published report of cholestatic hepatitis related to repaglinide. Latency approximately 2 months; 2-week history of pruritus and jaundice at presentation. Laboratory values: AST 83 U/l (normal <37), ALT 183 U/l (normal <40), ALP 307 U/l (normal <136), GGT 303 U/l (normal <85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dl; serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dl. Liver biopsy: expanded portal areas with mild bile duct proliferation, moderate inflammatory infiltrate (predominantly lymphocytes with some eosinophils), and hepatocyte ballooning. Viral serology negative, autoantibodies negative, MR cholangiography unremarkable. Rapid improvement and normalization within one month after drug withdrawal (positive dechallenge, no rechallenge). Authors note causal role strongly supported by temporal eligibility, exclusion of alternative causes, histology, and improvement after withdrawal; presence of eosinophils suggests a possible immune mechanism. Repaglinide is a meglitinide analog antidiabetic; its clearance depends on hepatic enzyme activity and hepatic blood flow, factors impaired in the elderly.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of symptomatic acute hepatotoxicity secondary to the use of bicalutamide, a nonsteroidal anti-androgen used during initiation of androgen deprivation therapy for metastatic prostate cancer, noting that while uncommon, acute drug-induced liver injury is possible with bicalutamide therapy, typically presenting as transient liver function derangement.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (81 years old) with metastatic prostate cancer receiving bicalutamide for anti-androgen flare suppression during androgen deprivation therapy; single-agent use.
raw_record.extra_details: An 81-year-old African American male with metastatic prostate cancer started bicalutamide 3 weeks before presenting with nonspecific symptoms and 1-day jaundice; physical exam showed scleral icterus; workup showed acutely elevated transaminases (>5x ULN), elevated alkaline phosphatase, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy. Competing etiologies (viral, common toxins, drugs, autoimmune, copper-induced hepatitis) were considered. Bicalutamide was discontinued and the patient managed with supportive care, with improvement of clinical and laboratory abnormalities within days. The authors note that while rare, clinically significant and potentially life-threatening liver injury can result from bicalutamide and that prompt recognition and discontinuation are necessary.

raw_record.support_text: An 83-year-old man treated with 0·2 mg moxonidine daily for moderate hypertension, with no other medication and an uneventful past history, developed itching, nausea, painless jaundice and a maculopapular rash 9 months after starting moxonidine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (83-year-old man); hypertension indication; single-agent therapeutic exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 0.2 mg/day; latency 9 months after treatment start; symptoms of itching, nausea, painless jaundice, maculopapular rash. Bilirubin rose to 173 µmol/L then 412 µmol/L, transaminases >1000 U/L (ASAT 1005, ALAT 1560) with only slight elevation of GGT and alkaline phosphatase. Liver biopsy showed severe localised intralobular and intraportal lymphoplasmocellular infiltrates with some neutrophils, intracytoplasmatic intracanalicular cholestasis, mild small-duct proliferation and considerable localised pericellular fibrosis. ANA, AMA, ANCA negative; α-1-antitrypsin, caeruloplasmin, copper normal; hepatitis B and C excluded, hepatitis A IgM negative. Patient recovered after drug discontinuation (vitamin K, albumin, diuretics), discharged within 4 weeks, liver indices normal 8 weeks after stopping and 1 year later. Authors note this is the first reported case and that in a manufacturer postmarketing surveillance programme none of >20,000 patients developed cholestatic hepatitis; they judge the case as drug-induced inflammatory intrahepatic cholestasis compatible with a causative role for moxonidine.

raw_record.support_text: In this single-patient case report, the authors state that the findings in their case are most consistent with acetaminophen-induced liver injury, concluding that acetaminophen protein adducts may aid identification of liver injury due to an adverse drug effect. The patient received therapeutic IV acetaminophen and developed hepatic injury characterized by elevated transaminases, coagulopathy, and elevated serum bilirubin and ammonia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (>75 years) with limited clinical experience of IV acetaminophen, post-operative and catabolic with NPO status, multiple doses administered over several days, and evidence of prior hepatic disease by ultrasound; the authors consider these uncommon circumstances to limit generalizability to a small number of patients.
raw_record.extra_details: IV route; no monitoring of hepatic transaminases or INR (recommended if IV acetaminophen is continued beyond 48 h); ALT elevation higher than that observed during heparin administration; coagulopathy and elevated serum bilirubin and ammonia; APAP-CYS serum adducts used to identify acetaminophen-induced liver injury; caution advised when acetaminophen is used in patients with prior hepatic disease; report acknowledges inability to draw causal inference inherent to a single case report.

raw_record.support_text: The case presents severe cholestatic jaundice induced by amiodarone in an elderly patient, illustrating the rarity of this complication after extensive diagnostic testing ruled out biliary or pancreatic malignancy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient; low-dose amiodarone with a total cumulative dose of 100 g; onset of jaundice more than 8 weeks after drug intake.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe cholestatic jaundice attributed to amiodarone; only seven cases of amiodarone-induced cholestatic jaundice have been reported worldwide, with total doses ranging from 4.2 to 648 g, and only five of the seven patients had severe cholestatic jaundice. Other causes of cholestasis were excluded by serologic, histologic, and imaging studies. Extrahepatic manifestations included corneal deposits, constipation, and dysthyroidism. Slow resolution of hepatotoxicity occurred after ursodeoxycholic acid administration. Amiodarone is an iodinated benzofuran derivative metabolized to desethylamiodarone by hepatic cytochrome P450; amiodarone and desethylamiodarone may accumulate in human liver at concentrations up to 800 and 6500 mg/kg respectively. Lysosomal lamellar bodies occur in almost all amiodarone-treated patients and denote drug exposure, not toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The 2 individuals with a fatal/liver transplant outcome within 6 months after DILI onset were elderly, had pre-existing chronic liver disease, and presented with jaundice and a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury. Patient 15, a 60-year-old woman with underlying nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, was treated with azithromycin for 3 days for a respiratory tract infection and underwent liver transplantation 1 month after initial presentation; patient 18, a 76-year-old man with daily alcohol abuse and COPD treated with a 4-day course for acute bronchitis, died 1 week later of multi-organ failure. Hepatocellular necrosis/damage with jaundice was the pattern in these fatal outcomes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patients with pre-existing chronic liver disease (nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in one case; daily alcohol abuse with COPD in the other); treated for respiratory tract/bronchial infections.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 15: 60-year-old woman, azithromycin 3 days, developed fatigue, anorexia, pain, nausea 4 days later, then jaundice and worsening mental status; bilirubin 13.8 mg/dL, ALT 1579 IU/L, Alk P 142 IU/L, INR 2.6; liver transplantation 1 month after presentation. Patient 18: 76-year-old man, 4-day course, nausea then jaundice 1 week later; bilirubin 7.2 mg/dL, ALT 8787 IU/L, Alk P 130 IU/L; small heterogeneous liver on imaging; died 1 week later of multi-organ failure.

raw_record.support_text: Lemire and Mitchell observed three cases of chlorpromazine jaundice in elderly people; in two, transient eosinophilia of 7-17% was noted. Liver-function tests showed hyperbilirubinaemia, increased serum alkaline phosphatase, and normal thymol turbidity; two had liver biopsies and all three underwent surgery. The authors concluded their patients were suffering from toxic hepatitis due to chlorpromazine, with the mechanism unknown; the presenting author notes these findings correspond with their own.

raw_record.support_text: Four patients are described in whom anicteric hepatitis appeared to be related to the use of nitrofurantoin. All had increased serum transaminase levels, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and liver biopsies suggestive of chronic active hepatitis; three showed cirrhotic features and two had circulating albumin-IgG-complexes ('tailing-albumin'). Serum transaminases became normal within weeks of drug withdrawal, while hypergammaglobulinaemia and biopsy findings persisted during 2-6 months of observation. One patient was re-challenged with nitrofurantoin, which resulted in recurrence of elevated serum transaminases after nine weeks of medication.

raw_record.support_text: Kaaber et al. report a series of 58 women and three men with nickel allergy and hand eczema treated with disulfiram; they found that hepatotoxicity was 'the most significant side effect.' Five patients had evidence of hepatitis, four of whom had symptoms so severe they required hospitalisation, and liver biopsy in four cases showed acute hepatitis. Six other patients developed raised serum aminotransferase activities. The authors conclude that 'hepatotoxicity is a frequent side effect of disulfiram treatment [for] nickel allergy' and recommend reserving disulfiram for severe, treatment-refractory cases, noting that none of the patients had sequelae from the liver damage and that the risk was not dose-related.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Evidence concerns patients with nickel allergy receiving disulfiram treatment, a population the paper suggests may be more susceptible than the general alcoholism-treatment setting; risk was reported as not dose-related.
raw_record.extra_details: Series of 58 women and 3 men with nickel allergy/hand eczema treated with disulfiram. Five patients had evidence of hepatitis (4 hospitalised), liver biopsy in 4 cases showed acute hepatitis, and 6 other patients developed raised serum aminotransferase activities. None of the patients had sequelae from the liver damage. The paper cites this ~8% incidence to argue the finding is idiosyncratic and specific to the nickel-allergy population.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the patient sustained severe hepatic necrosis from excessive therapeutic use of acetaminophen. They note the histologic features of the liver biopsy are consistent with this proposition, that the patient had a marked decrease in nutritional intake and may have had depletion of hepatic glutathione, and that this, with injudicious doses of the drug, produced a very severe liver lesion and illness. Serum acetaminophen was not measured at admission.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Excessive therapeutic use with injudicious doses; marked reduction in nutritional intake with possible hepatic glutathione depletion; not exposed to a known P-450 inducer.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report. Admission labs: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dl, leukocytes 4600/mm3, serum bilirubin 5.3 mg/dl (2.2 mg/dl direct), alkaline phosphatase 16.8 K-A units, SGOT 1321 Karmen units, prothrombin time 25 s (control 11.5 s), PTT 42.5 s (control 22 s), ammonia 189 ug/dl, HBsAg negative. Initial impression of stage I hepatic encephalopathy with acute fulminant viral hepatitis; biopsy showed centrilobular fibrosis, bridging necrosis, chronic inflammatory infiltrate, moderate fatty metamorphosis, rare coagulation necrosis, and was strongly suggestive of the toxic lesion induced by acetaminophen and atypical for viral hepatitis. Improved with conservative treatment, discharged asymptomatic after 8 days with bilirubin 1.2 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 17.4 K-A units, SGOT 17 Karmen units, normal prothrombin time.

raw_record.extra_details: 46-year-old-man (per case narrative) initially considered to have stage I hepatic encephalopathy with suspected acute fulminant viral hepatitis (HBsAg negative). Biopsy showed centrilobular fibrosis with bridging necrosis joining central areas, chronic inflammatory infiltrate, moderate fatty metamorphosis, rare coagulation necrosis of hepatocytes, and regenerative plates; findings deemed 'strongly suggestive of the toxic lesion induced by acetaminophen' and atypical for viral hepatitis. Abnormal labs at presentation: bilirubin 5.3 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 16.8 K-A units, SGOT 1321 Karmen units, prothrombin time 25 s (control 11.5 s), ammonia 189 µg/dl. Patient improved and was discharged asymptomatic after 8 days (bilirubin 1.2 mg/dl, SGOT 17 Karmen units, normal prothrombin time). The authors note he may have suffered previous, less severe episodes.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes an HIV-infected, drug-naïve female patient with a relatively low BMI, CYP2B6 516G>T (rs3745274) genotype and high efavirenz plasma concentration who was admitted 6 months after cART initiation (two NRTIs plus efavirenz) with drug-induced severe hepatotoxicity. Liver biopsy showed confluent parenchymal necrosis with mild-to-moderate portal tract inflammation and focal interface hepatitis; all other causes were excluded. The authors conclude that efavirenz has a potential harmful effect in patients with low BMI, specific genotyping, and interindividual pharmacokinetics affecting high plasma concentration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Female, HIV-infected, drug-naïve patient on cART (two NRTIs plus efavirenz); relatively low BMI; CYP2B6 516G>T (rs3745274) genotype; high efavirenz plasma concentration; interindividual pharmacokinetics.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity arose 6 months after cART initiation. Aspiration liver biopsy showed confluent parenchymal necrosis with mild-to-moderate portal tract inflammation and focal interface hepatitis. All other possible causes of the liver injury were excluded. Efavirenz is an NNRTI used in first-line cART in resource-limited settings.

raw_record.support_text: The paper treats anti-TB drug-induced hepatitis as caused by isoniazid (INH) during anti-TB treatment, noting the association of INH with hepatitis has already been reported and that the study's findings corroborate the hypothesis that acetylator status is a risk factor for the hepatic side effects of INH. Slow acetylators acetylate not only INH but also acetylhydrazine (the precursor of toxic intermediates) more slowly, and the study concludes that slow acetylators are prone to INH-induced hepatitis; the incidence of elevated serum transaminases was significantly higher in slow acetylators than in rapid/intermediate acetylators.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Finding applies to slow NAT2 acetylator phenotype/genotype individuals (slow acetylation was the only risk factor after multivariate adjustment); patients were treated with 400 mg INH in the anti-TB regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 hepatitis cases among 167 patients; slow acetylation associated with anti-TB drug-induced hepatitis, OR 3.59 (95% CI 2.53-4.64, p=0.02), confirmed with three-phenotype analysis OR 3.47 (95% CI 2.43-4.47, p=0.02). Slow acetylator phenotype OR 2.86 (95% CI 1.06-7.68) vs rapid/intermediate reference. Mechanistic basis: slow acetylation of INH and acetylhydrazine (precursor of toxic intermediates) to harmless diacetylhydrazine, with hydrazine production via direct INH hydrolysis as another route to hepatic injury; NAT2 is the main hepatic enzyme in INH metabolism. Age, sex, CYP2E1, GSTM1 and GSTT1 genotypes were not independent risk factors; CYP2E1*5/*5 rare (0.6%).

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized trial comparing NAT2 genotype-guided (PGx) with conventional standard (STD) dosing of isoniazid (INH) for drug-sensitive tuberculosis, isoniazid-related liver injury (INH-DILI) occurred in 7 of 9 slow acetylators receiving STD INH (5 mg/kg) within the first 4 weeks, versus 0 of 7 slow acetylators in the PGx group during the first 8 weeks (attributable risk difference 77.8%, p=0.003). Multivariable analysis showed the NAT2 slow acetylator genotype was associated with INH-DILI in the STD treatment. Few rapid acetylators had INH-DILI (4.2% STD, 4.6% high-dose PGx), equivalent to intermediate acetylators (4.7%). Standard-dose INH was concluded to be too much for slow acetylators. One slow acetylator required INH withdrawal after standard treatment was interrupted due to INH-DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Finding is genotype-restricted: NAT2 slow acetylator genotype at standard INH dose (5 mg/kg/day) within a first-line anti-tuberculosis combination regimen; association with slow-acetylator genotype in STD treatment only, not seen with genotype-guided lower dosing or in rapid/intermediate acetylators.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized controlled trial (n=155 evaluable patients) comparing NAT2 genotype-guided (PGx) vs conventional standard (STD) INH dosing for drug-sensitive tuberculosis. INH-DILI incidence: 77.8% (7/9) in slow acetylators on STD vs 0% (0/7) on PGx (p=0.003); 4.2% (2/48) rapid acetylators STD, 4.6% (2/44) rapid acetylators high-dose PGx, 4.7% (3/64) intermediate acetylators. INH doses: STD 5.5 mg/kg, PGx slow acetylators 2.6 mg/kg, PGx rapid acetylators 8.8 mg/kg. One rapid acetylator with INH-DILI showed no clinical improvement by week 8; 2 of 9 slow acetylators with INH-DILI on STD showed no improvement and INH was withdrawn in one. Derived from prior study assumptions of INH-DILI incidence 65% (control) vs 15% (test) in slow acetylators; combined unfavorable-event endpoint (INH-DILI or early treatment failure) reduced with PGx dosing (RR 0.354, 95% CI 0.177-0.707).

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents descriptive parameters of published amiodarone-induced liver injury case reports, comparing 20 cases that did not develop cirrhosis with 19 cases that did develop cirrhosis. Reported values include cumulative dose, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT, latency period, and recovery (period of remission) after amiodarone withdrawal, indicating these are published human cases of amiodarone hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings derived from published case reports of chronic amiodarone therapy; cirrhosis developed in 19 of 39 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Amiodarone-induced liver injury among 39 published cases (20 non-cirrhotic, 19 cirrhotic). Non-cirrhotic group: cumulative dose mean 222.7 g (median 189, range 4-1051.2), latency period mean 873.0 days, recovery 98.83 days on average. Cirrhotic group: cumulative dose mean 382.8 g (median 285), latency mean 1117.3 days. Recovery data available for 12 reversible cases: 2 within 15-30 days, 8 within 31-180 days, 2 within 6-9 months after withdrawal. ALT altered below 8x ULN in a majority; TB above 8x ULN in 3/36 (8%) of cases, about four times the general-population frequency. AP below 8x ULN in most cases, consistent with the non-cholestatic (hepatocellular) injury pattern most commonly described. Likelihood ratios favored age >65 years (2.27), ALT 1-3x ULN (1.98), and AP 3-8x ULN (2.55).; confidence_note: Overall relationship treated as established amiodarone-induced liver injury; one sentence (p:49) frames amiodarone as 'a possible cause' specifically for rare high-bilirubin cases.

raw_record.extra_details: Three of seven biopsied patients had abnormal liver biopsies (fibrosis grade 2 or 3); six of seven abnormal-biopsy cases had fibrosis grade 3, with cirrhosis (or early/very early cirrhosis) in most, including at post-mortem 5 months after DHS in case 1. Cumulative methotrexate doses were 1.0 g (case 1), 0.5 g (case 6) and 3.4 g (case 7). Liver enzyme monitoring was unhelpful in detecting fibrosis; frequent false elevations occurred with normal biopsies and one grade-3 fibrosis/cirrhosis patient had entirely normal enzymes. Dynamic hepatic scintigraphy had 83.3% sensitivity and 81.5% specificity for detecting fibrosis of grade 2 or worse, with 98.5% predictive value of a normal scan.

raw_record.support_text: The thiopurines 6-MP and AZA are useful for IBD but have significant hepatotoxicity. In a study of almost 3500 patients, AZA/6-MP-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in 3.4% of patients, with an overall incidence of about 1% per patient-year in IBD patients on 6-MP/AZA, with no difference between AZA and 6-MP. Most mild thiopurine-induced liver injury occurs in the first few months of therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in IBD patients on thiopurine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: AZA/6-MP-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in 3.4% of patients in a study of almost 3500 patients; overall hepatotoxicity incidence approximately 1% per patient-year. No difference in hepatotoxicity incidence between AZA and 6-MP. Most mild thiopurine-induced liver injury occurs in the first few months of therapy; transient enzyme elevations may resolve spontaneously without dose adjustment. Serious thiopurine hepatotoxicity grouped into three categories: hypersensitivity (arises 2-3 weeks after initiation, cholestatic profile with elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase), dose-dependent endothelial cell injury (manifesting at 3 months to 3 years as peliosis hepatis, nodular regenerative hyperplasia, veno-occlusive disease, sinusoidal dilatation and/or fibrosis), and idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction with severe jaundice that may not resolve after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate-induced pathological liver changes in IBD were described in two case series. In one, 11 patients treated for a median of 18 months (range 7-58) with a mean cumulative dose of 1225 mg (range 220-3400 mg) showed 5 cases of mild steatosis, one case each of granulomatous hepatitis with mild portal fibrosis, slight sinusoid dilation, and periportal fibrosis, and 3 normal biopsies. In another, 20 patients biopsied after a mean methotrexate duration of 131.7 weeks and mean cumulative dose of 2633 mg had normal or Roenigk grade I changes in 17 (85%) and grade II-IIIb changes in 3.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients receiving methotrexate therapeutically; histological changes assessed by liver biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Study 1: 11 IBD patients, median 18 months (7-58), mean cumulative dose 1225 mg (220-3400 mg); 5 mild steatosis, 1 granulomatous hepatitis with mild portal fibrosis, 1 slight sinusoid dilation, 1 periportal fibrosis, 3 normal. Study 2: 20 patients, mean duration 131.7 weeks (66-281), mean cumulative dose 2633 mg (1500-5410 mg); 17 normal or Roenigk grade I, 3 grade II-IIIb. Abnormal serum transaminase levels are not predictive of hepatic histological changes. Risk factors for liver injury: alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes mellitus, >1500 mg dose, and frequent dosing intervals (in psoriatic patients).

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate sodium is used as monotherapy in the long-term management of severe psoriasis, and liver fibrosis is described as its main disadvantage. The text notes that studies vary on the prevalence of methotrexate-induced liver injury in patients with psoriasis, and recommends evaluation of liver enzyme levels, procollagen III peptide (PIIINP) levels, and periodic liver biopsies during therapy. The conclusions further frame transient elastography and FibroTest as effective noninvasive tools for monitoring hepatotoxicity in patients receiving methotrexate for psoriasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in patients with psoriasis receiving long-term methotrexate; comorbidities such as obesity, alcohol intake, and diabetes mellitus may increase the risk of liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver fibrosis is cited as the main disadvantage of methotrexate; recommended monitoring includes serial liver enzymes, PIIINP, periodic liver biopsy, and (per 2009 AAD guidelines) biopsy consideration in low-risk patients with persistent abnormal LFTs or after cumulative methotrexate dose of 3.5-4.0 g. In the study cohort (77 patients), transient elastography was abnormal in 9/50 (18%; range 7.1-11.3 kPa) and FibroTest (METAVIR >F1) abnormal in 11/70 (16%); cumulative methotrexate dose (r=0.31) and duration of therapy (r=0.36) correlated with abnormal FibroTest results. All 5 biopsied patients showed steatosis, and 2 had hepatic fibrosis, 1 with a sinusoidal pattern attributed to steatohepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hospitalization rates for acute idiopathic liver injury among troglitazone-exposed patients were 55- to 124-fold greater than expected background rates (10-22 per million person-years), and that the incidence of idiopathic ALF among troglitazone-exposed patients was increased more than 240-fold. Additional evidence cited includes a 485-fold greater reporting of ALF with troglitazone than glipizide in the FDA adverse drug reaction database, three patients registered with the United Network for Organ Sharing for liver transplantation with troglitazone cited as the cause, whereas none were registered for sulfonylureas or metformin, and fatal/mortal ALF cases in postmarketing and randomized trial cohorts. The paper concludes that the high rate of ALF observed with troglitazone was not caused by type 2 diabetes itself.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings limited to type 2 diabetic patients treated with troglitazone; comparisons assumed to a general-population background rate.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the serious complications of methotrexate therapy, especially hepatic and pulmonary toxicity, warrant attention, and that hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis remain a major concern for regular prescribers of methotrexate. In a prospective ultrastructural study of 15 rheumatoid arthritis patients, an increase in hepatic sinusoidal collagen, the ultrastructural marker of fibrosis, was demonstrated in five of the 15 patients after 2 years of treatment, and noninvasive (radioisotopic) tests were found inferior to biopsy for detecting methotrexate-induced toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings reported in rheumatoid arthritis patients receiving therapeutic methotrexate; fibrosis detected ultrastructurally (increased sinusoidal collagen in 5 of 15 patients after 2 years).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis described as a serious complication of methotrexate therapy; prospective ultrastructural study showed increased hepatic sinusoidal collagen in 5 of 15 RA patients after 2 years despite normal light microscopic findings; radioisotopic noninvasive tests were inferior to liver biopsy for detecting methotrexate-induced hepatic toxicity. ACR Subcommittee on Hepatic Toxicity and Methotrexate monitoring recommendations (p.19) advise baseline CBC, creatinine, liver function tests, hepatitis B/C serology, serial liver function tests every 4-8 weeks, and liver biopsies under specified conditions (elevated AST in 5 of 9 or 6 of 12 yearly readings, or fall in serum albumin).

raw_record.support_text: The study defined atorvastatin-induced liver injury (AILI) as clinically diagnosed based on symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and jaundice, with physical examination and blood test findings after atorvastatin administration. From the BioBank Japan cohort, 30 Japanese patients clinically diagnosed with AILI were compared against 414 atorvastatin-treated patients without liver injury (non-AILI group).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to a Japanese population; patients were clinically diagnosed with AILI during atorvastatin therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: AILI diagnosis based on symptoms (nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, jaundice), physical examination, and blood tests after atorvastatin administration. 30 AILI cases versus 414 non-AILI controls from BioBank Japan. The paper hypothesized that higher atorvastatin concentrations can cause hepatocellular injury even at appropriate atorvastatin dosages, and reports that ABCB1 rs2032582 was significantly associated with AILI, with the G allele identified as an AILI risk factor in vivo and in vitro.

raw_record.support_text: In two Phase 1 studies, AB-506 (an HBV capsid inhibitor) was given at 160 mg or 400 mg daily for 28 days to subjects with chronic HBV infection. Four subjects (all Asian) had Grade 4 alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevations during HBV DNA decline, with three events leading to treatment discontinuation; in a follow-up study, 2 Asian healthy subjects had serious transaminitis events leading to treatment and study termination. No subjects had bilirubin elevations or signs of hepatic decompensation. The authors conclude that these findings suggest AB-506 hepatotoxicity contributed to the ALT elevations, and the AB-506 development program was terminated because of these findings.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to Asian subjects; observed in both subjects with chronic HBV infection and healthy subjects; transient severe ALT flares with treatment/study discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 1 randomized double-blinded studies; AB-506 doses 160 mg or 400 mg daily for 28 days; Grade 4 ALT elevations in 4 CHB subjects (2 at each dose) plus 2 serious transaminitis events in Asian healthy subjects; no bilirubin elevations or hepatic decompensation; mean HBV-DNA declines 2.1 log10 IU/ml (160 mg) and 2.8 log10 IU/ml (400 mg); AB-506 development program terminated because of these hepatotoxicity findings.

raw_record.support_text: In Chinese NSCLC patients receiving gefitinib, several NF-κB pathway SNPs were associated with gefitinib-induced hepatic toxicity: RELA rs11227247 (Fisher's exact test P=0.038, recessive model), NFKBIB rs2053071 (P=0.004, Fisher's; P=0.021 dominant model), and NFKBIA rs2233407 which was associated with severe hepatic toxicity (grade ≥2) (P=0.04, recessive model). Stepwise logistic regression confirmed RELA rs11227247 as a factor for gefitinib-induced hepatic toxicity (GG vs non-GG: OR=0.212, 95% CI 0.062–0.726, P=0.013). Gefitinib is thereby identified as the agent producing hepatic toxicity in these patients, with the studied SNPs framed as biomarkers predicting these adverse drug reactions.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to Chinese patients with non-small cell lung carcinoma receiving gefitinib as their anti-cancer therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic toxicity graded 0, 1, and 2+ (severe defined as grade ≥2). Associated genetic variants: RELA rs11227247 (hepatic toxicity, GG vs non-GG OR=0.212, 95% CI 0.062–0.726, P=0.013 on stepwise logistic regression; P=0.038 Fisher's exact, recessive), NFKBIB rs2053071 (P=0.004 Fisher's, P=0.021 dominant), NFKBIA rs2233407 (severe hepatic toxicity, P=0.04 recessive). Multiple other SNPs (ARFGEF3, DPT, IKBKB, IKBKE, NFKB1, NFKB2, NFKBIA, NR1H2, REL, SUMO4, TAB2, TAGAP, TNFAIP3) showed no significant association (NS). Gefitinib trough concentrations were available in 75 patients (median 231.15 ng/mL, range 47.8–773.6 ng/mL) with no significant genotype-dependent difference after FDR adjustment; the SNPs are presented as potential predictive biomarkers rather than the injuring entities.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that 6-TG-treated inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients are at significant risk for nodular hyperplasia, early fibrosis and, less often, venous outflow disease (Budd-Chiari). This is based on histologic study of 38 liver biopsies from patients treated with 6-thioguanine (6-TG), including 125 patients who received 6-TG for 1 to 3 years at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients treated with 6-thioguanine as an alternative to azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine; the majority of the 125 patients used 6-TG for 1 to 3 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 38 liver biopsies from 37 patients. Reticulin staining showed nodular regeneration of varying degree in 20/37 patients (53%); only 4/20 were seen with hematoxylin and eosin. Minimal fibrosis was seen with trichrome in 13 biopsies (34%); sinusoidal collagen deposition was seen in 14/23 cases examined by electron microscopy (60%). The single biopsy with nodular hyperplasia obvious on hematoxylin and eosin also showed changes of venous outflow obstruction. Background states 6-TG-related hepatotoxicity, including liver biochemistry elevations, sinusoidal collagen deposition, and veno-occlusive disease, had been described with its use in neoplastic disease, and that 6-TG caused liver cell necrosis and jaundice generally with veno-occlusive disease (VOD), with VOD regarded as the most characteristic 6-TG lesion; VOD and Budd-Chiari syndrome have also been reported in patients taking thioguanine alone or with other drugs. Authors recommend periodic rebiopsy for patients without nodular hyperplasia or fibrosis who continue 6-TG.

Despite ocular remission, tapering or discontinuation of MTX was required for 2 patients owing to MTX adverse effects, indicating the importance of monitoring cumulative adverse effects of MTX.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity observed in almost 50% of patients at some point during follow-up; mostly tolerable or improved with dose adjustment. raw_record.support_text: Long-term treatment with pexidartinib was reported to have a predictable effect on hepatic aminotransferases and an unpredictable risk of serious cholestatic or mixed liver injury. Prolonged pexidartinib treatment may be associated with hepatic laboratory abnormalities, including hepatic adverse reactions, of two clinically distinct types: frequent isolated aminotransferase elevations (>90%), which were reversible with dose interruption and dose dependent, and mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity (<5%), which in clinically significant cases presented as increases in alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin with aminotransferase elevations. All cases of serious liver toxicity presented in the first 8 weeks of treatment and all resolved in patients with TGCT.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to patients with tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT); open-label uncontrolled study with liberal dose reductions and holidays due to the non-life-threatening disease course and long cumulative therapy duration.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic adverse reactions fell into two clinically distinct types: isolated aminotransferase elevations (>90% of hepatic ARs), frequent, reversible with dose interruption and dose dependent; and mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity (<5%), which in clinically significant cases presented as increased alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin with aminotransferase elevations. Serious liver toxicity occurred within the first 8 weeks and all cases resolved in TGCT patients. Study is open-label and uncontrolled with centralized time-blinded TVS assessment; long-term pexidartinib showed tolerable safety with no late-emerging toxicity, most frequent TEAE being hair color change.

raw_record.support_text: In 49 psoriatic patients receiving long-term low-dose methotrexate who underwent liver biopsy, 12 were found to have hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis consistent with methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity, and the study concludes that ultrasound and radionuclide scans cannot reliably replace liver biopsy in detecting significant methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to psoriatic patients receiving long-term once-weekly low-dose oral methotrexate.
raw_record.extra_details: Cumulative methotrexate doses ranged from 0.5 g to 10 g (median 2.8 g) over 1-13 years (median 5.3 years); 49 patients studied (26 male, 23 female, age 22-69 years, median 46). Injury manifest as hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis (12 patients with fibrosis or cirrhosis). Ultrasound failed to detect any of the 12 patients with fibrosis/cirrhosis; radionuclide scans missed 1 of 3 cirrhosis and 5 of 9 fibrosis cases.

raw_record.support_text: The authors identified four individuals who, after consumption of Epistane (EPI, an orally administered 17α-alkylated testosterone derivative with a 2a-3a epithio ring), developed long-lasting cholestasis. In three patients the serum bile acid pool was increased 14- to 61-fold, mainly on account of primary conjugated bile acids (cholic acid conjugates). The paper concludes that EPI could cause cholestasis by inducing bile acid synthesis and favoring bile acid accumulation in hepatocytes, at least in part via androgen receptor activation, and anticipates that this explains the idiosyncratic nature of EPI-induced cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Four young males who took EPI orally in an intensive administration posology (body-builder misuse); onset was sudden and recovery of normal liver functions took many weeks after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: EPI is 17α-methylated epitiostanol (C20H32OS, CAS 2363-58-8), a potent AR agonist. Patients developed severe cholestasis with jaundice and pruritus; some required MARS albumin dialysis to lower bilirubin levels. Pure (bland) cholestasis with prominent conjugated bilirubin rise and moderate/minimal ALT, AST, AP elevations, no hepatocellular necrosis. In vitro: EPI (0.01 µM) upregulated CYP7A1 (~65%) and CYP8B1 (~67%) and BA transporters (NTCP, OSTA, BSEP), downregulated FGF19; 40 µM activated LXR and PXR; 0.01 µM activated AR and induced bile acid synthesis/accumulation in cultured human hepatocytes. Human liver bank samples showed AR expression positively correlated with CYP8B1 in men. Context: AAS DILI rose from 1% (2007-2009) to 8% (2010-2013) of Spanish DILI Registry cases.

raw_record.support_text: In the Mayo Clinic therapeutic trial of CDCA for gallstone dissolution, liver toxicity assessed by plasma aminotransferase activity was not present in most patients, and at doses up to 4 g/day there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity. A large NIH-sponsored multicenter placebo-controlled double-blind study (NCGS) and large French and Italian studies confirmed the safety of CDCA in gallstone subjects; a small percent developed elevated aminotransferase levels that returned to normal when CDCA was discontinued, with the mild toxicity attributable to CDCA per se.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Gallstone patients treated for gallstone dissolution; doses up to 4 g/day in some Mayo instances; NCGS used 10 mg/kg-day CDCA.
raw_record.extra_details: Explicit negative conclusion on human hepatotoxicity: no evidence of hepatotoxicity at Mayo and NCGS/large European trials confirmed safety of CDCA. A small percentage developed elevated plasma aminotransferase levels that returned to normal upon discontinuation; this mild toxicity appeared attributable to CDCA per se rather than to lithocholic acid (Fisher et al., 1991). British studies with liver biopsies showed only minor histological changes. Acute severe hepatotoxicity observed in fetal Rhesus monkeys is animal data and excluded from this human record.

raw_record.support_text: Tolcapone toxicity problems became apparent soon after its market introduction: three patients taking tolcapone died of hepatic failure, which was attributed to the use of the drug, leading to suspension of tolcapone in the EU and a black box warning in the US. Three deaths from fulminant hepatic failure in 40,000 patient-years is 10-100 times higher than the expected incidence in the general population, and the manufacturer's own information indicates the number is probably underestimated due to under-reporting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: General adult Parkinson's disease population on therapeutic dosing; no co-exposure restrictions reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Three deaths from fulminant hepatic failure in 40,000 patient-years, 10-100x higher than expected population incidence and probably under-reported. Phase III trials showed serum ALT increases ≥3x ULN in 1% of patients at 100mg three times daily and 3% at 200mg three times daily versus placebo, with some patients reaching serum ALT levels eight times above ULN; ALT was taken as an index of hepatocyte turnover/death, prompting routine ALT monitoring. One fatal case showed mitochondrial swelling, loss of cristae and reduced matrix density. Preclinical toxicology (rat, plasma AUC 14x human) confirmed rat liver toxicity and mitochondrial uncoupling, but these are supportive animal findings; entacapone showed no rat hepatotoxicity (AUC up to 21x human) and lacked the uncoupling activity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper analyzes annual reports of halothane-induced liver injury in Sweden, 1966-1973, with the hatched sections of the columns representing the number of fatal cases, and the arrows indicating when information was received from the Swedish Adverse Drug Reaction committee. This is a case series (94 patients) in which halothane anaesthesia is explicitly attributed as the cause of the reported liver injury, including 13 fatal cases (16% mortality).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: General adult surgical population undergoing halothane anaesthesia; one male not operated but exposed during work as a surgeon.
raw_record.extra_details: 94 reported cases of halothane-induced liver injury in Sweden 1966-1973 (13 fatal = 16% mortality). 4 men and 10 women among 14 fatal cases; operations included burns, plastic surgery, breast carcinoma, varicose veins, gall bladder extirpation, leg fracture, hysterectomy. Number of halothane exposures among 93 patients: 1 exposure in 23 (1 death), 2 in 44 (6 deaths), 3 in 20 (4 deaths), 4 or more in 6 (2 deaths). Operation duration recorded for 83 patients. Mean maximum serum bilirubin values increased with number of exposures. Australia antigen negative in all 39% of patients tested; moderate blood transfusion (1-4 units) given to 25% of patients; previous allergic manifestations in 10%. Age-related incidence per 10^6 inhabitants compared with infectious hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 64-year-old man was admitted with asthenia, jaundice and dark urine, after taking nimesulide 100 mg every 12 h for 6 months for bone pain until 2 days before admission; he had also received Klacid® (250 mg every 8 h) and Algidol® (every 12 h) for 2 days one week earlier. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated bilirubin (total 17.6, direct 13.5), GPT 1705, GOT 1397, alkaline phosphatase 512 and GGT 823; viral (A, B, C, HIV, CMV, Epstein-Barr), atypical-bacteria and autoantibody (AMA, ANA, SMA, anti-DNA, LKM-1) markers were all negative. The patient improved and was discharged after 3 weeks, framed as a clinical case of acute hepatitis caused by nimesulide.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: General adult therapeutic exposure; specific patient also took Klacid® (250 mg every 8 h) and Algidol® (every 12 h) for 2 days one week before admission as possible co-exposures; treated for bone pain; 64-year-old male.
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID and selective COX-2 inhibitor with a sulfonanilide group, metabolized in liver to 4-hydroxy-nimesulide; 0.1% eliminated unchanged in urine. Nimesulide hepatotoxicity risk was added to its product information in January 2000 after cases of hepatitis. In the Spanish Pharmacovigilance System (FEDRA) database there are 20 suspected hepatic adverse reactions with nimesulide; 84% were women with a mean age of 66.2 years, of which 8 had only liver enzyme abnormalities and the rest symptomatic hepatotoxicity. Reported manifestations are cholestasis and hepatocellular necrosis, which (if administration is not interrupted) can progress to acute liver failure, encephalopathy and even death. Mechanism described as idiosyncratic metabolic, dose-independent and host-dependent, through aberrant metabolic pathways producing toxic metabolites or converting hepatic antigens into neoantigens triggering an immunoallergic reaction (supported by peripheral and tissue eosinophilia) or by toxic accumulation after a long latent period. In the present case the patient recovered after 3 weeks with improving liver tests; laboratory and imaging findings are recorded.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of seven patients (ages 20-57) who received chloroform (CHC) as an anesthetic during open thoracic surgery is presented; post-mortem examination showed acute centrilobar necrosis of the liver in all seven. raw_record.support_text: The paper describes halothane hepatitis as a distinct human liver injury following halothane anesthesia, characterizing it as a hypersensitive reaction in which jaundice is uncommon within the first week after a single exposure but recurs with a shortened period upon re-exposure. Halothane hepatitis is distinguished from viral hepatitis by its shorter latent period (4-14 days versus 15-50 days) and different fever-jaundice pattern.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: General anesthesia exposure; considered rare in children.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis presents as a hypersensitive reaction; on deliberate rechallenge with brief halothane exposure, repeated episodes of hepatitis were reported in two cases. Australian antigen was not demonstrable in post-halothane hepatitis sera, militating against viral hepatitis. Serum mitochondrial antibodies similar to primary biliary cirrhosis and lupoid hepatitis were demonstrated. Reported lag from exposure to symptom onset varied from day 2 to day 10, with most patients having prior halothane exposures and unexplained jaundice or fever.

raw_record.support_text: Case series of two multiple-sclerosis patients who developed acute hepatocellular drug-induced liver injury after intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (MP) given for relapse. In patient 1, following a 3-day course of 300 mg/day IV pulse MP, causality assessment using the CIOMS scale scored 7 points (probable) for MP, and liver biopsy showed centrilobular necrosis with portal fibrosis and mixed inflammatory infiltrates, with a maximum total bilirubin of 12.6 mg/dL. raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1: 300 mg/day IV for 3 days; AST 1420 U/L, ALT 2194 U/L, ALP 229 U/L, TBL 3.6 mg/dL rising to 12.6 mg/dL; jaundice, nausea, weakness, weight loss; biopsy showed centrilobular necrosis, portal fibrosis, mixed inflammatory infiltrates; CIOMS (3) score 7 = probable; liver tests normalized within 70 days. Patient 2: 1 g/day IV for 5 days followed by prednisone 60 mg/day taper over 3 weeks; AST 419 U/L, ALT 630 U/L, ALP 193 U/L, TBL 0.8 mg/dL; abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver parenchyma and biliary ducts with biliary sludge; chemistries normal 8 weeks later; a later similar non-jaundiced episode occurred after a further IV MP course (1 g/day for 3 days) with AST 122 U/L, ALT 165 U/L, ALP 125 U/L, TBL 0.46 mg/dL, normal at 11 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: In a pilot study, 24 patients with hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer received hepatic artery infusion of floxuridine (FUDR) plus leucovorin (LV) through an implantable pump. Sclerosing cholangitis developed in 2 of 8 patients treated with FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d plus LV 30 mg/m²/d for 14 days within 4 months, and in 3 of 9 patients treated with FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d plus LV 30 mg/m²/d for 7 days; no biliary sclerosis occurred at the lower FUDR dose (0.2 mg/kg/d). The authors concluded that hepatic toxicity with FUDR and LV appeared to be greater than that previously reported with FUDR alone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Given by hepatic artery infusion via an implantable pump (unusual regional route); co-infused with leucovorin (LV) as biochemical modulator; sclerosing cholangitis occurred at FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d dose levels but not at the 0.2 mg/kg/d level, indicating a dose-related effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Pilot dosing study for hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer. Regimen 1: FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d + LV 30 mg/m²/d for 14 days alternating with 2 weeks saline, sclerosing cholangitis in 2/8 patients within 4 months. Regimen 2: FUDR 0.2 mg/kg/d + LV 30 mg/m²/d for 14 days, no biliary sclerosis. Regimen 3: FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d + LV 30 mg/m²/d for 7 days alternating with 1 week saline, sclerosing cholangitis in 3/9 patients. Overall response rate 72%; 18/25 patients alive at 1 year; median survival >27 months. Hepatic toxicity appeared greater than previously reported with FUDR alone.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Graves' disease patients on therapeutic MMI treatment; indication-restricted cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 MMI-DILI cases; dosage 20.0 (20.0-30.0) mg/day; days to DILI onset 30.0 (14.0-55.0); injury pattern cholestatic 20 (50%), mixed 13 (32.5%), hepatocellular 7 (17.5%); RUCAM causality possible 1, probable 37 (92.5%), highly probable 2; peak TBIL 12.0 µmol/L, peak ALT 85.5 U/L, peak AST 48.5 U/L; HLA alleles C*03:02 (OR=15.40, 95%CI 1.77-133.9, P=0.0011), A*02:01 (OR=2.9, 95%CI 1.39-6.22, P=0.0034) and C*01:139 (P=0.0157) more frequent in MMI-DILI cases than controls.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Healthy adult male volunteers (white Caucasian, 20-50 years, BMI 20-25); single oral gel-capsule doses of 2, 4, 10, and 20 mg; Phase I tolerability study.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver-function-relevant analytes measured in blood included total bilirubin, AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, albumin; all remained within normal range in every dose group. No QT interval prolongation on ECG. At 20 mg, five volunteers reported sleepiness (n=3), excitation (n=1), and paresthesia (n=1). Minor findings included a slightly elevated temperature (37.3°C at 10 mg; 37.1°C at 20 mg) in one volunteer per group and one transient systolic pressure rise at 20 mg.

raw_record.support_text: Panadiplon, an experimental non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic, produced evidence of hepatic toxicity in phase I clinical trial volunteers, which was not predicted by rat, dog or monkey preclinical studies. Subsequent studies showed that a carboxylic acid metabolite of panadiplon caused redistribution of cellular coenzyme A stores and inhibition of β-oxidation, rendering hepatocytes sensitive to secondary stress (e.g., hypoxia), which subsequently produced apoptosis and hepatocellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Healthy volunteer subjects in a Phase I clinical trial of an investigational anxiolytic.
raw_record.extra_details: A carboxylic acid metabolite of panadiplon caused redistribution of cellular coenzyme A stores and inhibition of β-oxidation, rendering hepatocytes sensitive to secondary stress (e.g., hypoxia), producing apoptosis and hepatocellular necrosis. Hepatic toxicity was not predicted by rat, dog, or monkey preclinical studies. In vitro, co-treatment with pyruvate reduced the level of LDH leakage caused by panadiplon under hypoxic conditions (Bacon et al. 1996). This ximelagatran-related review is anchored to prior mechanistic data on panadiplon.

raw_record.support_text: A 64-year-old man with pancytopenia who had his other medications withdrawn was treated with oxymetholone (50 mg/day, increased to 100 mg/day) as a bone marrow stimulant. Fifteen months after continuous oxymetholone was begun he was readmitted with hepatic enlargement and moderately deranged liver function, and postmortem examination showed peliosis hepatis with blood-filled spaces involving approximately 50% of the liver mass; he died in shock from an intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Peliosis hepatis was the only significant histologic abnormality.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents the first reported case of terbinafine-associated cholestatic liver dysfunction in a hepatic allograft recipient. Terbinafine therapy is generally well tolerated, but the incidence of symptomatic acute liver injury is 2.5 cases per 100,000 person-months of therapy, and liver injury has been reported both in patients with preexisting liver disease and in apparently healthy patients; many case reports describe prolonged cholestatic dysfunction, and rare cases of fulminant hepatic failure necessitating transplantation have been reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic allograft recipient (orthotopic liver transplantation ~5 years prior, for ethanol-related end-stage liver disease), on immunosuppression with tacrolimus and concurrent fluoxetine and insulin; initial biopsy was misinterpreted as acute cellular rejection and the patient was treated with high-dose steroids; pre-existing end-stage liver disease history.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 51-year-old man started on terbinafine (~4 weeks earlier) for onychomycosis who developed elevated liver enzymes (total bilirubin 55.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 392 U/L, AST 246 U/L, ALT 265 U/L). A second liver biopsy after terbinafine discontinuation showed marked centrilobular cholestasis and severe bile duct damage, along with portal inflammation, mild portal fibrosis, and hepatocellular iron accumulation. Symptoms included progressive jaundice, malaise, and nausea. Patient was managed supportively but died suddenly ~3 months after terbinafine was discontinued, with no autopsy performed; hepatic function was improving at the time.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 21 patients with liver metastases (predominantly colorectal carcinoma) receiving long-term hepatic arterial infusion of 5-fluorodeoxyuridine (5-FUdR) via an Infusaid pump, the reported toxicities of therapy included fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, toxic hepatitis, epigastric pain, and diarrhea. The drug was infused at 0.2-0.3 mg/kg/day (average 0.23 mg/kg/day) in a 2-week cycle alternating with a 2-week saline-heparin infusion.

Dosing: 0.2-0.3 mg/kg/day (average 0.23 mg/kg/day) on a 2-week cycle alternating with a 2-week saline-heparin infusion, cumulative 5-FUdR delivery of 1940 days. Six patients (29%) responded to therapy; median survival 17 mo from diagnosis of liver metastases and 13 mo from pump implantation.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 34 patients receiving hepatic arterial infusion pump (HAIP) chemotherapy after resection/ablation of colorectal liver metastases, delayed complications were predominantly pump infections, chemotherapy-induced hepatitis, and biliary sclerosis. Biliary sclerosis developed in 6 (18%) patients, usually after the second or third dose of FUDR (floxuridine); all affected patients discontinued HAIP chemotherapy. Two patients had bilirubin levels of 3.3 and 2.9 mg/dL with diffuse sclerosis on cholangiogram that was not amenable to stenting, while 4 others underwent biliary stenting, with bilirubin normalization in 3 and a decline to 2.9 mg/dL in the fourth.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIP) with FUDR in patients with resectable/ablated colorectal liver metastases; non-systemic route of administration; all affected patients discontinued therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: FUDR = 5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine (floxuridine). Biliary sclerosis developed in 6 of 34 (18%) patients, usually after the second or third dose. Two patients had bilirubin 3.3 and 2.9 mg/dL with diffuse cholangiogram sclerosis not amenable to stenting; 4 underwent biliary stenting (bilirubin normalized in 3, declined to 2.9 mg/dL in one). Comparison with published series showed biliary sclerosis rates of 0.5-35% across studies.
