raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies drug toxicity associated with hepatic artery infusion of floxuridine as a point of great concern. Drug-related chemical hepatitis, gastroduodenal ulcerations and biliary toxicity are the most common reported complications resulting in cessation of therapy in many patients. In Johnson's study, 50% of patients had to discontinue therapy because of therapy-related chemical hepatitis, three patients died of perforation and bleeding from peptic ulcers, and two patients died from severe sclerosing cholangitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic arterial infusion route (hepatic artery chemotherapy) in patients with colorectal hepatic metastases.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported complications of hepatic artery infusion of floxuridine include drug-related chemical hepatitis (drug-induced hepatitis), biliary toxicity, and gastroduodenal ulcerations. In Johnson's study, 50% of patients discontinued therapy due to therapy-related chemical hepatitis; three patients died of perforation and bleeding from peptic ulcers (non-hepatic) and two patients died from severe sclerosing cholangitis.

raw_record.support_text: In the hepatic arterial FUDR+LV+Dec trial, patients showed bilirubin elevations and biliary sclerosis attributed to the FUDR-based hepatic arterial chemotherapy. Across 61 untreated and treated patients, 11 (18%) had bilirubin >3 mg/dL by 3 months, increasing to 28 (46%) beyond 6 months, with 3% developing biliary sclerosis. In the prior FUDR+LV trial, 70% of patients had bilirubin >3 mg/dL by 6 months and 21% developed biliary sclerosis at any time. These findings document cholestatic/biliary liver injury attributed to the FUDR hepatic arterial regimen, with drug-free periods required because of elevated liver enzymes or bilirubin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic arterial infusion route; metastatic colorectal carcinoma population; FUDR administered in combination with LV and/or Dec.

raw_record.support_text: In the context of hepatic artery infusion (HAI) of FUDR (floxuridine) plus dexamethasone for liver metastases from colorectal cancer, hepatic toxicity was attributed to the FUDR dose. In the original adjuvant study using FUDR 0.25 mg/kg/day × 14 days, 18 patients (24%) developed total bilirubin elevations (>3 mg/dL) and four patients required biliary stents; in the present study with a lower FUDR dose (0.12 mg/kg × pump volume ÷ pump flow rate), this was reduced to seven patients (7%) with only two requiring stents.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic artery infusion (HAI) route with dexamethasone in patients with colorectal cancer liver metastases (unresectable or post-resection); patients also received systemic CPT-11 (irinotecan).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic/biliary toxicity characterized by total bilirubin elevation >3 mg/dL and need for biliary stents. Original adjuvant study: FUDR 0.25 mg/kg/day × 14 days, 18/75 patients (24%) with bilirubin >3 mg/dL, 4 required stents. Present study: FUDR 0.12 mg/kg × pump volume ÷ pump flow rate over 14 days of a 28-day cycle, 7 patients (7%) with bilirubin elevation, 2 required stents. Hepatic toxicity decreased with the lower FUDR dose. Biliary toxicity corresponds to cholangiopathy/biliary obstruction from HAI floxuridine.

raw_record.support_text: Hohn et al treated 35 patients with HAI FUDR, and all required dose reduction; early termination due to hepatic toxicity was required in 15% of patients. In five patients with persistently elevated alkaline phosphatase, cholangiograms showed biliary sclerosis of the common hepatic duct; two underwent cholecystectomy for presumed drug-induced cholecystitis with focal narrowing of the proper hepatic ducts; and liver biopsies in three patients showed focal pericholangitis with relatively normal hepatocytes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic artery infusion (HAI) route; biliary damage associated with hepatic artery delivery, manifesting even when liver function studies are normal.
raw_record.extra_details: 35 patients, all requiring dose reduction; 15% early termination due to hepatic toxicity. Five patients had biliary sclerosis of the common hepatic duct with elevated alkaline phosphatase; two underwent cholecystectomy for presumed drug-induced cholecystitis; three liver biopsies showed focal pericholangitis with relatively normal hepatocytes; cystic duct histology showed obliterative endarteritis and mural fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports FUDR (5-fluorodeoxyuridine) delivered directly to the hepatic artery causing drug-induced cholestatic jaundice/hepatotoxicity. It describes three patients with FUDR-induced cholestatic jaundice that markedly improved subjectively and objectively after treatment with oral corticosteroids, allowing chemotherapy to continue. The reported FUDR side effects include hepatocellular toxicity as evidenced by chemical hepatitis and/or cholestatic jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Cyclophosphamide is described as known to be toxic to hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells, with several clinical reports of hepatotoxicity after cyclophosphamide use. In the authors' previous report, 7 of 17 patients who received cyclophosphamide at 200 mg/kg developed SOS (five mild, two moderate) with maximum bilirubin levels of 4.2–21 mg/dl; maximum weight gain ranged from 3.5 to 29%. A recent study showed a correlation between exposure to cyclophosphamide metabolites and development of SOS.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose (200 mg/kg) conditioning prior to hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; findings from the authors' prior conditioning cohort and from published clinical reports.
raw_record.extra_details: Known to be toxic to hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells (mechanism); in a prior report 7/17 patients (five mild, two moderate) developed SOS with maximum bilirubin 4.2–21 mg/dl and weight gain 3.5–29%; a recent study correlated cyclophosphamide-metabolite exposure (4-hydroxycyclophosphamide interpatient variability) with SOS development. Also frequently associated with hemorrhagic cystitis, interstitial pneumonitis, and hypoxia (non-hepatic).

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a patient with Crohn's disease who suffered severe hepatic injury after high-dose mesalazine. Laboratory findings were consistent with cholestasis associated with mesalazine therapy: on admission, total bilirubin 6 mg/dl, ALT 393 IU/l (normal <23), GGT 166 IU/l (normal 6-28), and alkaline phosphatase 201 IU/l (normal 50-190), all returning to normal 6 weeks later. The patient, a 30-year-old man with ileal Crohn's disease, received 4 g mesalazine daily as the only medication; hepatitis/cytomegalovirus/EBV/herpes/HIV serology and autoimmune liver antibodies were negative, and he had no evidence of gallstones, gallstones, inflammatory or rheumatic disease, or alcohol abuse.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose (4 g daily) mesalazine used as monotherapy for ileal Crohn's disease; single case.
raw_record.extra_details: 30-year-old man with 9-month history of abdominal pain; Crohn's disease diagnosed endoscopically and histologically. No evidence of liver dysfunction before therapy; symptoms (nausea, fatigue, jaundice, severe right-upper-quadrant pain, 4 kg weight loss) developed 4 months after starting mesalazine. No other concomitant medication. Viral serology (anti-HAV IgM, HBs-Ag, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, anti-HCV, HCV-PCR, CMV IgM, EBV IgM, HSV IgM, HIV) and liver-kidney-microsomal, anti-mitochondrial, anti-nuclear, anti-cytoplasmic antibodies all negative; no gallstones, no alcohol abuse, no eosinophilia (4% eosinophils). Labs returned to normal 6 weeks after stopping mesalazine.

raw_record.support_text: One patient treated with high-dose BCNU developed abnormal liver function tests and the clinical picture of veno-occlusive disease with ascites. On liver biopsy, centrilobular necrosis was apparent without sclerosis of the central vein. Over a 6-week period the liver function returned to normal and the ascites resolved.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose (>1200 mg/m²) BCNU with autologous bone marrow rescue; centrilobular necrosis without central vein sclerosis; full recovery of liver function and ascites over 6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: One of 11 treated patients (C.P., astrocytoma grade IV). Discussion: when BCNU doses exceed 1200 mg/m², persistent liver-test elevations may indicate toxic centrilobular necrosis; the affected patient recovered from this hepatotoxic picture, and progressive hepatic failure may be minimized by limiting total BCNU dose to 1200 mg/m² given over a three-day period. Dose-limiting hepatotoxicity framed as dose-related direct toxic injury.

raw_record.support_text: At a BCNU (carmustine) dose of 1,200 mg/m², severe hepatotoxicity developed in four patients with malignant glioma: two had reversible hepatocellular dysfunction and two had fatal centrilobular hepatic necrosis. In the 1,200 mg/m² group (21 patients), severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 11% of all patients (4 cases, 2 fatal), contributing to an overall severe toxicity rate of 33% and fatal rate of 15%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose BCNU (carmustine) chemotherapy at 1,200 mg/m² in patients with malignant glioma.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity followed a single 1,200 mg/m² BCNU course (21 patients: 4 hepatotoxicity, 2 fatal); no severe hepatotoxicity in 2 patients receiving two courses totaling 1,350 mg/m², and none in the 1,050 mg/m² group (13 patients). Overall, severe hepatotoxicity affected 11% of all 36 patients. Two patients had reversible hepatocellular dysfunction; two had fatal centrilobular hepatic necrosis. No causality scoring instrument reported. Lung (interstitial pneumonitis) and CNS toxicities also reported separately.

raw_record.support_text: In one study patient, an elevation of liver enzymes was noted by the investigator and considered ceftriaxone-related hepatic toxicity, prompting discontinuation of ceftriaxone; therapy was switched to co-trimoxazole and the patient improved. On assessment by the expert committee, the case was classified as ceftriaxone-related biliary pseudolithiasis. No ceftriaxone-related deaths occurred. The discussion further describes biliary toxicity as a well-known complication of high-dose ceftriaxone treatment and cites a retrospective study in which a high dosage (4 versus 2 g) of ceftriaxone was a risk factor for hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose ceftriaxone (dosing up to ≥8–10 g/day in some patients) used to treat CNS infection in adults; only ceftriaxone-related hepatic case led to treatment discontinuation and resolved after switching to co-trimoxazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Expert committee classified the case as ceftriaxone-related biliary pseudolithiasis with sludge formation and elevation of liver enzymes; five (2.6%) ceftriaxone-related ADRs were initially notified by investigators, rising to 17 (8.7%, 95% CI 5.1%–13.4%) after expert adjudication. Biliary toxicity described as a well-known complication of high-dose ceftriaxone; a cited retrospective study found high dosage (4 versus 2 g) a risk factor for hepatic toxicity. No ceftriaxone-related deaths occurred in the study.

raw_record.support_text: Of the twenty RA patients completing the prospective high-dose aspirin study, 4 developed abnormal transaminase levels without abnormalities in other liver tests, near the end of the 2-week period. Levels returned to normal in all 4 after the aspirin dosage was reduced. Three had no clinical evidence of hepatitis; the fourth developed anorexia, nausea, vomiting, loss of taste, and a tender liver while transaminases were elevated, and reported similar symptoms in the past when taking high aspirin doses that resolved on dose reduction.

raw_record.extra_details: 4 of 20 completing RA patients developed abnormal transaminases (SGOT/SGPT) without other abnormal liver tests; 3 were asymptomatic hepatic enzyme elevations and 1 developed symptomatic hepatitis (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, loss of taste for cigarettes, tender liver). Enzyme levels normalized after aspirin dose reduction; the symptomatic patient had similar past symptoms on high aspirin that resolved with dose reduction. Buffered aspirin was used.

raw_record.support_text: High-dose BCNU given before autologous bone marrow transplantation produced dose-dependent hepatotoxicity: no liver enzyme alterations up to 10 weeks at doses up to 1000 mg/m², one death from liver failure with centrilobular necrosis at 1200-1400 mg/m², and mildly elevated transaminases and alkaline phosphatase without hyperbilirubinemia at 800-1200 mg/m². Another study showed transient reversible changes in 19 patients below 1200 mg/m² but fatal hepatotoxicity in 7/12 patients at 1500-2850 mg/m², with an important liver-damage threshold in the 1200-1500 mg/m² range.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose conditioning setting before autologous bone marrow transplantation; liver damage threshold in the 1200-1500 mg/m² dose range.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug referred to as BCNU. Dana-Farber Center: no enzyme alterations up to 10 weeks at doses up to 1000 mg/m²; 1 death from liver failure 6 weeks after 1200-1400 mg/m² with centrilobular necrosis on histology; mildly elevated transaminases and alkaline phosphatase without hyperbilirubinemia in longer follow-up at 800-1200 mg/m². Another study: transient reversible changes in 19 patients below 1200 mg/m², fatal hepatotoxicity in 7/12 at 1500-2850 mg/m²; fatal liver disease became overt only after 2 months then progressed rapidly.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase II study of amifostine given as protection before high-dose cyclophosphamide (HDCY, 7 g/m²) for PBPC mobilization in 29 non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patients compared with a historical group, amifostine reduced the intensity of cardiac, pulmonary and hepatic toxicity and significantly reduced the frequency and severity of mucositis. The hepatic toxicity is thus attributed to HDCY and mitigated by amifostine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose cyclophosphamide (7 g/m²) given for PBPC mobilization and tumor reduction in non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patients, with amifostine cytoprotection administered prior to it.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II study: 29 NHL patients (22 aggressive, 7 indolent) received 58 amifostine infusions before HDCY; comparison was a historical group of 33 aggressive-NHL patients treated with VACOP-B followed by HDCY. Amifostine reduced the intensity of hepatic (as well as cardiac and pulmonary) toxicity; no deaths in the protected group versus 2/33 in the historical group (from cardiac or pulmonary toxicity). Amifostine did not prevent the aplastic phase after HDCY.

raw_record.support_text: In a Phase I trial, three patients with advanced malignant melanoma received high-dose nitrogen mustard (Mustargen, HN2) at 33 mg/m2 i.v. as a bolus followed by autologous bone marrow reinfusion 48 hours later. The reported side effects included nausea, vomiting, anorexia, alopecia, phlebitis, hepatotoxicity, and neurotoxicity, and the authors state that the nonhematologic side effects of this dose of HN2 were severe and preclude the use of higher doses.

raw_record.extra_details: Three patients on Phase I protocol; HN2 given as i.v. bolus 33 mg/m2, bone marrow transfused 48 h post-dose; hepatotoxicity listed among nonhematologic side effects that the authors describe as severe, precluding further dose escalation; HN2/nitrogen mustard aliases; associated side effects included nausea, vomiting, anorexia, alopecia, phlebitis, neurotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and hypocalcemia.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes eight cases of oxacillin-associated hepatitis and concludes the hepatitis was probably a hypersensitivity reaction, based on eosinophilia in two patients and pruritus in one, variable oxacillin dose before onset, recurrence of hepatitis upon rechallenge with oxacillin in one patient, and a statistically significant association with previous or subsequent penicillin allergy (three of eight versus none of 46, P<0.01). Withdrawal of oxacillin led to resolution of the liver function abnormalities, and the authors recommend liver function test evaluation in all patients receiving high-dose intravenous oxacillin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose intravenous oxacillin; significant association with previous or subsequent penicillin allergy (3/8 vs 0/46). Several cases had concomitant drugs (methadone, acetaminophen, hydralazine, streptomycin, etc.) as potential co-exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: Eight-case case series. Presenting features included nausea, vomiting, hepatomegaly, hepatic tenderness, and abdominal distention; eosinophilia in two patients and pruritus in one. Hepatitis recurred on rechallenge with oxacillin in one patient; liver function abnormalities resolved on drug withdrawal. Prior reported oxacillin hepatitis cases: biopsy-proven cholestatic jaundice in a 65-y-old woman after 76 g oral oxacillin; hepatic injury in a 33-y-old woman after 270 g oral oxacillin; and three anicteric hepatitis cases after 9-12 days of high-dose intravenous oxacillin (Dismukes).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX, ≥1 g/m²) chemotherapy in osteosarcoma, although improving survival, 'can however lead to harmful toxicities including renal toxicity, myelosuppression and liver damage.' The study cohort consisted of 114 osteosarcoma patients treated with HD-MTX (12 g/m² per course, up to 12 courses, 4 h infusion) under the EURAMOS-1 protocol, and liver damage was assessed by measuring plasma alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase at 48 h after MTX infusion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose methotrexate chemotherapy (12 g/m² per course, up to 12 courses, 4 h infusion) for primary high-grade osteosarcoma in patients ≤45 years of age; administered in combination with doxorubicin and cisplatin, with or without ifosfamide/etoposide or interferon-α per EURAMOS-1 randomized treatment arm; given with leucovorin rescue, hydration, and urinary alkalinization.
raw_record.extra_details: HD-MTX defined as ≥1 g/m²; MTX plasma levels showed associations with alanine aminotransferase (liver damage marker) at 48 h after infusion; no specific liver-injury severity, biochemical pattern, or clinical phenotype beyond 'liver damage'/'MTX-induced liver toxicity' was stated; the study is a pharmacogenetic investigation of ADME gene variants (SULT1E1, CYP2B6, CYP4F8) on MTX pharmacokinetics and toxicities.

raw_record.support_text: This retrospective longitudinal study, coupled with genetic testing, provided a thorough examination of the hepatotoxic effects induced by HD-MTX, incorporating clinical and biochemical parameters, MTX concentrations at multiple time points, drug interactions, and MTX administration methods. The study established a nomogram predicting risk of moderate/severe DILI (grade≥2) and identified potential risk and protective genetic factors.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose MTX (HD-MTX) therapy in patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or osteosarcoma; Han Chinese population; some patients received intravenous plus triple intrathecal injection route rather than intravenous injection alone.
raw_record.extra_details: DILI graded ≥2 (moderate/severe). Nomogram predicting risk of moderate/severe DILI included sex, MTX dose, C24h MTX concentration, ABCB1 rs1128503, and SLCO1B1 haplotypes; model AUROC 0.805 (95% CI 0.750-0.859), AUPRC 0.515. ABCB1 rs1128503 identified as a possible independent risk factor and SLCO1B1 haplotypes as protective factors for moderate/severe DILI. Higher dose-adjusted MTX concentration was more prevalent with the intravenous plus triple intrathecal route.

raw_record.support_text: High-dose MTX-induced toxicity was recorded and graded per CTCAE 3.0 in osteosarcoma patients. At least one episode of grade 3-4 liver toxicity was experienced by 26 of 37 patients (70.3%), defined as the presence of grade 3 or higher symptoms. This attributes clinically significant dose-related liver injury to high-dose methotrexate therapy in humans.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose MTX infusion as part of osteosarcoma therapy in a CTCAE-graded prospective cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Grade 3-4 liver toxicity (CTCAE 3.0, defined as grade >=3) occurred in 26/37 patients (70.3%). Plasma MTX levels at 24, 48, and 72 h (median 4.7, 0.65, 0.3 µmol/L) were not significantly associated with severe liver toxicity; MTX levels at 48 h were associated with severe mucositis (P=0.007) and kidney toxicity (P=0.002), and at 72 h with severe mucositis (P=0.046) and kidney toxicity (P=0.002). No candidate SNP (SLC19A1 80G>A, MTHFR C677T/A1298C, ATIC C347G) correlated significantly with severe liver or kidney toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Ten patients with stage 4 disease were given oral busulfan (BU) at 20 mg/kg with dose adjustments to maintain a steady-state concentration of 1,350 ng/ml. One of these patients developed grade 4 hepatic toxicity and died of veno-occlusive disease (VOD) on day 68, his BU Css being 1,305/1,397 ng/ml. This attributes fatal hepatic veno-occlusive disease to the high-dose busulfan-based conditioning regimen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose myeloablative conditioning prior to autologous transplant for stage 4 (metastatic) breast cancer; busulfan co-administered with cyclophosphamide (and paclitaxel plus ciprofloxacin in the treatment cohort), an unresolved co-conditioning exposure; all patients had advanced (stage 4) disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral BU 20 mg/kg with dose adjustment to a target BU steady-state concentration (Css) of 1,350 ng/ml; affected patient had BU Css around 1,305-1,397 ng/ml; developed grade 4 hepatic toxicity and died of veno-occlusive disease (VOD) on day 68 post-transplant; a second patient in this group had grade 3-4 toxicity with pulmonary IPS. A historical comparison arm (BU/CY without paclitaxel and ciprofloxacin) also had a patient die of VOD on day 51 and another with grade 3 hepatic toxicity who died of RSV pneumonia on day 59; overall 4 of 25 (16%) in that arm had grade 3-4 regimen-related toxicity, 4 of 25 died of treatment-related mortality.

raw_record.support_text: The study shows that large MTX doses in a short period (6 months or less) produce a modest but significant impairment in galactose elimination capacity, without changes in antipyrine clearance and routine liver function tests, consistent with a defect in liver cell function detectable only by quantitative, dynamic tests.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose, short-duration (≤6 months) MTX chemotherapy with total dose described as far beyond the safe limits; post-surgical oncology patients.
raw_record.extra_details: At end of treatment (150-266 days after initial assessment), galactose elimination capacity (GEC) was reduced by 17% versus baseline, generally still within the normal range but markedly reduced (>30%) in four of the patients; difference from baseline was significant (P=0.013, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). AP clearance (available in 8 patients) and antipyrine half-life (12.7±5.3 h before vs 12.2±3.0 h after) showed no significant change; no significant changes in routine liver function tests (albumin, cholesterol, prothrombin activity). Data interpreted as a defect in liver cell function detectable only by quantitative dynamic tests. Discussion asserts the relationship of MTX treatment to chronic progressive liver disease is well established and probably dependent on cumulative dose; repeated MTX-related toxic hepatitis (transient transaminase increases returning to normal in days) may progress to chronic liver disease characterized by fibrosis or cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: In 22 high-risk uveal melanoma patients treated with adjuvant intra-arterial hepatic (i.a.h.) fotemustine, half of the patients experienced ≥ grade 3 hepatotoxicity, with one patient developing cholangitis 8 years later. The authors conclude that the treatment is feasible but that its toxicities are important.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-risk uveal melanoma patients receiving adjuvant intra-arterial hepatic (locoregional) administration of fotemustine.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 patients treated; planned 6-month duration starting with four weekly doses of 100 mg/m², then repeated every 3 weeks after a 5-week rest. Half (11) experienced ≥ grade 3 hepatotoxicity; one developed cholangitis 8 years later. Catheter-related complications occurred in 18%. Median follow-up 4.6 years for the fotemustine group vs 8.5 years for a 3:1 matched control group; median overall survival 9 years (95% CI 2.2-12.7) vs 7.4 years (95% CI 5.4-12.7; P=0.5). 5-year survival 75% vs 56%.

raw_record.support_text: In a case-control pharmacogenetic study of nevirapine (NVP)-treated patients in Mozambique, the ABCB1 c.3435C>T polymorphism was analyzed comparing 78 patients who experienced NVP hepatotoxicity against 78 controls; the 3435T allele was significantly associated with reduced risk of NVP hepatotoxicity (p=0.038, OR 0.42). The paper frames NVP hepatotoxicity as the studied adverse outcome of NVP-based combination antiretroviral therapy, occurring at roughly 5% frequency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV patients receiving NVP-based combination antiretroviral therapy in Mozambique with pharmacogenetic susceptibility assessed.
raw_record.extra_details: Case-control study with 78 NVP-hepatotoxicity cases and 78 controls; hepatotoxicity frequency about 5%; ABCB1 c.3435C>T T allele associated with reduced hepatotoxicity risk (OR 0.42, p=0.038); c.1459C>T (rs3211371) CYP2B6 SNP not polymorphic in this population; ABCB1 c.2677G>T/A not detected. Genetic/HLA markers themselves are not DILI-causal agents.

raw_record.support_text: In the Botswana clinical trial of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) in HIV-infected adults (n = 1,995), isoniazid-associated biochemical hepatitis (AST/ALT > 5× ULN, with or without symptoms) occurred in 19 participants (0.95%), clinical hepatitis (symptoms plus AST/ALT > 5× ULN) in 6 (0.30%), and one hepatitis death (50 per 100,000). These rates were compared with published INH studies and trials.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected adults (people living with HIV) receiving isoniazid preventive therapy in Botswana; isoniazid given as 6 months of preventive monotherapy rather than combination anti-TB therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Biochemical hepatitis (AST/ALT > 5x ULN) 19/1,995 (0.95%); clinical hepatitis (symptoms + AST/ALT > 5x ULN) 6/1,995 (0.30%); 1 hepatitis death (50 per 100,000) with 89% completion. For participants not on ART with at least 4 months of IPT (n=1,288): clinical 0.93%, biochemical 0.23%, deaths 78/100,000. Three-fourths of INH-hepatitis cases occurred in the first 3 months. Risk factors: CD4 < 200 cells/mm3 associated with increased risk (RR 2.80, 95% CI 1.14-6.84); age >35 yr RR 1.56, ART RR 1.56, NVP RR 2.09, co-trimoxazole RR 1.65, alcohol RR 1.42, CAGE>=1 RR 2.37; no evidence that efavirenz increased risk (RR 0.96). None of the INH-hepatitis cases had chronic HBV infection. Patient education about hepatitis symptoms (nausea, vomiting, yellow eyes, dark urine, fatigue, abdominal pain) and monthly monitoring were recommended.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized trial of 36-month continued isoniazid preventive treatment versus placebo in HIV-infected adults, there were nine cases of hepatitis (one with jaundice) in the continued isoniazid group, one of which (jaundice with disseminated herpes zoster) progressed to death from hepatic encephalopathy 9 months after enrolment; the participant stopped isoniazid 3 days after becoming jaundiced. A second death from hepatic encephalopathy attributed to isoniazid occurred during the open-label period. From enrolment there were 29 cases of severe isoniazid-associated hepatitis in more than 3100 person-years of isoniazid use: 8 (28%) had symptoms (including the two hepatic encephalopathy cases), 4 (14%) had jaundice, and 26 (90%) occurred during the first 9 months of therapy. Overall, 29 (1%) of 1995 participants had severe isoniazid-associated (biochemical) hepatitis (rate 14.5 per 1000 participants), 8 had clinical hepatitis (4.0 per 1000), and 2 had hepatic encephalopathy (1.0 per 1000).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected adults receiving continued (36-month) isoniazid preventive treatment with antiretroviral therapy in some participants; tuberculosis-endemic setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine hepatitis cases (one with jaundice) in the continued isoniazid group versus six hepatitis cases in placebo controls. One jaundiced continued-isoniazid participant died of hepatic encephalopathy with concomitant disseminated herpes zoster and lymphocytic pleiocytosis on CSF analysis, stopping isoniazid 3 days after becoming jaundiced. A second isoniazid-attributed death from hepatic encephalopathy occurred in the open-label period. Aggregate rates: severe biochemical hepatitis 14.5 per 1000 participants, clinical hepatitis 4.0 per 1000, hepatic encephalopathy 1.0 per 1000; 26 of 29 cases (90%) occurred within first 9 months of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In the Botswana trial of 36 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) among HIV-infected adults, severe (grade ≥3) hepatitis occurred in 2% (19 of 1,006) of recipients, with three cases of jaundice. Across trials there were no deaths attributed to study drug in the Soweto or Chennai trials. The authors place these rates in context of the trial finding that symptomatic isoniazid-associated hepatitis was very low during 36 months of IPT, with drug-induced hepatitis attributed to isoniazid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected adults receiving isoniazid preventive therapy for latent tuberculosis infection; unblinded pragmatic trial cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe (grade ≥3) hepatitis in 2% (19/1,006) at 36 months of IPT vs 28% (46/164) in the Soweto trial; jaundice in 0.3% (3/1,006, Botswana) vs 0.9% (3/339, Chennai). Symptomatic isoniazid-associated hepatitis was very low. Risk factors: baseline AST >1 to <2.5 ULN (HR 3.86, 95% CI 2.18-6.83), baseline CD4 <200 cells/µL (HR 2.57, 95% CI 1.47-4.50), positive hepatitis B core antibody (OR 2.81, 95% CI 1.1-7.0). Overall two deaths among 1,998 participants initiating IPT (0.1%) across both arms; none attributed to drug in other trials. Hepatitis risk highest during first 2 months of IPT. Concomitant efavirenz- or nevirapine-based ART did not significantly increase moderate to severe hepatitis risk.

raw_record.support_text: A 34-year-old HIV-infected woman with no other opportunistic infections presented a classic sulfone syndrome manifested by fever, rash, hemolytic anemia, and fulminant hepatitis due to a dapsone hypersensitivity reaction, with a fatal outcome. This is described as the first reported fatal complication of dapsone in an HIV-infected patient.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected patient receiving dapsone for Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia prophylaxis; co-medication zidovudine (AZT) as the only other medication; normal G6PD level.
raw_record.extra_details: Case occurred ~1 month after starting dapsone. Sulfone syndrome: fever, exfoliative dermatitis, hepatitis, hemolytic anemia; 15% eosinophils, markedly elevated liver enzymes, bilirubin peaked at 23 mg/dL, prothrombin time peaked at 36.2 seconds, hypocomplementemia. Hepatitis A, B, and C, infectious mononucleosis, syphilis serologies negative; drug-related hypersensitivity. Dapsone is a diaminodiphenylsulfone used for leprosy and dermatitis herpetiformis, now used for PCP prophylaxis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors reason that fulminant hepatic failure in the two HIV-infected patients can be ascribed to didanosine (ddI): both received ddI for 13 weeks, neither had prior liver disease, no superimposed infection including hepatitis viruses was found, and although both received concomitant therapy, those drugs were judged not responsible (zidovudine hepatotoxicity is rare with macrovesicular rather than microvesicular steatosis; ketoconazole had been given continuously for 22 months). They compare their two cases with the previously reported case (Lai et al., 1991), all showing fulminant hepatitis after 13-15 weeks of ddI with similar symptoms and prior normal liver function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected patients (CDC stage IV) receiving concomitant therapy (zidovudine, aerosolized pentamidine, ketoconazole); authors argued these co-medications were not responsible for the hepatic impairment.
raw_record.extra_details: Two own cases plus one previously reported case (Lai et al., 1991), all fatal. ddI doses 7.5, 11, and 12 mg/kg/day; duration from ddI start to first symptoms 13-15 weeks. Inaugural symptoms: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dyspnoea. Normal liver function before the episode; transaminases did not exceed 5-10x normal. Admissions showed moderate cytolysis, anionic cholestasis, and lactic acidosis; histology on post-mortem biopsy showed extensive diffuse microvesicular steatosis with mild centrolobular cholestasis and no necrosis or fibrosis. Death from major hepatic failure with cardiovascular shock. ddI and ketoconazole withdrawn on day 1; thiamin had no effect. Included for comparison: zidovudine-related fatty liver (macrovesicular) and one previous ketoconazole vesicular steatosis case were considered unlikely causes.

raw_record.support_text: In 522 HIV-infected pregnant women initiating triple antiretroviral prophylaxis, 14 (3%) developed severe hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or 4 ALT elevation), including 12 women who initiated nevirapine (NVP). Median time from ART initiation to severe hepatotoxicity was 68 days (IQR 35-127); symptomatic in 8 of 14 cases (rash n=7, jaundice n=4, fever n=3, abdominal pain n=2, nausea n=2). No deaths were attributed to severe hepatotoxicity. Nevirapine was discontinued in 11 of 12 severe hepatotoxicity cases and ALT elevations resolved in 10 of 11 women who switched to nelfinavir (NFV); one woman had persistent ALT elevations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected pregnant women receiving triple ART prophylaxis (NVP/3TC/ZDV or NFV/3TC/ZDV) in Kisumu, Kenya; 12 of 14 cases occurred in women who initiated NVP.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity defined as grade 3 or 4 ALT elevation. Median total bilirubin 43 umol/L (IQR 23-93), with 4 women having total bilirubin >210 umol/L (>5 x ULN). Rash preceded hepatotoxicity by median 8 days in 6 of 7 cases with rash. HBsAg negative in all 13 tested. HBV (hepatitis B surface antigen) negative. ALT resolved in 10 (91%) of 11 women switched to NFV; one woman had persistent ALT elevation. Regimens included lamivudine (3TC), zidovudine (ZDV), nelfinavir (NFV).; dose: None

raw_record.support_text: In HIV-infected South African patients receiving a blinded regimen of lamivudine or emtricitabine, stavudine, and either nevirapine or efavirenz, early hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or greater increase in serum aminotransferases within the first 12 weeks) occurred in 17% of the nevirapine group versus 0% of the efavirenz group, and was balanced between the lamivudine and emtricitabine arms. Two subjects died of hepatic failure, and independent risk factors included BMI<18.5, female sex, serum albumin<35 g/L, MCV>85 fL, HIV-1 RNA<20,000 copies/mL, AST<75 IU/L, and LDH<164 IU/L. The paper notes that the acute hepatic toxicity of nevirapine led to a product label change in the US and EU and that enrollment in the nevirapine stratum was terminated by health authorities.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected, antiretroviral-naive subjects with CD4+ cells >=200/mm3; given in fixed combination antiretroviral therapy with stavudine (30 or 40 mg twice daily) plus lamivudine (150 mg twice daily) or emtricitabine (200 mg once daily); female sex and low BMI identified as risk factors; nevirapine dosed 200 mg once daily for 2 weeks then 200 mg twice daily.
raw_record.extra_details: Early hepatotoxicity defined as treatment-emergent grade 3 (5-10x ULN) or grade 4 (>10x ULN) increase in serum ALT or AST within the first 12 weeks; observed in 17% of the nevirapine arm versus 0% in the efavirenz arm; 2 subjects died of hepatic failure; nevirapine acute hepatic toxicity led to US and EU product label change and termination of enrollment in the nevirapine stratum (trial put on hold). Independent risk factors: BMI<18.5, female sex, serum albumin<35 g/L, mean corpuscular volume>85 fL, plasma HIV-1 RNA<20,000 copies/mL, AST<75 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase<164 IU/L. Nevirapine brand Viramune; marketed by Boehringer Ingelheim.

raw_record.support_text: Remdesivir (RDV) usage is associated with elevations of AST and ALT; in most instances the enzyme elevations did not progress to severe liver damage, but cases of acute liver failure suspected as due to RDV have been reported. In two patients with RDV-induced acute liver failure, significant transaminase increases occurred between day 3 and day 10 of RDV use, associated with coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy. Using the Naranjo algorithm, both cases scored as 'probable' adverse drug reactions with a score of 6 each; after stopping the drug and treatment with N-acetyl cysteine infusion there was marked improvement in transaminases and liver function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hospitalized patients with COVID-19 and evidence of lower respiratory tract infection; intravenous RDV use.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with RDV-induced acute liver failure; significant transaminase increases between day 3 and day 10 of use, associated with coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy; Naranjo algorithm 'probable' adverse drug reaction with score 6 each; marked improvement after drug discontinuation and N-acetyl cysteine infusion. RDV suggested to be stopped if ALT >5x ULN or ALP >2x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN or in presence of coagulopathy or clinical decompensation; authors did not use RDV in decompensated cirrhosis patients.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 32 subjects with anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) manifesting after starting anticonvulsant therapy, the implicated drugs were phenobarbitone (2 cases), phenytoin (22 cases) and carbamazepine (8 cases), used either prophylactically after craniotomy or for epilepsy. Evaluation showed hepatitis in 18 of the 32 subjects (56.3%) as part of the systemic findings. Treatment consisted of stopping the causative drug, and no new lesions occurred after valproic acid was substituted for continued therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hypersensitivity syndrome cases; 19 of 22 phenytoin cases were craniotomy patients with concurrent anaesthetics, systemic antibiotics and analgesics (unresolved co-exposures), the remainder were epilepsy patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenytoin was the culprit in 22 of 32 AHS cases (19 post-craniotomy prophylactic, 3 epilepsy). Hepatitis occurred in 18 of 32 total cases (56.3%) as part of AHS, which also included fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, leucocytosis and lymphocytosis; latency from start of therapy to eruption was 2-4 weeks (mean about 3 weeks). Stopping the causative drug produced clinical response (approximately 13 days).

raw_record.support_text: In the eight cases studied, the reaction began 23 to 37 days after the start of p-aminosalicylic acid therapy and was characterized by fever (101-105 F), rash, nausea, cervical lymphadenopathy, and, in two patients, hepatomegaly with tenderness and splenomegaly, one of whom had obvious jaundice with a bilirubin level of 4.6 mg per 100 cc. Laboratory studies showed abnormal liver function tests (elevated alkaline phosphatase, thymol turbidity, bilirubin, positive cephalin flocculation, and sulfobromophthalein retention), and the reaction subsided rapidly on drug discontinuation but recurred on readministration even at fractional doses. The authors conclude that the picture, which includes hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and abnormal liver function tests, strongly suggests hepatitis caused by p-aminosalicylic acid therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hypersensitivity/allergic reaction during therapeutic p-aminosalicylic acid therapy for tuberculosis; reaction clinically resembles infectious mononucleosis with hepatic involvement (hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, jaundice in one patient) in 8 reported cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset 23-37 days after start of therapy; fever 101-105 F; generalized erythematous macular (one urticarial) rash; eosinophilia 11-50%; atypical lymphocytes 1-21%; elevated alkaline phosphatase (13.7, 21.4, 52.6 units), thymol turbidity, bilirubin, 3-4+ cephalin flocculation, and sulfobromophthalein retention (15%, 20%); dechallenge produced resolution within hours/days to a month; rechallenge even in fractional doses caused exacerbation with reappearance of atypical lymphocytes, eosinophilia, and left shift. One cited reference describes lethal p-aminosalicylic acid intoxication (Muri).

raw_record.support_text: Mild elevation of AST and ALT was induced by methimazole (MMI) treatment in patients with baseline normal hepatic function, and in 2 cases (3.5% of MMI-treated patients) AST and ALT rose above 2× the ULN, one of which had clinically significant hepatic dysfunction requiring MMI cessation with subsequent normalization of liver function tests. Levels under 2× ULN were attributed to thyroid dysfunction or subclinical MMI-induced hepatotoxicity, while levels above 2-3× the ULN were regarded as clinically significant hepatic dysfunction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hyperthyroid patients on methimazole (indication-restricted); one case of clinically significant hepatic dysfunction required MMI cessation; proposed susceptibility factors include alcoholism, malnutrition, concomitant enzyme-inducing medication, and diabetes.
raw_record.extra_details: 2/57 treated patients (3.5%) had AST and ALT >2× ULN, one requiring MMI withdrawal with normalization of LFTs. Rate of abnormal LFTs after >10 months was 10.8% (n=28) and 15.7% in LOCF analysis. LFT <2× ULN considered subclinical; levels >2-3× ULN regarded as clinically significant hepatic dysfunction. Cholestasis described as idiosyncratic with suspected polymorphism of drug-metabolizing enzymes; hepatocellular injury may be dose-related (Nakamura).

raw_record.support_text: Thioguanine is associated with liver toxicity, especially nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH). The paper assessed whether liver histology alters during long-term maintenance thioguanine treatment in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: IBD patients on long-term thioguanine maintenance after prior thiopurine (azathioprine/mercaptopurine) therapy; vascular abnormalities were non-progressive with limited clinical relevance over a median 25-month follow-up; portal hypertension occurred in 2 patients with phlebosclerosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Sequential liver biopsies in 25 IBD patients (median 25 months, range 14-54 between first and second biopsy). Rates: perisinusoidal fibrosis 91%, sinusoidal dilatation 68%, nodularity 18% (unchanged between biopsies); phlebosclerosis trended from 36% first to 68% second biopsy (p=0.092). Histological abnormalities were not associated with clinical outcomes. Nodularity resolved upon thioguanine withdrawal in 2 patients, and portal hypertension was observed in 2 patients with phlebosclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old ICU patient on prolonged ketamine infusions developed a persistent rise in alkaline phosphatase and GGT with normal bilirubin; MR cholangiopancreatography showed intrahepatic dilatation with a beaded appearance and a dilated common bile duct with distal narrowing, and liver biopsy showed biliary ductular reaction with lobular inflammation. The authors concluded the imaging and pathologic findings are consistent with a unique form of DILI: ketamine-induced sclerosing cholangitis (KISC).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: ICU therapeutic-use case during severe COVID-19 with mechanical ventilation and critical illness; co-administered sedatives (propofol, midazolam, hydromorphone) and later intravenous ketamine bolus; concurrent cavitary staphylococcal pneumonia and low-titer serum CMV DNA as competing/confounding conditions.
raw_record.extra_details: Prolonged/repeated ketamine exposure: 15 days of IV ketamine infusions, then 5 days oral ketamine, and a later IV ketamine bolus upon re-intubation. Cholestatic-biased laboratory findings: Alk P peaked at 2,239 U/L with GGT 773 U/L (AST 1260, ALT 1729 U/L, bilirubin normal 0.4 mg/dL); after recovery, re-administration of IV ketamine produced an abrupt repeat rise (Alk P 1,720, GGT 538, AST 266, ALT 407 U/L) with normal bilirubin and normal INR, consistent with a dechallenge/rechallenge response. Serologic workup (ANA, AMA, ASMA, ANCA) unrevealing; HAV/HBV/HCV/HIV/EBV/HSV ruled out. MRCP showed intrahepatic beaded dilatation and dilated common bile duct with distal narrowing; biopsy showed biliary ductular reaction, lobular inflammation, and a small non-necrotizing lobular granuloma.

raw_record.support_text: Seven dialysis patients with renal failure received cadaver kidney transplants and were treated with cyclosporin A (CyA) as the initial sole immunosuppressant. The summary reports that CyA was effective in inhibiting rejection but that there was clear evidence of both nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity; a cyclophosphamide analogue was added to CyA in six of the patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Immunosuppressed renal-transplant patients managed on dialysis with renal failure; CyA given initially as sole immunosuppressant, with a cyclophosphamide analogue added in six of the seven patients, leaving a possible co-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective pilot study of 7 patients with first cadaveric renal allografts from mismatched donors; CyA dosed 25 mg/kg, given intramuscularly in 'Miglyol' for the first 2-3 days then orally in olive oil (changed to Sandoz capsules in two cases in the third postoperative month); liver and renal function carefully monitored postoperatively. Hepatotoxicity was reported in addition to nephrotoxicity. Outcome: five patients out of hospital with functioning allografts, one allograft nephrectomy for pyelonephritis, one death from systemic aspergillus and candida infection.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 20 patients with chlorpromazine-induced jaundice/liver disease. Two patients were pregnant during the course of the chlorpromazine-induced liver disease; one recovered completely within four weeks of jaundice onset, and the other, who had marked intracanalicular bile stasis on needle biopsy, remained icteric until roughly two weeks after delivery but was normal four months postpartum. Follow-up data on all 20 patients indicate recovery from this drug-induced liver disease was complete in all.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Includes one patient in whom necrosis may have been due to concurrent alcoholic (nutritional) liver damage rather than chlorpromazine.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpromazine jaundice (drug-induced liver disease) in 20 patients; histology showed intact hepatic lobular architecture, marked intracanalicular bile stasis, and absence of hepatocellular necrosis in 14 of 15 biopsied patients (necrosis in only one, possibly alcohol-related). Must be differentiated histologically from infectious hepatitis and extrahepatic obstructive jaundice. Two cases occurred during pregnancy; eventual recovery was complete in all 20 patients, with no evidence of extrahepatic biliary obstruction in the operative case.

raw_record.support_text: A first large retrospective study on halothane-associated liver injury reported an incidence of 1:35 000 for fatal hepatic necrosis after halothane anaesthesia, and patients were at increased risk after repeated administrations. The paper states there is strong evidence that the fulminant form, halothane hepatitis, is mediated by the patient's own immune system; that severe form contrasts with a mild hepatocellular injury seen in about 20% of halothane-treated patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Increased risk after repeated administrations; immune-mediated fulminant form occurs in a small number of susceptible patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of fatal hepatic necrosis was 1:35 000 after halothane anaesthesia per the first large retrospective study. The fulminant halothane hepatitis is immune-mediated: reactive intermediates from halothane metabolism cause acetylation of intracellular proteins (first step), and antibodies directed against these acetylated neo-antigens form (second step), leading to severe and sometimes fatal hepatic injury in a small number of patients.

raw_record.support_text: We report a case of hepatotoxicity induced by methimazole treatment in a 54-year-old hyperthyroid man treated with methimazole (30 mg/day). Fourteen days later he developed scleral icterus, dark urine, and right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain; laboratory tests and liver biopsy led to a diagnosis of cholestatic hepatitis secondary to methimazole usage. The drug was withdrawn, laboratory parameters returned to normal within five days, and the Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable relationship between hepatotoxicity and methimazole therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Indication of hyperthyroidism; antithyroid therapy in a 54-year-old male patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis (confirmed by liver biopsy) with scleral icterus, dark urine, and right-upper-quadrant pain. Dose 30 mg/day; onset 14 days after starting treatment. Methimazole withdrawn and cholestyramine, ursodeoxycholic acid, and chlorpheniramine administered; abdominal pain resolved and laboratory parameters returned to normal within five days. Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable causal relationship. Author conclusion: physicians should be aware of hepatotoxicity risk with methimazole.

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old man with stage IIIB pulmonary adenocarcinoma received 100 mg daily erlotinib (an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor) after chemo- and radiotherapy failed. Twelve days after starting erlotinib he developed acute drug-related hepatitis complicated by renal deterioration (aspartate aminotransferase 1400 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 1299 U/L, creatinine 4.4 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 55 mg/dL). Viral causes of hepatitis were excluded and CT ruled out hepatic metastasis; by the Roussel-Uclaf causality assessment the erlotinib-related hepatitis was classified as 'probable'. The English-language discussion further states that in this patient renal function suddenly worsened as a consequence of acute liver failure, causing metformin accumulation and ensuing fatal lactic acidosis, with the patient dying two hours after admission.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 22 thioguanine (TG)-treated inflammatory bowel disease patients with sequential liver biopsies, thioguanine was associated with histopathological liver changes including mild inflammation, steatosis, fibrosis and vascular irregularities that were mostly asymptomatic and non-progressive. Perisinusoidal fibrosis (91%), sinusoidal dilatation (68%) and nodularity (18%) were present in both first and sequential biopsies, with a trend for phlebosclerosis (36% first vs 68% second, p=.092); nodularity of any degree was present in six patients (27%). Three patients ceased thioguanine due to hepatotoxicity, and in two patients nodularity of the liver resolved upon thioguanine withdrawal, while two patients had portal hypertension in the presence of phlebosclerosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Inflammatory bowel disease patients (including Crohn's disease) treated with thioguanine; three of these patients had previously received thiopurines (mercaptopurine, azathioprine).
raw_record.extra_details: 22 IBD patients (predominantly Crohn's disease) with sequential liver biopsies. Histological findings included nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH; nodularity in 27% of patients at any grade, grade 1-2 with none reaching grade 3), phlebosclerosis, perisinusoidal fibrosis, sinusoidal dilatation, and perivenular fibrosis. Three female Crohn's disease patients ceased thioguanine due to hepatotoxicity (TG duration 18-25 months); dechallenge biopsies showed reduced phlebosclerosis, perisinusoidal fibrosis, and nodularity with improved liver tests in two patients. Four patients had preexisting splenomegaly/liver test abnormalities, and thrombocytopenia occurred in three patients. Liver test abnormalities at first and second biopsy in nine (26%) and five (20%) patients; mild steatosis and elevated gamma-glutamyl-transferase (43-92 U/L) noted. Two patients had portal hypertension in the presence of phlebosclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: In Group I, 106 patients receiving chloroform anesthesia were studied with liver function tests (serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, prothrombin time, thymol turbidity, thymol flocculation, and cephalin flocculation) taken at delivery and on the third postpartum day. Although routine liver function tests were unsatisfactory for revealing liver damage from chloroform anesthesia, two patients showed clear liver damage: one developed clinical jaundice and a second had a subclinical significant elevation of serum bilirubin with 40% bromsulphalein retention after 45 minutes, while other tests remained normal. The paper frames these findings as toxic hepatitis from chloroform anesthesia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Inhalation anesthetic given during delivery; patients with a history of previous liver disease, diabetes mellitus, and severe toxemia were excluded from receiving chloroform anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 106 patients in Group I before SGPT was available; one patient developed clinical jaundice and a second had subclinical significant serum bilirubin elevation with 40% bromsulphalein retention after 45 minutes. Cephalin flocculation and alkaline phosphatase were normal in both affected patients. Fifty-two percent of patients had abnormal serum alkaline phosphatase (4 to 10 mM units) prior to delivery and 25% on day 3; 25% had 3- and 4-plus cephalin flocculation before delivery, falling to 7% on day 3. Study conducted at a local charity hospital with the highest incidence of toxic hepatitis; most patients were Negroes. Group II controls (39 patients, local or no anesthesia) showed only occasional minor SGPT variations and no such liver damage, aside from one incidental infectious hepatitis case.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old woman developed combined hepatic and renal toxicity after three intermittent doses of rifampicin, having previously taken rifampicin 450 mg daily and sodium aminosalicylate regularly for 16 months. The authors state this is apparently the first report of combined hepatic and renal toxicity due to rifampicin and the first to incriminate rifampicin taken alone, concluding that intermittent rifampicin therapy can cause acute hepatic and renal failure and that both toxic effects are reversible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intermittent (non-continuous) rifampicin dosing taken after 16 months of regular daily therapy; co-medication sodium aminosalicylate had been stopped 6 days earlier and was not implicated; no pre-existing renal or liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Case in a 62-year-old woman with active pulmonary tuberculosis. Rifampicin was taken as three intermittent doses (three tablets each); first intermittent dose produced chills, nausea, vomiting within 2 hours resolving after 24 hours; subsequent doses produced nausea/malaise and acute right loin pain with nausea/vomiting. On admission: jaundice, fever 38 C, bilirubin 4.3 mg/100 ml, prothrombin time 60%, alkaline phosphatase 165 IU, SGOT 1,450 IU/ml, indicating hepatocellular damage and early acute renal failure without haemolysis. Liver function returned to normal after 5 days; hepatic and renal effects reversible. Paper notes possible immune mediation via circulating antirifampicin antibody; influenza-like syndrome with anuric acute tubular necrosis reported. Comment section states intermittent rifampicin therapy can cause acute renal and hepatic failure. Clinical phenotype = acute hepatic failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Cases occurred in the extension phase of an open-label pilot study in adults and children with idiopathic and associated PAH (congenital heart disease, collagen vascular disease). raw_record.support_text: In a prospective randomized trial of hepatic arterial (I.A.) versus intravenous (I.V.) FUDR (floxuridine) for colorectal liver metastases, I.A. FUDR was associated with major hepatobiliary toxicity, described as chemical injury to normal hepatocytes and ductal structures. Chemical hepatitis occurred in 79% (19/24) of I.A. patients versus 7% (2/29) on I.V. therapy, and biliary sclerosis occurred in 21% (5/24) of I.A. patients. The biliary sclerosis led to a treatment-related death from liver failure, and the authors attribute the complication specifically to FUDR, noting no other reports of this complication with other drugs delivered through the hepatic artery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intra-arterial (hepatic artery) route of administration in patients with colorectal liver metastases being treated for cancer; I.A. dose significantly greater than I.V. dose during the first five courses.
raw_record.extra_details: N=24 I.A. and N=29 I.V. patients in a prospective randomized comparison; chemical hepatitis 19/24 (79%) I.A. vs 2/29 (7%) I.V.; biliary sclerosis 5/24 (21%) I.A., first described by Hohn et al., causing a treatment-related death from liver failure; reported as chemical injury to normal hepatocytes and ductal structures (hepatobiliary system); GI toxicity including peptic ulcers and gastritis/duodenitis in 38%; resolution required FUDR dose reduction or cessation; all patients received histamine H2 receptor antagonists without prevention.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of hepatocarcinoma patients treated with Yttrium-90 (Y90) radioembolization, nine patients (7%) experienced radiation-induced liver disease (REILD), a recognized liver-injury complication of Y90. Current guidelines advise against Y90 use in patients with clinical liver decompensation or significantly abnormal liver function tests, particularly with total bilirubin >2 mg/dL or albumin <3.0 g/dL, to avoid the risk of REILD. Other reported toxicities included elevated liver enzymes (2.5–34%) and bilirubin levels (24–26%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intra-arterial hepatic radioembolization (locoregional) in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma and portal vein thrombosis, many of whom had underlying cirrhosis and liver decompensation; REILD reported within this at-risk population.
raw_record.extra_details: Radiation-induced liver disease (REILD) occurred in 9/128 (7%) patients. REILD was described as contributing to worsening synthetic liver function, worsening liver failure, encephalopathy, and ascites/fluid retention, alongside progression of HCC. The paper also states Y90 can cause worsening liver failure (paragraph 56) and cites increasing MELD and CP scores post-treatment reflecting liver decompensation/REILD (paragraph 58). One death one day after Y90 was attributed to procedural complications rather than REILD specifically. Alias: Y90.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 59-year-old male on peritoneal dialysis for KDIGO stage 5 chronic kidney disease who developed DRESS, including hepatic involvement with elevated liver enzymes and eosinophilia, 25 days after initiating intraperitoneal vancomycin for bacterial peritonitis. The diagnosis was confirmed with the RegiSCAR scoring system and supported by skin biopsy showing lymphocytic and eosinophilic inflammation. The patient improved after vancomycin withdrawal and systemic corticosteroids. The paper states that although vancomycin is a known DRESS causative agent, DRESS associated with intraperitoneal vancomycin is extremely rare and highlights intraperitoneal vancomycin as a potential DRESS trigger, particularly in patients with impaired renal clearance.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intraperitoneal route of administration (unusual/formulation-route departure); patient with end-stage chronic kidney disease on peritoneal dialysis (impaired renal clearance) treated for bacterial peritonitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of 25 days after starting intraperitoneal vancomycin. DRESS diagnosis confirmed by RegiSCAR scoring and supported by skin biopsy showing lymphocytic and eosinophilic inflammation. Hepatic involvement characterized by hepatitis with elevated transaminases/elevated liver enzymes. Patient improved after drug withdrawal and systemic corticosteroid therapy. Background: type 2 diabetes, benign prostatic hyperplasia, systemic arterial hypertension. DRESS carries an estimated 10-20% mortality but no liver failure/death was reported in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: Dr. Ratz Bravo and colleagues present three cases of liver toxicity caused by intravenous amiodarone, including unpublished cases reported to the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products. Liver toxicity typically develops within 24 hrs (may take 2-3 days) of IV amiodarone, with liver transaminases rising rapidly to exceed ten times the upper normal limit; less frequently bilirubin, creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase increase and prothrombin time prolongs. Liver biopsy reveals centrilobular necrosis, and manifestations are usually reversible after discontinuation but may occasionally progress to a fatal outcome.

Latency typically within 24 hrs (up to 2-3 days). Transaminases rose to exceed 10 times upper normal limit; less frequently bilirubin, creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase increased and prothrombin time prolonged. Liver biopsy showed centrilobular necrosis. Manifestations usually reversible after drug discontinuation, but occasionally progressed to fatal outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Acute elevation of liver enzymes following IV amiodarone use ranged from mild asymptomatic to severe life-threatening and frequently necessitated drug discontinuation; in most reported cases the liver injury occurred within 24–48 h of therapy and reversed within 2–3 weeks of discontinuation. This describes acute hepatotoxicity attributed to intravenous amiodarone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intravenous (parenteral) administration to critically ill intensive/coronary care unit patients; reported predisposing factors include heart failure, hypotension from ventricular arrhythmias, high IV amiodarone dose, and postoperative therapy after coronary artery bypass grafting.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatic injury following IV amiodarone ranged from mild asymptomatic to severe life-threatening and frequently required drug discontinuation; injury typically occurred within 24–48 h of therapy and reversed within 2–3 weeks of discontinuation. Mechanism is controversial (possible ischemic injury, or immune-mediated alteration of hepatocellular membrane by solubilizers such as polysorbate 80); acute IV injury differs from chronic oral amiodarone hepatotoxicity. Study described: 180 ICU/CCU patients receiving IV amiodarone, with 90 AILI cases defined as acute rise in serum aminotransferase levels by at least 2-fold of baseline within 24–48 h of IV amiodarone, versus 90 controls without AILI.

raw_record.support_text: Patient data for 9 cases of severe hepatotoxicity attributed to intravenous amiodarone treatment are presented, listing total dose, period of administration, baseline and highest ALT, onset in days, recovery ALT and recovery time in days. ALT rose from baselines of 14-42 IU/L to peaks of 416-2554 IU/L within 1-7 days, with recovery over 5-18 days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intravenous administration; acute exposure (150-10200 mg over 0-168 h) in patients with arrhythmias or aortic dissection; patients received amiodarone for arrhythmia control.
raw_record.extra_details: 9 cases (8 male, 1 female, aged 42-73) of severe hepatotoxicity attributed to IV amiodarone. ALT peaked 416-2554 IU/L, onset 1-7 days after therapy, recovery over 5-18 days. Indications included ventricular premature contraction, atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and aortic dissection.

raw_record.support_text: A 79-year-old woman treated with intravenous (IV) amiodarone for atrial flutter abruptly developed coagulopathy, altered mental status and liver enzyme derangement, and was diagnosed with acute liver failure (ALF) secondary to an amiodarone adverse drug reaction, with a Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 7. Amiodarone was withheld and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was initiated; clinical improvement was seen within 48 hours of holding the drug and complete recovery was reported at follow-up.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intravenous amiodarone administration (IV push then infusion) for atrial flutter in a 79-year-old woman; N-acetylcysteine co-administered as treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Received 150 mg amiodarone IV push followed by an IV infusion totalling 930 mg over 24 hours, then transitioned to oral amiodarone 200 mg twice daily. Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 7 supports a probable causal relationship. Clinical improvement within 48 hours of holding the drug and within 24 hours of initiating NAC; complete recovery at post-hospital follow-up, making this the only reported survivor among seven total cases of amiodarone-induced ALF (the prior six reported cases were all fatal). Chronic oral amiodarone is noted to be associated with asymptomatic hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Therapy i.v. GCS may cause liver damage, described as a rare but potentially irreversible and even fatal side effect. In the analysed prospective clinical studies there were two cases (0.5%) of marked increase of serum aminotransferases after i.v. GCS and none in the oral GCS group; aminotransferase changes were associated especially with higher i.v. GCS doses and became smaller when the steroid dose was lowered. The prevalence of acute liver damage (ALD) associated with i.v. GCS therapy in a group of ~800 patients was estimated at 1.0% (eight patients), and the prevalence of fatal liver adverse effects at ~0.3% (three lethal liver complications/800 patients); in all four described lethal ALD cases after i.v. GCS therapy for Graves' orbitopathy the cumulative methylprednisolone dose exceeded 8.0 g.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intravenous high-dose glucocorticoid (methylprednisolone) pulses for Graves' orbitopathy; all four lethal ALD cases occurred with cumulative methylprednisolone dose >8.0 g; aminotransferase changes more pronounced at higher i.v. GCS doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases (0.5%) of marked serum aminotransferase increase after i.v. GCS vs none in oral GCS group; ALD prevalence 1.0% (8/~800 patients); fatal liver adverse effects ~0.3% (3/800); three proposed mechanisms: direct presumably dose-related hepatocyte toxicity, induction of viral hepatitis, and induction of autoimmune hepatitis; pre-existing viral or autoimmune hepatitis reported as risk factors.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase 1 trial of the investigational agent REM127 in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, adverse events in the hepatobiliary dysfunction system organ class were observed only in participants on active REM127 treatment and not in placebo recipients. One serious adverse event in the 350 mg dose group was considered related to study treatment and reported as toxic hepatitis. Drug-induced liver injury was reported in six participants leading to study discontinuation, and one case fulfilled Hy's Law criteria, led to hospitalization, and was reported as a suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction (SUSAR), prompting termination of the trial. Increased serum transaminases occurred in all 1400 mg (2/2) and 350 mg (2/2) participants and 1/5 in the 88 mg group versus none in placebo; increases typically started around the fourth week, peaked days to weeks after study discontinuation, and returned to normal in all participants over several weeks to months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Investgational agent evaluated in a phase 1 clinical trial in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease at daily oral doses of 88, 350, and 1400 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: AE terms reported included drug-induced liver injury, toxic hepatitis, hepatitis toxic, hepatic enzyme increased, alanine aminotransferase increased, blood lactate dehydrogenase increased, and transaminases increased. Six participants had hepatobiliary dysfunction leading to study discontinuation; trial was terminated early for safety. One case fulfilled Hy's Law, required hospitalization, and was reported as SUSAR. Transaminase elevations typically began around the fourth week (at last study-drug day or follow-up), peaked days to weeks after discontinuation, and resolved over several weeks to months; an associated decrease in total cholesterol was noted. No deaths or liver transplantations occurred. REM127 is a septin 6 (SEPT6) modulator; one participant received the co-medication quetiapine from Day 21 to Day 23.

raw_record.support_text: In a 7-year Seattle-King County cohort study, rates of isoniazid hepatotoxicity were derived by comparing hepatotoxicity cases from a 1989-1995 register with the number of patients who began isoniazid alone or in multiple-drug regimens. During the study, 11 patients experienced hepatotoxic reactions while receiving isoniazid (median age 34 years, range 27-67; 73% female; median latency 9 weeks, range 19 days to 5 months). All 11 had highly elevated serum hepatocellular enzymes, 9 (82%) were hyperbilirubinemic, 1 (9.1%) was hospitalized, and all recovered without sequelae.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Isoniazid given alone or in multiple-drug regimens (preventive or multi-drug TB therapy); two patients were also taking acetaminophen and two were taking ibuprofen at the time of diagnosis (possible co-medications).
raw_record.extra_details: 11 hepatotoxicity cases among the cohort; median age 34 (range 27-67), 73% female; median interval to diagnosis 9 weeks (range 19 days to 5 months), with 10/11 (91%) within 3 months; all had highly elevated hepatocellular enzymes and 9/11 (82%) hyperbilirubinemia; 1 patient (9.1%) hospitalized; all 11 recovered without sequelae. Rates computed per persons beginning therapy and per persons completing isoniazid single- or multiple-drug therapy; subgroup rates by sex, race, and age (0-14, 15-34, 35-64, ≥65); logistic regression odds ratios adjusted for sex, age group, and race.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients who received a cadaveric kidney transplant and were maintained on the immunosuppressant azathioprine (2.0-2.3 mg/kg) plus prednisone (10 mg) developed liver disease 16-24 months after grafting. They had no previous hepatic disease, normal pre-transplant liver function, no alcohol use, and no hepatotoxic drug other than azathioprine; HBsAg/HBsAb remained negative and serologic tests (CMV, brucellosis, toxoplasmosis, mononucleosis, syphilis, hepatitis A and B) failed to show an infective cause. Liver biopsy showed sinusoidal dilatation progressing to cirrhosis, with improvement after azathioprine dose reduction, implicating azathioprine as the cause of the hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Kidney transplant recipients maintained on azathioprine with prednisone (10 mg) as second immunosuppressant; onset 16-24 months after grafting.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 3 transplant patients (patients 1-3: ages 48, 37, 33; azathioprine doses 2.3, 2.0, 2.1 mg/kg/day). Injury featured hepatic sinusoidal dilatation progressing to cirrhosis, with splenomegaly, ascites, esophageal varices, increased wedged hepatic pressure, and marked 99mTc uptake reduction. Laboratory findings of frank hemolysis (increased reticulocytes, no detectable serum haptoglobin, elevated LDH first fraction, elevated bilirubin), macrocytic anemia, leuco- and thrombocytopenia; SGPT/SGOT, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT only slightly elevated in patients 1 and 2 and normal in patient 3; serum albumin decreased. Congestive heart failure and infective causes excluded. Improvement after azathioprine dose reduction in all 3 patients.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective randomized trial of LTBI contacts in Taiwan, clinically relevant hepatotoxicity was more common in the 9H (9-month daily isoniazid) group than in the 3 HP (weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid) group (5.3% vs 1.5%; p = 0.103). The trial assessed adverse drug reactions including hepatotoxicity in 263 participants (131 in 9H, 132 in 3 HP). Background text states that among patients receiving 9-month isoniazid treatment, isoniazid-associated hepatotoxicity was observed in 2.7% and Grade 3 or 4 hepatotoxicity in 0.3%.

raw_record.extra_details: The 9H (9-month daily isoniazid) group showed 5.3% clinically relevant hepatotoxicity in this trial of 131 patients; background cites isoniazid-associated hepatotoxicity in 2.7%, Grade 3 or 4 hepatotoxicity in 0.3%, and isoniazid treatment discontinuation in 2%. raw_record.support_text: In a series of studies of rifampin for latent tuberculosis, the paper reports the absence of hepatotoxicity: in the Hong Kong randomized trial none of the patients who discontinued due to adverse reactions developed hepatotoxicity; in the homeless Boston cohort there were no reports of hepatotoxicity; among 157 adolescents, 18 interrupted temporarily and two discontinued permanently; in a recent randomized comparison, 2/58 (3%) rifampin recipients permanently discontinued due to adverse events and none developed hepatitis; and in another observational study there were no cases of drug-induced hepatotoxicity among the 261 patients who received rifampin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Latent tuberculosis infection treated for latent infection; tolerability assessments in general adult populations (HIV-seronegative).
raw_record.extra_details: Multiple cohorts: Hong Kong randomized trial (patients discontinuing due to adverse drug reaction, none developed hepatotoxicity); homeless cohort in Boston (7/49 discontinued due to adverse effects, no hepatotoxicity reported); 157 tuberculin skin-test positive adolescents (18 interrupted temporarily, 2 discontinued permanently); randomized comparison of 4 months rifampin vs 9 months isoniazid (2/58, 3%, permanent discontinuation, none developed hepatitis); retrospective observational study where hepatotoxicity rates were 0.08% for rifampin vs 1.8% for isoniazid (p<0.001); another observational study with no drug-induced hepatotoxicity among 261 rifampin recipients.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial states that Klatskin and Kimberg's case report provides important evidence that halothane is a cause of liver injury: an anesthetist with recurrent episodes of hepatitis typically temporally related to working and thus anesthetic exposure had a flare-up precipitated by a carefully performed provocative exposure to halothane, and remained well for at least 12 months after returning to work without likely halothane exposure. Together with at least eight published cases of recurrent jaundice after separate halothane exposures and two similar patients known to the authors, the editorial concludes 'It seems highly probable that halothane was responsible for the recurrent episodes of liver damage in all these patients,' and notes the Fulminant Hepatic Necrosis Surveillance Study indicates halothane is an important cause of fulminant hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver damage recognized more frequently after re-exposure to halothane; index case was an occupationally exposed anesthetist; combined with retrospective evidence that massive hepatic necrosis is no more frequent after halothane than after other anesthetics.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury attributed to a hypersensitivity reaction rather than direct hepatotoxicity: no hepatic lesions in laboratory animals, injury in only a small proportion of exposed subjects, not dose-related, variable latent period, variable morphology with hepatitis-like lesions a common form, often with fever, eosinophilia, arthralgia, and skin rash. Retrospective studies of 856,000 patients plus an additional 300,000 patients were cited as major evidence against a cause-and-effect relationship with postoperative liver damage, with massive hepatic necrosis no more frequent after halothane than other agents, yet the editorial resolves in favor of a causal role. At least 8 published cases of recurrent jaundice after separate exposures and 2 personal cases; index anesthetist remained well for at least 12 months after avoiding exposure; less severe forms of liver damage occur and, as in the reported patient, may progress to cirrhosis; overall incidence remains unknown.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two cases of severe cholestasis associated with high levels of 6-mercaptopurine (6 MP) metabolites occurring after orthotopic liver transplantation. Applying the Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale, the temporal relationship of abnormal liver enzymes with high 6 MP metabolite levels, normalization of the liver biochemistry after drug withdrawal, absence of other offending agents, and other reported cases argue strongly in favor of 6 MP as the 'probable' cause of cholestasis. Histological features attributed to cholestatic 6 MP hepatotoxicity include severe intrahepatic cholestasis in a centrilobular location, centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis, and sinusoidal dilatation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver transplant recipients (post-orthotopic liver transplantation) receiving 6 MP as immunosuppression.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of severe cholestasis with high 6 MP metabolite levels; liver biochemistry normalized over several weeks after 6 MP withdrawal. Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale classified 6 MP as 'probable' cause of cholestasis. Histology: severe intrahepatic cholestasis (centrilobular), centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis, sinusoidal dilatation. 6 MP hepatotoxicity may present with varied manifestations ranging from asymptomatic rise in serum aminotransferases, cholestasis associated with nausea and vomiting, to venoocclusive disease (VOD) with portal hypertension, hepatoportal sclerosis, peliosis hepatitis, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia. 6 MMP (6-methylmercaptopurine) metabolite levels correlate with hepatotoxicity, whereas 6 thioguanine levels do not.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 86 liver transplant recipients with active tuberculosis, 35% (30/86) had MTB drug therapy stopped or changed due to an adverse effect attributed to therapy; of these 30, 24 (73%) had hepatotoxicity. Twenty-two of 24 hepatotoxicity patients received isoniazid, and 18 of these received isoniazid with rifampin or rifabutin. Mean time from initiation of MTB therapy to hepatotoxicity identification was 3.1 months (range 0.2-18). Most hepatotoxicity cases were reversible; 3 patients required liver retransplantation.
