raw_record.extra_details: 22 of 24 patients with drug-attributed hepatotoxicity received isoniazid; 18 of those received isoniazid with rifampin or rifabutin. raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that methotrexate is known to be hepatotoxic when given in high dosage, and that in the doses generally used for treating psoriasis, liver damage has only recently been recognized as a serious problem. In their studied patients, hepatic fibrosis developed after as little as one year of methotrexate treatment, and after three years of treatment cirrhosis or some degree of hepatic fibrosis was present in about 50% of cases. They note that, unlike many other methotrexate side effects, hepatic fibrosis is potentially irreversible and may progress to cirrhosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term (chronic) methotrexate use for psoriasis; most patients received a 'continuous low dose' schedule at minimum effective doses; severity of liver damage correlated with duration of treatment and the paper excludes three patients with disputed cirrhosis aetiology.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic fibrosis developed after as little as one year; after three years cirrhosis or some degree of hepatic fibrosis was present in about 50% of cases. Of 14 patients treated for more than 30 months, six had cirrhosis and another five showed fibrosis, in some cases severe. Liver disease severity correlates with treatment duration. Liver function tests were of little predictive value though raised alkaline phosphatase suggested fibrosis/cirrhosis; hepatomegaly during treatment was associated with considerable fibrosis or cirrhosis; liver biopsy was the only reliable assessment. Preliminary data suggest intermittent dosage may be less hepatotoxic than continuous low dose. In a Shapiro et al. (1970) study of 20 psoriatic patients no significant differences in liver function or biopsy findings were found between methotrexate-treated and topical-treatment-only groups after only 3-30 months of treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Long-term amiodarone administration causes hepatotoxicity in patients on chronic oral amiodarone therapy, attributed to iodine accumulation in the liver. Three clinical cases of amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity are presented. The paper also reports that hepatotoxicity and elevated transaminase levels occur in 15% to 50% of patients with long-term amiodarone use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term (chronic) oral amiodarone therapy at low dose for the prevention of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients underwent dual-energy computed tomography (DECT); iodine accumulation in the liver was proposed as the mechanism of hepatotoxicity. Liver enzymes were elevated in all three; abdominal DECT without contrast showed highly increased attenuation and increased hepatic iodine concentration. Case 1 showed a reversible course of liver function and decreased CT values after amiodarone discontinuation. Case 2 had increased hepatic iodine concentration and liver damage but died of multiple organ failure after rapidly progressive pneumonia (death not attributed to liver injury). Case 3 had increased hepatic iodine concentration and elevated liver enzymes, continued oral amiodarone, and required routine liver function tests every 3-6 months. The paper states hepatotoxicity/elevated transaminases occur in 15%-50% of patients on long-term use.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that long-term use of nitrofurantoin in moderate doses in patients with normal kidney function may cause or trigger chronic hepatitis. They cite a challenge (rechallenge) with the drug in patient no. 1 and rapid normalization of serum transaminases in all patients after withdrawal, together with no elevated transaminase levels in a well-matched control group, as strong evidence. Liver biopsies in all four patients showed chronic aggressive hepatitis with piecemeal necrosis and mononuclear/eosinophilic infiltration, with signs of developing cirrhosis in three patients; none were jaundiced and alkaline phosphatase was normal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term (chronic) use in moderate doses in patients with normal kidney function; exact dose not specified; none of the patients were jaundiced and clinical picture was not severe.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients; biopsies taken at maximal transaminase increase; first biopsies showed enlarged portal tracts with mononuclear and eosinophilic polymorphonuclear infiltration, piecemeal necrosis, irregular lobular margins, and swollen/eosinophilic hepatocytes; three patients (nos. 2, 3, 4) also showed lobular architectural irregularity with fibrous septa and signs of developing cirrhosis; patient no. 1 showed chronic aggressive hepatitis in follow-up biopsies 3 and 6 months after withdrawal. Rapid normalization of serum transaminases after drug withdrawal; rechallenge with drug in patient no. 1 confirmed the association; matched control group had no elevated transaminase levels. Hypoalbuminemia and hypergammaglobulinemia developed during treatment; normal eosinophile counts peripherally but eosinophilic granulocytes in liver biopsies. All but patient no. 2 (who had pulmonary infiltrates) had hepatic reaction without other obvious toxic manifestations.

raw_record.support_text: In the 'Hepatotoxicity' analysis of this long-term tacrine treatment study, six patients stopped their treatment within the first 6 months due to marked elevation of liver enzymes; after a short break (<30 days) treatment was resumed without complications in 2 patients, while the other 4 dropped out. Five patients had minor increases in liver enzymes without discontinuation. One patient with moderately elevated liver enzymes at 16 months was investigated with ultrasonic X-ray and diagnosed with liver cirrhosis, was excluded, and switched to donepezil. Elevated liver enzyme levels were detected in 24% (n=12) of patients, but only 10% (n=5) had to terminate treatment because of hepatic side effects. Paragraph 68 notes the second most common cause of first-year dropout was liver side effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term cholinesterase inhibitor therapy in unselected Alzheimer's disease outpatients followed over 5 years; hepatic side-effects stated as reason for treatment discontinuation/dropout.
raw_record.extra_details: Alzheimer's disease patients (n=50); drug under cholinesterase inhibitor class. 6 patients stopped within first 6 months for marked elevation of liver enzymes (2 resumed without complications after <30 day break, 4 dropped out); 5 patients had minor enzyme increases without discontinuation; 1 patient with moderately elevated enzymes at 16 months diagnosed with liver cirrhosis via ultrasonic X-ray, switched to donepezil. Elevated liver enzymes in 24% (n=12), treatment terminated due to hepatic side effects in 10% (n=5). Liver side effects were the second most common cause of first-year dropout. No significant correlation found between tacrine dose and outcome groups (RE vs UC) or 'time until NHP'.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe the histopathologic changes of methotrexate (MTX)-induced hepatotoxicity as well recognized, reporting on the hepatotoxic effects of long-term (10-year) MTX therapy. In most of the patients' biopsy material the pathologic findings ranged from normal to mild changes, including portal fibrosis, steatosis, inflammation, cholestasis, and sinusoidal dilatation/congestion, and the study failed to show progression to severe fibrosis and cirrhosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term chronic therapeutic exposure (10 years of MTX therapy) rather than short-course or single-agent-acute use; findings describe histologic spectrum rather than an acute idiosyncratic event.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 21 patients (with 5 repeat biopsies) on long-term MTX therapy. Initial biopsies: mild portal fibrosis with infrequent short septa and minimal patchy sinusoidal centrilobular (zone 3) fibrosis in 5 samples; no loss of architecture, complete septa, or nodular regeneration. Other changes included cholestasis (1 sample), epithelioid cell granulomas with inflammation (2 samples), lipogranulomas (1 sample), and sinusoidal dilatation/congestion with mild focal sinusoidal fibrosis (3 samples). Repeat biopsies (grade IIIA initial samples): no increase in fibrosis and no cirrhosis in 4 patients; 1 downgraded to grade II. Repeat biopsies in patients 3 and 21 (12-44 months after first biopsies, while still on MTX) showed portal/periportal inflammation, focal limiting-plate disruption, mild piecemeal necrosis, and perilobular inflammation (grade IIIB); patient 21 had >50% fat accumulation and moderate lymphoplasmacytic portal inflammation with eosinophils and polymorphonuclear cells involving one duct. Study concludes no progression to severe fibrosis or cirrhosis over 10 years. Pathogeneses (mechanism of liver cell damage/fibrosis) stated as unknown.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 415 long-term drug users treated with isoniazid 300 mg daily for latent tuberculosis infection, hepatotoxicity occurred in 20 patients (4.8%), including 6 (1.4%) with clinical hepatotoxicity; 34 patients (8.2%) had ALT and/or AST elevations to 3–5 times the upper limit of normal, and 71 (17.1%) abandoned or changed therapy. Isoniazid was the attributed cause, since hepatotoxicity was diagnosed by defined criteria and the drug was withdrawn when symptoms of hepatitis with enzyme elevations above 5x ULN appeared.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term drug users with latent tuberculosis infection; many in methadone maintenance (75.4%) or naltrexone (6.7%) programs; isoniazid 300 mg co-administered daily with pyridoxine 50 mg for 6 months under observed therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred in 20/415 patients (4.8%); clinical hepatotoxicity in 6 (1.4%); ALT/AST elevation to 3–5x ULN in 34 (8.2%); 71 (17.1%) abandoned or changed therapy. Diagnostic/drug-withdrawal criteria: symptomatic hepatitis with AST and/or ALT >5x ULN, or asymptomatic elevations >5x ULN on two consecutive weekly determinations or a single elevation >250 IU/L, with transaminases returning to baseline within 3 weeks and exclusion of viral hepatitis and other drug causes. Mean treatment duration 154.1 ± 51.4 days.

raw_record.support_text: In a report of a large population of patients who had received dantrolene for long periods, biochemical abnormalities of liver function (including moderate elevations of serum transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin) occurred in about 1.8% of patients, with symptomatic hepatitis in 0.6% and fatal hepatitis in 0.3%. The risk of hepatic injury appears about 2-fold greater in females, in patients receiving doses over 300 mg/day, and in those treated for over 60 days. The major histological pathology was subacute hepatic necrosis or chronic active hepatitis, although cholestasis has been reported; the reactions were considered unlikely to be due to hypersensitivity or autoimmune reactions. Reduced dosage recommendations for long-term use resulted in a marked decrease in severe hepatic disease reports.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term oral use; risk about 2-fold greater in females, in patients receiving doses over 300 mg/day, and in those treated for over 60 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Biochemical liver-function abnormalities (moderate elevations of serum transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) in about 1.8% of patients; symptomatic hepatitis in 0.6%; fatal hepatitis in 0.3%. Histology: subacute hepatic necrosis or chronic active hepatitis; cholestasis also reported. Reactions considered unlikely to be due to hypersensitivity or autoimmune reactions. Following reduction of long-term dose recommendations, the number of severe hepatic disease reports markedly decreased. Reference: Utili et al. 1977; data on file, Norwich Eaton.

raw_record.support_text: In this study, long-term treatment with atazanavir was generally safe and tolerable, and extended therapy was not associated with new safety issues. Atazanavir is a competitive inhibitor of uridine diphosphate-glucuronosyl transferase 1A1 and can lead to elevations in unconjugated bilirubin in a significant number of patients; elevated total bilirubin was the most common laboratory abnormality, but these elevations were asymptomatic, reversible, and not associated with hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term treatment of HIV-infected patients in an extended-study cohort (BMS AI424-044); findings in atazanavir-continuing and nelfinavir-switched groups.
raw_record.extra_details: Atazanavir use as a protease inhibitor, dosed once daily (400 mg or 600 mg). Elevated total bilirubin was the most common laboratory abnormality (observed in 76%-88% of patients across groups; Grades 3-4 in 13%-44%); elevations were asymptomatic, reversible, and attributed to UGT1A1 inhibition of unconjugated bilirubin, with the authors explicitly stating they were not associated with hepatotoxicity. Liver enzyme abnormalities (ALT/SGPT, AST/SGOT Grades 3-4) were minimal (0-3%).

raw_record.support_text: In a group of 37 patients treated with methotrexate, liver biopsies showed established or developing cirrhosis in 7 and varying degrees of hepatic fibrosis in another 10; among the remaining 20, non-specific reactive hepatitis was seen in 17 and 3 were normal. In a subgroup of 28 patients investigated regardless of whether liver disease was clinically suspected, 3 had cirrhosis, 9 had hepatic fibrosis, 14 had non-specific changes, and 2 were normal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term, chronic treatment for psoriasis (indication-restricted patient population).
raw_record.extra_details: Among 37 methotrexate-treated psoriatic patients, 7 had cirrhosis (active micronodular cirrhosis with inflammation and piecemeal necrosis in 4 cases, one with features of severe chronic aggressive hepatitis, and one inactive mixed micronodular/macronodular cirrhosis after discontinuing methotrexate four months previously). 10 patients showed mainly portal fibrosis (short septa extending around lobules, some with moderately severe portal and intralobular fibrosis), with nuclear vacuolation a constant feature and fatty change in 9 cases. Non-specific changes (mononuclear infiltration, focal necroses, acidophil bodies, fatty change, nuclear vacuolation) were found in 17. Severity of liver damage correlated with duration of methotrexate treatment: mean 17.7 ± 3.4 months for normal/non-specific histology vs 32.9 ± 6.6 months for fibrosis (P<0.05) and 46.9 ± 4.9 months for cirrhosis (P<0.001 vs normal/non-specific group); analogous values for the 28 unselected Newcastle patients were 19.6 ± 4.1, 35.2 ± 7.0, and 48.7 ± 5.9 months respectively.

raw_record.support_text: This clinical study of 49 psoriatic patients treated with long-term, low-dose, once-weekly methotrexate (MTX) examined sequential liver biopsy findings. No significant correlation was found between biopsy findings and cumulative dose or duration of treatment, and none of the 49 patients developed cirrhosis. The authors conclude that long-term, low-dose, once-weekly MTX may be significantly less hepatotoxic than previously stated, implying MTX hepatic damage is cumulative-dose related per published recommendations but this was not confirmed in their patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term, low-dose, once-weekly administration for psoriasis; patients with high alcohol consumption generally not treated with MTX and ongoing patients advised to minimize alcohol intake.
raw_record.extra_details: 49 patients with sequential liver biopsies; no cirrhosis occurred during long-term treatment. Histologic findings included steatosis and fibrosis (e.g., one patient deteriorated from steatosis to fibrosis with elevated liver enzymes). Biopsy findings did not correlate with cumulative dose, duration, or mean weekly dose (not above 20 mg weekly). 11 patients had fibrosis on the first biopsy; none deteriorated, 5 improved with no fibrosis on the last biopsy. Four patients stopped MTX due to liver biopsy findings (fibrosis or patient unwilling to continue monitoring). Authors suggest fibrosis alone need not contraindicate continued MTX therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old patient with pemphigus foliaceus, previously on corticosteroids, was started on azathioprine 100 mg daily (2 mg/kg per day). Three weeks after initiation he developed jaundice, dark urine and pruritus; laboratory investigations revealed severe hepatitis and cholestasis, with other hepatitis aetiologies negative. After azathioprine was withdrawn the jaundice regressed and hepatic tests normalised slowly; a low thiopurine methyltransferase activity (0.48 IU/mL red blood cells; normal 9.3–17.6) was found. The paper frames this as a severe case of azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity; concurrent chronic corticosteroid treatment for pemphigus foliaceus.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg daily (2 mg/kg/day); latency 3 weeks after therapy onset; jaundice, dark urine and pruritus; severe hepatitis and cholestasis on laboratory tests; other viral/aetiologic causes of hepatitis negative; dechallenge led to regression of jaundice and slow normalization of hepatic tests; TPMT activity 0.48 IU/mL red blood cells (normal 9.3-17.6). Discussion attributes toxicity to drug accumulation related to low TPMT activity.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate is reported to have hepatotoxicity as a rare side effect. Of patients with psoriasis receiving methotrexate daily, 3% to 5% developed cirrhosis after being given 1.5 g of the drug. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis who had received 1.5 g of methotrexate or 2 years of therapy, bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis (Roenick class IIIB or IV) was found in only 2 of 114 patients, one of whom was suspected of excess alcohol intake. The correlation of weekly pulse dosages of methotrexate with liver function tests is poor; enzyme elevations occur frequently but do not appear to reflect serious hepatic toxicity or the development of histologic fibrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low-dose methotrexate for psoriasis or rheumatoid arthritis; weekly pulse dosing; findings pertain to patients with risk factors (alcoholism, diabetes, obesity) excluded from certain comparisons.
raw_record.extra_details: 3% to 5% of daily-dose psoriasis patients developed cirrhosis after cumulative 1.5 g of methotrexate; bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis (Roenick class IIIB or IV) in only 2 of 114 rheumatoid arthritis patients after 1.5 g or 2 years of therapy, one case with suspected excess alcohol intake; correlation of weekly pulse dosing with liver function tests is poor, and enzyme elevations may return to baseline despite continued therapy; suggested association with hypoalbuminemia needs confirmation.

raw_record.support_text: A 60-year-old white woman receiving venlafaxine 75 mg daily for vasomotor symptoms presented after one month with abdominal pain; tests showed an enlarged liver and elevated ALT up to 372 U/L, AST up to 99 U/L, GGT up to 962 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase up to 758 U/L. After stopping venlafaxine, liver function improved markedly within a week. On rechallenge with venlafaxine 37.5 mg, liver enzymes rose again 6 days after resuming, and abnormalities resolved upon discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low-dose venlafaxine (75 mg daily initially, 37.5 mg on rechallenge) in a 60-year-old woman treated for postmenopausal vasomotor symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as drug-induced hepatitis. Hepatotoxicity characterized as rare and idiosyncratic. Naranjo probability scale rated the adverse drug event as probable. Dechallenge produced marked improvement within one week and full resolution after discontinuation; rechallenge reproduced the enzyme elevation (ALT 269, AST 49, GGT 256, ALP 263 U/L) 6 days after resuming therapy, confirming causality. Conclusion states venlafaxine can cause drug-induced hepatitis even at low doses, and recommends monitoring after therapy initiation.

raw_record.support_text: During low-dose methotrexate therapy, mild serum transaminase elevations frequently occur within 2 to 3 days of dosing and promptly return to normal, but these transient abnormalities do not predict hepatotoxicity. Liver enzymes are not necessarily elevated when cirrhosis or fibrosis develops; in one series 88 of 277 patients with biopsy-proven liver damage had no evidence of liver disease by history, physical examination, or serum transaminases, and liver biopsy was considered the only reliable means of monitoring for toxicity. A biopsy revealing portal fibrosis or cirrhosis mandates cessation of methotrexate, and a pretreatment biopsy is recommended in the setting of pre-existing liver disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low-dose weekly methotrexate therapy (initiated at 7.5 mg/week, up to 15 mg/week) in rheumatoid arthritis patients; risk relates to cumulative dosing; pre-existing liver disease is a consideration for pretreatment biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Transient transaminase elevations occur 2-3 days after dosing and resolve; serum enzymes are not reliably elevated when fibrosis/cirrhosis develops. Liver biopsy is the only reliable monitoring tool; in one series 88 of 277 patients with biopsy-proven liver damage had no evidence by history, physical exam, or transaminases. Routine pretreatment biopsy deferred until cumulative dose of 1500 mg (per Groff and coworkers); subsequent biopsies every 1-2 years; biopsy showing portal fibrosis or cirrhosis mandates drug cessation.

raw_record.extra_details: Combined data on 67 fatal/assessed cases (23 from Zimmerman and Ishak 1982 plus 35 other sources, 9 with no information). Presenting features included jaundice (15/23 and 21/35 cases), vomiting, drowsiness/malaise, fever, oedema, haemorrhage. Laboratory findings: abnormal SGOT in 56 cases, abnormal SGPT in 40, abnormal bilirubin in 40, coagulation disorder in 41, raised ammonia in 16/20 tested. Histology in 67 cases: necrosis only 20, steatosis only 8, cirrhosis only 1, steatosis and cirrhosis 4, steatosis and necrosis 22, unknown 12. Reversible hepatotoxicity: 21 patients recovering after valproate withdrawal (age 12 months to 73 years; 11 females, 6 males; 11 published cases).

raw_record.support_text: From our 30 cases and several other reports it appears that clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH) is idiosyncratic in nature: absence of dose dependence (dose was 4 times less than the pharmacological dose in 25% of patients), low incidence of toxicity under therapy (about 60 cases of hepatotoxicity reported per about 1 million people treated), and prompt recurrence following rechallenge, which also occurred in 7 of our patients. Some features of CIH resemble autoimmune chronic active hepatitis (lupoid hepatitis).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Marked female predominance (97%) in the series; autoimmune/lupoid-like features; rechallenge setting described separately.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 cases of clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH). Low incidence: ~60 hepatotoxicity cases per ~1 million treated. Dose was 4 times below the pharmacological dose in 25% of patients. Rechallenge in 7 patients reproduced chills, fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and jaundice with transaminase elevations; incubation periods shortened with each exposure (1-120 days, median 22 days for the second episode; 1 day for the third). No death from rechallenge; transaminases normalized within days to 2 months. Hypergammaglobulinemia and anti-tissue antibodies (anti-SM of anti-actin type and anti-N) present.

raw_record.support_text: Describing the safety profile of enzalutamide in men with metastatic prostate cancer who had not received chemotherapy, the authors state that, in contrast to other antiandrogens, enzalutamide was not associated with hepatotoxicity. This is an explicit statement that no human drug-induced liver injury relationship exists for enzalutamide at therapeutic dosing in this clinical-trial population.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Men with metastatic prostate cancer who had not received chemotherapy; safety evaluation during enzalutamide treatment in the PREVAIL-style trial cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Statement made in contrast to other antiandrogens. Other adverse events more frequent with enzalutamide included fatigue or asthenia, back pain, hot flush, and falls; grade 3 or higher AEs were 43% vs 37% in placebo.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of 647 metastatic breast cancer patients, 67 of 647 (10.36%) were confirmed to have docetaxel-DILI. Patients receiving docetaxel plus vinorelbine and/or docetaxel plus capecitabine/gemcitabine combination chemotherapy were at increased risk of docetaxel-DILI, with a docetaxel-based combination regimen containing capecitabine/gemcitabine and/or vinorelbine showing a 2.66-fold increased risk. Multivariate logistic regression identified premenopausal status, past HBV infection, liver metastasis, and docetaxel combination as significant contributors to the occurrence of docetaxel-DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Metastatic breast cancer patients under chemotherapy; occurrence increased with premenopausal status, past HBV infection, liver metastasis, and docetaxel-based combination chemotherapy (with capecitabine/gemcitabine and/or vinorelbine).
raw_record.extra_details: 67 of 647 patients (10.36%) confirmed to have docetaxel-DILI; incidence higher than early reported docetaxel-DILI rates. Combination regimen containing capecitabine/gemcitabine and/or vinorelbine gave 2.66-fold increased risk. Time to onset ranged 6.19-17.85 days. Cases classified as hepatocellular (n=41), cholestatic (n=16), and mixed (n=10) patterns; hepatocellular type had highest ALT/AST, cholestatic group highest bilirubin and ALP; jaundice and liver region pain most common in cholestatic group. Fever present in 31.34% of cases. Patients with more than three of the four risk factors had 36.61-fold (95% CI 10.18-131.62) increased risk; combined-risk AUC 0.7536. All patients received liver protectants concurrently.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of a 46-year-old female with metastatic lung cancer who presented with acute liver failure after being on crizotinib for two months; crizotinib was discontinued, she was treated with N-acetylcysteine for seven days, and her liver function tests returned to normal limits 26 days after admission. The authors describe this as crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity and note the precise mechanism and risk factors remain unknown.

raw_record.support_text: Of 203 patients with postoperative jaundice submitted to a panel of hepatologists, 76 were classified as having unexplained hepatitis following halothane anaesthesia (UHFH) after excluding those with identifiable causes. Hepatitis followed multiple exposure to halothane in 95% of cases, with repeated exposure within four weeks in 55%; 13 patients died in acute hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most cases followed repeated halothane exposure (95% multiple exposure; repeat exposure within four weeks in 55% of cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Nationwide survey of postoperative jaundice in the British Isles (November 1970 over three years) with hepatologist panel classification blinded to anaesthetic agent. 76 UHFH cases; 13 died in acute hepatic failure. 29 patients obese, 52 aged 41-70, 53 women. Rapid onset of jaundice, male sex, and obesity were poor prognostic signs; eosinophilia was the only impressive hypersensitivity stigma. UHFH group had higher incidence of liver kidney microsomal (LKM) and thyroid antibodies and autoimmune complement fixation than patients with identifiable jaundice causes. In 3 of 5 re-exposed patients jaundice did not recur. Paper notes that rapidly repeated exposure 'may cause hepatitis' but complication is probably rare, and comparative risks of halothane vs nonhalothane anaesthesia could not be determined.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that halothane use carries a small risk of liver damage and that the occurrence of hepatic necrosis could be largely prevented, since it only occasionally occurs after a single anaesthetic. Twenty-seven of the 35 patients of Trey and colleagues, 30 of the 42 patients of Klion and colleagues, and all of the authors' own patients had two or more anaesthetics with halothane before developing massive hepatic necrosis, and almost all showed prior features (jaundice, fever, or both) after earlier anaesthetics that could have alerted to halothane hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most cases occurred after two or more halothane anaesthetics; hepatic necrosis only occasionally follows a single anaesthetic.
raw_record.extra_details: As a general anaesthetic, halothane is described as the most widely used and its desirable properties outweigh the small risk of liver damage. Cases from Trey (27/35) and Klion (30/42), plus the authors' own patients, developed massive hepatic necrosis after repeated exposure; nearly all had earlier jaundice and/or fever indicating possible halothane hepatotoxicity. The authors also conclude that halothane hepatitis is a definite entity whose frequency is higher than currently accepted and that unexplained postoperative fever lasting longer than five days should deter further halothane use.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin can lead to a broad spectrum of liver injury with mild liver test abnormalities, acute liver failure with fatal outcome, or need for liver transplantation, and also liver cirrhosis. It was recently found to be one of the most common single agents associated with drug-induced liver injury (DILI) in a prospective study in the United States, and has been documented to induce autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH). Zone 3 necrosis was observed in the DIAIH cohort. All current-series DIAIH cases with laboratory parameters scored at least 'probable' by the new simplified AIH criteria.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most patients had been treated for a long period with the drug (median duration 24 months in the nitrofurantoin-induced AIH cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Broad spectrum includes mild liver test abnormalities, acute liver failure with fatal outcome, need for liver transplantation, and liver cirrhosis. Zone 3 necrosis observed in DIAIH cohort. Identified as one of the most common single agents associated with DILI in a recent prospective US study. Severe imaging abnormalities (low attenuation patches, confluent fibrosis and massive fibrotic bands) seen in 8/11 (73%) nitrofurantoin DIAIH cases. Inadvertent rechallenge reported to induce chronic liver injury and severe liver injury 17 years after an initial hepatitis-like illness. Cases scored at least 'probable' by simplified AIH criteria. Favorable prognosis in current DIAIH series; no cirrhosis found at presentation or on follow-up.; qualifying_conditions_note: None

raw_record.support_text: Over 30 cases of ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity have been reported, most involving individuals aged 55 years or older. Liver toxicity is dose-independent, onset of symptoms may be as early as 2 weeks after commencement, bland cholestasis is seen on liver histology, and cholestatic hepatitis with bile duct injury has been described. Recovery occurs within 3 to 6 months of discontinuing ticlopidine but may occasionally take longer than 1 year.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most reported cases involved individuals aged 55 years or older.
raw_record.extra_details: More than 30 reported cases; dose-independent; onset of symptoms may be as early as 2 weeks after commencement; bland cholestasis on histology with cholestatic hepatitis and bile duct injury described; recovery within 3-6 months of discontinuation but occasionally longer than 1 year. Clopidogrel has been used as a substitute in a patient with cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 5 published patients plus one new patient (6 total) with amitriptyline-induced jaundice. Hepatitis occurred 24-430 days after starting amitriptyline at 30-150 mg daily. Hypersensitivity manifestations (fever, rash, hypereosinophilia) were seen in 3 patients. Serum ALAT was markedly increased in 4 patients; alkaline phosphatase was usually increased. Liver histology showed necrosis, cholestasis, or both. The jaundice induced by amitriptyline is classified as 'mixed' with the hepatocellular component usually predominating. Two of the 3 patients with fulminant hepatitis died; our patient survived; patients without hepatic encephalopathy recovered in 53-128 days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most reported patients took concurrent psychotropic/sedative medications (diazepam, furosemide, amobarbital, secobarbital, chlordiazepoxide, perphenazine, sulpiride); the index patient received amitriptyline plus perphenazine (Mutanxion) before both episodes, clobazam only before the first episode and sulpiride only before the second, with amitriptyline reasonably assumed responsible.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency 24-430 days at 30-150 mg daily; fulminant hepatitis with hepatic encephalopathy in 3 patients (2 died); rechallenge led to recurrence sooner after second administration. Liver histology showed necrosis, cholestasis, and inflammation. Index patient had deep jaundice, asterixis, mild ascites, 9 mm Hg wedged-free hepatic vein gradient, and massive centrilobular/mediolobular necrosis on biopsy, with slow but complete recovery.

raw_record.support_text: The paper summarizes reported cases of jaundice due to isoniazid, describing them as hepatocellular-type (per Zimmerman's criteria). Most cases presented with fever, rash, or eosinophilia, and rechallenge with isoniazid reproduced jaundice in the present case, supporting a hypersensitivity (idiosyncratic) mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most tabulated cases also received PAS (and one also methyl prednisolone for sarcoidosis), so concurrent anti-tuberculous drug exposure with a debatable synergistic hypersensitivity effect was present; in the present case rechallenge with isoniazid reproduced jaundice twice.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine reported cases (ages 8-56 years) of isoniazid jaundice at doses 150-900 mg/day for 9 days to 7 weeks. Two patients died: Case 3 progressed to post-necrotic cirrhosis and died of ruptured varices after continuing isoniazid with jaundice; Case 8 died in hepatic coma after isoniazid readministration with PAS, with post-mortem acute massive hepatic necrosis. Most cases showed at least one of fever/rash/eosinophilia; liver biopsy in Case 1 showed acute hepatitis without bile stasis, with periportal lymphocytic/leucocytic/eosinophilic infiltrate.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report severe hepatic necrosis attributed to exposure to halothane anesthesia among patients they observed with acute hepatocellular disease, and note that multiple exposures to halothane and unexplained fever after each anesthesia-surgery procedure (each of the thirteen procedures in their seven patients with halothane necrosis was followed by fever) were characteristic of these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Multiple (repeated) exposures to halothane anesthesia; unexplained fever following each anesthesia-surgery procedure.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients with severe hepatic necrosis attributed to halothane; thirteen anesthesia-surgery procedures, each followed by fever. Clinical findings, course, laboratory data and liver pathology were indistinguishable from infectious/serum hepatitis. Severe acute hepatocellular disease with stupor/coma was associated with poor outcome: 30 of 31 such patients observed since 1958 died. The Glasgow group (Cook and Sherlock) noted similar overlap of severe hepatic necrosis due to hepatitis and various drugs.

raw_record.support_text: Safety data from carfilzomib trials show that this drug causes minimal hepatotoxicity. In an integrated safety analysis on 526 patients treated with single-agent carfilzomib, grade 3 or more hepatic adverse events occurred in 6.3% of patients, mainly as liver enzyme elevations. Reports of acute hepatic failure (0.6%), hepatic encephalopathy (0.2%), and veno-occlusive liver disease (0.2%) were also present in the safety summary, some fatal.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes clinical, laboratory, and histological data from three multiple sclerosis patients who developed idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity after high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP) administration. All three patients were hospitalized in the gastroenterology department of a tertiary Spanish hospital and followed by MS division neurologists. The paper proposes liver function surveillance 15–30 days after methylprednisolone administration and frames hepatotoxicity as a rare adverse event of methylprednisolone that should be considered in clinical practice.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Multiple sclerosis patients receiving high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone for relapse treatment; idiosyncratic reaction following IVMP administration.
raw_record.extra_details: High-dose IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg/day for 3–5 days; three patients described (clinical, laboratory, and histological data); paper proposes hepatic enzyme surveillance 15–30 days after administration and suggests ACTH, dexamethasone, or plasma exchange as alternate treatments.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a multisystemic reaction characterized by generalized erythroderma and renal, hepatic, and bone marrow failure in a patient who had started carbamazepine 50 days beforehand. A positive provocation test strongly implicated carbamazepine as the causative agent of this multisystemic reaction, which included hepatic failure attributed to carbamazepine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Multisystemic hypersensitivity reaction that also included renal and bone marrow failure; an underlying low-grade small lymphocytic lymphoma (B-cell, CD20+, CD5+) was diagnosed on bone marrow biopsy during the hospitalization.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient who had started carbamazepine 50 days before presentation; scleral icterus, hepatomegaly (liver margin 4 cm below costal margin), elevated liver tests at admission (ALT 88 U/L, AST 42 U/L, gamma-GT 751 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 294 U/L, bilirubin 73.4 mg/dL); serum carbamazepine 2 mg/L (therapeutic range 4-12 mg/L); eosinophilia (550/mm3) suggested an allergic reaction. Hepatic function tests returned to normal within four days after discontinuing carbamazepine. Positive rechallenge: one inadvertent 200 mg tablet of carbamazepine triggered severe cutaneous pruritus, rash, and hyperthermia within 2-3 hours. Viral/bacterial serologies and ANA negative.

raw_record.extra_details: SOS described as a fatal hepatic injury occurring after drug/toxin exposure, with abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, liver enzyme elevations and jaundice. In the cohort, splenic index rose from 25.6±10.4 to 29.6±11.2 cm2 after NAC (P<0.01), platelet counts were lower in the NAC group (16.9±5.5 vs 22.7±8.8 x10^4, P<0.05), and CD42b platelet staining correlated with SOS severity, especially zone III (P=0.009), with hepatocyte destruction in severe cases.

The authors conclude that carbamazepine-induced hepatitis can occur in association with prenatal and breast-feeding exposure.

raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis lasting approximately 5 weeks in the third to seventh week of life; infectious and metabolic etiologies and extrahepatic biliary atresia were excluded. GGT course compared with 2 previously published cases of neonatal carbamazepine-associated cholestatic hepatitis (Frey et al. and Merlob et al.); upper limit of normal GGT for 0-1 month: 147, 1-2 months: 123, 2-4 months: 90 U/L. Carbamazepine crosses the placenta and is excreted in breast milk. Authors recommend that this possible adverse effect be mentioned on the company drug information sheet.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective historical-control multicenter trial, 26 VLBWI given AmBisome (liposomal amphotericin B) were compared with 20 VLBWI given conventional amphotericin B for systemic candidiasis. Major adverse effects were lower in the AmBisome group, with hepatotoxicity in 25% vs 65% (AmBisome vs Amphotericin group, p = 0.014). The paper states that amphotericin B's use is limited by adverse effects including hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred in 25% of the AmBisome (liposomal amphotericin B) group vs 65% of the conventional amphotericin B group (p=0.014). No liver-injury phenotype, severity, or mechanism details are specified.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of seven patients (five female, one male, and one further female; ages 50-78 years) developed hepatotoxicity attributed to atorvastatin at therapeutic doses of 10-80 mg/day. Drug exposure to onset of the reaction ranged from 1 to 52 weeks. RUCAM causality scores ranged from 4 to 9. Liver histology showed cholestasis in two patients (cases 1 and 6) and hepatitis in one (case 5). Outcomes included death in one patient (case 5), persistently abnormal LFTs in one (case 4), and resolution in the remainder. Peak bilirubin reached up to 688 µmol/l and peak AST up to 1703 U/l.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: No non-default population or co-exposure restriction stated beyond general adult therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases reported as atorvastatin hepatotoxicity. Atorvastatin doses: 20, 10, 20, 10, 10, 80, 10 mg/day. Latency (weeks): 3, 4, 12, 5, 52, 1, 10. Duration of reaction (months): 10, 1, 3, >12, 1, 4, 2. RUCAM scores: 8, 8, 5, 8, 4, 9, 8. Case 1: 78-year-old male, jaundice with cholestatic biopsy showing non-specific cholestasis, distended bile canaliculi, feathery hepatocyte degeneration and a single focus of hepatocyte necrosis; peak bilirubin 184 µmol/l, ALP 1328 U/l, AST 175 U/l; resolved. Case 5: peak bilirubin 688 µmol/l, AST 1703 U/l, hepatitis histology; died. Case 4: persistently abnormal LFTs. Exclusion of other liver causes via normal ferritin, albumin, immunoglobulins, alpha-1 antitrypsin, prothrombin, viral serology, and negative liver autoantibodies; ultrasound excluded biliary obstruction. Competing co-medications present (e.g., atenolol, clopidogrel, lansoprazole, prednisolone in case 1) were not attributed as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: Thirty non-HIV-infected individuals who received short-term nevirapine as postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) after HIV exposure developed hepatotoxicity after a median of 20.5 days (range 8-35 days). Findings included ECOG grade 3-4 hepatotoxicity (n=14), fevers (n=11), skin rashes (n=8), eosinophilia (n=6), and fulminant hepatic necrosis requiring orthotopic liver transplantation (n=1); no other causes for severe hepatotoxicity were identified. After nevirapine discontinuation most improved within a median of 21.5 days, though one case required liver transplant and one resolved after corticosteroids. Liver biopsies showed extensive hemorrhagic central zonal necrosis with portal eosinophils and lymphocytes in one case and central zonal cholestasis with bile canalicular plugs without hepatocyte necrosis in another.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Non-HIV-infected individuals (health care workers, sexual contacts, clinical trial participants, and others) receiving short-term nevirapine as postexposure prophylaxis after potential HIV exposure (off-label use).
raw_record.extra_details: MedWatch FDA passive reports (n=19), HIV-specialist queries (n=6), pharmaceutical supplier (n=8), and published reports (n=9); severe hepatotoxicity defined as ECOG grade 3 or 4 (>5x normal ALT/AST, Alk Phos, and/or >1.5x normal total bilirubin). Grade 3-4 hepatotoxicity in 14 of 30; onset median 20.5 days (range 8-35); improvement after discontinuation in median 21.5 days (range 14-60); 1 patient had fulminant hepatic necrosis and coma requiring liver transplant 14 days after discontinuation; 1 case improved with corticosteroids after 2 months of persistent hepatotoxicity. Biopsy showed hemorrhagic central zonal necrosis with portal eosinophils and lymphocytes (patient 15) and central zonal cholestasis with bile canalicular plugs, no hepatocyte necrosis (patient 17). No positive HIV or hepatitis C serology.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports, to the authors' knowledge, the first case of hepatic peliosis caused by azathioprine (AZA) in a non-transplanted patient, a case that allows eliminating the transplantation factor and strongly incriminates AZA as an agent capable of inducing hepatic vascular lesions of the peliotic type. This is supported by Degott and colleagues, who found 12 cases of hepatic peliosis among 55 patients with hepatic alterations out of 500 renal transplant patients treated with AZA and corticosteroids.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Non-transplanted patient; intercostal shingles (zona) appeared simultaneously with the revealing hepatic pain and the authors cannot exclude that the herpes infection played a cofactor role with AZA; in transplanted patients the role of transplantation itself could always be discussed.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of AZA-induced hepatic peliosis in a non-transplanted patient. Peliosis is characterized by intralobular blood cavities distributed inhomogeneously; typical associated biologic findings include elevation of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl-transferase, isolated or with moderate transaminase elevation, frequent subicterus, almost constant hepatomegaly sometimes painful; lesions may regress, stabilize, or progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and death by hepatic failure or intraperitoneal hemorrhage. AZA hepatotoxicity was previously only invoked in renal transplant patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old man with pulmonary aspergillosis developed severe hepatotoxicity after six weeks of voriconazole (200 mg twice daily, initially intravenous then oral), with ALT 899 U/L, AST 821 U/L, ALP 256 U/L and γ-GGT 451 U/L; ALT and AST were more than five times the upper limit of normal. The patient had taken no other medications (including herbal products or supplements) recently, so voriconazole was discontinued due to consideration of voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity, and five days later liver enzymes slightly declined; he was re-admitted with hepatic insufficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Normal CYP2C19 metabolizer genotype with a low (not high) voriconazole trough concentration; history of old tuberculosis and chronic gastritis.
raw_record.extra_details: Standard dosing of 200 mg twice daily (IV then oral); onset of severe hepatotoxicity at six weeks; enzyme values ALT 899 U/L (≤41), AST 821 U/L (≤40), ALP 256 U/L, γ-GGT 451 U/L; ALT/AST >5x ULN; dechallenge led to slight decline (ALT 826, AST 598, ALP 227, γ-GGT 427) after five days; re-admitted with hepatic insufficiency; no concurrent medications.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate (MTX) is effective for treating psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, but its potential hepatotoxicity remains a concern. The paper frames liver biopsy as the gold standard for detecting MTX-induced liver injury, and the study investigated transient elastography for detecting MTX-induced liver fibrosis in Chinese psoriasis patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Observed in Chinese adult psoriasis patients receiving MTX; significant fibrosis was correlated with obesity and diabetes and not with MTX cumulative dose or duration of use.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 228 patients screened, 34 met inclusion criteria; 9 (26.5%) had significant liver fibrosis (Roenigk grade ≥3a). Transient elastography had an area under the ROC curve of 0.76 (95% CI 0.59-0.93; P=0.021); a cut-off of 7.1 kPa gave 100% sensitivity and 68% specificity. Liver biopsy was performed when liver stiffness was ≥7.1 kPa or total cumulative dose of MTX was ≥3.5 g. Fibrosis correlated with BMI ≥30 kg/m², waist circumference ≥138 cm, and glycated haemoglobin ≥7.8%.

raw_record.support_text: A 34-year-old nurse presented with sudden non-pruritic jaundice and elevated transaminases after inadvertent exposure to halothane in the surgical theatre where she works; viral, collagen, malaria, and sickling tests were negative. She improved with conservative management, then re-exposed to halothane after three weeks and developed a similar clinical picture, again improving on conservative management. raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old man with Crohn's disease, on mesalazine, azathioprine and steroids, developed altered liver tests with a cholestasis pattern seven months after his azathioprine dose was increased to 2.5 mg/kg/day (200 mg daily). Values showed AST 113 U/l, ALT 61 U/l, FA 284 U/l, GGT 462 U/l and total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dl, with thrombocytopenia (79,000/mm³), and abdominal ultrasound showed signs of portal hypertension (spleen 15 cm, portal vein 14 mm) and chronic hepatopathy; upper endoscopy showed small esophageal varices.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred after azathioprine dose increase to 2.5 mg/kg/day in a patient with Crohn's disease (ileocolic L3, fistulizing B3) also receiving mesalazine and steroids; features of chronic hepatopathy and portal hypertension present.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~7 months after the dose increase. Liver biopsy showed moderate architectural alteration with portal and sinusoidal fibrosis, regenerative nodules (reticulin staining) with lightly enlarged hepatocytes, perivenular fibrosis, sinusoidal congestion and areas of hepatocyte atrophy, compatible with nodular regenerative hyperplasia. After stopping azathioprine, aminotransferases, cholestasis enzymes and bilirubin improved and platelets normalized about one year later; follow-up ultrasound showed disappearance of portal hypertension signs (portal vein 12 mm, spleen 11.5 cm). Viral, autoimmune, alpha-1-antitrypsin, iron and copper workup were normal.

raw_record.support_text: As a complication of thyrotoxicosis treatment, methimazole (MMI)-induced hepatic dysfunction occurred in 4 cases (9.3%). The pattern of liver injury varied: 2 patients had hepatocellular injury, while 1 patient each showed cholestatic and mixed injury. All these patients underwent I-131 ablation therapy, and liver function tests normalized in 3 of the 4 patients; however, the patient with cholestatic liver injury continued to exhibit persistent cholestasis, and a liver biopsy confirmed cholangiopathy consistent with MMI-induced cholestasis.

raw_record.extra_details: 4 cases among 43 thyrotoxicosis patients (9.3%). Pattern: 2 hepatocellular, 1 cholestatic, 1 mixed. The cholestatic patient had persistent cholestasis with liver biopsy confirming cholangiopathy consistent with MMI-induced cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: The case report concerns a pregnant patient with significant propylthiouracil (PTU) hepatotoxicity, reported as PTU-induced hepatitis occurring in the second trimester of pregnancy. The authors note PTU-induced hepatitis is a recognized drug reaction with a small but potentially serious risk of hepatic failure, and they describe it as the first reported case of occurrence in the second trimester with a subsequent successful outcome following best supportive care and carbimazole (CBZ) therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred during pregnancy in the second trimester; the patient also had pre-existing deranged liver function at presentation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report; claimed to be the first reported PTU hepatotoxicity occurring in the second trimester; successful outcome achieved with early cessation of PTU, best supportive care and subsequent carbimazole therapy for relapse of hyperthyroidism; PTU may be used in women considering pregnancy, prolonging exposure and increasing risk of PTU-induced hepatitis; patients started on PTU should be warned of the small but potentially serious risk of hepatic failure and advised to seek medical advice on jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients suffered from fulminant hepatitis within 23, 59 and 22 weeks after having ingested a total dose of 16, 26 and 15 g, respectively, of amodiaquine for the prophylaxis of malaria. Amodiaquine administration was continued for 44, 21 and 25 days after the onset of jaundice. One patient underwent emergency orthotopic liver transplantation and survived; the other two died. The report states that fulminant hepatitis threatens patients in whom amodiaquine administration is protracted for several months and not interrupted when jaundice occurs.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred during protracted amodiaquine prophylaxis of malaria with administration continued 21-44 days after jaundice onset, which the authors link to the fulminant course.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients (including a 12-year-old girl, Case 1) with no prior liver disease or co-medication; serology negative for HAV, HBV, HSV, CMV, EBV; no pyrexia; normal leukocyte counts. Fulminant hepatitis attributed to severe liver cell necrosis. Total ingested doses 16, 26 and 15 g; onset at 23, 59 and 22 weeks. One patient (Case 1) underwent emergency orthotopic liver transplantation and survived; two died. Case 1 whole blood amodiaquine (AD) and monodeethylamodiaquine (MAD) 3 days after withdrawal were 173 and 725 ng/ml (normal ranges 0-5 and 75-92 ng/ml); hepatic tissue AD 27 and MAD 98 mg/g wet tissue. The authors note prior reports that amodiaquine is responsible for acute hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports isoniazid (INH)-associated hepatitis observed in a Philadelphia tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis and treatment program. A table of annual surveillance data (1969-1973) shows 7-9 annual cases of INH-associated hepatitis among the INH-treated population (rates of 0.12%-0.22% of the total INH population), including cases arising during both treatment and prophylaxis. The paper states that with proper surveillance isoniazid-associated hepatitis is readily reversible and shows no permanent defect on follow-up, and that the relatively low incidence of isoniazid-associated hepatitis does not preclude prophylactic use when there is a significant community problem.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred in a tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis and treatment program; described as reversible with surveillance and showing no permanent defect on follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: Annual Philadelphia surveillance data 1969-1973: total INH-associated hepatitis cases 7 (1969), 5 (1970), 7 (1971), 5 (1972), 9 (1973); rates of 0.15%-0.22% of the total INH population, including cases in both treatment and prophylaxis groups. The paper concludes the low incidence does not preclude prophylactic use given a significant community problem.

raw_record.support_text: In the DDI stage of this phase 1 study, all nine participants receiving GDC-2394 with midazolam experienced at least one AE, and two participants experienced SAEs of grade 4 drug-induced liver injury (DILI) on days 18 and 20 that were considered related to study treatment and met Hy's law criteria (AST or ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN or clinical jaundice). The sponsor halted all further enrollment, and both participants recovered, one receiving oral ursodeoxycholic acid. Additionally, three participants experienced events consistent with hepatic injury after completing GDC-2394 dosing, including one participant with a grade 2 ALT increase on day 11 considered related to study drug that resolved by day 20.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred in the drug-drug interaction stage where GDC-2394 was co-administered with midazolam in healthy participants; study enrollment was halted after these events.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 1 first-in-human SAD/MAD/FE/DDI study (NCT, 2021-2022). Two SAEs of grade 4 DILI reported on days 18 and 20, both meeting Hy's law criteria (AST or ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN or clinical jaundice), considered related to study treatment; both participants recovered, one treated with oral ursodeoxycholic acid. Seven (78%) DDI participants reported events considered related (fatigue and DILI most frequent). Three participants had events consistent with hepatic injury after completion of dosing; one had a grade 2 ALT increase on day 11 (related) resolving to grade 1 by day 20. No deaths. DILI was the reason the DDI stage (planned n=15) was halted at n=9.

raw_record.support_text: A 67-year-old man developed aplastic anaemia 11 weeks after a carbamazepine-induced DRESS. Among the systemic manifestations of the DRESS he had liver involvement with a pattern of cholestatic hepatitis. Carbamazepine was stopped at onset of the eruption, prednisone was started, the skin eruption resolved, and his liver function tests returned to normal values.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred within a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) hypersensitivity syndrome in a 67-year-old man; liver involvement was one of the systemic manifestations of carbamazepine-induced DRESS.
raw_record.extra_details: Carbamazepine was taken for facial post-herpetic neuralgia; rash and fever began about 2 months after starting therapy. Cholestatic hepatitis was documented by elevated alkaline phosphatase (855 U/L), gamma-glutamyl transferase (1267 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (161 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (51 U/L); bilirubin remained near normal (0.7 mg/dL). Liver tests returned to normal after carbamazepine withdrawal and prednisone. The patient later died of haemoptysis in the setting of probable pneumonia and severe thrombocytopenia during aplastic anaemia, not of liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes two distinct forms of liver damage associated with halothane anaesthesia. The milder form is characterised by elevation of serum aminotransferases, usually below three times the upper limit of normal, and occurs after about 20% of anaesthetics. The severer, much less frequent form is associated with fulminant hepatic failure and a high mortality, occurring more often after multiple exposures to halothane.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurs at anaesthetic (therapeutic) exposure; the severe form is much more frequent after repeated halothane anaesthetics, and cases may be preceded by earlier milder reactions to previous halothane anaesthetics.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe form associated with fulminant hepatic failure and high mortality; analysis of published reports of halothane hepatitis describing 10 or more patients shows high female:male ratio (1.6:1), previous halothane exposure in 78%, peripheral eosinophilia 21%, auto-antibodies 29%; Inman and Mushin reported 82% of cases had been exposed on at least one previous occasion and 80% within 28 days; shorter interval between exposures is associated with shorter period between last anaesthetic and onset of jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, an antidiabetic drug, caused life-threatening idiosyncratic reactions in patients. Mild, reversible hepatotoxicity appeared in pre-marketing clinical trials in <2% of patients; after marketing in early 1997 several cases of severe, even fatal, liver failure emerged, forcing market withdrawal in 2000. Affected patients had elevated serum enzymes and bilirubin and signs of hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis; livers showed necrosis and inflammatory infiltrates including neutrophils. Injury was idiosyncratic with no obvious dose relationship.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurs in a small minority of treated patients; no obvious relationship to dose or duration; onset of signs at widely varying times after therapy start.
raw_record.extra_details: Mild reversible hepatotoxicity in <2% of pre-marketing trial patients; several cases of severe, even fatal, liver failure after market entry in 1997; withdrawn from the market in 2000; elevated serum enzymes and bilirubin; signs of hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis; necrosis with inflammatory infiltrates including neutrophil accumulation; authors note it is not currently possible to predict which patients will develop liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: After exclusion of viral or toxic hepatitis, acute cholestatic hepatitis due to flutamide use was diagnosed. The patient, an 18-year-old woman treated with flutamide (375 mg/day then 250 mg/day) for minor acne and hirsutism, developed symptoms about 5 months after starting treatment and required admission with markedly raised aminotransferases and total bilirubin. Despite intensive care and multiple liver transplant attempts, the patient died 2 months after admission from septicemia and hemorrhage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Off-label therapeutic use in an 18-year-old woman for acne and hirsutism related to polycystic ovarian syndrome; an oral contraceptive was co-administered during the second course; no other drugs and no alcohol.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 375 mg/day for first month then 250 mg/day, renewed for a further 2 months; onset ~5 months after start. On admission: AST 4417 IU/L, ALT 4717 IU/L, GGT 140 IU/L, total bilirubin 222 µmol/L (rising to 547 µmol/L); symptoms asthenia, pruritus, diarrhoea, headache, hyperchromatic urine, sudoresis, nausea, jaundice. Abdominal ultrasonogram negative; EEG showed widespread discrete electrical alterations. Liver transplant 2 weeks after admission unsuccessful, with two further unsuccessful attempts; patient died 2 months after admission from septicemia and hemorrhage.

raw_record.support_text: About 10 days after admission the patient revealed she had been regularly taking 'natural' drugs for overweight over the last ten years, and that the therapy had recently been modified with the introduction of pemoline at a dose of 75 mg/day, within dosages recommended for its primary indication. The paper titles and develops this as a case of pemoline-induced hepatotoxicity, reporting that the patient developed acute hepatitis with submassive necrosis and required orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Off-label use for overweight; dose 75 mg/day (within recommended dosages for its primary indication).
raw_record.extra_details: Therapy recently modified with introduction of pemoline; liver dysfunction progressed rapidly (grade II encephalopathy, INR 2.6, bilirubin 28.4 mg/dl, glucose 49 mg/dl) and patient listed for transplant at UNOS status I; surgical biopsy and explant showed acute hepatitis with submassive necrosis and focal cirrhosis; underwent orthotopic liver transplantation on day 20. Discussion states pemoline-induced hepatotoxicity is supported by a large body of evidence: about 50 published cases of liver enzyme increases of variable entity reversible after withdrawal, at least 4 cases of acute liver failure leading to liver transplantation, and 3 fatal cases. Cases mostly paediatric because of the primary indication in attention/hyperactivity deficit disorders. Steroids (methylprednisolone 60 mg/day) tried but did not change disease course.

raw_record.support_text: In this prospective pharmacovigilance study of older adults' DILI, paracetamol was the culprit drug for 11% (50/458) of DILI cases, and one case was fatal. Ageing-related changes in liver blood flow and mass can increase paracetamol exposure, causing more frequently acute liver injury with paracetamol given at therapeutic doses, which led to a 2018 recommendation for a maximum paracetamol dose of 3 g per day (previously 4 g) for the elderly, achieving an 80% reduction in paracetamol-related DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Older adult (>65 y) patients from geriatric department cohorts; therapeutic-dose exposure in elderly; 2018 regulatory/clinical recommendation capped paracetamol at 3 g/day for the elderly.
raw_record.extra_details: Culprit for 11% (50/458) of DILI cases, one case fatal; 2018 recommendation lowering maximum elderly dose to 3 g/day (from 4 g) produced ~80% reduction in paracetamol-related DILI after 1 year; aging-related reductions in liver blood flow and mass increase paracetamol exposure and frequency of acute liver injury at therapeutic doses.

raw_record.support_text: Two older patients (83 and 91 years old) developed acute hepatotoxicity with elevated trough paracetamol levels (54 mg/l and 31 mg/l) while receiving a standard European oral dose of paracetamol (2 x 500 mg QDS = 4 g daily) with no risk factors for slowed metabolism (weight <50 kg, interacting medications, hepatic enzyme inducers, history of liver disease), following a recent dose escalation from as-needed to 4 g daily. The authors conclude that even when prescribed appropriately at the usual therapeutic dosage, paracetamol can be hepatotoxic.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Older patients (aged 83 and 91 years); therapeutic standard dose of 4 g daily with no risk factors for slowed metabolism; recent dose escalation from as-needed to 4 g daily; second patient also received co-codamol (paracetamol 500 mg/codeine 30 mg).
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (83-year-old female): LFTs rose from normal on Day 4 and peaked Day 6, trough paracetamol 54 mg/l, drug discontinued, treated with N-acetylcysteine, recovered completely with LFTs normalized in 2 weeks. Case 2 (91-year-old nursing home resident): on co-codamol for 3 weeks prior, acute hepatotoxicity with normal LFTs 2 weeks earlier, trough paracetamol 31 mg/l, received N-acetylcysteine but did not respond and died. Paracetamol = N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (acetaminophen).

raw_record.support_text: The glucose-containing chloroethylnitrosourea chlorozotocin showed hepatic toxicity: a few patients in phase I trials had reversible elevations of serum liver enzymes, and Belt et al. described three cases of liver damage following chlorozotocin at a dose of 225 mg/m². Peak bilirubin elevations ranged 3.5-12.7 mg/100 ml (mostly conjugated/direct), alkaline phosphatase rose up to 20 times normal while SGOT rose only 3-4 times, and liver histology showed centrilobular cholestasis in two cases and cholestasis without lobular localization in the third.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: One of the three described cases had a history of alcohol ingestion; whether the cholestatic histologic pattern is entirely characteristic of chlorozotocin-induced liver damage was not known.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as a glucose-containing chloroethylnitrosourea similar to other nitrosoureas. Phase I trials: a few patients with reversible serum liver-enzyme elevations. Belt et al.: three cases of liver damage at 225 mg/m², peak bilirubin 3.5-12.7 mg/100 ml mostly conjugated, marked alkaline phosphatase elevation up to 20 times normal, SGOT 3-4 times normal; histology showed centrilobular cholestasis (2 cases) and cholestasis without lobular localization (1 case). Mouse study (preclinical) showed principally hepatocellular vacuolation and necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The study demonstrated a clear relationship between methotrexate (MTX) therapy and chemically and histologically defined liver damage. The rapidity of onset and severity of abnormal liver function tests correlated with the intensity of therapy, with more hepatotoxicity observed in the group showing hematologic and gastrointestinal chemotherapy side effects. LFT abnormalities following intermittent MTX resolved completely within one month after cessation, and continued moderate-dose MTX therapy was associated with normal or near-normal liver function without progressive hepatic damage, including in patients with eye disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: One patient with pre-existing liver disease developed a somewhat more severe functional abnormality; his liver function returned to normal after cessation of therapy and repeated biopsies showed no further deterioration. Therapy was given for otherwise healthy ocular disease or as part of leukemia chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity included abnormal SGOT/SGPT and BSP retention, with histologic findings of portal fibrosis, fatty metamorphosis, mild toxic degeneration of hepatic parenchymal cells, and slight bile stasis. LFT abnormalities correlated with intensity of therapy and resolved within one month after cessation of intermittent MTX. Five patients received maintenance MTX 10-25 mg/m² IV once weekly for 3 months to 1.5 years; liver function returned to normal in 4 of 5, while one had persistent abnormalities (SGOT 30-60, SGPT 60-130, BSP 7-11%). Four intensive-therapy patients died of infectious complications of leukemia 4-6 months post-study with hepatic disease not involved; all showed leukemic portal infiltration, one with moderate fatty metamorphosis, one with slight portal fibrosis and moderate fatty metamorphosis.

raw_record.support_text: Human safety data on alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) are reported from more than 35 clinical studies (>1300 individuals, 600-2400 mg/day, up to 24 months). In the double-blind placebo-controlled ALADIN II study (24 months, 600 and 1200 mg/day), treatment-related adverse events were monitored across body systems and clinical chemistry parameters including SGOT, SGPT, gamma-GT, alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin; the authors report no differences in safety parameters between treatment groups and placebo over the entire study, and general tolerability was very good (94% for 1200 mg/day group versus 100% placebo). No drug-related liver injury is reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Oral supplementation/administration in humans; therapeutic doses of 600-2400 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: >35 clinical studies with >1300 participants, doses typically 600-2400 mg/day, durations weeks to 24 months. ALADIN II double-blind placebo-controlled study monitored liver chemistries (SGOT, SGPT, gamma-GT, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin) and found no differences vs placebo; tolerability very good (94% for 1200 mg/day group vs 100% placebo). General safety assessment (oral LD50 >2000 mg/kg bw in rats; no mutagenicity/genotoxicity).

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis developed acute hepatitis, probably due to orodispersible prednisolone (Solupred), which was started at 40 mg/d after intravenous methylprednisolone. Liver tests worsened after readministration of orodispersible prednisolone and improved after its withdrawal and replacement with oral prednisone, supporting causality. The case is titled prednisolone-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: At day 14 after starting prednisolone: ALT 165 U/L (3.3 N), AST 73 U/L (1.5 N), Alk Phos 369 U/L (3.2 N), GGT 706 U/L (12.8 N), bilirubin normal. Values improved on withdrawal and worsened on rechallenge (day 27: ALT 730 U/L (14.6 N), AST 313 U/L, Alk Phos 393 U/L, GGT 1097 U/L), then resolved after switch to oral prednisone (Cortancyl). raw_record.support_text: 95 patients had acute hepatitis with features of veno-occlusive disease during the trial, and all instances were related to 6-thioguanine exposure: 82 had been assigned that drug, one was taking non-randomised 6-thioguanine, and 12 were patients assigned 6-mercaptopurine who developed veno-occlusive disease whilst taking 6-thioguanine during intensification. Diagnosis was centrally validated and required at least two of: tender hepatomegaly, ascites, hyperbilirubinaemia (>17 µmol/L), or persistent thrombocytopenia out of proportion to neutropenia for more than 4 weeks. In the 82 assigned 6-thioguanine, 85% of veno-occlusive disease episodes occurred during continuing treatment or interim maintenance. Most patients had transient tender hepatomegaly with mild to moderate hyperbilirubinaemia and raised aminotransferases; one patient died of biopsy-proven adenovirus infection.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia patients treated within the ALL97/99 trial phases; treatment with 6-thioguanine as continuing therapy, interim maintenance, or intensification in comparison with 6-mercaptopurine.
raw_record.extra_details: 95 cases of acute hepatitis with veno-occlusive disease features; 82 patients assigned 6-thioguanine, 1 on non-randomised 6-thioguanine, 12 assigned 6-mercaptopurine who developed VOD while taking 6-thioguanine in intensification. Diagnosis required at least two of: tender hepatomegaly, ascites, hyperbilirubinaemia (>17 µmol/L), persistent thrombocytopenia out of proportion to neutropenia for >4 weeks. Among patients assigned 6-thioguanine, 85% of VOD episodes occurred during continuing treatment (75%) or interim maintenance (10%), 15% during intensification. >90% had transient tender hepatomegaly, mild-moderate hyperbilirubinaemia with raised aminotransferases, and moderate-severe thrombocytopenia. One patient died of biopsy-proven adenovirus infection after presenting with VOD features; two admitted to intensive care for pulmonary complications; ~20% needed platelet/RBC transfusions. All switched to 6-mercaptopurine after VOD. Liver tests normalised after mean 4 weeks (range 1-52). 24 patients (25% of affected) developed splenomegaly with persistent mild-moderate thrombocytopenia; a further 19 patients had splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia without antecedent acute VOD, all in 6-thioguanine recipients.

raw_record.support_text: Case 2: a 68-year-old man receiving intravenous amiodarone (bolus 450 mg then constant infusion and oral therapy) for refractory symptomatic ventricular tachycardia developed, 36 hours after starting amiodarone, a considerable rise in serum transaminases, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin with icterus and pruritus. Hepatitis A/B markers and viral and immunologic studies were negative and ultrasonography excluded obstructive biliary disease. Toxic cholestatic hepatitis was suspected; liver function returned to normal within 2 weeks along with gradual reduction of amiodarone dosage. The discussion states the clinical course, together with absence of known causes of acute liver damage, strongly suggests amiodarone as the cause of hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.extra_details: Two patients studied; liver enzyme/AST/ALT/AP/γ-GT/bilirubin elevations with icterus and pruritus appeared ~36 hours after starting amiodarone; viral (hepatitis A and B), immunologic studies and abdominal ultrasonography negative; liver biochemistry normalized within 2 weeks with gradual dose reduction. Discussion of 4 previously reported cases of early acute hepatitis due to parenteral amiodarone: 3 normalized promptly after stopping infusion, 1 died. In these two cases the drug was not stopped, only mildly reduced.

raw_record.extra_details: Aminoglutethimide 250 mg four times daily. Generalized pruritic eruption appeared after two months of therapy and resolved on discontinuation; therapy restarted at reduced dose and jaundice (icterus) developed. Labs: bilirubin 7.1 mg/dL (mostly direct), alkaline phosphatase 155 U, AST 128 U, ALT 207 U, GGT 1338 U, 7% eosinophils; hepatitis B surface antigen/antibody, Coombs' and alpha-fetoprotein negative; no biliary obstruction on ultrasound/ERCP. Jaundice and rash resolved upon discontinuation with supportive care; bilirubin fell to 3.0 mg/dL after two weeks and most values normalized within four weeks. Mechanism compared to phenytoin and sulfa hypersensitivity, possibly indicating latent direct hepatotoxic potential.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes a rare adverse effect of the antidiabetic drug repaglinide, a fast, short-acting meglitinide analog approved for type 2 diabetes. Although only elevated liver enzymes had rarely been noted before, the authors report a patient who developed cholestatic hepatitis while taking repaglinide, framed as the first published report of cholestatic hepatitis related to this drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient also had type 2 diabetes; no co-medications or herbal remedies reported.
raw_record.extra_details: 72-year-old man with 2-year history of diet-controlled type 2 diabetes and normal baseline liver function. Repaglinide started at 1 mg/day and increased to 2 mg/day one month before presentation; presented with 2-week history of itching and jaundice. Lab values: AST 83 U/L (<37), ALT 183 U/L (<40), ALP 307 U/L (<136), GGT 303 U/L (<85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. Viral serology and autoantibody screening negative; MR cholangiography showed no pathology. Liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with mild bile duct proliferation and moderate inflammatory infiltrate (mainly lymphocytes, some eosinophils) with hepatocyte ballooning. On withdrawal, laboratory findings normalized within a month. Causal attribution supported by temporal eligibility, exclusion of alternative causes, histologic features, and rapid improvement after withdrawal; presence of eosinophils suggested a possible immune mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute severe cytolytic and cholestatic hepatitis probably attributable (probablement imputable) to rofecoxib in a 69-year-old woman hospitalised for cutaneous-mucous jaundice. She had taken rofecoxib 12.5 mg per day for three days, four weeks before admission, for left shoulder pain. Liver tests showed cytolysis (ASAT 38x ULN, ALAT 42x ULN), cholestasis (alkaline phosphatase 4x ULN, γGT 40x ULN) and hyperbilirubinaemia (310 µmol/L total, 157 conjugated); prothrombin was reduced to 55% and factor V to 73%. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis compatible with drug-induced hepatitis. Her liver tests and prothrombin normalised within 6 months of rofecoxib discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient also used irbesartan (3 years, hypertension), zopiclone (insomnia), and self-medicated 1–2 g paracetamol daily for 4 months, representing concurrent co-medications; rofecoxib was taken intermittently at 12.5 mg/day for 3 days and was judged probably responsible.
raw_record.extra_details: Rofecoxib (Vioxx®), a selective COX-2 NSAID, was being self-medicated for left shoulder pain. Presented acute hepatitis with jaundice, hepatomegaly; no splenomegaly, ascites, or hepatic encephalopathy. Hypereosinophilia 0.49 g/L; positive anti-nuclear antibodies (1/320, homogeneous+cytoplasmic) at admission, negative at 6 months; viral, autoimmune and metabolic work-up otherwise negative. Biopsy showed acute hepatitis without portal/periportal fibrosis, centrilobular destruction, mixed portal-periportal-lobular inflammatory infiltrate with moderate cholangiolar proliferation. Prothrombin 55% with factor V 73%; improved to 65% at 1 week, normal 80% at 2 months, liver panel fully normal at 6 months. Adverse event reported Feb 2004 to Merck Sharp & Dohme-Chibret pharmacovigilance. Paper also notes four previously published cases of acute hepatitis in patients treated with rofecoxib.
