raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old man treated with benzbromarone (100 mg/d) for 4 months for hyperuricemia was admitted for icterus and nausea with severe liver injury and serious coagulation dysfunction. He deteriorated with grade II encephalopathy, underwent continuous plasma exchange six times, and received liver transplantation 26 days after admission. Liver pathology showed massive necrosis consistent with drug-induced liver injury, supporting the diagnosis of acute liver failure associated with benzbromarone; the patient recovered thereafter. The patient had a 10-year history of beer drinking (about 28 g/d alcohol), while autoimmune, viral hepatitis, and HIV tests were negative.

raw_record.support_text: In a 55-year-old female with lichen simplex chronicus and an autoimmune disposition (mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis and hypothyroidism), chronic nitrofurantoin therapy was implicated as the cause of autoimmune hepatitis-type 1. The positive ANA and ASMA results, hypergammaglobulinemia, histological chronic active hepatitis on liver biopsy, and clinical response to immunosuppressive drugs were strongly suggestive of nitrofurantoin-triggered autoimmune hepatitis. The Naranjo algorithm score was 6, indicating a probable drug-induced reaction. The patient was treated with drug withdrawal and parenteral glucocorticosteroids; azathioprine was considered if steroids failed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had a pre-existing autoimmune disposition (mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis and hypothyroidism); chronic nitrofurantoin therapy for UTI; 55-year-old female.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis with lymphoplasmacytic portal infiltrate and interface hepatitis. Positive ANA and ASMA, hypergammaglobulinemia. Naranjo algorithm score 6 (probable DIR). WHO-method rechallenge test considered confirmatory but not performed due to severity. Treatment: drug withdrawal and parenteral glucocorticosteroids; azathioprine if steroids fail. The paper also notes nitrofurantoin has been linked to autoimmune hepatitis (mostly single case reports/small series) and estimates nitrofurantoin-induced hepatic injury incidence at about 3 cases per 1,000,000 from Dutch and Danish national adverse-drug-reaction monitoring agencies.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old Asian patient with anaplastic lymphoma kinase-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma was started on crizotinib 250 mg twice daily as first-line therapy. On day 55 he was admitted with elevated AST (402 IU/L), ALT (215 IU/L) and total bilirubin (145 μmol/L) and was diagnosed with crizotinib-induced fulminant liver failure. Despite discontinuation and supportive therapy, enzymes continued to rise (AST 1075 IU/L, ALT 240 IU/L, bilirubin 233 μmol/L) and he died on day 60.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma with hepatic metastasis; 37-year-old Asian male.
raw_record.extra_details: First-line dose 250 mg twice daily; no adverse effects until day 46; admitted day 55 with elevated AST 402 IU/L, ALT 215 IU/L, total bilirubin 145 μmol/L; despite crizotinib discontinuation and supportive therapy levels rose to AST 1075 IU/L, ALT 240 IU/L, bilirubin 233 μmol/L and the patient died on day 60. Authors note crizotinib hepatotoxicity is rare and non-specific and may progress to fatal liver failure, and recommend King's College Criteria and weekly liver enzyme monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that several features of the case support pioglitazone as the cause of hepatic injury: other causes of acute hepatitis and biliary obstruction were reasonably excluded, liver biopsy findings were consistent with drug hepatotoxicity, and the patient improved within a few days of stopping pioglitazone until serum liver enzyme results were completely normal. Because a repeated liver biopsy was not performed, they could only presume, not prove, that a morphologically normal liver was restored.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had also received glyburide, metformin, lisinopril, and omeprazole; the authors could not exclude a combination effect or altered pioglitazone metabolism, though the patient did not become ill until pioglitazone was added. General adult patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic injury developed after 6 months of pioglitazone treatment (a recent case report by Maeda described hepatitis after 7 months, with elevated ALT and alkaline phosphatase). Liver biopsy showed mild portal lymphocytic inflammation, mildly altered bile duct nuclear polarity, and intraepithelial lymphocytes. The patient improved within days of discontinuation with complete normalization of serum liver enzymes; no repeated biopsy or rechallenge was performed. Authors frame hepatotoxicity as probably idiosyncratic, as with troglitazone and rosiglitazone. Premarketing trials: 0.26% of 1526 patients had asymptomatic ALT >3x ULN, similar to 0.25% of placebo patients; these were not clearly related to therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that rosiglitazone led to even more severe hepatotoxicity in their patient, manifested chiefly as a cholestatic hepatitis with nonsuppurative granulomatous cholangitis rather than hepatocellular injury, with serum aminotransferases within normal limits or only mildly elevated while alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin ranged from 3 to 20 times the upper limit of normal (peaks of 14.4 µkat/L alkaline phosphatase and 379 µM bilirubin). In paragraph 24, they state that severe and rapid worsening on inadvertent rechallenge with rosiglitazone provides additional strong evidence for rosiglitazone-induced liver injury, and that the overall course makes it unlikely the disease was due only to troglitazone.

raw_record.support_text: The authors reported the case of a patient undergoing hemodialysis (HD) who experienced acute liver dysfunction caused by febuxostat therapy. They noted that previous reports on acute severe liver dysfunction induced by febuxostat are scarce and recommended monitoring liver function test parameters to avoid progression of febuxostat-induced liver damage, especially in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and those undergoing HD.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had chronic kidney disease and was undergoing hemodialysis (HD), a non-default restricted population.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of acute severe liver dysfunction (acute liver injury) attributed to febuxostat in an HD patient. Febuxostat was administered as an alternative to allopurinol for hyperuricemia; the patient had previously been on oral allopurinol. The drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test (DLST) was negative for both febuxostat (92% SI) and allopurinol (101% SI). The case also involved severe hyperkalemia with severe liver dysfunction, and no HLA-B*58:01 (patient profile HLA-A*24:02, HLA-B*52:01, HLA-DRB1*15:02); no study has reported an association between these HLA alleles and DILI, so the HLA association with the febuxostat reaction remains unclear. Authors recommend frequent liver function monitoring and possibly lower than usual febuxostat doses in CKD/HD patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old Middle Eastern female presented with fatigue, malaise, and jaundice after recent treatment with albendazole for two large hydatid liver cysts. She had significant progressive transaminase and bilirubin elevation despite stopping albendazole; a transjugular liver biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with patchy necrosis, a distorted reticulin framework, and no plasma cell infiltration. She progressed to fulminant hepatic failure and received orthotopic liver transplantation 13 days into admission. RUCAM score was 6, indicating probable drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had echinococcal (hydatid) liver cysts; albendazole used for treatment of this indication.
raw_record.extra_details: Anthelmintic FDA-approved for echinococcosis; RUCAM score 6 (probable). Progressive transaminase and bilirubin elevation despite drug cessation; biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with patchy necrosis, distorted reticulin framework, and no plasma cell infiltration; progressed to fulminant hepatic failure and received orthotopic liver transplantation 13 days into admission. Introduction notes albendazole is documented through case reports to cause transaminase elevation that typically resolves with cessation.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 30-year-old woman with thyrotoxicosis treated with carbimazole 60 mg daily presented with one week of scleral and urine discoloration and pruritus. Investigations showed hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 208 µmol/L, conjugated 124 µmol/L) and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 224 U/L, AST 163 U/L, ALP 347 U/L). A probable diagnosis of carbimazole-induced cholestatic hepatitis was made; the drug was discontinued, other causes of hepatitis and cholestasis were excluded, and LFTs normalized within four weeks. The authors conclude that carbimazole-induced hepatitis, although rare, should be considered in jaundiced thyrotoxic patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had Graves' disease/thyrotoxicosis and was concurrently taking propranolol; carbimazole was discontinued and she was treated with steroids and switched to propylthiouracil. Dechallenge with drug withdrawal was followed by recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose carbimazole 60 mg daily; onset of symptoms (icterus, pruritus) approximately one month after starting treatment. Admission labs: total bilirubin 208 µmol/L, conjugated 124 µmol/L, ALT 224 U/L, AST 163 U/L, ALP 347 U/L; bilirubin peaked by day 6 (445 µmol/L) before declining; LFTs normalized within 4 weeks and remained normal at 6 months. Described as carbimazole-induced hepatitis with severe cholestasis. Other causes of hepatitis and cholestasis excluded. Radioiodine or surgery considered but not arranged; substitution of carbimazole with propylthiouracil reported without increased hepatotoxicity as the liver-injury mechanism is said to differ between the two thionamides.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with sarcoidosis and severe pulmonary hypertension was admitted for COVID pneumonia and developed Aspergillus fungemia, for which voriconazole was initiated. Two weeks into the voriconazole course, an acute liver injury was diagnosed that was stated to be most probably related to voriconazole. Despite discontinuation of the drug, her condition deteriorated and ultimately resulted in mortality.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had multiple concurrent medications (riociguat continued, treprostinil briefly initiated, prednisone) and severe comorbidities (stage IV sarcoidosis, severe pulmonary hypertension, COVID-19 pneumonia); voriconazole required discontinuation of macitentan due to a category X interaction before initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Voriconazole 300 mg BID started on day 39 of admission; acute liver injury developed about two weeks into treatment (approximately day 22 of voriconazole). Serial labs showed rising ALT (up to >3,600), AST (up to 1,364), and INR (up to 6.28); onset of abdominal fullness and fluctuating mental status. Voriconazole was discontinued on day 22 of therapy and supportive management including N-acetylcysteine was given, but the patient died. Diagnosis considers voriconazole the reason for acute hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old woman prescribed acarbose (50 mg three times daily) for NIDDM presented 5 months later with fatigue, dark urine, and jaundice; AST 2436 U/l, ALT 2556 U/l, total bilirubin 4.67 mg/dl, GGT 601 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 174 U/l. Viral hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV were ruled out, no autoantibodies, normal ultrasound. Acarbose was stopped and liver tests normalized within 5 months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had NIDDM and was not taking other medications or herbal remedies.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2 of the report: acarbose 50 mg three times daily for NIDDM; onset of fatigue/dark urine 5 months after starting; jaundice; AST 2436 U/l, ALT 2556 U/l, total bilirubin 4.67 mg/dl (direct 3.19), GGT 601 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 174 U/l; ultrasonography normal; liver tests normalized within 5 months after stopping. Causality supported by temporal relation, resolution on dechallenge, and absence of alternative explanations. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy rather than hypersensitivity (no fever, rash, or eosinophilia), involving the original compound or its metabolites, mainly 4-methylpyrogallol derivatives. Hepatotoxicity described as a very rare but potentially severe adverse event of acarbose therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Based on clinical history and histologic findings, lenalidomide-induced hepatotoxicity was suspected and the drug was discontinued. The patient had complete normalization of his liver function profile 16 days following discontinuation and follow-up MRI revealed complete regression of the hepatic lesions into simple regenerative nodules. The prompt resolution after lenalidomide discontinuation confirmed a lenalidomide-induced hepatotoxicity and liver nodules necrosis. The paper suggests the role of lenalidomide's antiangiogenic effect in hepatic regenerative macronodules infarction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had pre-existing cirrhosis (micronodular liver) with multiple (more than 30) well-circumscribed hepatic nodules measuring up to 20 mm in the right lobe; initial suspicion of multifocal HCC was excluded by biopsy, which showed multiple infarcted regenerative nodules.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single patient. Ultrasound and MRI showed multiple infarcted regenerative nodules with thick rim enhancement on arterial/portal phases and no washout. Histology showed localized hepatocyte proliferation with fibrotic bands and coagulation necrosis. Prompt improvement on dechallenge: complete normalization of liver function 16 days after lenalidomide discontinuation; complete regression of liver lesions on MRI at 3 months and 1 year. Authors note reported cases of lenalidomide-induced hepatotoxicity are rare and no prior report of liver necrosis; mechanism attributed to the antiangiogenic effect of lenalidomide.

raw_record.support_text: Case No. 1, a 52-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, ingested an extract of approximately 150 g of Taxus celebica (which contains the flavonoid sciadopitysin) to treat diabetes. Symptoms occurred 3 hours later. She was transferred to the ward under the impression of herb drug-induced acute renal failure, acute cholestatic hepatitis, hemolysis, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. Laboratory data at presentation showed AST 543 U/L, ALT 5 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 184 U/L, total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had pre-existing diabetes mellitus; sciadopitysin was administered as an herbal extract of Taxus celebica used in traditional medicine for diabetes; concurrent sciadopitysin-induced acute renal failure with hemolysis requiring hemodialysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute cholestatic hepatitis was part of the herb drug-induced diagnosis in this case. Onset ~3 hours after ingestion of a single large dose (~150 g Taxus celebica extract). Laboratory values: AST 543 U/L, ALT 5 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 184 U/L, total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL. The abstract additionally notes jaundice, hemolysis (100%), cholestatic hepatitis (50%), and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (50%) among all eight flavonoid-induced oliguric acute renal failure patients.

raw_record.support_text: Following captopril withdrawal, the patient's jaundice almost disappeared and her biochemical pattern progressively returned to normal. The paper concludes that both the onset of symptoms and the evolution of the picture support a diagnosis of captopril hepatotoxicity, and notes that clinical and biochemical normalization usually follows drug withdrawal, although at least one captopril case has been described with death due to hepatic failure secondary to hepatic necrosis. Mechanism discussion (paragraph 21) indicates the present case was attributed to hypersensitivity to captopril because the patient, despite renal failure, received a low dose and underwent haemodialysis three times a week without captopril supplementation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had pre-existing renal failure, was receiving a low dose of captopril, and underwent haemodialysis three times a week without captopril supplementation.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice and elevated liver biochemistry appeared around the time of captopril treatment; within three days of withdrawal the jaundice almost disappeared and the biochemical pattern progressively returned to normal, supporting dechallenge. A previously described captopril case resulted in death due to hepatic failure secondary to hepatic necrosis. Mechanism speculated to be hypersensitivity (the authors' view for this case) or a direct toxic effect via kinase II inhibition increasing prostaglandins and leukotrienes; the low dose was argued to weigh against dose-related direct toxicity. No cross-reaction between captopril and ACE inhibitors lacking a proline has been reported (reference [10]).

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old female on sorafenib (third-line for advanced follicular thyroid carcinoma) developed acute on chronic liver failure with a rapid rise in serum transaminases (AST 1,724 U/L), bilirubin (22 mg/dL), and INR 2.9. Liver biopsy demonstrated severe drug-induced necrotic hepatitis, prompting treatment with prednisolone at 1 mg/kg, which led to normalization of AST (to 70 U/L) and INR (to 1.36). The authors call this the first patient reported with sorafenib-induced liver failure, and note the patient had previously unknown well-compensated Child Pugh A cirrhosis, likely from nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had pre-existing, previously undiagnosed well-compensated Child Pugh A liver cirrhosis, likely due to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report, claimed first report of sorafenib-induced liver failure. Female, 65 yr, third-line treatment of advanced follicular thyroid carcinoma; dose reduction after 10 days due to skin rash, stomatitis, and diarrhea; treatment stopped after flu-like symptoms and fever about 1 week later; liver enzymes continued rising over the next 20 days until admission with beginning liver failure. Histology: severe drug-induced necrotic hepatitis with underlying fatty liver disease and early cirrhosis. Allergic-type immune-mediated liver injury was suspected. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg led to rapid recovery of liver function; bilirubin declined to 1.3 mg/dL under steroid taper. The patient later died from gastric ulcer perforation (not the liver injury). Liver function tests usually indicate cholestasis, with other symptoms including fever, rash, and pruritus, and the jaundice is considered probably attributable to 'hypersensitivity cholestasis'.

raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic jaundice with fever, rash, and pruritus; liver function tests indicated cholestasis; mechanism framed as hypersensitivity cholestasis. Both allergic and toxic mechanisms are suggested for macrolide hepatotoxicity, with the reactive metabolite possibly having mild hepatotoxic potential. An in vitro rat study (Dujoune and Salhab) showed erythromycin estolate, unlike the base, directly damaged rat liver cell plasma membranes (enzyme leakage, surface-scanning electron microscopy).

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old white man developed cephalexin-induced cholestatic hepatitis. He started a 10-day course of cephalexin (500 mg orally three times daily) for a postoperative wound infection and was taking no other medications at the start of therapy; previously he had tolerated penicillin and had received 1 g of cefazolin preoperatively. About 3 days after starting cephalexin he noted dark urine and pale stool, and within 24 hours of completing therapy developed fever, hives, pruritus and jaundice. A diagnosis of cephalosporin-induced (cephalexin) cholestatic hepatitis was made based on the temporal, clinical and biochemical course.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had prior preoperative cefazolin exposure and earlier analgesic co-medications (single doses of meperidine and morphine, a wound bupivacaine pump, short course of hydrocodone/acetaminophen) as competing/antecedent exposures; cephalexin taken for postoperative wound infection at 500 mg three times daily for 10 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented with 2 weeks of jaundice, pruritus, fatigue and anorexia; dark urine and pale stool ~3 days after starting cephalexin; fever, hives, pruritus and jaundice within 24 h of completing therapy. Labs: total bilirubin 17.9 mg/dL (nl 0.0–1.5), direct bilirubin 12.2 mg/dL (nl 0.0–0.3), AST 40 U/L (nl 0–37), ALT 87 U/L (nl 0–40), alkaline phosphatase 272 U/L (nl 30–120); albumin, prothrombin time and infectious/SMA autoimmune serologies, ultrasound, CT and ERCP unremarkable. Liver biopsy showed mild panacinar hepatitis with eosinophils and extensive cholestasis with canalicular bile plugs, no increased hepatic iron. Pruritus responded to ursodeoxycholic acid; symptoms resolved by 7 weeks postexposure and biochemical abnormalities resolved 5 weeks later. Cephalosporin-induced cholestatic hepatitis is rarely reported.

Histology excluded hepatic porphyria but revealed severe fatty changes thought to be caused by idiosyncratic metabolism of carbamazepine. The report frames this as a case of toxic hepatitis caused by carbamazepine, aggravated by the drug's effect on hepatic cytochrome P-450 involved in haem metabolism.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose 300 mg/day for 3 months prior to presentation. Lab findings: mild transaminase elevation (AST 70 IU/l, ALT 92 IU/l, both normal 7-45), alkaline phosphatase 406 IU/l, GGT 58 IU/l. Hepatic histology showed severe fatty changes thought due to idiosyncratic carbamazepine metabolism. Cutaneous features were bullous lesions and angio-oedema. Several fluorinated inhalation anesthetics have been associated with hepatotoxicity; although desflurane is considered safest, the authors diagnosed desflurane-induced hepatitis in this patient who may have been sensitized by previous halothane exposure.

raw_record.extra_details: Twelve days postoperatively developed macular erythematous rash, then jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, malaise, nausea, epigastric pain. Labs: eosinophils 1280/µL, ALT 1776 U/L, AST 1258 U/L, GGT 48 U/L, ALP 185 U/L, total bilirubin 29.4 mg/dL, ammonia 61 µmol/L, PT 37%, PTT 50 s, antithrombin III 27%. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with extensive centrilobular necrosis and mild lobular/portal inflammation. Anti-TFA IgG antibody titers rose (0.083 day 22 to 0.159 day 25, 0.108 day 27; 0.062/0.057/0.084 days 34/35/41; negative control 0.064, positive control 0.562), implicating trifluoroacetylated-protein hypersensitivity shared with halothane. Patient transferred to hepatology unit on postoperative day 30 for observation and potential liver transplantation; no encephalopathy at admission. Hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, infectious hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis excluded.

The authors concluded that they reported a severe Ligandrol (LGD-4033)-induced hepatotoxicity, and noted that despite an FDA warning, Ligandrol and other SARMs continue to be sold over the counter and via the internet as body-building products, requiring higher regulation to prevent life-threatening hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient self-administered LGD-4033 10 mg daily, 10 to 100 times higher than the doses (0.1, 0.3, 1.0 mg) used in a 21-day placebo-controlled clinical trial; purchased as an over-the-counter/internet body-building SARM product; possibility that the Ligandrol the patient took contained other different unapproved drugs was not excluded; genetic testing for hepatic transporter gene abnormalities was not performed.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of severe Ligandrol (LGD-4033)-induced hepatotoxicity with acute liver injury. Diagnosis based on timing of administration, dechallenge improvement of total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases, and liver biopsy findings, after ruling out other causes. A placebo-controlled randomized trial of LGD-4033 in 76 healthy men showed no serious adverse effects and no significant change in serum aminotransferases at 0.1, 0.3, and 1 mg daily over 21 days. Authors noted hepatotoxicity can be intrinsic (dose-dependent) or idiosyncratic, suggesting the patient's DILI was either intrinsic or idiosyncratic with a dose-dependent component. FDA warning exists for Ligandrol and SARMs.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman undergoing aftercare for chronic alcoholism (liver function tests normal at baseline) was started on disulfiram 250 mg daily; she took no medication except vitamin B1. Jaundice appeared 13 days after treatment onset, and acute liver failure was diagnosed on day 18 after a total disulfiram dose of 4.5 g (Quick value <10%, bilirubin 460 µmol/l, GPT 5099 U/l, GOT 4142 U/l) together with early renal failure (creatinine 300 µmol/l). Viral infection, autoimmune hepatitis and metabolic liver disease were excluded, and toxicology tests were negative. The patient died 25 days after starting disulfiram in hepatic coma from fulminant hepatitis with hepatorenal syndrome; biopsy and autopsy showed acute hepatic dystrophy without cirrhosis. The temporal relationship, exclusion of other causes, and histology compatible with chemical-toxic hepatitis indicated a disulfiram-induced fulminant hepatitis. The authors state that disulfiram hepatotoxicity is a very rare idiosyncratic reaction that is often fatal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient treated for chronic alcoholism (alcohol use disorder) after one year of in-patient withdrawal treatment; normal baseline liver function; no concurrent medications other than vitamin B1.
raw_record.extra_details: Disulfiram brand Antabus; dose 250 mg/d with total dose 4.5 g; jaundice latency 13 days, acute liver failure at day 18; laboratory values Quick <10%, bilirubin 460 µmol/l, GPT 5099 U/l, GOT 4142 U/l; hepatorenal syndrome with creatinine 300 µmol/l; death in hepatic coma 25 days after onset; liver biopsy and autopsy showed acute hepatic dystrophy/necrosis without cirrhosis; viral, autoimmune and metabolic causes excluded and toxicology negative. Paper also notes the first 1974 report of disulfiram-induced hypersensitivity hepatitis and roughly 30 published cases of severe or fulminant disulfiram hepatitis worldwide, and recommends immediate discontinuation on liver-enzyme rise or jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old man with metastatic prostate carcinoma was treated with bicalutamide as part of androgen deprivation therapy before starting chemotherapy. After 4 days of therapy he developed abnormal liver function tests and symptoms of hepatotoxicity, progressing to fulminant hepatotoxicity, multiorgan failure, and death 8 days after bicalutamide was begun. The Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale showed a probable (score of 5) causal relationship between bicalutamide and fulminant hepatotoxicity. The authors conclude fulminant hepatotoxicity is a rare but potentially fatal adverse effect of bicalutamide.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient used bicalutamide as part of androgen deprivation therapy with an LHRH agonist for metastatic prostate carcinoma before starting chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 59-year-old man; onset of symptoms 4 days after starting bicalutamide; ALT greater than 40 times the upper limit of normal; concurrent serum creatinine 4.2 mg/dL and troponin I 18 ng/ml; developed tachycardia and hypotension resistant to fluid resuscitation; died 8 days after therapy was begun secondary to multiorgan failure, most likely from fulminant hepatotoxicity; Naranjo probability score 5 (probable).

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe acute liver injury in a 61-year-old man who had undergone liver transplantation surgery 13 years previously and was on immunosuppressive therapy. After bilateral total knee arthroplasty under general anesthesia, during which a total of 200 mg bupivacaine was injected into each knee after wound closure, liver enzyme levels increased to more than 10 times the upper limit of normal after surgery and remained extremely high on postoperative day 1.

raw_record.extra_details: 200 mg bupivacaine injected into each knee after wound closure during bilateral total knee arthroplasty; liver enzymes rose to >10x ULN after surgery and remained extremely high on postoperative day 1; conservative management with hepatobiliary ultrasound; serum liver enzyme levels normalized 12 days after surgery and patient discharged 22 days after surgery; intra-articular bupivacaine is a widely used intraoperative analgesic method with rare complications, but there is a risk of inadvertent delivery into the systemic circulation.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old woman under allopurinol therapy for hyperuricemia was admitted with fever and a diffuse cutaneous erythematous eruption and shortly developed rapidly progressive signs of acute liver and kidney failure. Histologic findings from skin and liver biopsies were consistent with a toxic drug reaction, and the case was characterized as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome; the patient completely recovered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was also receiving losartan and low-dose hydrochlorothiazide, all of which were withdrawn together; adult female with newly diagnosed hypertension and hyperuricemia.
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS syndrome with fever (peaks up to 38°C), diffuse erythematous eruption on light-exposed regions, arthralgia, mild eosinophilia (12%), acute kidney failure and rapidly progressive acute liver failure with very high AST/ALT and declining serum proteins/albumin. Liver biopsy showed hepatocytic ballooning and scattered acidophilic bodies with moderate lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and few eosinophils; skin biopsy showed focal parakeratosis with necrotic keratinocytes and perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. Treated with prednisone (1 mg/kg) and later high-dose steroids; complete recovery, healthy at five years. No formal causality scoring instrument reported.

raw_record.support_text: A 47-year-old woman developed weakness, fatigue, pruritus, and scleral icterus 10 days after completing a self-prescribed 7-day course of oral methylprednisolone; she was also taking topiramate. Admission liver tests were ALT 2478 U/L, AST 1600 U/L, total bilirubin 10 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 138 U/L, and GGT 242 U/L; no other causes of liver dysfunction were identified. The final diagnosis was mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury caused by methylprednisolone, with enzyme levels returning to normal within 45 days after drug discontinuation. An objective Naranjo-scale causality assessment indicated hepatotoxicity was probably related to methylprednisolone, making this the third published case of methylprednisolone-induced toxic hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was co-exposed to topiramate (competing co-medication that was stopped before methylprednisolone was implicated); methylprednisolone was taken as a self-prescribed 7-day oral course for arm weakness rather than a standard indication, and the diagnosis relied on temporal association and dechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: In-hospital accidental rechallenge with topiramate caused no enzyme increase; resolution occurred within 45 days without treatment. raw_record.support_text: In the authors' patient, the temporal relationship between sertraline initiation and symptoms, along with biochemical and symptomatic improvement following drug discontinuation, strongly pointed toward sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity. The patient was also taking ranitidine and metoclopramide, but the paper judged their contribution theoretically possible yet unlikely to be of major clinical significance because ranitidine is only a minor substrate of cytochrome P450 2D6. The diagnosis of sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity requires exclusion of viral, autoimmune and hereditary causes.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity (acute liver injury). In a separate cited case (Persky and Reinus), inadvertent rechallenge with sertraline in a 23-year-old woman produced a prompt rise in ALT, suggestive of an anamnestic response; intentional rechallenge was not performed in the authors' patient due to medical risk. Theories of mechanism include immunologically mediated hepatitis supported by eosinophils on liver biopsy and the idiosyncratic reaction, and mitochondrial dysfunction with ATP depletion and inhibition of mitochondrial respiration. Sertraline inhibits cytochrome P450 2D6, which can raise levels of co-administered drugs. Sertraline-induced liver toxicity is considered rare.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with very high serum transaminases deemed most consistent with an acute toxic liver injury, with a time course and severity consistent with acetaminophen toxicity. The patient ingested not more than 11.5 g of acetaminophen, which ordinarily does not cause severe toxicity, had an initial acetaminophen blood level below the level usually associated with toxicity, and therefore appeared unusually susceptible to acetaminophen toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was concurrently receiving isoniazid, proposed to induce hepatic P450IIE1 and thereby increase acetaminophen susceptibility; also on oral contraceptives (deemed unlikely responsible); ingested up to 11.5 g acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report from University of Michigan Medical Center. Very high transaminases (peak AST about 209 µkat/L, ALT about 132 µkat/L) unusual for viral hepatitis and consistent with acute toxic liver injury; elevated bilirubin (peak 106 µmol/L); prolonged prothrombin time (up to 20.1 s); complete acute renal failure; initial blood acetaminophen level below the level usually associated with toxicity. Proposed mechanism: isoniazid-induced P450IIE1 conversion of a greater proportion of acetaminophen to toxic metabolites. Patient recovered and was discharged on day 10. Accompanying rat data (Addendum) show isoniazid pretreatment potentiates acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 91-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with flutamide (250 mg every 8 hours) and triptorelin (3.75 mg every 3 months) developed severe icteric hepatitis 6 months after starting treatment, with disorientation, asterixis, and elevated liver tests (GOT 496 U/L, GPT 342 U/L, GGT 223 U/L, total bilirubin 160 µmol/L with direct fraction 125 µmol/L, ammonia 420 µmol/L) and CA 19-9 359 KU/L, while hepatitis/pregnancy/cancer serologies, immunologic studies, and imaging were negative/normal. On suspicion of toxic hepatitis, flutamide was withdrawn; jaundice and encephalopathic signs resolved within 15 days and all parameters normalized by 6 weeks. The case is framed as severe toxic hepatitis caused by flutamide.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was concurrently receiving triptorelin as a co-medication; elderly male (91 years) being treated for benign prostatic hyperplasia.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg every 8 h; hepatitis onset about 6 months after starting treatment. Initial labs GOT 496 U/L, GPT 342 U/L, GGT 223 U/L, total bilirubin 160 µmol/L (direct 125), ammonia 420 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 194 U/L; CA 19-9 elevated to 359 KU/L and fell to 103 KU/L by 3 weeks and 55 KU/L by 6 weeks after discontinuation (dechallenge). Jaundice and encephalopathic signs resolved 15 days after stopping, all parameters normalized by 6 weeks. Flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen; proposed mechanism mitochondrial respiration inhibition; mild (<2x normal) transaminase elevation reported in ~30% (Rosenthal), and in the Gomez series 4 of 1091 prostate adenocarcinoma patients on flutamide 250 mg/8 h showed markers of severe hepatic toxicity, only 2 with clinical manifestations. The authors note severe flutamide hepatotoxicity causing acute liver failure may present with elevated CA 19-9.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, morbid obesity and other comorbidities, already on insulin glargine, glimepiride, metformin, simvastatin and sertraline, had pioglitazone 30 mg/day added 24 days before admission. She presented with markedly elevated AST (2,144 U/l) and ALT (2,760 U/l) with normal bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, ferritin and prothrombin; viral and autoimmune serologies were negative and no liver biopsy was performed. Using the Spanish Pharmacovigilance System algorithm, she was diagnosed with probable acute drug-induced liver disease and the case was reported to the Basque Country Pharmacovigilance Unit. After stopping all oral medication and treating with insulin, transaminases declined rapidly and normalized within 30 days.

raw_record.support_text: A letter to the editor titled 'Celecoxib-Induced Cholestatic Hepatitis' describes a 55-year-old nonalcoholic obese woman with a sulfa allergy who presented with a 5-day history of jaundice, malaise, and pruritic rash that began 3 weeks after taking celecoxib, 200 mg/d, for radiculopathy-associated pain. The patient stopped celecoxib 5 days before hospitalization.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose 200 mg/d for radiculopathy-associated pain; symptoms of jaundice, malaise, and pruritic rash began 3 weeks after starting celecoxib; drug stopped 5 days before hospitalization. Title frames the liver injury as cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that long-term benzimidazole therapy, preferably with albendazole, is mandatory in inoperable alveolar echinococcosis patients, and lists hepatotoxicity among its frequent adverse effects, as observed in their patient. It recommends screening for adverse reactions such as liver-test alterations and leukopenia during prolonged treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with alveolar echinococcosis undergoing long-term therapeutic benzimidazole (preferably albendazole) treatment; finding observed in an individual inoperable patient with disseminated disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a frequent adverse effect of long-term albendazole treatment together with alopecia and neutropenia. Authors recommend screening for liver-test alterations and leukopenia every 2 weeks for the first 3 months, then monthly during the first year, then every 3 months. Albendazole is metabolized in the liver to the active metabolite albendazole sulfoxide, whose blood levels should be monitored especially in case of hepatocellular dysfunction and/or cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old female with beta thalassemia major was admitted with fever, fatigue, abnormal liver function test results (aspartate aminotransferase 167 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 250 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 102 U/L, total bilirubin 3.79 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.37 mg/dL) and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis after 25 days of treatment with oral deferasirox 1500 mg/day for chronic iron overload. Despite extended examination no obvious cause of the fever, hepatitis, or hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis was found, and the diagnosis was compatible with tubular dysfunction, drug-induced hepatitis, and hypersensitivity reaction due to deferasirox. Use of the Naranjo probability scale revealed that the adverse reaction was probable; all pathological findings were fully reversible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with beta thalassemia major and chronic iron overload; diagnosis also included tubular dysfunction and hypersensitivity reaction as manifestations; prior deferoxamine therapy discontinued 25 days earlier.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 20 mg/kg (1500 mg/day oral); liver-function elevations (AST 167 U/L, ALT 250 U/L, GGT 102 U/L, total bilirubin 3.79 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.37 mg/dL); Naranjo probability scale scored the reaction 'probable'; all pathological findings fully reversible with excellent outcome; reported hepatitis alongside hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and tubular dysfunction; proposed mechanism of toxic effects via chelation of mitochondrial iron and ATP depletion in tubular epithelial cells.

raw_record.support_text: A 26-year-old female patient with CD and high TPMT activity stopped 2 mg/kg and then 1 mg/kg azathioprine (AZA) because of drug-induced hepatitis. She was then prescribed 0.5 mg/kg/day (25 mg/day) AZA concurrently with 200 mg/day allopurinol, which generated a satisfactory level of TGNs (350 pmol/8 x 10^8 erythrocytes) with no hepatotoxicity, and she remained asymptomatic with normal liver function tests for 5 years.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with Crohn's disease and high TPMT activity.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis attributed to AZA, prompting drug discontinuation at 2 mg/kg then 1 mg/kg. Subsequently AZA 0.5 mg/kg/day (25 mg/day) plus 200 mg/day allopurinol produced a satisfactory TGN level (350 pmol/8 x 10^8 erythrocytes) without hepatotoxicity and with normal liver function tests over 5 years; 6TU excretion was undetectable (<1% of AZA dose).

raw_record.support_text: In a 71-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis who had prior skin allergy to aspirin, penicillin, and cotrimoxazole, bosentan (62.5 mg twice daily, increased to 125 mg twice daily) was started for recurrent digital ulcers. About 6 weeks later she developed fever, generalized maculopapular exanthema, headache, and hepatitis with 20-fold increased ALT and marked eosinophilia (2500/ml). Bosentan was stopped and she improved within 4 days with normalization of eosinophils; hepatitis virus serologies and HHV-6 PCR were negative. The authors assume the case relates to DRESS (drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), which they suggest is the third case of hypersensitivity related to bosentan.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and a history of hypersensitive skin reactions to aspirin, penicillin, and cotrimoxazole (suggested sulfonamide-nonantibiotic cross-reactivity/overall allergic predisposition); single-patient case of DRESS with liver cytolysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Bosentan is an endothelin-1 receptor antagonist used for pulmonary arterial hypertension and digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis; it contains a -SO2NH2 sulfonamide moiety. Onset about 5-6 weeks after treatment start; fever 38°C, maculopapular exanthema, headache; ALT 20-fold elevated; eosinophil count 2500/ml; rapid clinical improvement and ALT improvement within 4 days of discontinuation plus normalization of eosinophils; RegiSCAR criteria for DRESS fulfilled; negative hepatitis virus serologies and HHV-6 PCR; ultrasound excluded biliary problems. Reported as the third case of hypersensitivity related to bosentan; DRESS death occurs in 10% of cases due to visceral complications such as fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a second operation on the same patient (in an orthopedic hospital, under N2O/O2/halothane anesthesia), the patient with suspected hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) received a total of 175 g sorbitol and 50 g fructose IV in two-thirds electrolyte solutions intraoperatively and on postoperative days 1 and 2. A few hours after surgery, the Quick prothrombin time was 19%, serum transaminase activity was increased, and renal retention values rose. The patient was transferred to a medical intensive care unit on postoperative day 2; the discharge diagnosis was again 'transient postoperative liver failure of unclear cause.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI); perioperative IV parenteral nutrition setting; co-exposure to fructose infusions.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: a 49-year-old woman with HFI who had experienced a similar transient postoperative liver failure two years earlier during a first orthopedic operation where sorbitol (125/50/75/50 g) and fructose (25/25/50 g) were infused IV. In the second episode, liver and coagulation values normalized within a few days after stopping glucose-exchange substances (sorbitol/fructose) and substituting coagulation factors, and the patient was discharged with the diagnosis of transient postoperative liver failure; she was later referred for metabolic diagnostics of HFI after her sister refused elective surgery due to prior experience. Laboratory values at peak included SGOT 726 U/l, SGPT 984 U/l, total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dl, Quick 9%, with renal retention (urea up to 84 mg/dl, creatinine 1.9 mg/dl). Sorbitol is metabolized to fructose and exerts its toxicity in HFI by this pathway.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with metastatic renal cell carcinoma presented with new-onset nausea, decreased appetite, and jaundice, with abnormal liver profile testing (ALT 484 U/L, AST 277 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 562 U/L, total bilirubin 7.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL). He had started pazopanib six weeks prior; liver enzymes and synthetic function tests had been normal during this treatment. He denied significant acetaminophen use or herbal supplements. ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, anti-LKM-1, anti-mitochondrial antibody, ceruloplasmin, ferritin/iron profile, and viral hepatitis (A, B, C) testing were unrevealing. Liver biopsy showed a moderate portal-tract inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes with admixed eosinophils and neutrophils) and cholestasis without cirrhosis. The patient was diagnosed with pazopanib-induced hepatotoxicity and offered supportive care; he did not develop signs or symptoms of acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (indication), with metastasis to ribs, thoracic vertebrae, and pancreas.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity noted 6 weeks after starting pazopanib. Cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy with portal and lobular mixed lymphocytic and neutrophilic inflammation and mild steatosis. Labs evolution: ALT rose to 484 U/L (from 25) and improved to 183 U/L; total bilirubin rose from 7.9 to 16.1 mg/dL; INR 1.02-1.25. No acute liver failure. Discussion notes clinical-trial incidence of hepatotoxicity as high as 53%; differential consideration of Stauffer's syndrome (paraneoplastic cholestasis).

Dechallenge was positive: after discontinuing carbamazepine, SGOT, SGPT, γ-GTP and LAP returned to normal. No rechallenge. Carbamazepine was given for painful tonic seizures and dysesthesia in multiple sclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: Eriksson reported a 29-year-old female with non-cirrhotic portopulmonary hypertension treated with bosentan for 18 months who developed DILI (mixed hepatic injury) and was treated with steroids with full recovery. Monthly liver monitoring throughout bosentan treatment is recommended, with permanent discontinuation advised if aminotransferases exceed 8× ULN.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with non-cirrhotic portopulmonary hypertension
raw_record.extra_details: DILI (mixed hepatic injury) developed after 18 months of bosentan; treated with steroids with full recovery. Monthly liver monitoring recommended; permanent discontinuation advised if aminotransferases >8× ULN. Proposed mechanism: inhibition of the hepatocanalicular bile salt export pump by the parent drug and metabolites, causing intracellular accumulation of cytotoxic bile salts.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of drug-induced hepatitis in a 50-year-old woman using spironolactone for the treatment of androgenetic alopecia. Six weeks after commencement of spironolactone the patient became unwell with extensive itch but no icterus or jaundice, and liver function tests found abnormally elevated bilirubin and enzyme levels; after withdrawal of spironolactone, symptoms resolved and liver function improved. The authors note only one other prior report of spironolactone-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old African American woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and congestive heart failure presented with fatigue, nausea, pruritus, loss of appetite, and dark brown urine. Pioglitazone was promptly discontinued because her symptoms were compatible with hepatic dysfunction and the drug was identified as a potential cause. Thirteen days later liver enzymes were abnormal (ALT 490 U/L, AST 360 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 851 U/L, total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL). Two and a half months after stopping the drug her symptoms resolved and liver function tests returned to normal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and congestive heart failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo causality algorithm indicated a probable relationship between pioglitazone and the liver injury. Laboratory values: ALT 490 U/L, AST 360 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 851 U/L, total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL. Symptoms (fatigue, nausea, pruritus, loss of appetite, dark brown urine) resolved and liver function tests normalized about 2.5 months after discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old woman developed hepatotoxicity days after starting clopidogrel (Plavix) for elective cerebral aneurysm coiling. Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 1362 IU/L, ALT 716 IU/L, ALP 160 IU/L) with elevated total and direct bilirubin, and the Maria and Victorino diagnostic scale of hepatotoxicity scored 10. Enzymes trended down after drug discontinuation, and a single 75 mg re-challenge produced a worsening pattern on day 2 that normalized by day 4, confirming the diagnosis of drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient's only new medication was clopidogrel, started 5 days prior; long-term co-medications included esomeprazole, levothyroxine, pregabalin, and risedronate.
raw_record.extra_details: Symptoms were nausea, vomiting and bloating. Maria and Victorino hepatotoxicity score 10. Positive drug re-challenge with a single 75 mg dose: worsening liver enzymes on day 2 followed by normalization by day 4. Patient improved and was discharged; complete normalization of liver enzymes at 2-week follow-up. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune antibody, blood culture, ultrasound, and HIDA scan work-ups were negative.

raw_record.support_text: In a case of pulmonary tuberculosis, treatment with ethionamide 1 g daily alone was started, and the next day the patient developed nausea, anorexia and malaise which persisted. On 22.3.62 liver function tests showed bilirubin 1.5 mg/100 ml, thymol turbidity 9 units/ml, and alkaline phosphatase 22 K.A. units. Ethionamide was stopped and treatment changed to isoniazid and PAS; symptoms disappeared and liver function tests returned to normal. The discussion notes that in this patient rechallenge with ethionamide after recovery from jaundice produced nausea, anorexia and malaise and renewed disturbance of liver function tests.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis; one patient (Case III) also received isoniazid concurrently. In Case II ethionamide was given alone and rechallenge reproduced symptoms and liver function disturbance.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases were reported. In Case II ethionamide alone produced nausea, anorexia and malaise with abnormal liver function tests (bilirubin 1.5 mg/100 ml, thymol turbidity 9 units/ml, alkaline phosphatase 22 K.A. units) within days; symptoms and LFTs resolved after stopping. In Case III (also on isoniazid) jaundice was noted with abnormal LFTs (bilirubin 5.8 mg/100 ml, thymol turbidity 6 units/ml, alkaline phosphatase 22.8 K.A. units) and urine showing bile and excess urobilin/urobilinogen; jaundice resolved within a month and LFTs normalized within six weeks after stopping drugs. Discussion: no other cases of jaundice occurred in the hospital except in patients receiving ethionamide; rechallenge in Case II and in previously reported cases (Rist; Moulding and Goldstein) produced recurrence. Differential diagnoses (homologous serum hepatitis, infectious hepatitis) were considered and excluded; isoniazid and PAS were given later without ill effect.

raw_record.support_text: In four patients with confirmed pathogenic POLG mutations and Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome, VPA (valproic acid) was administered for seizure control and ultimately led to liver failure and a genetic diagnosis; time to liver failure was approximately 3 months after VPA exposure. Patient 2 underwent an unsuccessful liver transplant. Patients 1-3 died of acute problems from liver failure or transplant, and patient 4 eventually died from complications of liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients carried confirmed pathogenic POLG mutations and had Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome, representing a genotype-restricted susceptibility; VPA was used therapeutically for seizure control in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Four case-series patients developed acute liver failure; latency to liver failure was ~3 months after VPA exposure. One patient (patient 2) had an unsuccessful liver transplant; patients 1-3 died of acute problems from liver failure or transplant and patient 4 died from complications of liver failure. The paper also notes that VPA-induced hepatotoxicity incidence decreases with age (about 1:40,000 in adults; up to 1/600 in children under 2 years on polytherapy with other antiepileptics) and suggests VPA exposure is related to POLG genotype and Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 150 renal-transplant patients included, azathioprine (AZA) therapy was reduced or withdrawn in 30 patients (20%) because of side effects. Among those 30, 18 patients showed hepatotoxicity (12 developed hematological toxicity such as leucopenia or pancytopenia, and none had both). These side effects, including the hepatotoxicity, resolved in all intolerant patients after azathioprine dose reduction or withdrawal, attributing the hepatotoxicity to azathioprine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients following renal transplantation treated with azathioprine as immunosuppressive therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Among the 30 patients whose azathioprine was reduced or withdrawn due to side effects, 18 showed hepatotoxicity and 12 showed hematological toxicity (leucopenia or pancytopenia); no patient had both simultaneously. Hepatotoxicity resolved in all intolerant patients after azathioprine dose reduction or withdrawal. Overall 20% (30/150) of cases had azathioprine reduced/withdrawn for side effects.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients with advanced bronchial carcinomas (large-cell and squamous cell) experienced severe hepatotoxic side effects during or immediately after a 5-day combination chemotherapy cycle with etoposide and ifosfamide. The injury was characterized by a massive rise in direct bilirubin, a drop in cholinesterase, a prolongation of thromboplastin time, a rise in alkaline phosphatase, and only modest rises in gGT and GOT. The reaction was lethal in one case and reversed over weeks in the other. Because ifosfamide was applied for the first time in both cases, it is regarded as the most likely cause of the hepatotoxicity, although an etoposide contribution could not be excluded in one case.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had advanced bronchial carcinoma and received combination chemotherapy that also included etoposide; an etoposide contribution could not be excluded; one case had prior etoposide/cisplatin exposure with liver enzyme changes.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred during or immediately after the 5-day therapy cycle and consisted of massive rise in direct bilirubin, drop in cholinesterase, prolonged thromboplastin time, rise in alkaline phosphatase, and only modest gGT and GOT rises; lethal in one of two cases, reversed within weeks in the other; ifosfamide was applied for the first time in both patients.

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with MTX (methotrexate) at 40 mg/m² for 5 doses for a lung neoplasm and psoriasis developed oral toxicity and thrombocytopenia after the 5th dose, then jaundice (total bilirubin 9 mg%, direct 5.4, indirect 3.6 mg%; BSF 58%; SGOT, SGPT and alkaline phosphatase normal), a palpable liver, pulmonary edema, and hepatic coma, followed by death; at autopsy the liver showed complete disruption of lobular architecture with blood and bile stasis, edema and atrophy of hepatocytes. The accompanying comment states the clinical and biochemical picture of hepatic and renal toxicity had a clear anatomopathological correlate. In another patient (case 2) bilirubin rose from 0.45 to 3.61 mg% and he died 9 days after a single 40 mg/m² MTX dose with a hepatorenal insufficiency picture. In case 5, BSF rose from 9 to 19% after the 4th dose and to 35% after the 7th, with parallel alkaline phosphatase rises and mild bilirubin increase; the comment concludes that although the terminal picture was attributable to progression of cerebral metastases, it seems probable that the therapy produced progressive hepatic toxicity, and BSF increase argues against a bone origin of the alkaline phosphatase rise.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had advanced lung neoplasms (some with bone/cerebral metastases) and received MTX as palliative systemic chemotherapy at 40 mg/m² per dose; one case received concurrent telecobaltotherapy; one patient had long-standing psoriasis. Case 5's terminal picture was partly confounded by progression of cerebral metastases.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 40 mg/m² intravenously, up to 7 doses; case 1 received 5 doses and died in hepatic coma (bilirubin 9 mg%, BSF 58%, transaminases and alkaline phosphatase normal, later palpable liver, pulmonary edema; autopsy: disrupted lobular architecture, blood and bile stasis, edema and hepatocyte atrophy, portal infiltrate); case 2 died 9 days after one dose with hepatorenal insufficiency (bilirubin rose 0.45 to 3.61 mg%, azotemia 20 to 115 mg%, uricemia 4.75 to 9.25 mg%); case 5 showed rising BSF 9 to 19 to 35% and alkaline phosphatase 1.80 to 3.24 to 7.70 U with mild bilirubin rise. A further case (case 3) treated with MTX plus telecobaltotherapy died with agranulocytosis and acute renal failure, without an attributed hepatic claim.

raw_record.extra_details: Representative index case details: grade 3 ALT/AST elevation starting day 28 of idelalisib monotherapy; transaminitis worsened after drug hold to max AST 1251 U/L and ALT 2237 U/L on day 35; liver biopsy on day 34; steroids initiated day 35; LFTs normalized after 3 weeks of steroid treatment. raw_record.support_text: Among 25 patients with hematological malignancies and invasive aspergillosis receiving voriconazole, abnormal liver function tests occurred in 48% (12/25). Voriconazole-related serious adverse events (SAEs) included hepatotoxicities in 5 patients, with patterns of abnormal liver function tests being cholestatic (n=3), hepatic (n=1), or mixed (n=1). One patient (patient 7) required discontinuation of voriconazole because of severe hepatotoxicity deemed to be probably related, but finally died from hepatic failure 11 days after discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had hematological malignancies and invasive aspergillosis; many had neutropenia, and some had undergone allogeneic HSCT, some with GVHD.
raw_record.extra_details: Abnormal liver function tests in 48% (12/25); voriconazole-related SAEs in 8/25 including hepatotoxicity in 5. Patterns of abnormal LFTs: cholestatic (n=3), hepatic (n=1), mixed (n=1). Two patients discontinued voriconazole due to SAEs; patient 7 had severe hepatotoxicity deemed probably related and died from hepatic failure 11 days after discontinuation. Median duration of IV voriconazole therapy 8 days (IQR 7-14); loading dose 12.0 mg/kg/day, maintenance 7.7 mg/kg/day. A trough plasma concentration of >=5.83 mg/l was the only independent risk factor independently associated with an SAE (adjusted OR 7.745, 95% CI 1.064-93.570; p=0.043). Trough concentrations did not depend on CYP2C19 genotype (EM/HEM/PM).

raw_record.support_text: The study reports three cases of jaundice attributed to ethionamide among patients with newly diagnosed previously untreated pulmonary tuberculosis. Jaundice developed after 3, 4, and 5 months of ethionamide therapy (1 g daily, co-administered with streptomycin or isoniazid), preceded by nausea, anorexia and malaise, and recovery was prompt when ethionamide was withdrawn. In 62 patients completing six months' therapy the incidence of jaundice was approximately 5 per cent, and liver function tests were transiently disturbed in 5 further cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had newly diagnosed previously untreated pulmonary tuberculosis; the three indexed cases received ethionamide with co-administered streptomycin or isoniazid (unresolved co-exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases of jaundice; onset after 3-5 months of therapy; jaundice preceded by nausea, anorexia and malaise; recovery after ethionamide withdrawal; ~5% jaundice incidence over six months in 62 patients; transient liver-function-test disturbance in 5 further cases. Hepatotoxicity from ethionamide was judged greater than expected from prior reports.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients developed liver injury attributed to acarbose: following cessation of acarbose, transaminase activities returned to normal; a 53-year-old woman with NIDDM developed symptomless hepatomegaly after 4 months of acarbose (300 mg daily) with AST 591 IU/L, ALT 1189 IU/L, and total bilirubin 24 µmol/L, and 1 month after cessation AST fell to 56 IU/L and ALT to 123 IU/L. Serology for hepatitis B and C viruses, PCR for hepatitis C and G viruses, antibodies against hepatitis A, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus, and antinuclear/antismooth-muscle/antimitochondrial antibodies were all negative, with normal iron and copper studies. The paper characterizes acarbose-induced liver injury as low in incidence, unpredictable, and idiosyncratic rather than intrinsic, and likely toxic-metabolic dependent rather than hypersensitivity-related due to lack of skin rash, fever, or arthralgia, long onset latency, and absence of granulomas and eosinophils on biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM) as the treated indication.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients (a series); dosages and latency: one 53-year-old woman received 300 mg acarbose daily for 4 months before onset. Lab values for that case: AST 591 IU/L, ALT 1189 IU/L, total bilirubin 24 µmol/L; 1 month after cessation AST 56 IU/L, ALT 123 IU/L. Dechallenge led to normalization/improvement of transaminases in all patients. Liver biopsies in the latter two patients (2 weeks and 1 month after hepatomegaly onset) showed mild lymphocytic infiltration in lobules and portal tracts, ceroid-containing macrophages, Councilman bodies, liver-cell regeneration, and mild partial portal fibrosis, without lysosomal glycogen accumulation. Alternative causes excluded (viral, autoimmune, iron/copper, ultrasound). Authors recommend regular serum aminotransferase monitoring during acarbose treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 17 patients with noninfectious scleritis treated with methotrexate (MTX), 47.1% experienced adverse effects of MTX at some point during follow-up, including 6 patients who had hepatotoxicity. In the majority of cases the adverse effects were tolerable or improved with dose adjustment, but 2 patients were switched to azathioprine or adalimumab owing to fatigue and hepatotoxicity. MTX was given at a median initial dose of 6 mg/week (range 4–10 mg), a median maximum dose of 16 mg/week (range 8–16 mg), and a median treatment duration of 22 months.

raw_record.support_text: As indicine-N-oxide showed promising results as an anticancer agent in in vitro and in vivo assays, clinical trials were conducted for acute leukemia; however, due to severe hepatotoxicity, the compound was not further tested. One clinical trial investigated indicine-N-oxide in patients with progressive acute leukemia refractory to standard chemotherapeutics (10 patients: 6 ALL, 3 AML, 1 AMML; ages 4–67 years). A lyophilized form at 3.0 g/m2 was given intravenously for five consecutive days; two patients achieved complete remission and one partial remission. Most patients experienced side effects such as mild nausea, mild diarrhea, maculopapular rash, and jaundice, and the authors concluded that indicine-N-oxide has anticancer activity but needs modification to remove unwanted side effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had progressive acute leukemia (ALL, AML, AMML) refractory to standard chemotherapeutics; ages 4–67 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Pyrrolizidine alkaloid from Heliotropium indicum. Lyophilized form given intravenously at 3.0 g/m2 for five consecutive days. Outcomes in the trial: 2 complete remissions, 1 partial remission. Reported side effects included mild nausea, mild diarrhea, maculopapular rash, and jaundice. The compound was not further tested owing to severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatotoxicity is a well-known side-effect of thiopurines (azathioprine) and describes patients who stopped AZA treatment due to liver dysfunction. In their cohort, five patients developed liver dysfunction on AZA: one of the two NUDT15 R139C homozygous patients and four other patients who carried no SNP. The authors note that thiopurine-induced liver dysfunction was not associated with NUDT15 gene polymorphisms and may be due to other unknown genetic factors. Table 2 lists 'Liver dysfunction' as an adverse effect of AZA occurring in 4 patients with no SNP, with a mean duration of AZA intake of 34.0 ± 11.5 days before the liver dysfunction (average AZA dose 1.64 ± 0.41 mg/kg/day).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients receiving AZA for severe/steroid-resistant dermatological diseases (connective tissue disease, autoimmune bullous disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa); indication-restricted cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients in the cohort stopped AZA due to liver dysfunction (4 with no SNP and 1 NUDT15 homozygous), occurring at a mean of 34.0 ± 11.5 days of AZA intake at average dose 1.64 ± 0.41 mg/kg/day. Hepatotoxicity was not associated with NUDT15 gene polymorphisms; the authors state thiopurine-induced liver dysfunction may be due to other unknown genetic factors. Reported in a small single-institution study of 15 AZA-treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present two cases of fatal fulminant hepatitis related to the use of cyproterone acetate (CPA), a drug normally well tolerated and used widely for treatment of prostatic carcinoma, and note that liver toxicity due to its use is not well known.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients receiving cyproterone acetate for treatment of prostatic carcinoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of fatal fulminant hepatitis attributed to CPA. Mechanism of toxicity unknown; absence of hypersensitivity evidence in all reported severe hepatotoxicity cases suggests a direct drug or metabolite effect, and CPA hepatotoxicity likely represents a rare idiosyncratic drug reaction. Several published cases of severe CPA hepatitis resolved once the drug was discontinued, supporting early cessation and liver enzyme monitoring. Physical stigmata of chronic liver disease (palmar erythema, gynecomastia, gynecoid hair distribution) were attributed to the drug's antiandrogen effect rather than to hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: In the analysis of toxicity attributable to treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (TLTBI) with isoniazid, elevated transaminase levels were found in 83.3% of oncohematological patients versus 37.3% of the control group (RR: 2.23; 95% CI: 1.56–3.20), and treatment had to be discontinued for severe hepatotoxicity in 3 patients (16.7%) with hematologic malignancies and 7 patients (9.3%) in the control group (RR: 1.79; 95% CI: 0.51–6.24). Severe hepatotoxicity was defined as a transaminase increase attributable to isoniazid greater than 5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), or between 3 and 5 times ULN together with attributable symptoms.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients treated for latent tuberculosis infection (TLTBI) with isoniazid; study compares oncohematological patients undergoing antineoplastic chemotherapy with a control group from Galicia's TB control program.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity defined as transaminase increase >5x ULN or 3-5x ULN with attributable symptoms. Elevated transaminases in 15/18 (83.3%) oncohematological vs 28/75 (37.3%) control patients (RR 2.2, 95% CI 1.6-3.2); severe hepatotoxicity in 3/18 (16.7%) vs 7/75 (9.3%) (RR 1.8, 95% CI 0.5-6.2). Overall discontinuation of TLTBI for any toxicity-related reason in 16.7% of hematologic patients vs 14.7% controls (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.35-3.66). No analyzed variable correlated with need to discontinue for severe hepatotoxicity. One oncohematological patient died during TLTBI due to causes not attributable to TB; none of 10 deaths during follow-up were TB-related.

raw_record.support_text: Human latent-tuberculosis treatment cohorts attributed hepatotoxicity to isoniazid: Nolan et al. treated 11,141 consecutive patients and observed 11 cases of hepatotoxicity (1 hospitalized, none died), a 0.10% rate among those starting isoniazid and 0.15% among those completing therapy; LoBue and Moser treated 3,788 patients and found 0.3% hepatotoxicity. raw_record.extra_details: Nolan et al.: 11,141 consecutive patients, 11 hepatotoxicity cases, 1 hospitalized, none died; 0.10% of those starting and 0.15% of those completing therapy. raw_record.support_text: Ceftriaxone-related liver toxicity was reported for several patients in a cohort of 196 patients treated for CNS infection. Patient 9 showed hepatic cholestasis and cytolysis (appearing 5 days after initiation, duration 3 days, grade 2 moderate severity on the CTCAE scale), and patient 10 showed hepatic cytolysis 5× the normal value with biliary sludge and liver steatosis on hepatic ultrasonography (2 days after initiation, 8 days duration, grade 2), which was attributed to ceftriaxone treatment by the investigators and led to ceftriaxone discontinuation. Both resolved without sequelae.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients treated with high-dose ceftriaxone for CNS infection (median initial daily dose 8 g/day, range 6-12 g); affected patients were older (median 76 years vs 59) and predominantly male (88.2%).
raw_record.extra_details: From table of ceftriaxone-related ADRs (19 ADRs in 17 patients). Patient 9: hepatic cholestasis and cytolysis, delay 5 days, duration 3 days, CTCAE grade 2, resolved without sequelae, attributed to ceftriaxone by investigators (yes). Patient 10: hepatic cytolysis 5× normal value, biliary sludge and liver steatosis on hepatic US, delay 2 days, duration 8 days, grade 2, resolved without sequelae, attributed to ceftriaxone and led to ceftriaxone discontinuation (yes). Patients 8 and 11 with isolated hepatic cytolysis were not attributed to ceftriaxone by investigators (no). Liver injury resolved without sequelae; no severe/fatal liver outcomes.

Other flucytosine toxicities included bone marrow suppression (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and gastrointestinal effects.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective analysis of patients treated for liver disease between 1992 and 2002 revealed eight cases of phenprocoumon-induced hepatotoxicity, including three cases of (sub-) acute liver failure that resulted in two orthotopic liver transplantations and one fatal outcome. Five patients with phenprocoumon-induced hepatitis recovered after anticoagulation was switched to another coumarin derivative or low molecular weight heparin. In all patients the liver injury was predominantly of a hepatitic type; massive confluent liver cell necroses were histologically present in the (sub-) acute liver failure cases, whereas patients without liver failure showed mild portal to moderate active lobular hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were being treated for pre-existing liver disease at the department, which limits generalization to the general population.
raw_record.extra_details: Eight cases of phenprocoumon-induced hepatotoxicity: three progressed to (sub-)acute liver failure (two orthotopic liver transplantations, one fatal outcome); five cases of phenprocoumon-induced hepatitis recovered after switching anticoagulation. Histology: massive confluent liver cell necrosis in the liver-failure cases; mild portal to moderate active lobular hepatitis in the non-failure cases. A BfArM (German Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices) retrospective analysis since 1990 reported 4390 possible phenprocoumon-related adverse reactions, 2% with hepatitis and 0.2% with liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses isoniazid as a cause of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), noting that moderate increases in ALT (up to two to three times the upper limit of normal) with enzyme levels returning to normal without discontinuing isoniazid are common and affect up to 20% of treated patients. The study itself enrolled 26 DILI cases all prescribed isoniazid 300 mg/day, with causality assessed by RUCAM, framed around the role of NAT2 genotype in isoniazid-related DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were co-prescribed other anti-TB drugs (all but one case); pyrazinamide co-exposure was a potential confounder. Cases were enrolled from a predominantly UK-based population including South Asian and Bangladeshi ethnicities.
raw_record.extra_details: Prescribed at 300 mg/day in line with UK/WHO guidelines; 26 DILI cases studied, 21 from the DILIGEN study (13 white European, 8 from the Indian subcontinent) plus 5 of Bangladeshi origin; enrolment criteria ALT >5x ULN, ALP >2x ULN, or ALT >3x ULN plus bilirubin >2x ULN; causality assessed by RUCAM (highly probable/probable/possible); moderate ALT increases up to 2-3x ULN occur in up to 20% of treated patients and normalize without discontinuation; slow NAT2 acetylator genotype associated with higher DILI risk in several populations.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report 81 patients (50 retrospective and 31 prospective; median age 34 years) who met criteria for efavirenz DILI. Among those biopsied (n=73), three histological injury patterns were observed: a nonspecific hepatitis associated with grade 1–2 transaminase elevation (n=17), a mixed cholestatic-hepatitis with grades 2–3 elevation of ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase and mild/moderate jaundice (n=20), and submassive necrosis with grade 4 ALT/AST elevation, severe jaundice and coagulopathy (n=36). Skin involvement was not observed, in contrast to nevirapine DILI. No patients fulfilled clinical criteria for tuberculous immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were HIV-infected adults receiving efavirenz-based antiretroviral therapy; in the prospective group 58% (n=18) were pregnant at ART initiation; 86% were Black, 73% female; 27% used or were currently using cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.
raw_record.extra_details: 81 patients total (50 retrospective, 31 prospective); median age 34 years; median CD4+ nadir 348 cells/µl (IQR 173–522); median duration on ART 20 weeks (IQR 12–24) at DILI onset. Liver-related mortality was 11% (n=9): 6% (n=3) retrospective and 19% (n=6) prospective; most deaths occurred within 1 week of presentation. Submassive necrosis was associated with an 'immuno-allergic' inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, conspicuous eosinophils), higher transaminases (ALT 679 vs 101 vs 114 U/l, P<0.0001) and bilirubin (232 vs 86 vs 8 µmol/l, P=0.003) compared with mixed cholestatic-hepatitis and nonspecific hepatitis patterns, and higher INR (1.68 vs 1.18, P=0.0002). In multivariate analysis, submassive necrosis was independently associated with CD4+ >350 cells/µl (OR 9.4, 95% CI 2.5–35.8) and female gender (OR 9.0, 95% CI 1.4–59.8); age >30 years was protective. Median hospital stay 28 days (IQR 11–60); slow median biochemical resolution >6 months. Submassive necrosis patients were treated with low-dose prednisone (0.25 mg/kg/day); protease inhibitor-based ART successfully introduced after resolution.

raw_record.support_text: A figure summarizes 23 cases of phenytoin-induced hepatotoxicity plus the present case. Most patients developed hepatotoxicity within 6 weeks of first phenytoin exposure, predominantly within 1 to 3 weeks, with no apparent relation to dosage or blood level.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were predominantly adolescents or young adults with equal sex distribution; Black persons outnumbered whites by nearly 2:1.
raw_record.extra_details: Based on 23 reviewed cases plus one present case. Onset typically within 1-3 weeks of first exposure, >80% within 6 weeks, sometimes delayed days after drug discontinuation; no dose- or blood-level dependence. Features included rash (all cases; desquamative in 66%, pruritic in 60%), fever (>90%, up to 40.9 C), clinical jaundice (55%), lymphadenopathy (75%), hepatomegaly (65%), splenomegaly (35%), hemorrhagic tendencies (40%), leukocytosis (two-thirds, up to 35,600/mm3), eosinophilia (70%), atypical lymphocytes (~40%). Pathogenesis interpreted as hypersensitivity reaction (eosinophilia, rash, lymphadenopathy, fever, exfoliative dermatitis); a direct toxic effect was excluded by lack of dose-level relation. Separate finding: Jacobsen and associates reported slight increases in serum alkaline phosphatase and ALT with few uni- or paucicellular necroses in asymptomatic chronic phenytoin patients, with no permanent liver damage.
