raw_record.support_text: The review compiles reported cases of acute pancreatitis associated with fatal liver failure in patients receiving valproic acid (VPA) for epilepsy (Sugimoto, Scheffner, Dickinson, and the present study), with VPA doses of about 20-55 mg/kg/day and serum VPA levels around 32-100 mg/L and latency from days to about 1.5 years; most patients either died or died after exploratory laparotomy. Separately, the text notes that the hepatic side effects of VPA, like the pancreatitis, appear to meet criteria of both toxic and idiosyncratic reactions, consistent with Eadie's view of a continuum of liver (or pancreatic) injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were predominantly children/young adults with epilepsy, several with mental retardation, treated with VPA at 20-55 mg/kg/day; several were concurrently on other antiepileptic co-medications (carbamazepine, ethosuximide, phenobarbital, primidone, clonazepam, phenytoin).
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal liver failure cases: Sugimoto 13F, VPA 20 mg/kg/day, serum level 37 mg/L, death; Scheffner 3.6F (55 mg/kg/day, 21 wk), 6.6F (30 mg/kg/day, 3 mo), 5.1M with CMZ/ETH/PB/PRM; Dickinson 25M; present study 21M with CL/PB, 39.2 mg/kg/day, serum VPA 91.1 mg/L, serum amylase 2.6x, death. Onset latency roughly 1 month to 1 year. The primary focus of the paper is VPA-associated pancreatitis, with the associated fatal hepatic failure documented during VPA therapy; hepatic side effects also discussed as meeting criteria of both intrinsic and idiosyncratic reactions.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone was reported to cause severe drug-induced liver injury in two patients treated for hyperuricaemia. A 58-y-old male treated for hyperuricaemia developed fever, jaundice and hepatic encephalopathy after 7 months of benzbromarone (unstated dose), with AST 736, ALT 1168, AP 792 and γGT 1102 IU/L; hepatic encephalopathy and increased PT ensued and liver biopsy at recovery showed fibrosis and bile-duct-like structures. A 53-y-old female took benzbromarone 100 mg/day with allopurinol for 2 months and developed fulminant hepatic failure (AST 3090, ALT 1140 U/L, PT 26.5 s); a positive lymphocyte stimulation test for benzbromarone was reported, she underwent living-related liver transplantation after failed haemodiafiltration/plasma exchange and died of sepsis 3 months later, with liver biopsy showing massive centrilobular necrosis consistent with fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were treated for hyperuricaemia/gout; one case (female) co-administered allopurinol with benzbromarone, and benzbromarone was used for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia in three of the four patients in the paper's case series.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (58-y-old male): onset after 7 mo, unstated dose; mild fever, malaise, anorexia, dark urine, pruritus, jaundice; total bilirubin 135 mg/L, AST 736, ALT 1168, AP 792, γGT 1102 IU/L; HBsAb positive but other hepatitis virus markers negative; LST for benzbromarone negative; co-medications allopurinol, tocopherol, niacin, alprazolam, theophylline, azelastine, nilvadipine; condition deteriorated despite stopping benzbromarone, with hepatic encephalopathy and prolonged PT; treated with prednisolone 30 mg/day, plasma exchange and haemodiafiltration; recovery biopsy showed fibrosis, bile duct-like structure, lymphocyte aggregation, nuclear enlargement. Case 2 (53-y-old female): benzbromarone 100 mg/day plus allopurinol for 2 mo; diarrhoea, nausea, anorexia, fatigue, jaundice; albumin 2.5 g/dL, AST 3090, ALT 1140 U/L, LDH 945 U/L, AP 123 U/L, total bilirubin 233 mg/L, NH3 160.6 µg/dL, PT 26.5 s; HAV/HCV/EBV/CMV negative, autoantibodies negative; LST positive for benzbromarone; massive centrilobular necrosis on biopsy; death from sepsis 3 mo after transplant. Paper also estimated incidence of benzbromarone-induced hepatotoxicity in Europe at approximately 1 in 17,000 treated patients (based on ~5 fulminant hepatitis cases over 1995-2000 among ~84,000 treated patients), possibly higher in Japan.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) treated for pneumocystis infection; pentamidine given 4 mg/kg/day intramuscularly for 2-28 days (median 12.5 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis seen in 9/30 patients (0 severe). raw_record.support_text: Eleven steroid-treated patients with active systemic lupus erythematosus received frentizole (150-350 mg/day) in combination with stable or decreasing prednisone doses in an open-label trial. Nine patients completed at least one 21- to 75-day course. Three patients developed reversible hepatic toxicity. Clinical and serologic improvement was noted in 3 patients who accepted a second 90-day course.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with active systemic lupus erythematosus on steroid (prednisone) therapy; frentizole given in combination with stable or decreasing prednisone doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Three of nine evaluable patients developed reversible hepatic toxicity. In protocol A, hepatic toxicity in patient #4 (6 mg/kg/day) led to dose reduction to 4 mg/kg/day for protocols B and C; in protocol B patients #5 and #6 developed hepatotoxicity and patient #6 was dropped from the trial. Frentizole doses ranged 150-350 mg/day; compound is 1-(6-methoxy-2-benzothiazolyl)-3-phenyl urea (Compound 53616, Eli Lilly Company).

raw_record.support_text: Regarding hepatic complications following busulfan (BU) administration in ADA SCID patients undergoing reduced-intensity conditioning for gene therapy, the paper states no clinically significant hepatotoxicity occurred, such as hyperbilirubinemia or sinusoidal obstruction syndrome. Transient ALT (27.5% of subjects) and AST (57.5%) elevations above age-based norms were observed in the 1-2 months after BU treatment, and 5 subjects (12.8%) had Grade II ALT elevation; however, these laboratory abnormalities self-resolved, did not require intervention, and were not significantly correlated with previous BU AUC values.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with adenosine deaminase severe combined immunodeficiency (ADA SCID) undergoing reduced-intensity conditioning (busulfan) for gene therapy; population is pediatric (infants).
raw_record.extra_details: No clinically significant liver injury (hyperbilirubinemia or sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) occurred. Transient ALT elevations above age-based norms in 11 subjects (27.5%) and AST elevations in 23 subjects (57.5%) in the 1-2 months after treatment, with peak ALT and AST at mean 35 days post-infusion; Grade II ALT elevation in 5 subjects (12.8%), mostly in the BSA cohort (44.4% of BSA cohort vs 5% of ABW and 0% of TDM cohort). These laboratory findings were not correlated with prior BU AUC and all self-resolved without intervention.

raw_record.support_text: An early report of a phase II trial in patients with advanced soft tissue sarcomas described 3 toxicity-related deaths among 59 patients treated with 1500 µg/m² ET-743 (trabectedin) as a 24-h infusion; in two patients death was due to neutropenic fever, renal insufficiency and liver failure, and the third died of neutropenic sepsis with elevated creatine kinase. A statistical analysis identified intercycle elevations of alkaline phosphatase and AST, and elevated baseline bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase, as prognostic factors for multi-organ toxicity in subsequent cycles.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with advanced soft tissue sarcomas; 1500 µg/m² as a 24-h infusion every 3 weeks
raw_record.extra_details: 3 toxicity-related deaths in 59 patients; 2 attributed to neutropenic fever, renal insufficiency and liver failure; a fourth patient later died of multi-organ toxicity; protocol amended to require normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase at entry and dose reduction to 1200 µg/m² for intercycle elevations, which improved safety.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report strong circumstantial evidence implicating halothane as the cause of acute hepatocellular jaundice in 6 patients. In all 6 cases, otherwise unexplained fever and/or bilirubinuria developed within 7 days after halothane anesthesia, and further exposure after a short interval resulted in acute hepatocellular jaundice; similar episodes have been ascribed to a hepatic injury resulting from hypersensitivity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with carcinoma of the cervix undergoing repeated (up to 4) halothane anesthetics for radium insertions at approximately weekly intervals; two of six patients (cases 5 and 6) died in hepatic coma.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients (aged 46-68) each received 2-4 halothane anesthetics; acute hepatocellular jaundice developing within 7 days of anesthesia with re-exposure after a short interval; death in hepatic coma in 2 cases (maximal serum bilirubin 12.6 and 38.0 mg/100 ml, SGOT 975 Karmen units); autopsy in case 6 showed submassive/massive hepatocellular necrosis with centrilobular cholestasis and fat-filled vacuoles in surviving cells; injury ascribed to hypersensitivity. Multiple other drug exposures (tetracycline, nitrofurantoin, penicillin, streptomycin, chlorpromazine, aspirin, chloramphenicol, prochlorperazine, sulphafurazole, thiethylperazine) were recorded but halothane was identified as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized controlled trial, 39 patients receiving repeated general anaesthetics for radium treatment for carcinoma of the uterine cervix were allocated to anaesthetics with or without halothane, and SGPT was monitored before each anaesthetic. Four of 18 patients in the halothane group had SGPT levels above 100 IU/l before the third radium treatment, whereas no patient in the 21-patient control group did (one-tailed test, P < 0.025). One halothane patient reached a maximum SGPT of 1800 IU/l and another 900 IU/l; neither had symptomatic illness or altered other liver function tests, but liver biopsies showed changes characteristic of hepatitis. Seven halothane patients showed an SGPT rise greater than 20 IU/l versus one control (P < 0.02).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with carcinoma of the uterine cervix undergoing repeated radium-treatment anaesthetics; repeated anaesthetic exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized controlled trial in 39 patients. 4/18 halothane patients had SGPT >100 IU/l before the third radium treatment vs 0/21 controls (P<0.025). raw_record.support_text: This single centre report describes three cases of significant hepatitis associated with rifampicin therapy used as an antipruritic agent in patients with primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC), a cholestatic liver disease. Two patients developed significant impairment of hepatic synthetic function, necessitating liver transplantation in one case. The authors report that rifampicin caused significant hepatitis in 7.3% (95% CI 2.5-19.4%) of patients treated for cholestatic liver disease in their centre, and note that prior reports of rifampicin hepatitis in tuberculosis patients were confounded by concurrent hepatotoxic antitubercular therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with cholestatic liver disease (primary biliary cirrhosis) receiving rifampicin as second-line antipruritic therapy; two of the three affected patients had significant impairment of hepatic synthetic function.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis occurred in 7.3% of 41 patients treated with rifampicin (95% CI 2.5-19.4%); three cases identified via a 50% increase in liver function tests (bilirubin, ALT, or ALP). One case required liver transplantation due to impaired synthetic function. Authors state these are the first reports of impaired hepatic synthetic function due to rifampicin monotherapy; prior tuberculosis-treatment reports were confounded by concurrent hepatotoxic antitubercular drugs.

raw_record.support_text: In a real-world cohort of patients with cholestatic pruritus treated with rifampicin, 95% of patients did not develop any liver injury, while 5% developed rifampicin-associated hepatitis. All patients who developed hepatitis recovered after drug cessation with only one patient requiring further intervention (corticosteroids and hospital admission); none developed life-threatening complications despite some having advanced liver disease at baseline.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with cholestatic liver disease receiving rifampicin for cholestatic pruritus; many had advanced liver disease and marked baseline jaundice (bilirubin >100 μmol/L); concurrent nonrifampicin medications (median 5) including long-term antibiotics, so drug-drug interactions could not be excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: 105 patients in cohort; median time to onset of hepatitis was 70 days (longer than the ~15-30 days reported in TB cohorts); two cases occurred after the period of biochemical monitoring suggested by recent guidelines; two of three rifampicin-induced hepatitis cases reported by Prince et al occurred at 11 and 14 months after initiation; no protocol liver-biochemistry monitoring, so subclinical cases may have been missed, potentially underestimating the rate; oral vitamin K co-prescribed for icteric patients; one patient required corticosteroids and hospital admission; no life-threatening complications or deaths.

raw_record.support_text: In this clinical trial of idelalisib monotherapy in patients with CLL, ALT increase was reported in 19 subjects (79%) including 13 (54%) grade 3-4, and AST increase in 19 subjects (79%) including 10 (42%) grade 3-4; blood bilirubin increased in 10 (42%) including 1 (4%) grade 3-4 and alkaline phosphatase in 8 (33%). raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL); transaminitis events adjudicated on idelalisib monotherapy during the trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy in 2 subjects with severe transaminitis showed increased perforin-positive (activated) CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell infiltrate and CD20+ periportal lymphocytes, suggesting an immune-mediated cause; steroids and/or mycophenolate mofetil treated the hepatotoxicity; median time from steroid initiation to reduction of transaminitis to grade ≤1 was 8 days (range 3-21). Rechallenge: 6 of 12 subjects developed recurrent transaminitis within 1-4 days of re-exposure; 4 of 5 rechallenged off steroids recurred (grade 2,1; grade 3,2; grade 4,1) vs 2 of 7 rechallenged on steroids. 16 subjects (67%) received steroids for transaminitis. Higher day-28 CCL-3 and CCL-4 were associated with hepatotoxicity; lower Treg percentages were associated with on-drug toxicity.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) receiving oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy; co-treatment with bevacizumab was associated with amelioration (protective effect) of oxaliplatin-induced SD.
raw_record.extra_details: Oxaliplatin causes sinusoidal dilatation (SD) with LSEC dysfunction, ECM remodeling, inflammation and LSEC injury that may progress to SOS/VOD. Associated gene perturbations include up-regulation of IL16, CCL2, TGFB1 (NHP), ERG, CDH5, vWF, MMP2/MMP9 and loss of vascular homeostasis markers (ICAM1, CCND1). Assessment of hepatic lesions attributed to oxaliplatin-induced hepatotoxicity also cited from Rubbia-Brandt et al. and amelioration of SD attributed to bevacizumab from van der Pool et al.; evidence based on a cross-sectional cohort of 65 clinical cases collected 2009-2012.

raw_record.support_text: Oxaliplatin-related sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) was identified in patients who had received preoperative oxaliplatin for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) but developed toxic liver injury, compared with controls having histologically normal livers (patients treated with oxaliplatin who did not develop SOS, and patients treated by surgery alone). 913 genes were found differentially expressed in oxaliplatin-related SOS.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with colorectal liver metastases receiving preoperative oxaliplatin as systemic chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Oxaliplatin-related sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) considered toxic liver injury; 20 SOS cases compared with 20 oxaliplatin-treated livers without SOS and 10 histologically normal livers. 913 genes differentially expressed; key implicated pathways included acute phase response signaling, coagulation system, hepatic fibrosis/hepatic stellate cell activation, and oxidative stress. CCL20 showed the highest mRNA upregulation, expressed in macrophages (hypoxia-inducible), and upregulation of HIF1 indicated hypoxia; IL-6/STAT (STAT1, STAT2, STAT3) pathways were implicated, with STAT1 contributing to liver inflammation/injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 104 patients with colorectal liver metastases who underwent liver resection after neoadjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, histopathologic evaluation found sinusoidal dilatation in 59 patients (57%) of the total study group. This finding is presented as chemotherapy-associated liver injury, and the study examined whether adding bevacizumab modified the degree of oxaliplatin-associated sinusoidal dilatation; moderate sinusoidal dilatation was present in 15/51 bevacizumab-treated patients (28%) versus 4/53 in the non-bevacizumab group (8%, P=0.01).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with colorectal liver metastases undergoing hepatic resection after neoadjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy; histologic assessment of sinusoidal dilatation by two pathologists with substantial inter-observer agreement (kappa 0.77).
raw_record.extra_details: Chemotherapy-associated liver injury; sinusoidal dilatation present in 57% (59/104) overall and not associated with postoperative complications (31% vs 27%, P=0.83). Moderate sinusoidal dilatation 28% in bevacizumab group vs 8% in non-bevacizumab group (P=0.01); severe dilatation in 1 bevacizumab patient vs 0 non-bevacizumab (P=0.45). No significant inter-group differences in perivenular fibrosis, portal inflammation, nodular regenerative hyperplasia, ballooning, lobular inflammation, or steatosis. Findings independent of number of chemotherapy cycles (>=6 vs <6) and of time interval from last dose to resection (<=5 vs >5 weeks).

raw_record.support_text: 6-Thioguanine (6-TG), a prodrug immediately converted into 6-thioguanine nucleotide (6-TGN), was tested in 40 azathioprine-intolerant and 9 azathioprine-resistant Crohn's disease patients at 20 mg/d. Five of 40 patients (13%) did not tolerate 6-TG, including two with an increase in liver enzymes. In a separate small prospective study of 16 patients on 20-40 mg of 6-TG, one severe case of hepatotoxicity occurred after 44 weeks with recovery within 24 weeks after withdrawal of 6-TG. The authors note the considerable risk of hepatotoxicity, predominantly nodular regenerative hyperplasia, even in patients with normal liver function tests, and conclude that 6-TG should only be given in controlled study settings.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as the second major, occasionally lethal side effect of antithyroid drugs. In an analysis of 18,558 Japanese patients with Graves disease treated with antithyroid drugs, severe liver injury (alanine aminotransferase >8-fold or total bilirubin >3-fold the upper limit) was significantly higher in the propylthiouracil (PTU)-treated group (6.3%) than in the methimazole (MMI)-treated group (1.4%); median time to development of antithyroid-drug-induced hepatic injury was 30 (range 7-314) days and no deaths were reported. Recent data from Taiwan and China are noted to challenge the older concept of a more hepatocellular injury pattern with PTU versus a more cholestatic pattern with MMI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with Graves disease; no deaths reported in the cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Japanese cohort of 18,558 patients; severe liver injury (ALT >8x ULN or total bilirubin >3x ULN) in 6.3% of PTU-treated patients; median latency 30 (range 7-314) days; no deaths. Recent Taiwan and China data challenge the older concept of a predominantly hepatocellular injury pattern with PTU.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with Graves' disease treated for hyperthyroidism; female predominance; greater susceptibility in the 20-50 year age group.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 39 PTU patients, dose at onset of severe hepatotoxicity was 212.8±105.0 mg/d (range 50-600 mg/d). Mean treatment duration before severe hepatotoxicity was 10 weeks for PTU; more than 60% of patients developed severe hepatotoxicity within 4 weeks and more than 80% within 12 weeks. PTU-induced hepatotoxicity is described as allergic hepatitis with hepatocellular injury, markedly elevated aminotransferases, and pathological findings ranging from hepatocellular inflammation to submassive or massive hepatic necrosis; cholestatic type frequency was 17.9% in the PTU group.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 8864 patients treated at a department of nuclear medicine in China, 90 cases of ATD-induced severe hepatotoxicity were identified (incidence 1.0%). Methimazole (MMI) was one of the antithyroid drugs implicated in causing severe hepatotoxicity; one patient was diagnosed with MMI-induced severe cholestatic hepatotoxicity within 9 weeks of initiating 20 mg/d MMI and died one week after radioiodine therapy because of progressively worsening liver function and complications.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with Graves' disease treated for hyperthyroidism; female predominance; greater susceptibility in the 20-50 year age group.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 51 MMI patients, dose at onset of severe hepatotoxicity was 19.1±7.4 mg/d (range 5-30 mg/d). Mean treatment duration before severe hepatotoxicity was 9 weeks for MMI; more than 60% of patients developed severe hepatotoxicity within 4 weeks and more than 80% within 12 weeks. MMI-induced hepatotoxicity is generally considered a cholestatic process with preserved hepatocellular architecture, intracanalicular cholestasis and mild periportal inflammation; cholestatic type frequency was 35.3% in the MMI group. Hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed types occurred at approximately equivalent rates in the MMI and PTU groups.

raw_record.support_text: Of the patients using thioguanine (TG), 14 (25%) had to discontinue therapy within 1 year, mostly due to adverse events or ineffectiveness. Out of 8 patients who had to discontinue TG due to hepatotoxicity, 5 were diagnosed with histologically proven nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) of the liver in biopsies taken as part of a long-term TG safety study. Of these, 2 were asymptomatic, 2 had thrombocytopenia (platelet counts 46 and 67 x 10⁹/L after 15 and 28 months of TG), and 1 had symptoms of noncirrhotic portal hypertension (esophageal varices grade III-IV, splenomegaly) after 44 months. NRH patients had comparable 6-TGN concentrations as non-NRH patients (481 vs 415 pmol/8 x 10⁸ RBC, P = 0.80).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis); one patient with thrombocytopenia had low platelets before TG initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 8 patients discontinuing TG for hepatotoxicity had histologically proven nodular regenerative hyperplasia; 2 asymptomatic, 2 with thrombocytopenia (platelets 46 and 67 x 10⁹/L after 15 and 28 months), 1 with noncirrhotic portal hypertension (esophageal varices grade III-IV, splenomegaly) after 44 months of TG. 6-TGN concentrations comparable between NRH and non-NRH patients (481 vs 415 pmol/8 x 10⁸ RBC, P = 0.80). Liver function test elevations in the total cohort were usually mild (<3.0 x ULN). NRH is a vascular lesion associated with liver injury; 2 TG-group deaths occurred during follow-up but were unlikely related to TG.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of patients with IBD, the authors confirmed the major relevance of 6-thioguanine (6-TG)-related drug-induced liver injury and the high risk for development of nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH). Unambiguous or most likely NRH was diagnosed on the basis of histological examination with silver-reticulin staining in 27.1% of the 59 patients with liver biopsy. 6-TG was used for a median of 18 months before liver biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease receiving therapeutic 6-TG; NRH diagnosis required liver biopsy with silver-reticulin staining.
raw_record.extra_details: NRH prevalence in the survey was 27.1% of 59 biopsied patients, lower than the 61.5% and 54.1% reported by the Los Angeles working group. 6-TG was given for a median of 18 months before biopsy in this population (median initiation dose 40 mg/day) versus 8.5 months in Dubinsky et al.; doses up to 100 mg/day were used in a US study. Higher 6-TG dosage may relate to higher NRH rates. Patients with NRH were older (median 44 years vs 35, p=0.002) and more often female (68.8% vs 44.2%), with hepatotoxicity in 56.3% of NRH-positive versus 25.6% of non-NRH patients (p=0.03); hepatotoxicity had 56.3% sensitivity and 74.4% specificity for NRH. Pathogenesis may relate to high 6-thioguanine nucleotide levels, though other mechanisms are debated. Multivariate analysis identified age as a weak independent risk factor.

raw_record.support_text: Liver toxicity was studied by sequential examination, liver function tests, and percutaneous liver biopsies (light and electron microscopy) during methotrexate treatment in patients whose leukemia or histiocytosis X remained in complete remission. Fibrosis was found even without hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function and persisted despite normalization of physical findings and liver function. Initially hepatocellular changes were seen by light microscopy, progressing to portal inflammation and fibrosis with continued therapy. The authors conclude that the pathologic changes are secondary to methotrexate therapy, not the basic disease process, and stress the insidious nature of this hepatic toxicity in nonmalignant uses of the drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with leukemia or histiocytosis X in complete remission receiving methotrexate therapy; finding specifically that fibrosis can develop absent hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 patients studied by sequential liver function tests and percutaneous biopsies (light and electron microscopy); hepatomegaly usually developed; fibrosis persisted despite normalization of physical findings and liver function; light microscopy initially showed hepatocellular changes progressing to portal inflammation and fibrosis; ultrastructural changes included double-nucleated hepatic cells with minor nucleolar changes and decreased perichromatin, varied cytoplasmic fat and glycogen, mitochondrial swelling, dilated endoplasmic reticulum, and sinusoidal slender filaments with collagen and basement membrane formation; authors state liver biopsy is the only accurate way to follow the extent of liver damage and discontinuation of therapy can result in return toward normal structure; toxicity also noted as concern for nonmalignant uses (skin disorders, immunologic diseases).

raw_record.support_text: Twelve patients with various malignancies (six MPM, two esophageal cancers, two lung cancers, two synovial sarcomas) were treated with mithramycin over twenty cycles. Nine patients experienced transient, asymptomatic dose-limiting transaminitis at 25 mcg/kg per infusion, and percutaneous biopsies revealed apoptotic hepatocellular death; three patients had no hepatotoxicity and tolerated dose escalation to 30 mcg/kg per infusion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with malignancies (malignant pleural mesothelioma, esophageal, lung cancers, synovial sarcomas); therapeutic intravenous infusion dosing; dose-limiting transaminitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Twelve patients treated, 20 cycles, all evaluable. Nine patients (75%) experienced transient, asymptomatic dose-limiting transaminitis at 25 mcg/kg per infusion; three patients (two MPM, one esophageal) had no hepatotoxicity and tolerated 30 mcg/kg per infusion. Eight patients experienced clinically significant (≥grade 3) transaminase elevations approximately 24 h after the third infusion. Mithramycin caused a >13-fold increase in geometric mean ALT (21 U/l [12–36] vs 363 U/l [138–895]) and AST (20 U/l [13–29] vs 269 U/l [116–622]), indicative of hepatocellular damage and/or injury. Biopsies showed apoptotic hepatocellular death. Peak and steady-state mithramycin plasma levels were 20 nM and 8 nM, respectively, below the 50–100 nM needed for tumor regression in preclinical models. No objective responses in seven evaluable patients. Pharmacokinetic parameters were not associated with transaminase elevations (P≥0.20).

raw_record.support_text: The study involved 129 admitted patients with metastatic breast cancer, all treated with docetaxel-based agents. Forty of these patients developed drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and were enrolled as cases, while 89 sex-, age-, and drug-matched patients without hepatotoxicity served as controls.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with metastatic breast cancer receiving docetaxel-based chemotherapy; case-control design restricted to this indication.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 129 docetaxel-treated metastatic breast cancer patients, 40 met DILI Network-based criteria and were compared with 89 matched controls without hepatotoxicity. DILI criteria included ALT/AST >5x ULN, ALP >2x ULN, or any enzyme elevation with total bilirubin >2.5 mg/dl, plus a causality assessment score >5 (categorized as probable or highly probable DILI). The study's main purpose was to assess IL10 and TNF single-nucleotide polymorphisms as susceptibility markers.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 34 patients with metastatic RCC treated with pazopanib, 4 patients (12%) were admitted to hospital because of liver toxicity and 3 patients (9%) were treated with prednisolone (median dose 50 mg, range 25–100 mg). One patient with grade 4 increased bilirubin had a liver biopsy demonstrating cholestatic hepatitis, responded to prednisolone 100 mg daily, had pazopanib interrupted for 215 days until normal liver tests occurred, and resumed pazopanib at ultra-low doses. The discussion frames liver toxicity as a significant adverse effect affecting patients treated with pazopanib, most often resulting in drug interruption and permanent discontinuation, and describes this as pazopanib-induced liver toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC); UGT1A1 (TA6/TA6 vs TA7 allele) genotyping informing dosing and rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: 34 patients evaluated; 4 (12%) admitted to hospital for liver toxicity; 3 (9%) treated with prednisolone (median 50 mg, range 25–100 mg); one patient with grade 4 increased bilirubin had a biopsy showing cholestatic hepatitis, responded to prednisolone 100 mg daily, pazopanib interrupted for 215 days until normal liver tests, then resumed at 200 mg every third day for 3 months and 200 mg every second day for 8 months. Of 9 patients with elevated liver enzymes and wild-type TA6/TA6 genotype, progressive disease was seen in 7 (78%). Discussion notes some outcome improvement may reflect very low dosing rather than the UGT1A1 polymorphism.

raw_record.support_text: In this multicentre, open-label study of long-term donepezil treatment (3, 5, 7 and 10 mg/day, step-wise) in patients with mild to moderately severe Alzheimer's disease, the most common adverse events were related to the nervous and digestive systems and were generally mild and transient. The authors state: 'There was no evidence of hepatotoxicity.' This is an explicit agent-specific negative conclusion that donepezil was not associated with human liver injury over up to 4.9 years of treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with mild to moderately severe Alzheimer's disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Open-label extension study in 133 patients who had completed a prior 14-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled donepezil study; donepezil doses 3-10 mg/day over up to 240 weeks (254 cumulative weeks). No hepatotoxicity was reported. Study provenance: 2000 Elsevier Science B.V.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 140 patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic dysfunction (Child-Pugh A or B) receiving voriconazole for suspected invasive aspergillosis, acute liver injury (ALI) occurred in 44 patients (31.4%). Drug causality was assessed with the RUCAM scale, and all 44 patients scored above six points, indicating a high probability of drug-related hepatotoxicity. High trough voriconazole plasma concentration (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.29-2.02, p=0.013) and voriconazole treatment duration (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.03-1.10, p=0.005) were identified as independent risk factors for hepatotoxicity in multivariate regression.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic dysfunction (Child-Pugh A or B); underlying hematologic malignancy (leukemia), immunosuppression, and hypoproteinemia were common; therapy for invasive aspergillosis/lung fungal infection.
raw_record.extra_details: ALI in 44/140 patients (31.4%); RUCAM scores above 6 (high probability of drug-related hepatotoxicity). Independent risk factors: trough voriconazole plasma concentration (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.29-2.02, p=0.013) and voriconazole treatment duration (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.03-1.10, p=0.005). Median trough concentration 5.07 mg/L in ALI group vs 2.70 mg/L control; median treatment duration 21 vs 9 days. Optimal cutoffs for ALI: trough VPC 3.81 mg/L (AUC 0.81) and treatment duration 10 days (AUC 0.74). All-cause mortality higher in ALI group (29.5% vs 10.4%, p=0.005) but fatalities mostly attributed to underlying hematologic malignancy. Tigecycline combination use not significantly associated (29.5% vs 18.8%, p=0.153). Possible mechanisms discussed: CYP450-dependent metabolism with hepatic impairment, reduced bile excretion retaining drug/metabolites including voriconazole N-oxide, and reduced glutathione reserves. Recommendations for therapeutic drug monitoring and dose adjustment.

raw_record.extra_details: Five patients with valproate-induced liver failure retrospectively identified. Four patients homozygous for POLG1 p.W748S and p.E1143G had hepatic mtDNA depletion; one of these died prior to anticipated transplantation and the other three survived 4-19 years after liver transplantation. POLG1 analysis recommended before introducing valproate therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Despite concerns over liver toxicity, bosentan was used successfully in portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH). In 11 patients with Child A cirrhosis and WHO functional class III-IV PoPH treated with bosentan for at least one year, bosentan was well tolerated and no drug-related liver injury was observed. In a separate retrospective noncomparative case series of 31 PoPH patients with Child A and B cirrhosis (18 treated with bosentan, 13 with inhaled iloprost), both treatments were safe in terms of liver function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH) with Child A/B cirrhosis; WHO functional class III-IV; bosentan given for at least one year in the 11-patient group; comparison cohort in the 31-patient series included inhaled iloprost.
raw_record.extra_details: In the 11-patient group (Child A cirrhosis) bosentan showed improved 6MWD and VO2max with reduced pulmonary vascular resistance at 1 year, with no drug-related liver injury observed. In the 31-patient series (18 bosentan, 13 inhaled iloprost; 3-year follow-up), bosentan showed better survival (p=0.029) and event-free survival (p=0.017) than inhaled iloprost and both treatments were safe in terms of liver function.

raw_record.support_text: In post-marketing surveillance in Japan, ticlopidine-induced liver injury characteristically occurred within two months of treatment initiation and included pruritus, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and more rarely marked progression of jaundice. In the present study (62 Cases), most patients developed liver function abnormalities within 30 days, and the disease type was cholestatic in the majority according to the ICM and DDW Japan 2002 criteria; effects of aging and dose were not significant, whereas pre-existing renal functional abnormalities tended to increase risk. The paper recommends monitoring ALT, ALP, and γ-GTP for at least 30 days to prevent serious ticlopidine hydrochloride-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with pre-existing liver or renal function abnormalities at initiation of ticlopidine therapy tended to develop abnormal liver function; risk was increased in those with pre-existing renal abnormalities, particularly for the cholestatic type.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 62 cases of liver function abnormalities on ticlopidine: 11 hepatocellular-type, 29 cholestatic-type, 11 mixed-type, 11 non-classified type (cholestatic >50%). Most (88.7%) abnormalities occurred within 30 days of treatment start; all abnormal LFTs normalized on discontinuation (or spontaneously with continued administration) except 7 with unknown outcome. Post-marketing surveillance: cholestatic injury within 2 months with pruritus, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, rarely marked jaundice. CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19, 3A4, 2D6 associated with ticlopidine metabolism; concomitant CYP2C9 substrate/inhibitor use significantly reduced cholestatic-type risk; no dose or age dependence. Dosing of UDCA (used as preventive) not effective.

It notes that alcohol, obesity, and diabetes increase the risk of MTX-induced fibrosis, with alcohol in particular increasing the incidence of hepatotoxicity, and that 50% of their patients continued drinking alcohol after starting MTX.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with psoriasis on MTX; alcohol, obesity, and diabetes increase the risk of MTX-induced hepatic fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Risk across studies: hepatic fibrosis 0-34%, cirrhosis 0-25.6%; studies not standardized for MTX dose, cumulative duration, risk factors, or pre/post-treatment histology. MTX-induced cirrhosis reportedly does not progress if the drug is continued and regresses if stopped. In the authors' cohort, three of five patients whose drug was discontinued had raised liver enzymes; half of patients had abnormal laboratory investigations. Alcohol increases the incidence of hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In ustekinumab psoriasis trials, INH-treated patients had significantly higher proportions of hepatic laboratory AEs, markedly abnormal ALT values, and various ALT elevations > 1 x ULN through week 12 compared with non-INH-treated patients, and events were characterized as consistent with INH toxicity (gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, or neurological disorders or hepatic laboratory AEs). ALT elevations > 3 x ULN were 12.9% in ustekinumab-treated and 17.9% in control INH-treated patients in the non-Asian trials. Six serious AEs among INH-treated patients were unrelated to INH toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with psoriasis receiving biologic or control therapy (ustekinumab 45/90 mg, etanercept, or placebo) during latent tuberculosis prophylaxis with isoniazid; co-exposure to biologic immunotherapy in trial setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Through week 12, rates of INH-related AEs (gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, neurological, or hepatic laboratory AEs) among INH-treated patients were 25.7% (non-Asian control), 20.0% (UST 45 mg), 22.2% (UST 90 mg); Asian trials 17.6%, 14.8%, 40.0%. Markedly abnormal ALT values (>150 IU/L with ≥100% increase from baseline): up to 22.9% in controls. Study-agent discontinuation due to INH toxicity through week 12: 4/101 (4.0%) non-Asian, 1/66 (1.5%) Asian; three PHOENIX 2, ACCEPT, and PEARL patients had clinically relevant ALT or AST ≥ 3 x ULN with bilirubin ≥ 2 x ULN while on INH, with enzyme/bilirubin levels returning to normal by week 20. ALT elevations > 3 x ULN were 12.9% (UST) vs 17.9% (control) in non-Asian INH-treated patients. No deaths, acute liver failure, or liver transplantation reported.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 278 liver biopsies taken over 30 years, MTX-induced liver fibrosis (≥Roenigk grade 3a) was seen in 15% (19 patients) of the psoriasis population. Progression to a higher stage of liver injury mostly occurred at a cumulative dose range between 1500 and 6000 mg (about 2 years at 15 mg weekly), and progressive liver damage was infrequent above 6000 mg. Additionally, fibrosis/cirrhosis (Roenigk ≥ 3a) was detected in 41 biopsies from 24 patients at some point during MTX treatment, and histological findings led to discontinuation in only 6/41 biopsies.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with psoriasis receiving low-dose, long-term MTX; findings restricted to a cohort managed per international biopsy monitoring guidelines.
raw_record.extra_details: 278 liver biopsies over 30 years; MTX-induced liver fibrosis (Roenigk grade ≥3a) in 15% (19 patients); fibrosis/cirrhosis detected in 41 biopsies from 24 patients; progression occurred mainly at cumulative dose 1500-6000 mg (about 2 years at 15 mg weekly) and was infrequent above 6000 mg; histology led to MTX discontinuation in only 6/41 biopsies; 16 patients had repeat biopsy after significant earlier abnormalities (mean 14 months) with improvement in 10, no change in 5, and worsening in 1; treatment was described as relatively safe despite hepatotoxicity risk.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of 224 tuberculosis patients treated with an isoniazid-based antituberculosis regimen, 33 (14.7%) were diagnosed with drug-induced hepatitis by the International Consensus Meeting definition. During isoniazid rechallenge, 14 of these patients (6.3%) developed serum ALT >3x ULN, which the authors classified as clinically significant isoniazid-induced hepatitis, prompting replacement of isoniazid with streptomycin or ofloxacin; the other 19 had transient hepatic dysfunction. Slow acetylator NAT2 status and older age were significant risk factors for isoniazid-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with pulmonary tuberculosis on isoniazid-based antituberculosis therapy; predominantly elderly cohort; age was a significant independent risk factor.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid rechallenge confirmed causality: 14 patients (6.3%) had ALT >3x ULN during rechallenge and were classified as clinically significant hepatitis; 19 (8.5%) had ALT <=3x ULN (transient hepatic dysfunction) and continued isoniazid safely. Peak ALT 393.6 ± 353.9 U/L (range 98-1609) and peak total bilirubin 3.25 ± 3.57 mg/dL (range 0.5-20.2) in hepatitis cases. Hepatitis risk was higher in slow acetylators (26.4% vs 11.1%; OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.32-6.23), and slow acetylators had higher peak ALT/AST and were more likely to exceed 3x ULN on rechallenge (64.3% vs 26.3%; P=.040). Multivariate OR for slow acetylator 3.66 (1.58-8.49) and age OR 1.09 (1.04-1.14). Rapid acetylator was protective (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.76).

raw_record.support_text: TGR-1202 is a PI3Kδ inhibitor studied in a Phase I trial in patients with relapsed/refractory hematologic malignancies. Notably, in comparison with other PI3Kδ inhibitors, no cases of hepatotoxicity or colitis were observed among the patients; in the combination trial with ublituximab, no hepatotoxicity or grade 3/4 toxicities were reported. These statements explicitly rule out hepatotoxicity for this agent.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with relapsed/refractory hematologic malignancies (CLL; phase I settings).
raw_record.extra_details: PI3Kδ inhibitor (also named Filanesol). In a separate phase I trial combining TGR-1202 with ublituximab (anti-CD20 mAb) in B-cell malignancies, no hepatotoxicity or grade 3/4 toxicities were reported.

raw_record.support_text: The study used the Roenigk grading system to assess liver damage in liver biopsy specimens obtained from patients with rheumatic disease or psoriasis who had received methotrexate (MTX) therapy. Grade I was normal histology, Grade II included fibrous spurs and patchy fibrosis, Grade IIIA mild portal fibrosis with septa, Grade IIIB spotty necrosis or septal fibrosis with bridging, and Grade IV was cirrhosis defined by bridging with regenerating nodules. The graded histologic spectrum (fibrosis, bridging fibrosis, cirrhosis) reflects liver injury attributed to chronic MTX exposure in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with rheumatic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, psoriatic arthritis, polymyositis, Sjogren's syndrome, UDCTD/CREST) or psoriasis receiving chronic methotrexate therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver biopsy specimens graded by the Roenigk criteria; Grades range from I (normal, including mild lobular hepatitis, mild focal fatty metamorphosis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia) to IV (cirrhosis with bridging and regenerating nodules). Graded features include fibrous spurs in the portal area, fibrosis in the space of Disse, thickened liver cords, septal fibrosis, portal-to-portal or portal-to-central vein bridging, spotty hepatocellular necrosis, and steatohepatitis. In the study cohort (29 patients), MTX cumulative doses ranged from 1.5 to 12.6 g, therapy exposure from 2 to 17 years, and weekly doses from 7.5 to 25 mg/week; observed grades ranged from 1 to 3b.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' experience, the risk of hepatotoxicity from methotrexate (MTX) is higher than earlier suggested. Three patients from a prospective study of 76 patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) followed with sequential liver biopsies developed cirrhosis, giving a point prevalence of cirrhosis of 2.63%; two additional patients of the 76 developed Roenigk Grade III B changes (moderate to severe fibrosis) requiring cessation of MTX. Over 14 years of clinic use, the 5-year cumulative incidence of cirrhosis was 9.4/1000 treated patients.

raw_record.extra_details: 5-yr cumulative incidence of cirrhosis 9.4/1000 treated patients; point prevalence of cirrhosis 2.63% (3/76) in a prospective serial-biopsy cohort; Roenigk Grade III B (moderate to severe fibrosis) changes in 2 additional patients; cirrhosis developed after >4 yr of MTX (case 2 had non-specific lobular hepatitis after 3.3 yr); monitoring of AST/ALT every 4-6 weeks recommended; supports ACR guidelines for hepatotoxicity monitoring; American/ACR guidelines recommend liver biopsy for AST elevations in 5 of 9 determinations within 12 months.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 210 patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with long-term, low-dose, pulse methotrexate (follow-up up to seven years), no cirrhosis was observed and only six persons had fibrotic changes, all graded as 'mild' hepatic fibrosis (grade III changes). raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis; long-term low-dose pulse methotrexate therapy; hepatic fibrosis was mild (grade III changes) with no cirrhosis in this cohort. raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective analysis of 210 methotrexate-treated rheumatoid arthritis patients, up to seven years of use; only six persons had fibrotic changes on liver biopsy, all 'mild' hepatic fibrosis; no cirrhosis. Mean age of patients with grade III changes was 59 years; five of six denied significant alcohol intake, all had normal renal function, five were obese, three had glucose intolerance/overt diabetes. Only one patient had LFTs greater than two times normal at grade III biopsy; three of six grade III patients never had elevated LFTs. Total dose/duration linked to eventual liver damage; three patients had received less than 1,200 mg at grade III biopsy. Five of six patients with grade III had methotrexate discontinued; one showed reversal to grade II on later biopsies while continuing therapy. Authors noted inadequate laboratory markers (LFTs, albumin) for hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: The authors contest the claim that hepatic fibrosis is an invariable consequence of prolonged low-dose oral methotrexate, noting that two reinvestigated patients showed no fibrosis whereas two others developed cirrhosis. raw_record.support_text: In comparing first and last liver biopsies among 49 patients receiving long-term, low-dose, once weekly oral methotrexate for severe psoriasis, there was improvement in 12, no change in 28, and deterioration in nine, with none developing cirrhosis. Liver biopsy findings prompted discontinuation of methotrexate in four of the 49 patients. The authors conclude that the risk of development or progression of liver disease during continued low-dose weekly MTX treatment is modest and that routine liver biopsy requirements should be reconsidered.

raw_record.extra_details: 182 liver biopsies performed over 10 years; 49 patients had two or more biopsies. Mean cumulative MTX dose at first biopsy 2743 mg (range 315-10,024) over 275 weeks (range 26-738); a further 2362 mg (range 390-7155) over 225 weeks (range 60-460) between first and last biopsies. Histologic groups: normal; steatosis alone; inflammation without fibrosis; fibrosis; cirrhosis. Deterioration in 9/49, no new cirrhosis; MTX discontinued in 4 patients due to biopsy findings. 124 biopsies performed in these patients (cost/morbidity consideration). The paper frames the study as prompted by concern over possible MTX hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that methotrexate remains one of the most effective treatments for severe psoriasis but that its use is often complicated by hepatotoxicity, which in the long term may result in severe hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis, both of which are contra-indications to further treatment with methotrexate. It also refers to methotrexate-induced liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with severe psoriasis receiving long-term once-weekly oral methotrexate, who were about to start or already taking long-term methotrexate.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 28 patients (20 men, 8 women, ages 30-74) comparing liver ultrasound with liver biopsy histology on 54 paired investigations. Fibrosis of sufficient severity necessitated methotrexate withdrawal in 4 cases where ultrasound suggested fatty change and in 2 cases where ultrasound suggested fibrosis; no patient with a normal ultrasound scan showed significant fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Oral methotrexate (MTX) used for severe psoriasis has potential hepatotoxicity; in this prospective study of 25 MTX patients (mean cumulative dose 3.9 g, range 0.2–11.1 g), liver biopsy grading showed 21 patients with normal liver histology (grade I), three with steatosis (grade II), and one with mild fibrosis (grade IIIA), assessed as MTX-induced hepatic damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with severe psoriasis receiving oral MTX; prolonged/chronic treatment with cumulative dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of 25 MTX psoriasis patients, mean cumulative MTX dose 3.9 g (range 0.2–11.1 g). Liver biopsy grading: 21 grade I (normal), 3 grade II steatosis, 1 grade IIIA mild fibrosis. Study compared dynamic hepatic scintigraphy (DHS) and serum PIIINP as screening tests against liver biopsy (gold standard); concluded DHS promising for early MTX-induced hepatic damage detection but not suitable to grade severity, and that regular liver biopsies remain mandatory for safe prolonged MTX use. Fibrosis and steatosis are attributed MTX-induced phenotypes.

raw_record.support_text: In pazopanib-treated patients with solid tumors, a key liver safety signal was concurrent elevation of ALT (>3 × ULN) and total bilirubin (>2 × ULN) without biliary obstruction, reflecting extensive hepatocyte damage. The authors characterized 26 such patients and performed detailed causality assessments per DILIN criteria (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely), adjudicating four cases that met criteria for Hy's Law, of which two carried HLA-B*57:01. Across the combined datasets, ALT >3 × ULN and >5 × ULN events occurred in 20% and 11% of pazopanib-treated patients, respectively, and HLA-B*57:01 carriage was associated with higher risk of ALT elevation ({OR, 2.0 for >3 × ULN and OR, 2.1 for >5 × ULN}).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with solid tumors (n=2,190 combined) treated with pazopanib at various doses either as monotherapy or in combination with other agents; baseline liver-metastasis and baseline ALT considered as covariates.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT elevation was the hepatotoxicity phenotype; 26 cases had ALT >3 × ULN plus total bilirubin >2 × ULN, adjudicated by DILIN causality criteria (definite/highly likely/probable/possible/unlikely); four cases met Hy's Law criteria; two Hy's Law cases were HLA-B*57:01 carriers; ALT >3 × ULN in 20% and >5 × ULN in 11% of pazopanib-treated patients; HLA-B*57:01 associated with ALT elevation (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.3-3.1 for ALT>3xULN; OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.3-3.6 for ALT>5xULN; HR 2.5 for time to >3xULN; HR 3.4 for time to >5xULN); no patients carried both Gilbert UGT1A1 and HLA-B*57:01 risk genotypes; no additional HLA genotype associations; HLA carriage frequency ~6%.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is well tolerated by patients with chronic liver disease. In a double-blind, two-period, cross-over study comparing acetaminophen, 4 g daily for two weeks, with placebo in 20 patients with stable chronic liver disease, laboratory tests and clinical evaluations revealed no evidence of hepatotoxicity and no adverse nonspecific effect on laboratory abnormalities associated with liver disease, no significant drug accumulation despite modestly impaired metabolism, no enhanced formation of the toxic metabolite as reflected in conjugate excretion, and no glutathione depletion. The authors conclude acetaminophen is preferred to salicylates in patients with chronic liver disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with stable chronic liver disease
raw_record.extra_details: Double-blind, two-period, cross-over study of 20 patients comparing acetaminophen 4 g daily for two weeks with placebo; weekly laboratory tests (bilirubin, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, 5-nucleotidase, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase, serum bile acids, prothrombin/partial thromboplastin time, serum creatinine) showed no adverse effects. No evidence of hepatotoxicity, no drug accumulation, no enhanced toxic-metabolite formation (normal conjugate excretion), no glutathione depletion. Authors frame acetaminophen as preferred antipyretic analgesic over salicylates in chronic liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: In 1,091 consecutive patients with stage C or D prostate cancer treated with flutamide plus the LHRH agonist [D-Trp6, des-Gly-NH2(10)] LHRH ethylamide, an increase in AST and ALT at four-fold or more above upper normal limits was observed in only four patients (0.36%). Only two developed clinical manifestations of liver disease (0.18%); a biopsy in one showed a mixed pattern of cytotoxic and cholestatic changes. All clinical and biologic manifestations of liver toxicity rapidly disappeared upon discontinuation of flutamide alone, with no sequelae at follow-up (18, 22, 31, and 62 months).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with stage C or D prostate cancer treated with flutamide in combination with the co-administered LHRH agonist [D-Trp6, des-Gly-NH2(10)] LHRH ethylamide (combination therapy co-exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of flutamide-related liver toxicity studied prospectively in 1,091 consecutive patients with liver function tests at 4, 8, 12 weeks and every 3 months. Four patients (0.36%) had AST/ALT at ≥4x upper normal limit; 2 (0.18%) developed clinical manifestations. Rechallenge positive in 2 patients (causal link assessed by temporal relationship and rechallenge). One biopsy showed mixed cytotoxic and cholestatic histopathologic changes. Peak lab values in patient 1: ALT 209, AST 106, gamma-GT 355, total bilirubin 126 mmol/L. All manifestations resolved on flutamide discontinuation; no sequelae at long-term follow-up (18, 22, 31, 62 months). Authors recommend serial aminotransferase monitoring at 2 and 4 weeks to detect early possible flutamide-induced hepatic injury.; confidence_note: None

raw_record.support_text: Acarbose-related liver injury has been reported in humans. Early trials reported increases in transaminases or rarely jaundice in 3.8% of acarbose users versus 1.1% on placebo. The first case report was a 65-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes taking acarbose 300 mg/day for 2 months, presenting with malaise and anorexia and a hepatocellular damage laboratory pattern, with spontaneous recovery after discontinuation. Subsequent case series indicated that acarbose-related liver toxicity reports mostly came from Japan and Spain, had an average latency of 2–6 months after therapy initiation, frequently recurred after rechallenge, and were predominantly hepatocellular injuries.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus on therapeutic acarbose; general treatment population, not restricted to renal impairment. Post-marketing reports predominantly from Japan and Spain.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: 65-year-old woman, type 2 DM, acarbose 300 mg/day for 2 months, malaise and anorexia, hepatocellular damage pattern, spontaneous recovery after discontinuation. Early trials: transaminase elevations or rarely jaundice in 3.8% of users vs 1.1% placebo. Case series: average latency 2–6 months, frequent recurrence after rechallenge. Indication: type 2 diabetes mellitus (alpha-glucosidase inhibitor). Putative mechanisms (unproven): CYP2E1 induction, increased reactive oxygen species production, and influence of sex hormones; acarbose hepatotoxicity likely not via metabolites given low and unpredictable incidence.

At the 1.3 mg/m2 trabectedin starting dose, grade 3-4 hepatotoxicity occurred in 59 of 84 patients (70.2%), and no grade 4 events occurred at the 1.1 mg/m2 dose (19/48, 39.6% G3).

raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity was reported in 70% of patients treated at 1.3 mg/m2 and in 40% at the lower 1.1 mg/m2 dose. The observed relevant liver toxicity, together with a small survival benefit, precluded additional development of trabectedin in MPM as a single agent at the investigated schedule. One toxic death due to multiorgan failure occurred in the trial.

raw_record.support_text: A 10-year-old girl prescribed erythromycin ethylsuccinate for a respiratory illness developed jaundice, pruritus, abdominal pain, nausea, pale stools and dark urine after two doses. Investigations showed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase; viral hepatitis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and Wilson disease were excluded. Liver biopsy showed moderate panlobular parenchymatous degeneration with cholestasis and numerous intra- and intracellular bile plugs, consistent with a cholestatic jaundice associated with erythromycin. Clinical condition and liver function improved over 6-8 weeks after cessation of erythromycin, and she remained well at 1 year follow-up.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (10-year-old girl); erythromycin ethylsuccinate formulation; prior single exposure to erythromycin without problem; respiratory illness indication.
raw_record.extra_details: Symptoms began after two doses. Labs: total bilirubin 246 umol/L (conjugated 224 umol/L), ALT 278 IU/L, AST 173 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase rising to 1,209 IU/L, GGT 121 IU/L. Liver biopsy at week 4 showed panlobular parenchymatous degeneration with cholestasis and bile plugs, no periportal fibrosis; consistent with cholestatic jaundice. Recovery occurred over 6-8 weeks after drug cessation; well with normal LFTs at 1 year. Mechanism of erythromycin liver injury thought to be hypersensitivity or direct toxicity from a metabolite eliciting an immunologic response (author's discussion).

raw_record.support_text: In Case 2, a 2-year-old male with Langerhans cell histiocytosis was started on second-line therapy with mercaptopurine and cladribine. After about 6 months of mercaptopurine he developed hyperbilirubinemia, hepatomegaly, and high alkaline phosphatase (1424 IU/L), so mercaptopurine was stopped considering drug-induced cholestasis. A liver biopsy to differentiate drug-induced cholestasis from hepatic histiocytosis was in favor of drug-induced hepatitis, and his liver enzymes continued to be mildly altered on follow-up, with imaging findings indistinguishable from sclerosing cholangitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (2-year-old male) patient treated for Langerhans cell histiocytosis; mercaptopurine given together with cladribine as second-line therapy; hepatic histiocytosis remained a competing differential for the cholangitis/fibrosis; liver enzymes did not fully normalize after stopping the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced cholestasis was clinically considered and mercaptopurine was stopped (dechallenge); liver biopsy favored drug-induced hepatitis. Presented with hyperbilirubinemia, hepatomegaly, and alkaline phosphatase 1424 IU/L after about 6 months of mercaptopurine. Follow-up imaging (ultrasound) showed sclerosing cholangitis with periductal band-like echogenicities, coarse echotexture, lobulated margins, findings indistinguishable from sclerosing cholangitis; liver enzymes remained mildly altered on follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: Case 5 is a 4-year-old boy who had a mole removed under general anesthesia with halothane. One week later he developed fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and increasing fatigue, and appeared pale; an emergency visit showed markedly elevated transaminases (AST 10,388; ALT 5,233), thrombocytopenia (platelets 58,000), coagulopathy (PT 23.2, PTT 38.6), and elevated total bilirubin (2.6, direct 1.6). He was admitted with acute liver failure, and a liver biopsy was consistent with halothane toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (4-year-old boy); exposure via general anesthesia with halothane during mole removal
raw_record.extra_details: Latency about one week after anesthesia. Admission AST 10,388 and ALT 5,233; platelets 58,000; PT 23.2; PTT 38.6; total bilirubin 2.6 with direct fraction 1.6. Liver biopsy consistent with halothane toxicity. Liver functions recovered with supportive treatment; stage 0 hepatic encephalopathy; did not require liver transplantation. Brain 1H MRS showed a mildly increased alpha 1H peak (3.75 ppm) in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: A 6-year-old Tunisian child treated for epileptic absences with sodium valproate and ethosuximide developed drug hypersensitivity syndrome with hepatitis. Imputability of both drugs was deemed probable from chronological and clinical features; positive rechallenge with ethosuximide confirmed its toxicity, and sodium valproate was also held responsible because patch testing was positive and followed by a generalized eruption. The outcome was favourable after drug discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (6-year-old child); treatment for epileptic absences with the anticonvulsants sodium valproate and ethosuximide as co-exposures, with both drugs implicated in the hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 500 mg/day (Zarontin, Parke Davis); serum ethosuximide 53 µg/ml (therapeutic range). Drug hypersensitivity syndrome included fever, morbiliform skin eruption with vesicular and target lesions, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia (2x10^9/l), lymphocytosis (8.95x10^9/l), monocytosis, leukocytosis, and abnormal liver function tests (AST 70 U/l, GGT 50 U/l, LDH 1020 U/l). Positive rechallenge with ethosuximide confirmed toxicity. HHV6 antibody titers rose from 40 to 120 within 15 days; favourable outcome after drug discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy. Reported as the first case of DHS with ethosuximide.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a fatal acute liver failure in a previously healthy 9-year-old female after repeated administration of four therapeutic doses of acetaminophen (500 mg each) at 4-hour intervals for dental pain following facial trauma. A diagnosis of paracetamol-induced hepatitis was deduced from the clinical picture of fulminant hepatitis and tubular necrosis with encephalopathy and edema, and liver biopsy showed typical acetaminophen-induced necrosis and microvesicular steatosis in periportal hepatocytes. The injury may have been favored by pre-existing mitochondrial dysfunction, such as a deficiency in an enzyme of mitochondrial beta-oxidation or the respiratory chain.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective analysis of 181 patients treated with methotrexate (MTX) for acute lymphoblastic leukemia who developed toxicity, hepatotoxicity was the most common MTX-induced toxicity (56.8%). Among these, transient elevated hepatic enzymes were noted in 84%, cholestatic hepatitis in 4%, and mixed hepatitis in 11.5%. Toxicity was most common during the chemotherapy induction phase (67.6%) at a dose of 5 g/m2, with a median time to MTX toxicity of 10 days after administration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia population (114 B-cell ALL, 6 T-cell ALL; mean age 17.4 years, 50% under 10 years) treated with combination chemotherapy protocols (EORTC 49%, HyperCVAD 32%, Saint Jude 15%); MTX given at 5 g/m2 during induction phase.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective single-center cohort (Farhat Hached University Hospital) 2008-2017, 181 patients, 55% male, patients selected for having developed toxicity while on MTX. Hepatotoxicity incidence 56.8%; transient elevated hepatic enzymes 84%, cholestatic hepatitis 4%, mixed hepatitis 11.5%. Median latency 10 days after MTX administration; toxicity most frequent at induction phase (67.6%). Other MTX toxicities: acute kidney injury 16%, cutaneous lesions 13.8% (mucositis most predominant), gastrointestinal disorders 6.9% (vomiting, diarrhea), hematologic disorders 4.4%, neurologic symptoms 2.2%. Conclusion notes MTX toxicity ranges from minor events to life-threatening reactions.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with idiosyncratic toxic hepatitis caused by valproic acid (ácido valproico), with a CIOMS causality scale score of 8, corresponding to a probable diagnosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric case report (published in Boletín de Pediatría); subclinical Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection was considered but explicitly not judged to justify the hepatic involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS causality score 8 (probable). Injury is dose-independent and mediated by an idiosyncratic metabolic-predisposition mechanism, in contrast to the hypersensitivity mechanism of other anticonvulsants. Causes hepatocellular injury with GPT increase ~2 times the upper limit of normal. Lipids reversed/declined and the patient was asymptomatic on follow-up; carbamazepine was replaced by phenobarbital during management. Clinical manifestations of valproate hepatotoxicity range from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to fulminant toxic hepatitis. L-carnitine treatment was considered but omitted as the patient had no risk factors and favorable evolution.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of 117 Korean childhood ALL patients receiving interim maintenance HD-MTX therapy, transient liver toxicity, which may include reversible chemical hepatitis, was seen in 85% of the patients and in 60% of the cycles, with hyperbilirubinemia seen in 30% of patients. Almost all patients had elevations in SGOT and/or SGPT after HD-MTX, which were framed as transient and reversible, of minor clinical importance, not requiring dose adjustment and not leading to chronic liver disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric childhood ALL patients receiving high-dose (HD-MTX) interim maintenance methotrexate therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Transient liver toxicity (possibly reversible chemical hepatitis) in 85% of patients and 60% of cycles; hyperbilirubinemia in 30% of patients and 20% of cycles; SGOT/SGPT elevations in almost all patients but described as clinically insignificant and not leading to chronic liver disease. Associated MTX-related toxicities in the same study included nephrotoxicity (5% of patients), stroke-like syndrome, and peripheral neuropathy.

raw_record.support_text: During hospitalization, ten NHL patients receiving 40 courses of methotrexate (MTX) infusions were monitored for renal, liver, oral, and hematological toxicities. All patients had normal liver, renal, and hematological functions before beginning each cycle. Toxicity of the MTX infusions was graded and hepatotoxicity was reported among the observed toxicities, with scores tabulated for the AA and BB therapeutic protocols.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric NHL patients (ages 3-13 years) treated with intravenous MTX 1 g/m² infusions; children are a departure from the general adult default population.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxicity graded over 40 MTX (1 g/m²) infusions in 10 patients, comparing an AA and a BB hydration/leucovorin protocol. Hepatotoxicity grades (Table 2): Mild AA 25% vs BB 30%; Moderate AA 20% vs BB 20%; Severe AA 5% vs BB 15%; Unacceptable 0% both. Plasma MTX measured at 24, 36, 48, and 72 h postinfusion (means 9.1 ± 1.4, 1.4 ± 0.4, 0.1 ± 0.05, 0.06 ± 0.05 µmol/l). No separate causality adjudication was performed; hepatotoxicity was reported as part of the toxicity profile of MTX infusions.

raw_record.support_text: A boy with delayed psychomotor development, attention deficit disorder, and therapy-resistant epilepsy was treated with valproate. The patient died of liver failure after 4 months of valproate treatment. Postmortem investigation of cultured fibroblasts suggested medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, an unexpected finding since the boy had not presented typical manifestations of this disease. Because MCAD is important in fatty acid beta-oxidation, the patient probably had a genetically reduced tolerance to valproate, and the drug should be omitted in treating seizures in patients with possible MCAD deficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (10-year-old boy). Possible underlying medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency, an inborn error of fatty acid beta-oxidation, was detected postmortem and is proposed as a genetically reduced tolerance/susceptibility to valproate. The patient had prior/ concurrent antiepileptic polypharmacy (phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine) and therapy-resistant epilepsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal fulminant hepatic failure occurred after 4 months of valproate treatment. Valproate-induced fatal hepatotoxicity has been regarded as an idiosyncratic reaction; risk factors noted include young age, polypharmacy, high valproate serum levels, and inborn errors of metabolism. Reduced MCAD activity was detected postmortem in cultured skin fibroblasts. Authors recommend omitting valproate in patients with possible MCAD deficiency.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of isoniazid (INH)-related fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) in a 10-year-old Caucasian boy treated by auxiliary partial orthotopic liver transplantation (APOLT). The authors state that isoniazid rarely causes FHF but, given its extensive worldwide use, better understanding of this adverse event is warranted, and note that several cases of successful OLT for INH-related FHF have been described.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (10-year-old Caucasian boy).
raw_record.extra_details: Case of INH-related fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) with grade III encephalopathy requiring mechanical ventilation; histology showed acute massive hepatocellular necrosis with spared portal tracts and marginal ductular proliferation. Treated with APOLT; the graft failed on post-transplant day 22 due to hepatic artery kinking and thrombosis, requiring urgent re-transplantation; recovered with signs of hepatic regeneration; patient healthy with normal liver function tests 24 months after APOLT. Authors note the risk of INH-related liver injury increases with older age, female gender, and Oriental ethnicity, but this case occurred in a child.

raw_record.support_text: A 10-year-old previously well girl prescribed erythromycin ethylsuccinate for a respiratory illness developed jaundice, hepatomegaly, pruritus, pale stools and dark urine, with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and elevated transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase. Viral hepatitis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and Wilson's disease were excluded, and a liver biopsy showed cholestasis with intracellular and intraductular bile plugs without significant hepatocellular damage, judged consistent with cholestatic jaundice associated with erythromycin. The jaundice and liver function tests improved over 6-8 weeks after cessation of erythromycin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (10-year-old girl; the accompanying CSM case series concerns children under 16 years of age); oral formulation (erythromycin ethylsuccinate) given for a respiratory illness.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute onset with nausea, abdominal pain, anorexia, fatigue, arthralgia; total serum bilirubin peaked at 360 umol/L, conjugated fraction 224 umol/L; alanine aminotransferase 278 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 173 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 1,209 IU/L; gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 121 IU/L. Liver biopsy (end of week 4) showed moderate panlobular parenchymatous degeneration with cholestasis and bile plugs, no periportal fibrosis; consistent with cholestatic jaundice/hepatitis. Recovery over 6-8 weeks after drug cessation; well at 1-year follow-up. Additional UK CSM/Medicines Control Agency spontaneous reports (1985-2002): 6 further pediatric cases of cholestatic jaundice suspected to be associated with erythromycin, 4 on the ethylsuccinate form, 3 recovered completely. Mechanism speculated to be hypersensitivity or direct toxicity via a reactive metabolite; no formal causality score reported.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes an 11-year-old girl who developed anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS), a potentially fatal multisystem disorder, after receiving oral phenobarbital for 10 days following a focal seizure. During the course, she developed jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, raised serum transaminases (AST 179 IU/dL, ALT 475 IU/dL), elevated bilirubin (total 6.5 mg/dL, direct 4 mg/dL), and reduced serum protein and albumin. Other etiologies (hepatitis A, hepatitis B, infectious mononucleosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Kawasaki disease) were ruled out. Using Naranjo's causality method, the event was assessed to be probably caused by phenobarbital. The patient recovered, with normalization of hepatic and renal parameters, after withdrawal of phenobarbital and treatment with methylprednisolone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (11-year-old girl); hepatic involvement occurred as part of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenobarbital given orally for 10 days after a focal seizure; fever on day 6, rash on day 9, drug withdrawn on day 13. On day 20 developed facial puffiness, jaundice, and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory values: AST 179 IU/dL, ALT 475 IU/dL, total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 4 mg/dL, creatinine 2.12 mg/dL, serum protein 5.36 g/dL, albumin 2.29 g/dL. Serum phenobarbital 14.2 µg/mL (within therapeutic range) on day 12. Naranjo causality assessment scored the event as probably caused by phenobarbital. Managed with methylprednisolone 0.5 mg/kg every 8 hours for 5 days; recovered by day 21 with normalization of hepatic and renal parameters; well at 2-year follow-up and switched to valproic acid.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-year-old girl with hyperthyroidism who had started treatment with propylthiouracil (PTU) 100 mg tid developed hepatitis. The drug was stopped and the clinical and laboratory findings of hepatitis disappeared within a week; she received no other hepatotoxic drugs and viral investigations were negative. The authors report this as the ninth reported case of PTU-induced hepatitis, with a clinical picture similar to viral hepatitis, noting that recovery usually follows drug withdrawal but that two fatal cases of PTU-induced hepatitis have been reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (12-year-old girl); indication of hyperthyroidism; prior urticarial rash with initial PTU exposure that resolved and recurred on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose PTU 100 mg tid. Onset of urticarial rash on day 3 after first administration; symptoms (diarrhea, fever, headache, nausea, vomiting) developed within days of the second administration. Dechallenge led to resolution of hepatitis within one week. Mild jaundice appeared two days after admission; enlarged liver and spleen. No other drugs used and viral investigations negative. Ninth reported case of PTU-induced hepatitis; two fatal cases previously reported; recovery usually follows withdrawal of the drug. Clinical picture similar to viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-yr-old girl was prescribed dapsone for PPD. Twenty days later she developed high fever, followed by a skin rash, and required hospitalization; dapsone was discontinued on HD 1. Laboratory findings showed elevated total bilirubin (1.8 mg/dL), ALT (141 IU/L) and AST (158 IU/L). Her liver function subsequently deteriorated with rising bilirubin, AST and ALT and coagulopathy, and she developed fulminant hepatic failure, hepatic encephalopathy (grade 3) and hepatorenal syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 14-year-old patient with osteosarcoma being treated with high-dose methotrexate. During the sixth high-dose methotrexate course, very high plasma methotrexate levels were measured together with renal insufficiency, hepatitis, mucitis, and moderate myelosuppression. The authors state that given the very high plasma methotrexate levels and the clinical (mucitis) and biological (hepatitis, renal insufficiency) picture, methotrexate may have been responsible for these complications, and the Naranjo adverse-event imputability algorithm concluded a probable relationship between the observed adverse events and methotrexate.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (14 years) with osteosarcoma treated with high-dose methotrexate; concurrent renal insufficiency; high-dose infusion regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis occurred during the sixth high-dose methotrexate course associated with very high plasma methotrexate levels, mucitis, renal insufficiency, and moderate myelosuppression. Naranjo imputability algorithm concluded a probable relationship. Intensified alkaline diuresis and increased folinic acid doses were insufficient; carboxypeptidase G2 and aminophylline were given as second-line rescue. Clinical symptoms regressed and laboratory parameters normalized within 2 weeks. Plasma homocysteine, measured as a marker of methotrexate antifolate activity, was significantly elevated during the intoxication. Methotrexate courses were resumed and the patient recovered.
