raw_record.support_text: The authors postulate that AmBisome (a lipid formulation of amphotericin B) had contributed to or directly caused serious liver damage in a 14-year-old girl with acute myeloid leukemia. There was no elevation of liver enzyme levels while the patient received ICE, ciprofloxacin, fluconazole and piperacillin-tazobactam, but initial cholestatic damage occurred immediately after AmBisome administration and resolved after its discontinuation; reintroduction of AmBisome was associated with a sharp, severe elevation of liver enzyme levels, suggesting AmBisome was an important factor.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (14-year-old girl) with acute myeloid leukemia receiving chemotherapy and antifungal therapy; competing co-medications (ICE, fluconazole, ciprofloxacin, piperacillin-tazobactam) were deemed unlikely contributors; a background of mild cholestatic liver disease was noted but considered unexplained.
raw_record.extra_details: Dechallenge: cholestatic damage resolved after AmBisome discontinuation; rechallenge-type finding: reintroduction of AmBisome produced a sharp severe rise in liver enzymes (γ-GT up to 3284 U/L, ALKP up to 3059 U/L, bilirubin up to 218 μmol/L on day 146). Cholestatic profile of liver enzymes evolved into a frank picture of obstruction with secondary hepatocellular damage at approximately day 133. Doppler ultrasonography suggested focal hepatic necrosis with an accompanying cholangitis-hepatitis type of flow hemodynamics, with sludge and sedimentation simulating an intraluminal mass. Indication: treatment of acute myeloid leukemia-associated infection (antifungal). No death, transplant, or acute liver failure reported; recovery evident by day 258 normalization trend.

raw_record.support_text: Propiltiouracil (PTU) is widely used to treat hyperthyroidism, and hepatotoxicity is among the rarest but most serious side effects associated with it. The paper reports a case of acute cholestatic hepatitis in a 15-year-old boy on PTU, in which viral, metabolic, and autoimmune causes were excluded and liver biopsy showed findings suggestive of drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Withdrawal of the drug led to remission of symptoms and progressive normalization of liver function tests; the paper notes that patients on PTU can rarely develop severe liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (15 years old) treated for hyperthyroidism; recent acetylsalicylic acid use noted as an additional (excluded) potential factor; propylthiouracil was withdrawn.
raw_record.extra_details: PTU 100 mg/day for 15 months; onset ~7 days before first consultation with asthenia, myalgia, coluria, pale stools, and jaundice; exclusion of hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV, Wilson disease, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, and autoimmune hepatitis (only FAN 1:160 granular nuclear positive). Laboratory: ALT 1070 UI/L, AST 1060 UI/L, total bilirubin 25.1 then 39 then 46.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 14.9-31 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 1319 UI/L, prothrombin activity reduced to 50%. Liver biopsy showed portal widening with mononuclear infiltrate, rare eosinophils, mild fibrosis, bile duct proliferation, hepatocyte ballooning with bilirubin pigment, and centrilobular congestion with subendothelial edema. Treated with prednisone (60 mg/day, tapered); full normalization of liver tests 2.5 months later; PTU hepatotoxicity has a known potential, with ~30 published cases up to 1996, some fatal, including severe cholestasis and submassive necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: After excluding glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, therapy with dapsone 1 mg/kg daily and prednisolone was initiated in a 15-year-old girl with linear IgA bullous dermatosis. Within 3 weeks of treatment, liver enzymes and cholestasis parameters rose up to 10-fold above normal and dapsone was discontinued; after normalization, reintroduction of dapsone again markedly increased liver enzymes, requiring withdrawal. The authors state this confirmed its causative role.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (15-year-old girl) with concurrent prednisolone treatment; dapsone reintroduction after normalization of liver parameters repeated the liver-enzyme increase.
raw_record.extra_details: Dapsone given at 1 mg/kg daily initially, then 0.5 mg/kg daily on reintroduction. Liver enzymes and cholestasis parameters rose up to 10-fold above normal within 3 weeks; parameters normalized after withdrawal and increased again upon rechallenge. Authors note hepatotoxicity is a very rare side-effect of dapsone that may occur as part of a hypersensitivity reaction ('dapsone syndrome'), mostly when combined with antimalarial or antileprosial agents. Skin disease relapsed upon dapsone discontinuation; patient also developed septicaemia.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year old patient with carbamazepine-induced hepatotoxicity, associated with hypersensitivity manifestations of fever, rash and eosinophilia, is described. Mononuclear leucocytes from the patient were more sensitive to oxidative metabolites of carbamazepine than control cells, and serum from the patient recognised a single 94 kDa protein band on human liver microsomes, which none of 25 control sera recognised. The paper presents this as a human case of carbamazepine hepatotoxicity with an immunoallergic/autoantibody basis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (16-year old); therapeutic anti-epileptic use for generalized epilepsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 400 mg/day; fever developed 4 weeks after start of therapy, generalized rash after 5 weeks, and jaundice after 6 weeks; associated with fever, rash and eosinophilia. In vitro mononuclear leucocyte susceptibility to carbamazepine oxidative metabolites generated by induced murine and human hepatic microsomes; patient serum, but none of 25 control sera, recognised a 94 kDa protein band on human liver microsomes via immunoblot. Proposed immunologic/immunoallergic mechanism, possibly with a deficiency in cellular detoxification (epoxide hydrolase) predisposing to idiosyncratic toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 17-year-old girl with a clinical diagnosis of adult-type juvenile rheumatoid arthritis developed a severe hepatotoxic reaction to 3.6 g of aspirin per day, associated with microangiopathic anemia and transient congestive cardiac failure. After laboratory values normalized she was rechallenged with five divided doses of aspirin (total 3.0 g), which produced a salicylate level of 9.1 g/dl with immediate deterioration in liver function test findings and return of microangiopathic blood features, reversed again by steroids. The authors conclude the case suggests that disseminated intravascular coagulation and its rare association with hepatotoxicity is a potentially fatal side effect of aspirin therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (17-year-old girl) diagnosed with adult-type juvenile rheumatoid arthritis; reaction associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation, microangiopathic anemia, and congestive cardiac failure; rechallenge reproduced the reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Therapeutic dose was 3.6 g aspirin per day; rechallenge was 3.0 g total in five divided doses producing a salicylate level of 9.1 g/dl with immediate deterioration of liver function tests. Responded to steroid therapy on both occasions. Outcome described as a 'potentially fatal' but not fatal side effect in this case. Case report, University of Chicago.

raw_record.extra_details: The girl developed severe hepatitis after the fourth administration of halothane. A circulating antibody acted specifically against hepatocytes from rabbits previously sensitized to halothane. The patient fully recovered from the hepatitis but 5 months later developed diabetes mellitus, which the authors judged coincidental. Neutrophilia was noted after the fourth administration; the white blood count rose to a peak of 32.4 x 10^9/L (84% neutrophils) after the second anaesthetic.

Adjuvant chemotherapy was then initiated according to the MAP protocol (which includes high-dose methotrexate, doxorubicin, and cisplatin), but because of the toxicity of high-dose methotrexate the patient suffered acute liver failure (hypertransaminasemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy), requiring treatment with cholestyramine and activated charcoal, so chemotherapy was changed to cisplatin with Adriamycin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (5 years of age) receiving high-dose methotrexate as part of adjuvant MAP chemotherapy for osteosarcoma, with co-administered doxorubicin and cisplatin.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure manifested as hypertransaminasemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy; required treatment with cholestyramine and activated charcoal, after which chemotherapy was changed from the MAP regimen to cisplatin with Adriamycin. High-dose (intravenous) methotrexate was the agent to which the toxicity was attributed.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a 5-year-old boy with chronic bronchial asthma who developed acute hepatitis after 2 years of montelukast 5 mg daily. Montelukast was discontinued with symptom onset, and liver tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin, ALP, glutamyltransferase) normalized within two weeks. Montelukast-induced hepatitis was suggested by rapid improvement after dechallenge, exclusion of other causes of hepatitis, and comparison with similar reported cases; no liver biopsy was done.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (5-year-old boy); therapeutic use for chronic bronchial asthma.
raw_record.extra_details: Montelukast 5 mg daily for 2 years prior to presentation; symptoms of fatigue, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain; AST 990 IU/L, ALT 658 IU/L, glutamyltranspeptidase 145 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL (direct 2.1, indirect 0.7), ALP 445 IU/L; normal albumin and PT; viral serologies negative; rapid normalization of liver tests within two weeks after dechallenge; described as first reported pediatric case of acute hepatitis while receiving montelukast; previously reported montelukast hepatotoxicity cases were all in adults; hypothesized mechanisms include hepatotoxic metabolites, idiosyncrasy, drug reactions and immunologic mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: Clinical and laboratory signs of liver injury in a 5-year-old child resolved over the next 5 days with a return to baseline AST and ALT after fondaparinux was discontinued and enoxaparin reintroduced. The authors concluded that fondaparinux was considered the probable cause of hepatotoxicity, and in the discussion stated that the role of fondaparinux was highly likely since signs occurred soon after introduction and disappeared rapidly after drug withdrawal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (5-year-old child, 12 kg); fondaparinux replaced enoxaparin while acetaminophen (paracetamol) and codeine were maintained as concurrent co-medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Fondaparinux (Arixtra) 2 mg/day given for a left-sided axillary veno-lymphatic malformation-related thrombosis. Onset of nausea and vomiting ~30 h after first fondaparinux dose. Hepatotoxicity evidenced by a 15-fold increase in ALT (509 IU/L) and AST (720 IU/L), and 5-fold increase in GGT (161 IU/L); ALP (278) and bilirubin (10 umol/L) remained normal. Signs resolved within 5 days after discontinuation with return to baseline ALT/AST. Viral serology (Hep A/B/C, herpes, adenovirus, enterovirus, parvovirus B19, HHV6, HHV8) negative; liver ultrasound normal without hepatic thrombosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 7-year-old boy given albendazole 400 mg single tablets for routine deworming on 4 occasions over three years developed jaundice each time within 7 days of administration, totaling four episodes of hepatitis with no other cause. Each episode resolved spontaneously and liver enzymes were normal at follow-up and between episodes. RUCAM/CIOMS score of 12 was compatible with drug-induced hepatitis, and the NADRPS score of 8 was suggestive of probable drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (7-year-old boy); routine deworming indications; four separate single 400 mg oral doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Four episodes of hepatitis/jaundice, each developing within 7 days of a single 400 mg albendazole tablet; no alternative cause identified; spontaneous resolution with normalized liver enzymes between episodes; RUCAM/CIOMS score 12; NADRPS score 8 (probable drug-induced hepatotoxicity). Albendazole is an orally administered broad-spectrum antihelmintic; hepatitis reported after prolonged use for hydatid cyst/neurocysticercosis, with this being the first report of repeated episodes following single doses.

raw_record.support_text: An 8-year-old boy started lamotrigine for seizures and presented with fever, generalized maculopapular rash, facial edema, and enlarged lymph nodes; serum AST and ALT were twice normal. He developed fulminant hepatitis with a fast rise in transaminases within 5 days and required liver transplantation despite glucocorticoid treatment, with histology showing massive hepatic necrosis with dense lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates. PCR detected high HHV-6 viremia before transplantation, and both a skin patch test and a lymphocyte stimulation test for lamotrigine hypersensitivity were positive, leading to a diagnosis of lamotrigine-induced hypersensitivity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (8-year-old boy); DIHS with concurrent HHV-6 viremia.
raw_record.extra_details: Given for multiple seizures (indication). Presentation included fever, generalized maculopapular rash, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia (18%), atypical lymphocytes (8%); transaminases initially two times normal then fulminant hepatitis with fast rise within 5 days; histology showed massive hepatic necrosis with lymphocytes and eosinophils; liver transplantation required despite glucocorticoid therapy; positive lamotrigine skin patch test and lymphocyte stimulation test; diagnosis of lamotrigine-induced hypersensitivity (DIHS/DRESS).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report an 8-year-old child with preexisting mild renal dysfunction who developed severe hepatic dysfunction after sevoflurane anesthesia. Sevoflurane was stated to be the only likely cause of hepatic failure in the patient, though the mechanism of the liver dysfunction was not well understood, and anesthesiologists were advised to weigh possible hepatic dysfunction when using sevoflurane in patients with preexisting renal dysfunction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (8-year-old child) with preexisting mild renal dysfunction; first exposure to inhalational anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Sevoflurane was the only likely cause of hepatic failure; mechanism of liver dysfunction not well understood; ~5% of sevoflurane undergoes hepatic metabolism principally by cytochrome P450 2E1 to inorganic fluoride and organic metabolites; hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP, 85% of organic metabolites) has low binding affinity for liver macromolecules and is rapidly glucuronidated and excreted in urine; not certain whether the decreased renal function impaired excretion of metabolites with resulting hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: A diagnosis of vanishing bile duct syndrome was made in an 8-year-old girl with unresolved jaundice and pruritus 5 months after beginning treatment with VPA. Severe interlobular bile duct loss and eosinophil-dominant mixed inflammatory infiltration with canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis were found. Elevated total bilirubin (20.2 mg/dL), direct bilirubin (12.9 mg/dL), gamma-GTP (1531 IU/L), ALP (2787 IU/L), total cholesterol (1398 mg/dL), AST (209 IU/L) and ALT (118 IU/L) were present; cholestasis and liver enzymes normalized after ursodeoxycholic acid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (8-year-old girl); onset 5 months after starting VPA.
raw_record.extra_details: Ultrasound showed slight hepatomegaly and splenomegaly without biliary tree dilatation; severe interlobular bile duct loss in portal areas with no interlobular bile ducts seen; eosinophil-dominant mixed inflammatory infiltration. No signs of chronic liver disease. Resolved after ursodeoxycholic acid treatment. Latency 5 months.

raw_record.support_text: The report concludes that vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) was caused by L-carbocisteine in a 9-year-old Japanese girl. Supportive findings included positive drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation tests for L-carbocisteine, fever, jaundice, skin rash, elevated serum transaminases, γ-glutamyltransferase and bilirubin, and histopathological features consistent with VBDS; the patient responded to discontinuation of L-carbocisteine and treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid, with gradual normalization of transaminase and bilirubin levels.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (9-year-old girl).
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 9-year-old Japanese girl presenting with fever, jaundice and skin rash; elevated serum transaminases, γ-glutamyltransferase and bilirubin; histopathology consistent with VBDS; drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test (DLST) positive for L-carbocisteine. Jaundice with elevated liver tests indicates clinically apparent cholestatic liver injury. The patient responded to discontinuation of L-carbocisteine and ursodeoxycholic acid administration, with gradual normalization of transaminases and bilirubin. No prior reports of children developing VBDS after L-carbocisteine.

raw_record.support_text: Un niño de 12 años y 10 meses, diagnosticado de enfermedad de Graves 2 años antes, desarrolló una hepatitis tóxica por propiltiouracilo 4 meses después de comenzar el tratamiento. Se había indicado este fármaco porque el paciente había presentado exantemas urticariformes con metimazol y con carbimazol. El cuadro clínico cedió de manera progresiva tras suspender el tratamiento e iniciar corticoterapia en dosis altas, y una vez controlada la hepatopatía la enfermedad de Graves se trató con radioyodo. Este fue el único efecto secundario grave detectado en la serie de 20 pacientes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (boy aged 12 years 10 months) with Graves disease; propylthiouracil was selected because the patient had previously developed urticarial skin rashes with methimazole and carbimazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis developed 4 months after starting propylthiouracil treatment; it resolved progressively after drug discontinuation and high-dose corticosteroid therapy, after which Graves disease was treated with radioiodine. This was the only severe adverse effect among the 20 antithyroid-drug-treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 10-year-old girl with Alpers syndrome (POLG1 mutations, c.248T>C p.L83P and c.2662G>A p.G888S) and refractory seizures was treated with valproic acid (VPA) among other antiepileptics. VPA was used for 2.5 months and then terminated due to acute liver failure after she developed edema and coagulopathy 52 days after starting VPA, followed 3 weeks later by jaundice and hepatomegaly with abnormal ALT, AST, total and direct bilirubin, total protein, albumin, and fibrinogen. After VPA was stopped, liver function improved and was near normal 6 months later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient with Alpers syndrome due to POLG1 mutations (c.248T>C p.L83P, c.2662G>A p.G888S), i.e., underlying mitochondrial hepatocerebral disease; VPA given for refractory seizures as part of a multidrug antiepileptic regimen (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, topiramate, lamotrigine, clonazepam).
raw_record.extra_details: VPA used for ~2.5 months. Acute liver failure developed with edema and coagulopathy 52 days after starting VPA; jaundice and hepatomegaly appeared 3 weeks later. Laboratory values: ALT 64 U/L (nl 0-40), AST 215 U/L (nl 0-45), total bilirubin 145.6 µmol/L (nl 1.7-20), direct bilirubin 113.1 µmol/L (nl 0-6), total protein 44.35 g/L, albumin 28.8 g/L, fibrinogen 0.64 g/L (earlier decreased fibrinogen 1.56 g/L). Liver function improved and was near normal 6 months after VPA was discontinued (dechallenge). Patient had known POLG1 genotype; VPA-triggered liver failure in setting of mtDNA polymerase gamma deficiency.

Liver failure diagnosed 4 days after VPA administration; VPA-associated liver failure reported generally at 2-3 days after VPA initiation; >100 VPA-associated liver failure cases reported worldwide. Supportive care after VPA cessation included nutrition and fresh-frozen plasma; patient survived but with severe neurological sequelae (cerebral atrophy, generalized seizures). Authors advise deferring VPA therapy in patients with status epilepticus/myoclonic epilepsy until Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome is excluded.

raw_record.support_text: Dactinomycin (Act-D) was implicated as the cause of sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) during treatment for Wilms tumor (WT), described as a life-threatening complication that is reversible in most cases with supportive care and diagnosis supported by blood count, liver function tests, and abdominal ultrasound. In the study, two patients were safely re-exposed to Act-D after complete recovery while a third patient's further Act-D doses were consciously replaced with doxorubicin; the authors note re-exposure can start at 50% dose and gradually escalate to full dose, though some physicians avoid re-exposure after severe, life-threatening episodes.

raw_record.extra_details: Act-D refers to dactinomycin/actinomycin D. In the study, two patients were safely re-exposed to Act-D following complete recovery, and one patient's further Act-D doses were replaced with doxorubicin (doxorubicin is not itself implicated as a DILI cause here).

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents histologic findings in the liver of 10 cases of valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, consistently showing microvesicular steatosis, vacuolar steatosis, ductular proliferation, necrotic areas, and fibrosis, with the architecture of the liver destroyed. In a larger series of 16 patients who died during valproate therapy, none had progressive neuronal degeneration of childhood (PNDC), and histologic findings clearly indicated a hepatogenic cause of death, supporting valproate as the cause of fatal hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with epilepsy treated therapeutically with valproate; some had underlying diseases such as urea cycle defects or were discussed as having carnitine deficiency as susceptibility factors.
raw_record.extra_details: Sixteen patients died during valproate (VPA) therapy; histology was evaluated in 10 cases (biopsy/autopsy). The most constant feature was microvesicular steatosis attributed to inhibited mitochondrial beta-oxidation of fatty acids, with swollen mitochondria and damaged cristae on electron microscopy; findings also included intracellular cholestasis, hepatocyte single-cell necrosis, ductular proliferation, necrotic areas, fibrosis, and destroyed liver architecture. Histology was Reye-like in appearance. VPA is described as 2-propyl-pentanoic acid. All pediatric cases were explicitly checked and none had progressive neuronal degeneration of childhood (PNDC), which some authors argued could confound attribution.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that salicylates (aspirin) therapy in patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis caused hepatic dysfunction and, in three of their patients, hepatic encephalopathy that resolved when aspirin was discontinued. Evidence of acute hepatic failure included severely impaired mental function with striking transaminase elevations, prolonged prothrombin time, elevated blood ammonia, and an EEG consistent with metabolic encephalopathy. All three patients were subsequently rechallenged with aspirin and developed recurrent hepatotoxicity, and hepatotoxicity to aspirin was obtained even in the absence of encephalopathy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis; chronic high-dose salicylate therapy producing salicylate levels of 25-44 mg/dl; Reye syndrome considered as a differential but excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients developed hepatotoxicity with hepatic encephalopathy and signs of acute hepatic failure while on aspirin for JRA; all three recovered when aspirin was discontinued and each had recurrent hepatotoxicity upon rechallenge. In Patient 2, liver biopsy one week after onset showed ballooned hepatocytes with regeneration, focal pseudoacinar formation around dilated canaliculi, and Kupffer cell hypertrophy. Mentation recovered and liver tests normalized (e.g., SGOT) after stopping aspirin. The paper notes prior reports of hepatic dysfunction in up to 60% of JRA/SLE patients treated with salicylates, generally considered benign with mildly elevated liver enzymes.

raw_record.support_text: In a Brazilian cooperative Wilms' tumor study, patients treated with actinomycin D developed hepatotoxicity. With a 60 µg/kg single-dose schedule, raised liver function tests occurred in 4 of 33 patients (12%) with no case of severe hepatotoxicity; with the standard schedule (15 µg/kg for 5 days), there was one case of severe hepatotoxicity among 32 patients and two others with raised liver function tests without ascites. The frequency of severe hepatotoxicity was similar in the two arms (0/33 vs 1/32).

raw_record.extra_details: Single-dose schedule 60 µg/kg (identical to dose in American National Wilms Tumor Study-4, which was later reduced to 45 µg/kg after severe hepatotoxicity was noted); standard schedule 15 µg/kg for 5 days. raw_record.support_text: The paper describes valproic acid (VPA)-associated liver failure and hepatotoxicity as a known side effect of VPA therapy, citing the 1988 German series of 16 patients with VPA-associated hepatotoxicity. Patient 13 in that series had normal laboratory tests initially with severe apathy 6 weeks after VPA initiation, recovered, but died of fatal liver failure 9 weeks later; 5 of the 16 patients showed apathy as the initial symptom of VPA-associated hepatotoxicity, 3 of whom had no pathologic laboratory tests at that time.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatal VPA-associated liver failure cases described (patients F1-F8) showed marked transaminase elevations (e.g., AST up to 20,850 U/L, ALT up to 6,900 U/L), hyperammonemia, impaired coagulation (low PT/PTT, DIC), elevated bilirubin, lactic acidosis and coma; VPA serum levels ranged from 15 µg/ml to 268 µg/ml. The 1988 German series included 16 patients with VPA-associated hepatotoxicity, and 5 of 16 had apathy as initial symptom. Also noted: stupor/coma during VPA therapy in 2-21% of patients with reversible encephalopathy and unaltered liver tests; mild transaminase/GGT elevations (pathologic GGT in up to 12% of VPA-treated patients) are usually transient and reversible. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with symptoms of impending hepatotoxicity during the second week of valproic acid (VPA) therapy, in whom fatal liver failure was a concern, and cites a report of a child who developed hepatotoxicity after only three doses of VPA. Serious signs were considered possibly attributable to comedication with phenobarbital (PB) and VPA, though serum concentrations of both antiepileptic drugs were within therapeutic ranges and no explanation of the severe clinical reaction was found.

raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 16 children on VPA with hepatotoxicity. Reported outcomes include reversible liver dysfunction during febrile illness in 7 children, reversible liver failure, reversible impairment of coagulation with bleeding manifestations, and fatal liver failure (autopsy findings included microvesicular steatosis, marked/acute diffuse severe/multifocal necroses, cholangiolar proliferation). Fatal cases showed elevated AST (up to 12,300 U/L) and ALT (up to 6,989 U/L), hyperammonemia, low prothrombin time. In one fatal case there was prior aspirin therapy; VPA-associated severe hepatotoxicity may be reversible if VPA is discontinued early. Some patients had increased 4-ene-VPA levels suggesting diversion of VPA metabolism to omega-oxidation.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity occurred in patients receiving valproate therapy. The median valproate dose was 39 mg/kg/day (range 14-92) for L-carnitine-treated patients and 43 mg/kg/day (range 12-108) for untreated patients, with median duration of valproate therapy of 81 and 72 days, respectively. Three L-carnitine-treated patients had received prophylactic L-carnitine to prevent toxicity, stopped 60 to 100 days before the hepatotoxic event.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (majority aged <10 years); chronic valproate use with frequent polytherapy (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, clorazepate, clonazepam, or lithium in bipolar patients); some patients received L-carnitine prophylaxis or treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: In this cohort of 92 patients with valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, hepatic survival was 20/42 (47%) for L-carnitine-treated patients vs 5/50 (10%) for untreated patients (p<0.001). Survival was better when valproate was stopped early (<5 days) and L-carnitine was given IV. Deaths attributable to the hepatotoxic event occurred in both groups. Initial symptoms included nausea/vomiting, anorexia, lethargy, increased seizures, and infection.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective observational cohort of 552 PLHIV, 12 of 284 participants in the isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT)-exposed group developed the outcome of interest (DILI) over 1128 person-months, while none of the 268 unexposed developed DILI. The incidence rate of DILI in the exposed group was 10.6 cases per 1000 person-months vs 0 in the unexposed (p = 0.002). The paper states the association of DILI with IPT was probable in all cases and that no alternative hepatotoxic explanation was found.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: People living with HIV (PLHIV) receiving isoniazid preventive therapy alongside anti-retroviral therapy (ART); most cases had concurrent drug exposure (3–4 or >4 total drugs).
raw_record.extra_details: 12 DILI cases (4.2% of exposed) among 284 IPT-exposed vs 0 among 268 unexposed; incidence 10.6 per 1000 person-months (exposed) vs 0 (unexposed), p=0.002; sensitivity analysis adding one unexposed case gave RR 11.32 (95% CI 1.68, 484.07). Time to onset (initiation of INH to DILI diagnosis) median 35 days (IQR 26.8, 60). Median ALT activity 7.3 and ALP activity 0.85; median R-value 8.8 (IQR 6.3, 14.2). Liver-injury pattern hepatocellular in all cases except one mixed. Severity mild in ten cases and moderate in two; all but two cases asymptomatic; two symptomatic cases received symptomatic vitamin B complex; DILI resolved (recovered n=9, recovering n=3). Only IPT was withdrawn in all cases as management.

raw_record.support_text: The paper recognizes that isoniazid (INH), shortly after its introduction, was known to cause toxic hepatitis and, rarely, death. A U.S. Public Health Service surveillance study (1971-1973) among 13,838 persons recorded eight deaths attributed to INH-associated hepatitis, and a 1989 California cluster reported 20 such deaths. The investigation focused on deaths attributable to INH-associated hepatitis in persons taking INH alone for preventive therapy within the United States.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Persons taking isoniazid alone for preventive therapy of tuberculosis within the United States; persons on multidrug treatment or reports from outside the United States were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: USPHS surveillance study (1971-1973) of 13,838 persons in 21 health departments reported eight deaths (seven in one city, six female of whom five were black). A 1989 California cluster comprised 20 deaths (16 in women, 10 Hispanic). Literature search (Medline 1965-1989) identified 48 deaths among persons on INH alone for preventive therapy; FDA Adverse Reaction Reporting System (reports dating from 1970) added 17 deaths not cited in the literature; state/territorial epidemiologists and TB control officers identified a further 59 cases. INH-associated 'toxic hepatitis' can progress to death.

raw_record.support_text: Spisulosine (compound 21, ES-285), a deoxysphingosine-based marine mollusk natural product isolated from Spisula polynyma, was evaluated in Phase I clinical trials in patients with established solid tumors using various regimens (24 h IV infusion every three weeks, or 3 h IV infusion for five consecutive days every three weeks). Despite infrequent drug-induced grade 3 or 4 adverse effects and an encouraging pharmacokinetic profile, spisulosine's potential as an anticancer agent was impeded by dose-dependent hepatic and neurotoxicity, and further development was therefore terminated; the human trials were discontinued due to poor clinical outcomes, with the death of one patient attributed to drug-related central neurotoxicity rather than to the liver.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I clinical trial dosing in patients with established solid tumors; development was terminated for poor outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: Also known as ES-285 and spisulosine 21. Dose-dependent hepatic toxicity was reported. Dose-limiting/grade 3-4 drug-induced adverse effects were infrequent. Regimens included 24 h intravenous infusion every 3 weeks and 3 h intravenous infusion for 5 consecutive days every 3 weeks. The single reported patient death was due to drug-related central neurotoxicity, not hepatic injury. In vitro data (not human DILI) showed anti-proliferative/cytotoxic activity against prostate (PC-3, LNCaP), breast, colon, HeLa, and other tumor cell lines.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I trial of PHA-793887, one patient treated at 66 mg/m² experienced a drug-related grade 4 hepatic failure with pancytopenia, and one patient treated at 44 mg/m² had a fatal hepatorenal failure. There was no dose relationship in the rate of clinical adverse events, but there was a clear dose relation with regard to their severity. Biochemical abnormalities related mainly to liver biochemistry tests, with evidence of a dose relation in the frequency and severity of AST, ALT and bilirubin elevations; all grade ≥3 liver biochemistry toxicity developed during cycle 1 within 2–4 days after initial drug administration and generally improved over 3–4 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I dose-escalation study in patients with advanced solid tumors; an investigational agent.
raw_record.extra_details: One drug-related grade 4 hepatic failure with pancytopenia at 66 mg/m²/day and one fatal hepatorenal failure at 44 mg/m²/day; two patients died during study (one from fatal hepatorenal failure, one from disease progression). Grade ≥3 AST and ALT elevations occurred in 2 of 9 patients at 44 mg/m² and 1 of 3 at 66 mg/m²; bilirubin grade ≥3 in 1 of 9 at 44 mg/m² and 2 of 3 at 66 mg/m². All grade ≥3 liver biochemistry toxicity developed during cycle 1 within 2–4 days of first dose and improved over 3–4 weeks; affected patients were not re-treated. Kinetic parameters: terminal half-life 6–13 h, Vss 1.9–2.2 L/kg, clearance 0.14–0.48 L/h/kg.

raw_record.support_text: In 102 patients with POLG-related mitochondrial disease and valproic acid (VPA) exposure from 46 articles, adverse drug reactions occurred in 91 patients (89%) and hepatotoxicity was reported in 87 patients (85%). There was no pre-existing liver disease in 92/102 (90%). Fatal outcomes occurred in 53/102 (52%), 8 unrelated to VPA (e.g., intractable seizures); liver transplant was required in 15 patients, 6 (40%) of whom died post-transplant. All patients with reported genotypes (97/102) had recessive POLG variants, with compound heterozygotes having worse outcomes than homozygotes (p<0.01).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: POLG-related mitochondrial disease with recessive POLG variants; 90% had no pre-existing liver disease; genotype-restricted finding
raw_record.extra_details: 102 patients from 46 articles; 91 (89%) had ADRs and 87 (85%) hepatotoxicity; 53 fatal outcomes (8 unrelated to VPA); 15 liver transplants with 6 (40%) post-transplant deaths; compound heterozygous variants associated with worse outcomes than homozygous (p<0.01); lower survival in VPA-exposure group vs no-VPA group among 280 recessive POLG patients (p<0.0001); age-at-onset 0-4 years had lower survival than 5-18 years (p=0.05); sex survival similar (p=0.7)

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 11 cases of well-documented acute liver injury associated with allopurinol use enrolled in the DILIN Prospective Study over a 16-year period, with all cases developing liver injury within the first 3 months of treatment and being severe (all 11 required hospitalization, the majority developing jaundice). Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor commonly used to treat and prevent gout and hyperuricaemia, and there was an overrepresentation of African Americans compared with the overall DILIN cohort (60% vs 13%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Population overrepresented among African Americans (60% vs 13% of overall DILIN cohort); severe cases all required hospitalization; DRESS/hypersensitivity presentation occurred in a subset of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 adjudicated DILIN cases of acute liver injury; latency within the first 3 months of treatment; majority developed jaundice. Most patients had a mixed or cholestatic biochemical profile at presentation, with prominent hypersensitivity features (rash in 10, fever in 5, eosinophilia in 5); four patients presented with DRESS features with initially normal liver biochemistries that rose after hospital admission, and two were confirmed as DRESS by skin biopsy. Histopathology showed a spectrum including granulomatous hepatitis, cholestasis with mild inflammation, ductopenia, and acute hepatitis with necrosis. Nine patients were treated with corticosteroids; three patients died 38, 45, and 182 days after DILI onset, with two deaths considered liver-related. HLA associations (HLA-B*58:01, potential HLA-B*53:01 and HLA-A*34:02) reported as risk factors, not causal molecules.

raw_record.support_text: In the report, non-HIV-infected healthcare workers developed severe hepatic toxicity, attributed to nevirapine, after use of a nevirapine-containing post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen; the toxicity occurred in conjunction with hypersensitivity reactions, and 2 workers did not improve until high-dose prednisone was administered. The paper concludes that non-HIV-infected individuals who receive nevirapine are at risk for severe and potentially life-threatening hepatic toxicity, with risk appearing higher than in HIV-infected persons.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Population restricted to non-HIV-infected adults receiving multiple-dose nevirapine-containing post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimens; findings explicitly do not apply to single-dose nevirapine use for prevention of perinatal HIV transmission.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatic toxicity described in non-HIV-infected healthcare workers after a nevirapine-containing PEP regimen, occurring with hypersensitivity reactions; 2 cases did not improve until high-dose prednisone was given (corticosteroid use is otherwise controversial). Risk for severe hepatotoxicity appears higher than in HIV-infected persons and may be associated with higher CD4 counts. The report concludes non-HIV-infected individuals should not receive PEP or other prophylaxis regimens including multiple doses of nevirapine.

raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old female patient with porphyria cutanea tarda died 13 days after taking 1250 mg chloroquine for P.c.t., ultimately from cerebral coma caused by an irreversible acute hepatic failure (akuter Leberzerfall), despite intensive therapy. Forensic autopsy, histology, and toxicology confirmed the clinical finding of chloroquine-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper explains the high hepatotoxic effect of chloroquine in this case and warns against exceeding the recommended dose of 2 x weekly 125-250 mg in the treatment of P.c.t.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Porphyria cutanea tarda patient; chronic hepatic porphyria considered a contraindication for chloroquine; dose of 1250 mg exceeded the recommended 2 x weekly 125-250 mg; concurrent moderate alcohol intake and long-term oral contraceptive (0.75 mg lynestrenol + 0.0375 mg ethinylestradiol per tablet).
raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~13 days from chloroquine intake to death; confirmed by forensic autopsy, histology and toxicology. Chloroquine also produced an expected mild (desired) liver damage ('flu syndrome') even at therapeutic doses in P.c.t., which the paper uses to explain the high hepatotoxicity. Cardiac arrhythmia was noted in usual chloroquine intoxication but was not the fatal mechanism here; fatal cardiac toxicity seen in other followed cases involved oral doses always above 10 g.

raw_record.support_text: All 53 patients with latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) received isoniazid chemoprophylaxis along with pyridoxine after liver transplantation (median time to initiation 5 days, range 3-12 days). Forty-nine of 53 (92%) completed 6 months of isoniazid, whereas treatment was prematurely discontinued in 4 subjects after a mean of 2.2 months (range 1-4 months) because of hepatotoxicity confirmed by liver biopsy and clear improvements after withdrawal. None of these 4 patients showed severe graft dysfunction, and none were retreated with isoniazid or alternative prophylactic regimens.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Post-liver-transplant patients with latent tuberculosis infection receiving immunosuppression (cyclosporine A/azathioprine/prednisone or tacrolimus-based regimens), treated with isoniazid chemoprophylaxis plus pyridoxine initiated a median of 5 days after transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 4 of 53 treated patients (7.5%) prematurely discontinued isoniazid after a mean of 2.2 months (range 1-4 months) due to hepatotoxicity confirmed by liver biopsy with clear improvement after withdrawal (dechallenge); none had severe graft dysfunction and none were retreated; 49/53 (92%) completed 6 months of isoniazid. No active TB reactivation occurred.

raw_record.support_text: The FDA received 11 reports (three fatal) of hepatocellular damage associated with labetalol in the United States. Temporal circumstances strongly implicate labetalol: nine patients improved after cessation of labetalol therapy and one had a recurrence after therapy was restarted. Follow-up with each reporting physician found no historic or laboratory evidence for other viral, toxic, or drug-induced causes, and the series lacked demographic/historic risk factors expected for non-A, non-B hepatitis. Microscopic examinations (5 cases) showed changes consistent with hepatocellular necrosis in four instances and chronic active hepatitis in one. The clinical presentation was most compatible with a metabolic idiosyncrasy mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Postmarketing cases received as spontaneous reports to the FDA; other pathogenetic explanations could not be entirely excluded; one patient (case 1) also received furosemide, prazosin, and nifedipine.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 US cases, three fatal. Histology showed hepatocellular necrosis in four cases and chronic active hepatitis in one; one case (#1) showed acute massive and submassive hepatic necrosis on explant. Nine patients improved after drug cessation; one had recurrent injury after rechallenge (restart). Case 1 was a 49-year-old black woman on labetalol (stabilized at 300 mg/day) who developed jaundice after ~60 days, with marked AST/ALT elevation, alkaline phosphatase ~2x normal, total bilirubin 308 µmol/L (18.0 mg/dL); negative for hepatitis A IgM, HBsAg, and anti-HBc (anti-HBs positive); no blood transfusion or alcohol history; referred for liver transplant on 20 Dec 1986 and died 4 days post-transplant. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy.

raw_record.support_text: Voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity is described as a relatively rare but serious clinicopathologic entity. The paper reports a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis who developed hepatic encephalopathy due to voriconazole administered for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis and who showed marked improvement in mental status with dose adjustment of the drug. Histopathologic examination of the explanted liver revealed numerous rhomboid-shaped crystals deemed secondary to liver injury after voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. Voriconazole was considered the likely cause of the hepatic encephalopathy; the drug was discontinued, mental status gradually improved, and therapy was restarted at a reduced dose that was tolerated without further supratherapeutic levels.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pre-existing alcoholic cirrhosis (advanced decompensated liver disease, MELD 37-41); supratherapeutic plasma voriconazole trough (13 μg/mL) despite standard therapeutic dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: 51-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and prior Crohn's disease; voriconazole (Vfend) dosed 400 mg twice daily for 1 day then 150 mg twice daily, later reduced to 175 mg/day after rechallenge. Presented with progressive jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly; labs at second admission serum ammonia 194 μmol/L, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 94 U/L, total bilirubin 21.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 20.8 mg/dL, INR 2.1. Developed hepatic encephalopathy (confusion and stupor) about 10 days after discharge; improved after discontinuation and tolerated lower dose. Native liver biopsy at deceased donor liver transplant showed severe hepatocellular degeneration associated with cholestasis and marked hepatic cholangial/ductular proliferation with cirrhosis, suggestive of acute/subacute liver injury, plus intracellular and extracellular deep amber-yellow rhomboid crystals staining golden yellow under polarized light (voriconazole drug crystals). Alcoholic cirrhosis and decompensated liver failure required liver transplant; death not attributed directly to voriconazole.

raw_record.support_text: A 92-year-old female developed acute hepatotoxicity attributed to intravenous acetaminophen given at 1 g every 6 hours (total 13 g) for postoperative analgesia. On hospital day 5 she had epigastric pain with serum total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, ALT 3,914 U/L, AST 4,698 U/L, INR 1.68, and ammonia 60 mcg/dL. The patient had no medication error, no additional acetaminophen source, no other hepatotoxic medications, and no history of shock, alcohol use, malnutrition, or viral hepatitis; serum acetaminophen-protein adducts (APAP-CYS) were elevated (1.79 µM on day 3, 4.81 µM on day 5, 2.92 µM on day 6), supporting acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. Acetaminophen was discontinued, intravenous acetylcysteine was given, and the patient improved and was discharged.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pre-existing hepatic steatosis and possible cirrhosis documented on ultrasound performed before acetaminophen initiation; advanced age (92 years).
raw_record.extra_details: Intravenous route at 1 g every 6 hours, given hospital days 3-6 for a total of 13 g; elevated serum acetaminophen level 15.3 mcg/mL at 26 h after last dose; APAP-CYS adducts 1.79-4.81 µM (expected <1.1 µM during therapeutic dosing); no acidosis or encephalopathy; treated with intravenous acetylcysteine (standard 21-h protocol) with transaminase improvement and discharge.

raw_record.support_text: Valproate-induced liver failure arises after a therapy duration of 6 weeks to 6 months and is not accompanied by hyperergic signs. Leading subjective symptoms include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, weakness, lethargy and somnolence, together with various neurological symptoms, shock, kidney failure and signs of hepatic insufficiency. Transaminases are moderately elevated (mostly below 400 U/l), bilirubin is variably elevated, platelets are often decreased and prothrombin time is prolonged. Histology shows variably expressed, preferentially centrilobular steatosis and inflammatory infiltrates. Of 18 patients with more detailed case history, 11 died within a few days as a consequence of liver failure; only three of the 18 were older than 20 years.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Predominantly pediatric population (only 3 of 18 detailed cases older than 20 years).
raw_record.extra_details: Valproate-induced liver failure latency 6 weeks to 6 months; no hyperergic signs; symptoms: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weakness, lethargy, somnolence, various neurological symptoms, shock, renal failure, hepatic insufficiency; transaminases moderately elevated (mostly <400 U/l), bilirubin variably elevated, platelets often decreased, prothrombin time prolonged; histology: variable, preferentially centrilobular steatosis with inflammatory infiltrates; 11 of 18 cases died within days of liver failure. Patient case showed marked metabolic (lactic) acidosis with anion gap 53 mval/l, resembling Reye syndrome with mitochondrial damage and disturbed fatty-acid beta-oxidation; mitochondrial swelling, reduced matrix and cristae disorganization observed in two children treated with valproate, which regressed after discontinuation; acidosis noted in 3 of the 18 cases.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective cohort study analyzed isoniazid (INH) hepatitis morbidity and mortality among patients at a U.S. prenatal clinic, comparing 3,681 pregnant/postpartum women in the 1981 INH preventive therapy program with an unmatched comparison group of 3,948 women aged 15-44 from the 1971 PHS multicenter INH hepatitis surveillance study. Two expert panels determined possible cases of INH hepatitis: five cases in the prenatal group and 10 in the non-pregnant group. Two Hispanic women aged 24 and 27 died at 3 and 5 months postpartum in the preventive therapy group, and one 38-year-old non-pregnant black woman died in the PHS group. The analysis raised the possibility of an association of pregnancy/post-partum state with INH hepatitis (risk ratio 2.5, 95% CI 0.8-8.2) and fatal hepatotoxicity (rate ratio 4, 95% CI 0.2-258), though groups were unmatched, followed a decade apart, and underpowered due to rarity of events.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy and post-partum state examined; cohorts were unmatched, followed a decade apart, and the analysis was underpowered because of the rarity of the events.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort comparing 3,681 pregnant/postpartum women in the 1981 INH preventive therapy (LTBI) program with 3,948 women aged 15-44 from the 1971 Public Health Service multicenter INH hepatitis surveillance study. Five possible INH hepatitis cases in the prenatal group and 10 in the non-pregnant group. Two Hispanic women aged 24 and 27 died at 3 and 5 months postpartum; one 38-year-old non-pregnant black woman died in the PHS group. Association of pregnancy/post-partum state with INH hepatitis risk ratio 2.5 (95% CI 0.8-8.2) and with fatal hepatotoxicity rate ratio 4 (95% CI 0.2-258).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports severe nevirapine-related hepatotoxicity and rashes among pregnant women. Kramer and colleagues described 14 cases of mild-to-moderately severe hepatotoxicity and 11 cases of mild-to-moderately severe rash among 125 pregnant women who received nevirapine. A second prospective, randomized, open-label study comparing nelfinavir/zidovudine/lamivudine versus nevirapine/zidovudine/lamivudine in pregnant women was stopped early because 5 of 17 women on nevirapine had events leading to treatment discontinuation, and one of the five experienced fulminant hepatic failure and death. Nevirapine prescribing information was subsequently changed and initiation of nevirapine is now contraindicated in women (pregnant or not) with a CD4+ cell count greater than 250/mm³ due to a greater risk of adverse events.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy; increased risk in women with a CD4+ cell count greater than 250/mm³ (initiation now contraindicated); nevirapine given as part of a combination regimen (nevirapine/zidovudine/lamivudine).
raw_record.extra_details: Severe nevirapine-related hepatotoxicity and rash described in pregnant women. Kramer study: 14 cases of mild-to-moderately severe hepatotoxicity (1/35 African-American, 13/86 non-African-American) and 11 cases of rash among 125 pregnant women. Second prospective randomized open-label trial stopped early: 5/17 women on nevirapine had adverse events leading to discontinuation, 1 of 5 experienced fulminant hepatic failure and death. Led to changes in nevirapine prescribing information; initiation contraindicated in pregnant or non-pregnant women with CD4+ count >250/mm³.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman with Graves' disease, started on a reducing regime of propylthiouracil (PTU), developed jaundice at week 20 of gestation. Bloods showed bilirubin 91 µmol/l, ALT 1,796 IU/l, ALP 200 IU/l, INR 1.2 and albumin 33 g/l. A presumptive diagnosis of PTU-induced hepatitis was made; PTU was immediately discontinued, and the bilirubin peaked at 378 before improving over the following two weeks. Autoimmune and viral hepatitis markers, ultrasound, ferritin and caeruloplasmin were normal, supporting PTU as the cause.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy; jaundice developed at week 20 of gestation while on a reducing PTU regime for Graves' disease.
raw_record.extra_details: PTU used as first-line anti-thyroid drug in pregnancy. Initial labs: bilirubin 91 µmol/l, ALT 1,796 IU/l, ALP 200 IU/l, INR 1.2, albumin 33 g/l; bilirubin peaked at 378 after PTU discontinuation, then fell (dechallenge improvement). After PTU cessation she became thyrotoxic and was started on carbimazole (not attributed as a cause); liver function tests improved and carbimazole was stopped at week 32; healthy baby delivered at 38 weeks. Reported as the first case of PTU-induced hepatitis in the second trimester with successful outcome.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of propylthiouracil (PTU)-induced fulminant hepatic failure in a pregnant patient who required liver transplantation and thyroidectomy, noting the case reflects a very rare complication of a presumed safe drug and echoes the FDA warning on propylthiouracil. Therapy for the condition involved immediate cessation of PTU with expectant management of hepatic-failure complications, and a fatality rate of 25% to 50% has been reported in these patients, with liver transplantation required in severe cases.

raw_record.extra_details: FDA warning exists on the drug (propylthiouracil). A fatality rate of 25% to 50% has been reported in patients with PTU-induced hepatic failure. Severe cases may require liver transplantation; 12 cases of liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure between the 13th and 27th weeks of pregnancy have been reported, with a fetal survival rate of 36%.

Six cases in one of the series shared fulminant hepatic failure presenting four to five weeks after starting therapy, in treatment-naive women with normal pre-therapy ALT and no hepatitis B or C history. All cases occurred in women with baseline CD4 counts above 250 cells/µL, and hepatitis progressed rapidly to hepatic failure despite nevirapine discontinuation and intensive clinical and laboratory monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case series of nevirapine-associated adverse events in pregnant HIV-infected women. Patient 1 (starting NVP-based ART at 27 1/7 weeks gestation) developed fever, diffuse urticarial rash, eosinophilia, clinical hepatitis, and renal failure; NVP was discontinued, and laboratory parameters returned to baseline 4 months after delivery. Patient 2, who added NVP at the 27th week of gestation, presented with pruritus, urticarial rash, and elevated ALT/AST with eosinophilia; after NVP discontinuation, repeat LFTs returned to baseline.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant HIV-infected women on nevirapine-containing antiretroviral therapy (third-trimester initiation); accompanies urticarial rash and eosinophilia.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1: ALT 235 U/L (grade 2), AST 309 U/L (grade 3), GGT 233 U/L at onset with fever, eosinophilia, and renal failure; improved after NVP discontinuation, resolved after cesarean delivery ~4 months postpartum; patient also on Combivir and treated with prednisone. Patient 2: ALT 295 (grade 3), AST 152 (grade 2) at onset; LFTs returned to baseline 4 weeks after stopping NVP; also on Combivir. Dechallenge supported by LFT return to baseline after NVP discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Among 107 pregnant women initiating HAART in the MTCT-Plus Program, eight developed grade 3 or 4 adverse events attributed to HAART. Two women developed grade 4 liver toxicity attributed to nevirapine (NVP), with alanine aminotransferase levels over 50 times and over 5 times the upper limit of normal, respectively. All events resolved with drug changes and no deaths were reported. In the short-course ARV (PMTCT) cohort, no grade 3 or 4 toxicities were observed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant HIV-infected women receiving a HAART combination regimen; concurrent antiretroviral co-exposure within HAART.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases with grade 4 liver toxicity attributed to NVP; alanine aminotransferase over 50x and over 5x upper limit of normal in the two respective women; events resolved with drug change (switched to nelfinavir); no deaths. Five other women in the same cohort developed grade 3 mucocutaneous rash also attributed to NVP.

raw_record.support_text: A 31-year-old primigravida was treated with nitrofurantoin 100 mg/day in the 36th week of gestation for dysuria with enterococcus in urine culture. After induced delivery, repeated labs showed elevated AST and ALT with negative hepatitis C and B markers, and the patient was subicteric. Nitrofurantoin was discontinued, and discontinuation plus methylprednisolone therapy significantly lowered liver enzyme levels. The authors concluded this was probably toxic liver damage caused by nitrofurantoin. The case is described as a rare case of acute toxic hepatitis in pregnancy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patient (31-year-old primigravida, 36th week of gestation); delivery was induced near term because of hypertension, which coexists with the exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg/day for treatment of dysuria from enterococcus urinary tract infection. Elevated aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase, negative hepatitis C and B markers, patient subicteric, normal coagulation and complete blood count, slight hepatomegaly on ultrasound without focal or diffuse lesions. Nitrofurantoin was discontinued and methylprednisolone therapy was introduced; liver enzymes significantly decreased to near normal. Authors described the injury as 'acute toxic hepatitis' (toxic drug-induced hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states there is now no doubt that isoniazid can occasionally produce liver damage, though the exact mechanism is unknown. It notes a relatively high incidence of biochemically demonstrable hepatic damage (10 per cent in Sharer and Smith's series and 13.3 per cent in the Public Health Service surveillance study), argues this argues against a hypersensitivity or idiosyncratic reaction, and suggests hepatic metabolic products of isoniazid may be responsible for hepatic necrosis. Concomitant drugs, preexisting liver disease, and inactivation rates of isoniazid are being explored as influences.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Preventive (prophylactic) therapy in tuberculin reactors/hospital employees; liver damage is rare in children and young adults but the incidence increases significantly in older adults, and it was predicted that preventive therapy would no longer be recommended for tuberculin reactors over age 35 without other risk factors.
raw_record.extra_details: In one study, 37 of 427 (9 per cent) hospital employees on isoniazid preventive therapy developed elevated SGOT; 5 had symptomatic hepatitis, isoniazid was stopped in 8 others with elevated SGOT plus abnormal total bilirubin and/or alkaline phosphatase, and in 5 others with SGOT greater than 100 on 2 occasions or greater than 250 on 1 occasion. Maddrey and Boitnott reported hepatitis attributed to isoniazid in 14 patients over 5 years, with 3 dying of fulminant hepatitis; rechallenge caused recurrent hepatitis in 2 patients and abnormal serum transaminases in a third; duration of symptoms before stopping ranged from 1 to 10.5 weeks, with longer duration associated with more severe hepatitis. Mechanism unknown; metabolic products of isoniazid may cause hepatic necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes disulfiram-induced hepatitis reported in humans: Keeffe and Smith first reported a case in 1974, Ranek and Andreason reported six additional cases in 1977 of whom five died, and Kristensen reported toxic liver damage in a nonalcoholic female treated with disulfiram for nickel dermatitis who developed liver-enzyme elevation upon rechallenge. Incidence of disulfiram-induced fatal hepatitis is reportedly 1 in 30,000 treated patients per year, and an analysis of reports to the Danish committee on adverse drug reactions implicated disulfiram in 5 of 52 (10%) drug-related fatalities.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Primary illustrative case is a pediatric (adolescent) patient; general use context is therapeutic aversion therapy in adults with chronic alcoholism. One reported case involved a nonalcoholic female treated for nickel dermatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset of hepatotoxicity occurs within 4-6 weeks (range 2-24 weeks) of starting treatment. Symptoms include fatigue, headache, fever, pruritus, rash, myalgia, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, light stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly; symptoms usually resolve within 2 weeks of stopping, and liver function may need up to 12 weeks to normalize. Biopsy may show predominantly hepatocellular degeneration with focal or extensive hepatocellular necrosis and portal/periportal eosinophilic infiltration. Disulfiram-induced liver failure requiring liver transplantation first reported in 1989 (Vanjak et al), with 3 total transplant cases reported; the paper's case is the first reported pediatric OLT for disulfiram-induced fulminant hepatic failure. Most reports suggest an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction as the primary mechanism; an alternative proposed mechanism is carbon disulfide-induced hepatic injury from covalent binding of electrophilic reactive metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced hepatotoxicity from methotrexate (MTX), a folate antagonist antimetabolite antineoplastic agent, may cause an acute increase in transaminase enzymes and, with long-term use, lead to liver fibrosis and cirrhosis; because liver damage does not correlate with enzyme rise, liver biopsy after a cumulative 1.5 g dose has been recommended. The report describes a 52-year-old male diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis 4 years earlier and started on MTX tablets, in whom hepatic fibrosis and prolonged cholestatic liver disease occurred secondary to prolonged MTX usage.

raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 52-year-old male with rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 4 years prior, on oral MTX tablets; prolonged MTX use resulted in hepatic fibrosis and prolonged cholestatic liver disease. MTX may also cause acute transaminase elevation, and long-term use may lead to fibrosis and cirrhosis. A liver biopsy was recommended after cumulative use of 1.5 g because liver damage does not correlate with liver enzyme increases.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old woman who had received an average daily dose of 200 mg of amiodarone for recurrent supraventricular tachycardia since December 1979 developed progressive liver enzyme elevations (alkaline phosphatase up to 317 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 225 U/L), ascites, and varices, and died 2 weeks after referral due to hepatic encephalopathy while still on amiodarone. At autopsy the liver showed histologic findings consistent with cirrhosis, with scant fatty infiltration, prominent fibrosis and bile duct proliferation, severely damaged hepatocytes, and widespread Mallory bodies. The authors report this as a case of fatal cirrhosis in a patient treated with amiodarone for over 4 years, adding evidence that asymptomatic liver dysfunction with prolonged amiodarone treatment may herald irreversible liver damage and that cessation of amiodarone should be considered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prolonged amiodarone therapy (over 4 years) at an average daily dose of 200 mg in a 76-year-old woman with recurrent supraventricular tachycardia and no pre-existing liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity presented as initially asymptomatic twofold alkaline phosphatase rise (195 U/L; normal 90 U/L), later aspartate aminotransferase rise (85 U/L then 225 U/L; normal 40 U/L), albumin 2.9 g/dL, normal bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, negative hepatitis B surface antigen and VDRL. Clinical findings included hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and esophageal varices; death from hepatic encephalopathy. Autopsy histology: cirrhosis with prominent fibrosis, bile duct proliferation, damaged hepatocytes, widespread Mallory bodies. Authors also note amiodarone induces alcohol-like hepatic changes, electron microscopy shows lamellar osmiophilic lysosomal inclusions even without clinical disease, and hepatotoxicity is suggested to be concentration-dependent in contrast to pulmonary toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a 6-month prospective, observational, multicentre, open-label evaluation of prolonged-release nicotinic acid (Niaspan, maximum dose 2000 mg/day) added to statin therapy in 1053 patients at increased cardiovascular risk, the authors report there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity or myopathy, and all patients recovered completely from ADRs after treatment discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prolonged-release nicotinic acid (Niaspan) added to statin therapy; patients with cardiovascular disease and/or type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Primary endpoint was safety and tolerability with special regard to treatment-related ADRs. Flushing occurred in 430 patients (40.8%); other ADRs in 125 (12.5%); serious ADRs 0.6%. 11.1% discontinued for flushing and 8.4% for other ADRs. No hepatotoxicity or myopathy observed; the hepatotoxicity claim is explicitly not supported by this study.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 1,091 prostate cancer patients all treated with the antiandrogen combination of flutamide and an LHRH agonist with serial liver-function monitoring, only 4 patients (0.36%) developed liver toxicity: 2 with clinical signs of liver toxicity and 2 with hepatic enzyme levels at least fourfold above upper normal limits without symptoms. All four displayed abnormal findings within 4 weeks of treatment onset, and the authors concluded that the clinical and biochemical sequence indicates cases of flutamide-induced liver toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prostate cancer indication; flutamide administered in a fixed combination regimen with an LHRH agonist. All four affected patients had pretreatment serum liver values within 20% of normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence 0.36% (4/1,091) of flutamide-related liver toxicity; 2 patients with clinical signs and 2 with asymptomatic enzyme elevations (transaminases up to 60-fold above pretreatment, one ~2-fold alkaline phosphatase rise, normal bilirubin in those three). One patient had a mainly cholestatic pattern with overt jaundice, fatigue, nausea, no pruritus; peak bilirubin >120 µmol/L, 6-fold alkaline phosphatase, 16-fold ALT, 5-fold AST; biopsy showed acute cholestatic hepatitis with mixed cytotoxic (spotty necrosis, acidophilic bodies) and cholestatic (bile plugs, bile pigment, feathery degeneration, periportal inflammation) findings, no zonal necrosis or portal fibrosis. The other three showed a 'pure' hepatocellular-type pattern. All patients recovered rapidly and completely within 2 to 8 weeks after flutamide discontinuation. Classified as an idiosyncratic response without signs of hypersensitivity, assumed toxic-metabolite dependent. Liver function tests remained within normal limits in almost all 1,091 patients during the 36-month observation. Upper normal values: ALT/AST 24 IU/L, γ-GT 28 IU/L, bilirubin 20.5 µmol/L.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity in prostate cancer patients, proposing that clinical flutamide hepatotoxicity occurs when CYP1A2 inhibition, reactive-metabolite production by extensive metabolizers, and lowered GSH content coincide. Preliminary clinical results from 11 prostate cancer patients showed that those who developed severe hepatitis with flutamide had lower CYP1A2 enzyme activity than the normal population, and higher flutamide and lower OH-flutamide plasma concentrations have been reported in patients with flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prostate cancer patients taking flutamide as an antiandrogen; susceptibility proposed to involve lower CYP1A2 activity (assessed by caffeine test), concurrent CYP1A2-inhibiting medication, and lowered glutathione content due to poor nutritional status and aging.
raw_record.extra_details: Referenced clinical findings: lower CYP1A2 enzyme activity in the 11 patients who developed severe hepatitis; higher flutamide and lower OH-flutamide (4-hydroxyflutamide) plasma concentrations in patients with flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity; higher FLU-1 plasma concentration in patients with flutamide-induced hepatic disorders. Proposed mechanism involves CYP1A2-mediated reactive-metabolite (originating from FLU-1) formation and glutathione (GSH) depletion; caffeine test (urinary caffeine metabolites) proposed as noninvasive CYP1A2 assessment.

raw_record.support_text: This cohort of 41 psoriasis patients receiving long-term methotrexate therapy was evaluated for methotrexate-induced liver injury using liver biopsy (Roenigk grade ≥3a) as the gold standard and transient elastography. Methotrexate is treated as the cause of the liver fibrosis/injury being monitored; TE values >7.0 kPa provided acceptable accuracy (AUROC=0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.93) and a high NPV of 84% for excluding methotrexate-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Psoriasis indication requiring long-term methotrexate therapy; non-obese Asian population; histopathologic assessment (Roenigk grading).
raw_record.extra_details: 41 patients evaluated by transient elastography and liver biopsy; histopathologic evidence of methotrexate-induced liver injury defined as Roenigk grades ≥3a. Total cumulative methotrexate dose and host factors (age, gender, metabolic syndrome and its components) were not significantly associated with TE values ≥7.1 kPa or Roenigk grades ≥3a. TE cut-off 7.1 kPa gave sensitivity 50%, specificity 83.9%, PPV 50%, NPV 83.9%, accuracy 75.6% in this study.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 183 methotrexate-treated psoriatics monitored with liver biopsies taken at average intervals of 1 year, liver cirrhosis was established histologically in 20 patients (mean cumulative methotrexate dose 2400 mg), and compared with 44 methotrexate-treated psoriatics without cirrhosis (mean cumulative dose 2200 mg). The paper frames these as 'methotrexate-induced liver cirrhosis' and investigates an HLA association, noting that liver damage can often be related to multiple factors such as alcohol intake, age, diabetes, obesity, previous arsenic intake, and possibly psoriasis itself.

raw_record.extra_details: HLA typing study; the A1+B8 antigen combination was increased among the 20 cirrhosis patients (present in 5/20) compared with methotrexate-treated psoriatics who did not develop cirrhosis (p<0.05), similar to data on drug-associated chronic active hepatitis. Cumulative methotrexate dose averaged 2400 mg in cirrhosis and 2200 mg in controls.

raw_record.support_text: The authors, who were the first to publish a detailed account of the hepatotoxic effects of methotrexate in psoriasis patients, respond to Dahl et al.'s suggestion that liver fibrosis is an invariable consequence of prolonged frequent small-dose oral methotrexate. They continue prescribing 2.5 mg methotrexate daily 6-8 days with 3-7 days' rest and report reinvestigation of four patients on this regimen for almost 10 years: two show no fibrosis (one with alcohol intake of 6 pints of beer per week), one presented with a full picture of cirrhosis one year ago, and one has histological evidence of cirrhosis. They state terms such as 'invariable' are not yet justified, but attribute hepatotoxicity (fibrosis/cirrhosis) to methotrexate.

raw_record.extra_details: Letter correspondence in response to Dahl et al. Authors were first to publish a detailed account of methotrexate hepatotoxicity in psoriasis patients. Described as still the best available drug for severe cases needing systemic therapy; authors emphasize ascertaining the safest schedule. Histology: two patients show no fibrosis, one presented with full picture of cirrhosis one year prior, one has histological evidence of cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report, based on their studies on methotrexate and the liver including considerable follow-up data on MTX-treated patients with liver biopsies, that MTX-induced liver cirrhosis is in general nonaggressive. They note a patient with ascites whose serum PIIINP and laboratory values for alkaline phosphatases and serum transaminases decreased after discontinuation of MTX, and state that psoriatics on long-term MTX should still have a liver biopsy at least once their total cumulative dose exceeds 1.5 g.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Psoriasis patients (some with arthritis) on long-term MTX treatment monitored by serial liver biopsies; biopsy recommended when total cumulative MTX dose exceeds 1.5 g; one case also involved reduced alcohol intake.
raw_record.extra_details: Discussion concerns monitoring of MTX-induced liver toxicity. In the referenced study, of 24 patients without arthritis with biopsy-proven fibrosis, six to eight (25%-33%) had normal serum aminoterminal propeptide of type III procollagen (PIIINP) below the 95% specificity cut-off, showing normal PIIINP is not a reliable basis to avoid or delay routine liver biopsies. MTX-induced cirrhosis in general described as nonaggressive; patients with fibrosis and negative PIIINP had low-grade, mostly inactive fibrosis. One patient with ascites showed declining PIIINP, alkaline phosphatases, and serum transaminases after discontinuing MTX.

raw_record.support_text: The follow-up investigation of MTX-treated psoriasis patients confirms the earlier study suggesting that MTX-induced liver cirrhosis is not aggressive. When biopsies were evaluated blind, no progression was found in most later serial biopsies, and in 14 cases the cirrhosis diagnosis could not be confirmed in the latest liver biopsy. The paper describes these as patients with MTX-induced liver cirrhosis, attributing the cirrhosis/ fibrosis to methotrexate therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Psoriasis patients on chronic MTX; the paper identifies prior heavy alcohol intake, previous treatment with arsenics and vitamin A, male sex, and ongoing alcohol intake as contributing factors to the cirrhosis frequency; a lowering of the weekly dose together with advice to avoid alcohol was proposed to explain histologic improvement.
raw_record.extra_details: 29 patients with MTX-induced liver cirrhosis (20 male, 9 female); average cumulative MTX dose at first cirrhosis diagnosis 3,130 mg, higher than in the 1980 study; serial-biopsy cumulative cirrhosis index grading (grades 1-4) showed no progression in most cases and in 14 cases cirrhosis was not confirmed on latest biopsy; alcohol intake proven to increase tendency to fibrosis and cirrhosis in MTX-treated patients; patients 3, 4, 20, 21, 25 died without signs of liver failure. The 29 patients plus 4 without follow-up biopsies represent 7.4% of all MTX-treated patients. Data from other studies comparing daily oral, 25-mg weekly single, and 15-mg divided intermittent oral schedules for relative hepatotoxicity were noted as inconclusive. Serial liver biopsies stated as the only reliable means of evaluating MTX-induced morphological liver changes.

raw_record.extra_details: MTX acts by inhibiting DNA synthesis and via anti-inflammatory effects on T-cell mediated immune responses. Long-term side effect includes liver fibrosis and cirrhosis due to MTX hepatotoxicity; dermatologic guidelines recommend liver biopsy at every 1500 mg cumulative dose. Study of 24 patients comparing Fibroscan (n=20, median 6.4 kPa, range 3.3-18.4 kPa) and Fibrotest against liver histology (Metavir score): Fibroscan correctly identified 88% without significant fibrosis (<F2, ≤7.1 kPa); Fibrotest identified 83% with significant fibrosis (≥F2, >0.31). Liver biopsy carries 0.01-0.1% mortality risk due to postprocedural pain and bleeding.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports MTX-related liver toxicity in psoriasis patients, with serial liver biopsies documenting perisinusoidal fibrosis, steatosis, regenerative activity, and regenerative nodules that progress with cumulative methotrexate dosage (Roenigk grades advancing from I to IV by 4 g cumulative MTX). The authors note that histological exams suggest stellate-cell proliferation mediates the toxic lesion caused by MTX, and that the incidence of cirrhosis in psoriatic patients treated with MTX is higher than in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

raw_record.extra_details: Serial liver biopsies in 13 patients (case series); cumulative MTX doses of 1 g, 1.5 g, 2 g, 3 g and 4 g; histology showed perisinusoidal fibrosis, steatosis, swollen hepatocytes, regenerative activity/nodules, sinusoidal dilation, congestion and cellular hyperplasia; Roenigk fibrosis/cirrhosis grades progressed from I to IV with increasing cumulative dose; sinusoidal dilation/congestion were not directly related to MTX dose; proposed mechanism involves stellate-cell proliferation.
