raw_record.support_text: The report of two additional cases of fatal liver injury related to the use of sitaxentan (Thelin; 100 mg sitaxentan tablets) in pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) patients enrolled in a randomised controlled study prompted Pfizer to voluntarily discontinue all ongoing clinical trials with this compound and to withdraw the commercial drug from the market worldwide. Thelin had been authorised in the EU since 2006 for treatment of PAH and marketed in 16 EU member states, Australia and Canada. The EMA advised patients taking Thelin to consult their physician to review treatment, and the ESC/ERS 2009 PH guidelines recommended no de novo initiation of Thelin and transitioning existing patients to another ERA (bosentan or ambrisentan) or to prostanoids/phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pulmonary arterial hypertension indication; cases occurred in a randomised controlled study population.
raw_record.extra_details: Two reported additional fatal liver injury cases led to Pfizer voluntarily discontinuing all ongoing clinical trials and global market withdrawal of Thelin (100 mg sitaxentan tablets). Drug authorised in the EU since 2006 for PAH, marketed in 16 EU member states, Australia, and Canada. ESC/ERS 2009 PH guidelines recommended against de novo Thelin initiation and advised transition to bosentan (Tracleer) or ambrisentan (Volibris) or other PAH drug classes (prostanoids, phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors) in cases of prior adverse reactions to those ERAs. Paper notes two types of ERA liver injury: a common dose-dependent, reversible toxic type, and a rare possibly idiosyncratic/immunologically mediated type that can result in severe liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses the risk of severe hepatotoxicity and death from pyrazinamide-containing regimens (rifampicin-pyrazinamide) used for LTBI treatment, citing McElroy and colleagues (2005): rates per 1000 rifampicin-pyrazinamide therapy initiations were 25.6 (95% CI 22.3-29.3) for asymptomatic aspartate aminotransferase level >5x upper normal limit, 18.7 (95% CI 15.9-21.9) for hepatitis, 7 fatalities (0.9/1000, 95% CI 0.4-1.9) and 23 hospitalizations (2.8/1000, 95% CI 1.8-4.3). Based on safety considerations, pyrazinamide-containing regimens are no longer recommended despite their proven efficacy.

raw_record.extra_details: Rates per 1000 rifampicin-pyrazinamide therapy initiations: asymptomatic AST >5x ULN 25.6 (95% CI 22.3-29.3); hepatitis 18.7 (95% CI 15.9-21.9); 7 fatalities, rate 0.9 (95% CI 0.4-1.9); 23 hospitalisations, rate 2.8 (95% CI 1.8-4.3). Data: McElroy 2005 comparison of state and city TB programme and healthcare-setting toxicity data with an historical isoniazid control. Pyrazinamide-containing regimens no longer recommended despite proven preventive efficacy on safety grounds.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses patients with halothane hepatitis (halothane-induced human DILI) who develop circulating antibodies to TFA neoantigens after halothane exposure. Using immunoblotting with liver microsomal proteins from halothane-treated rabbits or rats as test antigen, 42 of 68 (62%) patients with halothane hepatitis tested positive for halothane-induced antibodies. The paper notes prior halothane exposure would identify patients at increased risk of a hypersensitive reaction on further halothane exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Re-exposure to halothane after prior sensitization carries increased risk of a hypersensitive reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis patients produce antibodies to trifluoroacetyl (TFA) neoantigens. On immunoblotting, 42/68 (62%) were positive; ELISA results varied with antigen (TFA-RSA: 2/6, 16/24, 5/6, 12/40; halothane-treated rabbit microsomes: 16/24 (67%) and 28/39 (72%)). Neoantigen targets include ER proteins ERp99 (grp94/endoplasmin), calregulin, and 57/59/80/58 kd TFA proteins. Antibodies also cross-react with liver microsomal neoantigens produced by enflurane, suggesting potential cross-sensitization, though this remains speculative rather than a confirmed enflurane DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old Asian woman with tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis started triple therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide); all were stopped after a rash. One month later isoniazid was restarted and 28 days later she presented with nausea, abdominal pain, and jaundice and a hepatitic picture (bilirubin 310 µmol/L, ALP 314 IU/L, ALT 2175 IU/L). Isoniazid was stopped again, but she was readmitted 3 days later with grade 3 encephalopathy, coagulopathy (INR 3.0), and rising jaundice; she met criteria for emergency liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure and was successfully transplanted. Explanted liver showed severe confluent necrosis with collapse and granulomatous infiltration, consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rechallenge exposure: isoniazid restarted after a prior triple-therapy course; indication was tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 of four reported cases of fulminant hepatic failure caused by rifampicin, isoniazid, or both. Hepatitic laboratory picture (ALT 2175 then 2386 IU/L; bilirubin 310 then 399 µmol/L; ALP 314 then 350 IU/L; INR 3.0); grade 3 encephalopathy; successfully transplanted, discharged well at 7 weeks. Explanted liver histology: severe confluent necrosis with extensive collapse and granulomatous infiltration consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper notes isoniazid is among three potentially hepatotoxic anti-tuberculous drugs (with rifampicin and pyrazinamide).

raw_record.extra_details: Of 10 rechallenged patients, 6 manifested recurrent anicteric or icteric hepatic dysfunction within 48 h of re-initiation of daily chlorpromazine, while 4 maintained normal liver function during 1-3 years of daily dosing. raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with ecstasy (MDMA)-induced toxic hepatitis based on meeting criteria including no positive viral serology, exclusion of other hepatic diseases (autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease), exposure before symptom onset, clinical improvement upon discontinuation, relapse on self-reported re-exposure, and exclusion of pre-existing liver disease. A Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 11 rated ecstasy as the 'definite' cause of toxic hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Recreational ecstasy use with co-exposure to alcohol at a double dose; exact amount and contaminants unknown; CYP2D6 enzyme deficiency hypothesized as mechanism; outcome was recovery rather than chronic course.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic injury mimicked acute viral hepatitis with sharp serum aminotransferase elevation, jaundice (recurrent toxic hepatitis), elevated bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time/aPTT; treated with IV fluids and monitored over 6 days, followed 1 month, with liver enzymes and bilirubin returning to normal within 2 weeks. Naranjo score 11 corresponded to 'definite' causality. The paper notes ecstasy-induced hepatic injury ranges from benign viral-hepatitis-like forms to liver failure from massive hepatic necrosis, and cites Andreu et al who found ecstasy was the second most common cause of liver injury in patients under 25 years, with 5 of 10 such cases ecstasy-related. Mechanism thought to involve a reactive metabolite (glutathione depletion, calcium influx, oxidative cell-membrane lipid changes) partly via CYP2D6 metabolism; mortality described in MDMA- and 3,4-methylenedioxy-N-ethyl-amphetamine postmortem series. One reported case of fulminant hepatitis and two of acute hepatitis after a single ecstasy tablet.

raw_record.support_text: In 30 colorectal cancer patients undergoing isolated hepatic perfusion with 200 mg melphalan via hepatic artery infusion, veno-occlusive disease (VOD) occurred in 4 patients and portal hypertension (possibly a result of VOD) in 2 others. Grade 4 biliary toxicity occurred in 5 of 30 patients and 1 patient died of progressive liver failure. Toxic hepatitis was reported as a major complication in 1 patient. The discussion attributes these liver toxicities to the melphalan perfusion exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Regional exposure by isolated hepatic perfusion delivered via hepatic artery infusion/perfusion in colorectal cancer patients with liver metastases; not ordinary systemic therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: 200 mg melphalan given as 20-min hepatic artery infusion followed by 40-min perfusion; peak perfusate concentration 93.2 µg/mL, AUC 2841.6 µg·min/mL. Reported liver events: toxic hepatitis in 1 patient, veno-occlusive disease in 4 patients, portal hypertension in 2, grade 4 biliary toxicity in 5 of 30 patients, and 1 death from progressive liver failure. GGT, ALAT, ASAT and bilirubin elevations were graded per NCI CTC across 30 patients. VOD was noted as possibly resulting from accumulative exposure to chemotherapeutic agents; toxicity had a steep concentration-toxicity relationship independent of total melphalan dose (supported by a rat cholangiofibrosis model).

raw_record.support_text: Nineteen patients with hepatic tumors were treated with hepatic artery infusion chemotherapy using an implantable pump delivering floxuridine (FUDR), starting at 400 mg for 2 weeks with 2 weeks of rest. Reported toxicity included dyspepsia, elevated liver function tests in all patients, gastric ulcer in 2, cholecystitis in 2, and sclerosing cholangitis in 3, attributing these liver injuries to the FUDR regional infusion regimen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Regional hepatic artery infusion route of delivery; patients had colorectal adenocarcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, or carcinoid with liver involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: 19 patients treated; floxuridine (FUDR) 400 mg for 2 weeks with 2 weeks rest via implantable Infusaid pump; elevated liver function tests in all patients; sclerosing cholangitis in 3 patients; gastric ulcer in 2; cholecystitis in 2; dyspepsia in all. FUDR delivers high hepatic concentrations with near complete hepatic clearance.

raw_record.support_text: Nineteen patients with isolated unresectable liver metastases from a variety of tumors were treated with a 60-min isolated hepatic perfusion (IHP) using 200 mg melphalan. In the treated cohort, reversible grade 3 or 4 hepatotoxicity occurred in 10 (56%) patients and veno-occlusive disease occurred in 4 (22%) patients, with no treatment-related mortality.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Regional isolated hepatic perfusion (unusual route delivering high local exposure) in patients with isolated unresectable liver metastases from various primary tumors; 60-min perfusion with 200 mg melphalan.
raw_record.extra_details: Melphalan given as 200 mg via isolated hepatic perfusion in 19 patients (13 uveal melanomas, 2 neuroendocrine carcinomas, 2 gastrointestinal stromal tumors, 1 hepatocellular carcinoma, 1 high-grade sarcoma). Reversible grade 3 or 4 hepatotoxicity in 10/19 (56%); veno-occlusive disease in 4/19 (22%); no treatment-related mortality; one melanoma patient not perfused due to insufficient liver isolation. No formal causality instrument reported; toxicity attributed to the IHP melphalan treatment.

raw_record.support_text: In 20 patients with unresectable liver metastases treated with a 60-min hyperthermic isolated hepatic perfusion (IHP) using melphalan alone (1.5 mg/kg), three patients (15%) experienced grade 4 hepatic toxicity and died due to liver failure and subsequent multiorgan failure; six patients had significant (grade 3-4) but transitory hepatic toxicity (median time to recovery 15 days, range 9-58), and the remaining cases had grade 2 reversible hepatic toxicity. Hepatic toxicity did not correlate with tumor response, and none of the patient-related parameters (age, gender, preoperative liver function tests, percentage of hepatic replacement) correlated with postoperative liver toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Regional single-agent chemotherapy delivered by hyperthermic isolated hepatic perfusion (IHP) rather than ordinary systemic use; patients had unresectable liver metastases with 25-50% hepatic parenchyma replacement and had failed prior conventional treatments.
raw_record.extra_details: Melphalan dose 1.5 mg/kg body weight over 60-min hyperthermic IHP. Hepatic toxicity graded per NCI-CTC: overall grade 1-2 in 9 patients (45%) and grade 3-4 in 11 patients (55%); three patients (15%) had grade 4 hepatic toxicity with irreversible liver failure leading to multiorgan failure and death; six patients had transitory grade 3-4 toxicity (median recovery 15 days, range 9-58). Binary logistic regression found hepatic toxicity did not correlate with tumor response, and no patient-related parameter (age, gender, preoperative liver function tests, hepatic replacement percentage) correlated with postoperative liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients admitted for MDMA-related hepatotoxicity, whose case histories were published in 1997, had MDMA-induced fulminant hepatic failure and subsequent liver transplantation. Both had regularly taken MDMA on weekends for several months without side-effects, and after a further intake of MDMA developed fulminant hepatic failure with massive liver necrosis on histopathology; screening for hepatic viruses was negative.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Regular recreational weekend use over several months in non-overdose (ordinary recreational) exposure; both patients proved to be CYP2D6 extensive metabolisers.
raw_record.extra_details: MDMA-induced fulminant hepatic failure followed a further intake after a period of tolerance; histopathology revealed massive liver necrosis; required liver transplantation; viral screening negative; patients' genotypes were *1/*4, *2/*5, and *1/*1, so they were not poor metabolisers, and the hypothesis that hepatotoxicity results from genetically impaired (CYP2D6) metabolism leading to accumulation of MDMA/MDA/MDE was considered unlikely.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Relationship reported in the context of tolcapone used therapeutically as a COMT inhibitor for Parkinson's disease in conjunction with levodopa.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical trials demonstrated tolcapone can cause elevations of liver enzymes (potentially indicative of liver damage). It caused four cases of acute hepatotoxicity with three fatalities. The paper describes tolcapone as associated with idiosyncratic drug induced liver toxicity, and notes that rapid detection of tolcapone metabolites can provide mechanistic toxicity information related to drug metabolism and reactive metabolite formation.

raw_record.support_text: A renal allograft recipient on isoniazid 300 mg daily prophylaxis (given because of tuberculin reactivity and a Ghon complex) developed malaise, fever, epigastric tenderness, and bilirubinuria with markedly abnormal liver function about 2½ months after starting isoniazid. Isoniazid was immediately discontinued, and clinical and chemical recovery rapidly followed its withdrawal, supporting isoniazid as the cause of the hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Renal allograft recipient with chronic glomerulonephritis who had received a cadaveric renal transplant and was on immunosuppression (antithymocyte globulin, prednisone, azathioprine; azathioprine later replaced by cyclophosphamide); on concomitant Maalox, hydralazine, and chlorothiazide.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid 300 mg daily started May 1973 as prophylaxis; injury appeared after about 2½ months and on 26 July isoniazid was discontinued. SGOT rose from 65 (20 July) to 1830 IU/ml (26 July) and bilirubin to 5.9 mg/100 ml (28 July); alkaline phosphatase rose to 9.7 Bodansky units/ml. Percutaneous liver biopsy showed moderate diffuse hepatitis with ballooned hepatocytes, acidophilic bodies, mixed inflammatory infiltrate, hyperplastic Kupffer cells, small centrolobular zones of collapse without bridging, and moderate cholestasis. Hepatitis-associated antigen was negative; globulins and prothrombin time normal. Recovery followed isoniazid withdrawal. Authors note that the extreme hyperbilirubinemia and marked intrahepatic cholestasis without inflammatory reaction reported after azathioprine were absent here.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites Thomas et al (1979), who studied 119 renal allograft recipients receiving azathioprine as primary immunosuppression during isoniazid chemoprophylaxis. They found 11% had evidence of hepatic dysfunction attributable solely to isoniazid, 2.5% developed major hepatic dysfunction, and there were two deaths related to liver failure. The paper also notes that isoniazid hepatotoxicity usually occurs between 1 and 8 weeks after the start of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Calne in 1978 first introduced cyclosporin A (CyA) in seven patients with renal failure receiving transplants from mismatched cadaver donors. CyA was used initially as the sole immunosuppressive agent; it was effective in inhibiting rejection, but there was clear evidence of both nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity. The initial administered dose of CyA was 17 mg/kg and no therapeutic drug monitoring was used.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Renal transplant recipients with renal failure receiving cadaver-donor allografts; CyA given as the sole immunosuppressive agent; no therapeutic drug monitoring; initial dose 17 mg/kg.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported by Calne in 1978 as the first use of CyA in humans; hepatotoxicity accompanied nephrotoxicity; mentioned as evidence that further careful study of the drug would be required before clinical recommendation.

raw_record.support_text: A number of reports have suggested an association between azathioprine therapy and veno-occlusive disease, especially in renal-transplant recipients. Of 16 reported cases, 10 presented with jaundice as a predominant symptom, 5 had hepatomegaly, 3 ascites, and 1 splenomegaly. All patients became symptomatic 6 months to 9 years after renal transplantation; 8 had hepatic failure, 3 had progressive portal hypertension, 3 died of nonhepatic causes, 1 improved after azathioprine withdrawal, and 1 improved after a portacaval shunt.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Renal-transplant recipients on continuous azathioprine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Veno-occlusive disease characterized by non-thrombotic concentric luminal narrowing of sublobular hepatic veins without large hepatic vein obstruction. 16 reported cases; symptoms 6 months to 9 years after renal transplantation (11 between 12-24 months); among 16: 8 hepatic failure, 3 progressive portal hypertension, 3 died of nonhepatic causes, 1 improved on withdrawal, 1 improved after portacaval shunt. Some acute, some insidious progression to chronic liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 50-year-old woman who developed fever and jaundice with biochemical evidence of severe hepatitis 1 day after her third halogenated anesthetic (halothane), which evolved from acute hepatitis with bridging and piecemeal necrosis to quiescent cirrhosis over 10 months. The authors state that a causal association between halothane anesthesia and acute hepatitis with jaundice is accepted, and report the case as a further example of halothane hepatitis evolving to cirrhosis.

raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old woman with cancer of the cervix; fever and jaundice appeared 1 day after the third halothane anesthetic (cesium implant, March 5, 1979), the previous anesthetics being curettage with halothane (Feb 8) and cone biopsy with enflurane (Feb 23). Liver biopsy 10 days after jaundice onset showed acute hepatitis with bridging necrosis and piecemeal necrosis; a second biopsy after 10 months showed quiescent cirrhosis with residual piecemeal necrosis. Initial labs: serum aspartate transaminase 516 mmol/l (0-48), alkaline phosphatase 278 mmol/l (0-90), bilirubin 356 mmol/l (0-90); positive smooth muscle autoantibody (IgM, 1:320) and thyroid microsomal antibody (1:1,600); negative hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-hepatitis A antibody; no eosinophilia; abstinence from alcohol, no transfusions, no hepatitis contact. Clinical features included jaundice, spider nevi, smooth hepatomegaly (4 cm), and ascites that resolved after 6 weeks; full clinical recovery from hepatitis. Pathogenesis noted as undefined, with both direct toxicity and hypersensitivity implicated.

raw_record.support_text: Ten cases of crizotinib-induced liver toxicity have been reported since 2013, including the present case; all except the present case were hepatocellular-type liver toxicity in eight ALK-rearranged and one ROS1-rearranged NSCLC, and four cases were fulminant hepatitis including three fatal cases. Crizotinib was initially administered at 200-500 mg/day, and the onset of liver enzyme abnormalities ranged from 10 to 70 days (median 29.5 days), with a shorter median onset of 17 days for the three fatal cases. The authors conclude most crizotinib-induced liver toxicity is hepatocellular type, is not associated with initial prescribed dose, and that onset of liver enzyme abnormalities is shorter for fatal cases.

raw_record.extra_details: Initial doses 200-500 mg/day were not associated with injury risk; onset of liver enzyme abnormalities 10-70 days (median 29.5 days); 4 of 10 cases fulminant hepatitis with 3 fatal (median onset 17 days for fatal cases); the present case was ROS1-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma with fever and eosinophilia, interpreted as immune/adaptive-immune-related injury; rechallenge cases: successful desensitization only when starting at ≤50-100 mg/day (two cases), failures at 200-250 mg/day; crizotinib metabolized largely via CYP3A4; liver function tests every two weeks during the first two months recommended.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old HIV patient with anal carcinoma (and cirrhosis manifested by ascites) receiving oral budesonide 9 mg/day together with the CYP3A inhibitors ritonavir, clarithromycin, and fluconazole developed acute toxic hepatitis, with serum alanine aminotransferase flare up to 1,010 U/l and a liver biopsy showing ceroid macrophages and vesicular cytoplasmic inclusion bodies. Withdrawal of all medication lowered transaminases, while rechallenge with budesonide produced a significant increase in alanine aminotransferase. Budesonide trough levels were 8.0 and 7.8 ng/ml, far above reference levels, leading the authors to conclude that concurrent CYP3A inhibitors reduced budesonide phase I metabolism and caused hepatotoxicity, and that serious hepatotoxicity will occur if the budesonide dose is not reduced.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Required co-exposure to three CYP3A inhibitors (ritonavir, clarithromycin, fluconazole); patient with HIV infection, anal carcinoma, and cirrhosis with ascites.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral budesonide 9 mg/day; trough levels 8.0 and 7.8 ng/ml by LC/MS/MS on withdrawal day and one day prior, vs 0.5±0.3 ng/ml in noncirrhotics and 1.5±1.2 ng/ml in cirrhotics on the same dose. ALT flare up to 1,010 U/l; serology for viral and autoimmune hepatitis negative. Biopsy showed ceroid macrophages (sign of passed liver cell necrosis in resorption), no necroinflammatory activity, and vesicular cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in most hepatocytes. Withdrawal of all medication decreased transaminases; rechallenge with budesonide significantly increased ALT. Authors note hepatotoxicity of budesonide had never been reported before.

raw_record.support_text: Four patients aged 3–18 years of multiple ethnicities developed VPA-induced hepatotoxicity, all having received VPA for intractable partial seizures (three with epilepsia partialis continua). The time from VPA exposure to liver failure was 2–3 months, and liver failure was reversible in one patient. Molecular studies revealed homozygous p.R597W or p.A467T POLG mutations in two patients and compound heterozygous mutations (p.A467T/p.Q68X and p.L83P/p.G888S) in the other two; clinical findings and POLG mutations were diagnostic of Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome. The authors conclude VPA dosing at any stage of Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome can precipitate liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Restricted to children/adolescents (age 3–18 years) with POLG mutations/Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome who were treated for intractable partial seizures; three patients also had epilepsia partialis continua.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients across multiple ethnicities. Latency from VPA exposure to liver failure 2–3 months. Liver failure reversible in one patient. Molecular findings: homozygous p.R597W or p.A467T POLG mutations in two patients; compound heterozygous p.A467T/p.Q68X and p.L83P/p.G888S in the other two. Authors propose POLG gene testing consideration before VPA dosing in children/adolescents presenting with intractable seizures, particularly with psychomotor regression, given VPA dosing can precipitate liver failure in Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: The study identified 22 Japanese patients with ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity (cases) and 85 ticlopidine-treated patients with no adverse reactions (controls). The diagnosis of ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity was based on clinical history and laboratory findings (serum bilirubin >1.5 mg/dL or serum AST/ALT at least twice the upper limit of normal), and cases were divided into cholestatic (n=14), mixed (n=5), and hepatocellular (n=3) damage categories per Danan's criteria. There were no differences in age, gender, or ticlopidine dosage between groups; all subjects were Hondo Japanese.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Restricted to Hondo Japanese population; case-control genetic study context.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity cases vs 85 controls without adverse reactions. Diagnosis based on serum bilirubin >1.5 mg/dL or serum AST/ALT at least twice the upper limit of normal. Hepatotoxicity categorized by Danan's criteria as cholestatic (n=14), mixed (n=5), and hepatocellular damage (n=3). No differences in age, gender, or ticlopidine dosage between cases and controls. The study genotyped 12 drug-metabolism/oxidative-stress genes and HLA class I and II loci to assess associations with ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In all five patients with porphyria cutanea tarda treated with chloroquine, there was a 3.5- to 28-fold increase in urinary uroporphyrin excretion; serum transaminases were modestly increased in two patients (M.J., G.G.) and strikingly increased to up to 740, 810, and 670 units in three patients (C.W., C.K., W.C.). The transaminase elevation was transient, occurred during maximum uroporphyrin excretion, and in one patient (C.K.) serum bilirubin rose to 3.1 mg%. In patient W.C., liver biopsy at the time of maximum transaminase elevation showed distinct and rather marked centrilobular hepatic-cell necrosis, which had resolved 22 weeks later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Restricted to patients with porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) receiving chloroquine therapeutically.
raw_record.extra_details: Chloroquine doses of 0.5-1.0 g daily for 2-11 days increased urinary uroporphyrin excretion (up to 107.9 mg/24 hr, 3.5- to 28-fold) with transient SGOT/SGPT elevation; no change in serum bilirubin in two patients, but bilirubin rose to 3.1 mg% in C.K.; centrilobular hepatic-cell necrosis on biopsy in W.C. only, with normalization 22 weeks later. Patients experienced transient fever, malaise, nausea, and anorexia during initial treatment. Readministration of chloroquine to these patients after 1-26 weeks produced no effect (tachyphylaxis).; exact_agent_identity_note: Hepatotoxic transaminase elevation and hepatic necrosis attributed directly to chloroquine administration.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of Chinese patients with neuromyelitis optica treated with azathioprine (2 mg/kg) plus a low-dose corticosteroid, the most common side effects observed using the protocol were hepatotoxicity and neutropenia. Adverse effects were reversible with adjustment of AZA dose. The paper relates AZA metabolism by the TPMT enzyme and genetic TPMT*3C polymorphisms to higher likelihood of adverse effects, and excluded patients with the TPMT mutation from the cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Retrospective cohort of Chinese patients with neuromyelitis optica and normal TPMT genotypes; AZA given at 2 mg/kg in combination with a low-dose corticosteroid; patients with TPMT mutation excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity and neutropenia were the most common side effects of the AZA plus corticosteroid protocol; adverse effects were reversible with AZA dose adjustments. AZA is metabolized by TPMT and its activity is affected by genetic polymorphisms; about 5-10% of the Chinese population carries the TPMT*3C heterozygous or homozygous mutation and is more likely to experience adverse effects.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Retrospective cohort of myasthenia gravis patients treated with azathioprine.
raw_record.extra_details: Overall prevalence of AZA-associated hepatotoxicity was 15.2%. GGT-predominant elevation was the most common pattern, seen in 67.8% of patients with hepatotoxicity; isolated GGT elevation was seen in 6.9%. Hepatotoxicity and/or myelosuppression occurred relatively early (mean 5.3-6.0 weeks, median 3.5-6.0 weeks after initiation). AZA was discontinued in 53 patients (88.3%) with isolated hepatotoxicity, and 84.9% had normalization of test abnormalities after discontinuation; mean time to normalization was 5.8 weeks (median 5.0 weeks). The paper recommends monitoring liver enzymes, especially GGT, weekly for the first 6-8 weeks after AZA initiation.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate is reported to cause hepatic toxicity in rheumatoid arthritis patients: three of eight patients with adverse events in Weinblatt et al.'s study had hepatic toxicity, one with biopsy-proven cirrhosis and repeated transaminase elevations. A separate Australian group reported three male RA patients who developed cirrhosis after methotrexate therapy, with risk factors including advanced age (average 69 years), total methotrexate dose above 3900 mg, and alcohol intake in one case, and estimated a 5-year cumulative cirrhosis incidence of 9.4 per 1000 treated patients. Another cirrhosis case was reported in a male RA patient heterozygous for alpha-1-antitrypsin (PiMZ) deficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rheumatoid arthritis indication; cirrhosis cases occurred in elderly patients (average age 69), after high cumulative methotrexate dose (>3900 mg), with alcohol intake in one case, and in one patient with heterozygous alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiMZ phenotype); subjects with pre-existing risk factors or liver susceptibility.
raw_record.extra_details: Includes biopsy-proven cirrhosis, repeated transaminase elevations (marker of toxicity in ACR guidelines), 5-year cumulative cirrhosis incidence of 9.4 per 1000 treated patients; authors suggest screening methotrexate-treated patients with abnormal liver function tests for alpha-1-antitrypsin levels/phenotype. In a separate long-term prospective biopsy study (Kremer et al., 27 RA patients, mean 6.3 biopsies over 8.2 years, AST checked every 4-6 weeks, dose reduced by 2.5 mg/wk for abnormal AST), Roenigk score increased significantly with time but changes were not clinically relevant and other histologic/ultrastructural scores did not progress; this was deemed reassuring on methotrexate safety in a carefully monitored low-alcohol population.

Transaminase elevations after ingestion are very common, usually spontaneously reversible, and not associated with permanent hepatic injury; persistent transaminase elevations are considered an indication for liver biopsy. Among 98 specimens taken 28-40 months after starting therapy (cumulative dose 750-2,250 mg), 13 showed mild fibrosis and 2 moderate-to-severe fibrosis; no fibrosis in 16 patients with total dose >2,250 mg. 54% of mild-fibrosis patients and both moderate-to-severe-fibrosis patients had below-normal serum albumin during therapy vs 25% of no-fibrosis patients. Treatment: weekly oral low-dose pulse methotrexate, 7.5-15 mg, up to 12-18 weeks clinical trials, some patients on therapy up to 9 years.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 36-year-old pregnant Kenyan woman with Graves' disease (started on propylthiouracil/PTU therapy 3 months prior) who, at 19 weeks' gestation, developed acute liver failure attributed to propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity, requiring liver transplantation. This is framed as the first case of propylthiouracil-induced acute liver failure in a hyperthyroid second-trimester patient resulting in LT.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Second-trimester pregnancy (19 weeks' gestation); comorbid Graves' disease; therapeutic antithyroid treatment for hyperthyroidism.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of ~3 months after starting PTU. Presenting labs: total bilirubin 19.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 17.5 mg/dL, albumin 2.2 gm/dL, INR 2.99 (peak 5.64), PTT 60.2 s, ALP 217 U/L, AST 2549 U/L, ALT 1427 U/L, ammonia 104 umol/L. Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy requiring intubation; intraparenchymal pressure monitoring within normal limits. Attempted plasmapheresis and high-dose IV steroids before emergency listing for LT. Underwent liver transplantation at 19 weeks' gestation; thyroidectomy 2 weeks post-LT; subsequent delivery of a healthy infant at 38 weeks' gestation. Serologic workup for viral, autoimmune, and metabolic etiologies was unrevealing.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 103 selected patients receiving 2 cycles of systemic high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX, 3 g/m2) as ambulatory CNS prophylaxis for aggressive lymphoma, adverse events included 8 (8%) grade III hepatotoxicity events, mostly cytolysis, which was the most frequent grade III adverse event; 8 patients discontinued after 1 cycle for toxicity, including 3 with grade II hepatotoxicity. The paper further states that although severe hepatic cytolysis from MTX is rare, a simple increase in liver enzymes is frequently observed and is usually transient and spontaneously reversible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Selected patient cohort (age < 60, albumin > 34, PS 0-1, normal renal and hepatic function) receiving HD-MTX as ambulatory CNS prophylaxis for aggressive lymphoma after induction therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: HD-MTX at 3 g/m2, 2 planned cycles, ambulatory regimen, 2013-2016; among 103 patients, 92 (89%) completed 2 cycles; grade III hepatotoxicity (mostly cytolysis) in 8 (8%) events was the most frequent grade III AE; 3 grade II hepatotoxicity events contributed to discontinuation after 1 cycle; toxicity graded by NCI-CTCAE v4.0; MTX clearance not monitored; 84% grade I/II and 16% grade III/IV AEs overall. HD-MTX used across indications incl. osteosarcoma, ALL, CNS lymphoma.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 43-year-old woman who developed severe liver injury ~6 weeks after self-administering an artemisinin herbal supplement (125 mg orally two or three times daily for general health maintenance) that reportedly contained no other active ingredients. The temporal relationship to artemisinin intake and lack of other potential etiologies suggested HDS-induced liver injury secondary to artemisinin; the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score was 7, suggesting a 'probable' association. The liver-injury pattern at presentation was hepatocellular (R ratio >10), evolving into a prolonged cholestatic phase, with liver biopsy showing cholestatic hepatitis (marked cholestasis with mild portal and lobular inflammation), and the patient improved after discontinuation with normal liver tests one year later; rechallenge was not performed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-administered herbal supplement taken without medical supervision; monotherapy with reportedly no other active ingredients; no competing etiologies identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 125 mg orally two or three times daily for ~6 weeks for general health maintenance. Presentation: 1-week history of arthralgia and jaundice; total bilirubin 15.4 mg/dL, ALT 675 U/L, AST 175 U/L, ALP 208 U/L, INR 1.1. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with marked cholestasis and mild portal and lobular inflammation. RUCAM score 7 (probable). Pattern at onset hepatocellular (R ratio at onset >10) evolving into prolonged cholestatic phase. Improvement and normal liver tests 1 year after discontinuation; rechallenge not performed.

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective BICU study 01/01/07-30/06/18 including 1640 patients; annual mean ketamine consumption per patient used as population exposure index; three periods compared (P1 2007-2013 historical, P2 2013-2017 from first ISC case, P3 2017-2018 with ketamine restriction). raw_record.support_text: The paper states that halothane causes two types of hepatotoxicity in humans: a milder form (minor serum transaminase increases, ~20% of patients, attributed to cytotoxic effects of halothane metabolites) and the severe halothane hepatitis (1 in 10,000) that can lead to massive hepatic necrosis and death, possibly via an immune response to halothane-modified (trifluoroacetylated) liver proteins. Among 20 patients with clinically defined halothane hepatitis (otherwise unexplained hepatitis within 28 days of halothane anaesthesia), 13 had liver failure and 12 died; 17 (85%) had autoantibodies to human liver microsomal carboxylesterase (CES1), which the authors report as a target antigen localized to the centrilobular region, consistent with the pattern of halothane hepatitis damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severe idiosyncratic form typically followed repeated prior halothane anaesthesia (median 2 exposures, interval from 7 days to 10 years); mild intrinsic-like form in ~20% of patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old woman with concurrent squamous cell carcinoma of the anus and renal cell carcinoma developed severe hepatotoxicity while receiving paracetamol at recommended dosage (4 g daily) under medical supervision in hospital, without enzyme-inducing agents. She was severely malnourished and had recently fasted. Four days after starting paracetamol her ALT rose to 269 IU/L and AST to 252 IU/L; the next day she had nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort and tender hepatomegaly, with ALT 5920 IU/L, AST 4875 IU/L, bilirubin 30 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 169 IU/L, prothrombin time 20 s (control 13 s) and blood glucose 2.3 mmol/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severe malnutrition, weight loss and a recent ~20 h fasting period at therapeutic exposure; 53-year-old female hospitalized with concurrent anal squamous cell carcinoma and renal cell carcinoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of severe paracetamol-related hepatotoxicity based on highly typical enzyme pattern, with differential diagnosis of ischaemic liver injury excluded (no hypotension) and other medications considered unlikely; treated with N-acetylcysteine and glucose, normalizing over 4 weeks; hepatitis and other viral/metabolic/immune/her metastatic causes excluded. Authors attribute injury to glutathione depletion and shunting of metabolism from glucuronidation to microsomal oxidation producing N-acetyl-p-benzoquinonimine (NAPQI), and conclude the injury is dose-dependent rather than idiosyncratic; a later interval of lower-dose paracetamol (1.3-2.6 g daily up to three times weekly) after a further fasting period produced no liver injury. Patient was not encephalopathic and recovered.

raw_record.support_text: In a 30-patient series treated with BCNU (carmustine) for malignant tumors, hepatitis was severe in four patients and fatal in two: one melanoma patient given BCNU 1,200 mg/m² developed liver necrosis one month after treatment and died two weeks later in hepatic coma, with autopsy showing central lobular necrosis consistent with a toxic drug insult to the liver; one glioma patient given BCNU 600 mg/m² twice died of portal hypertension with ascites and liver dysfunction two months after the second course; and a glioma patient and a hepatoma patient had severe but reversible hepatitis. Overall, 14 of 30 evaluable patients (46%) had abnormal liver function tests unexplained by their primary disease, with toxicity occurring at all dose levels and most pronounced in hepatocellular enzymes (SGOT/SGPT).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severely ill patients with malignant tumors (glioma, melanoma, hepatoma, colorectal carcinoma) receiving concurrently dexamethasone (8-64 mg/day) and, in some, prophylactic nystatin/trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; two additional patients had liver-test abnormalities possibly related to underlying hepatoma or colorectal carcinoma.
raw_record.extra_details: BCNU (carmustine) at cumulative doses of 600-1,200 mg/m². Of 30 evaluable patients, 14 (46%) had one or more abnormal liver function tests (SGOT, LDH, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) unexplained by primary disease; in 10 of these, elevations were minimal (<2-3x SGOT/alkaline phosphatase), self-limited and asymptomatic, occurring a median of 3 months after treatment (range 2-6 months). Four patients had severe hepatitis, fatal in two (one with hepatic necrosis/central lobular necrosis and hepatic coma, autopsy-consistent with toxic drug insult; one with fatal portal hypertension, ascites and liver dysfunction). Eleven patients were evaluable at 3-4 months and 8 (73%) had abnormal liver tests; alkaline phosphatase abnormalities occurred later and resolved more slowly; hyperbilirubinemia occurred only in the four severe-hepatitis patients.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a severely malnourished 53-year-old woman who developed severe hepatotoxicity while receiving paracetamol at recommended dosage (4 g daily) following a period of fasting, in the absence of enzyme-inducing agents. A subsequent paracetamol exposure of up to 2.6 g daily thrice weekly, in the setting of ongoing malnutrition and fasting, did not lead to recurrent liver damage, leading the authors to conclude that paracetamol-related liver damage within recommended dosage guidelines can be dose-dependent rather than necessarily idiosyncratic in the setting of recent fasting and severe malnutrition.

raw_record.extra_details: Subsequent paracetamol exposure up to 2.6 g daily thrice weekly with ongoing malnutrition and fasting did not cause recurrent liver damage (failed rechallenge). raw_record.support_text: In pexidartinib registration trials, liver injury with jaundice developed in 5% of patients, with onset usually between 2 and 6 weeks and a pattern of liver enzyme elevations that was either mixed or solely cholestatic. Liver biopsy documented both bile duct injury and loss, and three patients treated for conditions other than tenosynovial giant cell tumors developed bile duct paucity and features of vanishing bile duct syndrome, leading to liver transplantation in one subject. The drug carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity requiring LIT monitoring, and should be avoided in patients with pre-existing elevations in ALT, bilirubin, or ALP or active liver/biliary disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Should be avoided in patients with pre-existing increased ALT, total or direct bilirubin, or active liver or biliary tract disease including increased ALP.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT elevation common in 50-90% of patients (G3/4: 12-20%); ALP elevation in up to 20%; jaundice in 5% of registration-trial patients; onset 2-6 weeks; biopsy showed bile duct injury and loss; three patients developed bile duct paucity/vanishing bile duct syndrome, one requiring liver transplantation; boxed warning for hepatotoxicity with recommended LIT monitoring and dose-holding/reduction rules; rechallenge at reduced dose may cause recurrence of increased ALT, bilirubin or ALP. Indication: tenosynovial giant cell tumors.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 50-year-old patient who, after accidental re-exposure to metamizole, developed a cholestatic liver disease within a few hours with a rapid and strong rise in bilirubin and elevations of transaminases (GOT 147, GPT 222, γ-GT 380, alkaline phosphatase 497 U/l; total bilirubin 43.9 mg/dl). Using metamizole and its four known metabolites (4-aminoantipyrine, 4-methylaminoantipyrine, 4-acetylaminoantipyrine, 4-formylaminoantipyrine) in the lymphocyte transformation test, circulating lymphocytes specifically sensitized against the metabolite 4-methylaminoantipyrine were demonstrated, indicating that allergic mechanisms can with high probability be considered the cause of the liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single 50-year-old patient with prior metamizole exposure (about 30 tablets of Dolo-Attritin 450 mg in 1984, plus 1986 Dolo-Neurobion (paracetamol) and Imbun 500 (ibuprofen)); current reaction followed accidental re-exposure within 5 hours, consistent with prior sensitization (allergic idiosyncratic reaction).
raw_record.extra_details: Allergic (immune-mediated) genesis demonstrated by lymphocyte transformation test performed five times over 232 days; first three tests positive with stimulation indices up to 2.3, showing sensitization to the metabolite 4-methylaminoantipyrine (formed first within 1-1.5 hours and representing about 40% of the four plasma metabolites). raw_record.support_text: Case 3: a 53-year-old housewife received erythromycin (600 mg, 3 days) for a sore throat in October 1976. Hemorrhagic papules appeared on skin and oral mucosa 10 days later and jaundice 20 days later. After steroid therapy her course (except jaundice) improved. On admission abnormal data included serum total bilirubin 29.1 mg/dl (direct 24.3), alkaline phosphatase 1054 IU/l, and cholesterol 1062 mg/dl (continued in next paragraph). A diagnosis of drug-induced intrahepatic cholestasis was made, with mechanical obstruction of the extrahepatic biliary tree excluded at laparotomy; a wedge biopsy showed marked centrolobular bile stasis with feathery degeneration of hepatocytes and mild septal fibrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single 53-year-old female case; co-exposure to steroid therapy; competing mechanical obstruction excluded at laparotomy.
raw_record.extra_details: Erythromycin 600 mg for 3 days for sore throat; jaundice appeared 20 days after drug exposure. Lab values: serum total bilirubin 29.1 mg/dl (direct 24.3 mg/dl), alkaline phosphatase 1054 IU/l, cholesterol 1062 mg/dl. Biopsy showed marked centrolobular bile stasis with feathery degeneration of hepatocytes and mild septal fibrosis; many portal tracts devoid of interlobular bile ducts with acidophilic degeneration and occasional rupture. Elevation of alkaline phosphatase, cholesterol, and bilirubin remained unchanged for 41 months with slight fluctuation; patient alive. Case table labels the diagnosis 'chronic intrahepatic cholestasis** = probably drug-induced'.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatitis was diagnosed when abnormal liver function studies developed that had not been present before 6-mercaptopurine initiation. Although hepatitis occurred in 11 patients, only 1 patient had hepatitis shown to be directly induced by 6-mercaptopurine: a 55-year-old man with intractable ulcerative colitis requiring continuous steroid therapy who became icteric about 6 months after starting 6-mercaptopurine. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with inflammation suggestive of drug hepatitis; liver tests returned to normal on withdrawal, and jaundice recurred upon self-rechallenge and resolved again on stopping 6-mercaptopurine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single 55-year-old patient with ulcerative colitis requiring continuous steroid therapy; patient refused surgery and self-rechallenged; jaundice and cholestatic changes on biopsy with recurrence on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Only 1 of 11 total hepatitis cases during 6-mercaptopurine therapy could be shown as directly drug-induced; the other 10 cases were attributed to infection. Icterus appeared ~6 weeks into the fourth month (about 6 months) of therapy. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with inflammation suggestive of drug hepatitis; liver function tests normalized on withdrawal; jaundice recurred on rechallenge and resolved on stopping again. Overall 6-mercaptopurine toxicity directly induced in 30 patients (7.6%), all reversed on withdrawal with no deaths.

Liver enzymes slowly returned toward normal values after phenprocoumon was discontinued and replaced by i.v. then subcutaneous heparin.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is described as virtually the only drug implicated in drug-induced liver injury in developing countries. Fifteen to 20% of individuals receiving isoniazid as a single agent for tuberculosis prophylaxis may develop increased transaminases, which usually stabilize or improve, so that <1% may develop severe hepatic necrosis; a large tuberculosis public health clinic recently estimated severe liver injury at 1:1000, with 11 of 11,141 patients developing isoniazid-induced liver disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single agent for tuberculosis prophylaxis
raw_record.extra_details: 15-20% of recipients develop increased transaminases that stabilize or improve; <1% may develop severe hepatic necrosis; recent estimate of severe liver injury 1:1000, i.e., 11 of 11,141 patients in a large tuberculosis public health clinic. Also reported as implicated in 5 otherwise presumed idiosyncratic DILI cases in the United States Acute Liver Failure Study Group registry (1998-2001).

raw_record.support_text: This is a case report of an adult female with severe jaundice after taking ibuprofen who developed persistent cholestasis, hyperlipidemia, and vanishing bile duct syndrome. The DILI from ibuprofen was identified by clinical features and liver biopsy, with a Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score of 6 and pathological features of cholestasis with stage four drug-induced injury as well as loss of bile duct structures. Laboratory abnormalities improved after cessation of ibuprofen, and a second liver biopsy on day 213 confirmed vanishing bile duct syndrome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case in a 40s female, no prior liver disease; ibuprofen 300 mg bid by mouth 2-3 days per month for menalgia; concurrent oral acarbose and metformin for type II diabetes.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 6; liver biopsy showed cholestasis with stage four drug-induced injury and loss of bile duct structures; persistently high bilirubin with hyperlipidemia over about one month; second biopsy on day 213 confirmed VBDS; negative autoantibodies (AMA-M2, ASMA, RO-52, LKM, SLA, anti-glycoprotein-210); jaundice, fatigue, dark urine; no ascites or hepatomegaly; spleen palpable 3 cm below left costal margin; symptoms began ~30 days progressive jaundice after intermittent ibuprofen over six months. Background notes ibuprofen may produce unpredictable, idiosyncratic type B reactions (hypersensitivity reaction).

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with type 2 diabetes developed liver injury 49 days after starting ipragliflozin (50 mg/day) to replace sulfonylurea: AST rose from 13 to 622 U/L, ALT from 9 to 266 U/L, ALP from 239 to 752 U/L, and γ-GTP from 19 to 176 U/L, with total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV serologies were negative, while a lymphocyte transformation test for ipragliflozin was positive. CT showed mild fatty liver. After discontinuing ipragliflozin with liver supportive therapy, he was discharged 18 days later with AST and ALT reduced to 20 and 13 U/L. The authors describe this as a case of ipragliflozin-induced liver injury, emphasizing the need to monitor liver function during SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case in a 75-year-old Japanese male with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and mild fatty liver (NAFLD background); sulfonylurea therapy had been replaced by ipragliflozin.
raw_record.extra_details: Ipragliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor) 50 mg/day; liver injury developed 49 days after start. Peak AST 622 U/L, ALT 266 U/L, ALP 752 U/L, γ-GTP 176 U/L; total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL (no jaundice), ZTT 3.5 U, TTT 0.4 U. Negative IgM hepatitis A antibody, hepatitis B antigen, hepatitis C virus antibody, IgM CMV antibody, and IgM EB VCA antibody; positive lymphocyte transformation test for ipragliflozin. Abdominal CT showed mild fatty liver with no nodular lesions. Patient was admitted for liver supportive therapy and discharged 18 days later with AST 20 U/L and ALT 13 U/L after discontinuation. Report recommends monitoring liver function during SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that cholestatic hepatitis is a rare side effect of phenprocoumon, and suggests an allergic (hypersensitivity) origin based on the presence of eosinophilia. This is drawn from a single case report in a 78-year-old woman who developed hepatitis after a first phenprocoumon course (hepatitis serology negative) and then cholestatic jaundice with rapid deterioration after rechallenge following a second knee prosthesis implantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case report in a 78-year-old woman receiving phenprocoumon for thromboembolism prophylaxis after total knee prosthesis implantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis occurred 10 weeks after the first phenprocoumon course; after rechallenge (second knee prosthesis 6 weeks before admission) cholestatic jaundice with rapid deterioration of general state developed. Hepatitis A/B/C serology was negative; elevated eosinophil count. Bilirubin 11.5 mg/dl; transaminases, gamma-GT and alkaline phosphatase increased; Quick value below 8%. Liver biopsy showed severe acute viral-type hepatitis with discrete eosinophilic infiltration. All drugs were stopped; prednisone (initial 50 mg/d, stepwise reduced) was given; cholinesterase parameters normalized and the patient was discharged in improved condition. Cholestatic hepatitis considered a rare side effect with suspected allergic/hypersensitivity genesis.

raw_record.support_text: A case of self-limited hepatitis with an influenza-like reaction to hydroxyurea therapy is presented. The association was strongly supported by recurrence on rechallenge with the drug. The patient presented with biochemical evidence of acute hepatocellular damage along with fever, malaise, drowsiness and delirium; symptoms and transaminase/bilirubin elevations settled within 36 hours of ceasing hydroxyurea, and a 1 g oral rechallenge on day seven re-triggered rigors, malaise, tachycardia (130 beats/minute), fever (40°C), drowsiness, delirium and mild re-elevation of hepatic enzymes within 5 hours, with liver function normal two weeks later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case report; low-dose hydroxyurea used for severe psoriasis in a patient for whom methotrexate was contraindicated.
raw_record.extra_details: Influenza-like reaction with fever, rigors/chills, malaise, drowsiness and delirium accompanying biochemical acute hepatocellular damage. Onset within 5 hours of ingestion and resolution within 36 hours of drug cessation; positive rechallenge with 1 g oral hydroxyurea on day seven re-triggered symptoms plus mild re-elevation of hepatic enzymes (resolved within 36 hours; liver function normal two weeks later). Self-limited hepatitis. The paper notes only one prior report of hepatic dysfunction caused by hydroxyurea, giving no details, and that Moschella reported an influenza-like reaction (fever, chills, malaise) in 6 of 60 psoriasis patients on hydroxyurea with no hepatic problems noted.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old woman with mild depressive episode was started on capsule fluoxetine 20 mg. Within 10 days she developed decreased appetite, malaise, and rashes, with serum bilirubin 4.34 mg/dl, glutamic-pyruvic transaminase 4790 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 316 IU/L; no other medication or comorbidity was present. Considering fluoxetine-induced liver injury and rashes, fluoxetine was stopped and prednisolone 30 mg was started; she improved significantly and liver functions normalized within 6 months, after which escitalopram 10 mg was given successfully.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case report; no other co-medications or comorbidities identified; possible role of genetic factors suggested.
raw_record.extra_details: Fluoxetine 20 mg capsule for mild depressive episode; onset of symptoms within 10 days; serum bilirubin 4.34 mg/dl, glutamic-pyruvic transaminase (transaminase) 4790 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 316 IU/L; concurrent rash over face, trunk, and upper limbs; treated with prednisolone 30 mg tapered over 15 days; significant clinical and laboratory improvement; liver functions normal within 6 months; switched to escitalopram 10 mg which was well tolerated. Dechallenge and rechallenge-with-different-agent support the attribution. Hamilton Depression Rating Scale score 12 at baseline.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of risperidone-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity in a 37-year-old male who developed a rapid increase in liver enzymes and cholestatic parameters after starting risperidone for paranoid psychosis. Work-up for other aetiologies was negative, and a percutaneous liver biopsy was consistent with drug-induced liver injury and cholestasis. Liver function tests returned to near-normal values over one month after discontinuance of all anti-psychotic agents.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case with a history of inactive Crohn's disease; subsequent exposure to haloperidol (10 mg/day) and later olanzapine also worsened the already-pathological liver tests, though risperidone is the designated culprit.
raw_record.extra_details: Risperidone (Risperdal) dosed 2 mg/day titrated to 6 mg/day within a week for paranoid psychosis; elevated AST (42 U/l), ALT (77 U/l), γGT (367 U/l) noted after 3 days, increasing over 10 days until discontinuation. On admission: AST 96, ALT 209, γGT 254, alkaline phosphatase 634 U/l, bilirubin 1.6 mg/dl, serum lipase 239 U/l. Percutaneous liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis: bile pigments in hepatocytes, portal and peri-cholangiolar inflammatory infiltrates, excess eosinophils; no autoimmune hepatitis, fibrosis, or cirrhosis. Viral and other aetiologies excluded; values returned near-normal over one month. Authors recommend monitoring cholestatic parameters plus liver enzymes at initiation and during the first weeks of risperidone intake.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a 51-year-old woman admitted with phenprocoumon-induced hepatitis. Three weeks after re-initiating phenprocoumon anticoagulation her transaminases rose (ASAT 588 U/I, ALAT 801 U/I) with elevated bilirubin (3.0 mg/dl), γ-GT and alkaline phosphatase; no other drugs were given that could have caused the liver damage. Liver biopsy revealed severe acute hepatitis of viral type with centrilobular liver cell necrosis. After phenprocoumon was discontinued, liver function improved within ten days. The patient previously tolerated a 6-month phenprocoumon course in 1994 without complications, and no hepatotoxicity was observed during six months of subsequent warfarin use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case; onset followed a prior phenprocoumon course (6 months in 1994) that was well tolerated; patient heterozygous for factor V R506Q and prothrombin G20210A mutations.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis began three weeks after re-initiation of anticoagulation; ASAT 588 U/I, ALAT 801 U/I, bilirubin 3.0 mg/dl, γ-GT 165 U/I, alkaline phosphatase 376 U/I; platelet count 82,000/µl; biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis of viral type with centrilobular liver cell necrosis; improvement within ten days of dechallenge (ASAT 131 U/I, ALAT 289 U/I, γ-GT 109 U/I, platelets 128,000/µl); viral and autoimmune serology negative; no cross-reactivity with warfarin.

raw_record.support_text: The DILI network collected detailed clinical data on 1212 patients with DILI between 2004 and 2012; of 41 patients in whom cephalosporins were implicated as primary agents, 33 were formally adjudicated as having cephalosporin-induced DILI. Nineteen of these patients developed clinically apparent DILI after a single intravenous dose of cefazolin, with all developing self-limited liver injury 3-23 days after receiving cefazolin during surgery, often during a minor outpatient procedure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single intravenous dose given during surgery, often a minor outpatient procedure; self-limited course.
raw_record.extra_details: 19 patients developed clinically apparent DILI after a single IV dose of cefazolin; part of a cohort of 41 patients with cephalosporins implicated as primary DILI agents (33 formally adjudicated), drawn from the DILI network database of 1212 DILI patients (2004-2012). Injury appeared 3-23 days after dosing with a reported latency period of 20 days. Clinical features included itching, jaundice, nausea, fever, and rash. No deaths or severe outcomes were reported for the cefazolin group.

raw_record.support_text: The project's impetus was a recent local case of iatrogenic hepatotoxicity secondary to Paracetamol reported within the trust, prompting a Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) audit cycle. The audit identified two problems with Paracetamol prescribing: patients were not always weighed in a timely fashion leading to incorrect dosing, and healthcare professionals lacked knowledge that IV Paracetamol is dose-adjusted for patients weighing less than 50 kg. Initial audit findings showed 25% of patients were on an inappropriate dose of IV Paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 19 patients with lipoatrophic diabetes treated with troglitazone (continued beyond the study period), one patient (U1) developed fatigue and an eightfold increase in ALT concentration after 10 months of therapy. While the patient was on troglitazone, ALT was within normal range 3 weeks before the elevation was detected; GGT, bilirubin, and synthetic function remained normal; viral hepatitis A, B, and C serology and autoantibodies were negative. A liver biopsy performed 3 days after troglitazone discontinuation showed an eosinophilic infiltrate consistent with toxicity due to hypersensitivity to the drug. Troglitazone was stopped and aminotransferase concentrations returned to normal 3 months later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single reported case in a patient with lipoatrophic diabetes receiving prolonged troglitazone treatment continued beyond a clinical study.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency about 10 months; ALT rose eightfold (prior transient ALT rise to 1134 nkat/L, normal <668 nkat/L, occurred 3 months before troglitazone started and normalized). Liver biopsy 3 days after discontinuation (6 days after peak ALT) showed chronic inflammatory infiltrate with many eosinophils and moderate piecemeal necrosis, small foci of lobular inflammation and hepatocellular apoptosis, preserved architecture, no steatosis, confluent necrosis, or fibrosis; electron microscopy showed no mitochondrial or peroxisomal abnormalities. Dechallenge led to slow improvement with ALT normalization 3 months after stopping; hypersensitivity/eosinophilic infiltrate attributed to the drug.

raw_record.support_text: An 84-year-old woman developed severe acute hepatitis 3 days after starting paroxetine 10 mg/day for chronic mild depression, with markedly elevated transaminases (AST 2208 IU/L, ALT 2110 IU/L), hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged INR (2.13), hyperammonemia and stage I hepatic encephalopathy. Viral, autoimmune and metabolic liver disease were excluded, and use of the Naranjo probability scale suggested that paroxetine was the probable cause of hepatitis (total score 7). The injury resolved after discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single reported case in an 84-year-old woman with chronic atrial fibrillation, arterial hypertension, brain atherosclerosis and prior transient ischemic attacks, taking concurrent verapamil, ticlopidine, spironolactone and nimodipine; a role for drug-drug interaction was considered unlikely by the authors.
raw_record.extra_details: Paroxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; hepatotoxicity is reported as very rare with only a few prior severe cases, all with favorable prognosis after discontinuation. Injury appeared 3 days after first dose at 10 mg/day. ALT rose to 2110 IU/L, AST to 2208 IU/L with normal alkaline phosphatase, mild GGT increase, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, INR 2.13, ammonia 335 mg/dL, hepatic encephalopathy stage I. Naranjo score 7. Patient advised to avoid future paroxetine and other SSRIs. Paroxetine is metabolized by CYP2D6; the authors note the mechanism is idiosyncratic.

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, initially controlled by diet and with normal liver function, began repaglinide (1 mg/day) and the dose was increased to 2 mg/day one month later. He presented with a 2-week history of itching and jaundice and was admitted to hospital; he denied any other drugs or herbal remedies.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-case report in an elderly (72-year-old) male with type 2 diabetes; findings may not generalize to the general population.
raw_record.extra_details: Repaglinide doses 1 mg/day increasing to 2 mg/day; latency of about 1-2 months before presentation; 2-week history of pruritus and jaundice. Labs: AST 83 U/l (<37), ALT 183 U/l (<40), ALP 307 U/l (<136), GGT 303 U/l (<85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl with direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dl, creatinine 1.3 mg/dl. Viral serology and autoantibody screening negative; MR cholangiography normal. Liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with mild bile-duct proliferation and moderate inflammatory infiltrate (mainly lymphocytes with some eosinophils) and hepatocyte ballooning. Rapid normalization of laboratory findings within one month after repaglinide discontinuation (positive dechallenge). Authors state this is the first published report of cholestatic hepatitis related to repaglinide, causality strongly supported by temporal eligibility, exclusion of alternatives, histology, and rapid improvement after withdrawal; presence of eosinophils suggests a possible immune mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old Japanese woman with relapsed ALK-rearranged NSCLC received crizotinib (250 mg twice daily) as second-line treatment. On day 15-16, she developed fever and rising AST/ALT (peak AST 437 IU/l, ALT 1,096 IU/l), with increased gamma-glutamyltransferase and total bilirubin but no rise in alkaline phosphatase; hepatocellular injury was suspected and hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus were excluded. Crizotinib was discontinued and symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved. The paper frames this as crizotinib-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-patient case report in a 51-year-old non-smoking Japanese woman with relapsed ALK-rearranged NSCLC treated with crizotinib as second-line systemic chemotherapy following carboplatin/pemetrexed.
raw_record.extra_details: Crizotinib 250 mg twice daily; first dose held on day 2 for abdominal pain, nausea and grade 3 diarrhea, then re-introduced at 250 mg once daily with dexamethasone 3 mg daily. On the second exposure the patient developed fever and nausea on day 15, crizotinib was stopped on day 16; peak AST 437 IU/l on day 18 and peak ALT 1,096 IU/l on day 19; gamma-glutamyltransferase and total bilirubin rose to grade 2, alkaline phosphatase did not increase; contrast-enhanced CT and ultrasonography showed no other cause; hepatitis A, B, C, EBV and CMV excluded. Abnormalities resolved fully without increase of steroids after 1 month. Later the patient was rechallenged with desensitized oral crizotinib starting at 50 mg/day (capsule contents dissolved in sterile water and diluted) with betamethasone 2 mg; grade 1 hepatotoxicity on day 12 of desensitization, then ursodeoxycholic acid and glycyrrhizic acid started and no further hepatotoxicity observed; achieved partial response.

raw_record.support_text: RUCAM causality assessment rated topiramate as a probable causal agent for acute liver failure in this patient. The timing of the elevated topiramate level, rapid decrease in ALT after discontinuation, and lack of a concomitant drug trigger supported the link; the total RUCAM score of 8 points placed the case on the border between 'probable' and 'highly probable' topiramate causally related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-patient case with chronic 10-year topiramate exposure; the drug level was >4-fold higher than it had ever been, with no medication or supplement changes, hypothesized to mimic a 'new drug' idiosyncratic-like effect.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM total score 8 (border of 'probable' and 'highly probable'); elevated ammonia level (ammonia >1300) also cited as supporting topiramate-induced hepatic toxicity, proposed via inhibition of type V mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase and reduced carbamyl phosphate synthesis in the urea cycle; both ALF and topiramate can cause hyperammonemia independently. Histology showed a hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern with microvesicular steatosis, consistent with DILI; no well-established characteristic pathology for topiramate hepatotoxicity exists. Three prior case reports of DILI attributed primarily to topiramate: Bjoro et al. (adult ALF requiring liver allograft 4 months after topiramate added to carbamazepine and days after a dose increase), Doan et al. (ALF in a young adult with topiramate added to valproate, liver tests corrected after discontinuation), and del Val Antonana et al. (hepatotoxicity in a 16-year-old male on topiramate monotherapy with elevated transaminases and coagulopathy but no hyperammonemia, resolving 2 weeks after discontinuation). Topiramate is an antiepileptic/metabolism inducer of CYP3A4; DILI mechanism not well understood.

raw_record.support_text: Six cases of flupirtine-associated liver injury (4 female, 2 male, aged 48-78) were described. One patient on flupirtine monotherapy presented with jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy and coagulopathy, requiring orthotopic liver transplantation for acute liver failure. Three presented with jaundice and mild coagulopathy without encephalopathy, and two were asymptomatic with elevated aminotransferases on routine controls. After discontinuation of flupirtine, aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin normalized. None had preexisting liver disease. One patient was accidentally re-exposed to flupirtine after 4 years and again developed elevated aminotransferases.

raw_record.support_text: Histologic alterations in 31 patients with hepatic injury after alpha-methyldopa exposure were investigated: 7 developed liver injury within 6 months and 24 after several years (mean 5 years). Short-term-exposed patients had acute and severe hepatitis, four with icterus, and two died of hepatic coma; long-term-exposed patients had fatty accumulation and increased fibrous trabeculae. The authors conclude that alpha-methyldopa may induce hepatocellular injury after both short- and long-term exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Some patients received concurrent therapy with digoxin, nitroglycerine, furosemide, glibenclamide, and occasional analgesics, kept unchanged during the study; none were alcohol abusers.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 31 patients (20 women, 11 men) with alpha-methyldopa-induced liver injury; diagnosis based on case history, biochemistry, serology, histology, and follow-up after drug withdrawal. Seven patients developed injury within 6 months (short-term) and 24 after several years (mean 5 years, long-term). Short-term group: marked parenchymatous degeneration, focal/confluent/massive necrosis and inflammation, acute and severe hepatitis, 4 with icterus, 2 died of hepatic coma. Long-term group: fatty accumulation and increased fibrous trabeculae, initially mild dyspepsia, nausea, colics. Histology findings included reactive hepatitis, chronic active/persistent hepatitis-like reactions, and massive necrosis (up to 47%). Liver function differences in serum albumin, bilirubin, and transferases; no change in alkaline phosphatase or Thrombotest. Patients 28D and 31D died.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials, treatment with the nonspecific MTP inhibitor lomitapide (formerly AEGR-733) induced an increase in hepatic steatosis in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. The liver-fat effect was highly variable (some patients had no change in liver content, others a large increase); liver-fat content returned to normal within a few months of drug discontinuation, and the drug was thereafter studied only at higher dosages in these patients. Separately, in 56 hypercholesterolemia patients studied by Samaha et al., hepatic fat was not assessed, but transaminase elevation occurred in 32% (18/56) and resulted in drug discontinuation in 9 patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Studied in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia; after the initial trial the higher doses were reserved for these patients where LDL-C reduction was judged to outweigh potential steatosis; in some trials lomitapide was given alongside other lipid-modifying medication (including LDL apheresis in a phase III study).
raw_record.extra_details: MTP inhibitor (formerly AEGR-733). Hepatic steatosis by MRI ranged from <10% to 40% (normal <1%) and was consistent with animal findings. MTP inhibition attenuates hepatic VLDL output, resulting in hepatic lipid accumulation and consequently hepatotoxicity. Variable effect (some patients no change in liver fat, others large increase); alcohol use in some cases may have influenced the effect, and liver fat returned to normal within a few months of discontinuation. Initial dose-escalation study: 6 patients, 0.1 mg/kg/day gave ~50% LDL-C reduction; subsequent trial: 10 patients up to 60 mg/day (~44% LDL-C reduction); Samaha et al.: 56 patients on lomitapide monotherapy (5.0/7.5/10 mg daily) with LDL-C reductions of 19%/26%/30%; transaminase elevation occurred in 32% (18/56) with discontinuation in 9. Authors raised the concern that lifelong accumulation of hepatic fat could progress to hepatic fibrosis.

raw_record.extra_details: 90 patients developed AILI among the cohort. Liver injury grades: 77.8% grade 4, 21.1% grade 3, 1.1% grade 2 (mean grade 3.76 ± 0.45). Grade 4 AILI showed mean ALT and AST rises of 8.53 ± 4.33 and 7.67 ± 5.12 fold from baseline. Predictors of severe (grade 4) AILI on multivariate analysis: inotropic support (OR 4.03, P=0.034), congestive hepatomegaly (OR 2.69, P=0.012), increasing baseline total bilirubin (OR 2.02, P=0.001), and increasing dose of amiodarone (OR 1.002, P=0.002). ROC: total bilirubin >1.3 mg/dl predicted AILI (AUC 0.72, 95% CI 0.64-0.79); >1.6 mg/dl predicted severe AILI (AUC 0.67, 95% CI 0.6-0.74). Post-amiodarone ALT/AST correlated with baseline ALT, AST, total and direct bilirubin, and ejection fraction.

raw_record.support_text: Among women who initiated nevirapine (NVP), 2 of 42 pregnant women (4.8%) and 43 of 211 nonpregnant women (20.4%) developed either rash or hepatitis after starting NVP (rate ratio 0.234 pregnant vs nonpregnant, 95% CI 0.0516-0.797). One pregnant woman developed grade 2 hepatitis and one grade 1 rash; both resolved upon NVP discontinuation. Two nonpregnant women with time to AE >90 days both had hepatitis, one also with lactic acidosis, and both normalized their transaminases upon medication discontinuation. None of the cohort developed fulminant hepatic failure or died.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study population of HIV-infected women starting NVP with standard dose escalation (lead-in 200 mg/day then 200 mg BID); all women also took other antiretrovirals, most commonly zidovudine/lamivudine (Combivir). Findings compare pregnant vs nonpregnant women.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 21 pregnant and 211 nonpregnant women. Onset within the first 30 days for 31 of 41 nonpregnant women with known onset, days 31-60 for 8, and day 408 and 487 for 2. Serious (grade 3-4) AEs occurred in 16 nonpregnant women (2 of whom had both rash and hepatitis: one grade 3 rash/hepatitis, one grade 1 rash + grade 2 hepatitis) and none in pregnant women. No significant interaction found for baseline CD4, age, or sulfa medication use, and no fulminant hepatic failure or death in the cohort. Package insert notes female gender and CD4 >250 associated with greatest hepatotoxicity risk.

raw_record.support_text: In a South African randomized study of HIV-infected patients, early hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or greater increase in serum aminotransferase levels within the first 12 weeks) occurred in 17% of patients in the nevirapine group. Fatal drug-related liver failure occurred in two of 385 women receiving nevirapine. The study population consisted of a high proportion of women with relatively high baseline CD4 cell counts (mean 398 cells/µl), and stavudine was part of the NRTI backbone of the regimen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study restricted largely to women with relatively high baseline CD4 cell counts (mean 398 cells/µl); stavudine was part of the NRTI backbone co-administered with nevirapine.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized comparison with efavirenz; early hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or greater aminotransferase rise within 12 weeks) in 17% of the nevirapine group versus 0% in the efavirenz group; fatal drug-related liver failure in 2 of 385 women. A separate study reported that among HIV patients one-third of all liver toxicities leading to hospital admission were associated with nevirapine use, and 80% of these occurred in patients with underlying chronic HCV infection.

raw_record.support_text: Among 3,377 adults (aged ≥25 years) started on isoniazid (INH) therapy for latent tuberculosis infection in a public health TB clinic over a 7-year period, 19 patients developed isoniazid hepatotoxicity defined as aspartate aminotransferase (AST) >5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), a rate of 5.6 per 1,000 patients. Only 1 of 19 patients had prodromal symptoms. Age >49 years (p<0.02) and baseline AST >ULN (p<0.0003) were identified as risk factors for INH hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study restricted to adults aged ≥25 years; exclusion criteria included pregnancy, INH initiation within 3 months postpartum, baseline AST >3 times ULN, and history of INH allergy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as AST >5 times ULN; 19 events among 3,377 patients (5.6/1000). Events per 1000 patients were 2.75 at 1 month, 7.20 at 3 months, and 4.10 at 6 months of therapy. Age-specific events per 1000: 4.40 (25-34 y), 8.54 (35-49 y), 20.83 (≥50 y). Risk factors: age >49 years (p<0.02) and baseline AST >ULN (p<0.0003). Moderate-to-severe hepatotoxicity frequently occurred without symptoms, supporting value of AST monitoring. Authors note INH is well documented to cause liver adverse effects ranging from mild transient aminotransferase elevations (approximately 10-20% of patients) to overt hepatitis; risk factors include age >35 years, female gender, and concurrent ethanol use, with some data suggesting African-American and Hispanic women at greater risk. Consistent with earlier trials, INH hepatotoxicity is age related.
