raw_record.support_text: In an observational study of adults with severe liver dysfunction treated with at least 4 doses of voriconazole, 69% of patients showed changes in liver function tests during therapy: elevated transaminases in 35%, cholestasis in 15%, or a combination of both in 45%. All patients with hepatotoxicity had a severe reaction per CTC classification, and the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score was greater than 8 in all hepatotoxicity patients. There was a correlation between an initial loading dose greater than 300 mg (4.5 mg/kg) and the risk of hepatotoxicity (p < 0.001).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study restricted to patients with severe liver dysfunction and following liver transplantation; higher risk correlated with an initial loading dose > 300 mg (4.5 mg/kg).
raw_record.extra_details: 69% of voriconazole-treated patients developed LFT changes (elevated transaminases 35%, cholestasis 15%, combination 45%); all hepatotoxicity cases scored RUCAM > 8 and were classified as severe per CTC; loading dose > 300 mg correlated with risk (p < 0.001); matched liposomal amphotericin B control group showed LFT alterations in only 10.3%.

raw_record.support_text: The most important factor limiting the tolerated dose of tacrine was liver toxicity. Raised liver enzyme concentrations have often been reported, with reported incidences ranging from 13% to 42%; in this trial 14 of 53 patients (26%) given tacrine during the dose-finding phase had liver enzyme concentrations three times the upper limit of normal. Although no permanent damage was reported and all subjects had normal concentrations within a month of withdrawing the drug, biopsies from patients with raised liver function test results showed damage ranging from focal inflammatory infiltration to extensive hepatocellular necrosis, and the authors consequently restricted doses to 100 mg daily.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study subjects were patients with Alzheimer's disease; report explicitly notes no permanent liver damage and resolution of liver enzyme concentrations to normal within a month of drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Tacrine is a cholinesterase inhibitor used in the Alzheimer's disease trial. Raised liver enzyme concentration incidences of 13% to 42% have been reported in previous trials; 14/53 (26%) treated patients in the dose-finding phase had liver enzymes three times the upper limit of normal. Biopsies showed damage ranging from focal inflammatory infiltration to extensive hepatocellular necrosis. Doses were restricted to 100 mg daily because of this liver toxicity; mean best dose was 72.6 (SD 28.94) mg daily.

The uniformity of the clinical picture and histologic findings affords strong presumptive data incriminating methyltestosterone as the causative agent.

raw_record.extra_details: 19 cases by 1954 from at least six medical localities; histologically characterized more consistently by intracanalicular bile thrombi alone without periportal inflammation than any other proposed cause of primary intrahepatic cholestasis; jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver injury from phenylbutazone has been described in at least 75 patients, less common than its myelotoxicity. Susceptibility increases with age and females are more commonly affected. About 65% of cases occurred within a month of starting therapy, while 10% developed after 12 months. Hepatotoxicity occurs in a generalized systemic illness (jaundice, abdominal complaints, rash, fever, arthralgia), and varying hepatic injury types include cholestasis, hepatocellular injury, mixed-hepatocellular injury, and granulomas; hepatocellular injury tends to occur with a generalized reaction whereas cholestasis tends to occur without systemic features.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Susceptibility increases with age and females are more commonly affected
raw_record.extra_details: DILI described in at least 75 patients; ~65% of cases within one month of therapy onset and 10% after 12 months; hepatotoxicity usually accompanied by systemic illness (jaundice, abdominal complaints, rash, fever, arthralgia), though a minority have liver disease without systemic illness; injury types include cholestasis, hepatocellular injury, mixed-hepatocellular injury, and granulomas; hepatocellular pattern associates with generalized reaction while cholestasis occurs without systemic features.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane had been widely used as an anesthetic and causes two forms of liver damage: a mild increase in serum aminotransferase seen in up to 20% of patients, probably from direct toxicity by drug metabolites, and a more severe form characterized by massive hepatocyte necrosis and acute liver failure. Susceptibility to the severe form was enhanced in adults, females, and obese persons, and increased with frequency of exposure. Severe halothane hepatitis was uncommon after first exposure (1 in 35,000 patients) but its incidence rose to 1 in 3700 after the second exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Susceptibility to the severe form was enhanced in adults, females, and obese persons, and increased with the frequency of prior exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Two forms described: mild aminotransferase elevation (up to 20% of patients, attributed to direct metabolite toxicity) and a severe immune-mediated form with massive hepatocyte necrosis and acute liver failure. Incidence of severe halothane hepatitis was 1/35,000 after first exposure and 1/3700 after second exposure. Mechanism: halothane is oxidatively metabolized by CYP2E1 with release of bromide to form trifluoroacetyl chloride, which covalently binds to proteins as trifluoroacetylated (TFA) adducts presented on hepatocyte membranes; anti-P450 2E1 autoantibodies detected by ELISA in 14 of 20 sera from patients with halothane hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a series of patients who developed hepatitis attributed to niacin, particularly following a switch from regular-release (R) niacin to sustained-release (SR) niacin; hepatitis often developed within days or several weeks of the switch. The authors note the mechanism of niacin-induced hepatitis is unknown and speculate that prolonged enzyme-system exposure with SR preparations may lead to shorter recovery and more severe toxicity, and that a sudden R-to-SR switch may be particularly harmful.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Sustained-release (SR) formulation; several cases followed switching from regular-release (R) to SR niacin
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis developed within days to several weeks of switching from R-niacin to SR-niacin; various commercial SR-niacin preparations were involved, making a contaminant unlikely; two affected patients were identical twin brothers and two others were sisters, suggesting a possible genetic susceptibility; use of SR-niacin without monitoring of liver function tests can lead to fulminant hepatitis. Mechanism of niacin-induced hepatitis unknown.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia taking crystalline nicotinic acid 6 g daily for over a year without side effects developed nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, dark urine and gingival bleeding 3 days after switching to sustained-release nicotinic acid (6 g daily). He progressed to fulminant hepatic failure with grade II hepatic encephalopathy progressing to coma, and required successful liver transplantation. The explanted liver showed massive hepatic necrosis with collapse of architecture and cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Sustained-release formulation at a 6 g daily dose, switched from crystalline nicotinic acid (also 6 g daily) taken for over 1 year without side effects; patient had hypercholesterolemia after coronary angioplasty; symptoms began 3 days after starting the sustained-release preparation.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure with grade II hepatic encephalopathy progressing to coma despite 10% dextrose and lactulose; admission labs: serum bilirubin 168 µmol/L (direct 101 µmol/L), ALT 86.20 µkat/L, AST 103.22 µkat/L, alkaline phosphatase 6.42 µkat/L, LDH 31.77 µkat/L, albumin 37 g/L, prothrombin time 64.6 s (control 12.5 s), ammonia 149 µmol/L; bilirubin rose to 333 µmol/L; prothrombin time improved to 19.5 s with fresh frozen plasma and vitamin K; successful liver transplantation and discharge after 3 weeks; explanted liver weighed 890 g with massive hepatic necrosis, collapse, pigment-laden macrophages, prominent cholestasis and minimal fatty change; hepatitis B stains negative; the sustained-release preparation contained on average 950 mg nicotinic acid and 50 mg nicotinamide per 1-g tablet.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report four cases of niacin-induced hepatotoxicity in patients using sustained-release niacin preparations; symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after the patients stopped taking niacin. Two patients had focal fatty infiltration of the liver on imaging, and one patient had a coagulopathy despite only mildly elevated aminotransferase levels. The authors recommend periodic liver-enzyme monitoring and discontinuation if abnormalities develop.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Sustained-release niacin formulation for treatment of hyperlipidemia.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients; all used sustained-release niacin preparations; symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved on discontinuation (dechallenge). Focal fatty infiltration of the liver seen on imaging in two patients, presented as a not previously described presentation of niacin hepatotoxicity. One patient had a coagulopathy despite only mildly elevated aminotransferases (prothrombin time 16.6 s, AST 86 U/L, ALT 86 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 136 U/L, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, albumin 3.3 g/dL) and a factor VII deficiency attributed to liver disease. Niacin is a water-soluble B vitamin used for hyperlipidemia therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a life-threatening toxicity syndrome consisting of an erythematous, desquamative skin rash, fever, hepatitis, eosinophilia, and worsening renal function in 78 patients receiving allopurinol. In a majority of cases the syndrome was associated with use of standard (200 to 400 mg per day) allopurinol doses in patients with renal insufficiency. Avoidance of allopurinol or use of reduced doses in patients with renal insufficiency is recommended to reduce the incidence of life-threatening allopurinol toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Syndrome most commonly occurred with standard (200-400 mg/day) allopurinol doses in patients with renal insufficiency; earlier reports also associated the syndrome with concurrent thiazide diuretic use.
raw_record.extra_details: 78 patients with a hypersensitivity-like syndrome including some or all of vasculitis, rash (usually toxic epidermal necrolysis), eosinophilia, hepatitis, and progressive renal failure, described as life-threatening. Allopurinol (4-hydroxypyrazolo pyrimidine), a xanthine analogue used for hyperuricemia, is converted to oxipurinol, its pharmacologically active metabolite; oxipurinol clearance correlates with creatinine clearance, and long-term 300 mg/day dosing produces elevated steady-state serum oxipurinol concentrations in renal insufficiency. Dose-reduction guidelines proposed for renal insufficiency may reduce life-threatening toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a teenager with a multisystem disorder, the clinical features of myoclonus, seizure, axonal sensory ataxic neuropathy, and hepatotoxicity induced by valproate, together with mild cognitive decline and cardiomyopathy, were described as indicative of a multisystem disorder suggestive of mitochondrial disease (MERRF-like). The patient was subsequently found to be homozygous for a recessive POLG mutation. Valproate is thereby explicitly attributed as the cause of the patient's hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Teenager with a suspected mitochondrial disorder, subsequently found homozygous for a recessive POLG mutation; valproate given in the setting of seizures. Underlying mitochondrial/genetic susceptibility context.
raw_record.extra_details: Article is a case report focused on POLG A476T/A467T homozygous mutation with a MERRF-like presentation (myoclonus, seizure, sensory ataxic neuropathy); hepatotoxicity is listed among the multisystem clinical features attributed to valproate. No biochemical pattern, histology, or severity of the valproate hepatotoxicity is reported.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: TG therapy for IBD in specialist settings only; use restricted to very limited circumstances (e.g., AZA-induced pancreatitis) where MTX, mycophenolate or surgery is impracticable.
raw_record.extra_details: Dubinsky et al study of 111 patients; 29 (26%) had abnormal liver enzymes or thrombocytopenia, with NRH in 76% of those biopsied. NRH produces non-cirrhotic portal hypertension. TG is a direct precursor of 6-TGNs used to avoid accumulation of the potentially hepatotoxic metabolite 6-MMP ribonucleotides.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the proportion of patients developing significant liver dysfunction from isoniazid (INH) therapy, attributed on the basis of a multiple logistic regression analysis of a prospective cohort. Age over 35 years and slow acetylation phenotype were the primary risk factors: in those ≥35 with slow acetylation 37.5% developed significant liver dysfunction versus 3.7% in rapid acetylators under 35. The discussion further states that INH is associated with overt hepatocellular disease, subclinical and overt hepatitis, with historical fatalities from INH-induced liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: The analysis was restricted to patients on INH chemoprophylaxis; the 12 patients who drank an excess of alcohol were excluded from the main risk-factor model, and patients with normal baseline laboratory studies were used for the prediction analysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Multiple logistic regression equation: log_e(theta/(1-theta)) = -1.90434 + 1.37376X1 - 1.35344X2, where X1=1 if age >35 and X2=1 if rapid acetylation (chi^2=10.5, d.f.=3, p=0.015). Observed rates of significant liver dysfunction: age<35 rapid 4.2% (1/24), age<35 slow 12.5% (3/24), age≥35 rapid 12.5% (2/16), age≥35 slow 37.5% (9/24). Historic evidence cited: Garibaldi et al. 2321 patients, 19 overt hepatocellular disease with 2 deaths; Bailey et al. 471 patients, 8.7% subclinical and 1% overt hepatitis, no deaths; Maddrey & Boitnott 14 overt biopsy-documented hepatitis cases ascribed to hypersensitivity; Black et al. 13,838 patients, 114 (0.82%) overt liver damage with 13 fatalities (11.4%). Discussion of proposed mechanism via acetylisoniazid, acetylhydrazine, and hydrazine metabolites (mainly animal evidence) that the paper notes is not clearly documented in humans prospectively.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of jaundice that appeared in a 37-year-old diabetic man during treatment with ethionamide; the hepatic abnormalities disappeared with drug withdrawal and recurred on rechallenge. This was noted as the fourth reported case of this complication.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: The index patient and two of the additional reported cases were diabetic; one additional case occurred in a patient with prior allergic reactions to isoniazid, streptomycin, and PAS.
raw_record.extra_details: Total of at least 4 cases reported: the index jaundice case (37-year-old diabetic man), plus 3 additional probable ethionamide-induced hepatotoxicity cases in an addendum (Oestreicher: one case of fulminating jaundice starting 11 days after starting ethionamide in a patient previously allergic to isoniazid, streptomycin, and PAS, and two cases of less severe abnormalities in diabetics; Kass: a case of liver function abnormalities presumably due to ethionamide). In all cases abnormalities cleared on discontinuation (dechallenge) and recurred on restart (rechallenge).

raw_record.support_text: Jaundice from chlorpromazine usually runs a self-limited course briefer than that of viral hepatitis, and during the acute course liver biopsies usually show only minimal hepatocellular damage. The paper also notes that hepatitis may occur without clinical jaundice, manifesting as liver enlargement or tenderness, fever, abnormal liver function tests, or histologic evidence of 'allergic cholangiolitis,' all of which are considered chlorpromazine jaundice.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: The paper notes a definite hazard of permanent liver damage if patients are re-treated following an attack of jaundice or if treatment is continued without interruption.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpromazine jaundice is attributed to drug allergy; the paper concludes the probability that jaundice is due to drug allergy is high. Nine of eleven challenged patients demonstrated objective evidence of sensitivity for up to seventeen months after an attack. Other reports also reproduced jaundice upon challenge. Jaundice can be mild (serum bilirubin 2 mg/100 ml or less) and short (3-7 days) and may occur without clinical jaundice (liver enlargement/tenderness, fever, abnormal liver function tests, histologic 'allergic cholangiolitis'). Acute liver biopsies show minimal hepatocellular damage. After an estimated four million treated patients, 26 deaths in jaundiced patients were reported, with the drug thought responsible in 13; most fatal cases were complicated by agranulocytosis, heart failure, possible viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, or recent surgery, and one death with acute hepatic necrosis occurred in an 81-year-old. Jaundice runs a self-limited course briefer than viral hepatitis. Animal toxicity studies failed to reveal hepatic damage, but continued use in sensitized patients appears to lead to permanent toxic liver changes.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 43-year-old Chinese woman who took viaminate (a derivative of retinoic acid/tretinoin, an amide of tretinoin and ethyl p-aminobenzoate) for severe acne for more than two months and died of hepatic failure, providing insight into viaminate-induced hepatotoxicity. They note that liver dysfunction due to viaminate therapy has not been well described and no prior death from viaminate-induced hepatotoxicity had been reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: The patient increased the viaminate dose from the routine 50 mg/day to 75 mg/day without medical advice after about 30 days of treatment before developing jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: 43-year-old Chinese female treated for severe acne; jaundice noticed after 60 days of viaminate, hospitalized 10 days later with worsening jaundice, mild fever and xiphoid tenderness; MRCP showed mild chronic cholecystitis, gallstone and splenomegaly; CT showed splenomegaly, uneven liver density and mild hepatic atrophy; labs on admission: TBIL 160.2 µmol/L, DBIL 135.4 µmol/L, ALT 1514 U/L, AST 939 U/L, TBA 91.3 µmol/L, INR 1.47; viaminate was stopped and hepatoprotective drugs given for 1 month but liver function deteriorated; typical hepatic encephalopathy (drowsiness, lethargy, asterixis, obnubilation, deep coma) developed and the patient died of liver failure on the 38th day post-admission; treatment drugs included compound glycyrrhizin, magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate, methionine vitamin B1, polyene phosphatidylcholine, ornithine aspartate and ceftazidime; viaminate is an amide of tretinoin and ethyl p-aminobenzoate, mechanism similar to isotretinoin.

raw_record.support_text: An analysis of 1100 cases reported to the Danish Committee of Drug-Induced Hepatic Injury between 1978 and 1987 confirmed that only 18 were due to paracetamol, yet damage did occur in non-alcohol-dependent patients after therapeutic doses of paracetamol. Acute cytotoxic as well as cholestatic reactions appeared after periods ranging from weeks to years, and three patients died. The number of case reports where therapeutic doses of paracetamol were implicated as the sole causative factor in hepatotoxicity is small, and if an unidentified at-risk group exists it must be very small.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic (non-overdose) doses; non-alcohol-dependent general population; rare reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Danish Committee of Drug-Induced Hepatic Injury 1978-1987 cohort (1100 cases, 18 attributed to paracetamol). Acute cytotoxic and cholestatic reactions appeared after weeks to years; three patients died. Chronic active hepatitis described in one report; acute biliary pain with cholestasis ascribed to inhibition of prostaglandin production potentially regulating the sphincter of Oddi/biliary duct pressure. The paper notes the mechanism here likely differs from NAPBQI-related toxicity given glutathione conjugation capacity.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical use, bromfenac at recommended therapeutic doses of 25–100 mg/d for at least 90 days (labeled recommended duration >10 days) was associated with severe symptomatic hepatocellular disease with associated hypoprothrombinemia. There was no evidence of a hypersensitivity reaction. Extensive confluent parenchymal necrosis originating in central zones was associated with lymphocytic infiltrate with nodular regeneration in 2 subjects with more prolonged disease prior to transplantation. Histologic lesions included acute lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis and fibrous expansion of portal tracts, and fulminant liver failure requiring liver transplant has been recorded after inadvertent rechallenge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic doses of 25–100 mg/d for at least 90 days, exceeding the labeled recommended duration of >10 days; delayed idiosyncratic onset.
raw_record.extra_details: During clinical trials bromfenac caused only reversible minor AST elevations. In clinical use it produced severe symptomatic hepatocellular disease with hypoprothrombinemia and no hypersensitivity reaction; extensive confluent parenchymal necrosis originating in central zones with lymphocytic infiltrate and nodular regeneration in 2 subjects with prolonged disease prior to transplant. Histology showed acute lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis and fibrous expansion of portal tracts. Prognosis is usually good with resolution, but fulminant liver failure requiring liver transplant occurred after inadvertent rechallenge. Risk-benefit: continued use was not justified once delayed idiosyncratic severe hepatotoxicity was identified given the availability of alternatives.

raw_record.support_text: Bromfenac, a phenylacetic acid derivative introduced in the United States in 1997, was withdrawn from further clinical use in 1998 after reports of several cases of acute liver failure causing death or necessitating liver transplantation. In a series of 4 patients with severe bromfenac hepatotoxicity, all had been treated for more than 90 days with therapeutic doses for musculoskeletal disorders, developed a prodrome of malaise and fatigue followed by severe hepatitis, and progressed to liver failure over 5 to 37 days. Histology showed extensive, confluent parenchymal necrosis beginning in zone 3 (perivenular) with predominantly lymphocytic infiltration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic doses taken for more than 90 days for musculoskeletal disorders; subjects had no underlying hepatic or renal disease and no extrahepatic features of drug allergy or reactive metabolite syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenylacetic acid derivative; introduced in the US in 1997 and withdrawn from clinical use in 1998. Series of 4 patients; prodrome of malaise and fatigue followed by severe hepatitis; progression to liver failure over 5-37 days. Histology: extensive confluent parenchymal necrosis starting in zone 3 (perivenular) with predominantly lymphocytic infiltration.

raw_record.support_text: Bellary and Isaacs reported Captopril-associated liver dysfunction cases, including a mixed hepatocellular cholestatic reaction in a 74-year-old man treated with 50 mg/day for hypertension, and an 88-year-old man who died with massive acute hepatic necrosis 7 weeks after starting Captopril (50 mg/day) for hypertension. At that time 29 cases of liver dysfunction due to Captopril had been recorded by the UK Committee on Safety of Medicine, with doses ranging from 12.5 to 150 mg/day; nine had hepatocellular jaundice with two deaths, eight cholestatic jaundice (one fatal), and three hepatorenal syndrome (all died). Worldwide (excluding UK) 164 adverse hepatic reactions had been reported to the WHO database by January 1989, 64 with serious clinical liver disease.

raw_record.extra_details: Reported cases include cholestatic jaundice with marked cholestasis and mild portal inflammation, mixed hepatocellular cholestatic reaction with jaundice and urticarial rash, and massive acute hepatic necrosis. 29 UK CSM cases (9 hepatocellular jaundice with 2 deaths, 8 cholestatic jaundice with 1 fatal, 3 hepatorenal syndrome all fatal); 164 WHO-database adverse hepatic reactions (64 serious). raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old man with psoriasis vulgaris, without prior liver disease, alcohol consumption, or cholelithiasis, was started on retinol 1 mg/kg/day in May 1984 and given for a 12-week period. At the end of the twelfth week he developed pruritus, dark urine, and acholic stool, with alkaline phosphatase up to 420 U/liter, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase up to 380 U/liter, and jaundice with bilirubin up to 400 µmol/liter (80% direct). The authors present this as the first case with clinical and pathologic evidence of acute cholestatic jaundice induced by retinol therapy, describing it as a biochemical and morphologic cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic use for psoriasis vulgaris at 1 mg/kg/day; patient without prior liver disease, alcohol consumption, or cholelithiasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Retinol (referred to by the brand names Tigason in Europe and Tegison in the USA) is described chemically as an aromatic retinoid. Symptoms and signs: pruritus, dark urine, acholic stool, jaundice; alkaline phosphatase up to 420 U/l (normal 10-85), gamma glutamyl transpeptidase up to 380 U/l (normal 20-53), bilirubin up to 400 µmol/l (normal 2-17), 80% direct. Authors note prior reports of transient slight transaminase elevations in <10% of treated patients, histologic changes resembling viral hepatitis, and mild cholestasis in a few cases.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old woman developed acute liver failure after taking paracetamol at a therapeutic dose (1 g four times daily for 8 days, cumulative 32 g) during prolonged fasting and a nil-by-mouth hospital period. Paracetamol levels were in the toxic range (238 µmol/L; therapeutic 66-132 µmol/L). Despite an N-acetylcysteine infusion she was listed for urgent liver transplantation but died before a donor became available; postmortem confirmed multisystem organ failure secondary to acute liver failure associated with paracetamol toxicity, with massive panlobular hepatic necrosis and mild fatty change.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic-dose exposure (1 g QID, 32 g cumulative over 8 days) during prolonged fasting and nil-by-mouth after abdominal surgery; patient had lost 10 kg weight, with subacute bowel obstruction and concurrent renal failure and metabolic acidosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol level 238 µmol/L (toxic range above 132 µmol/L); ALT 5859 U/L, INR 8.4, bilirubin 57 µmol/L, lactate 14.6 mmol/L; acute hepatic failure with haematuria, confusion and drowsiness requiring intubation; N-acetylcysteine intravenous infusion; listed for transplant but died; liver weighed 0.786 kg with massive panlobular necrosis, mild fatty change and increased sinusoidal inflammatory cells; paper notes paracetamol toxicity is the most common cause of acute liver failure in Australia and discusses therapeutic misadventure (48% of severe paracetamol hepatotoxicity cases in a US study were not intentional self-poisoning) and risk factors including prolonged fasting, heavy alcohol intake, CYP450 2E1 induction, and use in elderly patients.

raw_record.support_text: Severe hepatocellular damage occurred during isoniazid therapy in 114 patients reported here and in 60 or more additional patients reported by others. The authors conclude that isoniazid-related hepatic injury in humans results from the formation in the liver of a hepatotoxic metabolite, consistent with an occasional allergic mechanism involving acetylation of hepatic macromolecules by acetylhydrazine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapy for chemoprophylaxis of tuberculosis; increased mortality noted in patients presenting late in their course of isoniazid therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 114 patients with severe hepatocellular damage reported here; 60 or more additional cases reported by others. Severe liver damage incidence rises with age: rare under 20 years, up to 0.3% at ages 20-34 years, up to 1.2% at 35-49 years, and up to 2.3% at 50 years and over; rates may underestimate due to dropout. Moderate serum transaminase abnormalities occur in 10-20% of isoniazid recipients, mostly subsiding despite continued therapy. Mechanism attributed to a hepatotoxic metabolite (acetylhydrazine-related acylation of hepatic macromolecules), with an allergic mechanism in occasional patients. Authors recommend discontinuing isoniazid in patients over 35 whose liver function tests do not improve within a few weeks.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a patient who developed jaundice and elevated liver enzymes after 17 months of acetohexamide therapy for diabetes, with symptoms appearing shortly after a substantial dose increase. Peripheral eosinophilia and fever accompanied the liver damage, suggesting a hypersensitivity reaction. The hepatitis resolved after acetohexamide was discontinued and insulin therapy began, with bilirubin and liver enzymes normalizing gradually and the patient remaining in good health one year later. The authors discuss that a metabolite of acetohexamide might have been the offending agent at the higher dose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapy for diabetes (insulin likely for diabetic control); patient was asymptomatic for 17 months and developed symptoms after a substantial increase in acetohexamide dosage; the authors speculate a metabolite of acetohexamide may have been the offending agent at the increased dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as 'Acetohexamide-Induced Hepatitis'. Admission labs: total bilirubin 7.0 mg/dL (normal 0-1.0), alkaline phosphatase 567 U/L (0-110), SGOT 149 U/L (0-40), WBC 11.4 x10^3/µl, eosinophils 0.300 x10^3/µl; values peaked by day 2-6 then normalized by day 30 (bilirubin 0.8, alkaline phosphatase 183, SGOT 29, eosinophils normal). Peripheral eosinophilia and fever supported a hypersensitivity reaction. Recovery after discontinuation of acetohexamide and institution of insulin. The patient remained in good health 1 year after the jaundice episode. The authors note only two prior case reports of acetohexamide-induced liver disease: Goldstein and Rothenberg (jaundice 3 weeks after acetohexamide 500 mg daily plus chlorothiazide 500 mg daily, biopsy showing acute parenchymal disease and portal eosinophilia, resolution on discontinuation, but persistent hepatomegaly with macronodular cirrhosis on second biopsy and rechallenge with both drugs not inducing further damage), and Duncan et al. 1965 (patient on multiple medications including tolbutamide, phenytoin, phenobarbital, probenecid, colchicine, quinine, with past ethanol abuse, nonspecific biopsy changes). Balodimas et al. reported 20 cases of jaundice among an estimated 200,000 acetohexamide recipients up to 1965.

raw_record.support_text: Between 1/06 and 9/09, 6 of the 7 cases of DILI attributed to duloxetine in the DILIN Prospective Study were assessed as definite or very likely. Median patient age was 49 years, 6 (86%) were women, median latency from drug initiation to DILI onset was 50 days, 6 patients developed jaundice, and the median peak ALT in the 5 patients with acute hepatocellular injury was 1633 IU/L. All patients recovered without liver transplantation even though 3 had pre-existing chronic liver disease, and liver histology in 4 cases demonstrated varying patterns of liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The hepatotoxic effects of tacrine occur in nearly half the patients treated with it. Although some patients have had increases in serum ALT as high as 20 times the upper limit of normal, no deaths have been associated with tacrine hepatotoxicity. Tacrine is described as a relatively pure hepatocellular toxin, with ALT increases usually without concomitant increases in alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin, and hepatotoxicity does not seem to be dose related.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treated Alzheimer's disease patients; patients with significant pre-existing liver or kidney disease were excluded from the controlled trials and may constitute a predisposition in the general AD population. Patients should be withdrawn at an ALT above 3x ULN and monitored for at least 18 weeks after initiating therapy and 6 weeks after dose increase.
raw_record.extra_details: 47% of permanently withdrawn patients were withdrawn due to pronounced ALT increases; 49% of controlled-trial patients had at least one increased ALT, 25% had ALT >3x ULN, and 2% had ALT >20x ULN; no deaths from tacrine hepatotoxicity; raised ALT was delayed with peak incidence at 6-8 weeks of exposure and 90% of increases by week 12; not dose related; age, weight, and concomitant drug/alcohol/nicotine use did not predict risk; ALT increases usually without alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin rises; jaundice indicates severe liver injury and mandates drug withdrawal and supportive therapy; some patients have malaise or nausea/vomiting, many are symptom-free; data from controlled clinical trials (n=634 tacrine, n=342 placebo) and Cognex package insert.

Competing causes were excluded at autopsy: a normal heart ruled out congestive heart failure, there was no evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation in other organs, and severe hepatic damage from shock alone would have been accompanied by marked renal and other organ abnormalities. The paper frames this as a case of DTIC-induced hepatic veno-occlusive disease with a fulminant course.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treatment for melanoma as the indication; single-patient case with the authors uncertain whether the reaction reflects a distinctive DTIC effect or this particular patient's individual response to the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: initial clinical picture of fever, epigastric pain, and hepatomegaly with nonspecific hepatic laboratory tests (variable elevations of SGOT, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase). Pathologic findings were a rapidly progressive veno-occlusive disease of the liver; the brief clinical course precluded the fibrosis reported in other cases. The same VOD-like clinical syndrome may occur with many different chemotherapeutic agents; 4 of 5 previously reported evaluable cases had such liver failure contribute to or cause death. DTIC is metabolized in the liver but there is no evidence that its metabolites cause the lesion. No other reported patient had onset of liver dysfunction after as brief a drug exposure as this patient.

raw_record.support_text: Before marketing nevirapine, Boehringer-Ingelheim ran a series of clinical trials that concluded nevirapine can lead to both skin rash and liver toxicity in HIV patients. With a 200 mg/day lead-in dose for the first 2 weeks followed by 400 mg/day, liver toxicity was detected in 1% of the tested population. Postmarketing reports gathered by Boehringer-Ingelheim indicated the incidence of liver toxicity was greater than before approval, increasing from 1% to 3%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treatment of HIV-1 infection; nevirapine used with a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor or protease inhibitor (not monotherapy).
raw_record.extra_details: FDA-approved June 1996 (marketed as Viramune); 200 mg/day lead-in for 2 weeks then 400 mg/day. Clinical-trial liver toxicity in 1% of patients; postmarketing (pharmacovigilance) incidence rose to 3%. Abstract reports rare life-threatening liver failure associated with nevirapine therapy; first 6 weeks of therapy are most critical for adverse drug reactions with close clinical/laboratory monitoring urged during the first 12 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: In a DILIN (Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network) registry cohort of latent TB patients, 13 patients experienced fatal liver injury or required liver transplantation linked to isoniazid (INH) treatment. Of these, 4 (31%) stopped INH quickly (within 7 days of meeting stopping criteria), while 2 continued INH for more than 3 weeks yet had mild injury. One patient showed adaptation despite continued INH, with ALT peaking above 1000 U/L before decreasing; the paper refers to this as 'INH injury' and notes ALT level alone cannot fully predict serious INH liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (preventive therapy); patients were otherwise healthy before therapy. Patients harmed by suboptimal adherence, prolonged drug exposure, and delayed drug stoppage.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN registry data for latent TB patients on isoniazid. Of 13 fatal or transplanted patients, 4 (31%) stopped INH within 7 days of meeting stopping criteria; 2 continued INH >3 weeks yet had mild injury; one patient showed adaptation with ALT peaking >1000 U/L that decreased despite continuing INH. Authors note under-reporting makes the true incidence larger than captured, and state ALT level alone cannot reliably predict serious injury. INH for 3-9 months DOT is a recommended latent TB option; point-of-care ALT and automated text reminders proposed.

raw_record.support_text: The AKRENDO1 clinical trial, which assessed the efficacy and safety of the AKR1C3 inhibitor BAY1128688 as a potential treatment for endometriosis-related pain symptoms, was prematurely terminated by the sponsor due to cases of hepatotoxicity. Increases in serum ALT were detected after 12 weeks of treatment or thereafter, and individual bile acid levels were increased at isolated early time points; the in vitro BSEP inhibitory IC50 was 3.6 µM while total BAY1128688 concentration in human plasma was approximately 10 µM, and increases in androsterone and bilirubin were observed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Trial population comprised patients with endometriosis-related pain symptoms; treated with BAY1128688 at 60 mg BID.
raw_record.extra_details: Trial prematurely terminated by sponsor due to hepatotoxicity cases. ALT increases detected after 12 weeks of treatment or thereafter (from visit 7 onward). Proposed mechanism: BSEP inhibition (in vitro IC50 3.6 µM) with total human plasma concentration ~10 µM, leading to toxic bile acid accumulation; increases in androsterone (AKR1C3 inhibition pharmacodynamic biomarker) and serum bilirubin observed. Bile acid measurements had limited value for predicting ALT increases; biomarkers MCSFR, androsterone and six candidate biomarkers could not consistently predict ALT increases. Preclinical 13-week animal study showed transient bilirubin increases without liver enzyme or microscopic liver findings.

raw_record.support_text: INH (isoniazid) and its metabolic intermediates are indicated to be the cause of hepatotoxicity. INH is inactivated in the liver by NAT2, and slow acetylators may accumulate toxic intermediates and are prone to isoniazid-induced hepatitis, as supported by the present study and previous studies. In a Tunisian study, the incidence of INH-induced hepatitis was 21.2%, and one TB patient with a slow-acetylator profile (NAT2*5B/5B) died of acute fulminant hepatitis; slow acetylators with NAT2*6A/*6A and NAT2*5/*5 genotypes had a significantly higher risk of INH drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Tuberculosis (TB) patient population; slow-acetylator NAT2 genotypes (NAT2*6A/*6A, NAT2*5/*5, NAT2*5B/5B) associated with higher risk; possible concurrent anti-tuberculosis drugs (e.g., rifampicin) in the regimen are co-exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of INH-induced hepatitis in this study was 21.2%. One patient with slow-acetylator NAT2*5B/5B profile died of acute fulminant hepatitis. Slow acetylators dispose about 10 times more isoniazid via direct hydrolysis to hydrazine (a potent hepatotoxin), a pathway enhanced by rifampicin. Cytochrome P450 2E1 oxidation of monoacetylhydrazine yields toxic intermediates (acetyldiazene, acetylonium ion, acetylradical, ketene). Findings support NAT2 genotyping to pre-screen patients at high risk of INH-induced hepatotoxicity in the Tunisian population.

raw_record.support_text: Among 18 tuberculosis patients with INH (isoniazid)-related hepatotoxicity during anti-tuberculosis treatment, 11 (61%) were slow acetylators and 3 (17%) were fast acetylators. A significant association was observed between the slow acetylation profile and hepatotoxicity (P = 0.009, OR 3.71, 95%CI 1.38–9.93). This patient cohort in Belem, Brazil was studied for NAT2 and CYP2E1 polymorphisms as susceptibility factors for INH-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: 18 patients with hepatotoxicity among 270 tuberculosis patients. A significant association was observed between slow acetylation profile and hepatotoxicity (P = 0.009, OR 3.71, 95%CI 1.38–9.93). raw_record.support_text: In tuberculous meningitis (TBM) patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity (DIH) there was evidence of oxidative and ER stress compared to controls and baseline values. The paper attributes INH (isoniazid) hepatotoxicity to oxidative and nitrosative stress, with peroxynitrite (ONOO-) generation and mitochondrial dysfunction; acetyl isoniazid is metabolized to monoacetyl hydrazine (MAH) and other metabolites, and NAT2 acetylator polymorphism (fast/slow/intermediate) affects drug exposure. Isoniazid hepatotoxicity is described as resulting in non-zonal necrosis simulating viral hepatitis, which may be massive in 10% of patients, with severe fulminant and sub-acute necrosis reported in 30% of patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Tuberculous meningitis patients treated with an isoniazid-containing anti-tuberculosis regimen; co-exposure to other anti-TB agents in the regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: DIH occurred after a median duration of 11 (3-48) days; significant alterations in oxidative and ER stress markers (P < .001). Of 36 DIH patients, 58.3% had poor outcome (mRS>2) and 33.3% of poor-outcome patients died in hospital; 14 (39%) DIH patients died during follow-up. Massive necrosis may occur in 10% of patients and severe fulminant/sub-acute necrosis in 30%. Mechanistic support: acetyl isoniazid converted to monoacetyl hydrazine (MAH) and nontoxic diacetyl hydrazine; NAT2 polymorphism (slow/intermediate/fast acetylators) affects exposure; long half-life extends exposure. Supporting rat data: isoniazid reduced free-radical-scavenger thiols, glutathione peroxidase and catalase, increased glutathione reductase activity, and N-acetylcysteine pretreatment reduced injury; isoniazid also inhibits certain cytochrome P450 enzymes, raising levels of hepatotoxic drug.

raw_record.support_text: A series of 20 patients with chlorpromazine jaundice is described; jaundice lasted from 8 days to 10 months (two patients), two patients were pregnant during their jaundice without apparent effect on their pregnancies or fetuses, and follow-up in all patients showed eventual recovery without residual liver damage. The hepatic lesion produced by chlorpromazine was examined by liver biopsy in 15 of the 20 patients and could be differentiated from viral hepatitis (absence of hepatocellular necrosis) and from obstructive jaundice (absence of large bile accumulations), although it could not be morphologically distinguished from other drug-induced lesions such as those from methyltestosterone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Two patients were pregnant during their jaundice, without noted effect on pregnancy or fetus; all patients recovered without residual liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 20 affected patients; jaundice duration 8 days to 10 months (two patients). Liver biopsy in 15/20 patients showed absence of hepatocellular necrosis (differentiating from viral hepatitis) and no large bile accumulations (differentiating from extrahepatic/large bile duct obstructive jaundice). Lesion morphologically indistinguishable from other drug-induced lesions such as methyltestosterone. Steroid therapy was ineffective in five patients; a hepatitis regimen (high-carbohydrate high-protein diet, bed rest, vitamins) was recommended.

raw_record.support_text: Both patients in this report developed hepatic failure following flutamide treatment, and neither had been exposed to known hepatotoxins; the authors conclude that an unpredictable reaction caused by flutamide seems plausible. For patient 1, previous case descriptions also noted severe liver damage with jaundice, ascites, impaired coagulation and hepatic coma following flutamide, while in the present second patient jaundice resolved and liver function improved after flutamide cessation, with a liver biopsy read as drug-induced.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Two patients with prostatic cancer; patient 1 additionally received Zoladex and dextropropoxyphene, though Zoladex was argued unlikely to contribute, and had renal impairment possibly raising metabolite levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports. Case 1: severe liver damage with jaundice, ascites, impaired coagulation and hepatic coma; developed after therapeutic flutamide during period of therapeutic Zoladex. Case 2: serum alkaline phosphatase 1202 U/l, ALAT 56 U/l, bilirubin 255 µmol/l; liver biopsy showed slight portal lymphocytic/histiocytic infiltrate without obstruction, scattered focal necroses, and centrilobular cholestasis with bile thrombi and bile pigment in Kupffer cells, interpreted as drug-induced; liver tests improved and jaundice disappeared ~2 months after flutamide cessation; the patient died 1 year later from prostatic cancer. Flutamide is metabolized to hydroxyflutamide plus minor metabolites; renal impairment hypothesized to raise metabolite levels, though animal toxicology showed no serious hepatotoxicity. Prior reports described only slight transaminase elevations that normalized despite continued therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Two young male patients developed severe cholestatic DILI following low-dose ibuprofen intake (400 mg), lacking conventional risk factors. Genetic analysis revealed compound heterozygous mutations in ABCB11 (encoding BSEP), including p.V444A and p.A1028A, with Patient 1 additionally harboring p.A865V; immunohistochemistry showed abnormal BSEP membrane localization. The authors propose that NSAIDs may unmask latent BSEP dysfunction in genetically predisposed individuals, precipitating refractory cholestasis, and highlight ABCB11 polymorphisms as determinants of NSAID-related DILI susceptibility even at therapeutic doses.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Two young (32- and 29-year-old) male patients without conventional risk factors, one with prior Omicron (COVID-19) fever and one after jogging; both genetically predisposed through ABCB11/BSEP compound heterozygous mutations (p.V444A, p.A1028A, with p.A865V in Patient 1). Low-dose (400 mg) therapeutic ibuprofen exposure rather than overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1 (32 y, RUCAM 6, cholestatic, R=1.18): 20-day progressive jaundice, pruritus, malaise, nausea after ibuprofen 0.4 g for Omicron fever; ALT 173 U/L, AST 58 U/L, TBIL 162.9 μmol/L, DBIL 82 μmol/L, GGT 266/385 U/L, ALP 365 U/L; negative viral serology/autoantibodies; liver biopsy acute cholestatic hepatitis consistent with drug-related injury (G2/S2); improved after artificial liver support therapy; carried ABCB11 p.V444A, p.A1028A, p.A865V with intracellular BSEP retention on IHC. Patient 2 (29 y, RUCAM 8, hepatocellular, R=101.43): nausea, vomiting, jaundice after one ibuprofen capsule for muscle soreness; ALT 9575.3 U/L, AST 12,187 U/L, TBIL 148.4 μmol/L, GGT 306 U/L, PTA 7.6% (liver failure), plus myocardial damage (LDH 5913, CK-MB 40.8) and acute renal failure (BUN 10.23, Cr 246.7); diagnosed with acute severe drug-related liver injury (PTA 13%); improved with steroids/immunosuppressants; biopsy showed tendency toward chronicity and recovery; carried p.V444A and p.A1028A with reduced membrane BSEP distribution. Cases screened from a single-center prospective DILI cohort (winter-spring 2022-2023).

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old man developed severe drug-induced liver injury after using Ligandrol (LGD-4033), a selective androgen receptor modulator available over the counter. The diagnosis of DILI was confirmed by a liver biopsy that showed cholestatic hepatitis with mild portal, periportal, and perisinusoidal fibrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unapproved over-the-counter use as a muscle-building supplement in a previously healthy 32-year-old man; single-agent exposure with no other supplements or medications reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Ligandrol (LGD-4033), also known as VK5211, chemical name 4-((R)-2-((R)-2,2,2-Trifluoro-1-hydroxyethyl)pyrrolidin-1-yl)-2-(trifluoromethyl)benzonitrile. Patient took 1 mL (10 mg) daily for approximately 2 weeks (~15 mL total) starting ~50 days before presentation. Symptoms: fatigue, pruritus, weight loss (40 lbs), jaundice, acholic stool, nausea, intermittent abdominal pain. Lab values at our hospital: AST 33 IU/L, ALT 45 IU/L, ALP 425, total bilirubin 35.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 26.8, INR 1.1; hepatic patients negative for viral/serologic/autoimmune markers (ANA, AMA, ASMA, anti-LKM). Transjugular liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with canalicular bile plugs, mild portal inflammation, mild portal, periportal and perisinusoidal fibrosis, no ductopenia; no clinical liver failure, transplantation, or death reported.

raw_record.support_text: In this pilot study of 6 patients with corticosteroid-resistant grade III/IV hepatic GVHD who received low-dose MTX (with methylprednisolone) via catheter-directed intrahepatic arterial delivery, no hepatotoxicity was observed after IHA administration of MTX. The authors concluded that in patients with GVHD and normal renal function, IHA administration of low-dose MTX was not associated with liver or bone marrow toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Uncontrolled open-label pilot study; patients with corticosteroid-resistant grade III/IV hepatic GVHD; unusual route (catheter-directed intrahepatic arterial delivery) of low-dose MTX; co-administered with methylprednisolone and standard therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients (5 male, 1 female; median age 32 y, range 8-42 y). No hepatotoxicity was observed after IHA administration of MTX. In 5 patients with normal renal function, 24-h plasma MTX concentrations were 0.01-0.12 umol/L (mean [SD] 0.043 [0.042]); in 1 patient with renal failure plasma MTX was 1.0 umol/L at 24 h and 0.07 umol/L at 5 days, with severe hematologic and renal toxicity that may have contributed to death (renal/hematologic, not hepatic).

raw_record.support_text: In this clinical trial, hepatic arterial FUDR therapy was associated with hepatobiliary toxicity, defined as a ≥2-fold increase in alkaline phosphatase, ≥3-fold increase in AST, or serum bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL in the absence of tumor progression. Patients with bilirubin elevations that did not return to baseline underwent ERCP to distinguish biliary sclerosis from extrahepatic obstruction, and patients with documented biliary sclerosis were never retreated with hepatic arterial FUDR, implicating FUDR as the cause of this cholangiopathy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unusual regional route: hepatic arterial infusion rather than systemic use; colorectal cancer patients with liver metastases.
raw_record.extra_details: Given with leucovorin (LV) 15 mg/m2/d and dexamethasone 20 mg; initial FUDR dose 0.3 mg/kg/d as a 14-day continuous infusion (actually delivered ~0.21 mg/kg/d due to ~15 mL pump dead space) followed by a 14-day rest period. Hepatic toxicity defined as ≥2-fold increase in alkaline phosphatase, ≥3-fold increase in AST, or bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL absent tumor progression. Persistent bilirubin elevations prompted ERCP to distinguish biliary sclerosis from extrahepatic biliary obstruction; documented biliary sclerosis precluded retreatment with hepatic arterial FUDR. Dexamethasone (Dec) was used to treat hepatobiliary toxicity and may hasten recovery via anti-inflammatory properties.

raw_record.support_text: In a case report, the authors describe a patient who developed cholestatic hepatitis after vaginal application of AVC cream, a sulfonamide-based product. They state the temporal relation between AVC cream application and onset of symptoms, plus a prior history of fever with earlier use, strongly supports the diagnosis of sulfanilamide-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Exclusion of extrahepatic biliary tract obstruction and absence of other histologic changes also supported this diagnosis, even though absorption of sulfanilamide by the vaginal mucosa is incomplete.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unusual route/formulation: drug administered as a vaginal cream (AVC cream); systemic absorption by the vaginal mucosa is reported to be incomplete, with blood levels below 1.0 mg/100 ml.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of sulfanilamide-induced cholestatic hepatitis supported by temporal relation between AVC cream application and symptom onset, prior fever with earlier use, exclusion of extrahepatic biliary obstruction, and absence of other liver histology changes. The paper notes hepatic injury following vaginal sulfonamide application had not previously been recorded; a prior report concerned eosinophilic pneumonia after AVC cream application. The article concludes that hepatic injury may follow vaginal administration of a sulfonamide-based drug.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 35-year-old man with alcohol misuse history who received a subcutaneous implant of the oral drug disulfiram (Esperal) in his left buttock three months before presenting with severe acute liver failure. After surgical excision of the implant and supportive treatment, hepatic synthesis and detoxification normalized with uneventful recovery, supporting disulfiram as the cause. The learning points explicitly state that idiosyncratic drug induced hepatitis attributable to disulfiram is a rare but well described cause of acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unusual route: subcutaneous implant (Esperal) of the oral drug rather than standard oral dosing; patient had ongoing alcohol misuse with binge three days before admission; liver transplantation was considered but declined due to alcohol misuse under German transplant legislation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 35-year-old man presenting with fatigue, vomiting, jaundice and drowsiness. Laboratories showed massive increases in AST (60,620 U/l), ALT (16,726 U/l), LDH (38,180 U/l), GLDH (12,211 U/l), total bilirubin (179 µmol/l), lactate (5.2 mmol/l), severe coagulopathy (INR 8.29; factor V 12%; thrombocytopenia 16,000/µl) precluding biopsy. Progressive encephalopathy, fluid-refractory hypotension, anuric renal failure requiring haemodiafiltration. Common causes (viral hepatitis A-C, Wilson's disease, autoimmune liver disease, comprehensive drug screen) excluded. Implant placed three months prior; dechallenge by immediate implant excision with recovery and normalization of hepatic synthesis/detoxification after six ICU days, discharged without neurological sequelae. raw_record.support_text: The case report presents a case of cholestatic DILI from the SARM RAD-140, appearing histologically and serologically similar to that seen by anabolic androgenic steroids (AAS). Liver biopsy confirmed DILI with bland cholestasis, without evidence of autoimmune activity, and the patient's injury was attributed to RAD-140 based on the temporal relationship between drug initiation, symptom onset 4 weeks later, and serologic evidence of liver injury 4 weeks after symptom onset, with infectious and obstructive causes excluded.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Use as a performance-enhancement supplement (SARM) rather than an approved therapeutic; unresolved individual dose/exposure details not specified; patient was a young adult.
raw_record.extra_details: RAD-140 is a selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) taken as a supplement. Symptom onset 4 weeks after initiation and serologic liver injury 4 weeks after symptom onset. Liver biopsy confirmed bland cholestasis without autoimmune activity; total bilirubin remained >20 mg/dL for over 1 month after cessation. Cholestasis refractory to cessation, treated with prednisone 40 mg daily with bilirubin normalization over ~2 months. Infectious hepatitides A/B/C and obstructive biliary causes excluded. Pattern compared to anabolic androgenic steroid DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Belinostat, a new HDACI, was studied as a single agent in refractory/relapsed lymphoma as daily infusions on days 1–5 every 21 days. Adverse effects were nausea, fatigue, and fever; severe reactions included acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and toxic liver failure, with 7.8 % of patients dying of drug reaction. Fatalities were attributed to drug-related tumor lysis syndrome, hepatic failure, and ventricular fibrillation from QTc prolongation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first association of flutamide with serious hepatotoxicity in a woman using the drug for the treatment of hirsutism. Flutamide hepatotoxicity had previously been considered infrequent and had been reported by Wysowski and colleagues in 19 patients treated for prostatic diseases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Used for the treatment of hirsutism (a benign condition) in a 20-year-old woman, not for prostatic disease; the patient also continued taking an oral contraceptive pill (Demulen-30) concurrently.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose: flutamide 250 mg orally twice daily. Onset: therapy started in late January 1993; gastrointestinal symptoms appeared in early March and she presented on 13 March with severe pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools, deeply jaundiced. Labs: bilirubin 263 µmol/L (normal 3-20), INR 1.9, alkaline phosphatase 180 IU/L (normal 40-130), ALT 1481 IU/L (normal 5-55). History and viral serology excluded other causes of liver disease; ultrasound normal with non-dilated biliary tree. Bilirubin peaked at 480 µmol/L. Liver biopsy near the height of illness showed changes typical of drug toxicity, including zonal hepatic necrosis with cholestasis and ballooning degeneration of surviving zone 1 hepatocytes. On flutamide discontinuation, enzymes normalized within 6 weeks and bilirubin returned to normal by early June; pruritus controlled with subcutaneous naloxone. Authors state the features of the case are quite conclusive and note the potential for a life-threatening adverse effect.

raw_record.support_text: 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP), introduced in the 1950s as an antineoplastic agent for leukemias and lymphomas, is a thiopurine that has been implicated along with azathioprine in liver injury. Reports of liver injury, sometimes fatal, appeared shortly after introduction, and more than 100 cases of liver injury attributed to Aza and 6-MP have been reported. In large prospective and retrospective studies on drug-induced liver injury, Aza and 6-MP are frequently listed as common causes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Veno-occlusive disease and nodular regenerative hyperplasia are reported with higher doses and long-term treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 6-MP is an active thiopurine; Aza is its prodrug, and the two are blamed jointly. In many cases association was confirmed by prompt recurrence of injury upon readministration (rechallenge). Both are associated with transient, usually mild and self-limited serum enzyme elevations, and both are implicated in clinically apparent hepatotoxicity that can be severe, leading to prolonged intrahepatic cholestasis or acute liver failure, plus veno-occlusive disease and nodular regenerative hyperplasia at higher doses/long-term use. The current DILIN prospective cohort analysis enrolls thiopurine injury cases adjudicated as probable, very likely, or definite.

raw_record.support_text: A 92-year-old woman developed jaundice with dark urine and itching 16 days after starting memantine (5 mg/d for the first 8 days, then 10 mg/d for the next 8 days). Laboratory tests showed increased AST, ALT, gamma-glutamyltransferase, total and direct bilirubin, and ALP. Memantine was discontinued, symptoms resolved by 7 days, and liver enzymes normalized after 20 days. Based on biochemical, clinical, and instrumental parameters, criteria of drug-induced liver disorders, and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, the authors diagnosed probable cholestatic hepatitis induced by memantine. The conclusion states that memantine is a probable cause of drug-induced hepatitis with cholestasis, with alternative causes (mechanical obstruction, viral hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis) excluded.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Very elderly patient (92-year-old woman) with mixed moderate dementia and behavior disorders and comorbid hypertension and heart failure; patient was taking concurrent digoxin (0.125 mg/d), lisinopril (5 mg/d), tiapride (50 mg/d), alprazolam (0.25 mg/d), and promazine (10 mg/d), which were continued during the event.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose: memantine 5 mg/d for first 8 days, escalated to 10 mg/d for next 8 days; jaundice, dark urine, and itching onset on day 16. Lab values at day 1: AST 74 U/L (normal 5-30), ALT 132 U/L (5-56), gamma-GT 155 U/L (4-20), total bilirubin 4.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, ALP 912 U/L (38-126). Diagnosis of probable cholestatic hepatitis by Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale and criteria of drug-induced liver disorders. Dechallenge: signs/symptoms disappeared 7 days after memantine withdrawal; liver enzymes normalized after 20 days. Negative HAV, HBV, HCV, antimitochondrial antibodies, and direct Coombs test; ultrasonography excluded mechanical obstruction. Mechanism not identified; authors discuss memantine lysosomal accumulation/phospholipidosis and effects on canalicular transport proteins as possible mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: Three AML patients receiving prophylactic voriconazole developed hepatotoxicity manifesting as elevation of bilirubin, which was NCI CTC version 3.0 Grade 3 in two patients and required discontinuation of voriconazole. These patients were switched to prophylactic amphotericin B. Hepatotoxicity was noted on day 2 and day 14 of therapy respectively, and liver functions reverted to normal within 3 days of stopping voriconazole. The paper attributes this toxicity to voriconazole, since no other Grade 3/4 toxicity attributable to voriconazole was noted.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Voriconazole used as antifungal prophylaxis in AML patients undergoing induction chemotherapy (87% on daunorubicin + cytarabine-based induction); 3 of 75 patients affected.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity manifested as isolated bilirubin elevation (NCI CTC version 3.0 Grade 3 in two patients, requiring discontinuation; onset on day 2 and day 14 of therapy; liver functions reverted to normal within 3 days of stopping voriconazole after dechallenge); affected patients were switched to prophylactic amphotericin B.

raw_record.support_text: Among 30 patients who underwent single-session whole-liver radioembolization with Yttrium-90 (90Y)-labeled resin microspheres for nonresectable breast cancer liver metastases, clinically significant toxicities including increasing transaminase level, increasing bilirubin level, nausea and vomiting, gastric ulcers, and ascites occurred in eight of 30 patients. One patient's death was attributed to treatment-related hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Whole-liver intra-arterial radioembolization (not systemic oral/parenteral use) in patients with nonresectable, treatment-refractory breast cancer liver metastases who had prior polychemotherapy, hormonal therapy, and trastuzumab where applicable.
raw_record.extra_details: Mean delivered activity 1.9 GBq of 90Y. Clinically significant toxicities (increasing transaminases, increasing bilirubin, nausea/vomiting, gastric ulcers, ascites) occurred in 8 of 30 patients; one death was attributed to treatment-related hepatic toxicity. Median follow-up 14.2 months; partial response 61%, stable disease 35%, progressive disease 4%.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized trial, 4 of 18 patients in the halothane group developed S.G.P.T. levels over 100 I.U. per litre on admission for their third radium treatment (3 of the 4 had already had three halothane exposures), whereas no patients in the control group developed S.G.P.T. levels over 100 I.U. per litre. No abnormalities in other tests of liver function were noted.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Women with carcinoma undergoing radium (radiotherapy) treatment, receiving halothane general anaesthesia for the procedure; repeated halothane exposures in some patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 4 of 18 halothane-allocated patients developed SGPT >100 IU/L versus none of 21 controls. Two of these 4 patients had liver biopsies showing liver damage with histological changes characteristic of hepatitis (patients 1 and 17). Highest SGPT values were 1350 and 1800 IU/L. Comparison of log fractional SGPT increases between first and third measurement gave mean 0.71 ± 0.31 for halothane vs 0.03 ± 0.10 for controls (one-tailed P=0.013); four patients with SGPT >100 IU/L were all in the halothane group (one-tailed P<0.025). No patient became clinically jaundiced, and no bilirubin exceeded 1 mg/100 ml.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old male developed generalized pruritus and fluid-filled bullous skin lesions 2 days after taking Ciprofloxacin (obtained over-the-counter) for a surgical site infection, along with scleral icterus, markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (1390 U/L), conjugated bilirubin (13.7 mg/dl), and transaminases. Based on clinical findings, biopsy, and laboratory values he was diagnosed with toxic epidermal necrolysis and drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis. The Naranjo ADR probability scale gave a score of 6, implicating a probable adverse drug reaction caused by Ciprofloxacin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Young adult male on over-the-counter Ciprofloxacin; prior/co-exposure to paracetamol taken for fever before Ciprofloxacin onset; surgical site infection context.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of toxic epidermal necrolysis with cholestatic hepatitis; Naranjo ADR probability score 6 (probable, 5-8 range); lab findings SGOT 283 U/L, SGPT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L, total bilirubin 14 mg/dl, conjugated bilirubin 13.7 mg/dl, INR 2.70; skin biopsy consistent with epidermal necrolysis secondary to ciprofloxacin; normal hepatobiliary ultrasonography; no dose reported.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that, after a reasonable exclusion of all other possible causes, sevoflurane anesthesia caused fulminant hepatic failure in a young man who presented with a mild degree of microvesicular steatosis related to obesity. They note that alcohol consumption and obesity produce CYP2E1 induction and generate nitro-oxidative stress and energy depletion in the pericentral zone, where sevoflurane undergoes CYP2E1-catalyzed biotransformation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Young male patient with mild microvesicular steatosis related to obesity; CYP2E1 induction from alcohol consumption and obesity implicated in susceptibility; inhalational anesthetic exposure during anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of fulminant hepatic failure after sevoflurane anesthesia. Pericentral zone where cells are sensitive to hypoxia; sevoflurane undergoes CYP2E1-catalyzed biotransformation. Halogenated anesthetics are described as having a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes a fulminant hepatotoxic reaction during treatment with increasing doses of the antipsychotic clozapine, which is characterized as a rare reaction that progressed very rapidly. The patient had no pre-existing liver disease or biochemical evidence of liver vulnerability and complained only of sedation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Young patient (described as the youngest case in the literature) receiving increasing therapeutic doses of clozapine; psychiatric indication.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatotoxic reaction with marked liver test abnormalities and rapid progression; no pre-existing or biochemical evidence of liver disease. The patient recovered. Had recovery not occurred, liver transplant would have been considered; two fatal cases in the literature were deemed unsuitable for transplant, partly due to their psychiatric diagnoses. Suggested incidence in clozapine patients is 0.001% (MacFarlane et al., 1997). Only symptom was sedation; elevated bilirubin appears uncommon in benign transaminase elevations.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 70 young inflammatory bowel disease patients treated with azathioprine (15 of whom developed side effects), a correlation was found between the wild-type GST-M1 genotype (high activity) and an increased probability of developing adverse effects and leukopenia during treatment. The paper states that individuals with high GST activity are apparently predisposed to azathioprine side effects, which are listed as pancreatitis, hepatitis, myelosuppression, arthralgias and neuropathy, and these results require confirmation before GST testing can predict azathioprine side effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Young patients with inflammatory bowel disease; GST-M1 wild-type (high-activity) genotype as a susceptibility factor for side effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Based on the Stocco et al. study of 70 young IBD patients treated with AZA (15 developed side effects); hepatitis is listed among azathioprine side effects together with pancreatitis, myelosuppression, arthralgias and neuropathy. Proposed mechanisms include high 6MP formation leading to accumulation of active/toxic compounds and glutathione depletion causing cell damage; results require confirmation before GST testing can be used to predict side effects.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported clinical series, all severe cases of flutamide-induced acute liver failure (ALF) occurred in young women (mean age 29, range 20-44) treated with flutamide for benign pathologies (acne, hirsutism, alopecia). Histopathological study of 5 cases through the explanted liver confirmed ALF with massive or submassive hepatic necrosis, excluding other conditions such as autoimmune diseases, and severe cases required liver transplantation, with favorable evolution in 4 of the 5 cases. The authors attribute this to a hyper-acute inflammatory response through immunologic mechanisms and warn of a potential lethal complication.

raw_record.support_text: In the described flucloxacillin cohort, three patients experienced acute kidney injury, but the paper explicitly reports that there were no cases of hepatotoxicity or haematological side effects (neutropenia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia) observed during flucloxacillin treatment, including in the three acute kidney injury cases.
raw_record.extra_details: No cases of hepatotoxicity were observed during flucloxacillin outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy (OPAT); adverse events reported included acute kidney injury in three patients, axillary vein thrombosis in one, maculopapular rash in one, and other non-hepatic events.
